en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Five Treatises in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
Having taught the Vibhaṅga in eighteen divisions, the Great Hero, the Destroyer of Māra,
[taught] that which follows immediately after it: the Dhātukathā-ṭīkā.
He who elucidated the analysis of elements has taught the *Dhātukathā*;
I shall illuminate its meaning—listen to it with concentrated minds.
1. Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikā)
1. Commentary on the Schedule of Methods (Nayamātikāvaṇṇanā) It is said that this treatise is analyzed in fourteen ways by means of "inclusion" (saṅgaha), "non-inclusion" (asaṅgaha), and so forth.
All of that is established in two parts: the enumeration (uddesa) and the exposition (niddesa). Among these, the schedule (mātikā) is the enumeration. It is fivefold: [the five methods].

There are five matrices (mātikā): the matrix of methods (nayamātikā), the internal matrix, the matrix of method-entrances (nayamukhamātikā), the characteristic matrix (lakkhaṇamātikā), and the external matrix.
Therein, "comprehension" (saṅgaha), "non-comprehension" (asaṅgaha)... [and so on] ...

"that which is comprehended by dissociation" and "that which is not comprehended"—this is called the matrix of methods set forth by means of fourteen terms. For it is by this method beginning with comprehension that the phenomena (dhammā) in the *Dhātukathā* are analyzed.

Because it is established in order to demonstrate [the method], it is called the "Table of Contents of Methods" (*nayamātikā*). Because it serves as the root for these terms, it is also appropriate to call it the "Root Table of Contents" (*mūlamātikā*).
2. Commentary on the Internal Table of Contents:
"The five aggregates... [and so forth] ...attention"—this is the internal table of contents set forth by one hundred and twenty-five terms.
It is called the "Internal Table of Contents" (*abbhantara-mātikā*). For this [table] is not stated as "The entire *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* is the table of contents for the *Dhātukathā*";

rather, it is so called because it presents the aggregates and other phenomena—which are to be analyzed by way of categories such as "compendium"—in their own form and is placed within the *Dhātukathā* itself.
This is because the terms for the aggregates and so forth are not included in the table of contents of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
It is also appropriate to speak of the miscellaneous matrix (pakiṇṇaka-mātikā).
3. Commentary on the Matrix of the Doors of Method (nayamukha-mātikā):
"Inclusion by three, non-inclusion by three; association with four, dissociation with four"—this [is the matrix] by way of four.
The "matrix of the headings of methods" (*nayamukhamātikā*) is established by way of these terms.

For, regarding all the dhammas in the matrices—such as the five aggregates and so forth, as well as the triad of the wholesome and so forth—the inclusion (*saṅgaha*) and non-inclusion (*asaṅgaha*) should be applied by means of the three terms: aggregate (*khandha*), base (*āyatana*), and element (*dhātu*).

Likewise, there is association (*sampayoga*) and dissociation (*vippayoga*) by means of the four formless aggregates. These [terms] constitute the inclusion, non-inclusion, and so forth of these [dhammas].
Because it is established to show the "gates" (*mukha*) of the methods (*naya*), it is called the "matrix of method-gates" (*nayamukhamātikā*).
4. Commentary on the Matrix of Characteristics (*lakkhaṇamātikā*): 4.
This so-called matrix of characteristics is formulated by means of two terms: "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "heterogeneous" (*visabhāga*). For this [matrix] consists of homogeneous characteristics...

The method of inclusion by way of similar phenomena, the method of non-inclusion by way of dissimilar characteristics, and likewise the method of association and dissociation should be applied accordingly; thus,
because it is established to demonstrate the characteristics of inclusion and so forth by way of similar and dissimilar characteristics,
it is called the "matrix of characteristics" (lakkhaṇamātikā).
5. Explanation of the External Matrix (Bāhiramātikāvaṇṇanā) The entire *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* constitutes the matrix for the *Dhātukathā*.
This so-called "External Matrix" is set forth by condensing sixty-six triplets and two hundred couplets. For it begins: "The five aggregates... [etc.]..."
Because it is not included within the *Dhātukathā* itself— unlike [the section on] "attention" (*manasikāra*)—
but is instead placed outside the matrix (*mātikā*) of the *Dhātukathā*, it is called the "external matrix" (*bāhiramātikā*), as in the phrase "all of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
Having thus understood that the matrix exists in five ways, one should now consider "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) and "non-inclusion" (*asaṅgaha*) among such categories.
Thus, it is fourfold by way of birth, origin, action, and enumeration. Among these: “Let all khattiyas come;

let all brahmins, all vessas, and all suddas come,” and “Friend Visākha, whatever is right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these states are included in the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha)”—this is [the first type].
This is called "grouping by birth. For here, just as in the case where it is said, "Let those of one birth come," all [these factors] have entered into a single grouping by way of their genus.
It is like saying, "Let all the Kosalan people come, let all the Magadhan people come, let all the Bhārukacchan people come," or:
"And that which, friend Visākha, is right effort, and that which is right mindfulness, and that which is right concentration..."
"These states are included in the aggregate of concentration"—this is what is called "inclusion by genus" (*sañjāti-saṅgaha*).

For here, just as in the expression, "Let those born and raised in one place come," all [states] are brought together into a single inclusion by way of their genus, that is, the location in which they reside.
It is like saying, "Let all elephant-riders come, let all horse-riders come, let all chariot-warriors come."
“Friend Visākha, that which is right view and that which is right intention—these phenomena are included within the aggregate of wisdom.
This is called inclusion by action (*kiriyā-saṅgaha*). For all these [factors] have reached a single inclusion by virtue of performing their own respective functions.
[For example: “To which aggregate-count does the eye-base belong? It belongs to the count of the form aggregate. Indeed, the eye-base...
It goes into the enumeration of the aggregate of form; therefore, indeed, it should be said: "The eye-base is included within the aggregate of form.
This is what is called inclusion by enumeration. This is what is intended here. By its opposite, non-inclusion is to be understood.

From their various permutations, there arise [the categories of] inclusion and non-inclusion, and so forth. [These are determined] by way of simultaneous arising, simultaneous cessation, having a common basis, and having a common object.
Association is its opposite, dissociation. From their various permutations arise terms such as "associated" and "dissociated.
From the permutation of the combination of both, there arise terms such as "included by what is associated" and "dissociated from what is included.

Furthermore, [categories] such as "the five aggregates" should be understood according to the method explained in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* and other texts. Here, however, contact and the rest are treated by way of definitive determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*).
They are stated because they are common to all the types of consciousness mentioned.
This concludes the commentary on the Schedule (Mātikā). 2. Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesa).
1. First Method: Explanation of the Terms of Inclusion and Non-Inclusion.
1. Explanation of the Terms of the Aggregates. 6.

Now, regarding the matrix (mātikā) set forth by way of the five aggregates and so forth, [it is explained] by means of the terms of the method-matrix (nayamātikā) such as "inclusion" (saṅgaha), "non-inclusion" (asaṅgaha), and so on.

In order to demonstrate [the analysis] by combining [the categories], the section of the exposition (niddesavāra) is commenced in the manner beginning with, "The aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) by how many aggregates?

and so forth. Therein, because a matrix of introductory headings (nayamātikā) such as "comprehension" (saṅgaha) and "non-comprehension" (asaṅgaha) was established, and within that a sub-matrix of introductory headings (nayamukhamātikā) was set forth stating, "Comprehension by three;
non-comprehension by three," therefore, in order to show the comprehension of the aggregate of form and the others, [the text asks]: "By how many..."
Regarding the question, "By how many aggregates, by how many bases, and by how many elements [is it comprised]? only three items—aggregates, bases, and elements—are extracted.
Not even one among the categories such as "the four truths" and so forth is mentioned. And because the matrix of characteristics was established in this way:
"homogeneous" and "heterogeneous," therefore, in the answer to this question, it begins: "The aggregate of form is [comprised] by one aggregate," and so on.
It has been said: "For these aggregates and so forth are of the same class as that. In this context, "by one aggregate" means by the materiality aggregate alone.
For whatever form there may be, because it shares the same class as the materiality aggregate, it is included within the materiality aggregate itself;
thus, being counted by the materiality aggregate, it is delimited by the materiality aggregate alone. "By eleven bases" means excluding the mind base.
For the entire aggregate of form consists of ten bases (āyatana) and a portion of the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana);

therefore, it is reckoned and delimited by eleven bases. It is [reckoned] by eleven elements—namely, all except the seven consciousness-elements—for there is no form that is not included within these.
In the exposition on "not being included" (*asaṅgaha-naya-niddesa*), the question "By how many is it not included? is asked in brief.

In the answer, however, because the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpa-khandha*)—which are of a different class from the aggregate of material form (*rūpa-khandha*)—as well as one mind-base (*manāyatana*) and seven consciousness-elements (*viññāṇa-dhātu*), are [factors] that do not include the aggregate of material form, it is said:
"By four aggregates," and so forth. By this method, inclusion and non-inclusion should be understood in all instances.
In this Exposition of the Aggregates (*khandhaniddesa*), first, regarding the section beginning with "The aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) by how many aggregates [is it comprised]?
and so forth, there are five questions and five answers presented according to the method of inclusion (*saṅgahanaya*) based on single roots.

There are also five questions and five answers presented in brief according to the method of non-inclusion (*asaṅgahanaya*). By this same method, the questions and answers are to be understood for those based on double roots (*dukamūlaka*) and so forth.

These are to be understood. Here, only those dyads, triads, and tetrads rooted in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) have been shown. Regarding the pentad, however, the questions and answers are presented in two ways:

by way of differentiation, as in “the aggregate of form... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness,” and by way of non-differentiation, as in “the five aggregates [are comprised] by how many aggregates?
In this manner, the method of the Pāḷi should be understood.
2. Commentary on the Section on the Bases (Āyatanapadādivaṇṇanā) 22.
Regarding the exposition of the bases (āyatanapadaniddesa) and so forth: first, in the exposition of the bases, it is said that "the eye-base is comprised by one aggregate";
this means it is comprised solely by the single aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), and likewise by the single eye-base and the single eye-element (cakkhudhātu).
It should be understood. By this same method, the inclusion and non-inclusion [of phenomena] within the ear-base and so forth should also be understood.

Regarding the phrase "having set aside the unconditioned from among the aggregates": here, since the unconditioned is called the dhammāyatana (the base of mental objects), which is Nibbāna, and that does not fall within the inclusion of the aggregates, it is therefore said, "having set aside [it] from among the aggregates. [This refers to] "by means of four aggregates."

[It is] with the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations. For the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana), excluding Nibbāna, is included within these [four aggregates]. However, with respect to the aggregate of consciousness, it is not included within the remaining bases and elements, setting aside the base of mental phenomena and the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu).
Therefore it was said: “With one aggregate, eleven bases, and seventeen elements.”
"...is not included. And just as those [previous] sections were rooted in the aggregate of form, so too here the methods should be understood as being rooted in the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*).
However, having shown only a pair in the text, the question and answer are given without distinction simply as "the twelve bases" (*dvādasāyatanāni*).
This same method applies to the Exposition of Elements (*Dhātuniddesa*) as well.

40. In the Exposition of the Truths (Saccaniddesa): All the dyads, triads, and tetradic combinations have been shown in the text. Furthermore, because the analysis for the Truth of the Path is identical to that for the Truth of the Origin among the dyads, it is stated immediately after the latter.

50. In the Exposition of the Faculties (Indriyaniddesa): "The life-faculty by two aggregates" means that the material life-faculty is included within the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), and the immaterial life-faculty is included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained.
The determination of the textual tradition (*pāḷivavatthāna*) here is exactly like that in the exposition of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
6. Commentary on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādavaṇṇanā) 61.

In the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), rather than beginning with the question, "By how many aggregates (*khandha*) is ignorance (*avijjā*) comprised?", [the text] begins with ignorance.

"By one aggregate"—thus the answer itself has been shown. Therein, "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness" refers to all resultant consciousness, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. For this very reason, it is said: "It is comprised within seven elements.
Name-and-form should also be understood by way of both rebirth-linking and the course of existence. For this same reason, even the sound base is included here.
Inclusion is shown by means of the eleven bases (*āyatana*). Regarding contact (*phassa*) and the others, the classification according to the aggregates (*khandha*) should be understood.
For contact is included by one aggregate distinct [from the others], feeling (*vedanā*) by another;

however, craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) are included solely within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). Furthermore, the term "existence" (*bhava*) here is analyzed into eleven types by way of kamma-existence and so forth. Among these, kamma-existence...
Because they have similar modes of response (*visajjana*) to contact (*phassa*) and the other factors, they are shown together with them.

The existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*), sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), perception-existence (*saññābhava*), and five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) are shown together because they have mutually similar modes of response.

And since these are exclusively acquired phenomena (*upādinnaka-dhamma*), it is said: "by eleven bases (*āyatana*) and seventeen elements (*dhātu*). For the sound-base (*saddāyatana*) is unacquired (*anupādinna*); it is not included here.
68. In the description of the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*): "by five bases" means by the bases of eye, ear, mind, and mental objects.
"By eight elements" means by the elements of eye, ear, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, mental objects, mind-element, and mind-consciousness-element.

The three [existences] beginning with the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) are shown together because their answers are identical. Likewise for the non-percipient existence (*asaññābhava*) and the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*).
Therein, "by two bases" means by the base of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*) and the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*). The same method applies to the elements (*dhātu*) as well.
For, since the remaining Brahmās dwelling on the same level possess eyes, and because those [visible forms] are their objects, the base of visible forms is extracted there. 71.

"Birth by two aggregates" means that birth consisting of form is included in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), and birth consisting of non-form is included in the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
The same method applies to aging and death as well. Regarding sorrow and the rest, the differentiation of the aggregates (*khandha*) should be understood as follows:

sorrow, pain, and grief belong to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*); lamentation belongs to the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*); and despair and so forth belong to the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).

73. The basis of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) consists of two [aggregates]: the aggregates of mental formations and consciousness; the sense bases of mind and mental objects (*dhammāyatana*); and the elements of mental objects and mind-consciousness (*dhammadhātu* and *manoviññāṇadhātu*).

And: "Jhāna by two" means by the aggregates of feeling and mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). The immeasurables (*appamaññā*) and so forth are explained together because they have similar answers.
However, although consciousness (*citta*) was placed immediately after volition (*cetanā*), it is taken up later because it has a dissimilar answer.
Therein, regarding the immeasurables and so forth, "by one aggregate" means: feeling by the aggregate of feeling, perception by the aggregate of perception, and so on.
The remainder are included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); thus should the distinction of the aggregates be understood.
7. Commentary on the Triplets (Tikapada):
Having thus shown the inclusion according to the internal matrix (*mātikā*), he now shows the inclusion according to the external matrix.

The section beginning with “wholesome states” is commenced. Therein, in the triad of feeling, “by three elements” refers to the body-consciousness element, the mind-consciousness element, and the mental-object element.
“By seven elements” refers to the eye-, ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness elements, as well as the mind-element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
In the triad of resultants, “by eight elements” refers to those same [seven] together with the body-consciousness element. [This applies to] those states that are resultants of wholesome states.
However, because they share the same method of exposition as the "defiled and defiling" [categories], they are taken together.

And just as these are, so too in all the pairs of categories (*tikaduka*), whichever term has the same method of exposition as another term—even if it appears out of order—is taken together with that one and explained. In this regard, one should proceed exactly according to what has been stated.
The method of inclusion and non-inclusion is to be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the terms "included" and "not included. 2.
The second method: commentary on the terms "that which is included" and "that which is not included."
171. Now, in order to analyze the category of the "unincluded" by means of the "included," the section beginning with "by the eye-base" (cakkhāyatana) is commenced.

Herein, this is the characteristic: for in this chapter, whatever is included under the category of aggregates (khandha) but not included under the categories of bases (āyatana) or elements (dhātu), or whatever is included under the categories of aggregates or bases but not included under the category of elements—of that [the following analysis is made].

Having asked about non-inclusion by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, an answer was given. However, that [answer] is not tenable regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the others.
For it is the aggregate of form itself that is included within the aggregate of form; and there is nothing therein that is not included by eleven bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).

Likewise, it is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) itself that is included within the aggregate of feeling; and that too [is included] by the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*).

There is nothing that is not included. Because there is no such thing as being uncomprised in this way, these and other similar terms—such as the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*)—are not taken up in this section.
However, those terms which indicate a portion of form unmixed with the formless, and a portion of consciousness unmixed with anything else, are taken up here. And at the conclusion—
Ten bases, seventeen elements,
seven faculties, non-percipient existence, one-aggregate existence,
lamentation, and that which is visible and impinging.
"Furthermore, that which is non-indicative (anidassana) is indeed with resistance (sappaṭigha), having been derived (upādā).
Thus, these are precisely those shown in the summary verse (uddānagāthā). Therefore, inclusion and non-inclusion should be understood by means of those [categories] alone.
For in this section, by way of questions, twenty phenomena are combined together through similar answers according to the sense-bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).
One question was formulated; one by combining the seven consciousness-elements;

one by combining the seven faculties; one by combining the two types of existence; one by combining lamentation with the visible-with-resistance [phenomena]; one with the invisible-with-resistance [phenomena];
one with the visible [phenomena]; and one with the resistant derived phenomena—thus eight questions were formulated.
Among these, the classification into aggregates and so forth should be understood as follows: first, in the initial question, "by four aggregates" refers to the immaterial aggregates;
"by two bases" refers to the mind base together with each one of the eye base and the others;
and "by eight elements" refers to the seven consciousness elements together with each one of the eye element and the others.
In this regard, the method is as follows: by means of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is included within the classification of aggregates.
When that aggregate of form is so included, within the classification of bases (*āyatanasaṅgaha*), only the eye-base itself is included; the remaining ten bases are not included.
By means of the classification of elements (*dhātusaṅgaha*) as well, only the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*) is included by it; the remaining ten are not.
The elements are not included. Thus, those ten bases that are not included by it are not included within the two bases, namely the eye base and the mind base.
Likewise, those ten elements that are not included by it are not included within the eye element and the seven consciousness elements.
This same method applies to the visible-form base and the others as well.

172. In the second question: because there is no consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*) that is included within any consciousness element (*viññāṇadhātu*) which is not also included by the mind base (*manāyatana*), it is therefore said to be "included by inclusion through the bases" (*āyatanasaṅgahena saṅgahita*).
Here, however, "by four aggregates" refers to the four beginning with form (*rūpa*); "by eleven bases" refers to those excluding the mind base; and "by twelve elements" [refers to all elements].

Having excluded the corresponding consciousness elements (*viññāṇadhātu*), [the remaining] twelve [elements] are included. For the eye-consciousness element is included within the eye-consciousness element itself, while the others are not included. This same method applies to the ear-consciousness element and the rest as well. 173.

In the third question—the answer regarding the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*) and so forth is exactly the same as for the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth. Regarding the female-faculty (*itthindriya*) and male-faculty (*purisindriya*)...

However, together with the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana), two bases are to be understood; and together with the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu), eight elements are to be understood.
174. Regarding the fourth question: "By three bases" means by the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana), the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana), and the base of the mind (manāyatana).

For among those states of existence, only two bases—namely, the base of visible forms and the base of mental phenomena—are comprised by them. The remaining nine bases of visible forms [are not so comprised].

And likewise, they are said to be uncomprised by three: by those same two and by the mind-base (manāyatana). "By nine elements" means by the seven consciousness-elements together with the visible-form element (rūpadhātu) and the mental-object element (dhammadhātu).
In the fifth question—"by two bases"—this refers to the first phrase [of the previous question], meaning by the sound-base (saddāyatana) and the mind-base (manāyatana).
With reference to the second phrase, [the objects] are the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) and the non-base elements (anāyatana).
The elements (dhātu) should also be understood as seven consciousness-elements (viññāṇadhātu) each associated with those same [bases].
176. In the sixth question—“by ten bases” means excluding the visible-form base and the mental-object base; “by sixteen elements” means...

[This occurs] excluding only the form element (rūpadhātu) and the mental-object element (dhammadhātu). How so? Those phenomena (dhammā) called "non-visible and impinging" are the nine gross bases (oḷārikāyatana).
Within the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), which is included by way of the aggregate-inclusion (khandhasaṅgaha), these same nine bases are included by way of the base-inclusion (āyatanasaṅgaha).
The base of visible forms (rūpāyatana) and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) are not included. By way of the element-inclusion (dhātusaṅgaha) as well, those same nine [are included].
The elements are included. The visible-form element and the mental-object element are not included.
Thus, those two bases which are not included by them are not included by ten [bases]: by the nine gross bases excluding the visible-form base, and by the mind base.
Also, those two elements which are not included by them [are not included] by the nine gross elements excluding the visible-form element.
And it should be understood that [the mind-base] is not included among the sixteen by means of the seven consciousness-elements.
177. In the seventh question: "By two bases" means by the visible-form base and the mind base. "By eight elements" means by the seven consciousness-elements together with the visible-form element.
178. In the eighth question: "By eleven bases" refers to the phenomena with resistance (*sappaṭigha*), excluding the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*).
This refers to derived phenomena (upādādhamma), excluding the base of tangibles (phoṭṭhabbāyatana). The same method applies to the elements (dhātu) as well.
Furthermore, the interpretation of the meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated below.
This concludes the commentary on the terms "included" and "not included."
3. The Third Method: Explanation of the Terms "Not Included" and "Included. 179.
Now, in order to analyze the term "not included by what is included," the passage beginning with "by the aggregate of feeling" (*vedanākkhandhena*) is commenced.
Herein is the characteristic: for in this section, that which is not included by the term "aggregate" (*khandha*) [is considered] by the terms "base" (*āyatana*) and "element" (*dhātu*).

It has been included; having asked about its inclusion among the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, the answer was given. However, that [answer] is not applicable in the case of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*), the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), and so on. For, by means of the aggregate of form, the other four aggregates are not included under the category of "aggregate-inclusion" (*khandhasaṅgaha*).

Among those, there is not even a single phenomenon (*dhamma*) that is said to be included by it under the categories of "base-inclusion" (*āyatanasaṅgaha*) or "element-inclusion" (*dhātusaṅgaha*). But are not phenomena such as feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest included by the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*)?
Are they included? They are included. However, the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) is not the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) alone;

for from the aggregate of form, only subtle form (*sukhumarūpa*) belongs to the base of mental phenomena. Therefore, those things which are included by the base of mental phenomena are not said to be included by the aggregate of form.

Likewise, the other four aggregates are not included by the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*). Among those [bases], not even one is included by that [aggregate] through the inclusion of bases and elements.

There is nothing that is included [by way of being grasped]. Because of this absence of inclusion, these and other such terms, such as the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth, are not taken up in this section.

However, those terms which indicate a portion of the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) unmixed with consciousness or gross material form are taken up here. This is their summary verse (*uddāna*):
“Three aggregates and likewise truths, sixteen faculties;
fourteen terms in the mode of conditions, and fourteen above that.
There are thirty terms in the ten clusters.”
“There are two minor intermediate dyads, and eight major intermediate ones.
Now, among these sections, all twelve questions have been stated by grouping together those words that have identical answers.

Within them, the analysis of the aggregates (khandha) should be understood in this way; however, there is no division regarding the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu). Therein, in the first question:

The bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), however, should be understood by way of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).

Herein is the method: for Nibbāna and the subtle forms, perceptions, and mental formations are not included within the inclusion of the aggregates, yet they are included within the inclusion of the bases and elements. Among these, Nibbāna is not included in the inclusion of the aggregates...
The [remaining] factors go into the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), while the rest go into the aggregates of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and perception (*saññākkhandha*).

However, even *nibbāna* goes into the inclusion of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Therefore it was said: "Excluding the unconditioned from the aggregates, it is included by three aggregates, one base, and one element. But here, having removed perception from the side of the perception aggregate (*saññākkhandha*)...

Together with feeling, there are three aggregates; excluding the aggregate of formations from among the formations and so forth, the three aggregates consisting of form, feeling, and perception are to be understood. 180.

In the second [case]—“by four aggregates”—this refers to those excluding consciousness. For these, not being included by the cessation-aggregate-inclusion, are included by the inclusion of bases and elements.
181. Regarding the third [category]: "by two" means by the aggregates of feeling (vedanā) and perception (saññā).

For the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya), the immaterial life-faculty (arūpa-jīvitindriya), and the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness are not included within the same aggregate-grouping (khandha-saṅgaha). However, among those, only feeling and perception are included within the grouping of bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).
Therefore it is said: "by the aggregates of feeling and perception. By this method, the classification of the aggregates should be understood in all instances.
From here on, we shall state merely the names of the aggregates. 182.
In the fourth [case]: "by three aggregates" means, in the case of the femininity-faculty and masculinity-faculty, by the feeling, perception, and formations [aggregates];

in the case of the fivefold feeling, by the materiality, perception, and formations [aggregates]; and in the case of the faith-faculty and so forth ending with the contact-faculty, by the materiality, feeling, and perception aggregates.
Regarding feeling, the analysis is similar to that of the aggregate of feeling; regarding craving, clinging, kamma, and becoming, it is similar to that of the aggregate of formations.
183. In the fifth [truth], with respect to birth, aging, and death, it is similar to the life-faculty.

However, by means of jhāna, Nibbāna, subtle form, and perception—though not included within the classification of aggregates—are nevertheless included within the classification of bases and elements. Therefore:
With reference to that, two aggregates should be understood by way of the aggregate of form and the aggregate of perception.

184. In the sixth [section]—among sorrow and the rest—it is similar to feeling; among despair and the rest, it is similar to formations. Furthermore, among feeling, it is similar to the aggregate of feeling;
among perception, it is similar to the aggregate of perception; and among volition and the rest, it is similar to the aggregate of formations.
The exposition. By this method, the inclusion and non-inclusion [of factors] should also be understood in the seventh question and those that follow.

191. Now, in order to analyze the category of "included by what is included," the section beginning with "by the truth of origin" (*samudayasaccena*) is commenced.

That [answer] concerns even a single entire portion within the aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
It is not appropriate [to include] those passages where [the term] stands alone.

Therefore, such passages were not included in this section. However, those passages which [refer to] a portion of the formations (saṅkhāra)...
Or they explain it as unmixed with anything else—whether a portion of feeling, subtle matter, or a portion of sound;

“Two truths, fifteen faculties, eleven factors of dependent origination;”
"Furthermore, there are eleven above; thus, the section on clusters here is thirtyfold.

However, there are only two questions here. In that regard, whatever term has been extracted from the question, with reference to those phenomena by which it is included under the categories of aggregates and so forth, it is stated in every instance as "by one aggregate," and so on.

In this regard, the method is as follows: by way of the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*), all remaining formations (*saṅkhāra*)—with the exception of craving (*taṇhā*)—are included within the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth;
furthermore, those [remaining formations] include craving itself. That craving, in turn, is included by the formations themselves within the aggregates and so forth.

This same method applies everywhere. However, in the inquiries concerning immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) here, it is either the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) or the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).

Or, one aggregate is called a "single aggregate. Among inquiries concerning material phenomena, it is the aggregate of form. In the inquiry concerning lamentation, the sense base of sound is called a "single sense base.

The element of sound is called a "single element. In the remaining instances, the meaning should be understood by way of the sense base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*).
This concludes the commentary on the terms "included" and "not included."

There is no such thing [in this context]. Therefore, words of that kind have not been included in this section.

All the faculties as well, twenty-three by way of dependence.

“Sixteen terms were spoken within the *mahanta* [section], and eighteen beyond that;

[They] exist. In this context, regarding the term extracted from the question, it was stated "by one aggregate," and so forth, with reference to those phenomena not included among the aggregates and so on.

“Not included” means they are not included by one aggregate (khandha), one base (āyatana), and seven elements (dhātu).

By consciousness alone, they are not included within the three aggregates. And as for consciousness: from the perspective of the aggregates, it is one—the consciousness aggregate;
from the perspective of the bases, it is one—the mind base; from the perspective of the elements, there are seven consciousness elements.
Therefore, it is said: "by one aggregate," and so forth. By this method, in all cases, that very term which is raised in the question is [to be understood] by those phenomena...
Those not included by way of the aggregates and so forth should be understood as aggregates and so forth by way of those states themselves.
In that regard, first, in the second question, they should be understood by way of material phenomena and consciousness.

For feeling and the rest are not included in the inclusion of aggregates and so forth by way of material phenomena and consciousness alone. And these two [categories] constitute two aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements.
195. In the third question—since consciousness is not included among the four [bases] beginning with form—the aggregates and so forth should be understood by way of those [four]. 196.
In the fourth question—"the eye-base [is not included] among the four beginning with feeling"—by this same method, the aggregates and so forth should be understood in all instances.
At the conclusion—"form and the base of mental phenomena"—this refers to the very same phenomena shown in the summary verse (uddāna-gāthā), but presented in another aspect.

The sixth method: Commentary on the section of association and dissociation.
228. Now, in order to analyze the section on association (sampayoga) and dissociation (vippayoga), the passage beginning with "the aggregate of form" (rūpakkhandho) is commenced.

Therein, everything—both that which is applicable and that which is not—is included within the question. However, in the answer, that which is not applicable is rejected by stating "it does not exist.
[Thus it is said: "Association with four, dissociation with four; homogeneous (sabhāga) and heterogeneous (visabhāga)."
Indeed, according to the statement, association (sampayoga) is obtained only among the immaterial aggregates themselves—those which are similar and arise within a single continuum at a single moment.
However, there is no such thing as association between material phenomena and either matter or Nibbāna, nor between Nibbāna and matter.
Likewise, there is no association between matter and Nibbāna on the one hand and the immaterial aggregates on the other.

For they are of a different class from them. And just as there is no [connection] between the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) and material phenomena or Nibbāna, so too there is none with immaterial states that belong to a different continuity (bhinnasantāna) or exist at different moments. For these too are indeed of a different class because their continuity and moment are dissimilar.
This dissimilarity, however, is not present in the method of inclusion (saṅgahanaya), because it is contradicted by the sense of inclusion.

For the meaning of "comprehension" (*saṅgaha*) is simply being included in a count. However, in the method of association (*sampayoga*), there is [the category of] "associated," for the characteristic of association consists in such factors as arising together.

Thus, in this context, for that dharma for which even the characteristic of association with a single factor is not applicable, the negation "it does not exist" is made even after including it in the inquiry. But for that for which the characteristic of dissociation (*vippayoga*) is applicable—

Their dissociation has been shown. However, those words which describe mixed phenomena—where even a single one among the seven consciousness-elements is not dissociated from matter or Nibbāna—are entirely inappropriate here and have therefore not been included.
This is their summary verse (uddāna):
The sense-base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu), the truth of suffering and life-force (jīvita);

Birth, aging, and death—these are the nineteen [factors] within the triplets (tike).
In the *gocchakas*, there are fifty [terms], and eight words in the *cūḷantara*;

This total of two hundred and thirty-three words is not found in the *sampayoga* (conjunction).

For the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*)—because it is mixed with both form and Nibbāna—it cannot be said to be associated even with consciousness that is not included within the realms of existence (*apariyāpanna*).

The same principle applies to the remaining [bases] as well. Thus, since these [categories] do not apply in any case whatsoever, they are not mentioned here.

[The aggregates and so forth] have been taken up. Since the remaining aggregates and so forth are applicable, they have been included; thus, the answering of the questions has been done both individually and by way of their combination.
Among those questions, regarding the first: "by one base" means by the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
"By some" refers to feeling, perception, and volitional formations included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).

229. In the second [section], "with three" means with the remaining [factors], excluding those that have already been asked about. "Associated with some" refers to the feeling aggregate being associated with perception and mental formations;

Thus, in all cases, when there is dissociation from matter, it is non-material (arūpa) within the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu); and when there is dissociation from the non-material, [it is matter].
Form is to be seen. The third question is of obvious meaning. 231.
In the fourth [question], instead of saying “by how many aggregates,” etc., it is stated that “there is no associated [state].
That, however, should be understood by way of the aggregates and so forth alone. This same method applies to similar questions further on as well. For in the first question:
Having shown [the meaning] according to the form of the words, the text is abbreviated thereafter. In this manner, the application of the meaning should be understood everywhere.
However, where it might not be very clear, we shall proceed by making it clear. 234. Regarding "by means of the sixteen elements":
first, the eye-consciousness element consists of the six consciousness elements—excluding itself—and the ten material elements. The same method applies to the remaining elements as well.

235. “By three aggregates” means by the remaining aggregates, excluding the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). “By one element” means by the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu);
for there is no association with that truth-pair with any other element besides these.

“By one aggregate” means by the aggregate of mental formations. “By one base” means by the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana). “By one element” means by the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu). For among these, those two truths are associated with some [of the aggregates, bases, and elements].

238. In the question concerning the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and so forth: "By three" means by the aggregates of perception (*saññā*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*). Together with consciousnesses and the form-elements (*rūpadhātu*). For, excluding the sustained application of the second jhāna, the rest are called "without initial application but with sustained application.

Excluding joy (*pīti*), the rest are "accompanied by joy. Therein, sustained application is not associated with sustained application, nor is joy associated with joy; thus, they are included within the mental formations aggregate, the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).
"Associated with some" refers to [the states] excluding the dhamma-element and the mind-consciousness-element—thus, sixteen.

271. That which has a limited object (parittārammaṇa) is similar to that which is of the nature of fruition (vipākadhamma). "By one element" means by the mental-object element (dhammadhātu).

Those with exalted objects and so forth are similar to the wholesome [states]. 273.

The causes (*hetu*) and so forth are similar to the origin (*samudaya*). Those which possess a cause but are not themselves causes are similar to that accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagata*).

Form and Nibbāna. Because all aggregates and bases are included within these two, they are not dissociated from any aggregates or bases.

All these questions are indeed futile questions. For the four aggregates dissociated from the aggregate of material form have no association with anything else.
Material form and Nibbāna, which are dissociated from the aggregate of feeling, likewise have no association with anything.

The ninth method: commentary on the terms "associated" and "dissociated."

10. The Tenth Method: Commentary on the term "dissociated from the dissociated. 353.
Now, in order to analyze the term "dissociated from the dissociated," the passage beginning with "by the aggregate of form" is commenced. Therein:

Those phenomena, such as the aggregate of form and so forth, which were extracted in the "Exposition of Terms for Association and Dissociation" (Sampayoga-vippayoga-pada-niddesa) are the very same ones extracted in all the questions.
However, because the answers of similar type were taken together, the terms have appeared in a different sequence.
In that regard, whichever term was extracted from the question, the classification into aggregates and so forth is made by way of those phenomena with which it is dissociated.

Nibbāna, however, belongs to the category of subtle materiality. This same method applies everywhere.
This concludes the commentary on the terms "dissociated" and "dissociated from the dissociated. 11.
The eleventh method: the commentary on the terms "associated" and "dissociated" by way of inclusion.
409. Now, in order to analyze the section on the associated and dissociated states by way of inclusion, the passage beginning with "by the truth of the origin" is commenced.
Therein, those very phenomena such as the truth of the origin that were extracted in the exposition of the section on inclusion-by-inclusion are the same ones extracted in all the questions.

They have arrived. In this context, regarding those phenomena that are included within the aggregates and so forth by way of the categories extracted in the questions, their classification into aggregates and so on should be understood according to those with which they are associated or dissociated.

Herein is the method: first, by way of the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*), those phenomena comprised within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) are included within the aggregates and so forth.

However, with one form-aggregate (rūpakkhandha), ten form-bases (rūpāyatana), and the form-elements (rūpadhātu) [they are dissociated].
And they are dissociated from one dhammāyatana and from the dhammadhātu; because they are dissociated from material phenomena and Nibbāna, they are said to be "dissociated from some.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
This concludes the commentary on the terms "included," "associated," and "dissociated."
12. The Explanation of the Section on What is Included and What is Not Included by Way of Association (Sampayuttena-saṅgahita-asaṅgahita-pada-vaṇṇanā).

417. Now, in order to analyze the section on what is included and what is not included by way of association, the passage beginning with "by the aggregate of feeling" (*vedanākkhandhena*) and so forth is commenced.

Therein, those phenomena such as the aggregate of feeling that were set forth in the exposition of the section on "associated-with-association" (*sampayutta-sampayutta*) are [the subject] in all the questions.

These very [terms] have been extracted. In this context, regarding those phenomena that are associated with the terms extracted by the question, the classification into aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth should be understood according to whether they are included or not included within them.

Herein is the method: the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) is indeed associated with perception (*saññā*) and the others; those [factors], perception and the rest, are included within the three aggregates beginning with perception.

It is included by eight elements: by two bases—the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the base of the non-mental (*anāyatana*)—by the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), and by the seven consciousness elements (*viññāṇadhātu*).
It is not included by the remaining aggregates, bases, and elements. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all cases.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning inclusion and non-inclusion by way of association.
13. Thirteenth Chapter: Explanation of the Terms "Associated with the Unincluded" and "Dissociated from the Unincluded.

448. Now, in order to analyze the section on "associated with the unincluded" and "dissociated from the unincluded," the passage beginning with "by the aggregate of form" (*rūpakkhandhena*) is commenced.

In that regard, those phenomena which are similar to the questions concerning the aggregate of form, as presented in the fifth chapter in the exposition of the section on "the unincluded with the unincluded" (*asaṅgahitena-asaṅgahita-pada-niddesa*), [are as follows]:
Those [terms] which are similar to the formless existence (*arūpabhava*) have been extracted; the rest, however, were not extracted because they do not apply.

For by means of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), material and immaterial phenomena are not included under the category of aggregates and so forth, nor is there any association (*sampayoga*) between them.
Therefore, only those words that do apply have been extracted, having been combined with their corresponding answers.

In this context, those states which are not included among the aggregates and so forth by way of the categories already mentioned in response to the question, their classification into aggregates and so forth should be understood according to those [states] with which they are associated and those with which they are dissociated.

Herein is the method: first, consciousness alone is not included within the aggregate of material form by any of the three types of inclusion. That [consciousness], together with feeling and the rest...

It is associated with the three aggregates (khandhas) and with feeling and the other [mental states] within the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu). It is dissociated from one aggregate, namely the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha);
from the ten bases and elements of material form; and from the phenomena of material form and Nibbāna within the base and element of mental phenomena.
With reference to this, it was said: "those phenomena [are associated] with the three aggregates," and so forth. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all cases.
Commentary on the Terms "Associated with the Uncomprised" and "Dissociated. 14.
The Fourteenth Method: Commentary on the Terms "Comprised by the Dissociated" and "Uncomprised. 456.
Now, in order to analyze the term "Comprised by the Dissociated" and "Uncomprised," the passage beginning with "By the aggregate of material form" (*rūpakkhandhena*) is commenced.
In this context, those terms whose dissociation is not applicable have not been included in this section. Which ones are they?
They are the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and so forth. For the dissociation of the base of mental phenomena from even one of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so on is not possible.
The same principle applies to the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) and the rest. This is their mnemonic summary (*uddāna*):
“The sense-base of mental objects (dhammāyatana), the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu), and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya);
the term ‘name-and-form’ (nāmarūpa) and the sixfold sense-base (saḷāyatana).
The triad beginning with birth (jāti) is one [term]; these are the words in the twentieth triad.”
One at the end of the *Tikā*, seven in the *Cūḷantara*;
ten in the *Gocchaka*, fourteen in the *Mahantara*;
and six verses beyond that—thus, in brief, all of them.
"And the [remaining] steps are not found, forty-seven in total.
And at the conclusion, the verse beginning "The sense-sphere of phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu)" was also spoken to illustrate this very same meaning.

However, with the exception of these, all the others are indeed found. Among them, the classification into aggregates (khandha) and so forth should be understood according to the method already stated.
Commentary on the Terms "Included" and "Not Included" in Relation to the Dissociated.
Concluding Remarks:
And to this extent—
The exposition of the classification of the methods for the *Dhātukathā*— which the Tathāgata spoke,
being skilled in the analysis of the elements— is hereby completed. Indeed,
by means of this clear exposition of the classification of the methods, it is possible [to understand].
It has been said that all methods of exposition are merely brief statements for the sake of understanding.
However, if one were to speak at length on each and every word,
the discourse would become excessively voluminous, while the meaning would remain no different.
Thus, whatever merit has been gained by me through this recitation of the *Dhātukathā*,
which consists of two incomplete recitations, may that merit lead to the happiness of the world.
The Commentary on the *Dhātukathā* is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Designation of Human Types (Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā) in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
The Teacher, having taught the treatise named *Dhātukathā*, which is for the sake of subtlety and elucidates the classification of elements, in the abode of the gods;
immediately after that, the Victor [taught] the illumination of the classifications of designations.
He said: "The *Puggalapaññatti* is that which is the foremost person in the world.
Since the occasion for its commentary has now arrived, I shall therefore explain it; listen to it with concentrated minds."
1. Explanation of the Matrix (Mātikāvaṇṇanā) 1.
Six designations: the designation of aggregates... [and so on] ...the designation of persons. This, first of all, is the enumeration of the designation of persons.
Therein, "six" is a delimitation by number. By that, with respect to the number of those phenomena which he intends to designate here—
In brief, it shows the delimitation of designation (*paññatti*). "Designations" (*paññattiyo*) is a term for indicating delimited phenomena (*paricchinnadhamma*).
In that context, in passages where it is said, "He announces, teaches, designates, and establishes," *paññatti* means announcing, showing, making manifest, and establishing.
In passages where it is said, "The bed and chair are well-arranged," *paññatti* means placing and setting down.
[This is] the name. Here, both [meanings] are acceptable. "Six designations" (paññattiyo) means six ways of making known, six ways of showing or revealing;

it is precisely these that are intended here as the six ways of establishing or setting down. For a designation by name (nāmapaññatti) both shows those various phenomena and establishes them under their respective categories.
The passage beginning with “The designation of the aggregates” (*khandha-paññatti*) and so forth is a brief demonstration of the essential nature of those designations.
In this context, the act of making known, showing, manifesting, establishing, and setting down the aggregates as “aggregates” is called the designation of the aggregates.
Likewise, the designation of the sense bases as “sense bases,” of the elements as “elements,” of the truths as “truths,” of the faculties as “faculties,” and of persons as... [persons].
"Person" (puggala) means: making known, showing, manifesting, establishing, and setting down; this is called "person-designation" (puggalapaññatti).
Furthermore, according to the method of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), apart from those found in the canonical texts (*pāḷi*), there are another six designations:

designation of the existent, designation of the non-existent, designation of the non-existent by means of the existent, designation of the existent by means of the non-existent, designation of the existent by means of the existent, [and designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent].

"Designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent. In this context, the designation of a phenomenon that exists, is real, and has arisen—namely, what is wholesome or unwholesome—in accordance with its actual reality and ultimate sense, is called "designation of the existent.

Likewise, the designation of that which does not exist, such as "woman," "man," and so forth, which is established merely through worldly convention, is called "designation of the non-existent. In every respect...

Even the designation of something unfindable—such as the mere basis for speech consisting of a "fifth truth" and so forth, or the "atom," the "person," and so forth, as asserted by the sectarians—is indeed a non-existent designation (*avijjamāna-paññatti*).
However, because that [latter type] does not fall within the scope of the Buddha's teaching (*sāsana*), it is not included here.

Thus, the remaining types should be understood through the differentiation of these existent and non-existent [designations]. This is the case in expressions such as "one possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijjo*) or "one possessing the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñño*).

For while the three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*) and the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*) exist, the person (*puggala*) does not exist. Therefore, one who possesses the three knowledges is "one of three knowledges" (*tevijjo*), and one who possesses the six direct knowledges is "one of six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñño*). Thus, because the non-existent is designated by means of the existent, this is called a "designation of the non-existent by means of the existent.
However, in cases such as "the form of a woman" (*itthirūpa*) or "the form of a man" (*purisarūpa*), [it is a designation of the non-existent by means of the existent].
Woman and man do not exist [as substantial entities], while form exists. Therefore, "the form of a woman" is *itthirūpa*, and "the form of a man" is *purisarūpa*.
Thus, because the existent is designated by means of the non-existent, this is called a "conceptualization of the existent by means of the non-existent.
In such cases as "eye-contact" (*cakkhusamphassa*) or "ear-contact" (*sotasamphassa*), both the eye, ear, and so forth, as well as contact, [are designated in this manner].
It is indeed existent. Therefore, contact in the eye, contact born from the eye, or contact that is the fruit of the eye is "eye-contact.

Thus, because it designates an existent by means of an existent, this is called a "designation of the existent by means of the existent," as in the cases of "son of a kshatriya," "son of a brahmin," "son of a merchant," and so forth; for in these instances, the kshatriyas and others [are likewise designated].

[The son] does not exist; even the son [of a kṣatriya] does not exist. Therefore, because one designates the non-existent by means of the non-existent—such as when one says "the son of a kṣatriya" is a "kṣatriya-son"—this kind is called a designation of the non-existent by the non-existent (*avijjamānena avijjamāna-paññatti*).

Among those [five types of designation], only the first three designations are found in this treatise. For in this context, it says: "Designation of the aggregates... [and so on] ...designation of the faculties."

Because it is designated while actually existing, it is called a "designation of the existent" (*vijjamāna-paññatti*). In the phrase "person-designation" (*puggala-paññatti*), there is a "designation of the non-existent" (*avijjamāna-paññatti*).

However, in subsequent instances such as "one possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijjo*) or "one possessing the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñño*), a "designation of the non-existent by means of the existent" is obtained. Furthermore, according to the method of the teachers (Ācariya-naya) independent of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), there are another six types of designation:

designation by way of dependence (*upādā-paññatti*), designation by way of comparison (*upanidhā-paññatti*), [designation by way of connection (*sambandha-paññatti*), designation by way of location (*okāsa-paññatti*), designation by way of coexistence (*sahavutti-paññatti*), and designation by way of transformation (*vikāra-paññatti*)].

These are: designation by synthesis (*samodhāna-paññatti*), designation by juxtaposition (*upanikkhitta-paññatti*), designation by that which is produced (*tajjā-paññatti*), and designation by continuity (*santati-paññatti*).

Among these, that which—though its nature is not found as a reality in the ultimate sense (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*) like form, feeling, and so forth, either as identical to or different from them—is nevertheless conventionally accepted by depending upon, relying on, and taking as its cause the various aggregates such as form and feeling.
A "being" (*satta*). Depending upon various parts, there is a chariot, a house, a fist, or a hearth;
depending upon those very same [parts] such as visible form and so forth, there is a jar or a cloth; depending upon the revolution of the moon, sun, and so forth, there is time and direction;

and depending upon, relying upon, and making the cause of various elemental signs (*bhūtanimitta*) and the benefits of meditation (*bhāvanānisamsa*), that which is conventionally accepted appears in its respective mode.
The "learning sign" (*uggahanimitta*) and the "counterpart sign" (*paṭibhāganimitta*)—this is what is called a "derivative designation" (*upādāpaññatti*).

It is called a "designation" (*paññatti*) in the sense of that which is to be designated, not in the sense of the act of designating. However, the act of designating that object is itself merely a "designation of the non-existent" (*avijjamānapaññatti*).
Furthermore, [designations] such as "the second" or "the third" in relation to the first, second, and so on, and "long" in relation to one another, [are also derivative designations].
Descriptions such as "short," "distant," and "near" are called *upanidhāpaññatti* (descriptions by comparison).

Furthermore, this *upanidhāpaññatti* is classified as: comparison with something else (*tadaññāpekkha-upanidhā*), comparison with what is in the hand (*hatthagata-upanidhā*), comparison with what is associated (*sampayutta-upanidhā*), comparison through superimposition (*samāropita-upanidhā*), comparison with what is not far removed (*avidūragata-upanidhā*), comparison with a counterpart (*paṭibhāga-upanidhā*), comparison with what abounds in that quality (*tabbahula-upanidhā*), and comparison with what is distinguished by that quality (*tabbisiṭṭha-upanidhā*), and so forth.
By way of division, they are of many kinds.

Among them, those such as "the second" or "the third" are called *tadaññāpekkhūpanidhā* (comparisons relative to something else) because they are stated in dependence upon something other than themselves.

Those such as "one with an umbrella in hand" (*chattapāṇi*) or "one with a sword in hand" (*satthapāṇi*) are called *hatthagatūpanidhā* (comparisons based on what is held in the hand) because they are stated in reference to what has come into the hand.

[The term] *nāma*. [Expressions such as] *Kuṇḍalī*, *Sikharī*, *Kiriṭī*, and so forth, are called "comparison by association" (*sampayuttūpanidhā*) because they are spoken in reference to what is associated [with them].

[Expressions such as] *Dhaññasakaṭa* (rice-cart) and *Sappikumbha* (ghee-pot), and so forth, are called "comparison by attribution" (*samāropitūpanidhā*) because they are spoken in reference to what is attributed [to them].
[Expressions such as] *Indasālaguhā*, *Piyaṅguguhā*, *Serīsaka*, and so forth, are [called comparison] because they are spoken in reference to what is not far removed.
"Near-comparison by proximity" (*avidūragatūpanidhāna*) is so called because it is stated in comparison with a counterpart, such as "gold-colored" or "one who walks like a bull.
"Near-comparison by abundance" (*tabbahulūpanidhāna*) is so called because it is stated in comparison with what is prevalent therein, such as "a lotus pond" or "a brahmin village.
"Near-comparison by excellence" (*tabbisisthūpanidhāna*) is so called because it is stated in comparison with what is superior therein, such as "a jeweled bracelet" or "a diamond bracelet."
Because it is so stated, there is what is called "designation by way of comparison with that which is distinguished.

However, that designation which, having regard for the combination of various things, establishes such things as "the triple staff," "the eightfold board," "a heap of grain," or "a heap of flowers," is called "designation by combination" (*samodhāna-paññatti*).
That [designation] which, having set down each preceding thing one after another, [establishes] "two,"...
The designation of "three," "four," and so forth, is called *upanikkhittapaññatti* (designation by juxtaposition).

The designation of "earth," "fire," "hardness," "heat," and so forth, which depends upon the specific intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of each respective phenomenon, is called *tajjāpaññatti* (designation according to that [nature]).
Furthermore, the designation of "eighty years old," "ninety years old," and so forth, which depends upon the absence of a break in the continuum (*santati*), is [called *santatipaññatti*].

This is called "conceptualization of continuity" (*santatipaññatti*). Among these, however, "corresponding conceptualization" (*tajjāpaññatti*) belongs exclusively to the category of existing conceptualizations (*vijjamānapaññatti*). The remaining ones belong to the side of non-existent conceptualizations; furthermore, they fall under the side of non-existent conceptualizations by virtue of being non-existent.

According to the method of the teachers independent of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), there are another six types of conceptualization: conceptualization of function (*kiccapaññatti*), conceptualization of shape (*saṇṭhānapaññatti*), [conceptualization of number, conceptualization of direction, conceptualization of time, and conceptualization of relation].

There are four kinds of designation: designation by characteristic (*liṅgapaññatti*), designation by plane (*bhūmipaññatti*), designation by individuality (*paccattapaññatti*), and designation by the unconditioned (*asaṅkhatapaññatti*).
Among these, the designation by way of function, such as "reciter" or "preacher of the Dhamma," is called designation by function (*kiccapaññatti*).

The designation by way of shape, such as "emaciated," "corpulent," "round," or "quadrangular," is called designation by shape (*saṇṭhānapaññatti*). [The designation] such as "woman" or "man" is... [and so forth].

Designation by way of characteristic is called "characteristic-designation" (*liṅga-paññatti*). Designation by way of plane—such as "belonging to the sense-sphere," "belonging to the fine-material sphere," "belonging to the immaterial sphere," "of Kosala," or "of Madhura"—is called "plane-designation" (*bhūmi-paññatti*).

Designation by way of merely applying a personal name—such as "Tissa," "Nāga," or "Sumanā"—is called "individual-designation" (*paccatta-paññatti*). [Designations such as] "cessation" or "nibbāna" are...

The designation of an unconditioned phenomenon is called "unconditioned designation" (*asaṅkhata-paññatti*). Among these, certain designations of planes (*bhūmi-paññatti*) and unconditioned designations are indeed designations of what exists (*vijjamāna-paññatti*);
however, a designation of function (*kicca-paññatti*) belongs to the side of what does not exist (*avijjamāna-pakkha*) by means of what exists.
The remaining ones are called designations of what does not exist (*avijjamāna-paññatti*).
2. Now, regarding those designations for which a brief presentation of their essential nature was given in the section on the summary, he says “To what extent?
and so forth, in order to show them by way of analyzing their basis (vatthu) even briefly.
Therein, first, the meaning of the question should be understood as follows: that which is this designation of the aggregates as “aggregates,” and the seeing [of them],...

"Placement" (*ṭhapanā*): this is a question asked out of a desire to explain by how much [measure] it occurs. The same method applies to the subsequent sections, such as "To what extent are the bases (*āyatana*)?
and so forth. The meaning should also be understood in this way in the answers: by whatever means of designation—whether briefly as "the five aggregates" or in detail as "the aggregate of form...
up to ... the aggregate of consciousness"—and therein, the aggregate of form is that of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
Or there is a designation such as "the remaining [aggregates] belong to four planes"; by this much, there is the designation of the aggregates as "aggregates.
Likewise, by whatever means of designation—in brief as "the twelve sense bases" (*dvādaśāyatana*), or in detail as "the eye base... pe...
the mental-object base" (*dhammāyatana*)—therein too, one may designate that "ten sense bases belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while two sense bases belong to four planes. Such is the case.
There is a designation; by this much there is the designation of the bases as "bases.
4. By whatever means of designation—in brief, as "the eighteen elements," or in detail, as "eye-element... pe ...
mind-consciousness-element"—therein, sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and two elements belong to four planes of existence.
Or there is such a designation as this: by so much [of a definition], there is the designation of the elements as "elements.
5. By whatever means of designation—in brief, as "the four truths," or in detail, as "the truth of suffering...
up to ... the truth of cessation"; or even therein, as "two truths are mundane, two truths are supramundane"—such is the case.
There is a designation; by this much there is the designation of the truths as "truths.
6. By whatever means of designation they are designated—whether briefly as "the twenty-two faculties" or in detail as "the eye-faculty... pe ...
the faculty of one who has already known"—in that regard, ten faculties belong to the sense-sphere, and nine faculties are mixed.
Or there is such a designation as "three faculties are supramundane"; by this much, the designation of the faculties as "faculties" occurs.
Having thus briefly analyzed the basis, five designations have been shown by way of seeing.
Now, in order to show the designation of the person (puggalapaññatti) by way of seeing after analyzing the basis in detail, [the text says] "one liberated by occasion" (samayavimutto).

He said, "One liberated at any time," and so forth. For in the Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa below, the aggregates and other factors that serve as the basis for these five designations were explained in their entirety, like one winnowing sesame seeds or sifting chaff;
therefore, he explains them here only partially. The sixth designation of persons was [treated] below.
"Unstated" (akathita). Here too, in the section on the enumeration, they were stated only in part;

therefore, desiring to explain them in detail, he established the matrix (mātikā) starting from the singlefold up to the tenfold, beginning with "one liberated at times" (samayavimutta) and "one liberated not at times" (asamayavimutta).
This concludes the commentary on the matrix.
2. Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesavaṇṇanā) 1. Commentary on the Singlefold Exposition (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā) 1.
Now, in order to explain and demonstrate the matrix (mātikā) as it was established, starting from the beginning: "And what kind of person..."
He said, "One liberated by occasion," and so forth. Therein, "here" means in this world of sentient beings. "A certain person" means one individual.
Regarding "from time to time," the meaning should be understood in the sense of the locative case; it is equivalent to saying "at each respective time.
"From occasion to occasion" is a synonym for the preceding term. "The eight liberations" refers to the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
For it is called "liberation" (vimokkha) because it is liberated from opposing states. "With the body" means with the mental body (nāmakāya) that is co-nascent with liberation.
"Having touched and dwells" means having attained and remains in [that state]. At what time, then, does one dwell having touched liberation?
There is indeed a time when one desires to enter a meditative attainment (samāpatti), and there is a time when one does not.
There is. In this regard, the time for attending to the body and the time for performing the duties in the early morning are called "the wrong time" for entering attainment.

However, after having attended to the body, performed the duties, and entered one's dwelling place, the interval from when one has sat down until the time for going on almsround arrives is called "the right time" for entering attainment.
Furthermore, having observed the time for going on alms-round, the time for departing is not the time for entering [jhāna];
nor is it the time for standing at the thought-hall while surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, nor the time for wandering through the village for alms;

nor is it the time for drinking rice-gruel in the refectory or the time for performing the formal duties—this too is called "the wrong time" for attaining [jhāna]. However, in a secluded place within the refectory...
As long as the time for the meal has not yet arrived, this interval is indeed called the time for entering [jhāna].

However, the time for eating the meal, the time for going to the monastery, the time for putting away the bowl and robes, the time for performing the midday duties, and the time for giving questions for inquiry—this too is called the improper time for entering [jhāna]. That which is an improper time is itself the non-season. That...

Setting aside all [the aforementioned states], at other times and on other occasions, when one dwells having attained the eight liberations (*vimokkha*) of the type already described by means of the co-nascent mental body (*nāmakāya*), it is said: "In this case, a certain person... dwells.
Furthermore, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), one indeed touches the co-nascent phenomena through the co-nascent phenomena that possess contact.
It is indeed said that one touches absorption (appanā). One touches a subsequent absorption by means of a preceding absorption.
For when phenomena are co-nascent with something, they are said to be "attained" through it; they are also said to be "touched" by contact (phassa).
Even access concentration (upacāra) is a cause for the attainment of absorption, and likewise, a preceding absorption is a cause for a subsequent absorption. In this regard, for him—
In this way, the touching of co-nascent states by means of co-nascent states is to be understood: for the first jhāna consists of five factors, beginning with applied thought (*vitakka*).
Excluding those factors, the remaining fifty-six states—namely, the four aggregates (*khandha*)—constitute the "mental body" (*nāmakāya*).
Having touched and attained the liberation of the attainment of the first jhāna through that mental body, one dwells [therein]. The second...

The first *jhāna* has three factors consisting of rapture (*pīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*); the third has two factors consisting of bliss and one-pointedness of mind;

and the fourth has two factors consisting of equanimity (*upekkhā*) and one-pointedness of mind. Likewise for the base of infinite space … [and so on] … up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Excluding those factors, the remaining fifty-five states are called the four aggregates (*khandhā*).
By means of that mental body, having touched and attained the liberation of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells therein.

"And having seen with wisdom" means: having seen the conditioned phenomena with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), and having seen the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths with the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*).
"Some taints are utterly destroyed" refers to those taints that are to be abandoned by the first path and so forth, which are destroyed partially and partially.
"They have become completely exhausted. This is called a person "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimutta*).

In this context, it would be appropriate to say that an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) who has attained the eight meditative attainments dwells having touched [the formless realm] with that mental body (*nāmakāya*).

However, in the Canon it is stated, "some taints (*āsava*) have been completely exhausted. Yet, for an ordinary person, there are no such things as "exhausted taints"; therefore, he is not [liberated].

"He is included. It is appropriate to say that even one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) and whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) dwells having touched that mental body (*nāmakāya*).
