However, there is no such person among them whose taints are not yet exhausted; therefore, he too is not included.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the term "occasionally liberated" (*samayavimutta*) is a designation for the three types of noble ones: stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners.
2. In the exposition of "liberated at all times" (*asamayavimutta*): it should be understood according to the same method as previously stated.
Herein, "liberated at all times" is a designation for a dry-insight arahant (*sukkhavipassaka-khīṇāsava*).

However, in this dyad, dry-insight stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arahants who have attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), and worldlings (*puthujjana*) are not included; they are persons excluded from this dyad.

Thus they are called [by those names]. Therefore, the Teacher, by way of his own state as a perfectly awakened Buddha, having gathered together both what was previously mentioned and what was not, and establishing the textual tradition along with the summaries (*piṭṭhivaṭṭaka*), said:

"All noble persons (*ariyapuggala*)," and so forth. Therein, "in the noble liberation" (*ariye vimokkhe*) means in the supramundane liberation (*lokuttara-vimokkha*) which is reckoned as "noble" because it is remote from the defilements (*kilesa*). This is what was stated.
There is [a distinction]: for one entering the eight external attainments, there is both a proper time and an improper time;
but for one being liberated by means of the liberation of the Path, there is neither a proper time nor an improper time.
For one whose faith is powerful and who has initiated insight, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—
"There is no such thing as the penetration of the path and its fruits while one is eating or consuming food.
Thus, for one who is liberated by means of the liberation of the path, there is neither time nor non-time.

Having thus synthesized both what was previously accepted and what was not, the Dhamma King established this "Backbone" discourse (*piṭṭhivaṭṭaka-tanti*). Even for an ordinary person who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*)...

He has not yet grasped the lineage. However, if he were to associate with [worldly things], he would partake in the state of one liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimutta*) due to the defilements suppressed by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). 3.

Regarding the descriptions of those whose nature is subject to agitation and those whose nature is not subject to agitation: for one whose attained state of meditative attainment agitates or perishes...
That is subject to agitation. "Accompanied by form" means accompanied by form, which is designated as the sign of form;
the meaning is that they occur together with it, not without it, namely the four fine-material-sphere jhānas which have form as their object.
"Accompanied by the formless" means other than form, not form—that is, the formless. "Accompanied by the formless" means accompanied by that, occurring together with it, not without it.

The meaning is: "of the four formless-sphere jhānas which have formless objects. "Not one who attains at will" means not one who attains according to his wish because he has not mastered [the practice] through the five modes of cultivation; the meaning is that his attainment is unskilled (*appaguṇa*).
"Not one who attains without difficulty" means one who attains with difficulty, one who attains with hardship. One who, while suppressing defilements during the approach, [attains] access...

One who attains absorption, one who attains it with difficulty, hardship, exertion, and effort, and who only succeeds in reaching that attainment after becoming weary, is not called "one who gains it without difficulty. "Not one who gains it without ease" means one who does not gain it extensively;
having entered the attainment, they are unable to extend it for a duration of even one or two thought-moments.
The meaning is that he emerges suddenly after having turned [the mind] back.
"Wherever he wishes" means in whatever place he desires to sit after entering into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). "Whatever he wishes" refers to whichever [meditation] he desires:
either the *kasiṇa*-jhāna, or the *ānāpāna*-jhāna, or the *brahmavihāra*-jhāna, or the *asubha*-jhāna.
It is the attainment into which he enters when he wishes to sit; "as long as he wishes" means for whatever duration of time he desires.
This is what is meant: wherever and whichever attainment he wishes to enter and emerge for whatever length of time, there and then he enters that particular attainment for that length of time.

He is unable both to enter and to emerge from it. Having looked at either the moon or the sun and determined, “I shall emerge when the moon or the sun has reached such-and-such a position,” he enters the jhāna;
yet he is unable to emerge according to that determination and emerges prematurely, due to his lack of proficiency in the attainment.
"Having come to negligence" means depending upon negligence. "This is called" means that a person of such a kind is called one whose nature is subject to agitation.

This, however, is the name for three types of persons: the worldling who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*).
For in these [three], there are states that are obstacles to concentration and obstacles to insight.
Because they have not been well-suppressed and not well-washed away, their attainment is lost and declines.

And this occurs neither through a breach of virtue nor through a transgression of an offense. Furthermore, this grave matter of release does not perish on account of even a slight duty to be performed or merely a lapse in formal conduct.
In this regard, there is this story: It is said that a certain elder was practicing meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
When he had entered a village for alms, some children played in his courtyard and then departed. The elder returned and, thinking, "The courtyard must be swept," failed to sweep it;
instead, he entered the monastery and sat down, intending, "I shall enter an attainment. Being unable to enter it, [he remained there].
Reflecting on his virtue with the thought, "What indeed is an obstruction?", he saw not even the slightest transgression.
Looking to see if there was any breach of the proper conduct, he noticed that the courtyard had not been swept;
having swept it himself, he entered and sat down, sitting while entering into meditative absorption.
4. The description of the "unshakable nature" (akuppadhamma) should be understood by way of the opposites of what has already been stated.

Now, "one of unshakable nature" is a name for two types of persons: the non-returner (anāgāmī) who has attained the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti), and the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
For in these two, the states that obstruct concentration and the states that obstruct insight have been well-suppressed and well-washed away.

Even for those who spend their time in negligence—whether through such activities as delighting in talk and socializing, or through some other negligence suited to themselves—their attainment does not become disturbed and is not lost.

However, dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka) who are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, or those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) are not included in this dyad; they are persons outside the dyads.

Thus they are so named. Therefore, the Teacher—having gathered together both those previously mentioned and those not yet mentioned, and in order to establish the continuity of the teaching (tanti) within this pair of categories along with the "back-turners" (piṭṭhivaṭṭaka)—said: "All noble persons (ariyapuggala)," and so forth.
For while there might be the disturbance or loss of the eight attainments, the supramundane state (lokuttaradhamma), however, [is never lost].
There is no such thing as the agitation or loss of what has been penetrated; it is with reference to this that this was said.

5. The exposition of the states subject to decline and the states not subject to decline should also be understood by way of the exposition of the states subject to agitation and the states not subject to agitation.
For here, both the decline and the non-decline of states are taken in relation to the negligence of the person.
This is merely a teaching by way of synonyms; in all other respects, it is exactly the same as before. 7.
In the exposition of "one capable of volition" (*cetanābhava*): "one capable of volition" means one capable of attaining non-decline in volition.
"If he wills further" means if he enters into attainment. For one who enters into attainment is said to "will further. He...
One does not fall away; the other falls away.
8. In the exposition on "one capable of guarding": "one capable of guarding" means one who is capable of attaining non-falling through guarding.
"If he guards" means if, having abandoned unwholesome states, he enters upon the practice by cultivating wholesome states.
For one who practices in this way is said to "guard" [the attainment]. Such a person does not fall away, whereas the other falls away.

Both of these are capable of stabilizing and making the attainment firm by means of placing it [in the mind]. However, between the two—the one capable of volition (*cetanā-bhabba*) and the one capable of guarding (*anurakkhaṇā-bhabba*)—the one capable of guarding is indeed stronger.
For the one capable of volition does not distinguish between factors that are helpful and those that are unhelpful. Not knowing this, he [neglects] the helpful factors...
He pushes away and expels; he cultivates states that are non-beneficial. While cultivating those, he falls away from attainment.
One capable of preservation knows which states are beneficial and which are non-beneficial. Knowing this, he pushes away and expels the non-beneficial states and cultivates the beneficial states.
While cultivating those, he does not fall away from attainment.

For example, there were two field-watchers: one was afflicted with jaundice and unable to endure cold and other such conditions, while the other was healthy and could endure cold and other such conditions.
The sick man did not descend into the lower watch-tower; he abandoned his night-watch and his day-watch.
During the day, crows and other birds descended upon the field and ate the heads of the rice seedlings, and at night, deer, wild boars, and others entered it.
Having cut that field as if it were wood, they depart. Because of his own negligence, he does not obtain even a mere seed again.
The other, however, does not abandon his protection by night or his protection by day.
Because of his own diligence, he obtains four or even eight wagons from a single karīsa.
In this context, one capable of volition should be regarded as being like a diseased field-guardian, while one capable of preservation should be regarded as being like one who is healthy.

Just as a diseased person, through his own negligence, might not obtain even a mere seed again, so too for one capable of volition who—failing to distinguish between things that are beneficial and those that are not—abandons what is beneficial and cultivates what is not, there is a falling away from attainment. For the other [the one capable of preservation], it is otherwise.
By means of one’s own diligence, just as one might pull out four or eight carts from a single span of ground,

one should understand that for one capable of guarding [the attainment], there is no falling away from attainment when they know the helpful and unhelpful factors, abandon the unhelpful, and cultivate the helpful. Thus,
it should be understood that one capable of guarding is more powerful than one capable of volition alone to make the attainment stable.

9. In the Exposition of the Worldling (*puthujjana-niddesa*): "The three fetters" refers to the fetter of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbata-parāmāsa-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikicchā-saṃyojana*).
For these are said to be abandoned at the moment of the fruit (*phala-kkhaṇa*). However, this [worldling] is shown not even to exist at the moment of the fruit.
"Of those states" means of those states that are the fetters. For at the moment of the path (*magga-kkhaṇa*), one is practicing for their abandonment.

This [term] does not even exist at the moment of the path. Up to this point, it should be understood that one who has abandoned the meditation subject is described here as merely a "thick-headed" worldling (*puthujjana*). 10.
In the description of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*): "Of those states" refers to those more than fifty wholesome states that arise together with the knowledge of change-of-lineage.
"Of the noble Dhamma" means of the supramundane path. "There is an entry" means there is a descent, an arising, a manifestation.

"This is called" refers to that state where, by means of knowledge having Nibbāna as its object, one has transcended all the designation of a worldling (*puthujjana*), the lineage of a worldling, the circle of worldlings, and the concept of a worldling, and has entered the designation of a noble one (*ariya*), the lineage of a noble one, and the circle of noble ones.
One who has entered upon the noble designation is called a person of the lineage (gotrabhū). 11.
In the description of "restrained by fear" (*bhayūparata*): one who is restrained by fear is "restrained by fear.

Both the seven types of trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), having become afraid, refrain from evil and do not commit evil. In that regard, worldlings [refrain] out of fear of the miserable destinies and fear of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

They fear four fears: the fear of defilements (*kilesabhaya*), the fear of reproach (*upavādabhaya*), and so forth. Among these, in the sense of being something to be feared, it is precisely the miserable destinies (*duggati*) that are the "fear," thus "the fear of miserable destinies" (*duggatibhaya*).
The same principle applies to the others as well. In this regard, the worldling (*puthujjana*) thinks:
"If you commit evil, the four states of deprivation will stand with their mouths wide open like hungry pythons; experiencing suffering therein..."
Fearing the danger of an unhappy rebirth, one does not commit evil, thinking, ‘How will I fare?

However, the cycle of existence in saṃsāra, which has no known beginning, is what is called the danger of the round (vaṭṭabhaya). All unwholesome states are called the danger of the defilements (kilesabhaya). Censure, moreover, is called the danger of reproach (upavādabhaya).
Fearing these as well, the worldling (puthujjana) does not commit evil. But as for the stream-enterer, the once-returner, and the non-returner...
The three trainees (*sekkha*), having transcended the miserable destinies (*duggati*), do not commit evil after fearing the remaining three fears.

The trainees established on the path are called "those who have ceased from fear" either by way of their progress toward the goal or because they have not yet completely severed fear. One whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) does not fear even one of these four fears;
for he has completely severed all fear. Therefore, he is called "one who has ceased from fear through fearlessness."

It is said [that he does not fear]. But does he not even fear reproach? He does not fear it. However, it is appropriate to say that he guards against reproach, like the Elder Khīṇāsava in the village of Doṇupalāvī.
12. In the exposition of "one incapable of entering": "incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness" means one who is incapable of entering [it]. By "obstruction of kamma" (kammāvaraṇena):...
By the fivefold action of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*). By the obstruction of defilements (*kilesāvaraṇa*) means by fixed wrong view.

By the obstruction of karmic result (*vipākāvaraṇa*) means by rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) that is rootless or has two roots. "Lacking faith" (*assaddha*) means devoid of faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. "Lacking desire" (*acchandika*) means devoid of the wholesome desire for the wish to act.
Excluding those [of Jambudīpa], they should be understood as inhabitants of the other three continents.
For among them, humans are said to have entered into a state of lack of desire (*acchandikabhāva*).

"Lacking wisdom" (*duppaññā*) means being devoid of the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-paññā*). "Incapable" (*abhabbā*) means lacking the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for attaining the paths and fruits. "The certainty" (*niyāma*) refers to the certainty of the path (*magganiyāma*) and the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
"To enter" (*okkantuṃ*): they are incapable of entering—that is, of penetrating and becoming established therein—the certainty known as rightness regarding wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*).
13. The exposition on those capable of progress (*bhabbāgamana*) should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.

Thus, in this dyad, there are those persons who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya*), those with fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhika*), those who have taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with no root-cause or two root-causes, those who do not have faith in the Buddha and so forth, those who lack the desire to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*), and those whose wisdom (*paññā*) as a constituent of existence (*bhavaṅga*) is incomplete.
And those for whom there is no decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits are all incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*);
the opposite ones are said to be capable. 14.

In the exposition of the fixed and the unfixed: "those with immediate [retribution]" (*ānantarika*) refers to those possessing immediate kamma; "those with wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhika*) refers to those possessing fixed wrong view.

All these [beings] are called "fixed" because they are destined for hell. However, the eight types of noble persons (ariyapuggala) are called "fixed" because they are destined for the state of perfection, for the successive attainment of the paths and fruits, and for final Nibbāna through non-clinging. The remaining persons, however, have no fixed destination;
like a stick thrown into the air, as it falls to the earth, its tip—whether by chance or otherwise—will land on some spot.

Just as it is not known whether [a seed] will grow from its middle or its root, so too, because there is no certainty that "they will be reborn in such-and-such a destination," they should be understood as "indeterminate" (*aniyata*).
As for the statement that those born in Uttarakuru have a "fixed destiny" (*niyatagatika*), that is not by way of a fixed dharma (*niyatadhamma*).
For only those with the dharmas fixed in wrongness or fixed in rightness are called "fixed. And of these...
Thus, this classification of individuals has been explained by way of their function.
15. In the exposition of those practicing the path (*paṭipannaka-niddesa*): "those possessing the path" (*maggasamaṅgin*) refers to the eight types of persons on the paths.

For they are called "those practicing" (*paṭipannaka*) because they are practicing for the sake of the fruit. "Those possessing the fruit" (*phalasamaṅgin*) are so called because of their possession of the attainment of the fruit. From the attainment of the fruit...
For from that point on, even when they have not yet entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), they are indeed said to be "established in fruition.

In the exposition of the "Equal-Headed" (*samasīsī*): "Neither before nor after" means not earlier and not later; the meaning is "simultaneously. "Exhaustion" (*pariyādāna*) means complete destruction.
"This is called" means this person is called "equal-headed. Furthermore, he is of three kinds.
There is one who has the same end as his posture, the same end as his illness, and the same end as his life.
In this regard, there is one who, having established insight while walking, attains Arahantship and attains final Nibbāna while still walking, like the Elder Paduma;
and there is one who, having established insight while standing, attains Arahantship and attains final Nibbāna while still standing, like the Elder Tissa who dwelt at Koṭapabbata Monastery.
Or, while sitting, he applies insight, attains Arahantship, and while still sitting, he attains final Nibbāna;

or, while lying down, he applies insight, attains Arahantship, and while still lying down, he attains final Nibbāna—this is called one who reaches the summit simultaneously with his posture (*iriyāpatha-samasīsī*).

Furthermore, having fallen ill, while still within that illness, he applies insight, attains Arahantship, and through that very illness, he attains final Nibbāna—this is called one who reaches the summit simultaneously with his illness (*roga-samasīsī*).
What is meant by "having one's life terminated at the same time as the head"? "Head" refers to thirteen heads: the head of impediment, which is craving;
the head of bondage, which is conceit; the head of misapprehension, which is view; the head of distraction, which is restlessness; the head of defilement, which is ignorance;
the head of resolution, which is faith; the head of exertion, which is energy; the head of establishment, which is mindfulness; and the head of non-distraction... [and so on].
“Concentration has insight as its head; wisdom has the life-faculty as its head; liberation has the range [of experience] as its head;
and cessation has formations as its head. In this context, the path of arahantship exhausts ignorance, which is the head of the defilements.
The death-consciousness exhausts the life-faculty, which is the head of the process of existence. The consciousness that exhausts ignorance [exhausts] the life-faculty...
It is not able to exhaust it. The consciousness that exhausts the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is unable to exhaust ignorance (*avijjā*).
The consciousness that exhausts ignorance is one thing; the consciousness that exhausts the life-faculty is another.
One for whom these two "heads" reach exhaustion simultaneously is called "one whose head is level with life."

How is this equal? By equality of turn. For in whichever turn the emergence from the path occurs—namely, five reviews in the stream-entry path, five in the once-return path, five in the non-return path, and four in the arahant path—one establishes oneself in these nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge, descends into the life-continuum, and attains final Nibbāna. By means of this...
Due to the equality of their end, this exhaustion of both ends is called "equal. Therefore, this person is called "one whose life has an equal end.
And it is precisely this one who is intended here. 17.
In the description of the *ṭhitakappī* (one who remains for an eon): "An eon is stable" is *ṭhitakappo*; one who possesses such a stable eon is a *ṭhitakappī*.
The meaning is "capable of remaining for an eon" (*kappa*). "It would be the time for burning" means it would be the time for incineration. "Not yet indeed" means:
as long as this person possessing the path does not realize the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), so long the eon will not burn.
Even while burning, it would remain without having burned. For what is called the destruction of an eon is a great transformation and a great upheaval.
The great destruction of the world occurs by means of the incineration of a hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
He says that even this great destruction might endure. However, as long as the Dispensation (*sāsana*) exists, there is no such thing as the destruction of an eon (*kappavināsa*);

for the Dispensation does not exist during an eon-destruction. It is only when time has reached its ultimate limit that what is called the destruction of an eon occurs. Even so, the Teacher [declares] the absence of any obstacle.
To illustrate this, he cites the following reason: “Even this might occur, but it is impossible to create an obstacle for the fruit belonging to one who possesses the path.
Now, for how long a time does this person remain established in the *kappa*?
At whatever moment the emergence from the path occurs, there arises the mind-door adverting consciousness that turns back toward the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Then, one should maintain this state for as long as it takes for three conformities (*anuloma*), one change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū-citta*), one path consciousness (*magga-citta*), two fruition consciousnesses (*phala-citta*), and five reviewing knowledges (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*).
Regarding this matter, outsiders have illustrated it by means of the following simile of a visitor:
"Suppose there were a solid mountain a league high directly above the head of one who possesses the stream-entry path."
If one were to bind it with a triple-coiled rope and suspend it, when one coil is cut, it would be suspended by two; when two are cut, it would still be suspended by one;

and even when that too is cut, it would remain in the air like a mass of clouds, and it would certainly not cause any obstruction to the fruit immediately following the path for that person. However, this illustration is merely brief.
They are indeed great, like those of old. However, it is not only those standing on the path of stream-entry who suspend the eon;

others who possess the paths do so as well. Therefore, the Blessed One, having gathered together everything previously mentioned and what was left unmentioned, along with the individuals belonging to the "back-row" category, established this principle:
"All individuals possessing the paths are 'eons-suspenders' (ṭhitakappino)."

18. In the exposition of the *ariya* (noble ones): they are noble because they are far removed from the defilements (*kilesa*). They are noble because they are worthy of being sought after by the world together with its devas. The meaning of "noble" (*ariya*) is the meaning of "purified"; thus, they are noble also because of their purity. Others are non-noble because of their lack of purity. 19. In the exposition of those in training (*sekha*):

at the moment of the path for one possessing the path, and at the moment of the fruit for one possessing the fruit, they are indeed training in the three trainings beginning with the training in higher virtue;
therefore, they are called "those in training. However, for an *arahant*, at the moment of the fruit of *arahantship*, the three trainings—

They have trained; since there is no further duty for them to train in, they are "those beyond training" (*asekha*). Thus, the seven noble ones who are still training are "those in training" (*sekha*).

Those whose taints are destroyed are called "those who have completed their training" (*sikkhita-asekha*) because they have already trained in virtue and the other perfections in the presence of another.

Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas are called "those who have completed their training without having trained" (*asikkhita-asekha*) due to their self-enlightened nature. All other persons are "neither those in training nor those beyond training" (*neva-sekkha-nāsekkha*), because they neither train nor have trained.

20. In the exposition of the "Threefold Knowledge" (Tevijja): one who first produces the knowledge of past lives and the divine eye, and subsequently attains Arahantship, as well as one who first attains Arahantship and subsequently produces the knowledge of past lives and the divine eye, is indeed called a "possessor of the threefold knowledge.

However, in this context, the discourse on the Suttantas is an exposition by way of a figurative method (pariyāya-desanā), whereas the discourse on the Abhidhamma is an exposition not by way of a figurative method (nippariyāya-desanā).

In this context, the burden is indeed to be brought forward. Therefore, it is intended here that one who has first produced the two types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) and subsequently attained *arahantship* is meant.
The same method applies to those possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
22. In the description of the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*): "Regarding things previously unheard" refers to the penetration of the Truths in his final existence.
Previously, in the presence of others, they had never heard such things before.

However, in their successive previous existences, these omniscient Bodhisattvas, having gone forth in the Buddha’s Dispensation, mastered the Three Piṭakas, and having undertaken the practice of coming and going (gatapaccāgata-vatta), they established themselves at the very limits of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), reaching up to conformity (anuloma) and change-of-lineage (gotrabhu). Therefore, it was only in their final existence that they attained the state of being without a teacher.

This was said with this intention in mind. For at that time, the Tathāgata—having fulfilled the perfections—awakens to the four truths through his own direct knowledge, by means of a wisdom personally realized regarding the conditioned and unconditioned phenomena not heard from another: "This is suffering... [and so on] ...this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
In that context, "and therein" means in that path of arahantship known as the full awakening to the Four Noble Truths.
"He attains omniscience and mastery over the powers" means he attains both the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and mastery (*vasībhāva*) over the powers.
For from the moment the Buddhas attain both the knowledge of omniscience and the knowledge of the ten powers, there remains nothing further to be done.

It does not exist. However, just as it cannot be said of a well-born noble prince that "this or that sovereignty has not yet come" from the moment he receives his consecration— since everything has already arrived— so too,
from the moment the Buddhas attain the path of Arahatship, it cannot be said that "this or that quality has not yet come, has not been penetrated, or is not manifest."
It should not be said [that they have not been fully realized], for all the qualities of omniscience have indeed arrived, been penetrated, and become directly realized.
"This one is called" means that this person, having penetrated the quality of omniscience by means of the Noble Path through the power of the accomplishment of fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs),
is called a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).
23. Also in the exposition of the *Paccekabuddha* (Solitary Buddha), the meaning of the phrase "previously unheard" is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
For even a *Paccekabuddha*, in his final existence, being without a teacher, realizes the Truth by means of knowledge that exalts himself;
yet he does not attain either the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) or mastery over the powers (*bala*).

24. In the exposition on those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*): "Having touched the eight liberations with the body and dwells therein" means that he dwells having attained the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) by means of the co-nascent mental body (*nāmakāya*).

"And having seen with wisdom" means that having seen the conditioned phenomena with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), and having seen the four truths with the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*), his four taints (*āsava*) are exhausted.
“This is called” means that a person of such a kind is called “one liberated in both ways” (*ubhatobhāgavimutto*).
For he is liberated in two parts or twice; thus, he is one liberated in both ways. Regarding this, the tradition of the Elders (*theravāda*) is as follows:

First, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga said: “He is liberated by the liberation of suppression through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and by the liberation of eradication through the Path (*magga*).”
“Released in both ways on two occasions. The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, who was a master of the Tipiṭaka, said, “This is one who relies on names,” and recited:
“As a flame cast by the force of the wind, O Upasīva, goes out and can no longer be reckoned as such; (said the Blessed One).
"Thus the sage, liberated from the group of mental aggregates (nāmakāya), reaches the goal and does not come within the sphere of designation.

Having said this and cited the sutta, [he explained]: "Because he is well-liberated both from the group of mental aggregates and from the group of material form (rūpakāya), he is one who is liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)."

But the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya said: “One who is liberated once by means of the liberation through suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimokkha*) through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and liberated once by means of the liberation through eradication (*samuccheda-vimokkha*) through the Path (*magga*), is one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*).
Now, these three elders were wise, and seeing that there was reason in all three positions, they established the tradition (*tanti*) by accepting all three views.

In brief, however, one who is liberated from the material body by means of the formless attainments and liberated from the mental body by means of the Path is called "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) because he is liberated from both sides.

He refers to those four who, having emerged from each of the four formless attainments, contemplated conditioned phenomena and attained Arahantship; and those who, having emerged from the attainment of cessation, attained Arahantship.

It is fivefold by way of the stream-enterer and the non-returner. Among these, the first four are called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) in a figurative sense, because they do not enter cessation as the pinnacle of meditative attainments.
However, a non-returner who has attained the eight attainments, having entered that [cessation], emerged from it, and increased insight to reach *arahatship*, is so called in the literal sense.
[The highest type of Arahant is] called "the one liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta-seṭṭha*).

But is it not the case that the immaterial-sphere jhāna also possesses two factors—equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—and the fine-material-sphere fourth jhāna likewise; therefore, should one who attains Arahantship by taking even that [immaterial jhāna] as its proximate cause not also be "liberated in both ways"?
No, he should not. Why? Because he is not liberated from the material body (*rūpakāya*).
For that [attainment] is liberated only from the body of defilements, not from the body of form; therefore, one who emerges from it and attains Arahantship is not called "liberated in both ways.
However, the immaterial-sphere attainment is liberated from both the mental body and the physical body;
thus, it should be understood that one who takes that very attainment as a basis and attains Arahantship is "liberated in both ways."
25. In the explanation of "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*): one who is liberated by means of wisdom is "liberated by wisdom. This consists of five types:

the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*) and those four who have attained Arahantship after emerging from the four jhānas. For among these, not even one is an attainer of the eight liberations (*aṭṭha-vimokkha*).
That is why it says, "But indeed, he does not [possess] the eight liberations," and so forth. However, regarding the immaterial-sphere jhānas (*arūpāvacara-jjhāna*), in one...
When this is present, one is indeed called "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta).
26. In the description of the "body-witness" (kāyasakkhin): "certain taints" (āsavā) refers to those to be abandoned by the three lower paths.
"This is called" means that a person of such a kind is called a body-witness. For he realizes what has been touched [by direct experience]; thus, he is a body-witness.
One who first touches the contact of jhāna and subsequently realizes cessation, Nibbāna, is also a body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*).

He is of six kinds, beginning from the stage of one established in the fruit of stream-entry up to the stage of one on the path to Arahantship. 27. In the description of "one who has attained vision" (*diṭṭhippatto*):
"This is suffering" means this is suffering; "this much is suffering" means there is no more suffering beyond this.
It is suffering. This same method applies to the origin of suffering and the other [truths].
"He understands it as it really is" means that, setting craving aside, he understands the five aggregates of clinging as the "truth of suffering" according to their actual nature.
Craving, however, generates, produces, and brings forth suffering; from that, suffering originates. Therefore, he understands it as the "origin of suffering."

One understands it as it truly is. Furthermore, because this suffering and its origin cease, are stilled, and reach non-occurrence upon attaining Nibbāna, one understands it as it truly is: "This is the cessation of suffering.
And the Noble Eightfold Path goes toward that cessation of suffering; therefore, one understands it as "this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Up to this point, the determination of the truths at different moments has been shown.
Now, in order to show them at a single moment, he says: “Proclaimed by the Tathāgata,” and so forth.

Therein, “proclaimed by the Tathāgata” means that having sat at the seat of Great Enlightenment, they were penetrated, known, and made manifest by the Tathāgata. “Dhammas” refers to the Dhammas of the Four Noble Truths.
“Seen well” means clearly seen. “Well-practiced” means well-conducted; the meaning is that by means of these, his wisdom has been well-cultivated.
“This is called” means that a person of such a kind is called one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatto*).
For he has reached the end of vision. There arises the knowledge: “Conditioned phenomena are suffering; cessation is bliss. It is seen, it is known.
"Realized and seen by means of wisdom" refers to one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhappatta*). This person also, like the body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*), is of six kinds.

28. In the description of "one liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*): "But not as in the case of one who has attained vision" means that the taints (*āsava*) are not completely exhausted for the one liberated by faith in the same way they are for the one who has attained vision. What, then, is the difference between them regarding the abandoning of defilements?
Is there no difference [between them]? There is none. Then why does the one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*) not reach the level of the one who has attained through vision (*diṭṭhippatto*)?

It is due to the difference in their progress. For in progressing toward the state of one who has attained through vision, one is able to suppress the defilements without pain, without difficulty, and without fatigue;
whereas the one liberated by faith must suppress them with pain, with difficulty, and with fatigue.
He is unable [to progress further], and therefore he does not reach the stage of one attained to vision (*diṭṭhippatto*). Furthermore, there is indeed a difference in their wisdom as well.
For the insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) of the three paths higher than that of one attained to vision proceeds in a way that is sharp, keen, and clear.
But for one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutto*), the insight-knowledge does not proceed in such a way—neither sharp, nor keen, nor clear; therefore, for this reason too...
Thus, he does not reach the attainment of right view.
For example, when two novices are demonstrating a craft, one has a sharp sword in his hand and the other a blunt one.
When a plantain tree is cut with the sharp sword, it makes no sound; but when it is cut with the blunt sword, it makes a "kaṭakaṭa" sound.

It makes a sound. In this context, the sharpness, courage, and clarity of the insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) of the three paths for one who has attained vision is like the cutting of a plantain tree by a sharp sword even without making a sound.
The [insight-knowledge] of the three paths for one liberated through faith (*saddhā-vimutta*) is like the cutting of a plantain tree by a blunt sword even while making a sound.
The lack of sharpness, brilliance, and clarity in insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) should be understood.

Having rejected this method by saying "no," the conclusion was reached that the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta) does not reach the level of the one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatta) solely through the diversity of what is yet to be traveled.
However, it is stated in the Commentaries on the Agamas: "For among these, at the moment of the preliminary path, while the one liberated by faith has faith..."
For one who is thus settling, as it were, and resolving, as it were, there comes about the destruction of the defilements.
In the case of one who has attained through vision, at the moment of the preliminary path, the knowledge that cuts off the defilements proceeds unclouded, sharp, and courageous.
Therefore, just as when cutting a plantain tree with an excessively blunt sword, the place where it is cut is not smooth, so too [is the result] with a dull sword.
It does not cut swiftly, a sound is heard, and a more strenuous effort must be made; such is the development of the preliminary path for one liberated through faith.

But just as when one cuts a plantain tree with a very sharp sword, the place where it is cut becomes smooth, the sword cuts swiftly, no sound is heard, and there is no need for strenuous effort; such is [the development of the path for one liberated by wisdom].
“The prior-stage development of the path for one who has attained through view should be understood.
“This is called” means that such a person is called “liberated by faith” (*saddhāvimutta*). For he is liberated while being full of faith; thus, he is “liberated by faith.
Like the body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*), this one also is of six kinds.
29. In the exposition of the *dhammānusārī*: by the phrase "one who is practicing," the stage of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) is shown.
"Excessive" means powerful. "Bearing wisdom" (*paññāvāhī*) means that it carries wisdom; it is also said to mean that wisdom carries this person.
"Preceded by wisdom" means having made wisdom the forerunner. "This is called" refers to a person of such a kind.
He is called a "follower of the Dhamma" (dhammānusārī). For he remembers and recollects by means of the Dhamma known as wisdom; thus he is a follower of the Dhamma.
This name applies only to one who is standing on the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). But when the fruit is attained, he is called "one who has reached vision" (diṭṭhippatto).
In the exposition of the "follower of faith" (saddhānusārī) as well: it carries faith, thus it is "faith-bearing" (saddhāvāhī); or, faith carries this person, thus [he is a follower of faith].
It has already been stated that [the path] "carries faith. "Preceded by faith" means having made faith the precursor. "This is called...
means that such a person is called a *saddhānusārī* (follower by faith). For he remembers by means of faith; he is a *saddhānusārī* because he recollects through faith.
This name applies only to one who stands on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). But when the fruit is attained, he is called a *saddhāvimutta* (liberated by faith).
There are two yokes, two modes of application, and two heads for those who are producing supramundane states.

In this context, the "two yokes" are the yoke of faith and the yoke of wisdom. Furthermore, one bhikkhu applies himself through the mode of application of serenity (*samatha*), while another applies himself through the mode of application of insight (*vipassanā*); these are the "two modes of application."
And one who reaches the summit is "liberated in both ways," while another is "liberated by wisdom"—these are the two heads.

For whoever produces supramundane states, they all do so by making these two qualities their primary burden, fixing themselves upon these two positions, and attaining liberation through these two positions. Among them:

The bhikkhu who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), having made wisdom his primary vehicle and being intent upon calm (*samatha*), takes one of the formless attainments as his footing, establishes insight (*vipassanā*), and reaches Arahantship—he is called a "follower by Dhamma" (*dhammānusārī*) at the moment of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*).

Subsequently, however, in the six stages [of the higher paths], he is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*. Upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, he is called an "attainer of the fruit" [*phala-samāpanno*]).
One who is "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta).
Another, having made wisdom alone his primary burden and being intent upon insight, reaches Arahantship by comprehending either pure formations or one of the fine-material-sphere jhānas;
this person also is a "follower of Dhamma" (dhammānusārī) at the very moment of the stream-entry path.
...is so named. Furthermore, in six other instances, one is called "attained through view" (*diṭṭhippatto*). Upon attaining Arahantship, one is called "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutto*).
Here, two names are new; together with the previous ones, there are five.

Another person, having attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), makes faith the primary factor and, being intent upon concentration, takes a certain formless attainment as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
Having established insight and attained arahantship—he is called a *saddhānusārī* at the moment of the stream-entry path.
Beyond that, in the six subsequent stages, he is simply called a *kāyasakkhī*. Upon reaching arahantship, he is simply called an *ubhatobhāgavimutta*.
Here, only one name is new; together with it, there are six including the previous five. Another [type] is one who follows faith alone...

Taking this as his primary focus, he becomes intent through the means of insight (*vipassanā*). Having comprehended either pure formations or one of the fine-material-sphere jhānas, he attains Arahantship.
At the moment of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), he is called a "follower by faith" (*saddhānusārī*);
thereafter, in the six stages, he is called "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*); and upon reaching Arahantship, he is called "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*).
Here too, there is one name not mentioned before. Together with that, there are six or seven preceding ones.
These seven persons are called "the foremost in the world worthy of offerings.
In the exposition of "at most seven times" (*sattakkhattuparama*): "seven times" means seven occasions. Rebirth at most seven times.
He takes up a selfhood [only] seven times at most; beyond that, he does not undergo an eighth existence, thus he is called "one who has seven births at most.
Regarding the term "stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*): here, the "stream" (*sota*) is the noble path (*ariyamagga*); one who is endowed with that is called a stream-enterer.
As it is said: "This, Sāriputta, is called 'the stream, the stream. What, Sāriputta, is the stream? It is this very..."
"Indeed, venerable sir, the Noble Eightfold Path is the stream, namely: right view... [and so on] ...right concentration.
'One who has entered the stream, one who has entered the stream'—this, Sāriputta, is what is said. But who, Sāriputta, is one who has entered the stream?
One, venerable sir, who is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path—this is called one who has entered the stream."
"Or rather, this venerable one is of such a name and such a clan.

Thus, at the moment of the path, one is called a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). However, here the name of the fruit is given by means of the path; therefore, it is the state at the moment of the fruit that is intended as "stream-enterer.

"One whose nature is not to fall into the states of ruin" (*avinipātadhamma*) means one whose inherent nature is not to return to the lower realms (*apāya*), which are designated as "ruin," by way of rebirth. "Destined" (*niyata*)—
"Fixed by way of the path" means destined for full enlightenment (*sambodhiparāyaṇa*). He is "destined for full enlightenment" because he awakens by means of the path already attained;
or, he is "destined for full enlightenment" because he will certainly awaken by means of the three higher paths.
"Among gods and humans" refers to the world of gods and the world of humans. "Having run on and wandered through" means by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Going from one state to another": he makes an end of suffering; that is, he makes a limit and a boundary to the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"This is called... means that such a person is called "one who has seven births at most.
Furthermore, this should be understood as being described by way of a mixed existence, alternating between the world of the gods and the world of humans.
32. In the explanation of *kolaṅkola*: one who goes from family to family is called *kolaṅkola*.
From the moment of the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), there is no rebirth in a low family; the meaning is that one is reborn only in families of great wealth.
"Two or three families" refers to two or three existences (*bhava*) by way of gods and humans. Thus, this person also [attains Nibbāna] only through mixed existence.

This has been explained. This statement, “two or three [births],” is merely for the sake of instruction; however, even while wandering through existence up to the sixth birth, one remains a *kolaṅkola* (one who goes from family to family). 33.
In the exposition of the "single-seeded" (*ekabījin*), what is called the "stem-seed" (*khandhabīja*) is explained. For that stream-enterer who has only one stem-seed remaining—
There is one grasping of a personal existence; he is called a "one-seeder" (*ekabījī*). As for the phrase "in human existence," this is merely a conventional designation here;
it is indeed appropriate to say that he produces a divine existence. These names are given to them according to the names adopted by the Blessed One.
Having reached such a stage, he is called "one who has seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparama*); having reached such a stage, he is called "one who goes from family to family" (*kolaṅkola*).

The Blessed One has assigned these names—“one-seeded” and so forth—to them. However, there is no fixed rule such that this one is necessarily “seven-times-at-most,” this one “going from family to family,” or this one “one-seeded.
But what determines this distinction among them? Some elders, for their part, say: “It is determined by past causes (pubbahetu).”
Some say, "It is the first path"; some say, "It is the three higher paths"; and some say, "It is the insight of the three paths.

In that regard, according to the doctrine that "the prior cause determines [the result]," it follows from their statement that "the decisive support (upanissaya) for the first path has been established, while the three higher paths have arisen without a decisive support. According to the doctrine that "the first path determines [the result]..."
Otherwise, it would follow that the three higher paths are purposeless.
In the view that "the three higher paths determine [the result]," it follows that the three higher paths have already arisen even before the eighth path has arisen.
However, the position that "insight determines the three paths" is logical; for if insight regarding the three higher paths...

She becomes powerful and is called a "one-seed" (ekabījī); with even weaker [craving], she is "one who goes from family to family" (kolaṃkolo); with still weaker [craving], she is "one who has seven births at most" (sattakkhattuparamo).

For a certain stream-enterer (sotāpanna) may have a disposition toward the round of existence (vaṭṭa), delight in the round, and wander and be seen again and again within that very round—such as the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the female lay follower Visākhā, and the divine sons Cūḷaratha and Mahāratha.

The celestial youth Anekavaṇṇa, Sakka the king of the gods, and the celestial youth Nāgadatta—these individuals, whose inclinations were toward the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and who delighted in the round, will, after purifying the six heavenly worlds from the beginning and remaining in Akaniṭṭha, attain final nibbāna;
these are not included here. Nor are they alone; even he who, having transmigrated only seven times among human beings, will attain *arahantship*...
Even one who is reborn in the world of the devas and attains Arahantship after wandering from one state to another among the devas for seven times is not included here.

It should be understood that in this context, those who are "seven-times-at-most" (sattakkhattuparama) and "family-to-family" (kolaṅkola) are included only by way of mixed existences, and the "single-seed" (ekabījī) is included only as one who is reborn in the human existence. Therein, each [of these] is further distinguished by way of the difficult path (dukkhāpaṭipadā) and so forth.

They attain a fourfold state. With faith as the primary factor alone, there are twelve types: four who have seven births at most, four who go from family to family, and four who are once-returners (ekabījins).

If it is possible to produce [the path] through wisdom, then by making wisdom the primary factor with the thought, "I shall produce the supramundane Dhamma," one may likewise reach the state of having seven births at most and so forth.

It should be understood that these twenty-four stream-enterers (sotāpanna) are described in this context solely by way of their attainment in this very life and their realization through meditation. 34.
In the description of the once-returner (sakadāgāmin): one who returns only once by way of rebirth-linking is a "once-returner" (sakadāgāmin). "Only once" means...
"Only once. By the phrase "having come to this world," four out of the five types of *sakadāgāmin* are excluded, and only one is included.
For some, having attained the fruit of *sakadāgāmi* here, attain final nibbāna right here;
some, having attained it here, attain final nibbāna in the deva-world; some, having attained it in the deva-world, attain final nibbāna right there; and some, having attained it in the deva-world—
Having arrived here and been reborn, one attains final nibbāna—these four types are not included here. However, it should be understood that only this one type is included here:
namely, one who, having arrived here, dwells in the world of the devas for the full span of their life, and then, being reborn here once more, attains final nibbāna.
Whatever else might need to be said on this matter has all been stated below in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*.
This has already been stated in the description of supramundane wholesome states. Now, what is the difference between this once-returner and the one-seeder (ekabījin)?
For the one-seeder there is only one rebirth-linking, whereas for the once-returner there are two rebirth-linkings—this is the difference between them.

35. In the description of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*): regarding the "fettering bonds pertaining to the lower realm" (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), "the lower" (*oraṃ*) refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).

One for whom these five fetters have not been abandoned is drawn back to the sense-sphere realm itself by those fetters—just like a fish with a swallowed hook or a crow with its feet bound by a long string—even if he has been reborn in the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
"Occur" refers to the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*). "Lower parts" means they belong to the lower realm or constitute its constituent parts.
"By the complete destruction" means by the total exhaustion of those fetters. "Spontaneously born" (*opapātika*) means one whose mode of birth is spontaneous generation;
by this, his rebirth from a womb is excluded. "One who attains final Nibbāna there" means one who attains final Nibbāna in that very world of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*).
"Of a nature not to return from that world": by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), this refers to the state of not returning here from that world.
However, his coming for the purpose of seeing the Buddha, seeing the Elder, or hearing the Dhamma is not prohibited.
"This is called": such a person, because of not returning again by way of rebirth-linking, is called a Non-returner (*anāgāmī*).

36. In the exposition of the one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyin*): "Immediately upon being reborn" (*upapannaṃ vā samanantara*) means having become immediately after being reborn.
"Or not having reached the middle of the lifespan" (*appattaṃ vā vemajjhaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ*) means that he generates the Noble Path without having reached the midpoint of his lifespan;
such is the meaning. However, due to the alternative sense of the particle *vā*, it should also be understood as "having reached the middle."

Thus, three types of those who attain final nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyino) are established. "Of the higher fetters" means of the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) or of the eight defilements.
"For the abandoning" means that he generates the path for the purpose of abandoning these.
"This is called" refers to such a person because they attain final nibbāna in the very midst of their lifespan.
He is called one who attains parinibbāna in the interval.
37. In the description of one who attains parinibbāna upon arrival: "having passed beyond the middle of the lifespan" means having passed beyond the midpoint of the measure of the lifespan.
"Or dying upon arrival" means dying after having reached [the middle]. Of the exhaustion of the life-span...

The meaning is: "standing near. "This is called" means that such a person, having passed the middle period of five hundred kappas out of the lifespan of one thousand kappas in the Aviha heaven, and having remained for the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or even the tenth century of kappas, attains *arahatta* and, through the parinibbāna of the defilements...
Because he attains final nibbāna upon reaching the end of his life-span, he is called one who attains final nibbāna after having been reborn (upahaccaparinibbāyī).
38. Regarding the descriptions of the one who attains final nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī) and the one who attains final nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī):

one whose nature is to attain final nibbāna through the extinction of the defilements by means of non-exertion—that is, without difficulty and without applying excessive effort—is one who attains final nibbāna without exertion. By means of exertion...

One who is of a nature to attain final nibbāna through the extinction of defilements only after undergoing suffering, with difficulty, and by applying excessive effort, is one who attains nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*). 40.
In the description of the "Upstreamer" (*uddhaṃsota*): because his stream of craving or his stream of the cycle of existence flows upwards, he is called an "upstreamer."

"One who flows upwards" (*uddhaṃsota*): because he must attain [the goal] by going upwards, his stream of the path flows upwards; thus, he is "one who flows upwards. "One who goes to Akaniṭṭha" (*akaniṭṭhagāmī*):
having passed away from the Aviha realm, he goes to the Atappa realm, and so forth.
In those cases, while dwelling in the Aviha realm for a thousand eons, being unable to attain *arahantship*, he goes to the Atappa realm. There too, for two thousand eons...
Dwelling there for an aeon, if one is unable to attain Arahantship, one goes to Sudassa.
Dwelling there for four thousand aeons, if one is unable to attain Arahantship, one goes to Sudassī.
Dwelling there for eight thousand aeons, if one is unable to attain Arahantship, one goes to Akaniṭṭha. The meaning is that while dwelling there, one generates the Noble Path.
Furthermore, in order to understand the classification of these non-returners (*anāgāmin*), the tetrad of those who "go upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm" (*uddhaṃsota akaniṭṭhagāmī*) should be known.
Therein, one who, starting from the Aviha heaven, purifies the four celestial worlds and then goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm to attain final Nibbāna is called an "upstream-goer to the Akaniṭṭha.
However, one who, having purified the three lower celestial worlds, [goes to] the Sudassi heaven...
One who attains final nibbāna after having stayed [there] is called an "upstreamer" (uddhaṃsota), not one who goes to Akaniṭṭha.
But one who, from here, goes specifically to Akaniṭṭha and there attains final nibbāna is not an upstreamer; he is called one who goes to Akaniṭṭha.
Furthermore, one who, among the four lower deva-worlds, attains final nibbāna right there in each respective place is neither an upstreamer nor one who goes to Akaniṭṭha.
Thus, these constitute forty-eight non-returners. How so?

First, in the Aviha heaven, there are three who attain final nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyin*), one who attains final nibbāna upon arrival (*upahaccaparinibbāyin*), and one who goes upstream (*uddhaṃsota*);

these five, together with the five who attain final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāraparinibbāyin*) and the five who attain final nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyin*), make ten. Likewise...
Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī constitute four decades, making forty. In Akaniṭṭha, however, there is no one who goes upstream.

There are three who attain Nibbāna in the interval, one who attains Nibbāna upon arrival, and eight who attain Nibbāna—four who do so without exertion and four who do so with exertion. Thus, there are forty-eight.

All of these are illustrated by the simile of the spark: even when struck upon the iron surface of a fire heated throughout the day with a flint-stone, a splintering nail-cutter, or a fingernail, a spark arises and immediately goes out. Such is to be understood as the first type of *antarāparinibbāyin*. Why?
Because he attains final nibbāna by means of the nibbāna of the defilements at the very moment they arise. From that...
When struck by a still larger iron mouth, the spark leaps up into the air and goes out—such is the second type of one who attains final nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī) to be seen.
Why? Because he attains final nibbāna before reaching the midpoint.
Then, when struck by an even larger iron mouth, the spark leaps up into the air and, returning, does not strike the surface of the earth.
Having been offered as a sacrifice, it attains parinibbāna—such is the third type of one who attains parinibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyī*) to be understood.
Why? Because it attains parinibbāna after reaching the middle [of its flight] but without having struck the ground.

Then, when a much larger iron mouthpiece is being struck, a spark leaps into the air, falls upon the earth, and having struck the surface, it attains parinibbāna—such is the one who attains parinibbāna after striking the surface (*upahaccaparinibbāyī*).
This is how he should be understood. Why? Because, having reached the end of his time and exhausted his lifespan, he attains parinibbāna.

Furthermore, when a spark from a much larger iron flame is struck and falls upon a small amount of grass or wood, it burns that small amount of grass or wood and then goes out—such is the one who attains parinibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī). Why? Because he does so with little effort and by means of a swift transition.

Because of attaining final Nibbāna. When one being struck by an even larger iron-mouthed [torture] falls onto a vast heap of grass and wood, and having extinguished that vast heap of grass and wood, it goes out—such a person should be understood as one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*). Why?
Because he attains final Nibbāna through effort and with a non-swift course of progress. Another [being] falls onto vast heaps of grass and wood...

It falls there, and while great heaps of grass and wood are burning, a spark or a flame leaps up, burns the smithy, burns the village, town, city, and kingdom, and reaching the edge of the ocean, it is extinguished.
Such is the one who goes upstream bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm; why? Because he has exhausted the expansion of the seeds for manifold existences.
Because it reaches final nibbāna after being repeatedly touched and brought to an end.

Furthermore, since even small things such as thorns and so forth, as well as large things, are all merely iron cauldrons, for that reason the Sutta speaks of "iron cauldron" alone in every instance. As it is said:
"Here, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May there be nothing, may there be nothing for me; may it not come to be...'"
‘What exists and has come to be shall not be mine; I abandon that which is. Thus he attains equanimity.
He does not delight in existence, nor does he delight in becoming; he sees with right wisdom the further state of peace.
Yet that state is not fully realized by him in every respect. For him, the underlying tendency to conceit is not entirely eradicated in every respect.
The underlying tendency to sensual lust has not been entirely abandoned, nor has the underlying tendency to ignorance been entirely abandoned.
With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval.
Just as, monks, when a red-hot iron pan has been heated all day and is struck, a spark is produced and...
“...would be extinguished; even so, monks, a monk practicing in this way—though he does not [attain final Nibbāna]... becomes one who attains Nibbāna in the interval.
“Furthermore, monks, a monk practicing in this way—though he does not [attain final Nibbāna]... becomes one who attains Nibbāna in the interval.
Just as, monks, when an iron pan has been heated all day and is struck, a spark is produced and...”
Having risen up, it would go out; even so, monks, a bhikkhu practicing in this way—though he does not [attain final Nibbāna]...
becomes one who attains Nibbāna in the interval.
"Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu practicing in this way—though he does not [attain final Nibbāna]... becomes one who attains Nibbāna in the interval."

It happens thus: "Just as, monks, when an iron pan has been heated all day and is struck, a spark might be produced, fly up, and go out without reaching the ground; even so, monks, a monk practicing in this way—though he does not [attain final knowledge]...
becomes one who attains Nibbāna in the interval."
“Furthermore, monks, here a bhikkhu practices in this way: he does not [possess]... [as before] ...he is one who attains final nibbāna upon landing.

Just as, monks, when an iron pan has been heated all day and is struck, a spark is produced, which, having arisen and flown up, attains the surface and goes out; even so, monks, a bhikkhu practicing in this way...”
...he becomes one who attains final nibbāna upon landing (*upahacca-parinibbāyī*).

"But here, monks, a monk practices in this way—[and he does not have]... [as before]... through the total exhaustion [of the taints], he becomes one who attains final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*).
Just as, monks, when an iron pan has been heated all day and is struck, a spark arises..."
Having leaped up, it might fall upon a small heap of grass or a small heap of wood;

there it would produce both flame and smoke, and having produced both flame and smoke, it would consume that very same small heap of grass or wood and, being without fuel, go out. Even so, monks, does a bhikkhu...
He practices in this way: he does not [possess]... [as before] ... through the exhaustion [of the taints], he attains final Nibbāna without exertion.
"But here, monks, a monk practices in this way: he does not [possess]... [as before] ... he attains final Nibbāna with exertion.
Just as, monks, when an iron pan has been heated all day and is struck, a spark arises..."
Having leapt up, it might fall upon a large heap of grass or a large heap of wood; there it would even produce fire...
[and so on] ...having consumed that very large heap of grass or heap of wood, it would go out for lack of fuel.
In the same way, monks, a monk practices thus: he does not have... [and so on] ...he is one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion.

“Furthermore, monks, here a monk practices in this way: he does not [possess]... [as before] ... through the complete destruction of the taints, he becomes one who flows upwards, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.

Just as, monks, when an iron cauldron has been heated all day and is struck, a spark might be produced and fly up, and then fall upon a large heap of grass or a large heap of wood; there it would set fire to—”
...[he] would produce [fire]... having consumed that very great heap of grass or heap of wood, it might burn up the grove, it might burn up the forest;

and having burned up the grove and having burned up the forest, having reached a green edge, or a path’s edge, or a rock’s edge, or a water’s edge, or a delightful spot of ground, it would go out for lack of fuel. Even so...

“Monks, when a monk practices in this way—provided that he does not [fail to attain]... [as before]... through the complete destruction [of the taints], he becomes one who flows upwards, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
41–44. The explanations regarding those practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and so forth are already clear in meaning. This is called...
Regarding the statement "the person who is an Arahant," twelve types of Arahants should be understood here. How so? There are three liberations:
the void, the signless, and the desireless. Among these, one whose taints are destroyed and who is liberated by means of the void liberation is fourfold according to the way of practice;
likewise for those liberated by means of the signless and desireless liberations. Thus, twelve types of Arahants should be understood.

Thus, these twelve individuals—just like the twelve Arahants, the twenty-four stream-enterers (sotāpanna), and the forty-eight non-returners (anāgāmin)—having been liberated from here, do not arise externally;
they arise only within this very dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha. This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of Single Units.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of Pairs (Dukaniddesa) 45.

Regarding the exposition of pairs: "One who is prone to anger" (*kodhana*) means one whose nature is to be angry, possessing great wrath. Having thus questioned the person, he says, "In this context, what is anger?
and so forth, in order to show the person by way of the phenomenon (*dhamma*). This same method applies to the exposition of the "one who harbors resentment" (*upanāhī*) and the others as well.
“Anger,” “being angry,” and so forth have meanings already explained below. Likewise, in the description of resentment (*upanāha*) and the others, “anger” and so forth refer to the preceding stage.

“This anger is not abandoned” means that this much anger has not been abandoned either by suppression-removal (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*), or by partial removal (*tadaṅga-pahāna*), or by eradication-removal (*samuccheda-pahāna*). The same method applies to resentment and the others that follow.

53. In the explanations of shamelessness (*ahirika*) and so forth: “endowed with this shamelessness” means endowed with such a kind of unashamed state. The same method applies to the phrases “with this lack of dread” (*anottappa*) and so on.
63. “Internally fettered” (*ajjhattasaṃyojana*) means bound within. “Externally fettered” (*bahiddhāsaṃyojana*) means bound outside.
Both of these should be illustrated by the simile of the calf and the cow-pen. For in a cow-pen, a calf tied inside remains lying right inside.
This refers to the stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and once-returners (sakadāgāmin) who remain here [in the sense-sphere]. For them, both their bondage and their dwelling are right here.
However, the stream-enterers and once-returners in the fine-material and immaterial realms are like a calf tied inside but lying outside.
For them, the bondage is indeed here, but they themselves abide in the Brahma-world. They are like a calf tied outside but lying outside.
The non-returner (anāgāmī) exists in the realms of form and formlessness. For him, both his fetter and his own self are external.
However, the non-returner established here is like a calf lying inside while tied outside; for his fetter lies in the realms of form and formlessness, while he himself remains here.

65. In the exposition on the absence of anger (*akkodhana*) and so forth: “Abandoned” means abandoned by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), or by way of partial abandonment (*tadaṅga*), or by way of total eradication (*samuccheda*).
83. In the exposition on what is difficult to find (*dullabha*): “Difficult to find” means not easily obtained. “One who does good first” (*pubbakārī*) is one who acts first.

“One who recognizes what has been done” (*katavedī*) is one who experiences what was done; he makes it known and manifest. These should be illustrated by means of both householders and those who have gone forth from the household life. For among householders...

Parents are called "those who have done much" (*pubbakārin*). Sons and daughters, however, by looking after their parents and performing such acts as saluting them, are called "grateful" (*katavedin*).
Among those who have gone forth into homelessness, teachers and preceptors are called "those who have done much.
Disciples and co-residents, by looking after their teachers and preceptors and performing such acts as saluting them, are called "grateful. Of these...
To illustrate this meaning, the cases of the Elder Upajjhāyaposaka, Soṇa, and others should be related.

Another method: one who acts as a benefactor even when no benefit has been done by another, regardless of any benefit received for himself, is a "first-doer," such as parents, teachers, and preceptors. Such a person is rare, because beings are overwhelmed by craving.
One who recognizes and feels the benefit performed for oneself as a benefit, responding appropriately to the assistance rendered by another, is "grateful and appreciative.
This is exemplified by one who practices correctly toward parents, teachers, and preceptors.
Such a person is also rare, because sentient beings are overwhelmed by ignorance.
Furthermore: one who acts out of kindness without cause is a doer of good first; one who acts out of kindness with cause is a grateful and thankful person.
One whose actions are independent of such motives as "He will do for me" is a doer of good first; one whose actions depend on such motives as "He will do for me" is a grateful and thankful person.
One who is destined for darkness is a doer of good first; one who is destined for light is a grateful and thankful person. [The Buddha] is the teacher.
The first doer, the one who practices, the one who is grateful and appreciative of what has been done. In the world with its devas, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is the first doer;

the noble disciple is the one who is grateful and appreciative of what has been done. However, in the Commentary on the Second Book (Dukanipāta-aṭṭhakathā), it says: "'The first doer' means one who performs a service first;
'the one who is grateful and appreciative of what has been done' means one who, having recognized what was done by that person, performs a service afterwards. Of these two, the first doer..."
"He creates the perception: 'I am giving a debt'; the debtor creates the perception: 'I shall repay the debt. This much only was said. 84.
In the description of "difficult to satisfy": "difficult to satisfy" means those who cannot be satisfied by anyone.
For one who lives depending on a family of supporters or a family of relatives, when his robes have worn out, he sets aside the robe given by them; he does not...
He consumes it. Even when given again and again, he merely sets it aside after taking it.
And another person, by that same method, gives away whatever he receives, bestowing it upon others; even when receiving again and again, he acts in exactly the same way.
These two types of persons cannot be satisfied even by one who provides requisites with carts; thus they are called "difficult to satisfy."
85. In the explanation of “easy to satisfy”: “does not relinquish” means that, having not made it for oneself, one does not give it to another.
But when there is an excess, one does not set it aside; rather, one gives it to another. This is what is meant:
a monk who, having obtained a cloth or a garment from a family of supporters or from a family of relatives, makes a robe out of it and uses it, does not set it aside.
Even when one puts on a robe after giving its border away, if it is given again, one does not hastily accept it.
Furthermore, he who consumes whatever he has obtained for himself and does not give to others—these two are called "easy to satisfy" because they can be satisfied with ease.
86. *Āsava* means defilements (*kilesa*). "He feels remorse where there is no need to feel remorse" means he feels remorse regarding that which is not fit to be felt as remorse.
He feels remorse. Having obtained pork, he feels remorse, thinking it is bear meat; having obtained deer meat, he feels remorse, thinking it is leopard meat.
While it is still within the proper time, he thinks, "It is not yet time"; without being invited, he thinks, "I have already been invited";
while no food has yet fallen into his bowl, he thinks, "It has fallen"; and while fish or meat has not yet been prepared specifically for him, he thinks, "Meat..."
"He feels remorse for what was done specifically for him": he does not feel remorse for that which ought to cause remorse—that is, he does not feel remorse for what is appropriate to cause remorse.
Having obtained the flesh of a deer, he does not feel remorse, thinking it is the flesh of a pig...
[and so on] ...regarding fish or meat prepared specifically for himself, he does not feel remorse, thinking, "This was prepared specifically for me. (From the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*)

However, it is stated only as follows: “‘It should not be regretted’ means that not setting aside or not investigating the use of the Saṅgha’s property is what is called ‘not to be regretted,’ yet he regrets that.
‘It should be regretted’ means the setting aside or investigation of that very same thing; yet he does not regret that.
Regarding the phrase “of these,” it refers to these two persons on a favorable ground (subhūmi).
Just as grass, creepers, and the like grow both by night and by day, so too do the taints increase.

In the bright fortnight, having obtained allowable meat and taking it as allowable meat, one should not feel remorse; "one does not feel remorse" is how the meaning should be understood according to this method.
