88. “Of inferior inclination” means one whose disposition is inferior. “Immoral” means devoid of virtue. “Of evil nature” means one whose nature is base. 89.
“Of noble inclination” means one whose disposition is noble. “Of beautiful nature” means one whose nature is auspicious, pure, and excellent.
90. “Satiated” means satisfied, fully contented. “One who satisfies others” means one who brings satisfaction to others as well—referring to those who are paccekabuddhas.

And regarding the phrase "and the disciples of the Tathāgata": here, the Paccekabuddhas are themselves satisfied and fulfilled by the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*), yet they are not able to satisfy others. For there is no realization (*abhisamaya*) through their discourse on the Dhamma.
However, through the discourse on the Dhamma of the disciples, there is realization for immeasurable gods and humans. Even so, because—
Furthermore, when they teach the Dhamma, they do not speak by making it their own words; they speak by making it the word of the Buddhas.
The assembly seated to listen also shows respect, thinking: "This bhikkhu does not speak of a Dhamma realized by himself;
he speaks of a Dhamma realized by the Buddhas. Thus, that respect belongs to the Buddhas alone.
Thus, in that case, only the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is truly the one who satisfies.
For just as when a king commands, "Give such-and-such to so-and-so," and people bring it and give it—even though they are the ones giving—it is nevertheless the king who is the donor there.
And those by whom it is received accept it thinking only, "The king has granted us this position; he has bestowed upon us power and wealth."
"Not by royal officers. This should be understood in exactly the same way. The remainder is everywhere of obvious meaning.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Pairs (Dukaniddesa). 3. Commentary on the Exposition of Triads (Tikaniddesa).
91. In the Exposition of the Triads: “Immoral” (dussīla) means devoid of virtue. “Of evil nature” (pāpadhamma) means of base character.

Alternatively, one is immoral through failure in virtue, and of evil nature through failure in view. One is immoral through the breach of bodily and verbal restraint, and of evil nature through the breach of the remaining restraints.
One is immoral due to impurity of application, and of evil nature due to impurity of intention. [This is] by way of being devoid of wholesome virtue.
"Immoral": one who possesses unwholesome conduct and is of evil nature. "Impure": one who is endowed with impure bodily actions and so forth.
"Of suspicious conduct": one whose conduct is such that it must be scrutinized by others due to suspicion.
That is, having seen some slight impropriety, one's conduct becomes subject to the suspicion of others, who think, "This must have been done by him," or [one is suspect] by one's own suspicion.
“Conduct that should be practiced” means conduct that is attended by apprehension.
For when he sees monks gathered together in places such as the daytime quarters and discussing something, he thinks, “These are deliberating together;
perhaps they are discussing whether my own actions have been discovered. In this way, his conduct becomes attended by apprehension.
"Of concealed conduct" means one who is possessed of evil deeds that ought to be concealed.
"A non-recluse claiming to be a recluse" means one who, while being a non-recluse, claims "I am a recluse" because of his resemblance to a recluse.
"One who does not lead the holy life claiming to lead the holy life" refers to those other than those who lead the holy life, who are well-robed, well-clad, and carry clean alms-bowls.

Seeing those who maintain their livelihood by wandering for alms in villages, towns, market towns, districts, and royal capitals, he himself practices in such a manner that he is as if giving the declaration, “I am a practitioner of the holy life” (*brahmacārī*).

Furthermore, when he says, “I am a monk,” and enters the Uposatha hall and other such places, he indeed possesses the declaration of being a practitioner of the holy life; likewise regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha...
Taking profit. "Putrid within" means having entered inside with a putrid action; or, because of being devoid of virtue, he is putrid within due to the absence of the essence of virtue.
"Lustful" means soaked by passion and so forth. "Born of filth" means one in whom the refuse of passion and so forth has arisen.
Alternatively, *kasambu* refers to turbid water containing putrid corpses. And in this teaching, one who is immoral is called such because of being loathsome.
It is like water mixed with the putridity of rotting corpses; therefore, because it has arisen like a foul mass of refuse, it is called "arisen as a foul mass" (*kasambujāta*).

Why does it not occur to him in this way? Because that foundation, by being established upon which one would be able to attain *arahantship*, has been shattered. For just as [it occurs to] a low-caste boy, "Such-and-such a noble youth..."
Even upon hearing, “He has been anointed to the kingship,” it does not occur to one who was not reborn into that family from which those who are reborn receive the consecration:
“When indeed shall I too attain such anointment like that noble youth?
In the same way, even upon hearing, “A certain monk named so-and-so has attained arahantship,” it does not occur to one who is immoral...
Because that virtue by which one established in it might attain arahantship is absent, the thought does not occur:
"When indeed shall I too, like that virtuous person, attain arahantship?
This is called such a person being "hopeless" due to the absence of hope for arahantship.
92. "It occurs to him thus"—why does it occur? Because of the stability of that foundation by means of which one would be able to attain Arahantship.

For just as when a well-born noble youth hears, "A certain noble youth named so-and-so has been consecrated to the kingdom," he immediately recognizes the family into which those who are reborn attain consecration; so too [does it occur to him].
Thus it occurs to him: ‘When indeed shall I too attain the consecration, just as that prince did?

In exactly the same way, when a virtuous person hears, “A certain monk named so-and-so has attained Arahantship,” because of the firmness of his standing upon that very virtue by which one must be established to attain Arahantship, [he thinks]: ‘When indeed shall I too, like that monk, attain Arahantship?’
"May I attain it"—thus he thinks. "This is called" means that a person of such a kind is called one who has expectations (*āsaṃso*).
For he expects and aspires for *arahantship*, thus he is one who has expectations.

"Whatever [aspiration] he had previously when not yet liberated" refers to whatever aspiration that person with exhausted taints had previously, before being liberated by the liberation of *arahantship*.
His hope was liberated; it was calmed. Therefore, it does not occur to him thus.

For just as when a consecrated nobleman hears that "such-and-such a noble youth has been consecrated to the kingship," because one king lacks the second royal consecration and the second white parasol, it does not occur to him: "When indeed shall I too, like that youth, receive the consecration?"

“...might attain it”; even so, when one hears that “a certain bhikkhu named so-and-so has attained arahantship,” because there is no second arahant [present], the thought does not occur: “When indeed shall I too, like that bhikkhu, attain arahantship?
This is called such a person “one whose longing has departed” (vigatāsā) because of the departure of the longing for arahantship.

94. In the exposition of the simile of the sick person (*gilānūpama-niddesa*): first, in order to show the simile by which they are called "those who are like the sick," the passage beginning with "three kinds of sick persons" is stated.
Therein, "suitable" (*sappāyāni*) means beneficial and conducive to growth. "Appropriate" (*patirūpaṃ*) means fitting.
"He does not recover from that affliction" indicates one who is afflicted by an incurable disease such as wind-fever (*vātāpamāra*) and the like.

"One who has reached the end" refers to one who is ill. By the phrase "he recovers from that affliction," minor ailments such as scabies, prickly heat, carbuncles, old age, and so forth are indicated.
By the phrase "obtaining suitable food, not failing to obtain it," [the text indicates] that through the nursing of those [afflictions], one becomes comfortable.
All those ailments have been mentioned. And here, a "suitable attendant" should be understood as one who possesses the qualities of a sick-nurse: wise, skillful, and diligent.
"An attendant is permitted" means it is permitted that "he should be provided by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. For in the case of that sick person, [one should attend] to oneself...

If the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is unable to support him according to the nature of things (dhammatā), they should authorize another bhikkhu and a novice, saying, "Let this bhikkhu and novice look after him," and give them to him.

As long as those two look after him, the entire burden for whatever is needed by both the sick man and the two attendants rests upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus alone. Other sick persons, too, should be attended to.
The other two types of the sick should also be attended to. For what reason?
Even one who has reached the end of his life, if not attended to, might harbor mental resentment, thinking, "If they had looked after me, I might have been comfortable;
but they do not look after me," and thereby be reborn in a state of deprivation. But for one who is being looked after, it occurs thus: "By the Saṅgha of bhikkhus..."
‘All that was to be done has been done; yet such is the ripening of my karma. Having established loving-kindness toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he is reborn in heaven.

However, as for one who, even when afflicted by a minor illness, recovers whether or not medicine is obtained—for him, the illness is naturally subsided even without medicine, though medicine may be administered.
It is pacified more quickly. Thereafter, he will be able either to master the word of the Buddha or to perform the duties of a recluse.
For this reason it is said that other sick persons as well should be attended to.
"He does not enter" means he does not penetrate. "The certainty regarding wholesome states" refers to the rightness among wholesome states.
Rightness (sammatta) is defined as the fixed course of the path (magganiyāma). By this, the person who is "one for whom the word is supreme" (padaparama) is described.

In the second section, the one who gains knowledge through a condensed summary (ugghaṭitaññū) is included—such as the Elder Nāḷaka in the Teaching—and also one who, having received instruction from Paccekabuddhas once during the interval between Buddhas, has realized the knowledge of Pacceka-bodhi.
By the third section, the person who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū) is described.
But one who is to be led must rely on that very person.
"The teaching of the Dhamma is permitted" means that eight times during a month, a discourse on the Dhamma is permitted.
"The Dhamma should be taught to others as well" means that the Dhamma should be explained to others too. For what reason? Because for one who is a mere master of words in this present existence—
Even for one who is unable to penetrate the Dhamma now, it will become a condition for the future. Furthermore,
whether one obtains a vision of the Tathāgata or not, and whether one obtains the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya or not,
if one realizes the Dhamma, then while not obtaining [the vision], one does not yet realize it, but upon obtaining it, one will realize it very quickly.

For this reason, the Dhamma should be taught to them. However, for the third type, it must indeed be taught again and again. Those who are body-witnesses, those who have attained vision, those liberated through faith, and those liberated by wisdom have already been discussed above.
98. Regarding "one who speaks dung" and so forth: "gone to an assembly" means standing in an assembly.

"Gone to a gathering" means standing in a village gathering. "Gone into the midst of kinsmen" means standing in the midst of heirs. "Gone into the midst of a guild" means standing in the midst of trade associations. "Gone into the midst of the royal court" means...
He stands in the midst of the royal court at a great place of adjudication. "Abhinīto" means brought forward for the purpose of questioning.
"Sakkhipuṭṭho" means questioned by making him a witness. "Ehambho purisa" is a form of address.

"Attahetu vā parahetu vā" means either for one's own sake or for another's sake, such as for the sake of one's hands, feet, and so forth, or for the sake of wealth. Regarding "āmisakiñcikkhahetu vā": here—

"Āmisa" means gain (lābha). "Kiñcikkha" means something trifling or insignificant. The meaning is: for the sake of even a very small bribe, such as a partridge, a piece of meat, a lump of ghee, a lump of butter, and so forth.
"He speaks a deliberate lie" means he is one who utters false speech with full awareness.
"This is called... means that such a person is called a "dung-speaker" (gūthabhāṇī) because his speech is like dung. Just as...
For indeed, what is called excrement is undesirable and unpleasing to the great multitude;
even so, the speech of this person is undesirable and unpleasing to gods and humans.
99. "This is called" means that such a person is called a "flower-speaker" because his speech resembles a flower.
Just as blossoming *vassikā* flowers or *adhimuttaka* flowers are desirable and pleasing to the great multitude, even so the speech of this person is desirable and pleasing to gods and humans. 100.
*Nela*: "Ela" is said to mean fault (*dosa*). That which has no *ela* is *nela*. The meaning is "faultless," as in the phrase "the white-canopied chariot with faultless parts."
It is like salt mentioned in this context. "Pleasant to the ear" means it is pleasant to the ears due to the sweetness of its phrasing;
it does not produce ear-ache, like the piercing of a needle. It is "endearing" because, through the sweetness of its meaning, it generates affection rather than irritation throughout the entire body.
It is "heart-reaching" because it enters the mind easily without encountering resistance.
*Porī* means "of the city" because it is full of qualities (*guṇa-paripuṇṇatāya*). It also means "refined" (*sukumārā*) like a woman raised in the city;
or it means "belonging to the city" (*purassa esā*), which is to say, the speech of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers are speakers of appropriate discourse.
They call a mere father "father," a mere mother "mother," and a mere brother "brother. Such speech belongs to many people.

"Beloved by many" means beloved by a great multitude of people. Precisely because of being beloved by many people, one is "agreeable to many" (*bahujanamanāpa*), meaning pleasing and a source of mental growth for a great multitude.
"This is called" means that a person of such a kind is called a "sweet-spoken person" (*madhubhāṇī*).
There is also a reading *mudubhāṇī*; in both cases, the meaning is "one whose speech is sweet. For just as what is called "the four sweets" is indeed sweet and refined;
In the same way, the speech of this person is sweet to gods and humans.
101. Regarding the similes of the mind as a sore, etc.: "He becomes resentful" (*abhisajjati*) means he clings. "He becomes agitated" (*kuppati*) means he becomes disturbed by way of anger.
"He becomes corrupt" (*byāpajjati*) means he abandons his natural state and becomes putrid. "He becomes stubborn" (*paṭitthīyati*) means he falls into a state of dullness and rigidity.
“Anger” (*kopa*) refers to weak anger. “Hatred” (*dosa*) refers to that which is stronger than the former due to its state of malice.

“Indignation” (*appaccaya*) refers to mental distress in the form of dissatisfaction. “A chronic sore” (*duṭṭhāruka*) refers to an old wound. “With a stick” (*kaṭṭhena*) means with the tip of a staff. “With a shard” (*kaṭhalāya*) means with a potsherd.
“It exudes matter” (*āsavaṃ deti*) means it flows repeatedly. For an old wound, by its very nature, exudes pus and blood.
"These three things flow naturally, but when struck, they flow even more. "In the same way," here is the application of the simile:

a person prone to anger is like a malignant sore; the natural oozing of that sore is like the natural outburst of anger in an irascible person, and their walking about while in such a state is like the walking about of one who is bloated with rage.

Just as the slightest touch with a stick or a pebble causes even more swelling, so too should the state of extreme inflation—thinking, "He speaks thus to one such as me"—be understood as being like hearing even a trifling word.
"This is called" means that a person of such a kind is called one whose mind is like a sore; the meaning is that his mind is similar to an old wound.
102. "In the thick darkness of the night's gloom" means in the dense darkness that makes one blind by obstructing the arising of eye-consciousness during the night.
"In the interval of lightning" means at the moment when lightning flashes. Here too, this is the application of the simile:
the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) is to be seen as like the man with sight; the defilements (*kilesa*) to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) are like the darkness.
The time of the arising of the knowledge of the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa) is like the flashing of a lightning bolt.
The seeing of forms all around by a man with sight during the interval between flashes of lightning is like the seeing of Nibbāna at the moment of the stream-entry path.

Again, the enveloping of darkness is like the defilements to be abandoned by the once-returning path (sakadāgāmi-magga). Again, the flashing of a lightning bolt is like the knowledge of the once-returning path.
Arising. Just as a sighted person sees forms all around during a flash of lightning, so too is the vision of Nibbāna at the moment of the once-return path.

Again, just as there is the shrouding of darkness, so are the defilements to be abandoned by the non-return path. Again, just as there is the movement of another flash of lightning, so is the arising of the knowledge of the non-return path.
It is like the sighted person seeing forms all around during that flash of lightning.
The vision of Nibbāna at the moment of the non-returner path should be understood as being like that. "This is called" means that such a person is called one whose mind is like lightning;
the meaning is that his mind resembles lightning because of its brief flash of illumination. 103.
Regarding the state of having a mind like a thunderbolt, this is the application of the simile: for the knowledge of the path to Arahatship is like a thunderbolt.
It should be seen as follows: the defilements to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship are like a cluster of gems or a cluster of stones.

Just as there is no state of non-penetration once a diamond has pierced through a cluster of gems or a cluster of stones, so too there is no state of non-abandonment for those defilements that have been cut off by the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. It is like the non-replenishment of a hole pierced and penetrated by a diamond.
The non-arising again of the defilements severed by the path of arahantship is to be understood.

"This is called" means that such a person is called one whose mind is like a thunderbolt; the meaning is that his mind is similar to a thunderbolt because of its capacity to strike at the very root of the defilements.
104. "In those such as the blind, such an eye does not exist" means that the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*), which is of such a kind and of such a nature, does not exist.
"One should make it flourish" means one should make it prosperous and increased. "Blameworthy and blameless" refers to that which is faulty and faultless.
"Inferior and superior" refers to the low and the sublime. "Dark and bright with their counterparts" refers to the dark and the bright themselves, because they mutually oppose one another.
They are called "having counterparts" by way of their opposites. Here is the summary:
that eye of wisdom by which one would know wholesome states as "wholesome states," unwholesome states as "unwholesome states," and likewise for those that are blameworthy and so forth;
furthermore, among the dark, bright, and those with counterparts, one knows dark states as "having bright counterparts."
One would know with the eye of wisdom that "bright states have dark counterparts"; yet such an eye does not exist for him.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining cases as well.
"This is called" refers to a person of such a kind who lacks both the eye of wisdom for gathering worldly enjoyments and the eye of wisdom for purifying the welfare of future lives.

And because of the absence [of the former], he is called "blind. The second is called "one-eyed" because of the presence of the eye of wisdom that gathers wealth pertaining to the present life, but because of the absence of the eye of wisdom that clarifies the welfare of future lives.
The third is called "two-eyed" because of the presence of both.

107. Regarding the phrase "teaching the Dhamma to those with downcast wisdom" and so forth: they teach the Dhamma by setting aside their own work, thinking, "A lay follower has come for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
They teach it having made it "good in the beginning"—that is, making it auspicious, blameless, and faultless at the outset.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Herein, "beginning" (ādi) refers to the preliminary establishment.
The "middle" is the midpoint of the discourse. The "conclusion" is the final resolution.
Thus, when teaching him the Dhamma, they speak so as to make it beautiful, auspicious, and blameless at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
Herein, there are beginnings, middles, and ends of a teaching, and there are those of the Dispensation. Regarding the teaching first, in the case of a four-line verse:
The first word is the beginning; two words are the middle; the final word is the conclusion. In the case of a sutta with a single sequence of meaning:
the introduction (*nidāna*) is the beginning; the sequence of meaning (*anusandhi*) is the middle; "Thus he spoke" (*idamavoca*) is the conclusion.

In the case of one with multiple sequences of meaning: the first sequence is the beginning; from that point on, whether there is one or several, they constitute the middle; the last is the conclusion.
This, first of all, is the method of the teaching.
Furthermore, regarding the Dispensation: virtue is the beginning, concentration is the middle, and insight is the end.
Or, concentration is the beginning, insight is the middle, and the path is the end. Or, insight is the beginning, the path is the middle, and the fruit is the end.

The Path is the beginning, the Fruit is the middle, and Nibbāna is the end. Or, when treated in pairs: virtue and concentration are the beginning; insight and the Path are the middle; and the Fruit and Nibbāna are the end.
"With meaning" means they teach having made it meaningful. "With phrasing" means they teach having fulfilled the phonemes. "Entirely complete" means completely whole.
They teach having made [the teaching] complete. They teach "pure" by making it pure, free from tangles, and free from knots.
"They proclaim the holy life" means that while teaching in this way, they proclaim the Noble Eightfold Path, which is the supreme conduct, comprised of the three trainings.
"He does not attend to the beginning" means he does not attend to the prior establishment.
He attends to it. "Kumbho" means a jar. "Nikkujjo" means placed face down. "Evameva" (in the same way):
here, a person whose wisdom is overturned should be understood as being like a jar placed face down. The time of pouring water is like the time when the teaching of the Dhamma is received.
The time of the water spilling out is like the time when one sitting on that seat is unable to grasp it.
The time when one has risen but does not perceive [the object] should be understood as being like the time when water has no fixed shape.
"This is called" means that a person of such a kind is called one of "overturned wisdom" (*avakujjapañña*); the meaning is "one whose wisdom is face-downward.

108. "Heaped up" (*ākiṇṇāni*) means placed down. "He would scatter through loss of mindfulness" means he would disperse them due to his state of forgetfulness (*muṭṭhassatitā*). "In the same way" means...
In this context, the person of "lap-like wisdom" (ucchaṅgapañña) is to be understood as being like a lap. The various kinds of food are like the diverse teachings of the Buddha.
The time spent sitting while eating the various foods from the lap is like the time spent learning while seated on that particular seat.
The time when the food is scattered due to a lapse of mindfulness upon rising is like [the forgetting] after leaving that seat.
The time when one who has risen and is walking does not perceive [the object] should be understood.
"This is called" means that such a person is called "one of shallow wisdom" (*ucchaṅga-pañña*). The meaning is that his wisdom is like the palm of the hand.
109. "Upright" (*ukkujja*) means placed facing upwards. "It stands firm" (*saṇṭhāti*) means it remains stable. "In the same way" (*evameva kho*)—here, [it refers to] facing upwards.
A person of broad wisdom should be regarded as being like a jar that has been set down.
The time when water is poured in is like the time when the teaching is received. The time when the water settles is like the time of grasping while seated there.
The time of rising and departing should be understood as being like the time of contemplation (*sallakkhaṇa*). "This is called" means one who is of such a nature.
A person is called "of wide wisdom" (*puthupañño*); the meaning is "one whose wisdom is extensive. 110.

Regarding those who are not free from lust and so forth: just as the stream-enterer and once-returner are, so too the worldling (*puthujjana*) is not free from lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure and for the three realms of existence.
However, he is not included [in this specific category] because of his lack of skill. For just as a skilled carpenter, for the sake of building materials...
When one has entered the forest, one does not cut down every tree encountered from the very beginning; rather, one cuts down only those that serve as materials for one's purpose.

In the same way here, it should be understood that the Blessed One has included only those noble ones (ariya) who are of the nature of "materials" (dabbajātika), whereas ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) are not included because they lack such a nature.
"Free from lust for sensual pleasures" means free from lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa).
"Untamed with regard to states of existence" means untamed with regard to the realms of form and formlessness.
Regarding the similes such as "like an inscription on stone": "it persists" means it persists because it has not been abandoned. "It does not quickly crumble" means it does not perish in the interim;
it perishes only at the end of an eon (*kappa*). "In the same way" means that the anger of that person is likewise.
He does not become extinguished on the next day or the day after; rather, he is long-lasting.

The meaning is that he is extinguished only by death. "This is called" means that such a person, because his state of anger persists for a long time like a mark on stone, is called "one comparable to a mark on stone."
114. "And his anger is indeed [transient]": this refers to the anger of one who becomes angry impulsively even over a trifling cause.

"Not long" means that because it has not been abandoned, it does not persist for long. Just as a line drawn on the earth with a plow is quickly effaced by the wind and other elements, so too the anger that arises impulsively in him is extinguished very quickly; such is the meaning. This...

"He is called such" means that this kind of person is called "one comparable to a line on the earth" because, due to his habit of angering others, he does not remain for long, just like a mark drawn upon the ground.
(115) "With excessive harshness" means with extremely rigid speech that cuts to the quick; "with roughness" means that which is not pleasant to the ear.
"Disagreeable" means not by way of mental pleasure. "Mingles" means becomes one. "Joins" means connects.
"Rejoices" means becomes continuous. Alternatively: "Mingles" means it attains a state of harmony with the mind in mental activities and so forth;
the meaning is that it reaches a state of oneness like milk and water. "Joins" means [it joins] in bodily activities such as standing and walking.
"He unites with him in body" means that he reaches a state of mingling like sesame seeds and rice grains.

"He greets him" means that in verbal activities such as recitation and questioning, he unites with him in speech; even when living apart, he reaches a state of greater affection, like a dear companion.
Furthermore, in matters of duty and service, from the very beginning he shares a single mode of action with them.

As he approaches, he converges; as he proceeds as far as the middle, he joins together; and as he continues without turning back until the very end, he remains in harmony—this also should be understood.
"This is called" means that such a person, because he quickly converges like a line drawn on water, is called "one comparable to a line on water."
116. Regarding the Simile of the Cloth: in order to show the simile by which these are called "the similes of the cloth," the passage beginning with "three kinds of cloth" was stated.
Therein, "new" means newly woven. "Cloth" (*potthaka*) refers to a garment made of hemp (*sāṇa*).
"Discolored" means faded in color. "Painful to the touch" means rough to the touch. "Inexpensive" means being worth very little, having a value of only a few *kahāpaṇa* coins.

It exists. "Of middle age" means it is in the middle stage of its use. For, having passed beyond its newness but not yet reached the state of being worn out, even while in the middle period of use, it becomes discolored, unpleasant to the touch, and indeed of little value.
While it was worth a great deal, it is now worth half that. But in its worn-out state, it is worth only a half-māsaka or a kākāṇikā. "Rubbing on the mortar" means...
The sweeping of the black mortar.
"New" means one who is below five years of full ordination; even if sixty years of age by birth, such a person is still considered "new.
"By way of ugliness" refers to being ugly both in terms of physical appearance and in terms of the quality of one's character. For when one of immoral conduct sits in the midst of an assembly...
Due to his lack of luster, even the color of his body does not flourish; as for the color of his virtues, there is nothing at all to be said.
"And those who [follow] him" refers to those who attend upon this person, whether they be his supporters or his relatives and friends.
For them—that is, for those people who follow these teachers—[it is like] for those who follow Devadatta while holding wrong views.
And like that of Kokālika and others, such association leads to harm and suffering for a long time.
"Intermediate" means from the time of five years until the time of nine years; one is called "elder" (*thera*) from the time of ten years onward.
"They say thus" means they speak in this way. "What indeed is yours?"—what is the use of what you, a fool, have to say?
"It has meaning" is what is meant. "Of such a kind" means of such a nature, of such a character—that which constitutes the grounds for a *ukkhepanīya-kamma* (an act of suspension).
117. Regarding the similes of the Kāsika cloth: "Kāsika cloth" refers to a fine cloth woven from spun thread using three strands of cotton;
when newly woven, it is priceless. Even twenty [such cloths] are of middling value for use.
It is worth thirty thousand when new, but at the time it is worn out, it is worth only eight or ten thousand.
"That belongs to them" means that for those who cultivate it—just as those who serve the Fully Enlightened One and others—that cultivation leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
Indeed, by relying on even a single Fully Enlightened One, beings have been liberated until the present day.

There is no measure [to them]. Likewise, there is no measure of the beings who have gone to heaven by relying on the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and the remaining eighty great disciples; even until this present day, there is likewise no measure of the beings who have followed their example.
"It reaches its full extent" means that the speech of that Great Elder is grounded in that meaning.

Just as a Kāsika cloth is treated with care—being placed and kept inside a perfumed casket—in the same way, [the Buddha] is treated with care, being placed and kept upon the head and the heart, which are the most excellent parts of the body. The rest here should be understood according to what was stated below.
118. Regarding *suppameyya* and so forth: he is easily measured, thus he is "easily measurable" (*suppameyya*). "Here" means in this world of beings. "Uddhata" means...
"Endowed with restlessness": "Unnaḷa" means one whose reed (naḷa) has risen up; the meaning is that he stands having tossed up an empty pride.
"Fickle" means endowed with fickleness through such things as adorning oneself with a bowl. "Garrulous" means rough-mouthed. "Loose-tongued" means one whose speech is unrestrained.
"Unconcentrated" means devoid of one-pointedness of mind. "With wandering mind" means one whose mind is wandering, resembling a wandering cow or a wandering deer.
“With manifest faculties” means with open faculties. “This one is called such” means that a person of this kind is called “easily measurable.
For just as the measure of a small amount of water is easily grasped, even so the measure of one endowed with these unwholesome factors is easily grasped.
Therefore, he is called “easily measurable.”

119. “Difficult to measure” (*duppameyya*) means that he is to be measured with difficulty. The qualities beginning with “unagitated” (*anuddhata*) are to be understood by way of their opposites to those previously mentioned.
“This one is called such” means that a person of this kind is called “difficult to measure.
For just as the measure of the great ocean is grasped with difficulty, even so is the measure of one endowed with these factors of virtue difficult to grasp.
He is grasped [in this way]: he comes to be called "one who is a non-returner" or "one whose taints are destroyed";
therefore, he is called "difficult to measure.

(120) He is "immeasurable" because it is not possible to measure him. For just as it is impossible to grasp the measure of space, so it is with one whose taints are destroyed; therefore, he is called "immeasurable."
121. Regarding "not to be cultivated," etc.: "not to be cultivated" means not to be approached.
"Not to be associated with" means not to be relied upon. "Not to be attended upon" means not to be waited upon repeatedly by sitting near him.

In the phrases "he is inferior in virtue," etc., inferiority should be understood in relation to each respective standard. For one who observes the five precepts is [inferior] to one who observes the ten precepts.

He should not be associated with. Furthermore, one who observes the ten precepts should not be associated with by one who is observing the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), except out of compassion and sympathy—that is, setting aside both compassion and sympathy.
Indeed, such a person should not be associated with for one’s own sake; however, on account of compassion and sympathy, one may [associate with him].
It is appropriate to approach him.
"He is similar" means he is equal. "Of those who have attained equality in virtue" means of those who have reached a state of commonality through virtue.
"And there will be a discussion on virtue for us" means that for us, who possess such common virtue, the discussion will concern virtue itself.
"There will be conversation; and that will be comfortable for us"—that discourse on virtue will be a state of ease and a state of happiness for us.
"And that will be continuous for us"—that discourse of ours will continue even as we speak throughout the day;
it will not be interrupted. For when there are two virtuous people, by one [speaking] of virtue...
When one person speaks on virtue, the other rejoices; thus their conversation is both comfortable and productive.
However, if even one among them is immoral, the discussion on virtue is ill-spoken; consequently, there is no talk of virtue, it is not comfortable, and it does not proceed.
The same principle applies to discussions on concentration and wisdom. For when two who have attained concentration engage in a discussion on concentration, [it is likewise successful].
And those possessed of wisdom, while discussing the discourse on wisdom, do not even notice when night or day has passed.
123. "Having honored and revered" means having performed both honor and respect. "He becomes superior" means he becomes preeminent.
"The aggregate of virtue" means the mass of virtue. "I shall fulfill it" means that, by relying on that person of preeminent virtue, [I shall fulfill it].
"I shall bring my own incomplete mass of virtue to completion; in each respective instance, I shall support it with wisdom.

Here, by avoiding those things unsuitable and unhelpful to virtue and cultivating those things suitable and helpful, one is said to support the aggregate of virtue with wisdom in each particular instance.
The same method applies to the aggregates of concentration and wisdom as well.
124. Regarding the terms "to be loathed" and so forth: "to be loathed" means it should be loathed like excrement. "Then indeed" (*atha kho nan ti*) means "then indeed for him.
"Fame-sound" (*kittisaddo*) means the sound of talk. "In the same way" (*evamevaṃ*): here, immorality (*dussīlyaṃ*) should be regarded as a cesspool of excrement;
a person of immoral character is like one standing in a cesspool of excrement with his veins visible. By one being pulled out from the cesspool of excrement...
Just as when a snake has climbed onto a person's body, even though it has not yet bitten,
the body serves as the cause for that action; so too, for one who associates with the immoral,
the time when the sound of their evil reputation spreads abroad should be understood as being like the moment the snake has gone away after having smeared the body with excrement.

125. *Tindukālātaṃ*: a firebrand from a *tinduka* tree. "It crackles even more" means that while burning, it naturally emits sparks and makes a crackling sound—*cicciṭāyati*, *ciṭiciṭā*—and when struck, it makes an even greater noise;
such is the meaning. "In just this way" means that one who is prone to anger is, by his very nature, agitated.
Having become fierce, he behaves [with anger]. But when even a trivial word is spoken, thinking, "He speaks thus to one like me," he becomes even more excessively arrogant and fierce in his behavior.
"A cesspool" means a pit full of excrement, or simply a heap of excrement.
The application of this simile should be understood in the same manner as before. Therefore, such a person should be looked upon with equanimity.

"He should not be associated with" means that because one who is prone to anger becomes angry even when excessively served or approached, and becomes angry even when one steps back thinking, "What is the use of this?", therefore he should be viewed with equanimity like a fire of chaff;
he should not be associated with. What is meant? For if one approaches a fire of chaff too closely and is burned, his body—
He meditates. For one who moves too far away and burns with heat, the cold does not subside.
However, for one who does not approach too closely nor move too far away, but burns with heat while maintaining a state of equanimity, the cold subsides and the body is not consumed by fire.
Therefore, a person prone to anger is like a fire of chaff; he should be regarded with equanimity and should not be associated with.
One should not associate with him, nor should one attend upon him.
126. A "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*) is a pure friend. A "good companion" (*kalyāṇasahāya*) is a pure companion. A "companion" (*sahāya*) is one who goes together and travels along with another.

One who is "devoted to what is good" (*kalyāṇasampavaṅka*) is one who is devoted to those who are good and pure persons; the meaning is that his mind is inclined toward them, leaning toward them, and tending toward them.
127. Regarding the passage beginning with "one who fulfills the precepts" (*sīlesu paripūrakārī*):

"One who fulfills the precepts" refers to those noble disciples who, by not transgressing the four great training rules of the precepts known as *pārājika*—which constitute the beginning of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) and are the primary elements of the holy life—and by [not transgressing] those minor and lesser offenses they may commit, [fulfill the precepts].
Because they fulfill and complete whatever is to be done regarding the precepts through their emergence [from meditation],
they are called "those who practice the fulfillment of the precepts. However, because sensual lust and ill will—

which are obstacles to concentration— and the delusion that conceals the truth— which is an obstacle to wisdom— have not been eradicated, even while they are developing concentration and wisdom, they remain deficient in those two.
They are called "those who act moderately" in concentration and wisdom because they perform only a small portion, merely by way of measure, of what ought to be done.
By this same method, the meaning should be understood in the other two systems as well.
In this regard, there is also this further method from the Sutta:
“Here, monks, a monk is one who fulfills the training rules of virtue, but is only partial in his practice of concentration and partial in his practice of wisdom.
He commits those minor and lesser training rules and then emerges from them. Why is that?
Because, monks, I have not declared this to be a state of incapacity. As for those training rules...”
These are the practices fundamental to the holy life, appropriate to the holy life; therein he is firm in virtue and established in virtue, training himself by undertaking the rules of training.

With the complete destruction of three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, here a monk [is established] in the virtues... (as above)... [and so on].
With the total destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner;

having come back to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering. Furthermore, monks, here a monk is one who fulfills his duties regarding virtue, who fulfills his duties regarding concentration, and who practices wisdom to a moderate degree. He trains himself in those training rules... [as before] ...in the precepts of training.
Thus, with the five lower fetters... [he is] of a nature not to return from that world.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu is one who fulfills the precepts, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom.
He trains in those training rules, both the minor and the lesser ones... [he trains]. Through the destruction of the taints... [he] enters and dwells in... [the state of arahantship]."
130. In the exposition of the Teacher (*satthāra-niddesa*): "He proclaims full understanding" means he proclaims abandonment and transcendence.

"Therein" refers to among those three types of persons. "By that he is to be seen" means by that proclamation it is to be understood that this teacher is an attainer of the fine-material-sphere attainments (*rūpāvacara-samāpatti*).
The same method applies to the second section as well. "The Teacher is the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*); by that he is to be seen."
By virtue of this unique mode of teaching not shared with the *titthiyas*, this third Teacher, the Omniscient Buddha, is to be regarded as such.

For when the *titthiyas* teach the full understanding (*pariññā*) of sensual desires, they speak of existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*). When they teach the full understanding of material forms, they speak of existence in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*).
When they teach the full understanding of feelings, they speak of existence in the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*). Rightly...
While those who teach might propose it thus, they are not able to teach it correctly.

The Perfectly Enlightened One, however, teaches the full understanding and abandonment of sensual pleasures by means of the non-returning path; he teaches the full understanding and abandonment of form and feeling by means of the path of arhatship.
Regarding these three teachers: these two individuals are outsiders, and one is the Perfectly Enlightened One.
“In this world there are three kinds of teachers.
131. In the second section on the description of teachers: “In this very life (diṭṭhe dhamme)” means in this present personal existence.
“He describes the self as real and substantial” means he describes it as truly existing and stable, saying: “There is indeed a self, which is permanent, stable, and eternal.”

"And in the future life" means that he describes it as being exactly like this in another individual existence (*attabhāva*). The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of Threes. 4. Commentary on the Exposition of Fours.

132. In the Exposition of the Tetrads: An "untrue person" (asappurisa) is a base person. One who destroys living beings is a "destroyer of life" (pāṇātipātī). One who takes what is not given is a "taker of what is not given" (adinnādāyī).
One who engages in misconduct regarding sensual pleasures is a "misconducter in sensual pleasures" (kāmesumicchācārī). One who speaks falsely is a "speaker of falsehood" (musāvādī).
One who stands in the intoxication of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants is a "stander in the intoxication of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants" (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāyī).
133. “One incites another to the taking of life” means that one causes another to seize a living being in such a way that they actually take its life.

The same method applies to the remaining [offenses] as well. “This is called” means that because such a person is an heir to half of the immorality—both that which they have committed themselves and that which has been committed by the one they incited—they are therefore called an “unvirtuous person.”
He is called "one more base than a base person. A "true person" (*sappurisa*) is a supreme person (*uttamapurisa*). 135.

Because he is endowed with the excellent virtue (*susīlya*) performed by himself, and because he performs that which he is exhorted to do by a true person, he is "one more true than a true person" due to being an heir to half of that [virtue] from the supreme person; thus he is "one more supreme than a supreme person. 136.
"Evil" (*pāpa*) means one who is possessed of the tenfold evil consisting of the unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*).

138. *Kalyāṇo* means one who is endowed with the tenfold wholesome qualities known as the paths of wholesome action; he is pure and auspicious. The rest here is clear in meaning, as it follows the method already explained below.

140. Regarding *pāpadhamma* and so forth: one whose nature (*dhamma*) is evil is an "evil-natured" person (*pāpadhamma*). One whose nature is beautiful is a "beautiful-natured" person (*kalyāṇadhamma*).

The rest here is clear in meaning. 144. Regarding *sāvajja* and so forth: *sāvajja* means "with fault. By "faulty bodily action" is meant by a faulty action such as killing living beings and so forth.
By bodily action. The same method applies to the others as well.

"This is called" means that such a person, because their accumulated karma through the three doors is accompanied by fault, is called "blameworthy," like a place filled with excrement, corpses, and the like. 145.
"Abounding in the blameworthy" means that for such a person, blameworthy bodily action is abundant, while blameless action is slight.
He is said to be one who is frequently possessed of blameworthy bodily action and seldom of blameless bodily action;

the same applies to the other [types of action] as well. But who is such a person? One who, due to the customs of the village or the customs of the town, occasionally and at certain times undertakes the Uposatha and fulfills the precepts—such a person is called this.
Because among the kamma accumulated through the three doors, there is a great abundance of the blameworthy and a paucity of the blameless,
he is called "one who abounds in faults. Just as if, in one place, there were heaps of unsightly and foul-smelling flowers,
and upon them here and there were scattered *atimuttaka*, *vassika*, and *pāṭalā* blossoms— such is this person to be understood.
Just as if, in one place, there were heaps of *atimuttaka*, *vassika*, and *pāṭala* flowers, and upon them, here and there,
had fallen unsightly and foul-smelling *badara* blossoms and the like— such a person is to be understood as the third type. But the fourth,
because his accumulated karma through all three doors is free from fault, is like a golden bowl filled with the four sweets.

[The four types of persons] should be viewed as follows. Among them, the first is the blind, foolish worldling (*andhabāla-puthujjana*). The second is the worldly worldling who occasionally performs wholesome deeds.
The third includes the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*), and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
The fourth is the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), for he is exclusively blameless. This is according to the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*.
148. Regarding those who are "knowers by a condensed statement" (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth: here, "condensed statement" (*ugghaṭita*) means the opening up of knowledge;
the meaning is that one knows at the very moment knowledge is opened up. "At the time of being uttered" (*udāhaṭavelāya*) means at the very moment it is uttered during the recitation.
"Realization of the Dhamma" (*dhammābhisamaya*) is the realization through knowledge of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "This is called" (*ayaṃ vuccati*) refers to this [person].

When the summary matrix (*mātikā*) is established by way of the method beginning with “the four foundations of mindfulness,” a person capable of attaining *arahantship* by directing their knowledge according to the sequence of the teaching is called one who gains knowledge through what is condensed (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

One who knows the meaning only when it is explained in detail and expanded upon is called one who gains knowledge through what is expanded (*vipañcitaññū*). This is what is meant by “this [person] is called... (*ayaṃ vuccati*).

A person capable of attaining *arahantship* when the meaning is explained in detail after a brief summary of the matrix (*mātikā*) has been established is called one who "knows by expansion" (*vipañcitaññū*). 150.

One who is to be led by means of summaries and so forth is called "one who is to be guided" (*neyya*). "Gradual realization of the Dhamma" (*anupubbena dhammābhisamayo*) means the attainment of *arahantship* through successive stages.

151. One for whom the mere letter of the words is supreme is a "word-adept" (*padaparamo*). "There is no realization of the Dhamma through that birth" means that one is not able, by means of that personal existence, to produce either jhāna, insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), or the fruit (*phala*).
152. Regarding "possessed of appropriate eloquence" (*yuttapaṭibhāno*) and so forth: "eloquence" (*paṭibhāna*) refers both to knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and to the speech established upon that knowledge.
It is this latter sense that is intended here. One who possesses eloquence that is appropriate to the meaning and appropriate to the reason is "one possessed of appropriate eloquence."
Because he is unable to answer quickly immediately after being questioned, his ready wit (*paṭibhāna*) is not liberated; thus he is one whose ready wit is "not liberated" (*no-mutta-paṭibhāna*).
The others are to be understood in this same manner. Herein, the first type—after investigating for a short time, perceives only what is appropriate, like the Elder Cūḷanāga of the Three Piṭakas.
It is said that when questioned on a problem, he examines it thoroughly and speaks only with well-reasoned and well-applied arguments.

The second type—immediately after being questioned, deflects with whatever word or phrase available; and even after investigating, he does not perceive what is appropriate, like the Venerable Tissa, the Elder Paṇḍita of the Four Nikāyas.
It is said that when asked a question, he does not even reach the conclusion of the answer, but simply says whatever comes to mind.
Furthermore, when his words are investigated for their meaning, they do not hold together anywhere.

The third [type] is like the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya, who perceives the appropriate answer at the very moment of being questioned and provides the reply at that same instant. It is said that when asked a question, he speaks with great speed and his reasoning is both relevant and well-connected.
The fourth [type] is like the Elder Lāḷudāyi, who, when questioned, neither perceives the appropriate answer nor is able to deflect it in any way; he is as if submerged in thick darkness.
156. Regarding those who discourse on the Dhamma: "He speaks little" means he says only a small amount to an assembled assembly.
"And what he says is unconnected" means that while speaking, he does not speak what is consistent with the meaning or consistent with the reason.
"And his assembly is not skilled" means that the assembly seated there to listen does not know what is appropriate or inappropriate, what is reasoned or unreasoned, or what is coherent or incoherent.

The meaning is as follows: "Of such a kind" refers to one who is of this nature, a preacher of the Dhamma for fools; he receives the designation "preacher of the Dhamma" precisely because he belongs to a following of fools of such a kind.
In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. Furthermore, in this context, there are only two types of people who are preachers of the Dhamma by nature;
the others, however, are so described because they have entered among the ranks of the preachers of the Dhamma.
157. In the Simile of the Clouds, "clouds" refers to rain-clouds. "Thundering" refers to rumbling. In this context, to thunder without raining is considered a misfortune.
For when people hear the god thundering, they think, "There will be good rain," and they bring forth their seeds and sow them.
But if it does not rain, the seeds perish right there in the field, and the seeds [meant] for the house perish right there in the house.
"They perish" means there is a famine. Even the state of thundering without raining is evil.
For people, thinking, "In this season there will be drought," sow their seeds only in low-lying places.
Then, when the rain falls, it carries all the seeds out to the great ocean, and there is indeed a famine. But as for the state of thundering and raining...
It is auspicious. For at that time there is an abundance of food. However, the state of thundering without raining is exclusively evil. There is one who speaks but does not act;

he merely says, "Now I shall fulfill the duty of study (ganthadhura), I shall fulfill the duty of meditation (vāsadhura)," yet he neither takes up the recitation nor develops the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
There is one who acts but does not speak; he does not say, "I shall fulfill either the duty of study or the duty of meditation. When [the opportunity] has arrived...
But at the proper time, he fulfills that purpose. In this same manner, the others are also to be understood. All of this, however, was spoken by the donor of the requisites.
For one person invites the Saṅgha, thinking, “On such-and-such a day I will give a gift,” but when the time arrives, he does not do it.
This person falls away from merit, and the community of monks also falls away from gain. Another...
If one honors [the Sangha] without first inviting it, thinking, "I shall bring the bhikkhus," one does not succeed;
for all have already been invited elsewhere. This person also declines in merit, and the Sangha likewise declines from that gain.
Another, however, first invites the Sangha and subsequently offers gifts after performing honors; this person is one who fulfills his duty.
Another neither invites the Saṅgha nor gives alms; this person should be known as a "wicked person.
158. Regarding the similes of the mouse: "One who makes a lair but does not dwell" means that one digs a burrow, a hole, or a pit for one's own dwelling, yet does not live there;
instead, one dwells in some other place and thus falls under the power of enemies such as cats. "One who guards" (khattā) also...
The reading is as follows: "Thinking, 'We shall dwell having made a secure footing,' one does not dig oneself, but dwells in a hole dug by another;
thus one protects one's life. The third [type] does both and protects his life.
The fourth does neither and falls under the power of his enemies. Now, among the persons illustrated by this simile, the first is like that mouse.
He digs deep; in this way, he masters the ninefold teaching of the Teacher. However, just as that [woman] does not dwell there but, living in some other place, falls under the power of her enemies;
so too, this person, having directed his knowledge through the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), does not penetrate the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
Wandering only among places of worldly bait, he [falls under the power] of those known as Māra the Death, Māra the Defilements (*kilesa-māra*), and Māra the Son of a Deva (*devaputta-māra*).
He falls under the power of his enemies. The second is like that mouse which does not dig a secure burrow;

likewise, he does not master the ninefold teaching of the Master. But just as one living in a hole dug by another protects its life, so too, having heard the word of another and having penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, he transcends the power of the three Māras.
In this same manner, the correlation of the similes for the third and fourth [similes] should also be understood.

159. Regarding the similes of the mangoes: "The unripe one has the appearance of the ripe" means it is unripe within but resembles the ripe on the outside. "The ripe one has the appearance of the unripe" means it is ripe within but resembles the unripe on the outside.
This same principle applies to the other two as well. In that regard, just as with the mangoes, the state of being unripe...
It is raw; likewise, for a person, the state of being a worldling (*puthujjana*) is "rawness," while the state of being noble (*ariya*) is "cookedness.

And just as in that case "cookedness" was described by way of its similarity to what is cooked, so too for a person, the similarity of the Noble Ones to the act of stepping forward and so forth is described by way of "cookedness.
In this manner, the correlation of the similes with the persons illustrated by them should be understood.
160. Regarding the Simile of the Jar (*kumbhūpama*): "Jar" means a pot. "Empty" means hollow within.
"Covered" means placed after being closed. "Full" means filled within. "Open" means placed after being uncovered.

Among the persons illustrated here, one should understand that the person who is devoid of the essence of virtue within is empty, and who is covered by outward splendor is the "covered" person. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

161. Regarding the similes of the water pond: first, when there is even knee-deep water in a water pond, because the water is either mixed with fifteen colors or is thick, the bottom is not visible; this is called "shallow but appearing deep.
However, when there is water three or four fathoms deep, because the water is clear, the bottom is visible; this is "deep but appearing shallow."
There is [a type] so named. However, the other two should be understood from the presence of both causes.

A person who, due to the prevalence of defilements and the absence of profound qualities, possesses such things as "progress" that resemble those of the profoundly virtuous, is called "shallow yet appearing deep.
In this same manner, the remaining types should also be understood.

162. Regarding the Simile of the Bulls: First, as for the bull that agitates and terrifies its own herd of cows, yet is mild and gentle toward another's herd—this is called "fierce toward its own cows, but not fierce toward others.
Likewise, a person who agitates, strikes, and treats his own assembly with harshness, but shows gentleness toward another's assembly—[is likewise so described].
One who adopts a humble manner of living is called "fierce toward his own cattle" but not "fierce toward the cattle of others.

By this same method, the remaining cases should also be understood. In the section on the exposition (*niddesa*), however, the phrase "he becomes agitated" (*ubbejitā hoti*) means that by striking and piercing [others], he causes them to reach a state of agitation. 163.
Regarding the Simile of the Venomous Snake (*āsīvisūpama*): First, a venomous snake is one whose venom comes quickly (*āsuṃ*), spreads rapidly, and is terrible (*ghoraṃ*).
However, it does not persist and does not afflict for a long time—this is one whose venom has arrived but is not fierce.
The same principle applies to the remaining phrases as well. As for the classification of persons (*puggalavibhājana*), its meaning is self-evident.

Regarding the passage beginning with "one who speaks praise of one who deserves dispraise without having investigated or scrutinized": *ananuvicca* means without having weighed or without having grasped [the truth]. *Apariyogāhetvā* means without having delved into the virtues by means of wisdom (*paññā*).
166. "True" means it is *bhūta* because it exists, and *taccha* because it is non-erroneous.
"At the right time" means at the appropriate and suitable time. Regarding this, "he is one who knows the right time" refers to what was stated as "at the right time.

In that regard, for the sake of answering a question from a person who knows the right time—one who understands the proper occasion—one [should consider]: "Even if asked at this time, I should not speak;..."
“This is the time to speak”—this is what is meant by “speaking at the right time. “He dwells in equanimity” means he dwells established in a state of equanimity that is characterized by neutrality.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout. Regarding the phrases beginning with “one who lives on the fruit of exertion”:
one who spends the day solely in the energy of exertion and [lives on] merely its incidental fruit...
Having obtained some means of livelihood, one maintains one's life; yet, by relying on that exertion (*uṭṭhāna*), one does not obtain any fruit of merit.
It is with reference to such a person that it was said, "for the individual who exerts," and so forth.
Beyond that, "the gods" refers to the gods of the Brahma-world and above. For them, there is indeed no need for exertion or effort; they possess only the fruit of merit.

They subsist [on these]. And the phrase "of one who possesses merit" (puññavato) is said with reference to those possessing merit—namely, kṣatriyas, brahmins, and so forth, as well as the deities beginning from the Earth-deities up to the Nimmānarati gods.
All of these experience both the fruit of effort and the fruit of merit. However, those in hell are not able to produce a livelihood through exertion.
Nor does any livelihood arise for them through the fruit of merit.
Regarding these [terms]: he is "dark" (*tamo*) because he is possessed of darkness such as that expressed by the phrase "reborn in a low family.

He is "one whose destination is darkness" (*tamaparāyaṇo*) because, due to bodily misconduct and so forth, he goes again to the darkness of hell. "In a hunter's family" means in the family of deer-trappers and the like. "In a bamboo-worker's family" means...
In a family of basket-makers; "in a family of chariot-makers" means in a family of leather-workers. "In a family of scavengers" means in a family of those who throw away flowers.
"Of difficult livelihood" means of painful livelihood. "Ugly" means having the color of a burnt stump, like a dust-demon.
"Unpleasant to look upon" means even to one's own mother who gave birth to him, he is disagreeable to behold. "A cripple" means a hunchback. "One-eyed" means blind in one eye or blind in both eyes.
Or: *kuṇī* means one who has a withered hand in one arm or both arms; *khañja* means one who is lame in one leg or both legs;

*pakkhahata* means one whose wings are destroyed, that is, a cripple who crawls on a bench. Regarding *padīpeyyassa*: this refers to the equipment for lighting a lamp, such as an oil vessel and so forth.
Thus, regarding the statement "a person is dark and has darkness as his destination": here, one person, having seen no light externally, [remains] right there within the mother's womb...
Having passed away and being reborn in the states of misery (*apāya*), one wanders through the entire aeon (*kappa*). That person, too, is one who goes from darkness to darkness.
Indeed, such a rebirth occurs for a deceitful person (*kuhakapuggala*); for it is said that such an arising happens to the deceiver.

And here, by the phrases "reborn in a low family" or "in a family of outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) and so forth," both the failure of the destination (*āgamanavipatti*) and the failure of previously arisen conditions (*pubbuppannapaccayavipatti*) are indicated.

And [these] have been shown. By the terms "poverty" (*dalidda*) and so forth, the failure of the conditions for existence (*pavatti-paccaya-vipatti*) is indicated. By "a life of hardship" (*kasira-vutti*) and so forth, the failure of the means of livelihood (*ājīva-upāya-vipatti*) is indicated.

By "ugly" (*dubbaṇṇa*) and so forth, the failure of physical form (*rūpa-vipatti*) is indicated. By "afflicted by many diseases" (*bahv-ābādha*) and so forth, the conjunction with causes of suffering (*dukkha-kāraṇa-samāyoga*) is indicated.

By "not obtaining" (*na lābhī*) and so forth, both the failure of the causes of happiness (*sukha-kāraṇa-vipatti*) and the failure of enjoyment (*upabhoga-vipatti*) are indicated. By "misconduct of body" (*kāyena duccarita*) and so forth, the state of having the lower realms as one's destination (*tama-parāyaṇa-bhāva*) is indicated.

The conjunction of causes. By the phrases beginning with "with the breakup of the body," the attainment of light in the future life is indicated. The bright side (the wholesome) is to be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.
Furthermore, in this context, one is called "one who possesses light" (*joti*) because one is endowed with the manifestation of light such as rebirth in a noble family;

thus, it is said that one has become like light. Moreover, one is "destined for light" (*jotiparāyaṇa*) because, through bodily good conduct and so forth, one attains the state of light consisting in rebirth in the heavenly realms.
Regarding the phrase "in a great khattiya clan," and so forth: "great khattiyas" (*khattiyamahāsālā*) refers to khattiyas who possess great wealth (*mahāsāra*), having attained great riches.

For those khattiyas who have, at the very least, a hundred million stored as a hoard, and for whom three jars of *kahāpaṇa* coins are kept in the middle of the house set aside for daily use—these are called "great khattiyas. Of those...
Those Brahmins who had eighty koṭis of wealth deposited, and who kept one and a half jars of kahāpaṇas heaped in the middle of their houses for the purpose of daily expenditure,
were called *brāhmaṇamahāsālā*. Those householders who had forty koṭis of wealth deposited,
and who kept one jar of kahāpaṇas heaped in the middle of their houses for the purpose of daily expenditure...
They are established [as such], and thus they are called "wealthy householders" (*gahapati-mahāsāla*). The meaning is: "in their families. "Wealthy" (*aḍḍha*) means powerful.

"Of great wealth" (*mahaddhana*) is because of the vastness of the treasure stored away. "Of great possessions" (*mahābhoga*) is because of the vastness of articles for enjoyment, such as vessels of gold and silver.
"Of abundant gold and silver" (*pahūta-jātarūpa-rajata*) is because of the abundance of coined and uncoined gold and silver. [And] of the equipment of property...

“Possessing abundant wealth and requisites” means having a great abundance of things that cause satisfaction. “Possessing abundant wealth and grain” means having an abundance of cattle, wealth, and the seven kinds of grain.
“Handsome” (*abhirūpa*) means beautiful in form. “Pleasant to behold” (*dassanīya*) means worthy of being looked upon even for an entire day, setting aside other tasks.
“Charming” (*pāsādika*) means bringing clarity to the mind by the mere sight of him. “Supreme” (*paramāya*) means most excellent.
"By beauty of complexion" means by the quality of the lotus-like color. "Lotus" (pokkhara) refers to the body; the meaning is: by the excellence of its color.
"Endowed with" (samannāgata) means possessed of.
Regarding "bent-over-bent" (oṇatoṇata) and so forth: one who is bereft of success pertaining either to the present life or to the future life is "bent-over" (oṇata).
"Low" (*nīca*) means inferior; its opposite is "high" (*uṇṇata*), meaning elevated or lofty.

The rest here should be understood according to the method already explained regarding "that" (*taṃ*) and so forth. Furthermore: "Bent down and bent down" means low now and will remain low in the future.
"Bent down and raised up" means low now but will become high in the future. "Raised up and bent down" means high now [but will become low in the future].
"He will become low. "High and high" means: being high now, he will also be high in the future.
170. Regarding the Simile of the Tree: "A tree surrounded by softwood and heartwood" refers to a preeminent forest tree that is itself softwood while its surrounding trees are of heartwood.
The remaining cases should be understood according to this method. As for individuals:

The state of being "sapwood" (pheggutā) is to be understood as being devoid of the essence of virtue (*sīla*), while the state of being "heartwood" (*sāratā*) is to be understood through the possession of virtuous conduct (*sīlācāra*). 171.
Regarding "measure by form" (*rūpappamāṇa*) and so forth: one who makes form endowed with excellence his standard is "one whose measure is form" (*rūpappamāṇa*).

One who generates confidence therein is "one who has confidence in form" (*rūpappasanna*). One who makes fame and reputation, which are of the nature of sound, his standard is "one whose measure is sound" (*ghosappamāṇa*).
Regarding the terms *āroha*, etc.: *āroha* refers to height. *Pariṇāha* refers to the perfection of circumference, free from being either too thin or too thick.
*Saṇṭhāna* refers to the state of the limbs and sub-limbs being appropriately long, short, round, and so forth, in their respective places.
*Pāripūrī* refers to the absence of deficiency in the aforementioned qualities, or the state of being complete in its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*). *Paravaṇṇanāya* means by others.
"By means of a description of qualities uttered in one's absence" means by a description of qualities spoken when not face-to-face.

"By means of praise by others" means by praise expressed through the composition of verses and so forth by way of eulogy by others. "By means of praise from others" means by praise spoken by others in their presence.
"By means of the taking away of another's praise" means by the appropriation of praise set in motion by others through a succession of eulogies.
172. *Cīvaralūkha* means the coarseness of the robe due to its being discolored and so forth. *Pattalūkha* means the coarseness of the bowl by way of its color, shape, and material.
*Senāsanalūkha* means the coarseness of the lodging due to its lack of such amenities as theatrical performances and the like.
*Vividha* means manifold, consisting of various modes such as being naked (*acelaka*) and so forth. *Dukkarakārika* means the mortification of the body.

Another method: Among these four types of persons, one who has gained confidence by taking the physical form (*rūpa*) as the measure is called "one for whom the form is the measure" (*rūpappamāṇa*). "One who is confident in the form" (*rūpappasanna*) is a synonym for that same person.
One who has gained confidence by taking the sound (*ghosa*) as the measure is called "one for whom the sound is the measure" (*ghosappamāṇa*).

One who has gained confidence by taking the coarseness of the robe and the bowl as the measure is called "one for whom the coarse is the measure" (*lūkhappamāṇa*). [One who has gained confidence] by taking the Dhamma as the measure...
Having grasped [the teaching], one who is confident is called "one for whom the Dhamma is the measure. The others are merely explanatory statements regarding those very points.
Furthermore, having divided all sentient beings into three parts, two parts are measured by form (*rūpappamāṇa*), and one part is not measured by form.
Having divided them into five parts, four parts are measured by sound (*ghosappamāṇa*), and one part is not measured by sound. Having divided them into ten parts, nine...

The sections are of the measure of the coarse; one is not of the measure of the coarse. However, having divided [them] into a hundred thousand sections, only one section is of the measure of the Dhamma, while the rest are not of the measure of the Dhamma. Thus, this world-habitation is of four measures.
In this world-habitation of four measures, those who lack faith in the Buddhas are few and dull-witted, whereas those who have faith are many. Regarding the measure of form...
For indeed, there is no form more inspiring of confidence than the form of a Buddha.
There is no sound more inspiring of confidence than the sound of the fame of the Buddhas, which is as vast as the sky.

Having renounced even the most luxurious Kāsī garments, costly golden vessels, and magnificent palaces suited to the three seasons and endowed with every excellence, he instead makes use of rag-robes, stone bowls, and dwellings at the foot of trees.
There is no other austerity superior to that of the Buddha, the Blessed One, which brings about such confidence.

In this world with its devas, for the Tathāgata—who possesses the measure of the Dhamma and the extraordinary qualities of virtue and so forth—there is no other quality of virtue and so forth superior to his own that brings about such confidence.
Thus, the Blessed One [grasped] this fourfold world-dwelling with his fist...
"He stands as if having grasped [them]. 173.
Regarding those who have "entered upon practice for their own welfare" and so forth: "Endowed with virtue" means endowed or possessed of virtue.
The same method applies to "endowed with concentration" and the rest. And herein, both mundane and supramundane virtue is spoken of; likewise for concentration and wisdom. So too for liberation.
It is precisely the liberation of the fruit of arahantship. Knowledge and vision consists of nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).

Regarding the phrases "not another," and so forth: when one tells another person, "It is fitting for you too to be endowed with virtue," one does not exhort them to undertake virtue, nor cause them to take it up.
This same method applies everywhere. Among these four, however, the first—
One is like the Elder Vakkali; the second is like Upananda the Śākyaputra; the third is like the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna;
the fourth is to be understood as being like Devadatta. 174.
Regarding those who "torment themselves" (attantapa) and so forth: one who torments or causes suffering to oneself is an "atmātāpin. [This refers to] the practice of self-mortification...
The practice of self-mortification. "A naked ascetic" (*acelaka*) means one who is without clothes, one who is nude. "One of loose conduct" (*muttācāra*) means one whose behavior is unrestrained.
Devoid of the conduct expected of a worldly gentleman regarding the disposal of excrement and so forth, he voids excrement, urinates, eats, and consumes food while standing.
"One who licks his hands" (*hatthāpalekhana*) means that when the alms-food in his hand is finished, he licks his hand with his tongue.
This shows that having passed excrement, he scrapes it away with his hand while perceiving it as a stick (*daṇḍaka*).
It is said that they designate a stick as a "living being" (*satta*); therefore, fulfilling their practice, he acts in this way.
One who, when addressed with "Come, venerable sir" for the purpose of receiving alms, does not come, is a *na-ehi-bhadantika*. Consequently, [when addressed] with "Stay, venerable sir,"...
"Even when told, he does not stay"—thus he is called *natiṭṭhabhaddantika*.
For both of these, the sectarians do not act upon his word, thinking, "His word will be carried out. *Abhihaṭaṃ* means almsfood brought and received beforehand.
*Uddissakataṃ* means almsfood announced in this way: "This was prepared specifically for you. *Na nimantanaṃ* means [not accepting an invitation to] a specific family.
"or enter a street or a village"—even when invited in this manner, he does not consent to the alms-food, nor does he accept it.
"Not from the mouth of a pot": he does not accept alms-food that is being given after having been taken out from a pot (*kumbhi*).

"Not from the mouth of a vessel" (*kaḷopimukhā*): *kaḷopī* means a cooking pot (*ukkhalī*) or a basket (*pacchī*); he does not accept it even from there. Why? Because pots and vessels [are associated with] a ladle...
"He receives a blow" means: he does not accept food being given with a threshold placed between [himself and the giver].
Why? [He thinks: "Because of me, this person gains the status of having an intermediary. The same principle applies to sticks and pestles as well. "Of two" means:
when two people are eating and one stands up to give [food], he does not accept it. Why? Because it would cause an obstruction to his mouthful (*kabaḷantarāyo*).
Regarding the passage beginning with “not for a pregnant woman,” etc.: for a pregnant woman, the child in her womb suffers; for a nursing woman, there is an obstruction to the child’s milk;
for a woman who has gone over to another man, there is an obstruction to sexual pleasure—thus [the Buddha] did not accept [food from such women].
