“In collected alms” means in food prepared by collecting [offerings). It is said that during a time of famine, disciples of the Acelakas, for the sake of the Acelakas, [prepared food...].
Having had rice and other grains collected from here and there, they cook a meal; however, the strict naked ascetic does not accept it from there.

Nor does he take what has been brought from a place where a dog is waiting, thinking, "I shall receive an alms-offering," for he does not accept it if it is given without first giving to that dog. Why? Because this would be an obstacle to the dog’s alms.

"Moving in swarms" means moving in groups within groups. For if, upon seeing a naked ascetic, people enter a meal-house thinking, "We shall give alms to him," and while they are entering, flies that were hidden in baskets, at the mouths of pots, and so forth, fly up and move about in swarms, he does not accept the alms brought from there. Why? Because [he thinks]: "On account of me..."
"The flies have been obstructed from their range. *Thusodaka* is sour gruel made from all kinds of grain ingredients.
And herein, the drinking of fermented liquor (*surā*) alone is blameworthy; yet this person perceives it as blameworthy even in this case.

An "eater at a single house" (*ekāgārika*) is one who returns after receiving alms at only one house. An "eater of a single mouthful" (*ekālopika*) is one who sustains himself with only a single morsel of food.
The same method applies to the *dvāgārika* (two-day) meals and so forth. "By a single *datti*" means by one serving.
A *datti* is a small bowl in which the first portion of alms-food is placed and set aside.

"One-day interval" (*ekāhika*) means having a gap of one day between meals. "Half-monthly" (*aḍḍhamāsika*) means having a gap of half a month between meals. "Taking meals by turn" (*pariyāyabhattabhojana*)...
"Food received on specific days": this refers to eating food brought on a day-by-day basis, such as every other day, every two days, every seven days, or every half-month.
"One who eats greens" means one who eats fresh greens. "One who eats millet" means one who eats the grain of the *sāmāka* plant. Regarding *nīvāra* and the others:
first, *nīvāra* is a species of wild rice that grows spontaneously in the forest. *Daddula*... [text fragment] ...means parched grain.
“Leather refuse” refers to the scrapings discarded by leather-workers after they have scraped the hide. “Haṭa” means slime, or moss, or the resin of trees such as the *kaṇikāra*.
“Kaṇa” means broken rice (*kuṇḍaka*). “Ācāma” is the scum of boiled rice that clings to the mortar; one takes this from where it has been discarded and eats it.
Some also call it “boiled-rice gruel. “Piññāka” and so forth are well known. “One who eats fallen fruit” means one who eats fruit that has dropped [from the tree].

*Saṇāni* means garments made of *saṇa* fiber. *Masāṇāni* means mixed garments. *Chavadussāni* means cloths discarded from a dead body, or lower robes made by sewing together *eraka* grass and the like.
*Paṃsukūlāni* means rags cast away on the ground. *Tirīṭāni* means garments made from tree bark.
*Ajinaṃ* means the hide of the antelope (*ajina-miga*). *Ajinakkhipaṃ* is that same hide with a slit in the middle.
“Split” means it is split [from the stalk]. Some also say it is “with the husk. A “grass-cloth” (*kusacīra*) is a garment made by weaving together blades of *kuśa* grass.
The same method applies to garments made of *vāka* grass or bark. A “hair-blanket” (*kesakambala*) is a blanket made from human hair, with reference to which it was said:
“Just as, monks, among all woven fabrics, the hair-blanket is declared to be the most repulsive.”
"Coarse woolen blanket" (*vāḷakambala*) means a blanket made from horse-hair and the like. "Owl-wing" (*ulūkapakkha*) means a lower garment made by sewing together owl feathers.
"Standing upright" (*ubbhaṭṭhaka*) means standing up high.
"Devoted to the exertion of squatting" (*ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutta*) means devoted to the effort of squatting; even when walking, he remains in a squatting position.

He goes leaping up again and again. "One who uses a thorn-bed" means that having dug iron thorns or natural thorns into the ground and spread a hide over them, he performs standing, walking, and other postures there.
"Lying down" means that even while sleeping, he makes his bed right there. "Sāyatatiyakam" means three times a day; [namely] morning, midday, and evening. "Of the day..."
Thinking, “I shall wash away evil three times,” he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water.
175. One who torments others is a *parantapa*. The practice of tormenting others is the practice of torturing others (*paraparitāpanānuyoga*).

Regarding the sheep-slaughterers and so forth: “sheep” (*urabbha*) refers to rams. One who kills sheep is a sheep-slaughterer (*orabbhika*). The same method applies to the pig-slaughterers and the rest.
A hunter is one who is cruel and harsh. A fisherman is a fish-catcher, a *kevaṭṭa*. A jailer is a guardian of the prison.
Those of cruel occupations are those whose activities are dreadful.
(176) An anointed head is one sprinkled upon the head with the consecration of a *khattiya*. "To the east of the city" means...
To the east of the city. "Assembly hall" (*sandhāgāra*) means a sacrificial hall. "Having clothed himself in a rough antelope skin" means having put on an antelope hide complete with its hooves.
"With ghee and oil": indeed, setting aside the ghee, any other kind of unctuous substance is called "oil.
"Scratching" refers to the time when one must scratch because the nails have been cut short.
Scratching with that [tail]. "Not separated" means not covered by a rug. "With a calf of like appearance" means with a calf of similar appearance.
If the cow is white, the calf is also white; if she is brindled or red, the calf is likewise—thus it is "with a calf of like appearance.
"He spoke thus" means that king spoke in this way. "Calves" refers to the state of being young calves.

The heifers have passed away. The same method applies to the cows as well. "For the sake of sacrificial grass" means for the purpose of making an enclosure and for spreading it upon the sacrificial ground. 177.
"In this very life" (diṭṭheva dhamme) means in this very personal existence. "Free from hunger" (nicchāto): "hunger" (chātaṃ) is said to be craving; that [craving]...

"He has nothing" means he is free from hunger (*nicchāto*). Because all defilements have been extinguished, he is "extinguished" (*nibbuto*). Because of the absence of the defilements that burn within, he has become cool;
thus, he is "become cool" (*sītībhūto*). He experiences the bliss of the jhānas, the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna; thus, he is "one who experiences bliss" (*sukhappaṭisaṃvedī*).
"By himself, having become sublime" means by himself, having become the most excellent (*seṭṭha*).
To show this person starting from the appearance of a Buddha, he said:

"Here, the Tathāgata," and so forth. In that context, the Blessed One is a "Tathāgata" for eight reasons: he is a Tathāgata because he has come thus (tathā-āgata); he is a Tathāgata because he has gone thus (tathā-gata);
he is a Tathāgata because he has come to the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇa); he is a Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true dhammas as they really are (yāthāvato).
The Tathāgata is so called because he has seen thus; he is so called because he has spoken thus; he is so called because he has acted thus;
and he is so called in the sense of having overcome. The terms “Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One,” and so forth, have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
“That Dhamma” refers to that Dhamma characterized by the aforementioned excellences. As for the phrase “the householder hears”: why is it mentioned first?
Why does he point to the householder? Because of his humbled pride and because of his abundance. For those who have gone forth from khattiya families generally harbor pride based on their birth;
those who have gone forth from brahmin families harbor pride based on the mantras;
and those who have gone forth from families of low birth are unable to establish themselves due to their own low status. [This is] regarding the sons of householders.
However, with sweat pouring from their armpits and salt sprouting on their backs from having ploughed the earth, they become devoid of such pride and arrogance.
Having gone forth into homelessness, they refrain from pride or arrogance;
by learning the Buddha’s word according to their ability and performing the work of insight (vipassanā), they are able to establish themselves in Arahatship.
Furthermore, those who have gone forth after leaving other families are not many; householders are indeed numerous.
Thus, because of his humility and because of their abundance, [the Buddha] first specifies the householder.
"In another" means in one of the other families. "Reborn" means born again. Regarding the Tathāgata...
"He acquires faith" means that, having heard the perfectly pure Dhamma, he acquires faith in the Tathāgata, the Lord of the Dhamma, thinking:
"Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One. "He reflects thus" means he contemplates in this way:
"Household life is crowded," even if there are two spouses living in a house sixty cubits wide or a hundred leagues apart.
Although they dwell [there], nevertheless, for them, the household life is indeed a confinement in the sense that it possesses possessions and obstacles.

Regarding the "dust-path" (*rajo-patho*), it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that it is the place where the dust of passion (*rāga-raja*) and so forth arises; it is also appropriate to call it the "path of arrival.
It is called "open space" (*abbhokāsa*) because it is like an open area in the sense of being unattached. For one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*) [dwells] in a gabled house, a jeweled palace...
And even though he dwells in celestial palaces and the like, where doors and windows are well-shuttered and the place is concealed, he is neither attached, nor clings, nor bound.
Therefore it is said: "The life of renunciation is open space.
Moreover: "Household life is cramped" because there is no room for the performance of wholesome deeds; it is a path of dust, a place of uncontrolled refuse.
Just as one leaves behind a king, so too one leaves behind the dust of the defilements from the place where they gather.

The open air of renunciation provides a space for the performance of wholesome deeds according to one’s pleasure, because such an opportunity is made possible. Regarding the passage, "This is not easy... one should go forth," this is the brief explanation:
it concerns the holy life of the three trainings, which must be practiced without break for even a single day until the attainment of the final consciousness.

It is absolutely fulfilled (*ekantaparipuṇṇa*). It is absolutely pure (*ekantaparisuddha*) because it must be brought to the final moment of consciousness (*carimakacitta*) without being stained by the impurity of the defilements (*kilesamala*) for even a single day.
It is "scratched clean" (*saṅkhalikhita*), like a polished conch shell, resembling a washed conch shell;
thus it should be practiced. This is not easy to practice while living the household life, dwelling in the midst of a home—[absolutely fulfilled... etc.]—to be practiced.
— "What if I were now to shave off my hair and beard, and, having donned saffron-colored robes— the color of bitter astringent juice—
garments suitable for those leading the holy life, I were to go forth from the home into homelessness? And here,
because the work such as farming and trade that is beneficial to the household (*agāra*) is called "the state of the householder" (*agāriya*), [its opposite is "homelessness"].

And that [wealth] does not exist for one who has gone forth; therefore, going forth should be understood as "the homeless state. That is the homeless state. "I would go forth" means I would practice it.
"Little" refers to a mass of wealth below a thousand [pieces of gold]; from a thousand onwards, it is "great.
In the sense of being a bond, kinsmen themselves are the "circle of kinsmen. That too is "little" when it is below twenty.
[The term] "hoti" [is used] from twenty onwards, [and thus it is called] "mahā.
"One who has entered upon the training and way of life of the bhikkhus" means:

both that training of the bhikkhus known as higher virtue (*adhisīla*), and that which they live together in—whereby they share a single livelihood and lead a common life—consisting of the rules of training (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed by the Blessed One.
And [he is] endowed with the way of life (*sājīva*). In this context, "endowed with the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus" means one who has entered into them.
"Endowed" means that by fulfilling the training and not transgressing the way of life, one has approached both of these; such is the meaning.

Regarding the phrases "having abandoned the taking of life," and so forth, the discussion of the taking of life and the other [offenses] has already been explained in detail below. "Having abandoned" refers to this volition (*cetanā*) characterized as the taking of life.
"Having abandoned immorality": "He is abstinent" means that from the moment it is abandoned, he remains withdrawn from that immorality.
"One who has laid aside the rod, laid aside the weapon":
the meaning is that he has both set aside the rod and set aside the weapon because he no longer takes up a rod or a weapon for the purpose of harming others. And here, setting aside...
The staff and all other remaining implements should be understood as "weapons" because they have the nature of destroying living beings.
However, when monks go about carrying a walking stick, a tooth-stick scraper, or a needle case, it is not for the purpose of harming others.
Therefore, they are reckoned as those who have laid aside the staff and laid aside the weapon.
"Lajjī" means endowed with a sense of shame (*lajjā*) characterized by revulsion toward evil. "Dayāpanno" means having attained compassion, that is, a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī" means one who sympathizes with the welfare of all living beings.
The meaning is: by virtue of that state of having attained compassion, he possesses a heart of benevolence toward all living beings. "Viharati" means he conducts himself; he protects.
"One who takes only what is given" is *dinnādāyī*. "One who expects only what is given even with the mind" is *dinnapāṭikaṅkhī*.
"Stealing" (*thena*) means he goes by means of that; "not stealing" is *athena*. Because of being non-stealing, it is "purified.
"By himself" means by his own personal existence (*attabhāva*). What is meant is: "Having made his own personal existence non-stealing and purified, he dwells."

"Unchaste conduct" (*abrahmacariya*) means the practice of what is not noble. One who practices the sublime (*brahma*) or most excellent conduct is a "practitioner of the holy life" (*brahmacārī*). An "ārācārī" is one who conducts himself far from unchaste conduct.

"Sexual intercourse" (*methuna*) refers to those unrighteous acts (*asaddhamma*) designated by the conventional term "sexual intercourse" because they are practiced by those overwhelmed by lust due to their similarity [to it], and because they are to be indulged in. "Village-dharma" (*gāmadhamma*) means the practices of village-dwellers.
One who speaks the truth is a "truth-speaker" (*saccavādī*). One who joins truth with truth—that is, connects it—is a "truth-uniter" (*saccasandho*).

The meaning is that he does not speak falsehood from time to time. For a person who sometimes speaks falsehood and sometimes the truth, his truth is not joined with truth because it is interrupted by false speech;
therefore, he is not a truth-uniter. But this one is not like that.
Because he does not speak falsehood even for the sake of his life, but rather joins truth with truth, he is called "one who is bound by truth" (*saccasaṃdha*).
"Firm" (*theta*) means stable; the meaning is that he is one whose speech is stable.
For one person is not of stable speech, like turmeric dye, like a wooden stake driven into a heap of chaff, or like a gourd placed on the back of a horse. Another is like a line engraved upon stone.
He is firm in speech like a city gatepost; even when his head is being cut off with a sword, he does not utter two different words.
This is called "trustworthy" (*theto*). "Reliable" (*paccayiko*) means one who is to be trusted, that is, one who inspires confidence.
For there is a certain person who is not reliable; when it is said, "Who said this? It was so-and-so," [others might say], "Do not believe his word."
He falls into the state of being one who must be questioned. One person is an "authority" (paccayika). When it is said, "By whom was this spoken? By so-and-so," he falls into the state of saying:
"If it was spoken by him, then this alone is the authority; there is nothing further to be examined; it is exactly thus. This is called an "authority.
He is "one who does not deceive the world" because of that truthfulness in speech. Toward the world...
The meaning is "he does not deceive.
"For the sake of dividing these" means for the sake of dividing those in whose presence he has heard [the words] as stated in the phrase "having heard from them.
Or, "for the reconciliation of those who are divided" refers to two friends, or two who share the same preceptor and so forth, who have become divided due to some cause.
Having approached each one individually, he says things such as, "For those born into such a family and so highly learned, this is not fitting," and thus acts as a reconciler (*sandhāna*).
"One who provides reconciliation" (*anuppadātā*) means one who provides further reconciliation.
Seeing two people in harmony, he says, "For those born into such a family and endowed with such qualities, this is appropriate," and so forth.
The meaning is: having spoken thus, he should perform an act of strengthening. "A unified monastery" (*samaggārāma*) means one where the community is in harmony;
the meaning is that he does not wish to dwell even for a moment where there is no unity. There is also a textual reading *samaggarāmo*, which has the same meaning.
"Delighting in unity" (*samaggarato*) means he delights in those who are harmonious; the meaning is that he does not wish to go elsewhere, abandoning them. [In] the harmonious...
"He rejoices even upon seeing and hearing" means he is one who rejoices in concord (*samagganandī*).
"He speaks words that create concord" means he speaks only those words which bring beings into harmony—words that illuminate the virtue of concord—and not others.

"He speaks at the proper time" means he is a speaker at the right time (*kālavādī*); the meaning is that he speaks having observed the appropriate moment for what is to be said. "The truth" (*bhūtaṃ*)...
He is a speaker of truth (*bhūtavādī*) because he speaks exactly as it is, as it has come to be, and according to its very nature.

He is a speaker of what is beneficial (*atthavādī*) because he speaks only by relying on that which is for one’s welfare in this life and the life to come. He is a speaker of the Dhamma (*dhammavādī*) because he speaks by relying on the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*).

He is a speaker of the Vinaya (*vinayavādī*) because he speaks by relying on the discipline of restraint (*saṃvaravinaya*) and the discipline of abandoning (*pahānavinaya*). A "treasure" (*nidhāna*) is so called...
The occasion for setting aside. "Possessing a store" (*nidhānavatī*) means that she has a store [of speech].

The meaning is that she speaks words fit to be stored in the heart. "At the proper time" (*kālena*): even while speaking such words, she does not speak at an improper time, thinking, "I shall speak words possessing a store";
rather, the meaning is that she speaks only after having observed the appropriate time. "With a point of reference" (*sāpadesaṃ*) means with a simile.
"With cause" means with a reason. "With a limit" means having shown a boundary; the sense is that he speaks in such a way that its limit is made known.
"Beneficial" means that even when analyzed by many methods, he speaks what is endowed with meaning because it cannot be exhausted;
or rather, because it is connected with that very meaning which the speaker, being a proponent of the goal, declares.
He speaks speech that is connected with the goal. This means it is said that he does not set aside one thing and speak another.

179. "The destruction of seed-life and plant-life" refers to the fivefold category of seed-life—namely, root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, crown-seed, and seed-seed—as well as any kind of plant-life such as green grass, trees, and so forth.
And as for "undertakings": the meaning is that one abstains from the disturbance [of living beings] by way of cutting, splitting, cooking, and so forth.
"One who eats but one meal" refers to two meals: the morning meal and the evening meal.
Of these, the morning meal is delimited by midday; the other is from after midday until before dawn. Therefore, within midday, ten times—
Even while eating, he eats only one meal a day. It is with reference to this that it is said: "one who eats but one meal. Eating at night is "night";
he has abstained from that, thus he is "one who has abstained from night-eating" (*rattūparato*). Food taken after midday until the setting of the sun is called "untimely food" (*vikālabhojana*);
because he has desisted from that, he is "one who has desisted from untimely food. This is because [eating at such times] is not in accordance with the Teaching (*sāsana*).

"Visūkadassanaṃ" means the viewing of what has become a mere spectacle (*visūka*). "Naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā" refers to the viewing of spectacles consisting of dancing, singing, and instrumental music—whether performed by oneself through dancing or causing others to dance, and so forth, or even as little as watching a peacock dance or similar performances.
For dancing and the rest are spectacles whether one performs them oneself or [watches] others.
It is not permissible for either monks or nuns to cause these things to be made or even to look at them when they are suitable for such use.

Regarding garlands and so forth: “garland” (*mālā*) refers to any kind of flower; “scent” (*gandha*) refers to any kind of fragrant substance; “ointment” (*vilepana*) refers to that which colors the skin.
In this context, one who wears them is said to “wear” (*dhāreti*); one who fills a deficient place is said to “adorn” (*maṇḍeti*). This applies both by way of scent and by way of coloring the skin.
And "adorned" means taking pleasure [in them]. "Ground" (ṭhāna) is said to mean a cause. Therefore, the meaning is:
one who abstains from that unvirtuous volition by which the great multitude performs those acts such as wearing garlands and so forth.
"High bed" (uccāsayana) is said to mean exceeding the proper measure. "Large bed" (mahāsayana) is an improper covering; the meaning is: one who abstains from that. "Gold" (jātarūpa) means...
"Gold" refers to silver coins, copper māsakas, lac māsakas, and wooden māsakas—those which are known by trade.
"Abstaining from accepting both of these" means he neither takes them himself, nor causes them to be taken, nor consents to their being deposited for him. This is the meaning.
"Accepting raw grain" refers to the acceptance of the seven kinds of raw grain, namely: rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and kudrūsa grass.
Not only is the acceptance of these forbidden for monks, but even touching them is likewise not permitted.
Regarding "accepting raw meat," this refers to raw fish and meat other than those specifically permitted as exceptions.
For monks, only the act of receiving is not permitted, not the act of touching.

Regarding "receiving women and girls": here, a "woman" (*itthī*) is one who has entered into another man's household; the other is called a "girl" (*kumārikā*). For both of them, receiving as well as touching is indeed unallowable.
Regarding "receiving female and male slaves": here, it is not permitted to receive them specifically in their capacity as female and male slaves. [The text continues: "A kitchen attendant..."
However, it is permissible when it is said, "I give [it]," or "I give a monastery attendant.

Regarding goats, sheep, and so forth, ending with fields and land, the method for determining what is allowable and what is not allowable should be examined according to the Vinaya. In that context, a "field" (khetta) is that in which the first crop (grain) grows;
a "site" (vatthu) is that in which the second crop (vegetables, etc. grows; or, where both grow, that is a field.
A site is ground that has not been prepared for that purpose. By the term "field-site," ponds and similar places where crops are sown are also included here.
"Messengership" refers to the work of a messenger; it means going here and there after receiving a letter or a message sent by householders.
"Errand-running" refers to the minor errands of one who has been dispatched to another's house. "Devotion" (anuyoga).

The name [of this offense] refers to the performance of both [actions]. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "following after those who go on errands and for the purpose of abandoning [others].
"Buying and selling" means both buying and selling. Regarding "fraudulent scales," etc.—*kūṭa* means deception.
Therein, fraudulent scales (*tulākūṭa*) are fourfold: fraud regarding the material, fraud regarding the parts, fraud regarding the grasping, and concealed fraud. Therein...
*Ākāra-kūṭa* (the deception of form) means that when taking [the scale], one uses the large pan while making the two pans equal in appearance, but when giving, one gives using the small pan.
*Aṅga-kūṭa* (the deception of the limb) means that when taking, one presses down on the scale with the hand at the rear part, but when giving, one does so at the front part.

*Gahaṇa-kūṭa* (the deception of grasping) means that when taking, one grasps the rope at the base, but when giving, one grasps it at the tip. *Paṭicchanna-kūṭa* (the deception of concealment) means...
Having made a hollow balance-beam and filled its interior with iron filings, one who takes [the weight] places it at the rear end, while one who gives places it at the front end.
*Kaṃsa* refers to a golden bowl. Deception by means of that is *kaṃsakūṭa*. How so?
Having fashioned one golden bowl, they make two or three other bowls of base metal (*lohapaṭṭi*) colored like gold; then, having gone to a district, [they approach] some wealthy family...
Having entered, they say, "Buy these golden vessels! When asked about their price, they wish to give them at a higher price than usual.
Then, when those people ask, "How can it be known that these are gold?
they reply, "Take them after testing them," and having struck a golden bowl against a stone, they give away all the bowls and depart.

The deception of the measuring vessel (*mānakūṭa*) is threefold, according to the classification of the heart, the spout, and the cord. Among these, the deception of the heart occurs at the time of receiving ghee, oil, and so forth.

For one who receives them, having said "Pour slowly" while using a measuring vessel with a hole at the bottom, causes much of the liquid to flow out into the inner container before taking it. When giving, however, one covers the hole...
He gives after quickly filling [the measure]. The "breaking of the crest" (*sikhābheda*) occurs at the time of measuring sesame, rice, and so forth;
for one taking those, he takes them by slowly raising the crest, whereas the giver, having filled it rapidly, gives while cutting off the crest.
The "breaking of the cord" (*rajjubheda*) occurs at the time of measuring fields and lands; for those not receiving a bribe measure even a large field as being large.
Regarding "opening up" (ukkoṭana) and so forth: "opening up" means receiving a bribe to make that which has no owner have an owner.
"Deceit" (vañcana) means deceiving others by various means. Here is one story: it is said that a certain hunter was coming along carrying both a deer and a fawn.
A certain rogue asked him, "Sir, what is the price of the deer? What is the price of the fawn?"

When it was said, "The deer is two kahāpaṇas; the fawn is one," he paid a kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, and after going a short distance, turned back and said, "Sir, I have no need for the fawn; give me the deer.
The other replied, "In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas. He said, "But sir, did you not already give me one kahāpaṇa?"
“Yes, it was given. “Then take this young fawn as well; thus there will be two kahāpaṇas—this one kahāpaṇa and this young fawn worth a kahāpaṇa.
Perceiving that he was speaking reasonably, he took the young fawn and gave him the deer.

*Nikatī* means deception by means of a counterfeit, either through trickery (*yoga*) or through illusion (*māyā*), having made what is not a girdle into a girdle, what is not a gem into a gem, and what is not gold into gold.
*Sāciyoga* means crooked practice; this is a name for those very things such as "prying open" (*ukkoṭana*) and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: *ukkoṭana-sāciyoga*, *vañcana-sāciyoga*, and *nikati-sāciyoga*.

Some say that "crooked practice" (*sāciyoga*) refers to the exchange of one thing for another after showing something else; however, that is already included under "deceit" (*vañcana*). Regarding "cutting" and so forth:
"cutting" (*chedana*) means the cutting off of hands and so on; "killing" (*vadha*) means causing death; "binding" (*bandha*) means binding with ropes and so forth.
"Robbery" (*viparāmosa*) is twofold: robbery by snow and robbery by a thicket. For when, during the time of a fall of snow...
When they deceive people traveling on a road by hiding behind snow, this is "deception by snow" (*himaviparāmoso*).

When they deceive them by hiding behind thickets and the like, this is "deception by thicket" (*gumbaviparāmoso*). "Looting" (*ālopa*) refers to the act of plundering villages, market towns, and so forth.
"Violence" (*sahasākāra*) is a rash or reckless act; it is the thrusting of a weapon into the chest of people after entering their homes.
Except for taking the goods that are desired. Thus he abstains from this cutting... [and] from acts of violence. 180.
"He is content" means he is endowed with twelvefold contentment regarding the various requisites among the four requisites.
"Sufficient for the maintenance of the body" means merely enough to sustain the body. "Sufficient for the maintenance of the belly" means...

"Merely for the sake of maintaining the belly. "Having taken [only] this much and departed" means that having taken all eight types of requisites for a bhikkhu and having fastened them to his body, he goes away;

he has neither attachment nor bondage such as thinking, "This is my monastery, my cell, or my attendant. Like an arrow released from a bowstring, he has departed from the herd like a rutting elephant.

Enjoying whatever dwelling he desires—whether a forest grove, the foot of a tree, a jungle thicket, or a mountain cleft—he stands alone and sits alone. In all postures, he remains solitary and without a second.
He is equanimous toward the four quarters and free from aversion.
Content with whatever comes his way,
undaunted by hardships,
he should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus described, it attains the state of being like the rhinoceros horn.
Now, establishing that meaning by means of a simile, he says, "Just as," and so forth. Therein, *pakkhī sakuṇo* means a bird possessed of wings.
*Ḍeti* means it flies up. Here, however, the summary of the meaning is this: a bird [thinks], "In such-and-such a place..."
Knowing that "the tree has ripened fruit," birds come from various directions and, piercing and shaking its fruits with their claws, wings, and beaks, they eat them.
They have no thought such as, "This is for today; this will be for tomorrow.
But when the fruits are exhausted, they neither appoint a guardian for the tree nor do they leave behind even a feather or a claw there.
Or they place their beaks upon it; but then, having become indifferent to that tree, whichever direction anyone desires, he flies off toward it like one carrying a load of enemies.
In the same way, this bhikkhu departs entirely without attachment or expectation;
therefore it is said, "having taken [the requisites], he departs. "By the noble one" means by one who is faultless. "Internal" means within oneself.
"In one's own person. "Blameless happiness" means faultless happiness. 181.
"When he sees a form with the eye": the meaning is that this bhikkhu, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, having seen a form with visual consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*).
Regarding the remaining phrases as well, whatever needs to be said, all of it has been stated below.
This has already been stated. "The happiness of non-defilement" (*abyāsekasukha*) means the happiness that is not moistened by defilements (*kilesa*).

It is also called "the happiness of non-distraction" (*avikiṇṇasukha*); for the happiness of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvarasukha*) is undistracted because it proceeds by way of merely seeing what is seen, and so forth, regarding visible objects and the rest.
182. "In going forward and in returning": he is endowed with the restraint of the six faculties, including the mind.
The bhikkhu is one who acts with clear comprehension by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension in these seven instances, beginning with going forward and returning.
Regarding this, whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the *Jhāna Vibhaṅga*.
What does he show by the passage beginning with "By this" and so forth? He shows the excellence of the requisites for dwelling in the forest. For one who...
These four conditions being absent, his dwelling in the forest does not succeed; he falls into having to converse with animals or forest-dwellers.
The deities inhabiting the forest cry out terrifying sounds, saying, "What is the use of such an evil bhikkhu dwelling in the forest?
They strike their heads with their hands and make as if to flee.
“Such-and-such a bhikkhu, having entered the forest, committed this and that evil deed”—thus does he spread his ill repute.
But for one who possesses these four requisites, dwelling in the forest succeeds;
for when he reviews his own virtue and sees no blemish or stain whatsoever, he generates rapture and [views it] as subject to destruction.
Fully comprehending it as it passes away, he enters the plane of the Noble Ones. The deities dwelling in the forest, being delighted, proclaim his praise.
His fame spreads abroad like a drop of oil cast upon the water. The terms "secluded" (*vivitta*) and so forth have meanings already explained below.
Thus, with his mind thus concentrated... [as before] ...he understands beings according to their karma.
Everything that ought to be said regarding this point has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. 185.
Regarding the third true knowledge (*vijjā*), "when his mind is thus concentrated" should be understood as the fourth jhāna consciousness that serves as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*).

"For the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*)" means for the purpose of the knowledge of the path to Arahantship; for it is the path to Arahantship that [destroys] the taints.
The destruction of the taints is called the exhaustion of the taints. And in that regard, this knowledge is included within that [category]. "He inclines the mind" means he directs the insight-mind.

In such passages as "This is suffering," etc., he understands the entire truth of suffering—thinking, "Suffering is just this much, not more than this"—as it really is through the penetration of its specific characteristic.
He understands and penetrates it. He understands that craving which produces that suffering is "this is the origin of suffering";
he understands that the state where both of these cease upon reaching it is their non-arising, Nibbāna—“this is the cessation of suffering”;
and he understands the Noble Path that leads to its attainment as “this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,” through the penetration of the specific characteristics of each.
"One understands as it really is, one penetrates"—thus the meaning should be understood.

Having thus shown the truths according to their specific characteristics (*sarūpato*), he now speaks the passage beginning with "these are the taints" (*ime āsavā*) in order to show them by way of the defilements (*kilesavasena*) through a figurative method (*pariyāyato*).
"For one who knows thus, for one who sees thus" means for one who knows and sees in this manner, together with insight (*vipassanā*).
He speaks of the path that has reached its culmination. "From the taint of sensual desire" means from the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).

By the word "is liberated," he shows the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*). By the phrase "when it is liberated," he shows the moment of the fruit (*phalakkhaṇa*); for at the moment of the path the mind is being liberated, while at the moment of the fruit it has become liberated.
By the phrase "the knowledge 'it is liberated' in what is liberated," he indicates the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).
[The text] shows [this]. By the words “Birth is destroyed,” etc., it shows its plane. For by that knowledge, while reviewing, he understands: “Birth is destroyed,” and so forth.
“Vusitaṃ” means lived, fully lived, accomplished, practiced, and brought to completion;
this is the meaning. “Brahmacariyaṃ” refers to the holy life of the Path. Together with the virtuous worldling, there are seven types of trainees (sekha).
They are said to "dwell the life of purity" (*brahmacariya-vāsa*). One whose taints are destroyed has completed that dwelling.
Therefore, reflecting upon his own dwelling in the life of purity, he understands: "The life of purity has been lived. "What was to be done has been accomplished":
this means that the sixteenfold task—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing, with respect to the four truths and the four paths—has been brought to completion.

This is the meaning. For those such as the virtuous worldlings (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) still have that task to perform; one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) has already accomplished what was to be done.
Therefore, reflecting upon his own duty, he understands: "What was to be done has been done. He understands:

"There is no further task for this state of being"—that is, for this present existence, for the fulfillment of the sixteen duties, or for the destruction of the defilements through the cultivation of the path.

186. Regarding "with lust, etc. (*sarāgādi*): "Not abandoned" (*appahīna*) means not abandoned either by suppression (*vikkhambhana*), or by partial abandonment (*tadaṅga*), or by complete eradication (*samuccheda*).

187. Regarding "he is a possessor," etc.: "A possessor" (*lābhī*) means one who possesses [it], having attained and remained [in that state]. "Of internal mental serenity" (*ajjhattaṃ cetosamathassa*) means of the mental serenity arisen in one's own mind, which is reckoned as "internal" in its own right. "Of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanāya*)... [is]... [of]... [the insight into phenomena] characterized by higher wisdom.
[This refers to] insight (vipassanā) proceeding by way of impermanence and so forth regarding the phenomena of the aggregates, which is designated as "higher wisdom" (adhipaññā).

"Accompanied by form" means those fine-material-sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samāpatti) that have the sign of form as their object. "Accompanied by the formless" means those immaterial-sphere attainments (arūpa-samāpatti) that do not have the sign of form as their object.

And here, the first [type of person] is an ordinary worldling (puthujjana) who has attained the eight attainments; the second is a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) who is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka).
The third is the noble disciple who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*). The fourth should be understood as the worldling (*mahājana*). 188.

Regarding those who go with the stream (*anusotagāmin*) and so forth: "one who goes with the stream" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*) who follows the stream of cyclic existence (*vaṭṭasota*), submerged in that stream of cyclic existence.
"One who goes against the stream" means one who travels against the stream; this refers to one who, instead of going with the stream, proceeds against it.
This is a designation. "And he does not commit evil action" means that he does not do what is prescribed as a transgression.
"Even with pain and even with grief" means even together with the pain and grief that arise when there is an obsession of the defilements.
"Complete" means not deficient in even one of the three trainings. "Pure" means free from defilement.
"Brahmacariya" means the supreme practice (*seṭṭhacariya*). By this section, the stream-enterer and the once-returner are described.
But do they practice the holy life while weeping? Yes; they are said to "practice" while weeping with the weeping of the defilements (*kilesa*).
Even an ordinary monk (*puthujjana*) endowed with virtue (*sīla*) is included right here.

"Established" (*ṭhitatta*) means having an established nature. "Non-returner" (*anāgāmī*) means one whose nature is established because his mind cannot be shaken by sensual lust and ill will, and because he is subject to the law of not returning from that world.
"Crossed over" (*tiṇṇa*) means having crossed over the stream of craving. "Gone to the further shore" (*pāraṅgata*) means having reached the further shore of Nibbāna.
"He stands on dry land" means he stands on the dry land of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. "Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*)...

“Fruition-concentration” (phalasamādhi). “Liberated by wisdom” (paññāvimutti) refers to the knowledge of fruition (phalañāṇa). “This one is called” means that this one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is called “the brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land.
For it is because he has banished evil (bāhitapāpa) that he is named a brahmin.
Regarding “one of little learning” and so forth: “little heard” means that within the ninefold teaching of the Master, one has heard only a small amount.
"He does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma by misunderstanding the meaning or misunderstanding the Dhamma" means that although he knows both the commentary and the canonical text (pāḷi),
he does not practice the preliminary path (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā), which is the Dhamma corresponding to the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma).
In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
190. Regarding “The ascetic immovable” (*samaṇamacala*) and so forth: *samaṇamacalo* means the immovable ascetic; the letter *m* is used for euphonic junction (*padasandhi*).

The meaning is “an unshakable ascetic” or “a firm ascetic. “This one is called” means that this stream-enterer, because he is established in faith rooted in the Teaching, is called “the immovable ascetic.
However, the once-returner, because of the presence of the defilement of passion, is “the lotus-like ascetic” (*samaṇapaduma*).

It is said: "For here, the meaning of 'red' (ratta) is what is meant by the meaning of 'lotus' (paduma). Because of the absence of the defilement of passion known as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), the non-returner (*anāgāmī*) is called a "white-lotus ascetic" (*samaṇapuṇḍarīka*).
For it is said: "For here, the meaning of 'white' (*paṇḍara*) is what is meant by the meaning of 'white-lotus' (*puṇḍarīka*).
And because of the absence of those defilements that produce stiffness (*thaddhabhāva*), the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is called the "delicate ascetic among ascetics."
It has been said: "And in the sense of being free from suffering, he is indeed a delicate ascetic.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrad (Catukkaniddesa). 5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentad (Pañcakaniddesa).
191. In the *Pañcaka* [Nipāta]: "Therein" (*tattha*) means among those persons enumerated above in the manner beginning with, "He both initiates [an action] and feels remorse.

"Whoever" (*yvāyaṃ*) refers to this very person. Regarding the word "initiates" (*ārabhati*): here the term *ārambha* applies to undertaking an action, harming, exertion, agitation, an offense, and transgression.
For instance, it occurs in the sense of "action" (kamma) in the passage: "Whatever suffering arises, all that has its condition in undertaking."

“Great sacrifices, great undertakings, yet they do not yield great fruit”—this refers to *kiriyā* (action). “They slaughter living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama”—this refers to *hiṃsana* (harming).
“Exert yourselves, go forth, devote yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching”—this refers to *vīriya* (energy).
“He abstains from the destruction of seeds and the destruction of living plants”—this refers to *vikopana* (disturbance/destruction). “He undertakes [an action] and feels remorse.”

"And he becomes remorseful"—this, however, refers to the transgression of an offense (*āpatti*). Therefore, the meaning here is that by way of transgressing an offense, one both initiates [the act] and subsequently becomes remorseful because of it.

"One does not understand it as it really is" means that because it has not been attained, one does not know it according to its true nature (*yathāsabhāvato*). "In which" (*yattha*) means in whatever...
The meaning is: that state which, having reached it, the evil unwholesome states that have arisen in this person cease without remainder.
But having reached what do they cease? The path of arahantship (*arahatta-magga*).

However, for one who has attained the fruit (*phala*), they are said to have already ceased. Even so, it should be understood that here the fruit itself is spoken of by way of the function of the path.
The "arising of undertaking" occurs through the occurrence of transgressions of the precepts. The "arising of remorse" is born from remorse itself.
"Increasing" means they grow by arising again and again. "Well! is an expression of entreaty. This is what is meant:
"Indeed, the Venerable One has committed an offense; nevertheless, we entreat the Venerable One—to teach that which is worthy of being taught."
"By emerging from that which is subject to emergence, by disclosing that which is subject to disclosure,
by abandoning the taints born of undertaking, and by dispelling and removing the taints born of remorse through the reviewing of the state of being established in the pure end,
let him develop both the insight-consciousness and the insight-wisdom. By this fifth person— by this [means].
"By the fifth [type of person], the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). "He will become equal" means he will become equal precisely by way of equality in supramundane qualities;
this is the meaning of how one whose taints are destroyed should be exhorted.
"He undertakes it and does not feel remorse" means he incurs an offense. However, in order to confess that, he [seeks] a person of similar standing...
He searches for it. Therefore, he does not feel remorse. In the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated:
"Because he has emerged [from the offense], he does not feel remorse. "He does not commit [an offense] and thus does not feel remorse" means that he does not incur an offense;
yet, because he is unskilled in the Vinaya regulations, he perceives what is not an offense as an offense and consequently feels remorse. In the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*...

However, it is said: "Having once fallen into an offense and emerged from it, even if one does not subsequently fall into another, one is nevertheless unable to dispel remorse. "He neither undertakes nor feels remorse" means that he neither falls into an offense nor feels remorse.
But what kind of person is this? It is a person who has abandoned diligence. He...

For indeed, even one whose virtue is purified does not fulfill the practice if he thinks, "What is the use of my attaining final Nibbāna during this Buddha's time? I shall attain final Nibbāna in the future, at the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Metteyya.
Such a person [should be corrected by others] with the thought: "For what purpose does the Venerable One dwell heedlessly?
The destination of an ordinary worldling is uncertain. It may be that the Venerable One will obtain the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One Metteyya."

"Even if one does not obtain [the goal], one should nevertheless develop insight for the sake of Arahantship"—thus he should be exhorted. The remainder is to be understood everywhere according to the method already stated. 192.
Regarding "having given, he despises," etc.: there was a certain bhikkhu of great merit who was a recipient of the four requisites. He [gave] robes and so forth...
Having obtained something else, one of little merit asks for permission [to take it]. Even though he asks again and again, the other takes it nonetheless.
Then the former, becoming slightly angry and wishing to cause him embarrassment, says:
"This man does not obtain robes and so forth by his own nature; he obtains them by depending on us. In this way, a person despises after having given.
Furthermore, one person who has lived with another for two or three years may have previously held that person in high esteem, but as time passes, he no longer shows respect;
he does not rise from his seat, nor does he go to attend upon him.
In this way, a person disregards another through long association.
"Ādheyyamukho" means having the face [turned] toward what is to be placed [within him] from the beginning. The meaning is: "one whose face is fixed upon the very first word.
"Adhimuccitā hoti" means he becomes one who has faith. Herein, this is the method: a certain person describes a monk who is indeed worthy as "this one is unworthy";
having heard that, he reaches a conclusion. Then, by another monk of similar character, he is described as "worthy..."
Even when it is said, "This one is improper," he does not accept that person's word;
rather, he accepts the previous bhikkhunī’s statement, thinking, "So-and-so told us that this one is improper. Furthermore, another person tells him of an immoral man, saying, "He is virtuous.
Having placed faith in that person's word, he then hears from yet another: "This bhikkhu is improper; he should not come into your presence."
"Even when told, 'It is fitting to approach him,' he does not accept that person's word, but rather adheres to his own previous opinion.
Another accepts both what is said in praise and what is said in dispraise. This too is called "one whose mouth is for receiving" (ādheyyamukha).
The meaning is: one whose mouth is fixed upon whatever he hears; one who places his mouth [his judgment] upon each and every thing he hears.

"Lolo" means fickle because faith and the other [faculties] remain for only a short time, being shaken by lack of faith and so forth. "Ittarasaddho" means one of limited faith, one whose faith is incomplete.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. In this context, however, devotion (*bhatti*) is simply faith through repeated cultivation.
Affection (*pema*) includes both faith-affection and affection based on worldly attachment (*gehasita*). Clarity (*pasāda*) is simply clarity of faith.
"Thus a person is fickle": in this way, due to having limited faith and so forth, a person is called "fickle.
Like turmeric dye, like a wooden post pounded into a heap of chaff, or like a gourd placed on the back of a horse, he has no fixed station;
in one moment he is pleased, and in another moment he is provoked to anger.
“Dull and bewildered” means dull by way of ignorance and bewildered due to lack of clarity; the meaning is “greatly deluded. 193.

Regarding the similes of the professional soldier (*yodhājīva*): “professional soldiers” refers to those who live by war. “A cloud of dust” refers to a mass of dust rising from the ground broken up by the trampling of the feet of elephants, horses, and so forth.
“Does not steady itself” means it is unable to stand firm after having steadied itself.
"He endures the rising dust" means that even upon seeing a mass of dust, he remains patient.

"The tip of the banner" refers to the top of banners raised upon the backs of elephants and horses, or on chariots. "The shouting" refers to the loud and great clamor of elephants, horses, chariots, and the army.
"He strikes back" means even at a slight blow when [the enemy] has come close. "Is struck" means he is afflicted.
He encounters distress. "He is afflicted" means he encounters misfortune; he abandons his natural state.

"He endures the onslaught" means that even after receiving two or three blows, he endures them; he bears them patiently. "That very head of the battle" refers to that very place where the victorious camp is established.
"He dwells there" means he remains there for about seven days having overcome [the enemy]. For what reason? For the purpose of tending to the wounds of those who have received blows.
[This was said] for the purpose of granting a higher position and for the purpose of experiencing power and happiness, having recognized the distinction between their respective deeds. 194.

Now, since there is no need for the Teacher’s warriors (yodhājīva), this simile was brought forward to illustrate five types of persons within this teaching; therefore, showing those persons, he said, "In the same way," and so forth.
Therein, "sinks" means he desponds in wrong thought, he enters into it. He is not able to [fulfill] the holy life (brahmacariya).
"To sustain" means he is unable to protect the life of celibacy so that it remains uninterrupted.
"Having manifested weakness in the training" means having made known his state of frailty regarding the training.

"What is this 'dust-heap' for him?"—he says this to ask, "What indeed is this so-called 'dust-heap' for that person? "Beautiful" means possessing beauty. "Pleasant to behold" means worthy of being seen. "Inspiring confidence" means...

They bring serenity to the mind by their very sight. "Supreme" (paramāya) means most excellent. "By the beauty of complexion" (vaṇṇapokkharatāya) refers both to the color of the body and the symmetry of its limbs.

196. "She laughs at" (ūhasati) means she mocks. "She talks loudly" (ullapati) means she speaks. "She laughs aloud" (ujjagghati) means she laughs with a loud laugh, slapping her hands. "She ridicules" (uppaṇḍeti) means she speaks words of ridicule.

197. "Sits down" (*abhinisīdati*) means that having overcome [the other], he sits nearby or on the same seat. The same method applies to the second word as well. "Overwhelms" (*ajjhottharati*) means he covers over. 198.
"Having untied and having released" means having both untied his hand from the place where it was grasped and having released it. The rest here is of plain meaning. 199.
Among those who live on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*), due to dullness and delusion, he neither knows the undertaking nor the benefit; for himself—
However, due to dullness, delusion, and sheer ignorance, one becomes an alms-food eater. One who is of evil desire and overcome by craving thinks:

"Because I am an alms-food eater, they will show honor with the four requisites, thinking, 'This one is an alms-food eater,' and they will esteem me for qualities such as being modest and having few desires.
Thus, standing upon such evil desire, one is overwhelmed by that evil desire.

Having offered [the meal], he becomes an alms-food eater (*piṇḍapātiko*). However, one who wanders for alms due to madness is called an "alms-food eater" because of that madness and mental derangement.
Regarding the phrase "praised": this factor of the alms-food eater is praised and commended by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas;
thus, he is an alms-food eater. In the passage beginning with "relying on fewness of wishes alone," it says: "Thus I shall be one of few wishes..."
"This practice of eating only almsfood will lead to fewness of wishes for me; thus being content, this practice of eating only almsfood will lead to contentment for me;
thus I will wear away the defilements—this practice of eating only almsfood will lead to the wearing away of the defilements for me.
Thinking thus, he is one who eats only almsfood. This is called "having this as his purpose."

The meaning is: "relying on the fact that one has need of this noble practice, or the fact that one has need of this mere alms-food, and that one's livelihood is sustained by whatever is obtained. "Foremost" (*agga*) means the eldest; the remaining terms are synonyms for that same word.
Just as there is what is called "cow's milk" because it comes from a cow, and not without a cow; so too is it in the cases of "curd from milk," and so forth.

This is the method. "In the same way" means: just as, among these five products of the cow, the cream of ghee (*sappimaṇḍa*) is the foremost, even so, among these five types of alms-food eaters (*piṇḍapātika*), he who is an alms-food eater by relying on fewness of wishes and so forth—this one is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent.
However, among these five types of alms-food eaters, only two persons are [true] alms-food eaters.

Three are not alms-food eaters; however, they should be understood as "alms-food eaters" by name alone. This same method applies to the "those who eat only what is left over" (khalupacchābhattika) and the others.

202. Regarding the verse beginning with *chakke*: “*Tattha*” means among those six types of persons. “A *sammāsambuddho* is to be seen by that” means that person is to be seen as a *sabbaññubuddha* (All-Knowing Buddha) by virtue of the omniscient knowledge produced by himself without a teacher.
In the phrases “a *paccekasambuddho* by that,” and so forth, that person is a *paccekasambuddha* by virtue of the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*.
“By that *sāvakapāramīñāṇa* (perfection-knowledge of disciples), those persons [are Sāriputta and Moggallāna]. “By that making an end of suffering... [and so on].
Those remaining persons are Arahants. Because of not returning to this state of existence, that person is a Non-returner (Anāgāmī).
Because of returning to this state of existence, those persons—the Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and Once-returners (Sakadāgāmin)—are to be understood [as such].
