7. Explanation of the Section on the Sevenfold (Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā) 203. Regarding the section on the sevenfold: "sunk once" means sunk one time.

"By those that are exclusively dark" means by those phenomena of fixed wrong view known as the doctrine of non-existence (*natthikavāda*), the doctrine of no cause (*ahetukavāda*), and the doctrine of non-action (*akiriyavāda*). Such is the person.
For this reason, they say that such a person, having once sunk down, remains sunk just so; for there is no rising again from this renewed existence (*punabbhava*).
Like Makkhali Gosāla and others, he becomes mere fuel for the fires of hell below.
"Excellent is faith in wholesome states" (*sāhu saddhā kusalesu dhammesu*): because faith in wholesome states is rightly acquired, one emerges.
Thus, by that much alone of the wholesome, one is said to "emerge. The same method applies to the passages beginning with "Virtue is good" and so forth.
"He only declines" means that, like water poured on a slope, he declines absolutely. "Such a person" refers to one who thinks, "Faith is good," and so on;
having emerged once by way of these qualities such as faith, he sinks again due to their decline.

Like Devadatta and others. For Devadatta, although he had produced the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), subsequently became a thorn in the side of the Buddhas, and having fallen away from those virtues, committed the deed of shedding blood and the deed of causing a schism in the Saṅgha;
thus, with the breakup of the body, he was reborn in hell by the second moment of consciousness. Kokālika, having reviled the two chief disciples...
He was reborn in the Paduma hell.
"Neither decreases nor increases" means that it does not decrease even when there is insufficient food, nor does it increase even when there is sufficient food.
Both of these points, however, should be illustrated by way of both the householder and the homeless one. For a certain householder, when there is insufficient food...

Or he causes [the community] to receive fortnightly meals, tickets for meals, or rainy-season robes; yet later, even when there is sufficient time and means, he provides only those very same fortnightly meals and so forth.

Likewise, a homeless one might undertake a recitation or an ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) at the beginning when there is insufficient time, but even when there is sufficient time due to the attainment of intelligence, strength, and energy, he does not do anything further than that.
"Thus is the person": in this way, by means of the stability of faith and the other [faculties], the person is said to be "standing after having emerged.
"Having emerged, he sees clearly and looks about" means that the person who is a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), having risen up, looks toward the path to be traveled or the direction to be reached.
"Having emerged, he flies away" means that the person who is a once-returner (sakadāgāmi), having risen up due to the thinning of the defilements, flies away toward the direction in which he must go.

"He has reached a firm footing" means that a non-returner (anāgāmī), having risen, looked around, and stepped forward, has reached a place where he is firmly established; he stands there and does not return.

"He has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land" means that having crossed the flood of all defilements and gone to the further shore, he is one who stands on the dry land of Nibbāna. These seven types of persons are illustrated by the simile of water.
It is said that seven foot-trading merchants, while traveling along a long road, came upon a river full of water midway on their journey.
Among them, the first man, who was afraid of the water, sank down at the very spot where he had entered and was unable to rise again;

he remained right there as food for the fish and turtles. The second man, having sunk at the place where he entered, rose once and then sank again, unable to rise; he too remained right there as food for the fish and turtles. The third...
Having submerged himself, he emerged. Standing in the middle of the river, he was unable to come back from this side nor go over to the other side.
The fourth, having emerged and stood there, looked toward the landing place for crossing. The fifth, having looked toward the landing place for descending, stepped down.
The sixth, having crossed over and reached the opposite bank, stood in water reaching up to his waist. The seventh [reached] the opposite bank.
Having gone there, bathed with perfumed powders and other substances, put on fine garments, anointed himself with fragrant ointments,
adorned himself with blue lotuses and other flowers, and decorated himself with various ornaments, he entered the great city, ascended the excellent palace,
and partook of the finest food.
In this context, these seven types of persons are like the seven merchants on foot; the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is like the river.
The sinking at the very spot where the first man, who fears the water, enters is like the sinking into the round of existence by one of wrong view.
The person who, having emerged, sinks again is like the man who, having emerged merely by the arising of faith and so forth, sinks through their subsequent decline.
A person established [in the fruit] is like one standing in the middle of a river, due to the stability of faith and the other faculties.
A stream-enterer is like one looking toward the ford for crossing, or looking toward the path to be traversed or the direction to be gone.

A once-returner is like a person swimming across, because of the thinning of the defilements. One who has crossed and stands in water reaching only to the waist is like one whose nature is not to return.

The non-returner is one who stands [on the shore]. Like a man who, having bathed and crossed over to the further bank, stands on dry land, the brahmin whose taints are destroyed stands on the ground of Nibbāna after having transcended the four floods.

Just as that man standing on dry land enters a city, ascends a magnificent palace, and partakes of the finest food, so too the one whose taints are destroyed enters the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as its object.
The passing away [of the time] is to be understood. Those liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) and so forth have already been explained above.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the septad (sattaka-niddesa). 207.
The expositions of the octad (aṭṭhaka) and the nonad (navaka) are also to be understood according to the method stated above.
10. Explanation of the Exposition of the Decads (Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā) 209. Regarding the exposition of the decads: "Here" means in the sense-sphere plane (*kāmāvacarabhūmi*).

For in the sense-sphere plane, the culmination of those such as the "seven-times-at-most" [stream-enterer] occurs precisely within the sense-sphere plane. The meaning is that the attainment of Arahatship and the attainment of Nibbāna without residue occur by means of a sense-sphere existence alone.

"Having left this world" means that for those who have left their personal existence (*attabhāva*) here in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) and are established in a Pure Abode (*suddhāvāsa*) existence, there is finality (*niṭṭhā*).

For those such as the "one who attains Nibbāna in the interval" (*antarāparinibbāyin*), having reached the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) here and passed away from this world, they arise in the Pure Abodes and, by means of that personal existence, reach both Arahantship and the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*). Therefore...
It is said: “For these five, there is finality here, having left this world.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Decads. The Concluding Statement.
And to this extent—
the Teacher, who is indeed without equal in the world, taught the designation of persons (puggalapaññatti) in the abode of the Thirty-three gods, neither too briefly nor too elaborately.
Having plumbed without exception both the commentary on this [work] composed in the language of the Island,
as well as the commentaries on the Āgamas,
[he has presented] whatever meaning is clearly analyzed and unconfused, wherever it may be found.
Having taken from here and there that which was stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, avoiding excessive prolixity and not adopting everything,
this commentary is composed by way of a method that is neither too brief nor too extensive.
Whatever merit has been attained by me through compiling this tradition into seven recitation sections for the long endurance of the Dhamma—
by that merit, may the subtle and auspicious True Dhamma endure.
"Beholding with the pure eye of Dhamma all living beings.
The *Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā* is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the *Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā* of the *Abhidhamma-piṭaka*:
Seated in the world of the gods, honored by the assembly of deities;
The Teacher, without rival in the world with its devas,
skilled in all designations, having spoken the *Puggalapaññatti*—
the elucidation of designations— he is the supreme person in the world.
Because it serves as the basis for discourses such as those concerning persons (puggala),
he taught the *Kathāvatthu* treatise in brief.
By means of the laying down of the *mātikā* (matrix) alone, it was established in the abode of the gods.
Now that this [text], which was analyzed by Moggaliputta upon the earth,
has reached the stage for the exposition of its meaning,
I shall therefore explain it; listen to it with concentrated minds.
In the *Nidānakathā*,
at the conclusion of the Twin Miracle, the Blessed One, having entered the rains retreat upon the yellow-silk stone slab at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the City of the Thirty-three Gods,
delivered a discourse on the Abhidhamma to the assembly of deities, making his mother a bodily witness.
Having taught the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, *Vibhaṅga*, *Dhātukathā*, and *Puggalapaññatti* treatises, when it came time for the teaching of the *Kathāvatthu*, [the Buddha] said:
"In the future, my disciple, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa of great wisdom, having purified the defilements that have arisen in the Dispensation, will perform the Third Council;
seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, regarding his own doctrine..."
“Having combined five hundred suttas on the opposing doctrines with another five hundred suttas, he will expound this treatise. Thus granting him the opportunity,
[the author] begins with that eightfold method of debate consisting of two sets of five questions regarding the doctrine of the person (puggalavāda),
and proceeds through all the paths of discussion until reaching the measure of a complete recitation (bhāṇavāra).
He established the matrix (mātikā) of the *Tanti*. Then, having explained the remainder of the Abhidhamma discourse according to the method of detailed exposition, he spent the rains retreat.

Having descended from the deva-world into the city of Sāṅkassa by means of a stairway made of jewels, situated between stairways of gold and silver, he remained for as long as his lifespan lasted, accomplishing the welfare of beings, and finally passed away into the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa).
Then the community of masters headed by Mahākassapa, taking King Ajātasattu as their patron, compiled the body of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
One hundred years thereafter, the Vajjiputtaka monks proclaimed ten points.
Having heard of these, the Elder Yasa, son of the Brahmin Kākaṇḍaka, [confronted] Kālāsoka, the son of Susunāga.
Taking the King as his companion, he selected seven hundred elders from among the twelve hundred thousand bhikkhus;
having crushed those ten points, he compiled the body of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
However, the ten thousand Vajjiputtaka bhikkhus, who were refuted by those elders who compiled the Dhamma, [formed] a faction.
Seeking a weak faction suitable for themselves, they established a separate school known as the Mahāsāṅghika-ācariyakula.
After splitting from that, two other teacher-lineages arose: the Gokulika and the Ekavyavahārika.
From the Gokulika-nikāya, after further splitting, two more teacher-lineages arose: the Paṇṇattivāda and...
And because of their numerical majority, they were also known as the "Many-Knowers" (*Bahussutika*). Within their own ranks, other teacher-traditions called the *Cetiyavāda* arose.
Thus, in the second century [after the Parinibbāna], five teacher-traditions emerged from the Mahāsāṅghika school;
together with the Mahāsāṅghikas themselves, there are six.
In that very second century, having split from the Theravāda, two teacher-traditions arose:
the Mahīṃsāsakas and the Vajjiputtakas. Therein, having split from the Vajjiputtaka tradition, four other teacher-traditions arose:
the Dhammuttarīyas, the Bhaddayānikas, the Channāgārikas, and the Sammitiyas. Again, in that very same [period]...
In the second century [after the Parinibbāna], having split from the Mahīṃsāsaka school, two teacher-traditions arose: the Sabbatthivāda and the Dhammaguttika.
Again, having split from the Sabbatthivāda lineage, those known as the Kassapika were born. When the Kassapikas split, others known as the Saṅkantika were born.
When the Saṅkantikas split, those known as the Suttavāda were born; thus [the schools] arose from the Theravāda.
Having split apart, these eleven teacher-teachings (ācariyavāda) arose. Together with the Theravāda, they become twelve.
Thus, these twelve and the six teacher-teachings of the Mahāsāṅghikas—altogether eighteen teacher-teachings—arose in the second century [after the Parinibbāna].
They are also known as the "eighteen schools" (nikāya) or the "eighteen teacher-families. These are precisely those.
This is the name. Among these, it should be understood that seventeen schools are schismatic, while the Theravāda is non-schismatic. This is also stated in the *Dīpavaṃsa*:
"The Vajjiputtakas, those evil monks, were expelled by the Elders;
having gained another faction, many people became proponents of what is not Dhamma."
“Ten thousand [monks] having assembled together, performed the compilation of the Dhamma;
therefore this rehearsal of the Dhamma is called the Great Rehearsal (Mahāsaṅgīti).
The monks of the Mahāsaṅgīti acted contrary to the Teaching.”
Having shattered the *Mūlasangaha*, they composed another compilation.
They compiled the Suttas elsewhere and composed them elsewhere;
they split both the meaning and the Dhamma within the Vinaya and the five Nikāyas.
“Without understanding, O monks, that which was taught by way of a method, as well as that which was taught without a method; that which has a direct meaning and that which requires interpretation,
they— intending one thing when speaking— have established another meaning.”
By means of the mere shadow of the phrasing, those monks destroyed much of the true meaning.
Having discarded one part of the profound Sutta and Vinaya,
they composed another Sutta and Vinaya that were merely superficial imitations.
“The Parivāra, the Atthuddhāra, the Abhidhamma, the six treatises (Chappakaraṇa),
the Paṭisambhidā, the Niddesa, and a portion of the Jātaka—
having expounded these much, they composed other [works].”
The name, the insignia, the requisites, and the modes of conduct—
they abandoned their natural state and made it otherwise.
Those who were the leaders of the schismatic sects were the makers of the Great Council.
“By following their example, many schools of doctrine arose;
thereafter, at a later time, a further schism occurred therein.
The Gokulikas split into two groups: the Ekavyavahārikas and the Bhikṣus.”
There were two schisms among the Gokulikas, which arose at a later time:
"The Bahussutikas and the Paññattis—the monks split into these two groups;
then the Cetiyas and the Punavādins, who caused the division of the Great Council."
“All these five teachers were rooted in the Great Council;
they destroyed both the meaning and the Dhamma, as well as parts of the compilation.
Indeed, having discarded portions of the text, they composed something else.”
“Having abandoned their natural state, they changed their names, their gender, their requisites, and their modes of dress;
and thus another schism arose within the pure Theravāda.”
“The Mahīśāsakas and the Vajjiputtakas—the monks split into two factions;
within the Vajjiputtaka school, a fourfold schism arose.
The Dhammuttarikas, the Bhaddayānikas, the Channāgārikas, and the Sammitiyas.”
Two divisions of the Mahīśāsakas arose at a later time.
The Bhikkhus split into two: the Sabbatthivādins and the Dhammaguttas.
From the Sabbatthivādins [arose] the Kassapikas, and from the Kassapikas, the Saṅkantikas.
“The Suttavādin among the Saṅkantikas was gradually broken apart;
these eleven doctrines have branched off from the Theravāda.
They divided both the meaning and the doctrine, as well as a portion of the compilation.”
Having discarded a portion of the texts, they composed others.
Abandoning their names, gender, requisites,
modes of dress, and natural state, they made them into something else.
“There are seventeen schools that have split, and one school that has not split;
all together with that which has split, they become eighteen.
Like a great banyan tree, the Elder is the supreme among those who hold doctrines.”
Neither deficient nor redundant, it is the teaching of the Victor alone.
Like birds born upon a tree, they are but the remnants of the doctrine;
in the first century [after the Buddha’s passing], there was none [of such corruption], and in the second century as well.
“Seventeen distinct doctrines arose within the teaching of the Conqueror.

Furthermore, six other teacher-doctrines also arose—namely, the Hemavatikas, Rājagirikas, Siddhatthikas, Pubbaseliyas, Aparaseliyas, and Vājiriyas—but these are not intended here. As for the previous eighteen...
In the Dispensation that was proceeding according to the doctrines of various teachers,
King Asoka, having gained faith, gave one hundred thousand daily for the worship of the Buddha, one hundred thousand for the worship of the Dhamma, one hundred thousand for the worship of the Saṅgha,
one hundred thousand for his own teacher, the Elder Nigrodha, and one hundred thousand for medicine at the four gates.
By bestowing five hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he caused great gain and honor to circulate within the Dispensation.
The sectarians, their gain and honor destroyed so that they received not even so much as food and clothing, and longing for gain and honor, went forth among the monks;
yet they maintained their respective views, saying: "This is the Dhamma, this is..."

"Discipline is the Teacher’s instruction," they proclaim. Even though they do not receive formal admission, they cut their own hair, don yellow robes, and wander about the monasteries; when it is time for performing the Uposatha ceremony and other rites, they enter into the midst of the Saṅgha.
Although they are being restrained by the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, they [persist] in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya.
Failing to remain steadfast in their practice, they gave rise to many forms of growths, stains, and thorns within the Dispensation.
Some worshipped fire; some practiced austerities in the five heats; some circumambulated the sun;
and some, saying, "We shall split asunder the Dhamma and the Vinaya," exerted themselves in various ways. At that time, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
He did not perform the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies with them. For seven years, the Uposatha was suspended at the Asoka Monastery.
Although the king strove, thinking, "I shall have it performed by command," he was unable to do so;
rather, when many monks were deprived of life by a foolish minister who held wrong views, the king became remorseful. He [reflected] upon that remorse...
Desiring to pacify that corruption which had arisen within the Dispensation, he asked the Saṅgha, "Who indeed is capable in this matter?
Having heard, "Venerable Moggaliputtatissa, Great King," and by the word of the Saṅgha having summoned the Elder from Mount Ahogaṅga,
[he observed] the Elder’s power through the display of a miracle of psychic potency.
Free from doubt, he asked about his own remorse and pacified his regret.
The Elder, while staying right there in the royal park, had him master the ritual procedure (*samaya*) over seven days.

Having mastered the procedure, on the seventh day he convened the community of monks at the Asoka Monastery, had them enclose it with a screen-wall (*sāṇipākāra*), and sat down within that screen-wall.
Having grouped the bhikkhus according to their respective views—grouping those with the same view together—and having summoned each group of bhikkhus one by one, he asked:
"Venerable sirs, what does the Perfectly Enlightened One teach? Thereupon, those who held the doctrine of eternalism said, "He teaches eternalism.

Likewise, those who held the doctrine of partial eternalism, the doctrine of finitude and infinity, the doctrine of evasion through sophistry, the doctrine of fortuitous origination, and the doctrine of conscious existence [spoke accordingly].

They were proponents of non-perception, proponents of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, proponents of annihilationism, and proponents of Nibbāna in this very life—it was said of them, "proponents of Nibbāna in this very life.

Because the King had already grasped the true nature of the teaching, he realized, "These monks are not members of other sects," and having given them white robes, he caused them to disrobe. They numbered sixty thousand in all.
Then, having summoned other bhikkhus, he asked: "What is the doctrine of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, venerable sir?
"He is an analyst of doctrines, Great King. When this was said, the king asked the Elder: "Is the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, an analyst of doctrines, venerable sir?
"Yes, Great King. Thereupon the king thought: "Now the Dispensation is pure, venerable sir; let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus perform [the Uposatha]."
Having provided for protection, he entered the city. The Saṅgha, being in harmony, assembled and performed the Uposatha.

At that assembly, there were six million monks. In that gathering, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, for the purpose of warding off all those matters that had arisen at that time and those that would arise in the future, [proceeded].
Following the very method imparted by the Teacher, the Tathāgata himself established the framework (*mātikā*);

and while analyzing it, he brought forth five hundred suttas for his own school and five [hundred] for opposing schools, thus totaling one thousand suttas, and spoke this *Kathāvatthu* treatise, which crushes the doctrines of others and is characterized by its enduring nature.

Then, having selected sixty thousand bhikkhus from among those who upheld the three baskets of scripture (*tipiṭaka-pariyatti*) and possessed the analytical knowledges (*patisambhidā*), [he convened the council].

Taking one thousand bhikkhus, just as the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Yasa had compiled the Dhamma and the Vinaya, so too did he compile [this work], purifying the stains from the Dispensation and performing the Third Council.
While compiling the Abhidhamma therein, he included this treatise exactly as it was spoken. Therefore it is said:
“Because it serves as the basis for discourses such as those concerning persons (*puggala*),
he taught the *Kathāvatthu* treatise in brief.
By means of establishing the matrix (*mātikā*) alone, it was established in the Surālaya [monastery].”

By such statements as, “In the sense of ultimate actuality, form is apprehended,” the fifty-sevenfold classification of phenomena has been shown according to the aggregates, bases, elements, and faculties.

Here, however, it has come down as “Certainly (āmantā). Regarding this, the intended meaning is as follows:
for the Blessed One, taking up that discourse which was spoken later on—namely, the sutta that has come down stating, “There is a person practicing for his own welfare”—since the Blessed One...
One who speaks the truth does not utter speech with the intent to deceive, nor does he teach the Dhamma based on hearsay and the like;
rather, having personally realized the world together with its devas through direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), he proclaims it.

Therefore, taking the conviction that whatever he has stated—namely, "there is a person practicing for his own welfare"—exists precisely in the sense of the real and the ultimate (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*), one should accept it as such.
He [the opponent] admits, saying, “Yes.
Then, not giving him an opening for such ambiguous speech or for fallacious argumentation, the proponent (sakavādī) says: “That which is the ultimate truth,” and so forth.
Herein, this is the intended meaning: that which is subsequently described as “conditioned and unconditioned, formed and unformed, eternal... [and so on].
The seventy-sevenfold classification of phenomena, beginning with form and so forth, has been presented as being "eternal," "with signs," or "signless" in this way;
it should not be understood merely by way of conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*), nor by way of hearsay and the like.

Rather, it is the "actual reality" (*saccikaṭṭha*) precisely because of its own intrinsic existence, and the "ultimate meaning" (*paramattha*) because it is directly verifiable for oneself. With reference to this, he said: "That which is the actual reality..."
“The ultimate meaning; therefore, that person is found in the sense of a real and ultimate fact.
Here, “therefore” (tato) is an instrumental expression; thus, the meaning here is: “Therefore, by that sense of a real and ultimate fact, that person is found.
This is what is meant: by way of such modes as being subject to change (ruppana), or by way of such modes as having conditions (sappaccaya).
If that which is the true and ultimate reality is apprehended, is the person also apprehended in that same manner?
"It should not be said so"—this is the opponent's denial. For he denies it because he does not accept such a person.
Herein, this is the word-division: "It should not be said so," or "Indeed, it should not be said so. This applies to both as well.
The meaning is that it should not be stated in this way.

"Understand the refutation" refers to the statement of the proponent's own side. Since your subsequent admission that [the position] should not be stated contradicts your prior admission that it should be stated, and since your subsequent [admission] does not cohere with your prior one, for that reason as well you have incurred a refutation. That...

The meaning is: "Accept the censure, the fault, and the offense. Having thus caused him to acknowledge the censure, he now makes it clear by means of its establishment, as well as through the methods of leading forward and backward, and of bringing down and attributing, saying:
"If indeed a person is apprehended," and so forth. In that context, "if indeed a person is apprehended" means: if a person is apprehended; if a person exists.

The meaning is "in the sense of the ultimate reality of the actual state. First, this is called *anuloma-ṭhapanā* (establishment by way of conformity), which possesses the characteristics of establishing the opponent's position, bringing about their refutation, and assigning [the fault] to them.
In the phrase "tena vata re," etc., it is called *anuloma-pāpanā* (bringing about by way of conformity) because the refutation is brought about within the conforming position.
Therein, *tena* is a word expressing reason; *vata* is a word of conviction or acceptance; and *re* is a word of address.
This is what is meant: "By that [reason], O you who must indeed speak, O friend, O gentle-faced one, for that very reason it must certainly be spoken.
The passage beginning with "What you say therein... and so forth is called "the imposition of the favorable" (*anulomaropanā*), because a refutation is imposed upon the favorable side.
At the end of that, the word "wrong" (*micchā*) should be brought forward, preceded by the words "this is yours" (*idaṃ te*). This...
"Those are wrong"—this is the meaning here. Furthermore, this very point has already been established in the subsequent text.

As for the passage beginning with "But it should not be said," etc., because the position that was rejected—namely, "It should certainly not be said so"—has been set forth, this is called "contrary establishment," which is characterized by the application of refutation and the imposition [of consequences] in reverse order. The passage beginning with "But indeed, they do not... pertains to the contrary position.

Because it brings about a defeat (*niggaha*) in reverse order, it is called "reverse bringing-about" (*paṭilomapāpanā*). Furthermore, the passage beginning with "what you said there," etc., is called "reverse attribution" (*paṭilomaropanā*) because it attributes the defeat to the opponent in reverse order.
Here too, at the conclusion, the words "this is yours" (*idaṃ te*) must certainly be supplied before the word "wrong" (*micchā*).
This same method applies in similar instances hereafter as well.
In this regard, the summary meaning from the beginning is as follows:
If a person is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, then indeed, sir, it must be said that he is apprehended.

As for what you said there—"In the first question, he may be said to be 'apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact,' but in the second question, he cannot be said to be 'that very same person'..."
“...is apprehended,” this is wrong for you. Thus, first of all, there are the establishing, the leading astray, and the attribution in the direct order.
Then, in the second question, one cannot say, “He is apprehended from that”; nor can it be said in the first question either.
As for what you say here—that in the first question it can be said, “He is apprehended in the sense of a real, ultimate fact”—[that is not so].
And in the second question, one should not say, “That person is apprehended from that [basis]”;
thus, “This is wrong for you”—in this way there are the setting aside, the leading to, and the charging in reverse order.

Thus, because the refutation has been stated both in direct and reverse order, as well as the four leadings-to and chargings, this is called the "direct pentad" beginning with "it is apprehended. And here, although...
Two refutations (*niggaha*) are established: one through the application of the charge in direct order (*anuloma*), and one through the application of the charge in reverse order (*paṭiloma*).

However, since the person (*puggala*) is found here only in the phrase "Understand the refutation," and because the first refutation is applied in two ways based on that first thesis, this is considered a single refutation; thus it is called the "first refutation."
2. Now follows the method of opposition (*paccanīkanaya*). In this context, the question belongs to the opponent (*paravādin*).
For he, having grasped the position that "there is a person practicing for his own welfare," asks thus while refusing to accept [the proposition] that "he is not apprehended.

The proponent (*sakavādin*) admits [the non-apprehension], saying "Yes," on the grounds that [the person] is not apprehended in the same way that phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are apprehended. Again, the other...
He spoke the words beginning with "that which is the true sense" (*saccikaṭṭha*) with reference precisely to the true sense intended by himself.

Alternatively, he spoke thus even after combining conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) and ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) together. The proponent of the [opposing] view rejects [the question] with "No," because the person exists as a designation based on the aggregates (*upādāpaññatti*), and because the question was asked by combining the two truths together.
Now, although he first accepted non-apprehensibility by way of ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*),
and later rejected it— either by way of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) or by way of a mixed mode— the opponent,
relying on a quibble (*chalavāda*) based on the mere commonality of the term "non-apprehended," claims: "That which was first admitted by you has been subsequently rejected."

Just as one might offer a counter-argument to a quarrel, he said, "Understand the counter-measure (*paṭikamma*)," while performing a counter-measure against the act of censure (*niggahakamma*) committed by himself. Now, just as in the *Anulomapañcaka* [Sutta],

where the proponent established his position and made the refutation evident through the methods of leading forward (*pāpanā*) and leading backward (*āropanā*) in both direct and reverse order, so too is the counter-measure made evident.
He said, "If [the opponent] says 'it is a person' while doing so," and so forth. This should be understood in meaning according to the method explained below.

However, since "setting aside" (*ṭhapanā*) here consists merely in setting aside the opponent's position to show, "This is your fault," it does not constitute the making manifest of a refutation (*niggaha*) or a counter-argument (*paṭikamma*); rather, it is by means of "attributing" (*pāpanā*) and "imputing" (*āropanā*).

It becomes manifest. Therefore, this should be understood as one tetrad by way of the four modes consisting of the attainment and the application [of the factors] through direct and reverse order, because the counter-measure (*paṭikamma*) has been performed; thus it is called the "tetrad of counter-measures. 3.
Having thus performed the counter-measure, now, regarding that refutation which was made by the proponent (*sakavādin*) within the direct pentad (*anulomapañcaka*):
Showing the state of wrongdoing based on that very same fallacious argument, he said:
"But if you think... and so forth. Therein, "But if you think" means "if you think.

"It should be said" is stated with reference to the admission "Yes, it should be said" given in response to the challenge. "And it should not be said" refers, however, to the denial "No, it should not be said."
It has been stated. By that [reason], "therein for you" means: by that cause, you yourself are not apprehended therein;

thus, regarding the position—"admitting it to be so," [the answer is] "Yes, sir"—one who admits it in this way is "to be refuted in this manner. That is, one who again denies it, saying "it is not so," is to be refuted in this way.
"Then we shall refute him" means: then we shall refute him who is worthy of such refutation.
"And you are well-refuted" means that because you have been refuted by your own opinion, you are indeed well-refuted.
Having thus shown his state of being refutable, [the Blessed One] now says "If it be so," etc., while actually refuting him.

In this context, establishing, leading to a conclusion, and attributing [the fault] should be understood according to the method already explained below. At the conclusion, however, [he says]: "This of yours is wrong."

The meaning is: "This statement of yours is false. Because a refutation has been made through four modes by means of this fallacious argument (*chalavāda*), it is called the "tetrad of refutations" (*niggahacatukka*). 4.
Even after having thus effected the refutation, [the opponent now says]: "If this refutation made by me according to your own tenet is a 'bad refutation' (*dunniggaha*),"
Showing that "the refutation which you previously made against me in the *anuloma-pañcaka* was also difficult to refute," he said, "If this too is difficult to refute," and so forth.

Therein, "if this too is difficult to refute" means: either "this argument of yours has been poorly refuted by me," or alternatively, "this refutation made by me against you is difficult to refute. "In that very same way, one will see therein" means: even in that case...
"See it thus: by her, the refutation was made against me below.

Having now demonstrated that refutation which was made below by the proponent of his own position (*sakavādin*) through the words beginning with "it must be said," and leading that refutation toward the state of being no refutation at all, he said, "And we do not [admit] by you," and so forth.
In that context, regarding the phrases "And we do not [admit] by you there" and "by that admission of yours as a reason," etc.:

This is the meaning: because that refutation you have made against me is difficult to refute, therefore, even though we—by means of this very admission in the "Fivefold Conformity" (anulomapañcaka)—acknowledge it thus with the words "We agree," and even when a further denial is made with the words "It is not so," one should still not be refuted by saying "Understand the refutation.
You have refuted me, who am thus not to be refuted; by such [a method]...
"But we have been poorly refuted by this refutation.
Now, in order to show that refutation with reference to which he said, "And we have been poorly refuted," he said: "If a person... [etc.
...this is your error. Thus, this [refutation] has been demonstrated through four methods of attributing faults, both in direct and reverse order.

Because it has been brought forward, it is called the "tetrad of bringing forward. Now, the so-called "tetrad of refutation" begins with the words, "It should not be refuted in this way," and so forth. Therein, "it should not be refuted in this way" means: it should not be refuted in the manner that I have been refuted by you; for such a refutation as this— [The text continues: ...is not a valid refutation. Why? Because this [position] is established by means of a reason (*hetu*) and an example (*udāharaṇa*). For instance, when one says, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," the opponent might say: "If sound is impermanent because it is produced, then the 'being produced' must exist prior to the sound. But since the 'being produced' does not exist prior to the sound, how can sound be impermanent on account of being produced? Therefore, your reason is non-existent (*asiddha*). This is not a valid refutation. Why? Because the reason "because it is produced" is stated in reference to the state of sound at the very moment it is being produced (*utpadyamāna-avasthā*), not in reference to a time before its production. Thus, the reason is not non-existent. Furthermore, the example "like a pot" is stated in reference to a pot that is currently undergoing production, not in reference to a pot that has already ceased. Therefore, the example is not non-existent either. Consequently, this is not a valid refutation. This is called the first member of the tetrad of refutation. Next, the second member: "It should not be refuted by means of a reason. Suppose someone says: "Sound is permanent because it is incorporeal (*amūrta*), like space (*ākāśa*). The opponent might say: "If sound is permanent because it is incorporeal, then the 'incorporeality' must exist prior to the sound. But since the 'incorporeality' does not exist prior to the sound, how can sound be permanent on account of being incorporeal? Therefore, your reason is non-existent. This is not a valid refutation. Why? Because the reason "because it is incorporeal" is stated in reference to the state of sound at the very moment it is being perceived, not in reference to a time before its perception. Thus, the reason is not non-existent. Furthermore, the example "like space" is stated in reference to space as it is currently perceived, not in reference to a space that has already ceased.

Therefore, the example is not non-existent either. Consequently, this is not a valid refutation. This is called the second member of the tetrad of refutation. Next, the third member: "It should not be refuted by means of an example. Suppose someone says: "Fire is cold because it is a substance (*dravya*), like water. The opponent might say: "If fire is cold because it is a substance, then the 'substantiality' must exist prior to the fire. But since the 'substantiality' does not exist prior to the fire, how can fire be cold on account of being a substance? Therefore, your example is non-existent. This is not a valid refutation. Why? Because the example "like water" is stated in reference to water as it is currently perceived, not in reference to water that has already ceased. Therefore, the example is not non-existent. Consequently, this is not a valid refutation. This is called the third member of the tetrad of refutation. Next, the fourth member: "It should not be refuted by means of a conclusion (*nigamana*). Suppose someone says: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; whatever is produced is impermanent, like a pot; therefore, sound is impermanent. The opponent might say: "If sound is impermanent because it is produced, then the 'being produced' must exist prior to the sound. But since the 'being produced' does not exist prior to the sound, how can sound be impermanent on account of being produced? Therefore, your conclusion is non-existent. This is not a valid refutation. Why? Because the conclusion is stated in reference to the state of sound at the very moment it is being produced, not in reference to a time before its production. Thus, the conclusion is not non-existent. Consequently, this is not a valid refutation. This is called the fourth member of the tetrad of refutation. Thus, these four members are collectively known as the "tetrad of refutation. It should be understood that in all cases, a refutation is invalid if it fails to address the actual meaning intended by the proponent. One should not attempt to refute a position by attacking something other than what was actually stated. This concludes the explanation of the tetrad of refutation.
The state of being difficult to refute has been established by me. "By that" means for that reason;
because this refutation is difficult to refute, therefore, when you say to me, "If it is a person... [etc.
...this is wrong for you," the meaning is that this refutation of yours is incorrect. "By that" means for whatever reason this is wrong, for that reason.
The refutation made by you is wrong; that which was done by me as a counter-argument (*paṭikamma*) is well-done.
Furthermore, this presentation of the path of discourse by way of the fourfold counter-arguments and so forth is also well-done.

Thus, regarding the fivefold series of conforming arguments beginning with "a person is apprehended," there are the fourfold series of counter-arguments, refutations, lead-ins, and lead-outs beginning with "is not apprehended."
It should be understood that by way of this [sequence], what is called the "fivefold positive-negative" (anuloma-paccanīka) has been demonstrated.
Up to this point, while the proponent maintains his original position, the opponent achieves victory through a sophistical argument based merely on the commonality of the terminology used.
2. Explanation of the Negative-Positive (paccanīka-anuloma).

6. Now, in order to demonstrate how the opponent’s position is easily defeated by the True Dhamma of the proponent when that position exists, the pentad of questions on the inverse and the conformable—beginning with "the person is not apprehended"—is commenced.
Therein, the question in the inverse sense belongs to the opponent, referring to the ultimate reality as the true state of things consisting of the divisions of form and so forth.

The admission belongs to the proponent (*sakavādin*). Regarding the question of the opponent (*paravādin*), "Is that which is called 'the ultimate point of truth' (*saccikaṭṭha*) [found]?"—this is asked with reference to conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) either in its pure form or as mixed with the ultimate truth (*paramattha*).

The denial, "It is not so," belongs to the proponent, because it cannot be said that [the ultimate point of truth] is not found by way of convention, or because the question is confused due to being based on a mixture [of the two truths]. This is the admission.
"He rejects" means: understand that the opponent's statement "the person is not apprehended" is a mere verbal convention, such as the words "refutation" (*niggaha*) and so forth.
Thus, based on the second position, it should be understood that there is a second refutation: "this person is not apprehended.
In this way, a refutation has been leveled by him through a quibble (*chala*).
7–10. Now, in order to demonstrate victory for his own position through the Dhamma and justice, the proponent (sakavādī) asks according to the method of conformity (anulomanaya).
The opponent (paravādī) grants an admission based on his own tenet (laddhi). Without allowing room for that tenet, the proponent questions again from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha).
The opponent rejects [the person] because, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no person (puggala).

Following that, the entire passage beginning with "Understand the counter-argument for the purpose of showing one's own victory through the Dhamma and justice" is the statement of the proponent himself.

In this regard, the meaning of all four sets concerning the counter-argument (*paṭikkamma*), refutation (*niggaha*), leading [to the conclusion] (*upanayana*), and withdrawal (*niggamana*) should be understood according to the method explained below. Thus, regarding this pentad of counter-arguments beginning with "The person is not apprehended":

By means of the fourfold sets consisting of "it is apprehended" and so forth, as well as the refutation, the censure, the leading forward, and the conclusion, what is called the pentad of the inverse and the direct order is demonstrated.
Thus, these two pentads regarding the first sense of reality (saccikaṭṭha) have been demonstrated.
In that regard, within the first pentad, the refutation made by the proponent against the opponent is a sound refutation; however, the refutation made by the opponent against the proponent—
A victory achieved by oneself through a counter-argument based on fallacious speech (*chalavāda*) is difficult to win;

a defeat inflicted upon one's own proponent by an opponent is difficult to overcome. However, a victory achieved by oneself against an opponent through a counter-argument based on right speech (*dhammavāda*) is an easy victory.
This is the first point concerning the true meaning (*saccikaṭṭha*). Regarding this, it is said:
“In the first pentad, the refutation of the opponent’s argument is pure;
however, in that same case, the counter-refutation victory is impure.
In the second pentad, the refutation of one’s own argument is impure.”
But for him, there is purity, and in that case, it is a victory through counter-action.
Therefore, in both instances, victory belongs to our own side;
for victory by means of the Dhamma is true victory—how could there be victory by means of what is not the Dhamma?
“In this instance of the ultimate truth (*saccikaṭṭha*),
adorned by two sets of five, victory and defeat are stated solely by way of the wholesome and unwholesome.
In all subsequent instances of the ultimate truth, the wise one— ”
"In this very way one should discern both victory and defeat.

Commentary on the Positive-Negative Order (Anuloma-Paccanīka)

11. Having thus expanded upon the pure and actual meaning (*suddhika-saccikaṭṭha*), the passage beginning with "Again, a person is apprehended" is now commenced in order to expand upon that very same point through other methods such as the "locations" (*okāsa*) and so forth.
Therein, the question belongs to the proponent of one's own school (*sakavādin*), while the admission belongs to the opponent (*paravādin*).
Again, the inquiry "In all places" refers to the body; it is the proponent of one's own school who [raises] the objection regarding the fault of viewing the self (*attāna*) in form (*rūpa*).
Having seen the fault in the position that "the soul is one thing and the body another," there is the rejection of the opponent's view.

The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated below for the fivefold sequence of the positive-negative analysis (*anulomapaccanīka-pañcaka*). However, the text is abbreviated.
In that context, because it was said with reference to the body that "it is not apprehended anywhere," [the opponent might think] that it is apprehended outside of the body.
...one falls [into error]. Therefore, the negation in the counter-argument belongs to one's own side (the proponent);

whereas, having first granted [a point] and subsequently denying it, the counter-measure belongs to the opponent (the adversary) by way of a quibble (*chala*). The rest is self-evident. 3. The Meaning of Time and Reality (*kāla-saccikaṭṭha*)

In the second method, the opponent’s inquiry—"all [are] such"—refers to both the times of previous and subsequent births, as well as the times of being currently living and having attained final nibbāna.

This constitutes the fault of contradiction for the proponent’s own position, such as in the statements "that khattiya is that brahmin" and so forth, regarding those who are currently living and those who have attained final nibbāna.
Having seen the fault of the absence of distinction (*visesābhāva*), there is the refutation of the opponent. The remainder is exactly as stated in the first method.

The remainder is exactly the same.

14. Thus, having first distributed these three "fivefold sequences of the direct and the inverse" (*anulomapaccanīka-pañcaka*) in their proper order by way of the direct sequence alone, the passage beginning with "A person is not apprehended" is commenced in order to distribute them again by way of the inverse sequence alone in the "fivefold sequence of the inverse and the direct" (*paccanīkānuloma-pañcaka*).
Therein, regarding the inverse [sequences] which have been brought together in brief in the Pāḷi of the direct fivefold sequence, it is according to the method already stated.
The meaning of the "reverse" (paccanīka) sequence—which has been abbreviated in the text—should be understood according to the same method as that stated for the "direct" (anuloma) sequence.

Up to this point, for each of the four "points of actuality" (saccikaṭṭhāna)—namely, the pure [sequence] and these three—the meaning is established by way of two types of reverse sequences: the direct-to-reverse and the reverse-to-direct. This...
It should be understood that what is designated as "the eight-faced" (*aṭṭhamukha*) refers to a method of posing questions.

"In this manner, regarding the fourfold question, through the division into two sets of five..."
This is the method of debate known as the Eightfold Face, which has been explained.
In that [method], there are eight negations; of these, four are legitimate and four are illegitimate. In all cases, one should follow the position of our own school.
“Victory and defeat indeed belong everywhere to the opponent.

17–27. Now follows the reconciliation with the ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha*) regarding form and the other aggregates. Therein, "And as for form":
the question of the proponent (*sakavādin*) is asked with the intention of whether the person (*puggala*) is likewise apprehended in the ultimate sense as form is apprehended;
the affirmation of the opponent (*paravādin*) is based merely on accepting the verbal expression "there is a person. If, for you, form...

The opponent’s inquiry—"Does a person exist as an ultimate reality (paramatthato) like [the aggregates], or does it follow that the person is something other [than the aggregates] just as form is other than feeling and the rest?"—is directed against our own position.
The opponent’s rejection of this, having seen its contradiction with the *Samaya-sutta*, is directed against the other's position. The remainder is clear in meaning.
However, from the perspective of the Dhamma, here [the person is established] by way of the seventy-fivefold ultimate reality (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha).

In the section based on one's own position (*sakavādīpakkhamūlaka*) within the positive-negative method (*anulomapaccanīka*), fifty-seven positive pentads (*anulomapañcaka*) are shown; the counteraction tetrads (*paṭikammacatukka*) and so forth are abbreviated.
In the section based on the opponent's position (*paravādīpakkhamūlaka*) within the negative-positive method (*paccanīkānuloma*), fifty-seven reverse pentads (*paṭilomapañcaka*) are shown;
the counteraction tetrads and so forth are abbreviated. Therein, by the mere statement, "It was said by the Blessed One... [the following is established].

The opponent’s challenge is that the Blessed One spoke thus in order to demonstrate the existence of the person (*puggala*) and the cognizability of matter (*rūpa*) by way of their true and ultimate meaning (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha-vasena*), while simultaneously making it known that the two are distinct.

The proponent’s rejection is based on the fact that the question regarding the identity or difference between the conventional (*sammuti*) and the ultimate (*paramattha*) is one that must be set aside (*ṭhapanīya*). The rest here is also clear in its meaning.
Commentary on the Correlation of the Pure [States].
6. Commentary on the Correlation by Way of Simile (28–36).
Now follows the correlation with the ultimate truth (*saccikaṭṭha*) by way of similes together with form and the other aggregates. Therein:

The two questions—the question regarding the difference between form and feeling based on their commonality of apprehension, and the question regarding the difference between the person and form based on their commonality of apprehension—belong to the proponent (sakavādin).
Both acknowledgments belong to the opponent (paravādin).
Based on the commonality of apprehension admitted by the opponent, the proponent’s pursuit of the difference between form and the person, just as with form and feeling, is the refutation.

The other [side]. The rest here is also clear by way of meaning. By way of the principles (*dhamma*), however, nine hundred and twenty refutations (*niggaha-pañcaka*) are shown on the side of our own position (*sakavāda*) through the wheels (*cakra*) rooted in form (*rūpa*) and so forth. How so? First, regarding the aggregates (*khandha*):
there are four wheels rooted in form, and likewise four rooted in feeling and the others, making twenty. Regarding the bases (*āyatana*): in those rooted in the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*)...

There are eleven in the *cakra* [of the eye], and likewise in the remaining ones; thus, there are one hundred and thirty-two. In the case of the elements (*dhātu*), there are seventeen in the *cakra* based on the eye-element, and likewise in the remaining ones;
thus, there are three hundred and six. In the case of the faculties (*indriya*), there are twenty-one in the *cakra* based on the eye-faculty, and likewise in the remaining ones;
thus, there are four hundred and sixty-two. In this way, all together amount to nine hundred and twenty-five pentads of suppression (*niggaha*).

37–45. Even on the side of the opponent, since form (*rūpa*) is perceived, [the opponent] first establishes the admission of the distinctness of form, feeling, and so forth by way of conformity (*anuloma*).

Then, relying on the Sutta stating "there is a person" (*atthi puggalo*), he superimposes a commonality of perception between the person and form, etc., by way of trickery (*chala*), and thus carries out the application of their distinctness.
The rest here is also clear in meaning. From the standpoint of the nature of things (*dhammatā*) as well, on the side of our own position...
In the manner already described, nine hundred and twenty methods of counteractive measures (*paṭikamma*) have been shown.
This concludes the correlation with the ultimate truth (*saccikaṭṭha*) by means of similes together with form and the other aggregates.
7. Commentary on the Correlation According to the Fourfold Method.
46–52. Now, since that which is found in the sense of the actual ultimate truth must be one of the fifty-seven things found in the sense of the actual ultimate truth among form and so forth—
either residing in form and so forth, or apart from form and so forth,
or being the support for form and so forth— it is with this fourfold method that the correlation of the actual ultimate truth is commenced.

In this context, the proposition "form is the person" is the position of our own school (sakavādin). The denial "it is not so," due to the fear of the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi), is the response of the opposing school (paravādin).
The attribution of defeat belongs to our own school. But is this logical? Is it not the case that even what is stated as "form is feeling" must likewise be denied?
Yes, it must be denied; however, that [denial] is because feeling possesses a nature other than that of form.

It is not [the case that the person is other than the aggregates] because of the non-existence of anything other [than them]. Furthermore, this [teacher] does not accept that the person is other even from a single phenomenon such as form;
therefore, it is logical. Moreover, this line of inquiry—beginning with "Is form the person?

and continuing through to "Is the faculty of one who has final knowledge the person?"—is undertaken with reference to the entirety of ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*). However, it is impossible to state all of this together at once by way of their individual characteristics.

"It is not possible"—this is established merely as a characteristic of the formal inquiry (*anuyoga*) according to the system of the treatise (*tanti*). By means of this, the wise clarify the meaning.
However, one who desires to debate, having grasped this characteristic, should speak in such a way that no opportunity for the opponent arises.
Thus, it is indeed appropriate because the characteristic of the formal inquiry has been established according to the system of the treatise. By this...
The meaning is to be understood according to this method in all applications.

However, there is this distinction: just as it is appropriate to say that consciousness exists "in form" based on the physical basis (vatthurūpa) or based on one great primary element (mahābhūta) supported by three great primary elements, why do you not likewise [admit] a person in form?

And just as it is appropriate to say that all phenomena—such as feeling and the rest, or the four formless aggregates, or even Nibbāna alone—are "other than form" when analyzed according to their distinct classes, why is it not so for the person?
And just as it is appropriate to say, by way of dependence, that "form [is] in feeling... up to ... in consciousness" with respect to forms originated by mind, why is it not so for the person?

"Are they indeed such persons?"—in all these inquiries, however, the opponent's position is rejected both out of fear of the annihilationist view (*ucchedaditthi*) and because it contradicts the established doctrine (*samaya*).

The rest here is clear in meaning. As for the doctrinal aspect (*dhammata*), however, by applying four [negations] to each of the fifty-seven points of actual reality (*saccikaṭṭha*), there are two hundred and twenty-eight [positions] by way of refutation.
Five hundred [arguments] have been shown. On the side of the opponent as well, there are exactly that many by way of counter-argument.
As for the admission of the proponent when "a person" is mentioned here, that is by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*) as it appears in the Sutta.

The rejection in such cases as "form is the person" and so forth is because the question regarding the view of a real body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is to be set aside (*ṭhapanīya*). The opponent's counter-argument is likewise by way of the sixfold method (*chala*).
The Concordance of the Fourfold Method.
The discussion of the concordances is finished.
8. Explanation of the Application of Characteristics.

53. Now follows what is called the "application of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇayutti*). In this regard, with the exception of *nibbāna*, everything else is the ultimate reality in the sense of the truly existent (*saccikaṭṭhaparamattha*).
Because it is bound by conditions, it is "with conditions" (*sappaccaya*); because it is produced by the coming together of conditions, it is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*);
because it ceases after arising and is thus eternally non-existent, it is "non-eternal" (*asassata*); and because there exists a "sign" (*nimitta*) consisting of the cause for its arising—

Nibbāna is signless because it lacks the characteristics mentioned above; it is without conditions, unconditioned, eternal, and signless—this is the characteristic of the ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha*).
Therefore, if the person (*puggala*) is also an ultimate reality, it too must possess this characteristic.
With this in mind, the eight questions beginning with "Is the person conditioned? were posed.
The negation belongs to the opponent, while the affirmation belongs to one’s own proponent. Here, the passage beginning with "Understand the refutation" (*ājānāhi niggahaṃ*) has been abbreviated.
Thus, on the side of one’s own proponent, in the case of the positive-negative method, eight sets of five should be understood by way of the positive alone. 54.
On the side of the opponent, in the case of the negative-positive method, there are likewise eight [sets] by way of the negative alone. In that regard, because the opponent...
Conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) has been established by way of the Suttas; yet, conventional truth lacks the state of having conditions and so forth.

Therefore, the denial of things as they truly are is the position of our own school (*sakavādin*). However, everything that should be stated by way of the "Sophistry" (*chala*), such as "Understand the counter-argument," and so on, is likewise abbreviated here.
The commentary on the discussion of the application of characteristics is finished.
9. Commentary on the Purification of Statements (Vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā) 55–59.
Now follows the purification of statements. In this regard, as for the statement that "a person is apprehended," that—
"A person is apprehended for the sake of purification; a person is apprehended. This is the question of the proponent (sakavādī). Its meaning is as follows:
regarding these two phrases, "a person" and "is apprehended," do they have the same meaning or different meanings?
If, first of all, they have different meanings, then just as matter is one thing and feeling is another, so too the person would be one thing and that which is apprehended would be another.
[He] falls into [this position]. Then, as for the identity [of terms]: just as that which is *citta* (mind) is *manas* (intellect), so too the person (*puggala*) is apprehended;
thus he falls into [this position]. Therefore I say this to you: "If, for you, that person is apprehended, then this being the case, whatever is apprehended must be the person.
Do you accept this? Thereupon, because the proponent of the person (*puggalavādin*) [cannot maintain his position regarding the person's nature...]
He maintains that the person is apprehended, but not that the nature of a person belongs to the forms and so forth that are being apprehended. Therefore, he said: "The person is apprehended;
for some it is apprehended as a person, for others it is not apprehended as a person," and so on. The meaning of this is:
"The person exists" and "the person is apprehended" because of the Teacher’s statement; however, that which is apprehended—

Not every person [is such], but rather some persons are [persons] and some are not persons. In this context, the syllable *ke* has the sense of "some" (*ko*), and the syllable *hi* is merely a particle. "Some persons, some are not persons"—this is the meaning here. This is what is intended:
for even among the aggregates such as form and so forth, whatever dharma is apprehended is indeed a person; in that regard—
"A person is indeed a person. But among form and the other aggregates, there is no such thing as a "person" at all. To this, the proponent of the [opposing] view said:
"In some cases a person is apprehended; in some cases he is not apprehended. The meaning of this is as follows:

if, given the identity of meaning between the two phrases "a person is apprehended" and "[he is] not apprehended," that phenomenon which is admitted to be apprehended is not different from the person, [then...]
"One person exists, another does not; among persons, some are apprehended, while others are not"—this is what you fall into.
Do you accept this? Not wishing to admit the non-apprehension of a person, he rejects it by saying, "It is not so.
From here on, everything beginning with "Understand the refutation" is abbreviated. However, in detail:
It should be understood that the same method applies to such expressions as "the person is a real entity" (*saccikaṭṭha*) and so forth.

For all these are merely synonyms for "is apprehended. Furthermore, since this is the admission of the proponent of the person—that "the person is apprehended in the sense of a real entity and ultimate meaning"—therefore, just as he holds the view that "the person is apprehended," he likewise falls into the position that "the person is a real entity."

Furthermore, as for his tenet that "the person exists" (*puggalo atthīti*), this is merely a synonym for "being present" (*vijjamāno*). Therefore, all these statements have been proven consistent. 60.
Regarding what was stated at the conclusion—"The person exists; not every person exists"—and so forth, the intended meaning there is as follows:
As for that which was asserted by the opponent—"The person exists; the person exists in some cases, and does not exist in others"—it is as follows...

This has been stated; since, in terms of its meaning, it amounts only to this—that "the person exists" and "not every person exists"—therefore, having caused the proponent to accept that, he now interrogates him as follows.
For you have adopted the view that "the person exists" based merely on the statement, "There is a person practicing for his own welfare," just as [you accepted] by the Blessed One...
This has been stated; likewise, it has also been stated as "non-existent" in such passages as, "Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as empty.

Therefore, just as you hold the view that "the person exists, though not every person exists," so too would it follow that "the person does not exist, though not every person does not exist. Do you accept this?
Then, not accepting it, he rejects it by saying, "It is not so. The rest of the procedure regarding the refutation and so forth here should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the clarification of the statements is finished.
10. Commentary on the Application of the Formulations.

61–66. Now follows what is called the "Investigation of Designation" (*paññattānuyoga*). For the proponent of the person (*puggalavādī*) designates the person as possessing form (*rūpin*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and likewise as formless (*arūpin*) in the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*).

To refute that tenet of his, all the questions belong to the proponent of our own side (*sakavādī*), while the admission and the denial belong to the other. For when [the opponent] says "possessing form," [it is because of] the existence of the aggregate of form (*rūpakāya*).
When it is said "one who possesses desire" (*kāmī*), he denies [the person] because of the absence of one free from passion (*vītarāga*) and because of the non-existence of such a designation.
When it is said "one who is formless" (*arūpī*), he affirms [the person] because of the presence of the formless aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) and because of the existence of such a designation.
In both methods, the term "being" (*satta*) refers to the person (*puggala*).
This was stated by way of synonyms. 67.

Now, because he maintains that in the passage "contemplating the body in the body" (kāye kāyānupassī), the body is one thing and the person is another, the following inquiry—"Is it the 'body' (kāya) or the 'physical frame' (sarīra)?
and so forth—is posed by our own school (the Sakavādī) in order to refute that tenet. In this regard:
"Having made the body dear" means having made the body something to be cherished, something to be clung to, brought into a state of unity, and not to be divided;

this is the meaning of "I ask. "This very one" (eseso) means he is that very same person. There is also the reading "ese ese," which has the same meaning as "eso esoyeva. "Of one kind" (ekaṭṭhe) means of one kind.
"Equal, of equal portion, of the same sort" (same samabhāge tajjāte) means equal, of equal portion, and of the same nature. Here, it is merely a matter of words.
[The question is] "Is there a difference? But in terms of meaning, he asks: "Is this the body itself? The opponent, not seeing any diversity, admits, saying "Yes.

The same method applies to the questions "Is it a person? or "Is it a soul? However, when asked, "Is the body other [than the soul]?", he admits it because he holds such a view regarding the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).
But when asked, "Is the soul other [than the body]?", he [refuses to answer] because he cannot reject the Sutta spoken directly [to that effect].
Being unable [to answer], he disparages [the question]. Beyond that, the passage beginning with “Understand the refutation” (*ājānāhi niggahaṃ*) and so forth is of obvious meaning. 68.

However, on the side of the opponent's position, when asked whether the body is one thing and the person another, the proponent of our own position rejects it because it is a question to be set aside (*ṭhapanīya-pañha*). The opponent then makes a rejoinder by means of quibbling (*chala*). That too is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the application of designations (*paññattānuyoga*) is finished.
11. Commentary on the Investigation of Gati (Destinies) 69–72.
Now follows the investigation of death and rebirth-linking by way of the revolution of destinies.

In this regard, because the proponent of the person (puggalavādī), relying on such suttas as "That person, having wandered for at most seven times," maintains that it is the person who wanders, [the following is addressed].
He speaks having adopted a particular tenet; therefore, [the opponent] hastens toward him to shatter that tenet—this is the question of the proponent (sakavādin).
In this context, "hastens" means he transmigrates, performing coming and going. The admission is made by the opponent according to his own tenet.
The inquiry beginning with "That person" and so forth belongs to the proponent, while the refutation belongs to the other. In that regard, "he" means "that very same one."
The meaning is as follows. Thus, when questioned [whether the soul is] the same [as the body], he rejects it out of fear of the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

When asked if it is another, he does so out of fear of the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). When asked if it is both that and another, he does so out of fear of the partial-eternalist view (*ekaccasassatadiṭṭhi*). When asked if it is neither that nor another, he does so out of fear of the view of endless equivocation (*amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhi*).
Furthermore, when questioned about all four questions simultaneously, he rejects them all out of fear of all four views. Then again...
Showing those suttas on the basis of which his own doctrinal position (*laddhi*) arose, he said, "In that case, it is the person (*puggala*) who wanders," and so forth.

76. Again, the proponent of our own side (the Sautrāntika), with the intention of asking, "Is this one who wanders according to your doctrine the very same single entity in both this world and the next?"—having fixed the identity with the word "that very same"—asked him.
[The opponent], fearing the charge of eternalism (*sassata-bhaya*), rejected it; yet, being pressed further, he spoke firmly again.

When questioned in that same manner, he admits it because the person is not something other than a state of being (*bhāva*), and there is even a sutta stating, "Having passed away from there, he has reappeared here," and so forth.
When asked, "Is he himself a human? he denies it, because a human does not possess the state of being a deva.
Again, when questioned, he admits it on the basis of such suttas as, "At that time, I was the teacher named Sunetta."
Then the proponent of his own view, demonstrating that the statement [regarding] the diversity of rebirths among gods and humans is false, said: "Having been a human," and so forth.

(78) Therein, "In this way death will not come to pass" means that, such being the case, death will not occur. From here on, the diversity of the inquiry should be understood by way of the diversity of individual existence (*attabhāva*), such as "yakkha" or "petti.
(82) "Khattiya," and so forth, are stated by way of birth and by way of physical defects such as missing limbs.

87. "It should not be said again": when questioned by an opponent, the first admission [of the proponent] is based on the fact that one who exists here does not go to the next world by way of rebirth;
the second admission belongs to that same person, because even in another existence, a stream-enterer does not abandon the state of being a stream-enterer.
The statement beginning with "If it be so" (*hañci*) and so forth belongs to the opponent.
88. Furthermore, the proponent’s own position consists in demonstrating the absence of human status for one who has been reborn in the deva world.

89. Regarding the subsequent statement, "He is not another, he is not departed": here, "not another" means identical in every respect; "not departed" means not departed even in a single respect. He says "it is not so" because there is an absence of human status for one reborn in the deva world. 90.
Having again made his position firm, he assents to the tenet that "that very same person wanders on," as in the passage beginning with "one whose hand is cut off."
It is stated for the purpose of refuting the tenet that "one who has not departed runs on" by means of seeing the disappearance of the physical form (*ākāra*).

In this context, "one whose toes are severed" refers to one whose big toes have been cut off. "One whose tendons are severed" refers to one whose major sinews have been cut. Regarding the passage beginning with "possessing a physical form" (*sarūpa*) and so forth:
in the first question, he rejects [the notion] with reference to the non-accompaniment [of consciousness] with this material body (*rūpakāya*).
In the second case, he asserts [this] with reference to a person in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
For according to his tenet, that being enters the mother’s womb having gone there in its own form. Then that form of his breaks up.
He asks: "Is that very life-principle (*jīva*) which goes together with the body designated as 'form' the same as that body?"—thus the opponent asks.
Here, [the opponent] rejects [the view that the soul departs from the body] because it contradicts the Suttas and because of the disposal of the corpse.

Regarding the phrases "possessed of feeling" and so forth, he rejects them with reference to rebirth in the non-percipient realm (*asaññūpapatti*), while he accepts them with reference to other forms of rebirth.
That which is called the "life-principle" (*jīva*) is that which goes along with the body, designated by such things as feeling. What of this?

He asks whether that very soul is that body. Regarding the tenets "that soul is that body" and "the soul is one thing, the body is another," it is intended that all five aggregates are meant by "body.
The opponent rejects this on the grounds of contradiction with the Suttas. 92.

In the first question among those beginning with "Is it formless?", he rejects it with reference to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). In the second, [he rejects the idea that] the formless [attains] form.

He affirms with reference to one being reborn. When he asks, "Is the life-principle other than that body which is reckoned as form, [and] having abandoned it, the formless one wanders on?", he asks whether that body is one thing and the life-principle another. The other rejects this because it contradicts the Suttas.
In the cases of "without feeling" and so forth, he rejects with reference to existence as perception (*saññī-bhava*), but he affirms with reference to another mode of rebirth.
"Another [entity] lives" means: having abandoned the body known as feeling and so forth, that which wanders about without feeling and without consciousness—what is that other body of yours?
Thus he asks, "Is the life-principle another? The other rejects this on the grounds of its contradiction with the Suttas.
(93) Regarding the statements "form wanders about," etc., what are those aggregates such as form upon which you designate a person (*puggala*)?
He asks whether, while that person transmigrates, that form also transmigrates.

The opponent rejects this, because the statement "beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving transmigrate and wander on" refers only to a sentient being (satta) as the one who transmigrates.
When questioned again, [the proponent replies] that since there is no person apart from phenomena such as form, when that [person] transmigrates...
He asserts, based on the perception that "one must run about by means of that form. The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.
94. Regarding the statements "form does not run about" and so forth: since you say that the person is not form, yet that very person runs about, I therefore ask you:
what do you mean by "form does not run about"? When the other [the opponent] says that it is the person who runs about...
He denies that it is possible to transmigrate by means of form (*rūpa*) which has become a basis for clinging (*upādānabhūta*);
yet, when questioned again, he admits it because of the statement regarding the transmigration of beings (*sattā*). The rest here is self-evident.
As for the meaning of the verses, according to the Venerable’s view, it is like a shadow depending on a tree, or [fire] depending on fuel (*indhana*).

And like fire, the person exists dependent upon the aggregates. If, when there is no further wandering through form and the other aggregates, that person of yours were to perish along with those aggregates breaking up—this being the case, it would be the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*);
you would fall into the view of annihilationism. This is an unwholesome view which was avoided by the Buddha. As for the one who says, "The ascetic is an annihilationist..."
"Gotama"—this is spoken figuratively; he shows that he does not say [the person exists].
Furthermore, if that person were not destroyed when those aggregates are destroyed, then, such being the case, the person would be eternal. From that, it follows that he is exactly equal to Nibbāna.
"Exactly equal" (*samasama*) means exceedingly equal, or equal by way of equality, or equal precisely through the state of equality. Just as Nibbāna...
It neither arises nor breaks up; thus, that person is exactly equal to it.
