The investigation into death and rebirth-linking by way of the revolution of the destinies is finished. End of the commentary on the investigation.
12. Commentary on the Investigation into Designation by Dependence (Upādāpaññattānuyoga) 95.
Now follows the investigation into designation by dependence. Herein, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādin), while the denial of the admission belongs to the opponent (paravādin).
For [the opponent] holds that [designation exists] just as there is shadow in dependence upon a tree, or fire in dependence upon fuel.
If he intends that the designation, the description, and the comprehension of a person (puggala) are based upon form and the other aggregates, then, when asked, "Is it based upon form?

he admits it. Furthermore, just as a shadow is impermanent like the tree from which it is derived, and fire is impermanent like the fuel from which it is derived—so too, for you, the person derived from form and the other aggregates must likewise be impermanent like those very forms and so forth.
When asked whether [the person] is impermanent, he rejects it by standing upon his own tenet.

97. Regarding such statements as "blue form" or "derived from blue," he rejects them because he does not accept the identity of the person with the blue form, nor its multiplicity due to the existence of many blues and so forth within a single body. 98.
Regarding the statement "wholesome feeling," here too he rejects it because he does not accept identity with the feeling, nor the existence of many wholesome feelings within a single continuum.

Not desiring multiplicity by way of that [method], he rejects it. In the second method, because of the presence of such statements as "skilled in the path," he acknowledges it with reference to the sense of being "expert.
When asked about "together with its fruit" and so forth, he rejects it because such a conventional expression does not exist for him. 99.
On the side of the unwholesome, he acknowledges it with reference to the sense of being "unexpert."

100. He asserts [the position] with reference to its indeterminate nature by way of eternalism and so forth within the category of the indeterminate (*abyākata*). The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated below. 104.

Regarding the phrases "dependent on the eye," etc., he asserts [the person exists] because of the presence of such conventional usage as: "One who possesses eyes, like one avoiding uneven ground... [should] avoid evils. He rejects [the existence of the person] because he does not accept the cessation of the person through the cessation of the eye and so forth.
107. Regarding "dependent on form" and "dependent on feeling," other dyads, triads, and tetrads rooted in form should also be understood here.
Since, however, the designation of a person (puggala) is based upon the aggregates (khandha), he therefore admits that it is a designation based upon two, three, four, or even five [aggregates].
Yet, because two or five [aggregates] do not exist within a single continuum (ekasantāna), he rejects [the idea of a person as a separate entity].
This same method applies to the sense-bases (āyatana) and so forth as well.

112. Now, in order to show that—just as the designation of something is established based on something else, and just as the impermanence of that [basis] entails the impermanence of the designation, and its distinctness from it is thereby proven—so too does this apply to that person (*puggala*), he says: "Just as a tree," and so forth.
In this context, "based on" (*upādāya*) means depending upon or coming from; the sense is "not without that. But the opponent, not desiring it to be so, [objects].
He rejects [the proposition] while standing upon a particular tenet (*laddhi*).

115. *Nigaḷo* means a chain-bondage. *Negaḷiko* refers to one who is bound by that; "one who possesses form" (*rūpavā*) is so called because whoever possesses form is "one who possesses form. Therefore, just as it is not the chain... [etc. ...the meaning is that it is something other than "one who possesses form. 116.

In the passages beginning with "in mind, mind," etc., mindfulness of mind (*cittānupassanā*) is intended with reference to states such as "with lust" (*sarāga*), etc., by way of the mind being "with lust" and so forth.

He makes a formal admission (*paṭijānāti*). When questioned according to the method beginning with "Is he born?", he rejects [the question] because he does not accept the momentariness of the person (*puggala*).
When asked whether [the person] is "that same" or "another," he rejects it out of fear of the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism (*sassata-uccheda*).
Furthermore, when asked whether one should say "boy" or "girl," he admits that it should be said out of fear of cutting off worldly convention (*lokavohāra*).
The rest here is quite clear. 118.
Now, wishing to establish his position in another manner, the opponent says: "It should not be said that a person is apprehended," and so forth.
Regarding this, "it should not be said" means: what is the use of this extensive inquiry into designations based on the aggregates? First, say this:
Is it not to be said that "a person (puggala) is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact"?
When the proponent (sakavādī) says, "It is so," the opponent replies, "Is it not the case that he who sees... and so forth. In this context, "he" refers to the person;

"that" refers to the form (rūpa); "by which" refers to the eye; "he" refers to the person; "that" refers to the form; and "by which" refers to the eye. This is what is meant: Is it not the case that he...?
"The person who sees a form with a particular eye is that person.

Although the proponent [of the opponent's view] admits that it is the eye itself—which serves as the support for visual consciousness—that sees the form, and likewise the ear itself that hears the sound... pe...
and consciousness itself that cognizes mental objects, yet [he maintains]: "The Arahant has an eye; he sees..."
However, he admits by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*), saying, "An *arahant* [perceives] a form with the eye," and so forth.

Then, once the opponent has established that the person (*puggala*) must be spoken of by relying on that fallacious argument (*chalavāda*), [the respondent] turns that very argument around and says, "The person is apprehended," and so forth.
In that context, "he who does not see" refers to a blind man or a being without consciousness (*asaññasatta*).
One reborn in the formless realm who has attained cessation does not see, even though he is not blind, except at the time of seeing.
The same method applies to the remaining sections as well. The rest should be understood according to the meaning based on the text itself.
(122) In this collation of suttas, it is said that "he sees form" because the divine eye has form as its objective domain. In the second section...
Because of the statement, “I see beings,” he says that one sees a person. On the third occasion, because of the view that “having seen form, one discerns the person,” he says that one sees both.

However, since among the fourfold classification of the aggregate of form—namely, what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—it is only the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) that is included under "that which is to be seen," therefore the proponent of his own position...
“He poses the inquiry: ‘Is form the person? Is the person form? Are both form and the person? Its meaning is indeed evident.
This concludes the commentary on the inquiry into designation by way of clinging. 13. Commentary on the Inquiry into Personal Effort.

123. Now follows the application concerning human effort (*purisakāra*). In this regard, the opponent asks based on the thesis that "when there is karma, there must necessarily be an agent of that [karma].
The proponent agrees, asserting the existence of such karmas. Again, the opponent asks, "Is there an agent and one who causes [the agent] to act?
Here, "agent" (*kattā*) refers to the doer of those karmas; "one who causes to act" (*kāretā*)— [refers to one who instigates the agent].

One who causes [an action] to be done by means of methods such as commands and instructions. Now, since the opponent asks "who is the agent" (*kattā*) with reference to a person (*puggala*), and not merely to the instrument of action, the denial belongs to the proponent (*sakavādī*). 124.
Regarding the phrase "the agent of that is the one who causes it to be done": if, in this context, the agent of whatever is perceived is a person (*puggala*), [then the following applies].
"They are perceived; does another person who is both the doer and the instigator of that [action] also exist?"—this is the meaning.
The opponent, not desiring it to be so, rejects it out of fear of the doctrine of creation by a Supreme Lord (*issaranimmāna*). Being questioned again, he says:
"Since parents indeed give birth to a person, bestow a name upon them, and nourish them, they are therefore his doers. And furthermore...

He acknowledges this with reference to the meaning that spiritual friends or teachers who instruct one in various branches of knowledge and fields of craft are called "those who cause [the action] to be done.
What is intended is that his own prior action alone is both the doer and the causer of doing.

125. By the phrase "of that very one," he asks this: if for every agent of actions there is an agent, and for that agent there is another agent, and for that too another, then—this being the case—it would necessarily follow that by each preceding person a subsequent person must be made;
and thus, by that person who is the agent of the actions, another person must be made in the future, and by him as well...
There is no making an end of suffering for one who is "other"; there is no cutting off of the cycle of existence; there is no parinibbāna without conditions.
Since suffering, which is bound to conditions, would be absent due to the absence of conditions, that which is called Nibbāna would not exist for you.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "of that very [action]," if action were not merely action, then its agent—
"There is a person; there is an agent of that [action], and an agent of that as well"—thus there is a succession of persons (*puggala-paramparā*).
This being the case, the meaning is that the "making an end of suffering" which was previously stated by means of the non-occurrence of the cycle of kamma would not exist.
Not accepting this, the opponent rejects it. Hereafter, in other instances where the agent is asked about in general terms, [the same applies].

It is with reference to the person (*puggala*) alone that it is said, “the doer and the instigator,” and not with reference to the conditions (*paccaya*). For there are no conditions for the great earth and so forth. 135.
The question, “Is there another who is the doer of good and evil kamma? is rejected out of fear of views such as “the self possesses volitional formations” (*saṅkhāravantaṃ attānam*).
136. The passage beginning, “The result is found,” and so forth, is intended to shatter the position of one who demonstrates the person by way of the experiencer of the result.
It has been stated. In this context, the question "one who experiences the result" (*vipākapaṭisaṃvedī*) is from the opponent;

the denial, based on the fact that there is no experiencer other than the occurrence of the result itself, is from our own side (*sakavādissa*). Again, the question is from our own side, and the admission is from the other.
Regarding the phrase "the experiencer of that": since that which is to be experienced must be experienced by the experiencer of the result, [the opponent asks] "the experiencer of that."
The name is the result, but the person is not the result; therefore, the opponent’s position is rejected.

When questioned again, because he stands upon the basis of meritorious results, the opponent admits it with reference to such an experience as when a mother kisses or embraces her son, or a wife her husband, thinking, "I am experiencing the result."

"Of this very [person]" means: if the result were not merely the result itself, but rather there were a person who experiences it, and another who experiences that one, and yet another who experiences that one—in this way, there would be a succession of persons.
This being the case, the meaning is that the "making an end of suffering" which was described as occurring through the non-occurrence of the round of results would not exist.
From this point onward, the meaning should be understood according to the same method explained below in the questions concerning the experience [of results] by way of commonality.

142. The question, "Is there one who experiences the ripening of wholesome and unwholesome kamma as something other [than oneself]? is rejected out of fear of the view that "the self possesses feeling," and so forth.
143. The passage beginning with "divine happiness" is intended to show the ripening of wholesome and unwholesome kamma by way of classifying it.

This has been undertaken. All of this should be understood according to the method already stated below. Furthermore, in this context, the Proponent’s rejection of the "experiencer" (paṭisaṃvedī) should be understood as being by way of the person (puggala) alone, and not by way of the feeling itself (vedayita).
For the arising of feelings that take the great earth and so forth as their object is not denied.
170. “The agent, the one who causes to act, and the experiencer of the result,” and so forth, is introduced by way of the mixed method (*vomissakanaya*).
Therein, regarding the statement “He acts” and “You call him the agent and the experiencer”: does that very same person act, and does that very same person experience?
This inquiry belongs to the proponent of our own position (*sakavādin*); the rejection [of it] is made by the opponent (*paravādin*) out of fear of contradicting the Sutta.

171. Again, when questioned according to such suttas as, “One rejoices here and rejoices after passing away,” he admitted that very same [self-made] view. Then, forestalling an opportunity for him to speak, the proponent of our own position (sakavādī) stated: “Pleasure and pain are self-made. 172.
In this context, the statement “another does it” was spoken by way of questioning whether the agent and the experiencer are different.

Thereupon, the opponent (paravādī), having rejected it out of fear of contradicting the Suttas, was questioned again: “Having done it while being a human, one experiences the result while being a deva.”
One who conceives [a view] asserts it. However, when questioned on the basis of one who holds such a doctrine—that pleasure and pain are produced by another—he subsequently rejects it.
"He is one and the other is another" is stated by way of questioning whether the agent and the experiencer are identical or distinct. Thereafter, the opponent...
Having rejected [the position] solely out of fear of contradicting the Suttas, when questioned again, he admits both of the previous two methods combined.
However, because one who holds such a view falls into the position that pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by another, when questioned again on that account, he rejects it once more.
(176) "He does not do it" is stated by way of rejecting both the identity and difference between the agent and the experiencer. From that...
Having rejected [the opponent's position] by way of contradiction with the Sutta, the adversary, being questioned again, admits it while thinking: "Since a human being,
having performed the karma for rebirth in the world of the gods, does not experience the result while still being a human, nor does someone other than the one who performed the karma experience it,
therefore the experiencer is neither that same person as the doer, nor is he someone else."
"Is this merely a matter of obtaining [results]?"—one who speaks thus falls into the view that pleasure and pain are not self-caused, not caused by another, but have arisen fortuitously;
therefore, when questioned according to that [view], he again denies it.

Furthermore, in this method of synthesis (*vomissaka-naya*), the meaning should be understood from the beginning according to this same method. For this proponent of the person (*puggalavādī*) [asserts] both the agent of karmic actions and...
Since he accepts a feeler, it follows that he must either be identical with the agent, or the feeler must be one thing and the agent another, or both must be the same, or neither must be the same.
While pursuing this very line of inquiry, the proponent states all four alternatives beginning with "He who acts [is the same as he who feels]. The rest is exactly as previously described.
At the conclusion, however, all four questions were asked together.
In that regard, the denial, the admission, and the resulting fallacy of self-agency (*sayaṃkatādi*) are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

From here on, without stating "good and evil deeds," they are presented through the alternative formulation "kamma exists" and so forth, according to the method stated below. Of those too, [the explanation] is as follows: ...as stated below.
The meaning should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
This concludes the commentary on the application of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
"The Chapter on the Beautiful" (*Kalyāṇavagga*) is also a name for this very section.
14. Exposition of the Application of the Higher Knowledges (Abhiññānuyogavaṇṇanā) 193.

From here onwards, there is the accomplishment of Arahantship by means of the application of the higher knowledges and so forth. In that regard, when the proponent has assented with "Yes," the opponent [says]:
"There is no attainment of specific distinctions such as the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*) with respect to external matter not bound to the sense-faculties."

Thinking, "Since these exist internally, there must therefore be a person who produces psychic powers (iddhi) and so forth," he said, "Is it not the case that someone exercises psychic power? and so on. All of this is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the application of the higher knowledges (abhiññā).
15–18. Explanation of the Inquiry into Relatives, etc. 197.

Now, "mother," and so forth, is the inquiry into relatives (*ñātakānuyoga*). "Khattiya," and so forth, is the inquiry into birth (*jātianuyoga*). "Householder" or "renunciant" is the inquiry into practice (*paṭipattianuyoga*).
"Deva" or "human" is the inquiry into rebirth (*upapattianuyoga*). "Stream-enterer," and so forth, is the inquiry into penetration (*paṭivedhānuyoga*).

It is also called "the pursuit of the noble ones. All of these [terms] have their meanings already explained. However, the phrase "having been an Arahant, not an Arahant" is not mentioned here because it would constitute a futile question.
206. "The four pairs of persons," and so forth, refers to the pursuit of the Saṅgha; that too has its meaning already explained.
209. "The conditioned," and so forth, is an inquiry into the true nature of reality (*saccikaṭṭha-sabhāva*). In this context, "the third alternative" is the question of the proponent (*sakavādin*).
The denial is that of the opponent (*paravādin*), because such a true reality does not exist. When questioned again, the affirmation refers specifically to the person (*puggala*).
211. Even in the question "Is the person other [than the aggregates]?", the negation is directed at that very same person who does not accept otherness from the conditioned aggregates. 212.
The passage beginning with "The aggregates are conditioned" is stated to show the conditioned and the unconditioned by their own nature, for the purpose of asking about otherness. 213.
The passage beginning with "Form is conditioned" is stated to show the aggregates by way of analysis, for the purpose of asking about otherness.

214. "The arising of a person" is the question of the proponent (sakavādī). The opponent's (paravādī) admission is based on such suttas as, "Subject to birth, subject to aging, and likewise subject to death.
However, he does not accept its conditioned nature; therefore, he rejects it. 215.

When questioned again in the manner beginning with, "Is no arising perceived?", he admits that the arising and so forth of a person are untenable, based on such statements as, "For only suffering comes into being; suffering stands and passes away."

216. "Regarding 'atthatthamhi': *attha* is said to mean Nibbāna. In that regard, he asks, 'Does it exist? If it exists, eternalism follows; if it does not exist, annihilationism follows. Not desiring either of these two, he later rejects [the question].
Explanation of the inquiry regarding kinsmen and so forth. 19. Explanation of the inquiry regarding penetration and so forth."
217. Dependent upon existence (*bhava*), there arise questions concerning rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).

218. Regarding the question of one experiencing feeling (*vedanā*): one who experiences feeling and has discerned that feeling understands it as a practitioner (*yogāvacara*), whereas the foolish worldling (*bālaputhujjana*) does not understand it.
224. The questions on the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and so forth have their meaning already explained.
226. Regarding the verse from the *Pārāyana*: "Behold the world as empty," the meaning is: "Examine the world of the aggregates by way of their emptiness of a [substantial] being.

228. "Does a person behold?"—this is a question posed by one of our own school. For the opponent holds the view that the one who beholds according to the verse "Behold the world as empty" is a person (*puggala*); therefore, he asks him thus. "Together with form... [and so forth].
"Together with the form-body (rūpakāya). The meaning is: "not having emerged from that.

Having first granted this on the basis of the fivefold existence (pañcavokāra), he then, when asked whether they live [without it], rejects it for fear of contradicting the Sutta. "Without form" (vinā rūpena):

having first granted this on the basis of the fourfold existence (catuvokāra), he then, when asked about another way they live, rejects it for the very same reason—fear of contradicting the Sutta. "'Having gone within'..."
And the phrases “having gone outside” and “with form or without form” are descriptive terms for what was stated previously.
In this context, “situated inside” means situated within the form; the meaning is that one remains by way of the very delimitation of the form, without having gone either this way or that.
“Having gone out” means having transcended the delimitation of the form; the meaning is that one is no longer dependent on the form.
231. "Non-self" (*anattā*) means devoid of a self (*attan*), a life-principle (*jīva*), or a person (*puggala*). The meaning is that not even a single dhamma is a person.

Thus, the meaning of all the suttas should be understood according to the method stated in the *Āgama-aṭṭhakathā* (Commentaries on the Scriptures). Here, however, we shall speak only of what was intended by the underlying intention (*sandhāya-bhāsita*).
237. Regarding what was said by the Blessed One, beginning with "a jar of ghee," etc.: "All teaching, according to its literal expression, [is to be understood] in terms of its meaning..."
This has been brought forward for the purpose of showing that [the term] should not be taken [in its literal sense].
For just as a vessel made of gold, being a transformation of gold, is called a "golden vessel," there is no such thing as a "ghee-vessel" that is a transformation of ghee made by taking ghee;
rather, the vessel into which ghee has been poured is what is called a "ghee-vessel. This is the meaning here.
This is the meaning. The same principle applies to the "oil-jar" and so forth. Just as Nibbāna is permanent and stable, food or rice-gruel are not like that.

However, because it is established by way of a formal provision—namely, "we shall give this day after day"—without setting a time limit, it is called "permanent food" (*niccabhatta*) or "stable rice-gruel" (*dhuvayāgū*); this is the sense in this context.

In such passages as “There is a person practicing for his own benefit,” the person does not exist in the same way that phenomena such as form exist by way of their individual and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
However, when form and the other aggregates are present, there arises the conventional designation “one of such a name” or “one of such a clan.
Thus, by means of this worldly convention, worldly consensus, and worldly terminology, it is said that “there is a person”; this is the meaning here. As it has been said:
The Blessed One said: “Citta, these are indeed worldly designations, worldly expressions, worldly conventions, and worldly descriptions.
However, the phenomena such as form (rūpa) exist because they can be described by way of their individual and general characteristics even apart from worldly consensus;

this is the meaning here. Now, the Buddhas have two ways of speaking: conventional discourse (sammutikathā) and ultimate discourse (paramatthakathā). Among these, [terms such as] a being (satta), a person (puggala),...

Discourse concerning conventional designations (*sammuti-kathā*) refers to such terms as "deity" (*deva*), "Brahmā," and so forth. Discourse concerning ultimate reality (*paramattha-kathā*) refers to such terms as "impermanent," "suffering," "non-self," the aggregates (*khandhā*), the elements (*dhātuyo*), the sense bases (*āyatanāni*), the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānā*), and the right efforts (*sammappadhānā*), and so forth.
In this context, when it is said by way of conventional teaching that there is a "being" (*satta*)... pe ...or a "Brahmā," [one must] know and penetrate [the underlying reality].
If one is able to set forth and seize the victory of Arahantship, the Blessed One addresses that person from the very beginning as a "being" (satta), a "person" (puggala), a "creature" (posa),
a "god" (deva), or a "Brahmā. This is because, through the teaching of ultimate truth,
upon hearing any one of such terms as "impermanent" or "suffering," they are able to know, penetrate, set forth, and seize the victory of Arahantship.

He is able to do so. To one who understands through the discourse on conventional reality (*sammuti*), he does not first speak of the ultimate truth (*paramattha*) such as "it is impermanent" and so forth.
Rather, having awakened them through the discourse on conventional reality, he subsequently speaks of the discourse on the ultimate truth.
Likewise, even for a being who understands through the discourse on the ultimate truth, he does not first speak of the discourse on conventional reality.
In the *Paramatthakathā*, however, one first explains the ultimate truth (*paramattha*) and afterwards speaks of conventional discourse (*sammutikathā*).
For one who, by nature, speaks of the ultimate truth right from the beginning, the teaching becomes harsh in its form.
Therefore, the Buddhas speak of conventional discourse first and afterwards speak of the ultimate truth. Even when they speak of conventional discourse, they speak only the truth.
They speak only of what is natural, not falsely. Even when speaking of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), they speak only of what is true, what is natural, and not falsely. For it is said:
“The Fully Enlightened One, the best among speakers, proclaimed two truths:
conventional (*sammuti*) and ultimate (*paramattha*); a third is not found.”
In this regard:
“Conventional speech is true, being the cause for worldly consensus;
ultimate speech is true, being the suchness-characteristic of phenomena.”

Another method: There are two ways in which the Blessed One teaches—the teaching in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, and the teaching in terms of conventional designation (*sammuti*), by way of "a jar of ghee" and so forth.
For the Blessed One does not overstep conventional designations. Therefore, one should not form a dogmatic attachment based merely on the words, "There is a person. For the Teacher—
“Without overstepping conventional designation, the ultimate truth has been revealed;
one should not run beyond common usage. Therefore, any other wise person, when revealing the ultimate truth, should not run beyond common usage.”
The remainder is clear in meaning everywhere.
The Discussion on the Person (Puggalakathā) is concluded.
2. The Discussion on Decline (Parihānikathā).
1. Commentary on the Loss of Debate and Argumentation 239.
Now follows the discussion on loss (*parihāni*). [The Buddha said: "Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is still in training (*sekkha*).

"Bhikkhus, these five things... [and so forth]. Regarding the nature of decline and the nature of non-decline: "Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is still in training. "Bhikkhus, these five things... [and so forth].
Relying on such suttas as, "They lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is liberated by occasion," the Sammitiyas,
Vajjiputtakas, Sabbatthivādins, and certain Mahāsāṅghikas maintain that even an Arahant can fall away.
Therefore, whether they be these very schools or others, for the purpose of refuting the tenets of those who hold this view:
The question, "Does an Arahant fall away from Arahantship? belongs to the Sakavādin (the proponent of our own position). In this context, "falls away" refers to two kinds of falling away:

falling away from what has been attained (*pattaparihāni*) and falling away from what has not yet been attained (*appattaparihāni*). Among these, the statement, "A second time, the Venerable Godhika fell away from that temporary liberation of mind," is called falling away from what has been attained.
[And as for the statement: "Do not [be negligent], O you who seek the goal of recluseship..."

“The goal of recluseship has been lost”—this refers to the loss of what has not yet been attained. Among those [two types of loss], it is the loss of what has already been attained that is intended here.

With reference to that, the opponent’s admission is “Yes, sir. However, in their own system, they maintain that this so-called “loss of what has been attained” applies only to mundane attainments (*lokīyasamāpatti*), and not to the fruits of recluseship such as *arahantship*. This is also the case in the systems of others.
They do not admit [falling away] in any of the fruits of recluseship, in any state of existence, at any time, or for any persons.
However, since that is merely their own tenet, the teaching is further extended by the method beginning with "in all cases" and so forth, in order to shatter the entire web of such tenets.
In this regard, because the opponent has been gradually refuted, [the text now addresses] the falling away of an Arahant who is established in the fruit of stream-entry.

He does not desire it; he desires it only for one who stands in the higher realms. Because he does not desire it for one standing in the fine-material or immaterial realms, but rather desires it only for one standing in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*) due to the presence of qualities conducive to decline such as delighting in action (*kammārāmatā*), therefore, when asked "in all places," he refuses.
Then, being asked again more insistently, he speaks with reference to the sense-sphere realm.
He asserts this. For in the entire realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*), there are factors of sensual pleasure that cause decline; therefore, his tenet is that one declines therein.
In the third question, "decline" (*parihāni*) refers to those states that cause decline.

In that regard, since what is called decline consists of states such as delighting in action (*kammārāmatā*) and so forth—or specifically, sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*byāpāda*)—and these do not exist in the realms of form (*rūpabhava*) and formlessness (*arūpabhava*).
Therefore, "not indeed so" is the opponent's negation.
"At all times" is a question regarding time. In that regard, in the first inquiry, he negates because there is no decline at the time of wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
In the second, he admits it because for one who attends unwise (*ayonisomanasikāra*), there is decline at all times, whether during the night or the day.
In the third case, he rejects [the proposition] by stating that when there is an association with factors leading to decline, "decline" occurs only for a moment;
prior to that, for one who has not yet declined, and subsequently, for one who has already declined, there is no such thing as "decline.
Regarding the question "Are all [arahants] [subject to decline]?", he rejects it with reference to the first [type of arahant], the one with sharp faculties (*tikkhindriya*). In the second...
He makes his claim with reference to those of dull faculties. In the third case as well, only those of keen faculties are intended.
For it is his thesis that for all of them there is no falling away.
In the example of the treasurer, the first question belongs to the opponent, the second to our own side (the Sautrāntika). Herein, this is the intended meaning:
“As for what you asked me—‘Does an Arahant, falling away from Arahantship, fall away from the four fruits?’—in this regard I ask you a counter-question:

‘If a guild-leader, while exercising his leadership with four hundred thousand [pieces of wealth], were to lose one hundred thousand, would that guild-leader have fallen away from his leadership? Then the proponent, intending a partial loss, said:
When it was said, “Yes,” [the opponent] asks whether he has lost all his property. Since he has not actually lost it, the proponent says, “No.

Then, [the opponent], holding the view that has arisen, asks the second question concerning one capable [of falling away]: “In the same way, does an Arahant also fall away? But not from the four fruits.
The opponent states the certainty regarding the merchant’s incapacity [to fall away].

Having admitted that he does not see [the grounds for falling], yet being asked whether an Arahant is subject to falling away from the four fruits, he maintains his own tenet by taking the statement "he is fixed with enlightenment as his destination" in a superficial sense;
thus, referring to the impossibility of falling away from the fruit of stream-entry, he rejects it. However, that is merely his own tenet.
Thus far, what is called the "Method of Discussion" is completed.
2. The Exposition on the Comparison of Noble Persons and Decline. 240.
Now, the comparison of noble persons is commenced. In this regard, since some [hold that] there is decline even for Arahants—
Some maintain this even for non-returners (anāgāmi), and some even for once-returners (sakadāgāmi). However, no one at all maintains it for the stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

They maintain the possibility of falling away only for those who, having fallen from arhatship, remain in the state of non-returner or once-returner, but not for other non-returners or once-returners.
Furthermore, they do not maintain it for the stream-enterer in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, the question was asked by way of a formulaic repetition (*peyyālamukha*). In this regard, both the admission and the denial should be understood according to their respective positions.
For, regarding the question, "Does a non-returner fall away from the fruit of non-returning?", the denial is made from the perspective of those who do not accept the falling away of non-returners.
[The admission] is made from the perspective of those who maintain that one falls away from the state of a natural non-returner or from Arahantship.

Or, those who maintain that non-returners (anāgāmin) are subject to falling away (parihāni), it is on their account that this "admission" (paṭiññā) is stated; this is the methodological approach here.
Following this, all the elided passages (peyyāla) should be understood according to their meaning.
As for what is stated here—"Immediately after the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), one realizes Arahantship itself"—it is as follows:
This was said with reference to the attainment of Arahantship by one who has fallen away and is striving again.

The other [the opponent] rejects it because there is no attainment of Arahantship immediately after the fruit of stream-entry. Following that, [it is asked]: "This falling away would have to be due either to the weakness of the abandonment of defilements, or to the cultivation of the path and so forth..."
"Or because of a lack of resolute confidence, or because of not seeing the truths"—it is by way of such passages that it was said:

"To whom are the defilements more numerous [that have been abandoned]? and so forth. All of that is of plain meaning; however, the meaning of the suttas should be understood according to the method explained in the *Āgama-ṭīkā* (the commentaries on the scriptures).

262. Regarding the statement, "An Arahant liberated by occasion (samayavimutto) falls away from Arahantship": their tenet is that one with dull faculties is liberated by occasion, while one with sharp faculties is liberated non-occasionally (asamayavimutto).
However, in our own system (sakasamaye), an attainer of jhāna who has not reached mastery is liberated by occasion;
whereas an attainer of jhāna who has reached mastery, as well as all noble persons (ariyapuggala), are liberated non-occasionally in the noble liberation (ariye vimokkhe).
This is the conclusion. He, however, having adopted that personal view, falls away as one liberated by occasion (*samayavimutta*);
the other does not fall away—thus he said. The rest here is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the comparison of noble persons and falling away.
3. Commentary on the Attainment of the Sutta and the Decline 265.

Now follows the establishment by means of the sutta. In this context, "high and low" (*uccāvacā*) refers to those that are high and low according to the distinction between the superior and the inferior.

"Way of practice" (*paṭipadā*) means the path of practice (*paṭipadā*). "Proclaimed by the ascetic" (*samaṇena pakāsitā*) means illuminated by the Buddha-ascetic. For it is the way of practice leading to happiness (*sukhāpaṭipadā*).
The path with quick direct knowledge is high; the path with painful practice and sluggish direct knowledge is low.
The other two are high by one factor and low by the other. Or else, those mentioned first are high, while all three others are low.
By means of these high and low paths, they do not go twice to the further shore; that is, they do not reach Nibbāna twice by way of a single path.
The meaning [of the term *pāramitā*]. Why? Because those defilements which have been abandoned by a particular path cannot be abandoned again by that same path.
By this, he demonstrates the absence of the possibility of falling away (*parihāni*). This "ferrying across" (*pāra*) is not a virtue of a single quality;

furthermore, this "other shore" (*pāra*) is not something that can be reached by touching it only once. Why? Because all defilements are not abandoned by a single path alone. By this, [he shows] that by means of a single path...
This indicates the absence of arahantship.
"Is there anything further to be cut for what has already been cut? asks whether there is anything remaining of the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) that must be cut again.
The other [the respondent], having first denied this with reference to one of sharp faculties (*tikkhindriya*), when asked again, speaks with reference to one of dull faculties (*mudindriya*).

He admits [the point]. The proponent (sakavādī), having cited the sutta, demonstrates the state of non-existence. In this context, "flood-fetter" (oghapāsa) refers both to the flood of defilements (kilesogha) and the snare of defilements (kilesapāsa).

266. "The accumulation of what has been done" (katassa paṭicayo) means the further cultivation of the path already developed. Here too, the denial and the admission are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
267. "They lead to decline" (parihānāya saṃvattanti): regarding the five qualities mentioned by the opponent in the cited sutta, they lead to the decline of what has not yet been attained.
And they lead to the falling away from mundane attainments (*lokiyasamāpatti*). However, he observes that [these] lead to the falling away from the fruit of Arahantship already attained.
For this very reason, it was said: "There is for an Arahant delight in action" (*kammārāmatā*).

The other [teacher], having denied [this] with reference to one liberated at any time (*asamayavimutta*), admits it with reference to the other. Or rather, [the objection refers to] that which proceeds by way of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
Having rejected that [view], he admits to what proceeds in the opposite way. However, when asked about the existence of lust and so forth, he is unable to admit it. 268.
*Kiṃ pariyuṭṭhito*: by what is he obsessed, followed, or overwhelmed? This is the meaning.
In the inquiry regarding the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), the denial and admission should be understood as occurring precisely by way of those with keen faculties and those with dull faculties.

Alternatively, he may admit [the presence of] "wholesome underlying tendencies" merely on account of the commonality of the term itself. When it is said, "lust goes to accumulation," this is said with reference to that which has been abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The same method applies to hatred and delusion hereafter. However, as for personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the others, they are [abandoned] by vision (*dassana*).
Because it has been abandoned, it does not seek accumulation. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the demonstration by means of the Sutta. The Discussion on Decline is finished.
3. Discourse on the Holy Life (Brahmacariyakathā) 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Pure Holy Life (Suddhabrahmacariyakathāvaṇṇanā) 269.
Now follows the discourse on the holy life. Therein, there are two ways of living the holy life: the cultivation of the path and the going forth into homelessness.

Furthermore, there is no going forth (*pabbajjā*) among any of the devas. The cultivation of the path (*maggabhāvanā*), with the exception of the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), is not prohibited among the rest.

In this regard, those such as the Saṃmitīyas who do not even admit the cultivation of the path among the devas above the Paranimmitavasavatti devas—referring to them, the proponent of the first position asks:
"Is it not the case that [the path] does not exist among the devas? [The Buddha replied: "Monks, by three [factors]..."
"By three qualities, people of Jambudīpa surpass the people of Uttarakuru and the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Which three? They are brave, they possess mindfulness, and here [in Jambudīpa] there is the living of the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*).
Based on this sutta, the opponent’s admission—that there is no living of the holy life among the gods—arises from a particular view that has taken root. Furthermore, of these two...
The question "Are all the gods dull-witted? is asked by the proponent (sakavādī) on the basis of those things that are obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

In this context, "those who communicate by hand" refers to those who speak through hand gestures like the mute. The subsequent question "Is there [such] among the gods? is asked by the opponent (paravādī).
The affirmation is made by the proponent with reference to the cultivation of the Path (*magga-bhāvanā*). Failing to discern the intended meaning of that affirmation—
The opponent’s adherence is based on the premise of going forth (pabbajjā).
Regarding the question, "Where is there no going forth?", the denial was made with reference to the attainment of the path by householders and certain gods.
When questioned again, [the denial] was made with reference to those living in border regions and non-percipient beings.
The admission belongs to that very person. This same method applies to the questions such as "He who goes forth," and so on.

Furthermore, regarding the question "Is there [such a thing] among the devas?", the Sakavādin’s admission refers specifically to the cultivation of the Path; however, when it is said "among all devas," his own denial refers to the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*).

271. Regarding the two questions beginning with “Among humans,” the affirmation is made with reference to those of Jambudīpa. The denial should be understood as being made with reference to those living in the border regions.

“There is where there is” means: “Those gods exist, or that region exists where they are”; thus the reply of our own school (Sakavādī) is given by way of analyzing the seven locations. In this manner, all the alternating questions are to be understood.

272. Regarding the inquiry "Where does the arising of the fruit occur in the application of the Suttas?": this is the opponent's question as to where the arising of the fruit of Arahantship occurs for that Non-returner (anāgāmin).
"Right there" means in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa). "Handa hi" is a particle used in the sense of a reason. This is what is meant:
because a person who is a Non-returner realizes the fruit right there in the Pure Abodes by means of the Path developed here in this world, and does not develop another Path there.
"Therefore, there is no living of the holy life among the devas.
2. Commentary on the Concordance Regarding the Holy Life: 273.
Now, if the realization of the fruit occurs in one place by means of a path developed elsewhere, then [the same would apply] even for stream-enterers and the others.

The question regarding the connection of the terms "non-returner" (*anāgāmī*) and so forth, asked by the proponent (*sakavādī*), is intended to demonstrate the meaning of the word "might be" (*siyā*).
In this context, the opponent (*paravādī*) asserts the realization of the fruit for the non-returner, while denying the realization of the fruit for the others.

For here, one who has developed the path is called a "non-returner" and is said to have reached the final goal while remaining in this very world. Having developed the non-returner path in this world—

Based on the statement, “He is one of spontaneous birth who attains Parinibbāna there,” his tenet is that one realizes the fruit of Arahatship by way of rebirth alone, without further cultivation of the path.
However, as for the Stream-enterer and Once-returner, having cultivated the path there, they are said to be those who attain rebirth in that very place;
thus, for them, there is no returning here at all. Such is his [view] regarding the Non-returner.
When questioned about the realization of the fruit, he admits it. He denies it for others.

Regarding the question, "Does a non-returner (anāgāmī) person [realize the fruit] by means of the path cultivated there?", he denies it based on the tenet that "for a non-returner, there is no cultivation of the path there.
This is the inquiry: "Is the path cultivated, yet the defilements not abandoned?"

The admission of the proponent refers to the path of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-magga*). For by means of that path, he becomes one who has reached his final destination while remaining here [in this world].

Regarding the question, "Is the non-returner (*anāgāmī*) one who has done what was to be done?", because of the statement, "He is of spontaneous birth (*opapātiko*) and attains final nibbāna there," it follows that for him, [the goal] is attained through rebirth.

He makes his declaration with reference to the state of having duties yet to be performed and so forth. To the question "Is he an Arahant?", he denies it specifically in the case of an Arahant who attains Parinibbāna here and now.
When questioned again, he affirms it in the case of one who attains Parinibbāna there (after death).
In such passages as "Is there rebirth for an Arahant?", the meaning refers specifically to those who attain Parinibbāna there versus those who attain Parinibbāna here and now.

It should be understood as follows. When asked, "Does one who has not yet penetrated [the truth] attain final nibbāna right there?", he rejects it, desiring that the penetration to the unshakable state be achieved by means of the path developed right here.
The first example, "like a deer," belongs to the opponent; the second belongs to our own school. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The Discussion on the Holy Life is finished.
3. Exposition of the Discussion on the Specific (Odhisokathā). 274.

Now follows what is called the Discussion on the Specific. Therein, regarding those such as stream-enterers and others, by way of their various clear realizations through the vision of suffering and so forth—
They maintain that the abandoning of defilements occurs only partially and in part, just as the Saṃmitīyas and others do today.

To refute their tenet, the question "only partially" (odhiso) is posed by the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission [of this] is made by the opponent (paravādī). Again, the inquiry belongs to the proponent;
the denial follows from the opponent because of the non-existence of the state of a stream-enterer and so forth even in part.
By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Specific (Odhisoka-kathā). 4. The Discourse on Abandoning (Jahati-kathā).
1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Non-Existent (Nasuttāharaṇakathā) 279.

Now follows the discourse known as the "Discourse on Abandoning" (Jahatikathā). In this regard, there is the following tenet: "An ordinary person who has attained jhāna becomes an non-returner simultaneously with the clear realization of the truths;
for him, sensual lust and ill will were abandoned even during his time as an ordinary person. This is, for example, the view held by [certain sects].
Now, regarding the Saṃmitīyas: the question "Does he abandon [the defilements] as an ordinary person? belongs to the proponent of his own school (sakavādin), intended to refute their tenet.

However, the affirmation of the opponent (paravādin) is made from the perspective of one who does not perceive the active manifestation (*paryuṭṭhāna*) of those defilements which have been suppressed by meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Since even for those [defilements] suppressed by absorption, their absolute abandonment occurs only through the path of the Non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*), therefore, once again—
The proponent of our own position (sakavādī) maintains that there is an absolute abandonment [of the fetters], while the opponent rejects this because such an abandonment does not exist for him.
When the text says "it suppresses," the question of the proponent refers specifically to absolute suppression.
Beyond that, there occurs a comparison of the worldling (puthujjana) with one who stands on the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga); the meaning of this is self-evident.

280. When asked, "Does he thereafter stand firm in the fruit of non-returning? he admits it, referring to the non-returning of the meditative attainments (*jhāna*). When asked, "Does he stand firm in arhatship? he denies it, because the higher fetters have not yet been abandoned by means of the path of seeing (*dassanamagga*).
When asked, "Do the three paths [arise] neither before nor after one another? he denies it, because such a mode of cultivation does not exist.
Being asked again, he admits it, referring to the presence of the functions of the three paths. This is also the case regarding the questions on the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
The same method applies here. When asked, "By which path?", he says, "By the non-returner path," referring to the non-returning state pertaining to the jhānas.
Again, when asked about the abandoning of fetters, he denies it because those particular defilements cannot be abandoned by the [first] three non-returner paths.
When asked the second time, he admits it, referring to the fact that the first path itself constitutes the non-returner path for the jhānas.
The meaning here is entirely obvious.
The Discussion on Abandoning. 5.
The Discussion on "Everything Exists."
1. Commentary on the Mode of Expression: 282.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Theory that Everything Exists. In this regard, because of such statements as, "Whatever form there is—past, future, or present...
this is called the aggregate of form," it is held by some that all phenomena (dhammas), categorized as past and so forth, possess the essential nature of an aggregate (khandha-sabhāva).
“They do not abandon [it]; therefore, everything indeed exists”—such is their tenet, just like that of the present-day Sarvāstivādins.
For the purpose of purifying their tenet, the question “Does everything exist? is asked by the proponent (sakavādī).
The other [the opponent] gives his assent while standing upon the aforementioned tenet. “In all” means he asks: “Does everything exist in every body? “At all times” [means...]
He asks: "Does everything exist at all times? He asks: "In every way does everything exist?

He asks: "In all things does everything exist? "Non-conjunction" means that which is unfit for conjunction; for there is conjunction between things of different natures, but not for that which is of a single nature.
Thus, in this question, [does] form [conjoin] with feeling, or feeling with form?
Having made all non-existent things possess the single characteristic of existence, he asks: "Does everything exist?

He asks: "Even that which does not exist, does that exist?"—meaning, even that which is established as non-existent, such as the sixth aggregate (*ṣaṣṭha-skandha*) or a rabbit's horn (*śaśaviṣāṇa*), does that exist for you?
"Everything exists"—is this view a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) or is this view a right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?

By the phrase "all this exists," he asks this: "Is that view of yours which holds 'all exists' a wrong view because it is not according to reality (ayāthāvaka), whereas our view is a right view because it is according to reality (yāthāvaka)?
In this way, he asks whether [the object] exists according to your system. The other [responds] regarding all these methods, concerning the existence of the kind already described.

He rejects [the opponent's position] on account of its non-existence. Now, in all these methods, the entire classification of the paths of discourse—beginning with "Understand the refutation" and so forth—should be understood in detail.
This, then, is the propriety of debate (*vādayutti*) in this context.
2. Commentary on the Coordination of Time (*kālasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā*)

283–284. Now follows the correlation of time by way of the statement, "the past exists. Therein, "the past exists" and so forth is the correlation of the pure [factors]. "The past form exists" and so forth is the correlation of time by way of the aggregates (*khandha*).
285. "Having made present form unlovely": having set aside the past and future, one makes only present form unlovely and indivisible.
Regarding the question, "Does it abandon the state of being form?": because even form that has ceased is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

He rejects it. Regarding the statement "he does not abandon the state of being form," even in the counter-question, he admits it precisely because it is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

As for the phrase "having made a white cloth unlovely," although not every cloth is white, when one says "having made a white cloth unlovely" instead of simply saying "a cloth," there is identity of meaning with the proponent's position.

It is permitted. Regarding the question, "Does it abandon its state of being white? the proponent's admission refers to the disappearance of the color. However, regarding the question, "Does it abandon its state of being cloth?
there is a denial by that same person because the designation (paññatti) has not ceased. The same method applies to the reverse order as well. 286.
When asked, "Does the past not abandon its state of being past? [the opponent replies: "If it were to abandon it, then it would be either future or present..."
Thinking, "It might be so," he admits it. But when asked whether the future does not abandon its future state, he denies it, thinking:
"If it did not abandon it, it would remain only the future and would never reach the state of the present.

In the question concerning the present as well, he denies it because there would be the fault of its not attaining the state of the past. This is also the case in the questions on conformity (*anuloma*).
The meaning should be understood in this very same manner.

Having thus explained the pure method (*suddhikanaya*), the passage beginning with "past form" and so forth was stated in order to show it again by way of the aggregates (*khandha*). All of that can be understood by following the canonical text (*pāḷi*) itself.
This concludes the commentary on the clarification of the terminology.
288. Now follows the clarification of the statement beginning with, "Does the past exist? and so forth.

In this context, if it is asked, "Does the past exist?"—meaning, "If the past does not exist"—then the claim that "the past exists" is false; for it would be incorrect to say that the past both is and exists.
When asked whether that very same [past] is the future or the present, since its state of being present occurs only at the moment of the future...
He rejects [the first question] by means of the diversity of time, intending [the answer] in terms of non-existence.
When asked the second [question], he affirms that which was previously future before its arising, because at the time it has arisen, it possesses the state of being present.
Regarding the phrase "having been, it is; having been, it is," this refers to what you said: "having been future, it becomes present."
By speaking according to the view that "the future itself is the present," it was said: "Having been future, it becomes present. [The questioner asks:
"Does that too become after having been? The other rejects this, saying "No," because what has already become does not exist again after having been.
When asked a second time, the opponent admits it because that [dharma], having been future, while becoming present, has come to be designated as "having been, it is. Then the proponent asks him:

"If, for you, that which was future, while becoming present, has come to be designated as 'having been, it is,' does it then 'have been, it is' again—that which was future, not having been [present]?"
The horn of a rabbit, which is not existent and has never been known as "having existed and then not existing," is it also "not having existed, it does not exist" again?
With this intention, he asks the question: "Not having existed, it does not exist; not having existed, it does not exist.

The other replies: "That which does not exist, by its very non-existence, is likewise 'not having existed, it does not exist' in the future, because it does not exist in the present after not having existed."
Thinking, "Let it be for now that it exists; but from where could there be its state of having not been after having been?", he rejects [the proposition].

Regarding the question, "Is that which is present the same as that which is past?", he also rejects it on account of the difference in time, intending thereby that in the very moment of being present, its state of being past is absent.
In response to the second question, he admits that what was present in the past has become the present; because that very thing has now passed away, he says, "having been, it is.

By saying "having been, it is," you—who asserted that "having been present, it becomes past"—are doing so on the basis of the view that "the present is the same as the past," [expressing it] as "having been either present or past, it is."
It was asked: "Does that [past] become having been that [present]? The other denies it, saying, "No," because there is no further becoming after what has already become and passed away.
In the second question, since that which, having been present, becomes past, is designated as "having been, it becomes," he therefore admits it.
Then the proponent asks him: "If that very same thing, having been present, becomes past..."

The phrase “having been, it is” refers to what is conventionally designated as such; yet having been, it is again. That which is present—neither having been nor becoming past—is conventionally designated as “not having been, it is not,” like a rabbit’s horn.

With this intention, he asks the question, “Not having been, it is not; not having been, it is not,” asking whether even that [rabbit’s horn] is again “not having been, it is not. The other [responds]:
“Let it be for now that what does not exist, by virtue of its very non-existence, does not become past after having been present;
thus let it be called ‘not having been, it is not. But from where does its state of ‘not having been, it is not’ come?”—thinking thus, he rejects [the position].
This same method of application should be employed for the third question as well, when both [positions] are combined and presented together.

Another method: If that very same future thing is that present thing, then it follows that the state of being "having been" is predicated of the future in relation to the present, and the state of "not having been" is predicated of the present in relation to the future.
This being so, even the future would be called "having been," and even the present would likewise be called "having been. Therefore, we ask you this: regarding these two...
"Does each one, having been, become [the other]? The other, having rejected the question "Is that very future [state] that present state?
by the same method of rejection used previously, when questioned again, admits it by the method of admission used for the second question. Then the proponent [asks him]:
"By way of the question 'Is that very future [state] that present state?', does each one, having been..."

To one who asserts that "having been, it becomes," he asks—turning back the previously rejected question—"does it not become after not having been? Does it not become after not having been? The meaning of this is:
when you stated, "Is that very future [state] the present?", did you not, by rejecting the first question, [admit] the state of becoming for the future and the state of being for the present?
And having been, it does not exist; thus, non-existence is rejected. By that, the future is said to "not have been," and the present is said to "not have been.
In the second question, it was admitted that "that which is the future is that which is the present.
This being so, even the future has not "not been" and does not exist; likewise, even the present has not "not been" and simply does not exist. Therefore, we ask this of you.
—“Is it that each one among these, having not been, does not exist; having not been, does not exist?
The opponent, like one shrouded in total darkness on all sides, unable to see their state of “not having been, not existing,” rejects it, saying, “No, it is not so.
In the second instance as well, if that very present were that past, then the state of “existing” would have been predicated of the present in relation to the past.
Furthermore, for that which has passed away, it follows that its state of having existed in the present is reached;
this being so, even the present would be called "having existed," and even the past would likewise be called "having existed. Therefore we ask you:

"Of these, does each one exist by having existed, or does it exist as having existed? The other [responds] according to the very same method of refutation used for the question: "Is that very present the past? and so forth.
Having rejected [the first position], when questioned again, he admits to the second question by way of affirmation alone.

Then the proponent, having turned back to the previously rejected question—asking him who admitted "having been, it becomes" regarding each of those [factors] individually through the method of questioning whether "that which is present is that which is past"—asks: "Does it not become after not having been? No.
He asks, "Having been, it does not exist. The meaning of this is:
When you stated that "the present is indeed the past," did you not, by rejecting the first question, reject both the state of existing for the present and the state of having existed for the past?
Therefore, the present is called "not existing," and the past is called "not having existed."
And in the second question, you have admitted that "that which is present is the same as that which is past.
This being so, it follows that even the present does not "not having been, it ceases to be," and the past likewise does not "not having been, it ceases to be. Therefore we ask you:
"Regarding these two, is each one 'not having been, it ceases to be,' or is it 'not having been, it does not cease to be'? The opponent, being completely shrouded in darkness on all sides—
As if shrouded, not seeing their state of being "has been" (nahotibhāva), he denies it by saying "it has not been.

In the third instance as well, if that very same future thing is that present thing and that past thing; then the state of being "has been" would have been predicated of the future and present things in relation to the present and past, and the state of being "has been" would have been predicated of the present and past things in relation to the future and present.

[Otherwise] it would follow that it exists having already been non-existent. This being so, even the future would be called "having been, it exists"; and even the present and the past would likewise be called "having been, they exist.
Therefore we ask you: "Of these three, does each one exist having already been, or does it exist as 'having been'?
The other, by the very same method of rejection used for the question "Is that which is future the same as that which is present, and that which is past?"...
Having rejected [the first question], when asked again, he admits it in the second question by way of affirmation.

Then the proponent, addressing him as one who affirms that "that which is future is the same as that which is present, and that which is present is the same as that which is past," turns back the previously rejected question and asks him, using those [three times] one by one as the basis for the questions: "Does it exist having existed? and so forth.
"Having been, it is not; having been, it is not," he asks. Its meaning is this:

When you stated that "the future is that very same thing, the present is that very same thing, and the past is that very same thing," did you not, by rejecting the first question, reject the state of "being" for the future and the present, and the state of "having been" for the present and the past? Therefore, [regarding] the future and the present...
It is called "not having been. Both the present and the past are called "not having been.
And in the second question, you have admitted that "that which is future is the same as that which is present, and that which is present is the same as that which is past.
This being so, even the future has not "been," yet it is called "not having been"; and likewise, even the present and the past have not "been," yet they are called [so].
It is indeed called "it exists. Therefore, we ask him: "Is it that each one among these does not exist having not existed, or does it not exist having not existed?
The opponent, like one shrouded in total darkness on all sides, not seeing their state of "not existing having not existed," rejects it by saying, "No, it is not so.
The refutations and so forth here should be applied according to the method already stated below.
The commentary on the Purification of Words is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Past Eye, Visible Objects, and so forth (289):

In such statements as "the past eye exists," he asserts its existence precisely by way of its not having abandoned its status as an eye and so forth. However, when questioned whether it "sees" and so on, he denies it on the grounds that those [past] consciousnesses lack their respective functions.
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Past, etc.

(290) Regarding the question, "Does one perform the function of knowledge by means of that knowledge?"—because that knowledge has ceased, he rejects it, not seeing its status as a functional activity.
When asked again, [he says] that present knowledge having the past as its object [performs the function] of past phenomena.

By way of a mere hint, he asserts that because there is a function of knowledge to be performed by means of that "knowledge of the past"—which is actually just the present moment designated as "knowledge of the past" for one who knows it as such—the opponent (the proponent of his own view) does not allow him any room for ambiguity and says:
"By means of that knowledge, one fully understands suffering," and so forth. The other [responds] that these four functions are performed by means of knowledge whose object is precisely the past.

He rejects [the existence of lust] because of its non-existence. The same method applies to the question concerning the future. The questions concerning the present and the questions for cross-referencing are of obvious meaning.
291. Commentary on the Discussion of the Arahant, etc.:

In such statements as "Does past lust exist in the Arahant?", he admits it precisely while not abandoning the state of lust and so forth. In cases such as "Is he possessed of lust?", he rejects it both out of fear of contradicting the Suttas and out of fear of contradicting logical reasoning.
Commentary on the Purification of Terms (Padasodhanakathāvaṇṇanā) 295.

Having thus understood everything according to the sequence of the text, the meaning of the subsequent passage—"there may be the past, there may be the not-past"—should be understood as follows: that which is only past exists is "the past. That which is present or future...
"It exists; that does not exist for us; that is past for us. For this reason, it is "the past is indeed past," and "indeed past, it is the past";
thus, by that cause, the past is not [simply] the past, nor is the non-past the past. This same method applies to the questions concerning the future and the present.
*Commentary on the Proof by Sutta*
296. It should not be said that "the past exists, the future exists" for the purpose of establishing this by means of a sutta;

this is the question of the opponent (paravādin), and the admission (paṭiññā) is that of our own side (sakavādin). Again, based on his own tenet, "Whatever, monks, is form..."—this is the inquiry of the opponent alone.
In the second method, the question is that of our own side, and the admission is that of the other. Thus it is in all cases regarding the question.
And the admission [of the opponent] must also be understood. As for that which was shown by the opponent at the conclusion of the sutta beginning with "If,
monks, in regard to material food..."— namely, the statement "there is there the production of renewed existence in the future"—
which was intended as a proof of the existence of the future, that does not prove the existence of the future.
For that was stated there with reference to what has necessarily been developed because the causes have been brought to completion. This is the intended meaning of the sutta.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the discussion of "everything exists" is finished.
6. Discussion on Past Aggregates, etc. 1. Explanation of the Discussion on the Non-establishment by Sutta. 297.
Now follows the discussion beginning with “The past [consists of] aggregates. In this context, because they do not abandon their status as aggregates and so forth, both the past and the future...
For one who asserts existence, the opponent’s question is whether the past [aggregates] are aggregates; the proponent’s admission is "yes," because the past is included within the aggregates.
Again, the opponent’s question is whether the past does not exist; the proponent’s rejection follows because its existence has been refuted by the *Niruttipatha Sutta*.
This applies likewise to the questions regarding the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), as well as to the questions concerning the future.

Having correlated [the present] with the present, the meaning should be understood by this same method even in questions presented in forward and reverse order, as well as in questions such as "past form" and so forth. 2.
Commentary on the Proof by Sutta.

298. Regarding the statement "it should not be said in the proof by sutta," this is the question of the proponent (sakavādī). Therein, the meaning is: "there is no volition" and "these phenomena do not exist.
Since he does not accept their non-existence despite the fact that they possess the nature of aggregates and so forth, the opponent's (paravādī) admission is "yes [they exist].
Then, the proponent cites the sutta for the purpose of proving their non-existence. The second question is also [of the same nature].

The opponent’s admission is for the proponent, while the citation of a sutta is for the opponent. However, since that [citation] establishes for them only the status of being aggregates and so forth, and not their actual existence, even though it has been cited, it is as if it were uncited.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion beginning with "The past is the aggregates."
7. Discussion on Whether Some Things Exist 1. Explanation of the Discussion on Whether Some Past Things Exist 299.
Now follows the discussion on whether some things exist. In this regard, there are those who maintain that "some past things exist."
It is just as in the case of the Kassapikas. For the purpose of refuting their tenet, the question "Does the past exist?

is from the proponent (sakavādī), and the reply "A portion exists" is from the opponent (paravādī). This is the intention: "That which has not yet ripened as result exists, while that which has already ripened as result does not exist.
The inquiry "A portion has ceased" is from the proponent. Its meaning is: if...
They [assert] that some of the past exists and some does not exist;

this being the case, they fall into the position that some of the past has ceased while some of the past has not ceased, and likewise remains as it was. The same method applies to the terms "vanished" and so forth.
As for the phrase "some things whose result is yet unripened," this is because [the opponent] desires the existence of those very things whose results are unripened.

These too are indeed past. Therefore, just as for them some of the past exists, it was stated [in the objection] to challenge [the opponent]: "In that case, do some phenomena whose results have not yet ripened exist, while others do not?
The term "those whose results have ripened" (*vipakkavipākā*) was stated to challenge [the opponent] from the perspective of those for whom he maintains that non-existence.
The term "those without results" (*avipākā*) was stated to challenge [him] from the perspective of the indeterminate (*abyākata*) phenomena.
Thus, by way of these three groups, both the admission and the rejection are to be understood in all forward and reverse sequences.
Those [kamma-formations] whose results have partially matured and partially not matured are called "incompletely matured results" (*vippakata-vipāka*).
For the kamma by which rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is produced, its result is also the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the death-moment (*cuti*).
Therefore, from rebirth-linking until death, that [kamma] is called "incomplete fruition. This was said with reference to such phenomena.
The question—"Do they exist?"—is asked by the proponent of the opposing view (sakavādī), taking into account that "they will ripen" and thus "they exist.
Just as it is said that many phenomena exist even while a person who has mastered the Dhamma is sleeping, so too is their existence [asserted] according to worldly convention.

The opponent’s admission is made with a hidden intention (*sandhāya*). Regarding the second question, "They will ripen," it is an admission by the opponent based on the position that "there exists a certain thing called the accumulation of karma (*kammūpacaya*), which is characterized by the non-destruction of karmas.
2. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning Certain Future [Karmas], etc. (*Anāgatādi-ekacca-kathāvaṇṇanā*)

300. Regarding the statements such as "the future exists," etc., when it is said that "some things exist," this is said with reference to phenomena that are subject to arising. The rest is already clear in meaning everywhere because it follows the method explained below.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of "some things exist. 8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna).
301. Now follows the discussion on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Regarding this, according to the method stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta:

“Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness,” there are those who—having taken the body and so forth as objects of mindfulness—hold the view that “all phenomena are foundations of mindfulness,” just as is the case today.
Regarding the Andhakas: the Andhakas consist of these later-arisen schools—the Pubbaseliyas, Aparaseliyas, Rājagiriyas, and Siddhatthikas.
For the purpose of examining their tenets, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission belongs to the opponent (paravādī).

In this context, since they "are established in these," they are called *paṭṭhānā*. What is it that is established? Mindfulness (*sati*). Because mindfulness is established therein, they are "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānā*).

In this sense, the objects of mindfulness are also called foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). [The word] "foundations" (*paṭṭhāna*) means "they establish themselves. What establishes itself? Mindfulness.
Thus, "mindfulness itself is the foundation" is the meaning of "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*); in this sense, mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness.
Therefore, both explanations are tenable as alternative ways of speaking (*pariyāya*). However, those who reject that alternative way of speaking and maintain exclusively that "all phenomena..."

When they say, “The foundations of mindfulness,” the question is posed by the proponent (sakavādin) with reference to them; the admission is made by the opponent (paravādin) on the basis of the objects.
However, for one who maintains that “all phenomena are mindfulness,” the denial is likewise his own, because all phenomena lack the intrinsic nature of mindfulness.
In that context, terms such as “leading to destruction” are qualifications of the Path. For the “one-way path” leads to Nibbāna, which is the destruction of the defilements.
