It goes toward destruction, thus it is "leading to destruction" (*khayagāmī*). It goes while awakening to the Four Truths, thus it is "leading to awakening" (*bodhagāmī*). It goes while wearing away the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), thus it is "leading to diminution" (*apacayagāmī*).
Thus, by means of these terms, he asks: "Are all those phenomena such that this is your one-way path?
The phrases beginning with "taintless" (*anāsava*) and "not subject to fetters" (*asaṃyojaniya*) are also for the purpose of asking about their supramundane nature (*lokuttarabhāva*).
These have been stated. The sections beginning with "The recollection of the Buddha" were stated by way of a question regarding their specific classifications.
The section beginning with "The eye-base is a foundation of mindfulness" was stated by way of a question regarding the classification of all phenomena.
Even therein, there is a denial from the standpoint of mindfulness itself, but an affirmation from the standpoint of the object. In this manner, the meaning should be understood for all questions.
The *Suttasādhanā* is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Purpose.
304. Now follows the discussion on existence (hevatthika). In this regard, there are those who hold the view:

"All phenomena, whether past and so forth, exist by way of [their own] form and so on; yet the past does not exist by way of the future or present, nor do the future and present exist by way of the past and so on;
therefore, all this exists in this way and does not exist in that way"—just as is the case with those of various classifications mentioned nowadays.
[This refers] to the Andhakas. With reference to them, the proponent’s question is: "Does the past exist? The opponent’s reply is:
"In one way it exists, and in another way it does not exist. In this context, "heva" means "thus" (evaṃ). Then the proponent asks him:
"If you hold the view that the past exists only in this way and does not exist in this way, then in that case, that very same thing both exists and does not exist. Thus he questions him.
He said, "It exists; it does not exist. The other person rejects this, referring to existence by that very same intrinsic nature and non-existence by that very same [nature].
When questioned a second time, he admits it, referring to existence by its own nature and non-existence by another nature.
Beyond that, the meaning of "exists" and the meaning of "does not exist" refers to what is called the nature of existence and the nature of non-existence.
He asks. By this same method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
But at the conclusion, having said, "In that case, does the past exist or not? and "In that case, does form exist or not?
and so forth—even though the opponent has established a tenet, because it was established through improper means, it is indeed not established at all.
The commentary on the discussion regarding rain.
The Mahāvagga is concluded.
2. The Second Chapter.
1. Explanation of the Charge of Falsehood (Parūpahāra-vaṇṇanā) 307.

Now follows the discussion on the charge of falsehood. In this context, it refers to the offense of *sukkavissaṭṭhi* (emission of semen) committed by those who falsely claim to have attained *arahatta*, who perceive themselves as having attained what they have not attained, who are conceited (*adhimānika*), or who are hypocrites (*kuhaka*) claiming to have attained *arahatta*.
Having seen this, they imagine: "Deities belonging to Māra’s host are offering impurity to an Arahant"—just as is the case now among the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas.
With reference to them, the proponent of the first position asks, "Does an Arahant exist?", and the other assents.
Now, since what is called the emission of semen originates from lust, [the question arises: "Does an Arahant [possess lust]?"
The pursuit of "lust" has been undertaken. All of that is indeed of plain meaning.

Regarding the question beginning with "the deities of Māra’s host as themselves," since those deities have no such thing as the emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*), nor do they take the semen of others and apply it [to themselves], and furthermore, since an *arahant* has no semen at all, therefore [it is not so].
"Hevanti" means he rejects.

Regarding the question "Does he not [bestow it] upon himself?", he admits to the position that he manifests [himself] and bestows [it]. Regarding the question "By means of the pores of the skin?", seeing that there is no bestowing by means of the pores of the skin—as there is with ghee or oil—he rejects it.
(308) "Handa hi" is a particle used for emphasis in speech. [The intention is: "I shall cause him to fall into such doubt as, 'Am I an Arahant or not?'"
The meaning is that, having spoken thus, he concludes [his argument] in this way. When asked, "Does an Arahant have doubt?

he rejects it, referring to the eightfold doubt (*vicikicchā*). When asked a second time, he admits it, referring to the absence of certainty regarding the names, clans, and so forth of women and men.
309. "There is a receptacle for it": he asks whether there exists a place of support for that semen, just as there is for feces and urine.
312. "Skilled in his own Dhamma" means skilled in the mere Dhamma of his own Arahantship. He says this with reference specifically to one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*).
"Skilled in another's Dhamma" refers to being skilled even in the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), which are other than one's own Dhamma.
Regarding "of the wholesome": he speaks thus with reference specifically to one liberated in both ways. The rest here should be understood according to the text itself.
End of the commentary on the discussion on external importation. 2-3-4. Commentary on the Discussion on Ignorance, etc.
314. Now, there are three discourses known as ignorance (*aññāṇa*), doubt (*kaṅkhā*), and being made aware by others (*paravitaraṇā*).
In this regard, for those who hold that "there is ignorance because of the absence of the occurrence of knowledge regarding the names, clans, and so forth of Arahants, such as women and men;
there is doubt because of the absence of certainty in those very matters; and since these matters are made known, explained, and declared to them by others, therefore..."
They hold these views, such as "there is no transfer of merit for them," just like those of the Pubbaseliyas and others nowadays.
To refute those views, in all three discourses, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), while the admission and the denial belong to the other.
In this regard, the meaning of both the questions and the answers should be understood by following the canonical text (pāḷi) itself.
Commentary on the Discussion of Ignorance, etc.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of Verbal Expression 326.
Now follows the discussion called "Verbal Expression. In that regard, for those who hold that "at the moment of the path of stream-entry, first..."
The tenet is: "For one who has attained *jhāna*, speech ceases, [therefore] there is no suffering. This is just as it is for the Pubbaseliyas and others nowadays.

With reference to them, the question—"Is there vocal utterance for one who has attained [jhāna]?"—is asked by the proponent of the first position (*sakavādin*). The admission is made by the opponent (*paravādin*) while standing upon that tenet.
Again, when asked regarding "everywhere," he refers to the three realms of existence and denies it with reference to the formless realm (*arūpa*).
When asked "at all times," he denies it with reference to all other occasions of attainment, excluding the first moment of the first path and the first jhāna attainment.
When asked "of all those who have attained," he denies it with reference to those who have attained mundane attainments.
When asked "in all attainments," he [denies it] with reference to supramundane attainments such as the second jhāna and so forth.
And he rejects it with reference to all mundane attainments (*lokīyasamāpatti*).
"Bodily dissolution" (*kāyabheda*) refers to bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) occurring by way of approaching and so forth.

This is for the purpose of raising the objection: "Those very same consciousnesses that produce vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*) also produce bodily intimation; this being so, why does bodily dissolution not also occur?"
He asks. The other both denies and affirms according to his own attainment.
Now, if he utters the word "suffering" at the moment of the Path, he might also utter "origination," and so forth;
or if he does not utter that, he would not utter the others either—it is for the purpose of such an objection that the questions beginning with "one who knows suffering" were stated. But the other...
He both asserts and denies according to his own specific tenets.
For it is his tenet that one who has attained the supramundane first jhāna contemplates it as "suffering among sufferings.

(328) "Knowledge" refers to supramundane knowledge of the Four Truths. "Ear" is intended to mean ear-consciousness, by means of which one hears that sound. "Of the two contacts" refers to ear-contact and mind-contact.

329. "Indeed, it should not be said" means that if there is no vocal expression for anyone who has attained [jhāna] without distinction, then it should not be said without distinction that "there is vocal expression for one who has attained.
The rest here is of plain meaning, together with the supporting evidence from the Sutta. As for the Sutta cited by him at the conclusion: "Of the Blessed One Sikhī, Ānanda... [and so forth].

It has been brought forward that the vocal expression is originated by the attainment-consciousness; however, the bodily expression is likewise originated by that very same consciousness, and that first-jhāna consciousness is not supramundane.
Therefore, it is not a proof [of the existence of a separate mind-made body].
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of vocal expression.
6. Explanation of the Discourse on the Conveying of Suffering (Dukkhāhārakathāvaṇṇanā) 334.
Now follows the discourse known as the Discourse on the Conveying of Suffering. In this regard: "One who utters the words 'suffering, suffering' brings forth knowledge regarding suffering;
that is called the conveying of suffering. Furthermore, this is a factor of the Path (maggaṅga) included within the Path."
Regarding those whose tenet is as follows, such as that of the Pubbaseliyas at present: with reference to them, the question "Is it a nutriment of suffering?

is asked by the proponent of his own view (sakavādī), and the admission is made by the opponent (paravādī). In the first question, he rejects [the proposition] with reference to those who lack insight (avipassaka);
in the second question, he admits it with reference to those who possess insight (vipassaka), yet that is merely his own personal tenet. Therefore, "all... [and so forth].
He said, “They [are fools and worldlings],” etc., for the purpose of refuting that doctrine. That has an obvious meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Nutriment of Suffering. 7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Consciousness.
335. Now follows the discussion on the stability of consciousness (*cittaṭṭhitikathā*).

In this regard, there are those who, seeing that both the attainment-consciousness (*samāpatti-citta*) and the life-continuum-consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) proceed in uninterrupted succession, hold the view that "a single consciousness persists for a long time," such as the Andhakas of the various types mentioned below. For the purpose of purifying that view, [it is said]: "A single consciousness..."
The question, "Does it stand for a day? belongs to the proponent (sakavādin), while the admission belongs to the opponent (paravādin).

Regarding the statement, "Half a day is the moment of arising," this question was formulated solely in terms of arising and passing away—according to the method of teaching that "Impermanent indeed are formations, subject to the nature of arising and passing away"—without touching upon the moment of stability.
When asked, "Are those states quick to change compared to the mind? he rejects it because he does not perceive any state that changes more quickly than the mind.
When asked the second question, he affirms it with reference to that mind which he considers to have a long duration.
Regarding the question, "Does it remain for the full length of its life-span? [he answers] by way of such statements as: "The Maruts remain for eighty-four thousand aeons."

He rejects [the existence of consciousness] apart from the formless realm (*ārūpya*) and asserts it within the formless realm. Regarding the question, "Does it arise moment by moment?", the opponent asserts this for fear of contradicting suttas such as "subject to arising and passing away" (*uppādavayadhammino*).
However, he maintains its stability (*ṭhiti*) by way of its having attained [a state of persistence]. The rest here is of plain meaning.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Consciousness. 8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Burning Embers (Kukkuḷakathā). 338. Now follows what is called the Discussion of the Burning Embers.

In this regard, for those [who hold] that "everything, monks, is burning; all... ...the commentary on the discussion of the stability of consciousness. 8. Commentary on the discussion of the burning embers (kukkuḷakathā). 338. Now follows what is called the discussion of the burning embers. In this context, for those who [hold]: "Everything, monks, is ablaze; all..."
Having taken such suttas as "conditioned phenomena are suffering" in an improper manner, they hold the view that "all conditioned phenomena are, in an absolute sense (nippariyāya), burning,
like a mixture of glowing embers and ashes, resembling the Niraya hell"— just as is the case today for the Gokulikas.
In order to separate them from that view by demonstrating the various kinds of happiness, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), and the answer is their admission.

[This refers to] the opponent’s argument. In that context, "without making a limitation" means not establishing a limit, a boundary, or a specific portion; the meaning is "without distinction, all [beings] indeed.
The rest of it all should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi, together with the proof from the Sutta.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Pit of Embers (Kukkuḷakathā).
9. Explanation of the Discourse on Gradual Realization (Anupubbābhisamaya-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 339.
Now follows the discourse known as the "Gradual Realization. In this regard, for those who hold:
"The wise person, step by step, little by little, moment by moment;..."
“Just as a smith blows away the dross from silver, so should one blow away one’s own impurities.

Having taken such suttas out of context (*ayoniso*), [some] maintain: “One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry abandons some defilements by seeing suffering, some by seeing the origin, cessation, and the path; likewise for the others. Thus...
"By gradually abandoning the defilements through sixteen stages, the attainment of Arahatship occurs"—
such various views regarding the realization of truth (abhisamaya) arose, just as they do now among the Andhakas, Sabbatthikas, Sammitiyas, and Bhadrayānikas.
For the purpose of examining their views, the proponent of the first position asks whether there is a gradual realization, while the other admits that there is.
When asked about the "gradual path of stream-entry," he refuses, fearing that one single path would become many.
When asked about the second [path], he admits it by way of the vision of suffering and so forth. Alternatively, he admits that those four knowledges are indeed just a single stream-entry path;
however, since he maintains that the fruit is only one, he refuses [to accept multiple fruits]. The same method applies to the paths of once-returning and the others as well.

344. Regarding the question, "When the path is seen, one is established in the fruit": because the vision [of the truths] through the seeing of suffering and so forth is not yet finalized, whereas it is said to be finalized through the vision of the path, at that time one comes to be designated as "established in the fruit"; therefore, he makes this admission. 345.
The question, "When suffering is seen, are all four truths seen? belongs to the opponent; the admission is made on the basis of a single simultaneous realization (*ekābhisamaya*).

[This is] the proponent's own position. Again, when questioned whether the truth of suffering is all four truths, the denial of that same [position] follows because all four possess distinct intrinsic natures.
The question "Has the aggregate of form been seen as impermanent? belongs to the proponent;

for just as when the taste of a single drop from the ocean is penetrated, the rest of the water is likewise penetrated, so too when one phenomenon is penetrated as impermanent and so forth, all [phenomena] are penetrated.
"By way of tenet" refers to the admission of the opponent.

"By four knowledges" means by the knowledge of suffering and so forth. "By eight knowledges" means by the knowledges of the truths shared by disciples as well as by the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
"By twelve knowledges" means by the knowledges of the twelvefold dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
"By forty-four kinds of knowledge" means by those knowledges stated in the Nidāna-vagga thus: "Knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death," and so forth.

"By seventy-seven kinds of knowledge" means by those knowledges stated in that same place thus: "Bhikkhus, aging-and-death, monks, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation."
The rest here is to be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi itself, together with the supporting suttas.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Gradual Realization. 10.
Commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Designation.

347. Now follows the discussion on conventional usage (*vohārakathā*). Regarding this, those who hold the view that the Buddha, the Blessed One, employs supramundane conventional usage—such as the Andhakas do today—are the ones intended by the questioner of the Sakavādin’s position.

The opponent’s admission is made according to their own tenet. The statements beginning with “supramundane ear” are spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the irrationality of that [opponent’s] position.
This is the intended meaning here: “Is it only the sense-base of sound that is supramundane, or are the ear and the rest as well?
If the verbal expression of the Buddha, the Blessed One, were to strike against a mundane ear, then it might strike against a supramundane one;
however, one must not understand the meaning in such a way as to imply that [the ear] would be supramundane. Rather, for that which strikes against a mundane [ear],...
The intended meaning here is that there is no such thing as "supramundane-ness. Regarding the phrase "by mundane consciousness," the meaning here too is "by what is exclusively mundane";
otherwise, there would be an inconsistency, for the supramundane is indeed known by mundane knowledge. Thus, everything should be understood according to its appropriate application.
Regarding the questions, "Do all those develop the path?", those who do not attain the path [are meant].
He rejects it with reference to those who do not obtain it; he admits it with reference to those who do obtain it. "Made of gold" means made of gold.
This is the example of the opponent (the *paravādin*). "Made of *eḷaṇḍa*" means made of *eḷaṇḍa*. This is the example of our own school (*sakavādin*).
To say that one who uses worldly conventions is "worldly" (*lokiya*) is also one tenet; this is currently the tenet of certain Andhakas. The rest here is of plain meaning.
Exposition of the Discussion on Conventional Designation. 11. Exposition of the Discussion on Cessation. 353.
Now follows the discussion called "Cessation. In this regard, for those who [assert] both non-deliberate cessation (*appaṭisaṅkhā-nirodha*) and deliberate cessation (*paṭisaṅkhā-nirodha*),...
The view that even these two, taken together, constitute the truth of cessation belongs to those such as the Mahīśāsakas and the Andhakas today.
With reference to them, the question "Are there two cessations? is asked by the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is made by the opponent (paravādī).
Regarding the questions "Are there two cessations of suffering?", he rejects them because he does not accept two truths of suffering. Because [he accepts] in two ways...
He accepts that "suffering ceases" because he desires it; therefore, he acknowledges it.
Regarding the questions on "two truths of cessation," he rejects them because he does not accept two cessations of the truth of suffering; he acknowledges them because suffering ceases in two ways.
The same method applies to the passages beginning with "two refuges."
Regarding the questions such as "Are there two kinds of Nibbāna?", he rejects them because he does not perceive any such distinctions as high or low.
"Cessated through non-reflection" refers to those formations which, having not been ceased by supramundane knowledge through reflection,
are said to be "ceased" either because they are merely the natural state or because they do not manifest due to the influence of recitation, interrogation, and so forth.
"Ceasing through reflection" means they cease by means of supramundane knowledge;
they are brought to a state of non-arising. "Are not formations ceased even without reflection?"—this is the question of the opponent.

In that regard, because there is no further fueling for those things already broken, or because they cease in that very manner when the Noble Path has arisen, the proponent [the Theravādin] asserts their absolute destruction (*accantabhaggata*) regarding those formations ceased without reflection.
He acknowledges it. The rest here is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Cessation.
The Second Chapter.
3. Third Chapter: 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Powers (Balakathāvaṇṇanā) 354.
Now follows what is called the Discourse on the Powers. Therein, regarding those [powers] mentioned in the Anuruddha Saṃyutta: "And furthermore, I say of these..."
“Friend, through the development and cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, I understand, as it really is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible”—
having wrongly grasped such ten discourses as these, they hold the view that “the power of a Tathāgata is shared with disciples,” just like the Andhakas nowadays.
It is with reference to them that the question of the proponent is asked.
The opponent’s admission is made while standing upon their own tenets. Furthermore, this power of the Tathāgata is shared with disciples, unshared, and both shared and unshared.
Among these, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*) is shared; the knowledge of the degrees of others’ faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*) is unshared;
and the remainder is both shared and unshared. [This includes] the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*), and so forth.

For disciples know by way of partiality, whereas Tathāgatas know without partiality. Thus, those [powers] are common in terms of their general description (*uddesa*), but not in terms of their detailed exposition (*niddesa*).
However, this [power] is said to be common in its entirety without distinction.

To distinguish it from that, the further inquiry was undertaken as to whether it is a power of a Tathāgata or a power of a disciple. In that regard, in the first question, [it is distinguished] by way of detailed exposition.

He rejects [the first question] with reference to the state of having all modes as its object. In the second question, he affirms it by way of knowing, through mere indication, what is possible and what is impossible, and so forth.
In the questions beginning with "That very same," he rejects it because there is an absence of non-difference in every mode.

Furthermore, "prior application" (*pubbayoga*) and "prior conduct" (*pubbacariyā*) are one in meaning; likewise, "proclamation of the Dhamma" (*dhammakkhāna*) and "teaching of the Dhamma" (*dhammadesanā*).

In the question concerning the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (*indriyaparopariyatti*), he acknowledges [this power] within the domain of a disciple (*sāvaka*) with reference to its partial commonality. 355.
Now, since a disciple knows such things as the possible and the impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*) by way of enumeration, he first demonstrates the disciple’s knowledge in that manner;
then, by means of this mere commonality of knowing, he establishes their shared status with disciples. Thus, the disciple...
"Knowing what is possible and what is impossible," and so forth, are the questions of the opponents.

In that context, the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriyaparopariyattiñāṇa*) is not included because it is one of the six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*). Or, regarding "the destruction of the taints through the destruction of the taints":
this would refer to the destruction of the taints in a disciple in relation to the destruction of the taints in the Tathāgata.
There is no difference; that does not exist. This same method applies even to the phrase "liberation of liberation. The rest here is of plain meaning. 356.

Now, in order to inquire about the commonality of the remaining [knowledges] as well, by correlating them with what the proponent has admitted—that "the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava) is common"—there follow again the opponent's questions beginning with "In the destruction of the taints... and so forth.

They exist. In the response to those [questions], because there is no distinction regarding the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) for the proponent (*sakavādin*), that knowledge was admitted to be common.

In the case of the others as well, their commonality was rejected due to the absence of distinction. Again, by correlating "the possible and the impossible" (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*) and so forth with the destruction of the taints itself, the questions concerning what is not common belong only to the opponent (*paravādin*). In that regard, concerning the knowledge of the destruction of the taints:
There is a negation; and regarding the remaining [bases], the admission belongs to the proponent (sakavādin).
Then, having correlated it with the knowledge of the faculties of others (indriyaparopariyatta), the unique question belongs to the opponent (paravādin). That has been shown in brief.

Nevertheless, in the case of the knowledge of the faculties of others, there is an admission by the proponent, and regarding the remaining [bases], there is a negation by the proponent. Then, having correlated it with the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭṭhāna) and so forth...
The opponent’s common inquiry concerns the knowledge of the degrees of others’ faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta*). That too has been shown in brief.
In that regard, there is a denial by the proponent concerning the knowledge of the degrees of others’ faculties, while there is an admission regarding the remaining [knowledges].
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of powers (*bala*).
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Noble Ones (Ariyantikathāvaṇṇanā) 357.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Discussion of Noble Ones" (Ariyantikathā). In this regard, there are those who hold the following tenet:
"Not only is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) noble, but the nine preceding powers (balas) are also noble," such as is the case with those of the present day.
Regarding the "noble ones" (*ariya*): the question from the proponent (*sakavādin*) refers to them, while the other [the opponent] grants that they are indeed noble.
Furthermore, if they are noble, they must be one or another of those such as the Path; thus, the question from the proponent is by way of the Path and so forth, while the other denies it.
Again, the question regarding the object of emptiness (*suññatā-ārammaṇa*) and so forth belongs to the proponent of our own school (*sakavādin*). In this context, there are two kinds of emptiness:

the emptiness of beings (*satta-suññatā*) and the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-suññatā*). The "emptiness of beings" refers to the five aggregates being empty of a "being" as imagined by views.
The "emptiness of conditioned phenomena" refers to *nibbāna*, which is empty, secluded, and escaped from all conditioned phenomena. Regarding this, the opponent...
He rejects [the proposition] with reference to having Nibbāna as its object, but he affirms it with reference to having conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as its object.
When asked, "Does one attend?", he likewise rejects it with reference to Nibbāna alone, but affirms it with reference to conditioned phenomena.
Thereupon, the proponent [states]: "Attention to what is possible and impossible, etc., has conditioned phenomena as its object; attention to emptiness (suññatā) has Nibbāna as its object."
Adopting this method, when asked, "Is there a convergence of two contacts and two consciousnesses?
he refuses, finding no room for evasion. The same principle applies to the signless (*animitta*) and the wishless (*appaṇihita*).

For the aggregates are signless because of the absence of the signs of the seven [types of] signs; Nibbāna is signless because of the absence of the signs of formations (*saṅkhāra*). Having applied this even to a single phenomenon, it is established by what is termed that which is to be placed [therein].
The aggregates are "wishless" (appaṇihita) because they are devoid of the seven wishes that have come to be reckoned as "wished for" (paṇihita) in the sense of being objects to be wished for.
Nibbāna is "wishless" because it is devoid of the wish of craving, or of craving itself as an object, or of the wish for any conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
Therefore, here too, both the negation and the affirmation should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

358. Then the questions arise in direct and reverse order: “Just as the supramundane states such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are both noble (ariya) and have emptiness (suññatā) and so forth as their object, are the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa) likewise?
In this regard, all the admissions and all the denials belong only to the opponent. By this same method, the questioning and answering regarding the remaining types of knowledge should be understood.
In the Pāḷi, however, the others are abbreviated, and at the end only the knowledge of death and rebirth (cutūpapātañāṇa) is analyzed.

Following that, even within our own system, questions regarding the noble state (*ariyabhāva*) are posed both in forward and reverse order for the remaining knowledges, in conjunction with the "noble" knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*), which is established [in the texts]. All of these are the opponent's admissions.

And the refutation belongs to one's own position. Those [terms] are indeed of obvious meaning. However, in this passage of the Pāḷi, only the first and ninth [knowledges] are shown, while the seven knowledges are abbreviated.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Noble One (Ariya).
3. Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation (Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā) 363.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Discussion of Liberation. In this regard, some hold the view: "For minds that are free from lust, there is no such thing as a purpose for liberation.
However, just as a soiled cloth is freed from its stains when it is washed, so too is a mind possessed of lust [freed from its stains]."

The view is that "the mind is liberated from lust," just as is the case with the Andhakas today. With reference to them, the proponent's question is whether [the mind] is "with lust," and the other's admission is that it is.
Then, when questioned by way of the method beginning with "accompanied by lust" and so forth, he says that at the moment of the Path, the mind is indeed called "liberated.
Yet, he denies it, saying that at that time such a mind does not exist.

Even when questioned in the manner beginning with "With contact," etc., he denies it because he does not perceive the liberation from lust in such a way that both contact and consciousness are liberated from lust. The meaning should be understood by this same method regarding those [states] with hatred and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Being Liberated.

366. Now follows the discussion on "being liberated. In this regard, concerning those who hold the view that "by means of jhāna there is liberation through suppression, and at the moment of the Path there is what is called liberation through eradication," the question "Is it liberated or being liberated?
is asked by the proponent of the first position (Sakavādī), and the affirmation is given by the other.
"Puna ekadesan" (Again, "one part") is the question of the proponent. In this context, "ekadesaṃ" is a neuter noun in the accusative case.
Just as [the mind] is liberated, or as it might be partially liberated or partially not liberated, he asks: "Is it thus that one part is liberated and one part is not liberated?
Why does he ask in this way? Because of the state of being unfinished, as expressed by the phrase "liberated and being liberated."

Because it has been stated thus. For just as mats and the like, while being made, are partially made and partially unmade because they are unfinished, so too this [mind] would follow as being partially liberated and partially unliberated.

Therefore, the opponent, having rejected the first position on the grounds that the mind lacks parts—unlike mats and the like—[proceeds to] the second [position] regarding that which is being liberated...
He claims [to be liberated] because his liberation is not yet final. Alternatively, he denies it with reference to the moment of a mundane jhāna;
for at that time, one is not being liberated by means of the liberation through eradication (*samucchedavimutti*). He claims it with reference to the moment of a supramundane jhāna;
for his view is that at that time, one is being liberated by means of a portion of the liberation through eradication.
Then the proponent of the first position (sakavādī), in order to challenge him with the argument, "If for you a single consciousness is partially liberated and partially unliberated,
then it follows that even one who becomes a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) by means of that very same consciousness would be only partially a stream-enterer and partially not a stream-enterer," said,
"partially a stream-enterer," and so forth. The other [responded] to that formulation...
Not seeing [the distinction], he rejects it. The same method applies to the remaining sections as well.

Regarding the question on the moment of arising: if the very same consciousness is both "liberated" (*vimutta*) and "being liberated" (*vimuccamāna*), then it follows that what is liberated at one moment is being liberated at another. What kind of consciousness is this for you? This is the meaning. 367.

In establishing the proof by means of the Suttas, the first Sutta belongs to the opponent. His intention therein is as follows: "It is being liberated" (*vimuccati*) is a description of the process of liberation.
Therefore, for that yogi who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from these taints; and as it is being liberated, it is said to be "being liberated.
This is the second sutta of the proponent's own school. In this regard, his intention is as follows:

if [the opponent claims] that because of the statement "it is being liberated," that which is already liberated is "being liberated," then here, because of the absence of the statement "it is being liberated," it must be only that which is already liberated.
“Could it be that it is not being liberated?

Now, in order to raise an objection—namely, “Just as there is ‘being liberated’ due to the state of liberation being incomplete, are there also states of ‘being impassioned’ and so forth due to passion and the like being incomplete?”—the passage beginning with “there is mind” is commenced again. Even by the opponent, such a kind of mind...
Since he did not see anything [else], everything was rejected. Then the proponent, making him understand that there are only two alternatives and no third, said:
"Is it not the case that it is either 'passionate' (ratta) or 'not passionate' (aratta)," and so forth. The meaning of this is:

"Is it not true, friend, that there are only two alternatives—a mind associated with lust is 'passionate,' and one dissociated from it is 'not passionate'—and that there is no third alternative called 'one who is currently being impassioned'?"
The same method applies to the corrupt and so forth as well. Then, having acknowledged him by saying "I am," he stood there.
To show that even on the side of liberation there are only two alternatives, he said, "If it is both lustful... and so on. The meaning of this is:
if you accept these two alternatives, then accept these as well—namely, "both unliberated and liberated. For a consciousness associated with defilements is unliberated.
It is dissociated and liberated. As for the term "being liberated," from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), there is no third category.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of being liberated. 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Eighth Person (*Aṭṭhamaka*).

368. Now follows the discussion on the "eighth person" (*aṭṭhamaka*). In this regard, there are those—such as the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas—who hold the view that for the eighth person, the individual standing at the path of stream-entry, two types of obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) are abandoned because of the absence of the manifestation of defilements (*kilesa*) at the moments of conformity (*anuloma*), lineage (*gotrabhū*), and the path (*magga*).
It is with reference to one of these [views] that [the following is said]:
The question belongs to the proponent; the other’s admission refers to the non-arising of views starting from the moment of the path.
Since this view is abandoned only by one who has attained the stream-entry (sotāpanna) and not by one standing on the path, the proponent’s challenge is:
"Is the person at the eighth stage (aṭṭhamaka) a stream-enterer? The same method applies to the question regarding doubt. Regarding the question on latent tendencies (anusaya):
Their tenet is that the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is something other than the active outburst (*pariyuṭṭhāna*); therefore, [the Buddha] rejects it, saying, "Certainly not.

In the question regarding the misapprehension of rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), he likewise does not perceive the conventional expression "outburst of misapprehension of rules and observances," and therefore he rejects it. Their tenet is that for such a person, the outburst itself has been abandoned.
369. Regarding the question "Is the path cultivated?": at that moment, one is cultivating it; it is not yet cultivated. Therefore, he rejects it.
In the inquiry beginning with "Is it not by a non-path?", he denies [its abandonment] with reference to the fact that it has already been abandoned by the first path itself.
For if it were abandoned by a non-path, it would follow that even for persons such as those at the stage of lineage (gotrabhū), it would be abandoned. The question "Will it arise?
belongs to the opponent (paravādin), while the response belongs to one's own side (sakavādin). The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Eighth-Stage Person. 6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties of the Eighth-Stage Person. 371.
Now follows the discussion of the faculties of the eighth-stage person (*aṭṭhamaka*). In that regard, for those who hold that "the eighth-stage person [attains] the path at the moment of the path..."
The tenet is that "one acquires the faculties, yet they have not been acquired," as is the case with the Andhakas today.
With reference to them, the proponent's question is, "Does the faculty of faith not exist? and the other's admission is, "It does not.
However, when asked, "Does faith not exist?", he rejects it after perceiving the distinction between faith and the faculty of faith.

The same method applies to the remaining [faculties] as well. However, just as for one who possesses mind (mano), there is also the mind-faculty (manindriya), so too for one who possesses faith and the rest, there are also the faith-faculty (saddhindriya) and the others.

It is for the purpose of illustrating this that the passage beginning "there is mind, there is the mind-faculty" has been undertaken. All of that is already explained in its obvious meaning along with the supporting Sutta citations.
The Explanation of the Discussion on the Faculties of the Eighth-Rank Person.
7. The Explanation of the Discussion on the Divine Eye. 373.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Divine Eye. In this regard, for those [who have attained] the state of the fourth jhāna, which is firmly established...
The view that the fleshly eye itself is called the divine eye belongs, for example, to the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas at present.
With reference to them, the question "the fleshly eye" is asked by the proponent of his own position (sakavādī), and the other [the opponent] admits it.

When questioned again, "Is the fleshly eye the divine eye? Is the divine eye the fleshly eye?", he rejects it, saying, "That is not so to that extent. In the questions beginning with "Of what kind," etc., he likewise rejects them because there is no identity of nature between the two.
In the passage beginning with "The object," the object for both is exclusively the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*). However, the fleshly eye sees only that which has come into its range;

the other [the divine eye] sees even what is not within its range, such as what is behind a mountain and so forth. Furthermore, even extremely subtle form is the domain of the divine eye, whereas such is not the case for the other.
Thus, their power and their domains are dissimilar.

When asked, "Having been appropriated (*upādiṇṇa*), does it become non-appropriated (*anupādiṇṇa*)?", he rejects [the proposition] because he maintains that the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) is appropriated, whereas the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) is non-appropriated, and he does not accept that the fleshly eye itself is the divine eye.
When asked the second question, he [rejects it] because, based on the statement, "The arising of the fleshly eye is the path to the divine eye," [he sees it as] conditioned by the fleshly eye.
The divine eye arises, and he maintains that it is the sensitivity derived from the four great elements of the fine-material sphere;
therefore, he affirms it. When asked, "Is it while remaining in the sense-sphere?", he denies it because he does not maintain that the fleshly eye itself is the divine eye.
When asked the second question, he [affirms] because it has arisen by way of the condition of fine-material-sphere jhāna.
He claims that what is called "belonging to the fine-material sphere" (rūpāvacara) has arisen.

When asked whether, having been of the fine-material sphere, it is now of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), he denies it because, following that, at the moment of the immaterial-sphere development (bhāvanā), there is no mind belonging to the fine-material sphere.
When asked about the second [case], regarding the four [consciousnesses] belonging to the immaterial sphere...
He admits to the tenet that [the divine eye] arises as a clarity (*pasāda*) of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). However, he does not accept its state of being "unincluded" (*apariyāpanna*);
therefore, he simply rejects it. 374.
"The divine eye is supported by states" means it is supported by states belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). Again...
"Supported by the Dhamma" means supported by the supramundane Dhamma.

When asked, "Are there two eyes?", although he does not accept that the divine eye—which is supported by the Dhamma—is the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), he nevertheless denies it because of the existence of the eye of wisdom.
When asked again, he says: "The fleshly eye, when supported by the Dhamma, becomes the divine eye."
He acknowledges it by way of attainment. The rest here is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Eye. 8.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Ear.
375. Now follows the discussion on the divine ear (*dibbasota*). In this regard, when asked whether there is only one ear, he denies it because two exist.
When asked again, he affirms it because that very [organ], when fortified by the Dhamma, is called the divine ear.
The rest is exactly as explained below.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Ear. 9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Passing Away According to Kamma. 377.
Now follows the discourse known as the Knowledge of Passing Away According to Kamma. In this regard, for those who [say], "Thus, by means of the divine eye..."

Having misunderstood the Sutta passage, “With the purified... [pe] ...he understands beings according to their destination as they pass away and reappear,” he holds the view that the knowledge of beings according to their destination is itself the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

With reference to him, the questioner (the proponent) asks the question, and the other (the opponent) gives his assent. When asked again, “Does he also attend to those who have passed away according to their destination?
he denies it, because two objects cannot be the focal point for a single moment of consciousness. When asked the second time...
One makes a claim based on various states of mind. Furthermore, when asked, "Do two contacts arise simultaneously? one denies it without leaving any room for ambiguity.

Thus, just as the meaning should be understood through the application of this phrase "according to their respective deeds" (*yathākammūpagatā*), so too should it be understood through the applications of these phrases beginning with "these, indeed, venerable sirs, are beings" (*ime vata bhonto sattā*).
378. Regarding the statement, "The Venerable Sāriputta knows the knowledge of the destination according to kamma":
because some do not know that the Elder does not employ the higher-knowledge cognitions due to his fewness of desires, they imagine that he does not possess them at all.
Therefore, thinking that "the Elder has not attained the divine eye," the proponent of the opposing view asks this. For that very reason...
When asked by another, "Does the Venerable Sāriputta possess the divine eye? he denies it.

When asked a second time, he affirms that whatever can be attained by a disciple has all been attained by the Elder. Now, the proponent of the opposing view (sakavādī), creating a diversion for him, says:
"Was not the Venerable Sāriputta... and so forth. Indeed, the Elder [uttered] this verse with the intention of employing it as a means of communication.

He spoke thus because of the absence [of that specific knowledge], not because of the absence of the knowledge of direct higher power (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*). However, the opponent perceives the meaning as being due to its very absence.
Therefore, according to his own tenet, the Elder possesses only the knowledge of the destination according to karma (*yathākammūpagata-ñāṇa*), but not the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
Hence it was said: "In that case, it should not be said that the knowledge of the destination according to karma is the divine eye."
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of Rebirth According to Deeds. 10. Commentary on the Discussion of Restraint (Saṃvara-kathā). 379.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Discussion of Restraint. In this regard, first concerning those [beings] starting from the Tāvatiṃsa devas and above...
Because those among the devas do not practice the five types of enmity (*vera*), they hold the view that "restraint (*saṃvara*) exists.
The question directed toward them belongs to the proponent of the first position (*sakavādin*). The other’s admission is made by one who does not perceive the actual occurrence of enmity.

Then, because what is called "restraint" exists only when there is non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) of that which ought to be restrained, the proponent of the first position asks about non-restraint; [this concerns] killing and so forth among the devas.
The negation of the other [non-restraint] occurs by way of its non-existence.

The passage beginning with "There is [restraint] among human beings" is stated for the purpose of showing the occurrence of non-restraint when restraint exists, and the occurrence of restraint when non-restraint exists.

380. Regarding the questions beginning with "Abstention from taking life," the affirmation is to be understood as the non-practicing of taking life and so forth, while the negation is to be understood as the non-existence of taking life and so forth. The reverse questions have their meaning already explained.
Regarding the question, "In the end, there is no restraint among the gods," the proponent's admission refers to the absence of restraint after having committed acts such as killing.
Then, by way of a dilemma, the opponent asks, "If there is no restraint, then all gods are killers of living beings," and so forth.
The proponent's rejection is based on the fact that there is an absence of the manifestation of enmity among the gods. [The response is: "Indeed not."
The proponent of the opposing view establishes his own tenet by merely taking up [the opponent's] words; yet, a tenet established in such a manner remains truly unestablished.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Restraint.
11. Commentary on the Discourse on Non-perception (Asaññakathāvaṇṇanā) 381.

Now follows what is called the Discourse on Non-perception. In this regard, for those who hold that because of the statement, "With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises," there is no rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) without consciousness; and [who hold that] "With the arising of perception, those deities pass away from that body"—

Based on their verbal expression, the Andhakas hold the view that even for non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), perception (*saññā*) exists at the moments of death and rebirth-linking, just as it does now.
With reference to them, the question was asked by the proponent (*sakavādī*), and the other party gave his assent.

Thereupon, the proponent, in order to challenge him with such questions as "Is that state a realm of perception (*saññābhava*)?", said: "Perception is a realm of perception," "Perception is a destination," and so forth. All of that—
Beyond this, it should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi itself.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on Non-perception (Asaññakathā). 12. Commentary on the Discourse on the Base of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakathā).
384. Now follows the discussion on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).

In this regard, there are those—such as the Andhakas of the present—who, because of the expression "the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," hold the view that "perception exists in that state.

With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent of our own position (*sakavādin*), and the other party gives his assent. All else here is to be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi itself.
Exposition of the Discourse on the Base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
The Third Chapter.
4. The Fourth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether a Householder Can Be an Arahant (387).

Now follows the discussion titled "Whether a Householder Can Be an Arahant. In this regard, there are those such as the Uttarāpathakas of the present day who, having seen the attainment of Arahantship by certain sons of good family and others while they remained in the outward appearance of householders, hold the view that "a householder can be an Arahant."

These questions are posed by the proponent (*sakavādin*) with a specific underlying intention (*sandhāya*). In this context, "a householder" (*gihī*) means one who is a householder by virtue of being associated with the fetters of a householder;

the meaning is that such a person could be an *arahant*. However, the opponent (*paravādī*), failing to perceive this underlying intention and seeing only the mere outward appearance of a householder, admits [the point].
Now, for him [it is explained]: "One is called a householder by reason of the fetters of a householder, not by mere outward appearance. As the Blessed One said:"
Even if one were adorned, yet should live equanimously—
peaceful, tamed, self-restrained, and living the holy life—
having laid aside the rod toward all beings, [he would be a true ascetic].
“He is a brahmin, he is a recluse, he is a bhikkhu.
To demonstrate this method, the passage beginning with “There is an arahant” was commenced. All of that is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether there can be an arahant who is a householder.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Rebirth (Upapattikathāvaṇṇanā) 388.

Now follows the discussion known as the "Discussion of Rebirth" (upapattikathā). In this regard, there are those who, having misinterpreted the statements, "He is one of spontaneous birth (opapātiko), attaining final nibbāna right there," hold the view that one is worthy of rebirth in the Suddhāvāsa heavens;
or those who [misinterpret] the statement, "one who attains final nibbāna after passing away (upahaccaparinibbāyī)."

Having transposed the term, those who master the phrase “one who attains Parinibbāna upon rebirth” (upapajjaparinibbāyī) hold the view that one becomes an Arahant simultaneously with rebirth—just as is the case among the people of the Northern Path today.
With reference to them, the question belongs to the proponent of our own position (sakavādī), while the admission belongs to the other.
In this regard, since what is called the “rebirth-consciousness” (upapatticitta) is mundane (lokiya), by means of that [consciousness], even stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and others [are included].
They do not exist, let alone an Arahant. Therefore, in order to demonstrate this principle to him, the passage beginning with “a stream-enterer together with rebirth” is commenced.

(389) The passage beginning with “Sāriputta” is stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent] by asking: “Among these great elders, is there even one who is called an Arahant together with rebirth?

(390) “By means of that which pertains to rebirth” means by means of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*). For that [consciousness] seeks and searches for rebirth; therefore, it is called “pertaining to rebirth. The rest here is of plain meaning.
Commentary on the Discussion of Rebirth. 3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Taintless. 391.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Taintless" (anāsava). In that regard, whatever states belong to the taintless Arahant, all those...

"Those who hold the view that [the aggregates] are 'without taints' (anāsava)—such as the people of the Northern Path nowadays—with reference to them, the proponent of the first position asks whether they are "Arahants," and the other admits this.

Then, in order to challenge him by asking whether those very things called "without taints"—namely the Path and so forth—actually arise for him, the passage beginning with "The Path, the Fruit... is commenced. [And when he is asked: "Is the eye without taints?"...
Because it is associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*), he rejects [the first question]. When asked the second time, he admits that it is "without outflows" (*anāsrava*).

392. Regarding the question on robes, he rejects [the first question] for fear of contradicting the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that there is only one single phenomenon which is both without outflows and with outflows.
When asked the second time, he admits that "having been without outflows, it becomes with outflows. In both questions, he maintains that it is precisely that same thing which is without outflows.

The same method applies here. However, because the proponent has conceded that it is "that very [same thing]," the opponent challenges him with the arguments beginning with, "the path, having become untainted," and so forth.
By this means, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Untainted (*anāsava*).
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Possession (Samannāgatakathā) 393.
Now follows the discussion called "Possession" (*samannāgata*). In this context, there are two kinds of possession:

possession as being currently endowed with something in the present moment (*samaṅgībhāva-samannāgama*), and possession as acquisition through reaching a particular plane, such as the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth (*paṭilābha-samannāgama*). This [latter] lasts as long as the specific distinction attained...

It does not fall away; it is obtained at that very moment. However, for those who hold the view—such as the Uttarāpathakas of the present day—that there exists another "possession" (*samannāgama*) by way of the nature of rebirth (*upapattidhammavasena*), apart from these two [possessions], they have no such thing as "the nature of rebirth" (*pattidhamma*).
Therefore, in order to refute this, the proponent asks: "Is an Arahant possessed of the four fruits? This is the question of the proponent.
Having made a promise to the first person, he then makes a counter-promise to the other.

Then, for the purpose of challenging him with the words, "If the Arahant possesses four fruits just as he possesses four aggregates, then, that being so, you must also possess the four types of contact and so forth that exist within those four fruits," the passage beginning with "The Arahant [possesses] four contacts" is commenced. All of that—

The opponent rejects [the position] because the four factors beginning with contact do not exist simultaneously in a single moment. This same method applies to the questions concerning the Non-returner and so forth.
(395) "One who has transcended the fruit of stream-entry" does not mean one who has attained the second jhāna in the same way as one who has attained the first jhāna;

rather, he asks [about one who has transcended it] by way of its non-recurrence. The passage beginning "the path of stream-entry" is undertaken to show that he does not possess those things again, having transcended them.
And regarding the question, "Is he not fallen away from those [attainments]?"— since mundane jhāna states are lost through the manifestation of opposing factors,
whereas supramundane states are not; for those defilements which are abandoned by the Path and suppressed by the Fruit remain abandoned and suppressed exactly as they were,
therefore the proponent has admitted this by saying, "Yes."
This very point has already been explained elsewhere in such passages as, "The four paths were attained by the Arahant," and so forth. The remainder is of obvious meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of possession (*samannāgata*). 5. Commentary on the Discussion of Possession of Equanimity (*upekkhā-samannāgata*).
397. The meaning of the discussion stating that "the Arahant possesses six kinds of equanimity" should also be understood by this same method.

For the Arahant is said to be "possessed of them" because of the possibility of the arising of equanimities at the six doors, not because of the simultaneous arising of all of them in a single moment.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of being possessed of equanimity.
6. Explanation of the Discussion on the Enlightenment as the Buddha (Bodhiyā-buddhoti-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 398.

Now follows the discussion known as "The Enlightenment as the Buddha. In this context, "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is a designation for both the knowledge of the four paths and the knowledge of omniscience.
Therefore, just as those who possess a white complexion are called "white," and those with a dark complexion are called "dark," so too regarding enlightenment—

The view that "there is a Buddha" is held, just as it is now among those of the Northern Path (Uttarāpathakas). With reference to them, the question and the inquiry belong to the proponent of his own doctrine (Sakavādī), while the admission and the denial belong to the other.
Regarding the question "in the past," he denies it because [the Buddha] did not exist at that moment. Being asked the second time, he [admits it] with reference to the attainment [of Buddhahood].
He acknowledges it. Again, when questioned from the perspective of duty (*kicca*), he denies it because of the absence of such duty.
When questioned for the second time, he acknowledges that there was no delusion regarding what ought to have been done by him through that [state].
However, when questioned in the manner beginning with "he fully understands suffering" without leaving any room for evasion, he denies it because of the absence of that duty.
In the *Anāgatapañha*, he denies [the first question] because at that moment there is an absence of path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*).
When asked the second time, "Has the Buddha gone to Rājagaha?", he affirms it, imagining that he will attain Buddhahood through his future enlightenment.

When asked, "Is he performing the duties of enlightenment?", he denies it because at that moment those duties have not yet come to pass. When asked the second time, [he would affirm it], for if he were not to perform them...
He would not say "Buddha. Because he will certainly do so, he admits that he is indeed called "one who acts.
Again, when questioned without being given any room for evasion, he denies it. The question regarding the present, along with its reconciliation, is clear in meaning. 399.

When questioned by combining the three types of enlightenment into one, [the Buddha] refers to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), because by means of all three, one may be called "Buddha."
He makes a formal claim. When questioned again with the words "by three," he denies it because all [knowledges] do not exist simultaneously.
When questioned a second time regarding the omniscient knowledge of the past, future, and present, he claims it by way of that [omniscience].
Again, when questioned with the words "constantly and continuously" without allowing for any room for partiality, he denies it.

"It should not be said, 'He is enlightened'" is the opponent's question; "Because at the moment enlightenment is absent, he would fall into the state of being a non-Buddha" is the proponent's admission.

However, regarding the question, "Is it not the case that [he is called a Buddha] upon the attainment of enlightenment?", the admission is that very person's, because the conventional designation "Buddha" exists in that same continuum wherein the path-knowledge known as enlightenment has arisen. His intention...
The opponent’s position is the establishment of the thesis: "One kills without knowing. Now, in order to make his lack of discernment evident, the proponent asks:
"Is one a Buddha because of the attainment of enlightenment (bodhi), or is one a Buddha by means of enlightenment? The meaning of this is:
"Is it because you are a Buddha due to the attainment of enlightenment that you are a Buddha by means of enlightenment? The other [the opponent] says: "The so-called 'attainment of enlightenment'..."
Even though enlightenment has arisen and ceased, its state of having arisen within the continuum remains.
It is precisely because he fails to perceive this distinction—that "enlightenment" (bodhi) refers to knowledge at the moment of the Path—that he asserts it once again.

Then, when questioned by the proponent of the opposing side as to whether enlightenment is so called because of the attainment of enlightenment, he is unable to find an opportunity for speech and thus rejects the position.
The Commentary on the Discussion of Awakening and Buddhas.
Thus, these three discussions belong specifically to those of the Northern Route (Uttarāpathaka).
7. The Commentary on the Discussion of the Marks (Lakkhaṇa).

400. Now follows the discussion on the marks (lakkhaṇakathā). In this regard, there are those who, having misinterpreted the Sutta passage, “For one endowed with these [marks], only two destinies exist for a Great Man,” hold the view that only a Bodhisatta is one endowed with the marks—such as the followers of the Northern Path (Uttarāpathakas) do nowadays.
With reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is given by the opponent (itaro).

Regarding the question "Is he a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti-satta)?": since both a wheel-turning monarch and a bodhisatta are referred to by that term, he denies it with reference to one who is not a bodhisatta, but affirms it with reference to a bodhisatta.

The sutta on the thirty-two marks was spoken specifically concerning the bodhisatta; for he becomes a Buddha in his final existence, whereas in other [existences] he is a wheel-turning monarch. Therefore, even what has been brought forward is just like what has not been brought forward.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion of the marks.
8. Explanation of the Discussion on Entering the Path of Certainty (Niyāmokkantikathāvaṇṇanā) 403.

Now follows the discussion known as the "Entering the Path of Certainty" (Niyāmokkantikathā). In this regard, concerning those [who hold that] the Bodhisatta had already entered the path of certainty during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, with reference to Jotipāla’s going forth in the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta, it is said:
"The Bodhisatta had entered the path of certainty and lived the holy life under the Blessed One Kassapa."
"Adherence" (*laddhi*) is, for example, like that of the Andhakas nowadays. With reference to them, the question "Is he a Bodhisatta? was asked by the proponent of his own view;

the other's affirmation was made while standing upon that adherence. Then, since "entry into the fixed course" (*niyāma*) or "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*) are names for the Noble Path, and there is no so-called "exit from the fixed course" for Bodhisattas other than the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramī*). If...
[If that were so,] the Bodhisatta would have been a stream-enterer disciple. But this is not the case. For the Buddhas, standing upon the power of their own knowledge, declare of him:
"This one will become a Buddha. Therefore, the opponent's argument is that he is called a "Bodhisatta" [only later];
the other's denial refers to his final existence (*pacchimabhava*). Regarding the second question, at the time of Jotipāla...

The promise was made with reference to that very [final] existence. The same principle applies to such phrases as "having become a disciple" and so forth. "One who has heard" (*anussaviyo*) means one who has penetrated the Dhamma through oral tradition (*anussava*).
Having rejected [the claim] with reference to his final existence, he acknowledges it with reference to the oral tradition during his time as Jotipāla.

(404) "Another teacher" is said with reference to Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta. The passage beginning with "Venerable Ānanda" is stated to show: "Only those disciples who have entered the fixed course of rightness (*okkantaniyāma*) become such; others who have not entered the fixed course do not become like this."

"A disciple has transcended birth": he asks this because one might think that the disciple has transcended that very birth in which he was a disciple, and thus would no longer be a disciple in another existence.

The other [the respondent] rejects this, because those who have entered the stream and so forth still possess the status of disciples—namely, stream-enterers and the rest. The remainder here is of plain meaning. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Entering the Path of Certainty (Niyāmokkantikathā).
9. Further Exposition on the Discourse Concerning Endowment 406.

Now, there is another discourse known as the "Discourse Concerning Endowment. In this regard, there is the tenet held by certain people—such as the Andhakas at present—that "the person standing on the fourth path is endowed with three fruits by virtue of the dhamma already attained."
These questions were posed by the proponent with a specific underlying intention (*sandhāya*), while the other [the opponent] gave his assent.
The rest here should be understood according to the same method explained below in the discussion on being endowed with the four fruits.
This concludes another commentary on the discussion of being endowed [with qualities].
10. Explanation of the Discussion on the Abandonment of All Fetters (Sabbasaṃyojanappahānakathāvaṇṇanā) 413.

Now follows the discussion known as the "Abandonment of the Fetters. In this regard, there are those who hold the view that "the abandonment of all fetters in the direct sense is Arahantship," such as the Andhakas of the present day.
With reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of our own position (sakavādī).
The other’s reply is "Yes. Again, when asked, "Are all fetters abandoned?", he denies it with reference to those already abandoned by the three lower paths mentioned above.
When asked the second time, he affirms it because there is nothing remaining to be abandoned by that [fourth] path.

Regarding personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the others as well, he denies it with reference to their abandonment by the first path, but [affirms] their abandonment without remainder by the fourth path.
Having intended [this], he makes the declaration. This same method applies everywhere.
The commentary on the discussion of the abandoning of all fetters.
The Fourth Chapter.
5. The Fifth Chapter: 1. Explanation of the Discussion on Liberation (Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā) 418.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Discussion on Liberation. In this context, there are four factors: insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), the fruit (phala), and review (paccavekkhaṇa).
Among these four knowledges, the name "knowledge of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇa*) is applied as follows:

insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*) is "knowledge of liberation" because it is liberated from the signs of permanence and so forth, or because it is liberated by way of liberation through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimutti*). The path is liberation by eradication (*samucchedavimutti*), and the fruit is liberation by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhivimutti*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of reviewing is called "knowledge of liberation" because it knows liberation. Thus...
Regarding the fourfold knowledge of liberation (*vimutti-ñāṇa*), in the absolute sense (*nippariyāyena*), only the knowledge of the fruit (*phala-ñāṇa*) is liberation.
The remaining [three] cannot be described as either "liberated" or "unliberated.

Therefore, it is with reference to those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas—that "this specific knowledge of liberation is liberated," rather than stating generally that "the knowledge of liberation is liberated."
The question is from the proponent’s side; the admission is from the opponent’s side. Again, when asked "whatever [it may be]," he rejects it with reference to reflection and so forth.
When asked "of one who has entered upon the path," he admits it with reference to the untainted nature of path-knowledge.
However, because that knowledge does not exist for a stream-enterer established in the fruit, it is therefore not called "liberated."

The proponent of the opposing view (sakavādī) spoke again, beginning with "of the stream-enterer," for the purpose of challenging [the opponent's position]. In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
Explanation of the Discussion on Liberation. 2. Explanation of the Discussion on the Knowledge of the Adept (asekha-ñāṇa).

421. Now follows the discussion on the "Asekha" (the one beyond training). In this context, since those who are still in training (*sekha*), such as the Elder Ānanda and others, know the Asekha by way of such expressions as "The Blessed One is sublime," there are some—such as the Uttarāpathakas—who hold the view that "the one in training possesses knowledge of the Asekha.
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent of the first position (*sakavādin*), and the admission is given by the other. [The text continues: "He knows, he sees."

This is stated by way of knowing what has been personally attained. The passage beginning with "one who is a lineage-attainer" (gotrabhu) is stated for the purpose of showing the absence of higher and higher knowledge for one who remains on a lower plane.
Does not the Venerable Ānanda, being a trainee (sekha), know that "the Blessed One is sublime"?
Thus the opponent maintains that this is "knowledge of the Asekha" because it occurs in reference to the Blessed One, who is an Asekha.
But this is not the knowledge of one beyond training (asekha). Therefore, even though such a tenet has been established in this way, it remains unestablished.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of one beyond training. 3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Perversion.

424. Now there is what is called the "discourse on the perverse. In this regard, concerning those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas—that "the knowledge of one who enters attainment perceiving earth in the earth-kasiṇa is perverse knowledge," the question belongs to the proponent of his own position (Sakavādī), and the admission belongs to the other.
For the sign that arises dependent upon the earth is not the earth itself.
And in that case, one perceives this as earth. Therefore, [the opponent's claim] that it is "perverted knowledge" (viparītañāṇa) is his intended meaning.

To this, the proponent replies: "Whether it be the earth of characteristics (lakkhaṇapathavī), the earth of constituent parts (sasambhārapathavī), the earth of signs (nimittapathavī), or the earth-deity (pathavīdevatā)—all are simply 'earth.
Knowledge that these are 'earth' is not perverted. Rather, the inversion such as taking the impermanent to be permanent is what constitutes perverted knowledge."

"Is this one of those?"—with this intention to challenge him, [the Buddha] said, "In the impermanent, [perceiving it as] permanent," and so forth. The other [the monk] denies it, referring to the absence of the characteristic of perversion (*vipallāsa-lakkhaṇa*);
he affirms it, referring to the sign of earth (*pathavī-nimitta*).

"Wholesome" (*kusala*) is said with reference to the knowledge of trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*). Even in the questions such as "Does the Arahant exist?", [it is said] because of the absence of the characteristic of perversion.
He rejects it. He admits [it] with reference to the sign of earth (*pathavīnimitta*).
When [the opponent] asks, "Is all that 'earth' merely the earth-kasina, which is indeed the earth as a characteristic (*lakkhaṇapathavī*)? the proponent rejects it because such is not the case.
The question, "Is there not earth, and is there not someone who enters into earth through earth? belongs to the proponent. Its meaning is as follows:
— But surely there is a "sign-earth," and there are some who enter into that earth as earth alone, and not as water or fire.

[The text] beginning with "Earth exists" means: if the knowledge of one who enters into whatever exists in such a way is erroneous, then even regarding Nibbāna—which exists and which one enters into as the eradication of all perversions—[the same would follow].
It was said for the purpose of showing that even their knowledge of the path would be erroneous.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Erroneous. 4. Commentary on the Discussion of Certainty (Niyāma).

428–431. Now follows the discussion on "the certainty" (niyāma). In this regard, because the Blessed One knows that a person who will enter the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma) is "capable of realizing the Dhamma," there are those—such as the followers of the Northern Path (Uttarāpathakas) nowadays—who hold the view that "even for a person who is an indefinite worldling (puthujjana), there exists knowledge for the sake of entering the certainty."

The question "with reference to whom [is it] 'not fixed'? belongs to the proponent of the first position (sakavādī). In that context, "for the sake of entering the certainty" (*niyāma*): *niyāma* is called the path;

the meaning is "for the sake of going upon the path" or "for the sake of setting out upon the path. However, the admission [of the second position] belongs to the opponent (paravādī), referring to that knowledge by which the Blessed One, having seen [the potential], knows: "This person is capable."
Then, in order to demonstrate that his own position is illogical, the proponent states "of one who is fixed" (*niyatassa*) as a counter-objection.

Therein, regarding the first question, he rejects it by stating that for one who is fixed by the Path, there is no such thing as knowledge for going by a non-path. Regarding the second, he admits it precisely because of its non-existence.
Regarding the third, since he was asked whether [knowledge] exists for one who is not fixed, he rejects it because it contradicts his established tenet. Again...
Having made the first question itself the fourth, three questions are formulated regarding the attainment of certainty (*niyāma*) by one who is already destined (*niyata*).
Among these, in the first, he rejects [the possibility] because for one who is destined by the initial path, there is no further knowledge required for that same purpose.
In the second, he admits it precisely because of its non-existence. In the third, he rejects it precisely because of the contradiction with what has been attained. Again, the first question...

Having made the eighth [question], three questions were formulated concerning the entry into the fixed course (*niyāma*) and so forth for one who is not yet fixed (*aniyata*). Their meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
Then, having made the very first question the twelfth, questions rooted in that—beginning with "Is there a fixed course?
and so forth—were formulated. In that context, since the knowledge for entering the fixed course is indeed the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*), therefore, with reference to that:
"It is said that 'there is the fixed course' (niyāma). But the other one rejects when 'the fixed course' is mentioned, yet admits it when 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) is mentioned.
