The same method applies to the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth. The counter-argument is of obvious meaning.

The passage beginning with 'of those who have reached the lineage' (gotrabhu) is stated for the purpose of showing that whatever has not been attained by someone does not belong to them. 'The Blessed One knows' [is said] by virtue of his own power of knowledge."
He knows [them], because he possesses the knowledge of entering the fixed course (niyāma). Therefore, for this reason, even though his own tenet is established, it remains unestablished.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Fixed Course (Niyāmakathā).
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidākathā) 432–433.

Now follows the discussion known as the "Analytical Knowledges. In this regard, there are those who, holding the view that "whatever knowledge belongs to the Noble Ones is entirely supramundane," maintain the tenet that "all knowledge is analytical knowledge" (*paṭisambhidā*), such as [the following].
Regarding the Andhakas: the question was directed at the proponent of his own school (the Sakavādin), while the answer was given by the other.

In the questions concerning conventional knowledge (*sammuti-ñāṇa*), he denies with reference to the attainment-knowledge (*samāpatti-ñāṇa*) regarding the earth-kasiṇa convention, but he affirms with reference to linguistic knowledge (*nirutti-ñāṇa*).
In the question "Whatever is conventional," he denies with reference to the worldling (*puthujjana*). Regarding the questions on the penetration of others' minds (*cetopariyāya*):
He rejects with reference to the knowledge of an ordinary person (puthujjana), and he affirms with reference to the knowledge of a noble one (ariya).
Among all the questions concerning wisdom, he rejects with reference to the question of the totalities (kasiṇa) attainments, and he affirms with reference to the supramundane (lokuttara).

Regarding the attainment of the earth-totality (pathavī-kasiṇa) and so forth, [the question is]: "Is all that wisdom which exists in these various instances analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā)? He rejects this.

This was stated for the purpose of inquiry. Therefore, regarding the phrase "all knowledge": since all supramundane wisdom (*paññā*) is analytical insight (*paṭisambhidā*), the word "all" establishes this in conjunction with the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of analytical insight.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Knowledge (Sammutiñāṇakathā) 434–435.
Now follows the discussion known as "Conventional Knowledge. In this context, there are two truths:

conventional truth (sammutisacca) and ultimate truth (paramatthasacca). However, some, without making such a distinction, include even conventional knowledge under the term "truth" based on the commonality of the word "truth."
“They say, ‘It has only truth as its object,’ just like the blind. Since they are proponents of an improper view, this discussion was undertaken for the purpose of purifying their position.

In that context, “it should not be said” is the question of the opponent (the *paravādin*); “with reference to ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*), I agree,” is the response of our own proponent (the *sakavādin*).
“In conventional truth (*sammutisacce*)” means in the truth that has entered into convention (*sammuti*); or it may mean [conventional truth] itself.

The meaning is that it is a term for the mundane and conventional truth (*sammutisacca*). The question, "Does conventional knowledge have only truth as its object? belongs to the proponent of the first position;

the affirmation belongs to the other. Thereafter, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If that [knowledge] has only truth as its object without distinction, then one should effect the full understanding of suffering and so forth by means of that knowledge," he says, "By means of that knowledge," and so on.
Commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Knowledge.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of Mental Objects (436–438).
Now follows the discussion called "Mental Objects. In this context, the phrase "knowledge of the penetration of others' minds" (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) is merely a verbal designation.

Having taken up [this position], regarding those who hold the view that "that knowledge has mind alone as its object"—just as the Andhakas do today—the question belongs to the proponent of the first position (sakavādī), while the affirmation belongs to the other. Then [the opponent] says to him:
"For one who knows the mind by way of lust and so forth, lust and the rest are also objects; therefore, it should not be said that it has mind alone as its object."
"Is there not someone for the purpose of questioning? and so forth, is begun. "In the object of contact" means in the object designated as contact.

The same method applies to "in the object of feeling" and so on. Again, when asked that "knowledge regarding the object of contact should not be stated," he, while attending to the characteristic of touching belonging to contact, admits that "contact itself is the object. But what is this?
When asked, "Is there knowledge of the modes of contact? he rejects it because no such scriptural passage exists.
The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates. Now, in order to establish his own position by demonstrating the very basis upon which that view rests, he says:
"Is there not knowledge of the modes of mind? However, although this view is established through a mere adherence to the literal expression, it remains truly unestablished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Mental Objects (Cittārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā). 8. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Future (Anāgatañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 439–440.
Now follows the discussion called "Knowledge of the Future. In this context, "the future" refers both to what is yet to come and to the immediate interval.

Regarding "immediately after" (*anantara*): among those [factors], there is absolutely no knowledge regarding what is immediately subsequent. And just as with what is immediately subsequent, so it is with that which is included within the same cognitive process (*vīthi*) and the same impulsion (*javana*).
In this context, the question belongs to the proponent (*sakavādin*), who addresses those—such as the Andhakas—who maintain that there is knowledge regarding the entire future;
the other’s response is his admission. Then [the opponent asks him]: "As for that knowledge of yours regarding the future, is it immediate?"
In order to prompt [the questioner] to ask, "He knows the future by way of its root and so forth," he said, "The future by way of its root," and so on.
In that context, all these terms beginning with "by way of its root" (*mūlato*) are synonyms for cause (*kāraṇa*).

For that which produces its own fruit is called a "root" (*mūla*), because it roots itself there—that is, it establishes itself. And because it leads from that [root] and sets it in motion, it is a "cause" (*hetu*). That very same thing indicates it, saying: "Come now..."
"Do not take it. It is called *nidāna* because it is like handing over [the object]. It is called *sambhava* because it arises from that; it is called *pabhava* because it originates from that.
Furthermore, it is called *samuṭṭhāna* because the [craving] arises therein, or because it causes that [object] to arise. It is called *āhāra* because it brings that very thing [to oneself].
And in the sense of being something not to be relinquished, it is its *ārammaṇa* (object). And it is precisely this [object] which, depending upon it—
"It goes," thus it is a condition (*paccaya*). Because it arises from that, it is called "origination" (*samudaya*).
However, because it is not possible to know the immediately succeeding consciousness through these modes, he rejects [the idea] by saying "not so.

"The state of being a root-condition for the future" means that he knows the state of being a root-condition in the immediately succeeding future consciousness; those phenomena which therein function as root-conditions, [he knows].
The meaning is "he knows them. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
The passage beginning with "of those destined for lineage" (*gotrabhū*) is stated in order to show by way of its specific form that knowledge does not arise regarding the future.
The *Pāṭaliputta* sutta was brought forward to show that knowledge does arise regarding the future. However, since this [knowledge] does not [arise] regarding every kind of future...
It is effective; therefore, it is indeed "unbrought.
Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge of the Future. 9.
Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge of the Present.

441–442. Now follows the discussion on knowledge of the present (*paccuppanna-ñāṇa*). In this regard, there are those—such as the Andhakas—who, relying on the statement, "When all conditioned phenomena have been seen as impermanent, that very knowledge is also seen as impermanent," hold the view that "knowledge exists without distinction regarding everything that is present.
With reference to them, [the text says] "of the present" (*paccuppanne*).
The question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission belongs to the other. Then, for the purpose of challenging him with the argument:
"If knowledge exists in the present in general, it must also exist in the momentary present (*khaṇapaccuppanna*).

This being so, since two knowledges cannot exist simultaneously, that [object] must be known by that very same knowledge," the inquiry "by that" (*tena*) belongs to the proponent. Regarding that, in the first question:

The denial that "one cannot know that by means of that very [knowledge]" refers to the other [knowledge]. In the second question, the affirmation is made with reference to the continuity (*santati*) of that same [knowledge].
The intention is that one who sees dissolution in its successive order sees the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution by means of the contemplation of dissolution itself.
This same method applies to such statements as "one knows that knowledge by means of that knowledge. By that contact...

The phrases beginning with "he touches that" are stated for the purpose of preventing the appearance of a subtle substrate (*lesokāsa*). However, as for what was said by him—beginning with "Is it not all conditioned phenomena"—for the purpose of establishing his own tenet:
therein, the opponent's admission is made on the grounds that, according to the method [of analysis], that knowledge has been seen, but not as an object (*ārammaṇa*).
Therefore, even though his tenet is thus established, it remains truly unestablished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Presently Arisen. 10. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Fruits (443–444).
Now follows the discussion known as the knowledge of the fruits. In this regard: "Even the Buddhas [strive] for the attainment of the noble fruits by sentient beings..."

“Even the disciples teach the Dhamma,” they say; thus, by this commonality, those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas—that the disciples also possess the knowledge regarding the fruits attainable by various beings, just like the Buddhas, are the ones intended here.

With reference to them, the question “Of the disciple? is asked by the proponent (sakavādin), and the affirmation is given by the other. Then [the opponent asks]: “If, for the disciple, regarding the fruit...”

"There is knowledge [of this]; for just as the Buddhas, even though they are equal in the fruit of stream-entry, describe the specific nature of that fruit by their own power of knowledge—saying, 'This one is a single-seeder (ekabījī), this one is one who goes from family to family (kolaṃkolo), this one is one who has seven births at most (sattakkhattuparamo)'—does a disciple likewise do so?
To challenge him with this, he said, "Does a disciple describe the specific nature of the fruit? The other denies it.

The passage beginning with "There is for a disciple the knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the fruits" is stated for the purpose of asking about the conditions for the existence of such knowledge regarding the fruits.

This is the intended meaning here: for the Buddhas there exists what is called "knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the fruits" (*phale paropariyatti*), which consists in knowing the superior and inferior status of the fruits, thinking, "This fruit is higher; this one is lower. Likewise, there exist the knowledges of the higher and lower degrees of the faculties (*indriya*) and of individuals (*puggala*).
Because of their existence, they know the respective fruits according to the respective faculties of each individual.
Do these higher and lower knowledges (*paropariyatti*) also belong to the disciple? They do; for the disciple possesses the designation of the aggregates (*khandha-paññatti*), and so forth.
[The text continues: "If those [knowledges] were like the fruits of the Buddhas for the disciple..."
"Knowledge exists; for these must also be his designations (paññatti). Do they exist for him?

Is he able, by his own power, to know or to designate these designations?"—these were stated for the purpose of such an objection. The passage beginning with "The disciple is a Victor" [is intended to show]:
"If the disciple possesses knowledge regarding the fruits (phala) as the Buddhas do, then he himself would be a Victor."
This was stated for the purpose of exhortation. This same method applies to the question regarding the disciple who has not yet arisen [in the path].

Regarding the question "one who lacks knowledge," he is excluded because the ignorance (aññāṇa) known as *avijjā* has been destroyed; however, it is not that he possesses the knowledge of the fruits (phala-ñāṇa) in the same way as the Buddhas.
Therefore, the opponent's doctrine remains without foundation.
Exposition of the Discussion on Knowledge of Fruition.
The Fifth Chapter.
The Great Fifty-Section is completed.
6. The Sixth Chapter: 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Certainty of Destiny (Niyāmakathā) §§445–447.

Now follows the discourse known as the "Certainty of Destiny" (niyāmakathā). In this context, "certainty of destiny" (niyāma) refers to [the state] such that one is "capable of entering the certainty of destiny regarding wholesome states."
Because of the statement, "Rightness regarding phenomena," the Noble Path is what is meant.

However, since a person does not become "undetermined" even when that [Path] has arisen and ceased, those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas—that "this determination (niyāma) is unconditioned in the sense of being eternal," are the ones referred to by the questioner’s inquiry, while the other’s response is an admission. Then, "If..."

He spoke the words beginning with “Nibbāna” while demonstrating that it must be of such an unconditioned nature. The questions concerning the correlation are of plain meaning. The passage beginning with “Are there some...
was stated for the purpose of illustrating the conditioned nature of the fixed order (niyāma). Regarding the question “Is the path unconditioned?
he rejects it because of its state of arising and ceasing. Regarding the question “Is the fixed order conditioned? even when the path has ceased—
He rejects [the question] with reference to the existence of *niyāma* (the fixed course).
In the questions concerning "the stream-entry *niyāma*" and so forth, the meaning should be understood by this same method, both in direct and reverse order.

When asked about "five unconditioned things" (*asaṅkhata*), he rejects it because he does not see any passage where five unconditioned things have been mentioned. When asked the second [question], [he rejects it] regarding the four *sammattaniyāmas*.
He acknowledges [the path] because of the mention of "certainty" (niyāma) and because of the unconditioned nature of Nibbāna.

The question regarding the certainty of the wrong state (micchattaniyāma) was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that it is inappropriate for it to possess unconditionedness merely by virtue of the term "certainty. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Certainty (Niyāmakathā).
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā) 448.
Now follows the discourse known as the "Exposition of Dependent Origination" (Paṭiccasamuppādakathā).

In this regard, because of such statements in the Nidāna-vagga as, "Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed; it is the stability of phenomena," it is said that "dependent origination..."

The tenet is that "the unconditioned" (asaṅkhata) exists, as held by the Pubbaseliyas and the Mahīṃsāsakas; the question is directed at the proponent (sakavādī) with reference to them, and the answer is given by the other. 449.
Questions such as "Is ignorance (avijjā) unconditioned? and so forth are for the purpose of demonstrating that ignorance and the rest are indeed part of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).

...have been stated. However, the specific sense in which each individual factor therein is called "dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda) has already been explained in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*.

Regarding the statement "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*), this was spoken for the purpose of shattering the tenet by demonstrating its true meaning, through the very sutta—beginning with the words "the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*)—by means of which that tenet was established. This is the meaning here: that which was [stated] below...
“It is this very element that has been called ‘the stability of phenomena,’ ‘the fixed course of phenomena,’ and ‘the regularity of phenomena.
It does not exist as something separate or distinct from ignorance and the other factors. Rather, this is merely a name for the conditions themselves, such as ignorance.

For whether a Tathāgata has arisen or has not arisen, volitional formations arise from ignorance, and consciousness and the rest arise from volitional formations and so forth. Therefore, [it is said]: ‘With ignorance as condition…’”

Regarding the phrase “formations” (*saṅkhārā*): the fact that these factors of formation abide in the sense of being causes is the "stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*). Furthermore, the fixed regularity of those very same phenomena in the sense of being causes is the "regularity of phenomena" (*dhammaniyāmatā*);

thus, ignorance (*avijjā*) is so called. [The opponent] asks: "Is that [ignorance] unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), and is Nibbāna also unconditioned? Having admitted this on account of his own tenet, the opponent says: *...saṅkhārā*—the stability of phenomena is the fact that these factors of formation abide in the sense of being causes. And the regularity of those very same phenomena in the sense of being causes is the regularity of phenomena; thus, ignorance is spoken of. That [ignorance] is unconditioned, and Nibbāna is also unconditioned. He asks this. The opponent, having acknowledged it by way of his own doctrine, says:
When asked again, "Are there two unconditioned things?", he rejects it on the grounds that they do not exist as sutta-passages, yet he affirms it by way of what has been attained.
The same method applies to the remaining phrases. However, what was stated previously should be understood according to the method explained therein.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
3. Commentary on the Discourse on Truths (Saccakathāvaṇṇanā) 452–454.

Now follows what is called the Discourse on Truths. In this regard, there are those who, relying on the sutta beginning, “Bhikkhus, these four are suchnesses, not otherwise,” hold the view that “the four truths are permanent and unconditioned,” such as [the Vajjiputtakas].
[This refers to] the Pubbaseliyas. With reference to them, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādin), and the admission belongs to the other. For this is his intention:
regarding the origin and the path, the truth of the basis (*vatthusacca*) is conditioned (*saṅkhata*), while the truth of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇasacca*) is unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).

In the case of cessation (*nirodha*), there is no such thing as a "truth of the basis"; the continuum is exclusively unconditioned. Therefore, he said, "Yes. However, that is merely his own personal opinion.
For he maintains that suffering is the truth of the basis (*vatthusacca*), and likewise origination and the path.

However, those characteristics of these [three]—namely, oppression, arising, and leading out—are called the "truth of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇasacca*). Furthermore, there are no such things as suffering and so forth apart from the characteristic of oppression and the rest.
The intended meaning in passages such as "refuges" (*tāṇāni*) and so on should be understood according to the method already stated.
Regarding the question "Is it the truth of suffering?", he affirms it with reference to its characteristic as established by his own tenet (*laddhi*).
Regarding the question "Is it suffering?", he denies it with reference to its objective basis (*vatthu*).

From here on, both the pure questions and the cross-referencing questions are to be understood according to the Pāḷi text itself. At the end, the Sutta cited for the purpose of establishing his tenet misrepresents the meaning.
Because it has been grasped, it is just like that which has not yet been brought forth.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on Truth (Saccakathā). 4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Formless (Āruppakathā).

455–456. Now follows the discussion on the formless (ārūpya). In this regard, concerning those who hold the view that "all those states are unconditioned (asaṅkhata)" based on the statement, "The four formless attainments are imperturbable (āneñja)," the question "the base of infinite space" is posed by the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is given by the other.
The rest here is of plain meaning. There is also a supporting sutta for this point.
Because it was brought [to him] without his knowing, it is as if it were not brought at all.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Formless Attainments (Āruppakathā). 5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Attainment of Cessation (Nirodhasamāpattikathā).
457–459. Now follows the discussion on the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). In this context, the attainment of cessation is the non-occurrence of the four aggregates.
However, because it is performed when being performed and entered when being entered, it is said to be "accomplished" (nipphanna).
Yet, due to the absence of both conditioned and unconditioned characteristics, it cannot be [categorized] as such.

“Is it conditioned or unconditioned? In this context, regarding those who hold the view that “it is unconditioned because it is not conditioned”—such as the Andhakas and the Uttarāpathakas—the proponent asks about the attainment of cessation, and the other party assents.
The phrase “they produce,” and so forth, refers specifically to the act of entering and the subsequent acquisition [of the attainment].
It has been stated. However, while form and the other aggregates give rise to unconditioned phenomena, it is not the case that anything gives rise to that [unconditioned state] in such a way.
"Cessation, purification, emergence"—this should be understood as the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). But the unconditioned itself does not exist as such [an entity];
therefore, he rejects it. "Therefore indeed" means: because it is not conditioned, it is thus held to be unconditioned. This...
Furthermore, the statement that there is no cause for the state of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) is just like what was not said at all.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Attainment of Cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). 6. Commentary on the Discussion of Space (*ākāsa*).

460–462. Now follows the discussion on space (*ākāsa*). Therein, space is threefold: delimited space (*paricchedākāsa*), space cleared by the removal of a kasiṇa (*kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa*), and unadulterated space (*ajaṭākāsa*).
Its name is also "empty space" (*tucchākāsa*). Among these, delimited space is conditioned (*saṅkhata*); the other two are mere designations (*paññatti-matta*).
However, for those who hold the view that "both [the latter two] are unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) because they are not conditioned," [the following applies].
It is just as with the Uttarāpathakas and the Mahīśāsakas; referring to them, the question "Is it space?
is from the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is from the other. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Space.
7. Commentary on the Discussion: "Is Space Visible? (463–464).

Now follows the discussion titled "Is Space Visible? In this regard, there are those—such as the Andhakas—who hold the view that "all unobstructed space is visible" based on the occurrence of cognition through apertures such as the holes in a drum; it is with reference to them [that the following is said].
The question, "Is space visible? is from the proponent; the other's admission follows.
Then, for the purpose of challenging him with the thought, "If it were visible, it would be of such a nature," the words beginning with "matter" (rūpa) are spoken.

Having rejected [the opponent's position] because there is no such sutta as "dependent on the eye," etc., he admits [visibility] based on the perception of the space between two [objects], and so forth. Of the two...
Regarding the phrase "between trees": here, having seen the form of the trees with the eye, mind-door consciousness arises perceiving it as space because of the absence of form in the interval;
visual consciousness does not arise there. This same principle applies to the other cases as well. Therefore, this [argument] is not a proof.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether space is visible.
10. Explanation of the Discussion Beginning with “The Earth Element is Visible,” etc. (465–470).
Now follows the discussion known as “The Earth Element is Visible,” and so forth.

In this regard, those who—having seen the color-sphere (*vaṇṇāyatana*) in the movement of stones, water, nets, and trees, as well as in the locations where the five faculties are established, and the visible forms of hands, feet, and so forth at the time of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*)—[hold that the earth element is visible]...
The tenet that "the earth element and so forth are visible" belongs to those such as the Andhakas.
With reference to them, in all discussions, the initial question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission belongs to the other.
The remainder in all cases should be understood according to the Pāḷi text and by the method explained above, beginning with "the earth element is visible" up to "bodily action is visible."
The concluding discussion is finished.
The sixth chapter.
7. The seventh chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Included (Saṅgahitakathāvaṇṇanā) 471–472.

Now follows what is called the discourse on the included. In this regard, since there are no phenomena that are "included" by other phenomena—unlike oxen and the like which are bound by ropes and so forth—it is said: "There are no phenomena that [are included] by..."
Regarding those who hold the view that "if things are thus comprised by [other] phenomena, then the statement 'there is a singlefold inclusion of form' and so forth is purposeless"—
such as the Rājagirikas and the Siddhatthikas— the question of the proponent (sakavādī) is intended to show the state of being included according to another meaning,
while the admission of the other is made according to his own tenet. Now, as for the meaning by which...
Inclusion is obtained; to demonstrate that, the passage beginning with "Are there not some states...
has been commenced. All of that is of plain meaning because it follows the method explained below.

As for the simile brought forward by the opponent for the purpose of establishing his own position—namely, "just as by a tethering-rope," etc.—the proponent, neither approving nor rejecting it, says: "If, by a tethering-rope..."
Thus, it should be understood that his tenet is refuted. This is the meaning here:
if those oxen and so forth are indeed "included" by means of the nose-rope and so forth, then there must be certain phenomena that are included by other phenomena.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of inclusion (*saṅgaha*).
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Association (Sampayutta-kathāvaṇṇanā) 473–474.

Now follows the discussion called the "Association" (sampayutta). In this regard, since feeling and the other [mental factors] do not enter into perception and the others—unlike oil within sesame seeds—it follows that "there are no states associated with any states; thus..."

For those who hold the view—such as the Rājagirikas and Siddhatthikas—that "when [the mind] is wholesome, it is associated with knowledge" and so forth would be meaningless, the proponent asks a question in order to demonstrate association in another sense; the opponent’s affirmation is made according to his own tenet.
The rest here is also of plain meaning, as it follows the method explained below. As for this which was [raised] by the opponent...

The question regarding the simile beginning with “as oil in sesame seeds” was brought forward because, unlike feeling and perception, there is no defining of difference by way of characteristic between the sesame and the oil.
For in all cases—whether it be the sesame seed, the husk, or the shell—it is merely a conventional designation that they are called “sesame.

Consequently, once the sesame has been produced and removed, nothing is perceived as being called “sesame” by virtue of its prior shape; therefore, this case is just like one that was not brought forward at all.
Commentary on the Discussion of Conjoined Factors. 3. Commentary on the Discussion of Mental Factors (Cetasika). 475–477.
Now follows what is called the discussion of mental factors. In this regard, since there are no such things as "contact-based" factors and so forth, therefore—

Regarding those who hold the view that "there should be no mental factor (cetasika), thus there is no mental phenomenon," such as the Rājagirikas and Siddhatthikas—the question is posed by the proponent of our own position (sakavādī) with reference to them, and the admission is made by the other.

The term "co-arisen" (sahajāto) is stated with reference to associated co-arising (sampayutta-sahajāta). The question "pertaining to contact" (phassikā) is asked by one who does not see such conventional usage.

[This is] for the opponent. What is the point of conventional usage? Just as [a dharma] is called "mental" (*cetasika*) because it is dependent on the mind, so too there is no fault in calling this [contact] "contactual" (*phassika*) because it is dependent on contact;
such is the admission of our own school (*sakavādin*). The rest is of obvious meaning. Thus ends the commentary on the Discussion of the Mental Factors (*Cetasikakathāvaṇṇanā*).
4. Explanation of the Discourse on Giving (Dānakathāvaṇṇanā) 478.
Now follows the discourse known as the "Discourse on Giving. In this context, giving is threefold:

the volition of relinquishment (*cāgacetanā*), abstention (*virati*), and the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*). In passages such as, "Faith, moral shame, and wholesome giving," it is the volition of relinquishment that is called "giving. [In the passage], "Fearlessness..."
In the passage where it says, “he gives,” it refers to abstention (*virati*). In the passage where it says, “he gives a gift of food and drink,” it refers to the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*).
In that context, the volition of relinquishment (*cāgacetanā*) is called *dāna* (giving) because “one gives by means of it, or they give the object to be given by means of it.

Abstention is also called *dāna* in the sense of cutting off (*avakhaṇḍana*) or in the sense of lopping off (*lavana*). For when it arises, it cuts off the volition of misconduct (*dussīlya-cetanā*), which consists of fear, terror, and so forth.
It is called *dāna* because it cuts, breaks, reaps, or blows away [defilements]. It is called *dāna* because the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*) is given.
Thus, although this is threefold in name, in terms of its actual meaning it is twofold: namely, the mental state (*cetasika-dhamma*) and the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*).
In this regard, those who hold the view that "only the mental state is *dāna*, not the object to be given"—such as the Rājagirikas and Siddhatthikas—[hold such a position].
The question, "Is it a mental concomitant (cetasika) by way of intention? belongs to the proponent (sakavādin); the admission belongs to the other.

Then, in order to challenge him by way of the object to be given, the question, "Is it possible to give [it]? belongs to the proponent; the denial, "It cannot be given like food and so forth," belongs to the other.
When questioned again more firmly, his admission, "He gives fearlessness," is based on the Sutta.
In the *Phassapañhā* and other such texts, however, one rejects [the idea of giving contact] precisely because one does not see the conventional usage of such expressions as "giving contact.
(479) The passage beginning with "an undesirable fruit" is stated for the purpose of illustrating that a non-mental state (*acetasika*) can function as a gift;

for a non-mental state such as food and so forth does not itself yield a future result (*vipāka*). Rather, this [passage] is intended to establish the certainty regarding the nature of the desirable fruit.
It should be understood that this has been said. This, too, is the intended meaning here:

if a non-mental phenomenon such as food were itself the gift, then for one giving an unpalatable or disagreeable medicine with a mind of benevolence, an undesirable fruit would be produced—just as neem seeds and the like produce neem trees and so forth.
But since, in this case, the gift is the volition of relinquishment characterized by the diffusion of a benevolent mind, therefore...
"Even when the object to be given is undesirable, the gift still has a desirable fruit.

When the opponent has thus established that a mental state constitutes the act of giving, the proponent, by way of another method, seeks to prove that the object to be given also constitutes the act of giving, and says:
"The Blessed One stated that a gift has a desirable fruit," and so forth. The opponent—
However, one rejects [the proposition] because one does not see that robes and so forth have desirable results.

The application of the sutta is applicable both to the opponent's doctrine and to one's own doctrine, yet not in the same sense. Since it is said that "the object to be given has a desirable fruit," only the state of having a desirable fruit is rejected.
Therefore, the fact that it "should not be stated" by him is appropriate precisely in terms of its having a desirable fruit.

In the sense of being something to be given, however, the object to be given is simply "giving" (*dāna*). Indeed, this discourse is intended solely for the purpose of releasing [the giver] from the state of confusion regarding what has been given and what constitutes giving.
*Commentary on the Discourse on Giving* 5. *Commentary on the Discourse on Merit Consisting in Use* (*paribhogamaya-puñña-kathā-vaṇṇanā*)
483. Now follows the discussion on so-called "merit consisting in enjoyment" (*paribhogamaya-puñña*).

In this regard, those who hold the view that "there is such a thing as merit consisting in enjoyment," having misinterpreted suttas such as, "For them, merit increases day and night, always," and, "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is enjoying a robe," and so forth, [assert that there exists merit consisting in enjoyment]. Just as...

[This concerns] the Rājagirika, Siddhatthika, and Sammitiya schools. Referring to them, the question "consisting of enjoyment" (*paribhogamaya*) was posed by the proponent of our own school (Sakavādin), and the admission was given by the other.
Then, in order to challenge him with the argument that "merit (*puñña*) consists of wholesome states such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth, and nothing beyond that;
therefore, it must increase through contact and the rest," the passage beginning with "Contact consists of enjoyment" (*paribhogamayo phasso*) was commenced. That...
Everything else is rejected because there is no growth for them. The phrases beginning with "like creepers" are stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent]:
"Even without action or cultivation, just as creepers and so forth grow by themselves, why do they not grow in that way?
However, because such growth does not occur for him, it is rejected with the words "it is not so."
Regarding the question, "Does he not attend to it?": [The Buddha] acknowledges that "it becomes merit" by way of the recipient's enjoyment, through which the prior volition increases.
Then, when questioned by such terms as "not regretting," he denies [the increase] with reference to the donor’s volition of relinquishment (*cāgacetanā*).
In that context, "not regretting" refers to that which precedes the volition of giving.
For one who does not turn back or reverse the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) by means of adverting (āvajjana). "Without effort" (anābhoga) means without exertion (nirābhoga).

"Not attending" (asamannāharanta) means not bringing [the object] to mind. For adverting, having interrupted the life-continuum, is said to "attend" to the volition of giving as it arises on its own path. By this consciousness, which has such a function...
He asks: "Does merit accrue to one who does not attend? "Amanasikarontassa" means to one who does not direct the mind.
For by means of adverting (āvajjana), one is said to "make" the mind that arises immediately thereafter; thus, the meaning is "to one who does not do so.
This locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. "Acetayantassa" means to one who does not generate volition (cetanā). "Apatthentassa" means...
For one who does not exercise wholesome desire, which is termed "aspiration" (*patthanā*). "Not directing [the mind]" (*appaṇidahantassa*) means placing the mind by way of the volition of giving;
this is the meaning. [Objection: Is it not the case that for one who "turns [the mind] toward" (*āvaṭṭentassa*), there is an application of attention (*ābhoga*)?

[Response: It belongs to one who possesses such application of attention (*ābhogavato*). Alternatively, the meaning is that this merit arises either for one who has such application of attention, or immediately after that application of attention.
485. Regarding the statements "of two contacts," etc., he rejects them because, in a single moment, the donor lacks two contacts and so forth;
yet he affirms them with reference to the contacts and so forth of both the donor and the one consuming [the gift].

Furthermore, he holds the view that there is a simultaneous conjunction (*samodhāna*) of the five consciousnesses, and it is on the basis of this that he affirms [those statements]. Then, he [addresses] him...
The proponent (sakavādī), having closed the door to the opponent's method, asks a question on "wholesome" (*kusala*) and so forth in order to challenge him with a direct counter-argument.
Therein, he rejects [the opponent's position] by referring to the absence of association between the wholesome and the unwholesome within a single moment.
However, he admits it by asserting the thesis that "that which consists of enjoyment (*paribhogamaya*) arises dissociated from consciousness. Then, the proponent refutes him by means of a Sutta.

486. Regarding the statement "merit always increases," this refers to the merit arising from time to time through the recollection and reflection upon those who plant groves and so forth during the practice of the suttas.

As for the phrase "his flood of merit is immeasurable," this is because he is one who dwells in the immeasurable states, and it also refers to the act of rejoicing [in the merit] by thinking, "He is using such a robe as a requisite given to me."

And it has been said: "He perceives that [merit] consists in enjoyment. However, since merit indeed arises even when the gift has been accepted by the recipient but not yet enjoyed, the position of our own school (sakavādin) is stronger;
in this context, the meaning should be understood as "having been accepted by the recipient. The rest is self-evident.
Commentary on the Discussion of Merit Consisting in Enjoyment. 6. Commentary on the Discussion of What is Given from Here (Itodinnakathā). 488–491.
Now follows the discussion known as "What is Given from Here. In that regard, for those [who hold] that "the departed (petā) subsist by what is given from here,"...

Based on the statement, "They have passed away there," the tenet [held] is that "they subsist by means of exactly those robes and other requisites given from here," as is the case with the Rājagirika-Siddhatthikas.
With reference to them, the question "given from here" is asked by the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is made by the opponent (itarassa).
Again, when pursued regarding robes and so forth, he rejects it. [The phrase] "one person is the doer for another" [is used].
It is meant that one who gives the result of another’s karma is a different agent; it is not the case that one performs karma for oneself by means of oneself.
When questioned thus, the other person rejects it out of fear of contradicting the Suttas.
“Giving a gift” means seeing one who is giving a gift. In that regard, because of their own act of rejoicing, their wealth [arises] there.
They arise; therefore, for one who establishes a doctrine on this basis, that doctrine remains unestablished.
For they do not subsist solely on the material given from here. This same method applies to the remaining scriptural proofs as well.
Thus ends the commentary on the discussion of what is given from here.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Threefold Ripening of Karma Regarding the Earth (Pathavī-kamma-vipāka-otika-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 492.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Threefold Ripening of Karma Regarding the Earth. In this context, regarding the statement:

"There is karma that leads to sovereignty (*issariya-saṃvattaniya*), there is karma that leads to lordship (*ādhipacca-saṃvattaniya*)," here "sovereignty" (*issariya*) is the state of being a ruler (*issara*), and [lordship] is the state of being a master (*adhipati*).
It has been stated that "existence" (bhāva) means sovereignty, and there exists karma conducive to the sovereignty of mastery over the earth.
Therefore, with reference to those who hold the view that "the earth is the result of kamma," such as the Andhakas, the proponent asks, "Is the earth [the result of kamma]?
and the other admits it. The passage beginning with "conducive to pleasant feeling" is for the purpose of demonstrating the essential nature of the result of kamma.
It has been stated: "Contact exists," and so forth. Among the resultant states indicated by such a method, contact is divided into that which is to be experienced as pleasant and so on.
That [contact], as well as perception and the others, are associated with pleasant feeling and the rest; feeling and the others are associated with perception and the rest.
All of them have an object, and they possess advertence—consisting of preliminary application, turning toward, and so on—and they function as a condition for kamma.

Volition (*cetanā*), which is the aspiration for the desirable result therein—the root-craving that functions by way of longing—is what [the first speaker] asks about when he asks, "Is such earth yours?
The other denies it. The questions in reverse order (*paṭilomapucchā*) and so forth have their meanings already explained. 493.
Regarding the question, "Is the ripening of kamma common to others?", he denies it with reference to contact (*phassa*) and the other factors; however, that which is originated by kamma—
And he admits [the existence of] form (rūpa) with reference to its commonality (*sādhāraṇabhāva*) among earth and the other [elements].
He presents a sutta cited from another school (*parasamaya*) which considers it uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). To the question, "Do all beings enjoy the earth?
he denies it with reference to those not dependent on the earth, but admits it with reference to those who are dependent. Without enjoying the earth...
Regarding the question, "Do they attain final Nibbāna? he affirms this with reference to those who attain final Nibbāna in the formless realms (*ārūpa*).
The phrase "without exhausting the ripening of kamma" is stated according to the tenets of other schools (*parasamaya*);

for it is their doctrine that one attains final Nibbāna only after exhausting the ripening of kamma. However, in our own school (*sakasamaya*), there is no attainment of final Nibbāna without exhausting the ripening of kamma that has already found its opportunity to arise.
And according to their tenet, because the earth is a common result (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*), it is indeed a result that has already arisen.

It is appropriate to challenge this by saying that it is not possible for final nibbāna to occur without exhausting that which remains in the state of being a result. The other rejects this on the basis of their own tenet.
Regarding the question, "Is the karma-result of a Wheel-turning Monarch [common]?", he rejects it with reference to contact and so forth, which are not common.
He asserts [this] with reference to what is common. For it is their tenet that the earth, the oceans, the sun, the moon, and so forth, are the result of karma common to all.
494. Regarding the phrase "conducive to sovereignty": here, "sovereignty" (*issariya*) means the possession of great wealth.

"Lordship" (*ādhipacca*) means the state of being a lord (*adhipati*) in the sense of exercising authority over other people and being held in high esteem by them. In that regard, karma functions by way of acquisition.
It is called "conducive to that" (*taṃsaṃvattanika*) by way of its leading toward it, not by way of producing it. Therefore, this [argument] does not prove that [the earth] is a result of kamma.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether the earth is a result of kamma. 8.
Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Aging and Death are Results of Kamma.
495. Now follows the discussion on the ripening of aging-and-death, titled "The Discourse on the Extremes of Ripening.

In this regard, for those who hold that "there is karma conducive to ugliness and karma conducive to short life," where "ugliness" is aging and "shortness of life" is death—and since there is indeed karma conducive to these—therefore they maintain the thesis that aging-and-death is a result of ripening (*vipāka*), just as [in the case of other results].

[This refers to] the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission belongs to the other. In the counter-question (*paṭilomapañhe*), [the answer is] "without an object" (*anārammaṇa*).

First, material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*) are indeed without an object. Furthermore, for immaterial phenomena (*arūpa*), aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is without an object because of the absence of the characteristic of association (*sampayoga-lakkhaṇa*).
496. Regarding the question: "Is the aging-and-death of unwholesome states the result (*vipāka*) of unwholesome states?"—by means of aging-and-death...

He admits to the tenet that "it must have an undesirable result. For that very reason, he rejects the idea that the aging and death of wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) constitute a wholesome result (*kusala-vipāka*). Furthermore, he subsequently admits that they are indeed an unwholesome result (*akusala-vipāka*).

The phrase "of both wholesome and unwholesome" is formulated as a single unit by way of a question; however, such a thing does not exist within a single moment. [This applies] to the indeterminate (*abyākata*)...
There is no way in which aging and death could be said to be the result of kamma that is non-resultant; therefore, the question was not asked with reference to the indeterminate (abyākata).
Regarding the phrase "conducive to ugliness" (*dubbaṇṇasaṃvattaniya*): here, "ugliness" (*dubbaṇṇiya*) means impurity of complexion.
"Shortness of life" (*appāyukatā*) means the incapacity for the life-span to persist for long. In this context, unwholesome kamma [is the cause] of that which is originated by kamma...
It is a condition for ugliness by way of kamma-condition; however, because it is dissimilar, it is not its result.
But it is a condition for temperature-originated [matter] and so forth by way of its acquisition, and for life by way of its interruption.
Thus, this is called "conducive to that" in a figurative sense, not by way of being a producer like resultant contact and the rest; therefore, in the state of being a result—
It is not a producer [of kamma]. The rest here is exactly as stated below.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning aging-and-death as a result of kamma.
9. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Result of Noble Dhamma.
498. Now follows the discussion titled "The Ripening of Noble Dhamma.

In this context, there are those—such as the Andhakas—who hold the view that the fruit of recluseship consists merely in the abandonment of defilements, and not in the mental states and mental factors themselves.
With reference to them, the proponent asks: "Is there no ripening of noble dhamma? Herein, "the ripening of noble dhamma" refers to that which is comprised by the Path.
It is the fruition of the noble Dhamma. According to the tenet that the noble fruit is merely the exhaustion of the defilements, this is the admission of the other [position].
"Asceticism" (*sāmañña*) means the state of being an ascetic; this is a name for the Path. For it has been said: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you asceticism and the fruit of asceticism.
The same method applies to "brahminhood" (*brahmañña*) as well.

In such passages as "The fruit of stream-entry is not a result of kamma-result," he asserts that the noble fruits are not results by referring to the fact that the path of stream-entry and so forth lead to the diminution [of defilements], while he rejects [the application of this term] to the fruits of giving and the like.

For he maintains the following meaning for the term *ācayagāmi*: they are "leading to accumulation" because they go toward an accumulation known as kamma-result, or because they proceed while accumulating that [result].
They are called "leading to diminution" because they go about diminishing kamma-result (*vipāka*). Therefore, he both admits and rejects [the opponent's position] in this way. 500.
The question beginning with "Is wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere accompanied by result leading to accumulation? belongs to the opponent;
the admission and the rejection belong to the proponent. For mundane wholesome kamma consists of result, death, rebirth-linking, and the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

It is "leading to accumulation" (*ācaya-gāmi*) because it goes while accumulating. Supramundane wholesome [kamma] is "leading to dispersal" (*apacaya-gāmi*) because it goes while dispersing both death and rebirth-linking as well as the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Thus, this [supramundane wholesome kamma] is indeed with result (*savipāka*); it is not without result merely by virtue of the term "leading to dispersal.
It is with reference to this meaning that the admission and the rejection of our own position (the Sautrāntika) should be understood here.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Ripening of Noble Qualities. 10. Commentary on the Discussion: "Ripening is a Dhamma that has the nature of ripening. 501.
Now follows the discussion known as "Ripening is a Dhamma that has the nature of ripening. In this regard, since ripening is [the result] of ripening...

It is a condition by way of conditions such as mutuality (*aññamañña-paccaya*) and so forth. Therefore, regarding those who hold the view that even a resultant state (*vipāka*) is a phenomenon subject to resultancy (*vipākadhammadhamma*)—such as the Andhakas—the question is posed by the proponent of the orthodox position (*sakavādin*), and the other party gives his assent.
For him, "its resultant" means that whatever resultant belongs to that resultant phenomenon subject to resultancy, that too is, for you, a phenomenon subject to resultancy.
He asks, "Does it exist? The other denies it, referring to the absence of the giving of a result in the future.
When asked a second time, he affirms it, referring to the arising of another result conditioned by that [first one].

Such being the case, just as there is a result for the wholesome and unwholesome, there would also be a result for that result, and a result for that result as well; thus, when questioned, [he sees that] the non-cessation of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) would follow.
He rejects [the position] out of fear of contradicting the established doctrine (*samaya*).

Regarding the phrase "or it is a result" (*vipāko vā*) and so forth, in the context of establishing the meaning through the word, he rejects it by arguing that if there were identity of meaning between a result (*vipāka*) and a phenomenon subject to ripening (*vipākadhammadhamma*), then wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena would also fall into a state of identity. Thus: "The result and the phenomenon subject to ripening..."

And here, this is the intended meaning: for he, regarding each one among the four resultant aggregates as being "of a nature to result" (*vipākadhammadhamma*) in the sense of being a condition—such as through the condition of mutuality—and as "resultant" (*vipāka*) in the sense of being conditionally arisen, admits when asked, "Is the resultant of a nature to result?
by saying, "Yes. Then the proponent [of the thesis] says to him: "Since, in a single moment..."
He spoke thus in order to challenge [the opponent] by saying: "In the four aggregates, both the resultant (vipāka) and that which is of the nature to result (vipākadhammadhamma) are admitted;

therefore, it follows that they possess the state of being co-nascent and so forth. The other [respondent] rejects this, referring to that which is called wholesome or unwholesome as being of the nature to result.
[The challenger asks: "If those [aggregates] are both resultant and of the nature to result, then that which is an unwholesome resultant—"

Thus, one falls into what is unwholesome. Why? Because it is of the same nature as that which has the quality of ripening (vipākadhammadhamma). This same method applies to the cases of "that very thing is wholesome," and so forth. 502.

As for the phrase "mutually related conditions" (aññamaññapaccaya), this is stated merely in terms of the conditionality of co-nascent factors; therefore, it is not a proving factor. Furthermore, the mutual conditionality of the great primary elements (mahābhūta) is also taught, yet they are neither results of kamma (vipāka) nor do they have the quality of ripening.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding "resultant state" (vipāka) and "state having the quality of ripening" (vipākadhammadhamma).
The Seventh Chapter.
8. The Eighth Chapter: 1. An Exposition on the Discourse Concerning the Six Destinations.

503–504. Now follows the discussion on the six destinations (*chagatikathā*). Regarding this, there is the tenet held by some—such as the Andhakas and the Uttarāpathakas—that there are six destinations including the host of asuras (*asurakāya*).
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent (*sakavādī*), and the other [the opponent] gives his assent.
Then the proponent, citing the *Lomahaṃsanapariyāya* [Sutta], says: "But, Sāriputta, these five destinations..."
He said, "Are there not five destinies? and so forth, in order to urge [the opponent] by means of the limited number of destinies.
The other [opponent] admits [this], fearing contradiction with the Sutta. But why does the proponent not accept six destinies?

Is it not the case that in the passage, "And he is liberated from the four states of deprivation," the host of asuras is also included? True, it is included, but this is not a destiny. Why? Because it is separate.

Because of their non-existence [as a separate realm]. For among the asura hosts, the Kālakañjika asuras are included within the destiny of the hungry ghosts (petagati), while the assembly of Vepacitti is included within the destiny of the gods;
thus, there is no such thing as a "separate destiny" called the asura host.
Now, in order to demonstrate this very point, the passage beginning with "Is it not the case that the Kālakañjikās... is commenced. In that context, "of similar appearance" means...
"Of similar form and shape" means they are ugly, misshapen, and unsightly. "Sharing common enjoyments" means they engage in similar sexual conduct.
"Sharing common food" means they consume similar secretions such as saliva, mucus, pus, blood, and so forth. "Sharing a common lifespan" means they have an identical limit to their life-span.
"Marriage" refers both to the taking of a bride and the giving away of a bride. In the bright (wholesome) side, "of similar color" means having similar form and shape.

They are beautiful, pleasing, lovely to behold, and endowed with radiance. "Sharing enjoyments" means they share in the enjoyment of the fivefold qualities of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) alike.
"Sharing food" means they share in food such as celestial nectar (*sudhā*) alike. The rest is exactly as previously stated. As for the objection:

"Is there not a body of asuras?"—this indeed establishes the existence of a body of asuras; however, because that [body] lacks a distinct classification as a separate destiny (*gati*), it does not establish [it] as a separate destiny.
Commentary on the Discourse on Chagaṭika. 2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Intermediate State (Antarābhava). 505.

Now follows what is called the discourse on the intermediate state. In this regard, for those [who hold that] there is a scriptural passage stating, "one who attains final nibbāna in the interval" (*antarā-parinibbāyī*),...
Having grasped this without proper reflection, they hold the view: "There is such a thing as an intermediate state (antarābhava), wherein a being—

whether lacking divine vision like one who possesses it, or lacking psychic power like one who possesses it— remains for seven days or more than seven days while awaiting the union of the parents and the proper season," just as is the case with the Pubbaseliyas and the Sammitiyas.
Referring to this, the question "Does it exist? belongs to the proponent of the thesis; the admission [of its existence] is made by the other, standing upon his own tenet.

Then, desiring to challenge him by means of those three states of existence (*bhava*) spoken of by the Blessed One, he says: "The sensual state of existence," and so forth. Herein, the intended meaning is as follows:
if there is for you some state of existence called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), then by that very fact, it must be one of the others, such as the sensual state of existence.
It must exist like the existence consisting of the five aggregates (pañcavokāra-bhava); therefore, I ask you:

"Is this so-called intermediate state (antarābhava) the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), or is it the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) or the immaterial existence (arūpabhava)? The other, not desiring it to be so, rejects everything.
And as for the phrase "of the sense-sphere existence," etc., if there were such a thing as an intermediate state, it would have to be between these two existences.
He began to urge: "May the boundary be like the space between boundaries.
However, the opponent, not desiring it to be so, rejected every question solely on the basis of his own tenets and not according to the Dhamma.
For that very reason, the proponent refuted him, saying: "Indeed, no, sir!"

506. The statements beginning with "The fifth is that womb" and so forth were spoken in order to challenge [the opponent] by suggesting that since he does not find a synthesis within the wombs and so on as they have been defined, there must therefore be something additional to those. As for the phrase "kamma leading to the intermediate state":
if that too is a single existence (*bhava*), then why did the Teacher analyze it—just as he analyzed the kamma leading to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and others—by distinguishing it?
It is stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent] that since [the intermediate state] has been shown [in the suttas], there must likewise be a specific karma leading to it. However,

because in the systems of others (parasamaya) there is no separate karma called "leading to the intermediate state," but rather their tenet is that one is reborn in the intermediate state by the very same karma that leads to whichever existence one is to enter, the phrase "not indeed" is used as a rejection [of that view].
When asked, "Is there a being who goes to the intermediate state (antarābhava)? he rejects it because of his tenet that there are only those who go to the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava).
When asked about "being born" and so forth, he also rejects it, as he does not admit to birth, aging, and death therein, nor to the succession of death and rebirth-linking.
Even when asked by way of form and other such qualities, [he rejects it] because for the being of the intermediate state, form is non-manifest (anidassana).
His view is that feeling and the other aggregates are not coarse (*oḷārika*) like those of others; therefore, he rejects [the classification].
For this very reason, his rejection should also be understood to apply to the existence of the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*). 507.
Now follows the "Concordance of Existence" (*bhava-saṃsandana*), beginning with "sensual existence is existence, it is a destination," and so forth. Herein, this is the intended meaning:

If there were some state called "intermediate existence" (antarābhava) that existed in its own right—just as distinctions such as the realms of existence (bhava) and destinies (gati) are found within the realms of sense-desire (kāmabhava) and so forth—it would likewise be found there.
Or, just as it is not found there, it would not be found in these [realms] either.
For if the nature of being a state of existence (bhava-bhāva) is common to both, why is this distinction present only in these and not in the other? What is the reason for this?
Regarding "due to specific reasons": the other, however, by way of mere opinion, both asserts and denies various points.

(508) When asked whether there is an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) for all beings, he denies it because he does not accept an intermediate existence for those bound for hell, those born among non-percipient beings, or those bound for the formless realm;
for that very reason, he asserts it in the reverse order.
Regarding the phrase "of one who has committed an immediate offense" (*ānantariyassa*) and so forth:

this was stated in order to analyze and demonstrate the views of those who do not accept the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). All of that should be understood according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*), together with the supporting suttas. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Intermediate State (*Antarābhavakathāvaṇṇanā*).
3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Strands of Sensual Pleasure (Kāmaguṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 510.

Now follows the discourse known as the "Strands of Sensual Pleasure" (kāmaguṇakathā). In this regard, first of all, according to our own school (sakasamaya), the term "sense-sphere" (kāmadhātu) refers to both sense-objects (vatthukāmā) and defilements (kilesakāmā), as well as the existence of the sense-sphere (kāmabhava).
Among these, sense-objects are called "sensual pleasures" (kāmā) in the sense of being desirable; they are [also] empty in the sense of being devoid of intrinsic nature (sabhāvanissatta-suññata).
“Dhātu” means the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*). Defilement-desires (*kilesakāma*) are called “desires” (*kāma*) in the sense of being desirable and in the sense of craving;

and by the same meaning already stated, they are called an “element” (*dhātu*), thus “sense-sphere element. Sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is a “desire” for three reasons: in the sense of being desirable, in the sense of craving, and in the sense of being the locus for the occurrence of objective desires (*vatthukāma*);
and by the same meaning already stated, it is called an “element,” thus “sense-sphere element. Furthermore, in the systems of others: “These five... [etc.]

Relying merely on the statement, “O monks, these are the strands of sensual pleasure,” it was understood that only the five strands of sensual pleasure constitute the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu).
Therefore, with reference to those who hold this view—such as the Pubbaseliyas today—the proponent of the first position asks, “Are there only five?
in order to clarify the diversity of the sense-sphere element. The other’s admission is made according to their own tenet. [The opponent then asks: “Is it not the case that...? and so forth.

This is stated for the purpose of showing that [the desire realm] consists of defilements and sensual pleasures. In this context, "connected with that" means connected with the strands of sensual pleasure;

the sense is that they have the strands of sensual pleasure as their object. Indeed, it should not be said that there are only five [objects], for when these—desire and so forth—are connected with those [strands], one cannot say that only the five strands of sensual pleasure constitute the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). For these factors, such as desire, are both "sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) in the sense of being desirable and "elements" (*dhātu*).

And "also" refers to the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*). The meaning of "sense-sphere of desire" (*kāmadhātu*) is that it is a sphere (*dhātu*) designated as "desire" (*kāma*) in the sense of being desired.
The passage beginning with "the eye of humans" is stated for the purpose of showing the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*).

Therein, the opponent, having rejected the status of the six bases (*āyatana*) as not being the sense-sphere of desire on the grounds that they are themselves objects of sensual desire, is then asked about "mind" (*mano*); [he replies] "the sublime and supramundane."

Having in mind [the fact that] it does not possess the state of the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), he claims [it to be so]. However, since all mind belonging to the three planes is indeed the sense-sphere, the proponent refutes him with a Sutta.

(511) The passage beginning "The strands of sensual pleasure are existence" is stated for the purpose of showing that existence is the sense-sphere; for it is in the mere strands of sensual pleasure...
There is no conventional expression "becoming" (bhava); therefore, the opponent rejects [the view] with "it is not so.

The passage beginning with "kamma that leads to the strands of sensual pleasure" is stated entirely for the purpose of showing that the mere strands of sensual pleasure do not constitute the realm of sensual desire (kāmadhātu).

For it is only kamma that leads to the existence of sensual desire (kāmabhava), which is designated as the "realm of sensual desire," and only beings who lead to the existence of sensual desire [are included therein]. In that [existence], they are born, they age, and they die.
By this method—that they pass away and are reborn, and not [merely] among the strands of sensual pleasure—the meaning should be understood in all instances.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Strands of Sensual Pleasure. 4. Commentary on the Discussion of Desire.

513–514. Now follows the discussion on sensual desire (*kāma*). In this context, there are those—such as the Pubbaseliyas—who, based merely on the statement, “Bhikkhus, these five strands of sensual pleasure,” hold the view that the five sense bases, beginning with the visible-form base, are themselves sensual desires.

To show that for them only defilement-sensual-desire (*kilesakāma*) possesses the status of sensual desire in the primary sense, the proponent of the true doctrine (Sakavādī) asks: “Are there five? and so forth.
The admission is for the other. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of sensual desire (kāmakathā). 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).

515–516. Now follows the discussion on the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding this, there are those who hold the view that "material phenomena (*rūpino dhammā*) are called the form realm," such as the Andhakas.
With reference to them, the proponent asks, "Are they material? and the opponent assents.
Then the proponent [argues] that since what is called the form realm is actually a state of existence consisting of form (*rūpabhava*), and not merely form itself, therefore—

In that sense, he says "the fine-material element" (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth, in order to challenge [the opponent]. All of this is to be understood according to the method already stated in the discussion on the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
When asked, "Is that itself the desire-element" (*kāmadhātu*), he rejects it, seeing a contradiction with the delimitation of the planes (*bhūmi*).
When asked again more firmly, he admits it according to his own position. But this being so, by means of two existences...
The proponent states, "He incurs possession [of both] by means of that [existence] and by means of the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*)," and so forth.

The opponent rejects this because it is impossible for a single [being] to possess two [types of existence] simultaneously. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
6. Explanation of the Discussion on the Formless Realm (Arūpadhātukathāvaṇṇanā) 517–518. The meaning of the discussion on the formless realm should also be understood by this same method.

However, regarding formless phenomena, the teaching here is presented by taking only the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) as the basis, according to the method beginning with "feeling is existence" (*vedanā bhavo*). In that context, what are those formless phenomena?

The meaning should be understood as follows: it is "gone to the category" (*saṅkhaṃ gatā*) because it is one of the [factors] beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated below.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*). 7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Bases (*āyatana*) in the Material Element (*rūpadhātu*).
519. Now follows the discussion on the sense bases (*āyatana*) regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

In this context, there are those—such as the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas—who, relying on the Sutta passage, "Possessing form, mind-made, complete in all limbs and parts, not lacking any faculties," maintain the thesis that even the nose and other [faculties] of the Brahmakāyika deities are indeed sense bases, and thus their personal existence (*attabhāva*) consists of six sense bases.
Having in mind those [six], the question "Is there the sixfold base? was asked by the proponent of the first position (sakavādī), while the other’s admission was made according to his own tenet.
Then, in order to challenge him by way of that which is not a base therein, the passage beginning "Is there the nose-base therein?
was commenced. Thereafter, the opponent [replied] regarding the shape-characteristic of the three internal bases therein, such as the nose and so forth...

He admits [it] on the basis of the tenet that "that very thing is the sense-base. When questioned regarding external sense-bases such as odors and so forth, he does not accept the nose-faculty and the rest therein;
therefore, he rejects them by denying their objective domain.
The meaning should be understood in this same manner even for the questions concerning the reverse order and the cross-referencing questions.
521. "Therein exists the nose-base (ghānāyatana) and there exists the odor-base (gandhāyatana);
by means of that nose, one smells that odor"—this was said with reference to certain teachers within that very same other system (parasamaya).
For it is said that they maintain that the six internal bases (ajjhattikāni āyatanāni) are complete therein, and that a base must indeed possess its own specific function (sakiccaka). By them...
They also maintain that those odors and so forth are smelled, tasted, and touched by the nose and the other [senses].
With reference to this tenet, the opponent acknowledges it, saying, "Yes.
However, when questioned regarding the statements beginning with "Is there a root-odor there?", he denies them, being unable to establish their existence.
[Objection: "But surely such passages as 'Is there there the sign of the nose? establish only the mere shape, not the sense-base (āyatana);
therefore, even what has been cited is just like what was not cited.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the sense-bases within the element of form.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Form in the Formless Realm (Arūpe Rūpakathāvaṇṇanā) §§524–526.

Now follows the discussion of form in the formless realm. In this regard, there are those who hold the view that because of the statement, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]," there exists in the formless existence a subtle form that has escaped coarse form; for example, [the Andhakas].
And for the Andhakas; referring to them, the question "Is there form? belongs to the proponent (sakavādin), and the affirmation belongs to the other. The rest here is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of form in the formless realm. 9. Commentary on the Discussion of Form as Being Kamma.
527–537. Now follows the discussion on matter as action (*rūpakammantikathā*).

In this regard, there are those—such as the Mahīśāsakas and the Saṃmitīyas—who hold the view that bodily and verbal intimation (*kāyaviññatti* and *vacīviññatti*), which are themselves material form, constitute bodily action and verbal action respectively;
and that these are wholesome when originated by the wholesome, and unwholesome when originated by the unwholesome. With reference to them, [the text says] "by the wholesome..."
"Arising from the mind" is the question of the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is that of the other.

Then, in order to challenge him—asking, "If that is wholesome, does it possess those qualities such as having an object (*sārammaṇa*) which are found in wholesome [states]?"—the passage beginning with "having an object" is commenced.
In this context, "aspiration" (*patthanā*) and "resolve" (*paṇidhi*) are synonyms for volition (*cetanā*) itself; for it is indeed wholesome volition that...
"Formulating an aspiration" (*pakappayamānā patthanā*). Because it exists by way of formulating, it is also called "resolution" (*paṇidhi*).

However, in the subsequent passage concerning feeling, perception, volition, faith, and so forth—which arise from a wholesome mind—it is only among these factors, such as feeling and the rest, that "aspiration" and "resolution" are applicable, and not to volition.
Why? Because two types of volition cannot exist simultaneously.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the tradition (tanti) has proceeded in this way because it has entered the ear.
The passage beginning with "the base of visible form" is stated for the purpose of showing the detailed classification of what was abbreviated as "all that is wholesome" in the previous section.

The remaining methods of correlation, as well as the entire discussion on verbal action beginning with "arisen from an unwholesome mind," should be understood strictly according to the canonical text (pāḷi).
In this context, however, "impurity" (asuci) refers to semen. The grammatical derivation of the term is self-evident.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding matter as an action-resultant (kammaja-rūpa). 10. Commentary on the Discussion of the Life-faculty (jīvitindriya).

540. Now follows the discussion on the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). In this context, there are those who hold the view that the life-faculty is a non-material phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*) dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*), and therefore there is no material life-faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*); such as the Pubbaseliyas and the Sammitiyas.

With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent of his own position (*sakavādin*), and the other party gives his assent. [The question: "Is there no [life-faculty] for those possessing form?"...

In the question regarding the "life-span of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ āyu*), he accepts that even for appropriated matter (*upādinnarūpa*) and for grass, wood, and so forth, it is precisely their occurrence by way of continuity (*santāna*) that constitutes life-span (*āyu*), stability (*ṭhiti*), subsistence (*yapanā*), maintenance (*yāpanā*), movement (*iriyanā*), persistence (*vattanā*), and preservation (*pālanā*); therefore, he rejects [the opponent's position].

In the question "Does it exist?", he likewise affirms it for this reason. In the question "Does the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpajīvitindriya*) exist?", [he affirms it] regarding immaterial phenomena.
He asserts that there exists a continuum of the life-faculty dissociated from consciousness; therefore, he makes this admission.

(541) Regarding the question, "Is the life-span of material phenomena the immaterial life-faculty?"—whether they belong to the continuum of a sentient being as material or immaterial—he asserts that for all of them, it is exclusively the immaterial life-faculty dissociated from consciousness; therefore, he makes this admission.

(542) Even in the questions concerning those who have attained the attainment of cessation, he denies [the existence of material phenomena] with reference specifically to the immaterial life-force dissociated from consciousness.

And he also admits it. But the proponent, not accepting that, says "If so" and so forth, in order to challenge [the opponent] by arguing that if there were no occurrence of the formless, there would have to be form.

In the question regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), he denies it with reference to the aggregate of formations consisting of contact and so forth, but he admits it with reference to the aggregate of formations consisting of bodily action and so forth. [This concerns] bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).
"Vocal intimation, right speech, right action, the life-faculty," and so forth—such phenomena are also included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); such is his doctrine.
