However, the proponent of our own position (the Theravādin), not accepting that, says "Is there an aggregate of feeling? and so on, in order to challenge him:
"If the aggregate of mental formations exists even when the immaterial process has ceased, then let there be the existence of all four aggregates."

The other denies it with reference to the internal attainment (*samāpatti*), while he asserts it with reference to the preceding and succeeding moments of one who is entering or emerging from that attainment.
This same method applies to the section on non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*). For according to his tenet, at the time of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) for non-percipient beings—
The mind, having arisen, ceases; together with it, the immaterial life-faculty dissociated from mind arises and continues for the duration of the lifespan.
Therefore, when asked whether they possess the life-faculty, he denies it;

when asked whether they possess it, he affirms it. He likewise denies that the aggregates such as feeling exist for them by way of their continued occurrence (*pavatti*), but affirms them by way of death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-patisandhi*).
[The opponent] admits [this]. But the proponent, not accepting that, says "fivefold existence" (*pañcavokārabhava*) in order to challenge him:
"If feeling and the other [aggregates] exist there even for a single moment, one attains the state of fivefold existence. The other rejects this for fear of contradicting the Suttas. 544–545.
Regarding the question, "Is it partially broken?"—it is the associated [factors] that are broken, while the dissociated [factors] remain. His...
This is their tenet; therefore, he admits it. "There are two life-faculties" is the question of the opponent; "Yes" is the admission of our own school.
For there are two life-faculties by way of the material and the immaterial; by means of these alone a being lives, and it is said that through their dissolution one dies.
Indeed, at the moment of death, both life-faculties perish together.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Life-faculty. 11. Commentary on the Discussion of the Cause of Karma. 546.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Cause of Karma. In this regard, concerning an Arahant by whom another Arahant was previously misaccused in a former existence:

Regarding those who hold the view that one falls away from Arahatship because of such karma—namely, the Pubbaseliyas and the Sammitiyas—it is with reference to them that the proponent asks, "Is it because of karma?
and the other admits, "Yes. The rest is exactly as stated in the discussion on falling away (*parihānikathā*).
"Indeed, he slanders the Arahants"—this [statement] is said by the opponent to make the other accept that very karma on account of which one falls away.
Then the proponent, having made him admit that position, says "ye keci... and so forth, in order to challenge him:
"If that were so, then all those who have never before slandered the Arahants would attain Arahantship. The other [responds]: "The Arahantship of that karma..."
He rejects it because he does not see a fixed rule regarding its attainment.
End of the commentary on the discussion of the cause of kamma.
The eighth chapter.
9. The Ninth Chapter: 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Seeing the Advantage (Ānisaṃsadassāvī-kathā). 547.
Now follows the discourse known as "Seeing the Advantage. In that regard, within one's own system, [one views] conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as disadvantageous and Nibbāna...

"It is certain that for one who sees [the practice] in terms of its benefits, there is the abandoning of the fetters. However, regarding those who—having adopted a one-sided doctrine concerning both of these points—hold the view, "Only for one who sees the benefits is there the abandoning of the fetters," such as the Andhakas:
the question is directed at the proponent of our own school (Sakavādī), and the affirmation is from the other. Then, for him, [regarding] the one-sided doctrine...

"Since it has been grasped by her, the danger must also be seen"—with this in mind, for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction, the proponent (sakavādī) says, "He attends to formations as impermanent," and so forth.
Regarding the question, "He attends to formations as impermanent and perceives the benefits in Nibbāna," this is the intended meaning:
their doctrine is that for one who perceives the benefits [of Nibbāna], there is the abandoning of the fetters. Is it not the case that he attends to formations as impermanent?
When asked, "Are the fetters abandoned by one who attends [to them]? he admits, "Yes.
Thereby it follows that he attends to those formations as impermanent and perceives the benefits in Nibbāna; do you accept this?
Then the opponent denies this, referring to a single moment of consciousness; when asked a second time, he does so on account of various moments of consciousness.

[The opponent] admits [this]. However, the proponent, having crushed his intention and because the perception of the benefits of contemplating impermanence has been admitted as one and the same, asks:
"Is there a convergence of two contacts and two consciousnesses?
The other, not seeing such a convergence of two, denies it. The same method applies to the questions beginning with "as suffering" and so forth.
What, then, is the conclusion here? Is it that the fetters are abandoned by one who attends to [the object] as impermanent and so forth;
or rather, by one who sees the benefits in Nibbāna; or perhaps by one who does both together?

If the abandonment were to occur for one attending to it as impermanent and so forth, it would happen through the mind of insight (vipassanā-citta) alone. If, on the other hand, it were for one who sees the benefits...
For one who perceives the benefits of Nibbāna by way of hearsay, it would occur through the mind of insight (vipassanā-citta) alone;
or, if one were to combine both [the path and insight] together, there would be a convergence of two contacts and so forth.

However, at the moment of the Noble Path (ariya-magga), the function of the mental attention to impermanence and so forth reaches its fulfillment, because the apprehension of permanence and so forth has become a state of non-arising.

And the direct perception of the benefits of Nibbāna is accomplished; therefore, it should be understood that for one who perceives the benefits of Nibbāna by taking it as an object through the process of mental attention directed toward impermanence and so forth— both by way of the accomplishment of what is to be done and by way of its occurrence—
the abandoning of the fetters takes place.

548. The sutta, “One who contemplates happiness in Nibbāna,” establishes only the state of contemplating happiness in Nibbāna and so forth; it does not establish the abandoning of the fetters merely by seeing its benefits. Therefore, even though it has been cited, it is just like what was not cited.
Commentary on the Discussion of Seeing Benefits. 2.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Deathless Object.

549. Now follows the discussion on the object of the Deathless (*amatārammaṇakathā*). In this regard, there are those—such as the Pubbaseliyas—who, having grasped the meaning of such passages as "he conceives Nibbāna" in an improper way, hold the view that the fetter has the Deathless as its object.

With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent (*sakavādī*), and the admission is made by the opponent (*itaro*). Then [the proponent asks]: "If the fetter has the Deathless as its object..."
He said, "The Deathless is a fetter," and so forth, in order to challenge [the opponent] by suggesting that it would follow that the Deathless possesses the nature of being a fetter and so on.
The other [opponent], fearing contradiction with the Suttas, rejects everything. The meaning in all instances should be understood by this method.

As for the Sutta cited from the perspective of "Nibbāna as Nibbāna," however, it was spoken with reference to *diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna* (Nibbāna in the present life); therefore, it does not prove [the point].
Commentary on the Discussion of the Object of the Deathless. 3. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Matter Has an Object. 552–553.
Now follows the discussion known as "Whether Matter Has an Object. In this context, matter has an object in the sense of being conditioned.
"It is called [consciousness] because it does not take another object" refers to the condition of the object (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

However, regarding those who hold the view that matter (*rūpa*) possesses an object without distinction—such as the people of the Northern Path (Uttarāpathakas)—the question of the proponent is intended to demonstrate the differentiation of the meaning of "object," while the other's response is an admission.
The rest here should be understood according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

It should be understood thus. Regarding the statement "it should not be said," the opponent's admission in the first question refers to the object that is clung to (*olubbha-ārammaṇa*). In the second question as well, the opponent's admission likewise refers to the object that serves as a condition (*paccaya-ārammaṇa*).
Thus, in this context, the state of having an object (*sārammaṇatā*) is established solely in the sense of being conditioned (*sappaccaya-ṭṭhena*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether material form (*rūpa*) has an object.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Latent Dispositions (Anusaya) Are Without an Object (Anārammaṇa). §§554–556.

Now follows the discussion known as "The Latent Dispositions Are Without an Object. In this regard, there are those—such as the Andhakas and certain others—who hold the view that what are called latent dispositions are dissociated from consciousness, rootless, and indeterminate; and for that very reason, they maintain that they are without an object.

[This concerns] those from the Northern Path (Uttarāpathakas). With reference to them, the question regarding the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) was asked by the proponent of our own school (Sakavādī), and the other [the opponent] admitted it.
Then, in order to challenge him by suggesting that there must be such a thing as a "non-object" (*anārammaṇa*), he said, "Is form... and so forth.

The passage beginning with "sensual lust" (*kāmarāga*) is shown because it is not distinct from the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). Regarding the question, "Is the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) without an object?", [it refers to] the aggregate of volitional formations associated with consciousness.

He rejects [the proposition] with reference to that [consciousness]. He affirms it with reference to the underlying tendency (*anusaya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and the form of bodily action and so forth, which are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
By this same method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.

However, in the question "Is he one who possesses underlying tendencies? the state of possessing underlying tendencies is admitted because the underlying tendencies have not been abandoned, not because of the actual presence of their active manifestation (*pavatti*). For whoever...
That which has not been abandoned is neither past, nor future, nor present. However, because these defilements to be destroyed by the Path have not yet been abandoned, they are said to "exist.
And for such [defilements], it cannot be said that "this is their object"; therefore, that [position] is rejected.

Furthermore, this applies not only to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), but is exactly the same for lust (*rāga*) and the others as well; thus, it does not prove that the underlying tendencies are without an object.
Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Latent Dispositions (anusaya) Are Without an Object.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Knowledge (ñāṇa) Is Without an Object. 557–558.
Now follows the discussion known as "Knowledge Is Without an Object. In this regard, because an Arahant who possesses eye-consciousness...
"One is called 'possessing knowledge' (ñāṇī), yet at that moment there is no object for that knowledge; therefore, knowledge is without an object (anārammaṇa).
Regarding those who hold such a doctrine—just like the Andhakas—the question belongs to the proponent of his own view (sakavādin), and the affirmation belongs to the other.
The rest here should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Anusaya-kathā*.
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge Having No Object.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of Objects Past and Future (559–561).
Now follows the discussion known as "Objects Past and Future. In this regard, since there is an object past and future...
There is no such thing [as a past object]; therefore, because the object does not exist, the consciousness that would have that as its object must necessarily be without an object.
With reference to those who hold this view—such as the Northerners (Uttarāpathakas)—who maintain that "the past is without an object," the proponent asks, "Is the past without an object?
and the other assents. The rest of this section is to be understood exactly according to the text.
Commentary on the Discussion of Past and Future Objects. 7. Commentary on the Discussion of Thoughts that Have Intruded. 562.
Now follows the discussion known as "Thoughts that Have Intruded. Therein, those called "thoughts that have intruded" are of two kinds:

[This is] both from the perspective of the object and from the perspective of association. In this regard, because there is no fixed rule stating that "such-and-such a consciousness does not have applied thought (*vitakka*) as its object," it might follow that all consciousness is accompanied by applied thought;
however, because consciousness dissociated from applied thought exists, not all consciousness is accompanied by applied thought.
Thus, without making this distinction, [if one were to speak] without qualification... all [consciousness].

Regarding the view held by those such as the Uttarāpathakas—that "the mind is accompanied by applied thought" (cittaṃ vitakkānupatitaṃ)—this question was posed by the proponent of the orthodox position (sakavādī), and the other party gave his assent.
The rest of this matter is resolved according to the scriptural text itself.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion on the Mind Accompanied by Applied Thought.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Sound of the Projection of Applied Thought (Vitakkavipphārasaddakathā) 563.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Sound of the Projection of Applied Thought.

In this context, because it has been stated that "applied thought and sustained thought are verbal formations" (*vacīsaṅkhāra*), therefore, for one who is entirely engaged in applied thought and sustained thought—even at the time when the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is functioning—there is a projection of applied thought.
"Those who hold the view that 'it is sound alone'—such as the Pubbaseliyas—with reference to them, the proponent asks, 'Is it entirely? and the other assents.

Then, in order to challenge him by suggesting that if sound were merely the vibration of thought (*vitakkavipphāramatta*), then contact (*phassa*) and so forth would also be sound, he says, 'Does it cause contact in every way?
and so on. The other, not seeing such a scriptural fragment (*suttalesa*), [remains silent]."

He rejects [the proposition]. He asks, taking the view that "sound cognizable by the ear is merely the diffusion of thought," meaning sound as the mere diffusion of thought itself, and not the sound produced by the diffusion of thought in those who are asleep or inattentive; the other rejects it.
"Is not the sound of the diffusion of thought cognizable by the ear?"—this demonstrates his own particular tenet, for he...
One [teacher] says that the sound consists merely of the vibration of thought (*vitakkavipphāra*) and is therefore not cognizable by the ear;
the other, however, says it is cognizable by the ear because of the statement, "Having heard the sound of the vibration of thought, he points it out.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the sound of the vibration of thought.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Speech Not Corresponding to the Mind (Nayathācittassa vācātikathāvaṇṇanā) 564.
Now follows the discussion known as "Speech Not Corresponding to the Mind" (nayathācittassa vācā).
In this regard, because someone may speak one thing while intending to say something else, speech does not correspond to the mind nor follow the mind; it occurs even without [the mind's intention].

"‘It proceeds by means of consciousness’—this is the tenet of those such as the Pubbaseliyas. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is from the other.

Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, ‘If the consciousness that originates it did not exist, then contact and the rest would also not exist at that moment,’ he said, ‘Of one who is without contact,’ and so forth.
In the phrases ‘not wishing to speak,’ etc., because [the mind] is something else..."
Even one who says something else while thinking "I shall speak," is indeed still desirous of speaking; therefore, he rejects it by saying "not so. 565.
Is it not the case that in instances such as "I shall speak something else," one who intends to say "robe" might instead say "cloth"?
In that case, because of the dissimilarity between the preceding mind—the desire to speak something else—and the actual mind of speaking something else, [the intention is not established].

What is called "without intention" (ayathācitto) means that for him there is merely no offense; however, it does not mean that the speech which gives rise to the verbal transgression lacks the underlying intention.
Thus, with reference to the meaning that such speech is "without intention," this example establishes that the statement "speech of one without intention" is indeed established.
Yet, [if taken otherwise], it would remain unestablished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Verbal Action Not Conforming to the Mind.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of Bodily Action Not Conforming to the Mind (566–567).
Now follows the discussion known as "Bodily Action Not Conforming to the Mind. In this regard, since someone [might act] otherwise...

"If one goes elsewhere when intending 'I shall go,' therefore bodily action does not conform to the mind, follow the mind, or correspond to the mind, but proceeds even without the mind"—this is the tenet of those such as the Pubbaseliyas.
With reference to them, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission belongs to the other. The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated above.
Commentary on the Discussion of Bodily Action Not Conforming to the Mind.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of Possession of the Past and Future. 568–570.
Now follows the discussion known as "Possession of the Past and Future. In this regard, there is the designation of possession (*samannāgata-paññatti*).
Regarding the "description by way of acquisition," two descriptions should be understood. Among these, one who possesses present phenomena is said to be "endowed.

Now, although for one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), those attainments do not occur simultaneously—since some are past, some are future, and some are present—nevertheless, because they have been penetrated and are not lost, [he is said to be endowed with them].

He is called "one who has attained. In this context, since those who have attained meditative absorption (jhāna) possess past and future absorptions as well—provided one does not take this specific classification into account—the Andhakas hold the view that "they are endowed with both the past and the future.
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent of the orthodox position (Sakavādī), and the other party gives his assent. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The passage beginning with “One who meditates on the eight liberations,” however, establishes the state of being an attainer (*lābhī*), not the state of being fully possessed (*samannāgata*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of possession regarding the past and future.
The Ninth Chapter.
10. The Tenth Chapter: 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Cessation (Nirodhakathā) §§571–572.
Now follows the discourse known as "Cessation" (nirodhakathā). In this regard, for those who hold that [the self] "exists after having reached the state of rebirth..."

Simultaneously with the moment of the dissolution of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), it is their view that five aggregates arise—namely, the four aggregates classified as either wholesome or unwholesome functional (* kiriya *) states, and mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*). For they hold the opinion:

"If those [functional states] were not to arise when the life-continuum has ceased, there would be a rupture in the continuity [of existence]," just like the Andhakas. It is with reference to them [that this was said].
"Regarding 'in those who have been reborn' (upapattesiyesu): this is a question from the proponent (sakavādī), and the other's response is an admission.

In that context, in the four locations [of the compound], the singular locative form is used in the sense of the plural locative. The meaning here is: 'while the five aggregates (khandhas) of those who have been reborn have not yet ceased. The word 'ten' is stated by way of both the aggregates of those who have been reborn and the aggregates of the action (kiriyakhandhas)."
In that regard, to the first question, he denies that there are five aggregates by way of the characteristic of an aggregate and by way of activity.
To the second question, he affirms it with reference to diversity in terms of priority and posteriority and by way of rebirth-linking activity.
However, when asked about the conjunction of two contacts and two consciousnesses, he denies it because of the absence of a scriptural indication (*sutta-lesa*).
"Four functionals" means that four—either wholesome or unwholesome—have been taken up without form (*rūpa*).

"Functional knowledge" (*kiriyāñāṇa*) is the objectless knowledge admitted by the opponent at the moment an Arahant possesses eye-consciousness. "The path arises when [the consciousness] has ceased" is the question of the opponent;
"because it does not arise while [the consciousness] has not ceased" is the admission of our own school (*sakavādin*). "One develops the path while dead."

The opponent’s question is based on a deceptive pretext. However, because a being is indeed said to "live" from the moment of rebirth-linking until the final death-consciousness, the proponent does not assent and thus rejects it.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Cessation.
2. Commentary on the Discussion:

Is Matter the Path? (573–575) Now follows the discussion titled "Is Matter the Path? In this context, regarding those who hold the view that "right speech, right action, and right livelihood are matter"—such as the Mahīśāsakas, Saṃmitīyas, and Mahāsaṅghikas—it is said: "of one possessing the path."
The question is from the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is from the other (the opponent).

Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If for you right speech and so forth are matter (rūpa) and not abstinences (virati), then that matter would likewise possess the nature of having an object (sārammaṇa) and so on, just as the path consisting of right view and so forth does," he says "having an object" and so forth.
In this context, both the denial and the admission by the opponent should be understood according to the tenets of their respective positions. The rest here is of plain meaning.
Commentary on the Discussion of Form as the Path.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Path for One Possessing the Fivefold Consciousness. 576.
Now follows the discussion known as "The Path for One Possessing the Fivefold Consciousness. In that context, regarding those [who hold] that "by the eye, form..."

Based on the Sutta passage, "Having seen [it], he does not grasp at signs," there is the thesis: "There is cultivation of the Path for one possessing the fivefold sense-consciousness," as held by the Mahāsāṃghikas.
With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of our own position (Sakavādī), and the admission is from the other. Then, [the opponent asks]:

"If there is cultivation of the Path for him, is it by means of a path belonging to the fivefold sense-consciousness, or by means of paths belonging to those [who possess] the fivefold sense-consciousness?"

Or else, one must admit that the fivefold sense-consciousnesses (pañcaviññāṇa) are present [during the path]; yet they cannot be said to have the path as their destination because they do not have Nibbāna as their object and because they are supramundane (lokuttara).

Nor can it be said that the path has the fivefold sense-consciousnesses as its destination, because they are not included within its characteristics. To challenge this, he says: "Are not the fivefold sense-consciousnesses arisen with a physical basis?
and so forth. Herein, the intention is this: if the cultivation of the path occurs for one possessing the fivefold sense-consciousnesses...
It might be argued that the mind-consciousness associated with the Path could also belong to one possessing the fivefold sense-consciousness.
This being the case, instead of stating the characteristic as "the five consciousnesses have arisen bases," etc., it would have had to be stated as "the six consciousnesses.
Yet, it was not stated thus; rather, it was stated specifically as "the five consciousnesses. Therefore...
"It should not be said that 'for one possessing the fivefold sensory consciousness, there is the cultivation of the Path'.

Since this is precisely the intended meaning here, the proponent (sakavādī), having caused the opponent (paravādī) to accept that characteristic, said: "Indeed, it should not be said that for one possessing the fivefold sensory consciousness, there is the cultivation of the Path."

Another method: The five sense-consciousnesses have arisen bases, whereas the Path may be without a base. Those [consciousnesses] have arisen objects, whereas the Path has an object that cannot be so described.

Those [consciousnesses] have bases that are co-nascent, whereas the Path may be without a base. Those [consciousnesses] have objects that are co-nascent, whereas the Path has an object that is not co-nascent.
Those [consciousnesses] have internal bases, whereas the Path may also be without a base. And those [consciousnesses] are by way of form and so forth...
The [five] doors have external objects, whereas the path has Nibbāna as its object. Because they proceed by depending on a basis that has not yet ceased, they are of undivided basis;
the path, however, is without a basis. Because they proceed by taking as their object precisely those forms and so forth that have not yet ceased, they are of undivided object;
the path has Nibbāna as its object. They have various bases, whereas the path is either without a basis or has a single basis.

Alternatively: those [two] have various objects, whereas the path has a single object. Because they proceed within their own respective spheres of form and so forth, they do not experience one another’s sphere of activity; nor does the path take even a single object among form and so forth as its sphere.
Since they arise having made the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) their precursor, they are neither without attention nor without mental engagement.
The path arises as entirely free from fault. These [defilements] arise interspersed with the functions of receiving and so forth, whereas for the path there is no such interruption.
They arise in relation to one another through the sequence of preceding and succeeding moments; however, for the path, there is no such priority or posteriority alongside them.
At the time when they do not arise—namely, during the period of sharp insight—and in the place where they do not arise:

And because they also arise in the formless realms. Since these [consciousnesses] are separated by the receiving consciousness (*sampaṭicchana*) and others, they do not arise as immediate antecedents (*samanantara*) to one another;

however, for the Path, there is no such separation by the receiving consciousness and so forth. Apart from the actual falling upon the object, these have no function other than mere attention (*ābhoga*);
whereas the function of the Path is the eradication of the defilements (*kilesa*). And because here—

This too is the intended meaning; therefore, having caused the opponent to accept through these modes that the Path does not fall within the range of the fivefold sensory consciousness, the proponent says:
"Indeed, it should not be said that for one possessing the fivefold sensory consciousness there is the cultivation of the Path.
(577) "With reference to emptiness" means: just as the supramundane Path has emptiness, Nibbāna, as its object, so too the mundane [Path] has the pure heap of formations as its object.
He asks, "Does eye-consciousness arise depending on something? Is it thus [that you say] 'eye-consciousness'?

The other rejects this because of the statement, "Dependent on the eye and forms. When asked a second time, he admits it, referring to that which is signless therein as "emptiness," because of the statement, "one who does not grasp at signs. This same method applies to both questions beginning with "dependent on the eye."
578–579. Regarding the statement, "Eye-consciousness arises by taking the past and future as its object," this is the intended meaning:
For one possessing mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*), there is the cultivation of the Path (*magga-bhāvanā*), and mind-consciousness arises even by taking the past and future as its object;
why then should eye-consciousness be any different? This same method applies to the statements "by taking contact as its object" and so forth. Having seen a form with the eye...
Regarding the phrase "one who grasps signs," here it is not said that there is grasping of signs at the moment of the impulsion (javana), nor at the moment of eye-consciousness.
Therefore, even with reference to the mundane path, this [argument] is not a proof.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the path for one possessing the fivefold sense-consciousness.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether the Five Consciousnesses are Wholesome Joy (Pañcaviññāṇā kusalāpītikathāvaṇṇanā) §§580–583.
Now follows the discussion entitled "Whether the Five Consciousnesses are Wholesome Joy. This should be understood in meaning according to the method already explained above.
[End of] the Commentary on the Discussion of Whether the Five Consciousnesses are Wholesome Joy.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Consciousnesses Being With Effort (Sābhoga) (584–586).
Now follows the discussion known as "The Five Consciousnesses Are With Effort. In this context, "effort" (ābhoga) occurs by way of the wholesome and the unwholesome;
and it was said by the Teacher: "Having seen a form with the eye, one seizes upon its signs, or one does not seize upon its signs," and so forth.

This has been stated; however, taking that [statement] out of context, those who hold the view that "the five consciousnesses are accompanied by mental effort" (*sābhoga*)—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—regarding them, the question belongs to the proponent of the first position (*sakavādin*), and the admission belongs to the other. The rest here is exactly like the previous discussion.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether the five consciousnesses are accompanied by mental effort.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Two Kinds of Virtue (Sīla) §§587–589.

Now follows the discussion known as "By means of the two kinds of virtue. In this context, because of such statements as, "A wise man, established in virtue," it is understood that by means of mundane virtue (*lokiya-sīla*), the virtuous person develops the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*). Therefore, [the text says]: "And by the former, which is mundane..."

Regarding those who hold the view—such as the Mahāsāṃghikas—that "at the moment of the path, one is said to be endowed with two types of virtue, namely the supramundane and the mundane," the question "one who possesses the path" is asked by the proponent of the first position (Sakavādī), and the affirmation is given by the other. Then [the opponent asks]:
"If he is endowed at one and the same moment with both mundane and supramundane virtues..."

In order to challenge [the opponent] by suggesting that one who possesses that [right speech] must also possess two [other factors], such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth, [the text] says "by two contacts," and so on.
The other [opponent], not seeing such a logical sequence, rejects it.

Regarding the question "both the mundane and the supramundane," he admits it with reference to both what was previously undertaken and the right speech (*sammāvācā*) and so forth that arise at the moment of the Path (*magga*).
The question, "Does he cease from worldly virtue? belongs to the opponent; the admission, "He ceases through momentary dissolution," belongs to our own teacher.
However, the other [the opponent], perceiving that as if it were a transgression, says, "He is immoral," and so forth.

But his attempt to establish this position merely illustrates that virtue was previously unbroken; it does not demonstrate that one is possessed of both [virtue and its cessation]. Therefore, the position remains unestablished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Two Kinds of Virtue.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of Virtue Not Being a Mental Factor (590–594).
Now follows the discussion titled "Virtue is not a Mental Factor. In this regard, because even when virtue has arisen and ceased...
There is what is called the accumulation of virtue (sīlopacaya) caused by undertaking [the precepts], by which one truly becomes "virtuous" (sīlavā).

Therefore, regarding those who hold the view that "virtue is not mental," such as the Mahāsāṅghikas, the question belongs to the proponent of our own position (sakavādī), while the admission belongs to the other.
The rest here should be understood according to the same method explained in the discussion on "giving is not mental."
Even the establishing of alms-food is indeed non-establishment because it is undertaken in an improper manner.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the non-mental concomitants of virtue (sīla). 8.
Commentary on the Discussion that Virtue Does Not Follow the Mind.

595–597. Now follows the discussion titled "Virtue Does Not Conform to the Mind. In this context, the phrase "does not conform to the mind" refers merely to a difference in terminology; the rest is exactly like the previous discussion.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion titled "Virtue Does Not Conform to the Mind.
9. Commentary on the Discussion on the Cause of Undertaking.

598–600. Now follows the discussion on the cause of undertaking (samādāna-hetuka). In this context, there are those—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—who, having grasped the meaning of the verse “Those who plant groves,” etc., in an improper manner, hold the view that “virtue increases due to the cause of undertaking,” based on the statement “merit always increases.
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent of his own position (*sakavādin*); [the virtue] is dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*).
The opponent’s admission refers to the accumulation of virtue (*sīlopacaya*). The remainder is exactly like the previous discussion.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse concerning the cause of undertaking [precepts]. 10.
Commentary on the Discourse Concerning Intimation as Virtue.

601–602. Now follows the discussion entitled "The Nature of Intimation as Morality" (*viññatti-sīla-kathā*). In this context, because bodily intimation is taken to be bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal intimation is taken to be verbal action (*vacīkamma*), there are those—such as the Mahāsāṃghikas and the Saṃmitīyas—who hold the view that "intimation is morality" (*viññatti-sīla*).
With reference to them, the question "Is intimation [morality]? is asked by the proponent of our own position (*sakavādī*), and the admission is made by the other. Then...

Because what is called "virtue" (*sīla*) is actually abstinence (*virati*), not a material phenomenon (*rūpadhamma*), he said "abstention from taking life," and so forth, in order to correct that point.
As for the statement "reverence is virtue" and so on, this was said to set aside and demonstrate that kind of manifestation (*viññatti*) which he mistakenly considers to be "virtue.
However, because that [manifestation] is not abstinence, he again said "taking life," and so forth. But his own [wrong] view is as follows:
Because it is established by means of intimation, it is indeed non-established. This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the end of morality as intimation. 11.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the End of Immorality as Non-intimation.
603–604. Now follows the discussion on non-intimation as the end of immorality (*dussīlyantika*).

In this regard, concerning those—such as the Mahāsāṃghikas—who hold the view that "non-intimation is immorality" with reference to the completion of the factors (*aṅga*) for killing and so forth through a command, which is dissociated from consciousness and constitutes an accumulation of demerit (*apuñña*), the question belongs to the proponent (*sakavādī*), and the admission belongs to the other. Then...
In order to challenge [the opponent] by asking, "If she were unvirtuous, would she be guilty of any one of the offenses such as taking life?

he said, "Taking life," and so forth. "Having undertaken an evil deed" means having made a commitment to evil, thinking, "I will have such-and-such a person killed" or "I will steal such-and-such property.
When asked, "Do both increase?", [he replied] with reference to the non-arising of evil at the moment of giving.
He rejects [the first point]. When questioned a second time, he admits [it] with reference to the accumulation of evil dissociated from consciousness.

The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated in the discussion on what consists in enjoyment (*paribhogamaya*). His establishment of this tenet also proves only that evil was previously undertaken, not that there is a state of immorality (*dussīlabhāva*) through non-intimation (*aviññatti*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Non-intimation as the End of Immorality.
The Tenth Chapter.
The Second Fifty is completed.
11. The Eleventh Chapter: 1–3.
The Exposition of the Three Discussions on Latent Dispositions (Anusaya), 605–613.
Now follows the three discussions on latent dispositions (*anusaya*), namely: that they are indeterminate (*abyākata*), rootless (*ahetuka*), and dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*).

They are so named. In that regard, because an ordinary person (puthujjana) must be called "possessing latent tendencies" (sānusaya) while wholesome or indeterminate (abyākata) states of consciousness are occurring—
yet the latent tendencies are neither caused by whatever cause exists at that moment, nor are they associated with that consciousness— therefore,
those who hold the view that "they are indeterminate, rootless, and dissociated from consciousness," such as the Mahāsāṅghikas and others...
And [the same applies] to the Saṃmitiyas. With reference to them, in all three discourses, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādin) and the admission belongs to the other.
Since the remainder can be understood through the method of the Canon (pāḷi) as explained below, it has not been elaborated here.
This concludes the commentary on the three discourses on latent tendencies (anusaya).
4. Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 614–615.

Now follows what is called the "Discussion on Knowledge. In this context, although ignorance has been removed by means of path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*), when consciousness dissociated from knowledge—such as eye-consciousness and so forth—arises again, that path-consciousness does not occur. Therefore, it should not be said: [that the path is present].

Regarding those who hold the view that one is "possessed of knowledge" (*ñāṇī*), such as the Mahāsaṅghikas: the question is posed by the proponent of his own position, and the affirmation is given by the other.

Then, in order to challenge him—thinking, "If the designation 'possessed of knowledge' does not exist when ignorance has ceased, then the designations 'free from lust' and so forth would also not exist when lust and the rest have ceased; thus you are unskilled in the designation of persons"—[the text addresses] lust...
He says, "They have departed," and so forth. The opponent, seeing no logical consistency in the state of being "with lust" and so on when those [defilements] have departed, rejects it.
At the conclusion, because he deserves to be called "possessed of knowledge" (*ñāṇin*) due to the acquisition of knowledge, the rejection "it is not so" belongs to the proponent (*sakavādin*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge. 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the End of Knowledge Dissociated from Consciousness. 616–617.
Now follows the discussion known as "Knowledge Dissociated from Consciousness. In this regard, because an Arahant possesses eye-consciousness and so forth, [knowledge arises].
One is called "possessing knowledge" (*ñāṇī*) with reference to the knowledge of the path already attained; yet that knowledge is not associated with that [attaining] consciousness.

Therefore, regarding those who hold the doctrine that "knowledge is dissociated from consciousness," such as the Pubbaseliyas—the question is posed by the proponent of the first position (*sakavādī*), and the admission is given by the other.
Then, [the opponent asks him]: "If for you knowledge is dissociated from consciousness, among those things dissociated from consciousness..."
In order to challenge [the opponent] by suggesting that it might be any one among form and so forth, he says, "Is it form? and so on. The other denies this. The rest is exactly as explained below.
At the conclusion, however, when asked, "Is it wisdom (paññā)? he accepts it because he intends its occurrence in the sense of acquisition; therefore, he admits it.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning knowledge dissociated from consciousness.
6. Explanation of the Discourse on "This is Suffering" (Idaṃ dukkhaṃ). [Verses 618–820].

Now follows the discourse known as "This is Suffering. In this regard, for those who hold that "at the moment of the supramundane path, the practitioner of yoga utters the words 'this is suffering,' and while he thus utters the words 'this is suffering'..."
"The knowledge 'This is suffering' occurs"—this is the tenet of the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent (sakavādin).
The other's admission is made with reference to the occurrence of knowledge and the utterance of such words at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa).
However, because he utters speech connected with the remaining truths as an ordinary person (puthujjana), and not for him [the Noble One] in that manner...
He maintains that "the occurrence of knowledge" (*ñāṇappavatti*) is intended; therefore, he rejects [the application of this term] to questions concerning the origin and so forth.

The statement beginning with "form is impermanent" is spoken by way of showing a synonym for suffering (*dukkha*). However, the other [teacher], not seeing such a conventional usage within his own school, rejects it.
As for the passage beginning with "iti ca daṃ ca," if knowledge regarding suffering were to occur to him, then the vowel *i* and the consonant *daṃ*...
This was stated to show that [the path] should proceed by means of the four knowledges in successive order within the syllables *du* and *kha*.
However, the other [opponent] does not accept this, and therefore he rejects it.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the end of suffering (*dukkhanta*).
7. Explanation of the Discourse on the Power of Supernormal Success (Iddhibala-kathā) 621–624.

Now follows the discourse known as the "Discourse on the Power of Supernormal Success. In this context, there are those who, having wrongly grasped the purpose of the benefits arising from the development of the bases of supernormal success, hold the following tenet:
"One endowed with the power of supernormal success could remain for an eon," just as [the Vajjiputtakas].

[This concerns] the Mahāsāṃghikas. With reference to them, the question of the proponent of the internal view (sakavādin) is: "Could one endowed with the power of psychic potency (iddhibala) remain for an eon (kappa)?
In this context, an "eon" (kappa) is threefold: the great eon (mahākappa), a portion of an eon (kappekadesa), and the life-span eon (āyukappa).

For in the passage, "Monks, there are these four incalculables (asaṅkhyeyya) of an eon," it is the great eon alone that is called "an eon. [In contrast, regarding] the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm...

In the phrase "an eon is the measure of life," it refers to a portion of an eon. In the phrase "He is cooked in hell for an eon; he rejoices in heaven for an eon," it refers to a lifespan-eon (*āyukappa*).
The meaning of "the determination of a lifespan" (*āyukappana*)—or the allotment of life—is the delimitation of a lifespan either by way of the ripening of karma or by way of a calculation of years.
Among these, he asks with reference to a great eon (*mahākappa*), while the other assents.

Then the proponent of the opposing view (sakavādī), wishing to challenge him by saying, "If you are endowed with the power of psychic potency (iddhi), then since the lifespan is limited such that 'whoever lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more,' he ought to live beyond that—
either for a great eon (mahākappa) or a portion of a great eon—
by means of a life span consisting of psychic potency," said: "That life span is made of psychic potency," and so forth.
The other [teacher] rejects it because it has been stated that "there is no such thing as a supernormal (iddhimayika) life-faculty; it is produced solely by kamma.
But what is the distinction here for one possessing supernormal power? Is it not the case that even one without supernormal power could remain for the duration of a lifespan? This is the distinction:

for one possessing supernormal power, having warded off by the power of supernormality those factors that would create an obstacle to the continuation of the life-faculty for as long as the natural lifespan lasts—
It is capable of preventing untimely death in the interim; this power does not belong to one who lacks supernormal power (*iddhi*). This is the distinction between them.

Regarding the phrase "the past and the future," this challenges [the opponent] because it was promised without qualification that [the body] might endure for an eon (*kappa*). The passage beginning with "two eons" means:
"If one possessing supernormal power is able to transcend the limit of his lifespan, he can do so not only for one, but for many eons."

"May he remain"—this was said for the purpose of an exhortation. The passage beginning with "contact has arisen" and so forth was stated to show that not everything is obtainable through psychic power (*iddhi*), and that there are things which even lie outside the scope of psychic power.
The rest here is of plain meaning. The commentary on the discussion of the power of psychic power is concluded.
8. Explanation of the Discourse on Concentration (Samādhikathāvaṇṇanā) 625–626.

Now follows what is called the "Discourse on Concentration. In this context, there are those who do not take even that one-pointedness of mind which arises in a single moment of consciousness as "concentration" in the sense of being concentrated;
rather, they rely on such statements as: "He dwelt experiencing exclusively happiness for seven days and nights," and so forth.
Based on this, there is the tenet that "the continuity of consciousness (*cittasantati*) is concentration (*samādhi*)," as held by the Sabbatthivādins and the Uttarāpathakas.

With reference to them, the question "Is the continuity of consciousness [concentration]? is asked by the proponent of our own school (*sakavādī*), and the affirmation is given by the other. Then, he [the opponent] is addressed:

"If the continuity of consciousness is concentration, then the so-called continuity of consciousness exists in the past and also exists in the future. For it is not only the single present moment of consciousness [that constitutes it]."
To challenge [the opponent] by asking, "Is there such a thing as a mental continuity (cittasantati), and is all of that concentration (samādhi)?
he says, "The past... and so forth. The other, not accepting that, rejects it.
[The opponent asks: "Is it not true that the past has ceased? and so forth. [The response is: "In the mental continuity, only the present consciousness performs a function; the past and future..."
This was stated in order to show: "Since it has ceased and since it has not yet arisen, it does not exist; how then can it be called 'concentration'?

The question, "Is it momentary? belongs to the opponent. Thereafter, the admission belongs to our own school (the Sautrāntika), referring to that one-pointedness associated with a present wholesome state of mind which is called "concentration" in our own tradition in such passages as, "Monks, develop concentration."
The statement beginning with “one possessing eye-consciousness” and so forth was spoken through a quibble, having merely grasped the expression “occurring in a single moment of consciousness”;
for that very reason, it was rejected by the proponent himself. Is it not said by the Blessed One?

This Sutta establishes the uninterruptedness of concentration as it proceeds from one preceding to one succeeding moment, but it does not establish that there is a state of concentration in a continuum; therefore, it is not a proof [for your position].
Commentary on the Discussion of Concentration. 9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitatā). 627.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Stability of Phenomena. In this regard, based on the statement, "That element remains ever stable," [the following is said]:

Regarding those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas—that there exists a single entity called "the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*), which is comprised of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and is itself fully established (*parinipphannā*):
the question is posed by the proponent of the first position (Sakavādī), and the answer is given by the other. Then [the opponent] says to him:
"If there is a distinct 'stability of phenomena' that is fully established, separate from the ignorance and so forth that are themselves fully established..."

"There exists, and by that stability of the Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitatā), another established state (ṭhitatā) that is fully accomplished (parinipphannā) follows," [the opponent] says this beginning with "by that stability" in order to challenge [the position].
The proponent rejects it because he lacks such a tenet (laddhi).

Being asked for a second time, he admits it, referring to both the condition of immediate succession (anantarapaccayatā) and the condition of mutuality (aññamaññapaccayatā). The rest is as explained below.
Because it follows the method already stated, its meaning is self-evident.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitatākathā). 10. Commentary on the Discussion of Impermanence (Aniccatākathā).

628. Now follows the discussion on impermanence (*aniccatā*). Regarding this, there are those—such as the Andhakas—who hold the view that "the impermanence of impermanent things such as form (*rūpa*) is also a fully established entity (*parinipphanna*), just like form and the other aggregates.
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent (*sakavādin*), and the other party gives his assent.
Then [the proponent says to him]: "If, for you, impermanence is a fully established entity just like form and the others, then of that [impermanence]..."

In order to challenge [the opponent] by asserting that there must be impermanence (*aniccatā*) once full knowledge (*aññā*) has been perfected, [the proponent] said, "by that impermanence," and so forth.

The other [opponent], having rejected it on the grounds that the impermanence of two things cannot exist simultaneously, then admits it because that impermanence is not permanent and therefore disappears along with that very impermanent thing. Then the proponent [continues]:

Without granting it a separate place, he says "by that very [impermanence]" and so forth, attributing the fault of non-interruption through a continuous succession— starting from the second impermanence admitted by him,

then the one following that, and so on. As for the passage beginning "Aging is fully accomplished," it is stated by way of investigating the divisions of impermanence, because there is no such thing as impermanence other than the aging and death of what has arisen.
In that case as well, the opponent’s admission and refutation are to be understood in the same manner as before.
The statement beginning with “Form is fully established” is stated for the purpose of correlating it with those who hold that impermanence [belongs to such things].
Therein, “Just as there is impermanence, aging, and death for fully established forms and so forth, so too for fully established [things]... [is said].
Thinking, "Those [characteristics] such as impermanence do not exist in them," he rejects [the view] with absolute certainty.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Impermanence.
The eleventh chapter.
12. The Twelfth Chapter. 1.
Explanation of the Discussion on Formal Acts of Restraint (Saṃvara-kammantikathāvaṇṇanā) 630–632.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Formal Act of Restraint. Therein: "Having seen a form with the eye, one who grasps at its signs..."

Based on the Sutta passage, "He does not grasp at signs," those such as the Mahāsaṅghikas who hold the view that "both restraint and non-restraint are kamma" are the ones referred to by the questioner of the Sakavādin school, while the other provides the affirmative response. Then,
regarding that which is called "kamma" in our own tradition as volition (*cetanā*), when it proceeds through the doors of body, speech, and mind—

It receives the name "bodily action" (kāyakamma) and so forth. Likewise, in order to challenge [the opponent] by saying, "If restraint (saṃvara) were action, then that too, while occurring in the eye-faculty and so on, would receive the name 'eye-action' (cakkhukamma) and so forth," he said, "Eye-faculty restraint is eye-action," and so on.
The other, not seeing such a scriptural passage, having rejected it at the four doors, [proceeds] at the fifth door, the body-door.
He rejects with reference to the body of clarity (*pasādakāya*), but admits with reference to the body of intimation (*viññattikāya*).

For he maintains that both the body of clarity and the body of intimation are simply the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*). Regarding the mind-door (*manodvāra*) as well, he rejects with reference to the resultant door (*vipākadvāra*), but admits with reference to the kamma-door (*kammadvāra*).
The same method applies to non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). [As for the phrase] "having seen a form with the eye":
The sutta merely illuminates restraint and non-restraint regarding those doors; it does not establish their status as kamma. Therefore, it is not a proof.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of restraint as kamma.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Kamma.

633–635. Now follows the discussion on action (*kamma*). In this regard, there are those, such as the Mahāsāṅghikas, who hold the view that "all action has a result" based on the scriptural passage: "I do not say, monks, of intentional actions" (*nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sañcetanikānaṃ kammānaṃ*).
To them [the Teacher replies]: "Monks, I say that volition (*cetanā*) is action," thus the Teacher has stated without qualification that volition is "action."

It has been stated [that all action is volition]. To show this distinction—that wholesome and unwholesome [action] alone possess fruition (*savipāka*), while the indeterminate (*abyākata*) is without fruition (*avipāka*)—the question "All action?

is posed by the proponent (*sakavādin*), and the affirmation is given by the other. Furthermore, regarding the questions "All volitions?", the denial should be understood as referring to the indeterminate, while the affirmation refers to the wholesome and unwholesome. [The passage beginning with] "Fruition-indeterminate... and so forth [follows].
This was stated in order to show, by way of its formal characteristics, volition that is both with and without fruition. The rest here is of plain meaning.

As for the sutta beginning, "I do not say, monks," it was spoken with reference to the experiencing of fruition in the present life and so forth when conditions exist; therefore, it is not a proof [to the contrary].
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Kamma.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of Sound as Ripening (Saddo vipākotikathāvaṇṇanā) 636–637.

Now follows the discussion entitled "Sound as Ripening. In this regard, some—having grasped such passages as, "Because that karma was performed, accumulated, intensified, and expanded, he possesses the voice of Brahmā," and so forth—to be literal, maintain that "sound is ripening."

This is a tenet, such as that of the Mahāsaṃghikas. To show that for them "only immaterial phenomena arising from kamma receive the designation 'result' (vipāka), whereas this conventional usage does not apply to material phenomena," the question is posed by the proponent (sakavādī) and the admission is made by the other.
The passage beginning with "to be experienced as pleasant" is stated for the purpose of showing that "such is what is called a result."
The sutta beginning with “So tassa kammassā” is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the acquisition of the characteristics [of a Great Man].
For a Great Man possesses a pure retinue because he has performed that karma; yet the retinue itself is not the karmic result (vipāka). Therefore, this [argument] is not proving anything.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding sound as a karmic result.
4. Explanation of the Discourse on the Six Bases (Saḷāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā) 638–640.

Now follows the discourse known as the "Discourse on the Six Bases. In this regard, since the six bases arise from the performance of karma, there are those who hold the view that they are "resultant" (vipāka), such as the Mahāsaṃghikas; it is with reference to them [that the following is said].
The question, "Is the eye-base result? is from the proponent; the admission is from the other. The remainder is exactly according to the method stated below.
Regarding the statement "the six sense bases are results": here, the mind-base might be a result. The remaining [five] are produced solely by kamma and are not results.
Therefore, this [argument] is not proving.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Six Bases (Saḷāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā). 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the One Who Has Seven More Births at Most (Sattakkhattuparamakathāvaṇṇanā) 541–545.

Now follows the discussion known as "The One Who Has Seven More Births at Most" (sattakkhattuparama); therein, because [the term] "one who has seven more births at most" (sattakkhattuparamo) [is used].

Since this has been stated, in order to show the distinction— namely, that for those such as the Uttarāpathakas who hold the view that "a person who is 'seven-times-at-most' is fixed by way of being seven-times-at-most," there is no other fixation for him apart from the Noble Path by which he would be fixed to the state of being seven-times-at-most— [the following is said].
The question is from the proponent; the admission is from the other.

Regarding the phrases "the mother lives" and so forth, this is the intended meaning: there are two fixed courses (niyāma), namely, the fixed course of rightness (sammattaniyāma) and the fixed course of wrongness (micchattaniyāma).

The fixed course of rightness is the Noble Path (ariyamagga). It determines both the state of not falling into the lower realms (avinipātadhammatā) and the arising of the fruit. The fixed course of wrongness...
This is an action of immediate retribution (*ānantariyakamma*). It determines rebirth in hell immediately thereafter.

In that regard, one who has at most seven more births is determined by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) through the quality of being no longer subject to falling into states of misery and through the arising of its fruit.

However, there is no determination by the remaining paths for him because they have not been attained; moreover, he is incapable of committing an action of immediate retribution. But you [ask] about his determination...
If you desire that, we shall say this to you: "Is he fixed by this wrongness-in-determination (micchattaniyāma)?

Regarding the questions on "incapable of [reaching] the interval," he denies with reference to the absence of immediate retribution (ānantariya), and he affirms with reference to the limit of seven more births.
Regarding the question "Does that determination exist?", not seeing a determination in the sense of a limit of seven more births, [he denies].
He rejects it. The passage beginning with "Do you have the foundations of mindfulness? is stated to show the Dhamma of the Path, which is termed "certainty" (niyāma).
However, since he has not yet attained even the first path, he does not possess those [foundations] either; therefore, he rejects it. The rest here is of plain meaning.
Regarding the statement, "Is he one who will be reborn seven times at most?", the Blessed One said: "This person, in this many births..."
"He will attain final Nibbāna after running through [seven more births]; this much is his lot"—thus he declares by the power of his own knowledge.

He does not declare some fixed destiny of existence (*bhavaniyāma*) such that one is called "one who has seven births at most," "one who goes from family to family," or "one who has only one seed remaining. Therefore, this [argument] is not a proof.
*Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Has Seven Births at Most.*
646–647. The stories of the kolaṃkola and the ekabījika should also be understood by this same method.
This concludes the commentary on the stories of the kolaṃkola and the ekabījika.
8. Commentary on the Story of Taking Life.

648–649. Now follows the discussion on the taking of life. In this regard, since the destruction of life occurs through a mind associated with hatred, and hatred has not been abandoned by one who is endowed with right view, it is with reference to those—such as the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas—who hold the tenet that "one endowed with right view might intentionally deprive a living being of life," that [the following is said].
“Endowed with right view” is the question of the proponent; the other’s reply is an admission.
However, regarding the questions beginning with “intentionally [killing] one’s mother,” he rejects them out of fear of contradicting the Sutta which states, “This is impossible, this cannot happen.

The passage beginning with “one who has no respect for the Teacher” is stated to show that for one who possesses respect for the Teacher and the rest, there is no transgression of the training rules. But the other...
Having rejected the claim that he lacks respect for it on account of unwholesome states (*akusala*), and having admitted his state of possessing respect,

when asked again whether he is disrespectful, he confesses— referring to the absence of salutation and circumambulation at the *cetiya* due to lack of mindfulness and lack of mental attention caused by distraction while occupied with various duties. Then, [the text continues] with "he might neglect," and so forth.
When questioned according to the method, he denies such an action because of his intentional non-performance of it. The rest here is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the taking of life. 9. Commentary on the Discussion Regarding an Evil Destination.

650–652. Now follows the discussion on the "bad destination" (*duggati*). In this context, there are those—such as the Uttarāpathakas—who take both the bad destination itself and the craving for the objects of sense (form, etc.

belonging to beings in that bad destination to be the "bad destination," and who then state without such further analysis or distinction that "the bad destination has been abandoned by one possessed of right view.
It is with reference to them that the question of the proponent (*sakavādin*) is asked.
The other’s admission is as follows: “One might take delight in form belonging to the states of deprivation,” and so forth.

This was stated in order to challenge the opponent on the basis of his own tenet that for one endowed with right view, an unhappy destination has not been abandoned. The rest here is of plain meaning. “One might be reborn in hell,” and so forth, illustrates the very abandonment of the unhappy destination, or rather, the abandonment of the craving leading to the unhappy destination; it does not [refer to] beings in the unhappy destination.
The abandonment of craving for objects such as visible forms is therefore not the means of accomplishment.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the miserable destinies. The same method applies to the discussion regarding those in their seventh existence as well.
The Twelfth Chapter. 13.
The Thirteenth Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Kappaṭṭha Sutta.
654–657. Now follows what is called the "Discourse on the World-Age" (*kappaṭṭha-kathā*). In this regard, there are those who hold the view:
"Having split a united Saṅgha, one roasts in hell for an eon," and "A schismatic of the Saṅgha remains in hell for the entirety of an eon," such as the Rājagirikas.
With reference to them, the question "Is he an eon-dweller? is asked by the proponent of our own position (*sakavādin*), and the other [the opponent] admits it.
The phrase "and the Buddha in the world" is stated for the purpose of showing that there is no schism in the Saṅgha in the absence of the arising of a Buddha.

The passage beginning with "the aeon dissolves and the Saṅgha splits" is stated to show: "If he were to remain for the entire aeon, having performed that deed from the time of the dissolution [of the world], he would arise and remain therein. The passage beginning with "in the past," etc., [is stated to show...]

The intended meaning is exactly as stated above. Regarding the question, "Is one who possesses supernormal power (iddhimā) a worldling (kappaṭṭha)?", he denies it with reference to that power consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya).

However, in other systems, they maintain that such a person possesses supernormal power consisting in birth (jātimaya); it is with reference to this that he affirms it. As for the passage beginning "the basis of supernormal power consisting in will" (*chandiddhipāda*), etc., [the opponent argues]:

"To call one 'possessing supernormal power' on account of supernormal power consisting in birth is merely a conventional designation; what is the use of that? For if he actually possesses supernormal power," [then he must be so].
This was stated for the purpose of exhortation, [thinking]: "In this manner, the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) would be developed.

As for the sutta stating "one who is subject to ruin, destined for hell," that was said with reference to an *āyukappa*—a single *kappa* divided into eighty parts, and one remaining for only a portion of that time; therefore, it is not proof [of the point].
Commentary on the Discussion of the Kappaṭṭha. 2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Attainment of the Wholesome (Kusalapaṭilābhakathā). 658–659.

Now follows the so-called "Discussion of the Attainment of the Wholesome. In that context, according to our own system, the *kappaṭṭha* possesses only wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
He does obtain it. However, he does not obtain that which is sublime (mahaggata) or supramundane (lokuttara), by means of which he might ward off that rebirth.

But for those, such as the Uttarāpathakas, who—without making this distinction—hold the view without qualification that "he does not obtain a wholesome consciousness," [this passage] is intended to refute that view by demonstrating the distinction.
The question is from the proponent; the admission is from the other. The rest here is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning the attainment of the wholesome. 3. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning What is Immediately Connected.
660–662. Now follows the discussion on the "one who has been incited" (*anantarāpayutta*).
In this context, one who is "incited" is one by whom an immediate (*ānantariya*) deed—such as matricide—that yields its result immediately after the breakup of the aggregates, has been commanded.
In that case, he for whom the act is performed due to a command given with certainty is "fixed in falsehood" (*micchattaniyata*), because of the arising of a volition that accomplishes that purpose.

He is incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*). However, one who has been commanded by an indefinite command and will perform that action is not fixed in wrongness because he has not yet produced the volition that accomplishes the goal;

thus, he is capable of entering the fixed course of rightness—this is the established conclusion within our own school (*sakasamaya*). But for those [who hold] that "even by an indefinite command, he is indeed incapable..."
The tenet is: “One enters the certainty of rightness”; this is the view of the Uttarāpathakas.

To refute that tenet of theirs, the proponent (sakavādī), having stated the prima facie position (pubbapakkha), asks the opponent (paravādī) to confirm it as being connected to what immediately follows.
Thus, the first question here belongs to the opponent, who is asked to admit [the point] with reference to the absence of volition that accomplishes the purpose.

This is the position of our own school (sakavādin). Thereupon, the opponent, because of the fact that the act of matricide and so forth has been commanded, thinks, "He is fixed in falsehood (micchattaniyata).
Therefore, he asks the question: "And [is one] fixed in falsehood?
The proponent, however, rejects this by saying "No," referring merely to the fact that a single individual cannot enter into two fixed courses (niyāma) simultaneously.
"Is that not karma? refers to such acts as matricide and the like. In this context, the proponent’s admission of "Yes" refers to the indeterminate (aniyata) instruction.
For even when one has employed an indeterminate instruction and stands [therein], remorse certainly arises in the form of "I have done what is unseemly," and regret certainly is born.
The phrase beginning with "If indeed... takes up merely the arising of remorse.
This was stated by the opponent for the purpose of establishing his own thesis.

Now, taking up that very same person for whom even the entry into the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*) has been denied by the opponent—despite being immediately connected to the triad of undetermined [factors]—the proponent of our own school (Sakavādī) poses the question: "Is such a person incapable? because he is immediately connected [to those factors].

The other’s admission is made according to his own conviction. Then the proponent (sakavādī), in order to challenge him with the question, "One who is incapable [of such acts] cannot be a doer of deeds such as matricide;
were those deeds committed by you?", says, "Your mother was deprived of life," and so forth.
The other, seeing no such action that would render those bases (vatthu) incurable, rejects it, saying, "Certainly not."
"Having withdrawn that action" refers to an indefinite act of formal instruction (*aniyata-āṇattika-kamma*).
For that is indeed called "withdrawn" by one who prevents what was instructed with the thought, "Do not do what I have instructed.
And it is precisely because it has been withdrawn that remorse is dispelled and regret is said to be removed. Even though this is so, here—
Assuming that the previous *āṇatti* (command) itself possesses a fixed nature, the opponent admits, "Yes.
Then the proponent, having caused him to accept the fact that the action has been withdrawn and having established his own position, says "Indeed, etc. 662.
Again, in the final question, "one who is subsequently engaged," the question is directed at the opponent just as it was in the first question.
The admission belongs to the proponent (sakavādin). "Is that not karma? is the inquiry of the opponent (paravādin).
The proponent’s admission refers to the time when [the action] was performed prior to the time it was withdrawn.

Taking the mere fact that it was previously performed, the opponent establishes his own tenet by saying "yes" according to the principle of indeterminate injunction. However, because this tenet is established through improper reasoning (ayoniso), it remains truly unestablished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Immediate Sequence. 4.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Certainty of the Certain. 663–664.
Now follows the discussion known as "The Certainty of the Certain. In this regard, certainty is of two kinds: certainty in the wrong state (*micchattaniyāma*)...

There is the karma of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*) and the noble path of rightness (*sammatta-niyāma*). Apart from these two fixed courses (*niyāma*), there is no other so called "fixed course.
For all remaining phenomena of the three planes (*tebhūmaka-dhamma*) are called "unfixed" (*aniyata*); even one endowed with them remains unfixed.
However, when the Buddhas, by the power of their own knowledge, have declared: "This being will attain enlightenment in the future," [then he is fixed].

Because the Bodhisatta is overflowing with merit, he is said to be "fixed. Thus, taking this as a mere conventional expression, there are those—such as the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas—who hold the view that "the Bodhisatta in his final existence is capable of realizing the Dhamma in that very birth," and [therefore] that "the fixed one enters the fixed course.
It is with reference to them that this question is asked.

The first is the admission of one’s own position, while the second is that of the other. The passage beginning with "one fixed in falsehood" is stated for the purpose of showing that what is fixed by one destiny lacks any other destiny.
The passage beginning with "having previously developed the path" is stated for the purpose of showing the different types of destinies.

The passage beginning with "the foundation of mindfulness" is stated for the purpose of showing the different factors within even a single destiny. The statement "a Bodhisatta is capable" is merely...
This demonstrates the potentiality of a bodhisatta, not the entry into the fixed course (niyāma) of one who is already destined; therefore, it is not conclusive.
For he was previously undetermined even by a single factor of destiny, yet at the foot of the Bodhi tree, through the vision of the Truths, he entered the fixed course.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the destined one’s entry into the fixed course.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Enveloped (Nivuta-kathā) 665–667.

Now follows the so-called discourse on the enveloped. In this regard, there is the tenet held by some—such as the Uttarāpathakas—that one who is "enveloped," "covered," and "shrouded" by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) abandons those very hindrances, because for one who is already pure, there can be no further function of purification.

Having taken these into account, there is the concealment of the questioner’s own position and the admission of the other’s. The passage beginning with "One who is lustful [sees] lust" is stated for the purpose of showing the fault in the abandonment of the hindrances by one who is concealed.

The passage beginning with "In that which is purified and cleansed" is stated for the purpose of showing the purification through eradication (*samuccheda-visuddhi*) of that which has already been purified by suppression (*vikkhambhana-visuddhi*).
The passage beginning with "For him who knows thus" refers to one who knows.
It illuminates the destruction of the taints for one who has seen, but not the abandoning of the hindrances for one who is shrouded; therefore, it is not effective.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Shrouded. 6. Commentary on the Discussion of Presence.

668–670. Now follows the discussion on "manifestation" (*sammukhībhūta*). In this context, "one who has manifested" refers to one who has reached the state of the fetters being manifest, that is, having come into possession of them. The rest here is exactly like the discussion on "being shrouded" (*nivuta*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion on manifestation.
7. Commentary on the Discussion: "Having Attained [Jhāna], One Relishes It."
671–673. Now follows the discussion titled "One who has attained [jhāna] relishes it.

In this regard, based on such statements as, "Having entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, he relishes that," there are those—such as the Andhakas—who hold the view that "one who has attained relishes it, and his craving for jhāna (jhānanikanti) has jhāna as its object.
With reference to them, [the text says] "one who has attained" (samāpanno).

The question is from the proponent; the admission is from the other. Regarding the questions, "Is that jhāna the object of that jhāna?", [the opponent], not seeing its status as having that as its object, rejects it for fear of contradicting the Sutta; yet he admits it merely on the basis of the statement, "He relishes that.
He [interprets] the Sutta passage, "He relishes that," as meaning that one who has attained jhāna, having emerged from jhāna, relishes the gratification of the jhāna.
It is not only within the attainment that there is attachment to the jhāna; rather, there is attachment to the object of the jhāna. Therefore, [the opponent's argument] is not a proof.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether one who has attained relishes the attainment.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Lust for What is Unpleasant.
