674. Now follows the discussion on lust for what is unpleasant (*asāta-rāga*). In this regard, it is stated in the Sutta: "Whatever feeling one feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one delights in that feeling and speaks in praise of it.

This was said with reference to delighting through wrong view (*diṭṭhābhinandana*). Relying on the expression "delights in," [some claim] there is delight even in painful feeling by way of the gratification of lust (*rāgassāda*).
"Therefore, there is lust for what is unpleasant"—this is the tenet held by certain schools, such as the Uttarāpathakas.

With reference to them, the proponent asks: "Is there lust for what is unpleasant? Herein, "lust for what is unpleasant" (*asāta-rāga*) means the attachment that thinks regarding an unpleasant feeling, a painful sensation:
"O, may this very thing happen to me! "Yes" (*āma*) is the admission of the other party on account of their tenet. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
675. Thus, in the Sutta, "he delights in that feeling" is explained by turning it back [to its true sense] as follows: there is no arising of lust directed toward a painful feeling itself;

rather, by grasping at a collection [of factors], one regards a phenomenon characterized by being felt as a painful feeling, or indeed as a self, and thereby delights in the feeling through the delight in views known as the conceiving of views.

One delights in the transformation of painful feeling; even one who, being overcome by painful feeling, longs for sensual pleasure as its antidote, is said to "delight in painful feeling. This is the intended meaning of how there is delight in painful feeling.
Therefore, this [argument] regarding "one who has lust for what is unpleasant" is not proving anything.
Commentary on the Discourse on Lust for the Unpleasant. 9. Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Whether Craving for Phenomena is Indeterminate. 676–680.
Now follows the discussion known as "Whether Craving for Phenomena is Indeterminate. In that context: craving for forms... [etc. ...craving for phenomena.

Since, among these six types of craving, the very last is called "craving for phenomena" (*dhammataṇhā*), those who hold the view that it is indeterminate (*abyākata*)—such as the Pubbaseliyas—with reference to them, the proponent of our own position asks the question, and the other admits it.
The meaning of the remaining questions follows the text. [The six types of craving] are also [classified] by way of the three divisions beginning with "craving for sensual pleasures" (*kāmataṇhā*).

Craving has been shown by way of its condensation. For craving that occurs with respect to the six objects, beginning with visible forms, by way of sensual delight (*kāmasāda*), is craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).
Craving accompanied by the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*)—namely, "The self and the world will exist"—is craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).
Craving accompanied by the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*)—namely, "It will not exist"—is craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*). But is this not craving for phenomena (*dhammataṇhā*)?
The passage indicates that craving occurs by taking a mental object (*dhammārammaṇa*) as its basis; it does not indicate its neutral (*abyākata*) nature. Therefore, it is not a proof [of the thesis].

This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether craving for phenomena (*dhammataṇhā*) is neutral. 10. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Craving for Phenomena is Not the Origin of Suffering.

681–685. Now follows the discussion entitled "Is craving for phenomena not the origin of suffering? In this regard, since it is stated that "it is craving for phenomena," there are those who hold the view that it is therefore not the origin of suffering—such as the Pubbaseliyas themselves.
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent of the first position (Sakavādī), and the admission is given by the other. The remainder is exactly like the previous discussion.
Commentary on the Discussion: "The Craving for Dhamma is Not the Origin of Suffering.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
14. The Fourteenth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Linking of the Wholesome and the Unwholesome (686–690).
Now follows the discussion known as "The Linking of the Wholesome and the Unwholesome.

In this context, there is no such thing as the wholesome arising immediately after the unwholesome, nor the unwholesome arising immediately after the wholesome; thus, there is no mutual linking between them.

This is not tenable. However, as for those who—because one lusts and becomes dispassionate toward the very same object—hold the view that "therefore, that [consciousness] reconnects with the other," such as the Mahāsāṅghikas;
it is with reference to them that the questioner (the Sakavādin) asks the question, and the other (the Itaravādin) gives the admission.
Both "turning toward" (*āvaṭṭanā*) and "intention" (*paṇidhi*) are names for advertence (*āvajjanā*) itself; for that indeed...

It turns back the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), thus it is "turning-back" (āvaṭṭanā). It directs and places the consciousness upon an object other than the object of the life-continuum, thus it is "directed application" (paṇidhi).

"Without turning back the wholesome" means: he asks whether that wholesome [consciousness] which arises immediately after an unwholesome one and links rebirth arises without turning back [the life-continuum]. But the other [responds]: without an act of adverting (āvajjana)...
Not seeing the arising of the wholesome, he rejects it. The statement, "One attends to the wholesome by way of improper attention," is said for the purpose of challenging [the opponent]:
"If the wholesome were to arise immediately after the unwholesome, then it would arise for one who attends improperly by means of the adverting [consciousness] directed toward the unwholesome itself.
The rest follows exactly as in the text. Is it not the case that "in the very same object"?

The statement illustrates the arising of passion and dispassion toward a single object; it does not illustrate the immediate succession of wholesome and unwholesome states. Therefore, it is not a proof [for that].
Commentary on the Discussion of the Reconnection of Wholesome and Unwholesome States. 2.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising of the Six Sense Bases.

691–692. Now follows the discussion on the arising of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*). In this regard, for those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), the six sense bases arise simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) of the existence-to-be-born. For those born from a womb (*gabbhaseyyaka*), only the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the body base (*kāyāyatana*) among the internal sense bases arise at the moment of rebirth-linking;
the remaining four arise during the seventy-seven nights [of the embryonic period]. And these, moreover, by which...
"Rebirth-linking is grasped by means of karma, whether it is that very same [karma] or another that has been performed"—this is the doctrine within our own tradition (sakasamaya).

However, for those such as the Pubbaseliyas, who hold the view that because it arises from a single act of karma, the mere seed of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) arises in the mother's womb at the very moment of rebirth-linking—just like the sprout of a tree whose branches and foliage are already fully developed; [for them, this is their position].
Referring to these [six sense bases], the question "the sixfold base" (*saḷāyatana*) was asked by the proponent of our own school (*sakavādin*), and the admission was made by the other.

The passage beginning with "possessing all limbs and parts" was stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent] as to whether, when the sixfold base exists, one could enter [the womb] having become such [a being].

The question "of one who has gone into the mother’s womb" was asked by the opponent (*paravādin*). Subsequently, the question "after [the formation of] the hair" was asked by the proponent of our own school. The rest here is of plain meaning.

Now follows the discourse known as the "Condition of Immediate Proximity. In this context, regarding dancing, singing, and so forth, there are the seeing of forms and hearing of sounds, and so on.

Seeing that [consciousness] changes rapidly, those who hold the view—such as the Uttarāpathakas—that "these consciousnesses arise immediately after one another," are being addressed by the proponent of the first position (sakavādī) with the question, "Of eye-consciousness...? and the other party's admission follows. [The opponent asks:
"Is ear-consciousness also exclusively having visible form as its object immediately after eye-consciousness?"

This was stated in order to challenge [the opponent] by suggesting that there might be a material object as an objective support (rūpārammaṇa) for the resultant mind-element (vipākamanodhātu), just as there is for others.

Having rejected this on the grounds that there is no such sutta in the questions "Dependent on the eye and forms, ear-consciousness arises," etc., he admits it by way of acquisition, observing its immediate succession: "That very same eye-consciousness is that ear-consciousness. Just as...
Immediately after the first impulsion, the second impulsion is that very same [consciousness] in its nature as mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*);
thus he asks you: "Why is this pair also one and the same? In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.

The statement beginning with "dances and sings" illustrates the state of being intermingled due to the rapid turnover when objects coincide; it does not indicate immediate conditionality (*anantarapaccayatā*), and therefore it is not a proof [of such a relationship].

Regarding those who hold the view that "all form consists of the four great elements and the derived form (upādāyarūpa) dependent upon the four great elements"—such as, for example, the people of the Northern Path—it is with reference to them that the proponent of the internal position (sakavādī) asks:
"Is noble form (ariyarūpa) derived from the great elements? In this context, "noble form" means either the form of the Noble Ones (ariyānaṃ rūpaṃ) or form that is noble (ariyaṃ rūpaṃ).
"Noble form" (*ariyarūpa*). "Yes," is the admission made by the other while standing upon that tenet. When asked whether it is wholesome (*kusala*), he admits it solely on the basis of his tenet.

The same method applies to the questions regarding the "taintless" (*anāsava*) and so forth. With the exception of the sutta stating "whatever form," the [definition of] primary elements (*bhūta*) demonstrates the state of being derived (*upādā*) for all remaining forms, but not for right speech and right action. For in their case, even the mere status of being "form" (*rūpa*) is not established.
How, then, could there be derived matter? Therefore, [the argument] is not proof.

This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Noble Matter (Ariya-rūpa-kathā). 5. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether the Latent Disposition (Anusaya) is Something Other [than the Defilement].

700–701. Now there is the discussion called "The Other Underlying Tendency" (*anusaya*). In this regard, since an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is to be described as "possessing an underlying tendency" (*sānusaya*) when a wholesome or indeterminate state of consciousness is occurring, but not as "obsessed" (*pariyuṭṭhita*), therefore, for those who hold the view that the underlying tendency is one thing and obsession is another—such as the Andhakas—it is said:
"There is an underlying tendency of sensual lust which is distinct [from obsession]."

The question belongs to the proponent; the other’s response is an admission. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated below in the discussion on the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).

As for the passage beginning with “one who possesses an underlying tendency” (*sānusayo*), this indicates that at that time one is to be called "possessing an underlying tendency" because the underlying tendency has not been abandoned, yet one is not to be called "obsessed" (*pariyuṭṭhito*) because [the obsession] has not arisen.
It does not, however, indicate any difference between the underlying tendency and the obsession; therefore, [that argument] is not a proof.

6. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Manifestation (pariyuṭṭhāna) is Dissociated from Consciousness. 702.
Now follows the discussion titled "Whether Manifestation is Dissociated from Consciousness. In this regard, because [it arises] from the perspective of impermanence and so forth...

Even when one is attending [to an object] as unattractive, lust and other defilements still arise. For this has been said: "Sometimes, Master Bhāradvāja, thinking 'I shall attend to it as unattractive,' one attends to it precisely as attractive.

Therefore, regarding those—such as the Andhakas—who hold the view that "obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) is dissociated from the mind," the question was asked by the proponent of our own position (sakavādī), and the admission was given.
For the other [type of person]. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of obsession as dissociated from consciousness.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Included (Pariyāpanna).

703–705. Now follows the discussion on what is "included" (pariyāpanna). In this regard, since sensual lust (kāmarāga) underlies the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) and is said to be "included in the sense-sphere realm," those who hold the view that sensual lust for the fine-material realm (rūparāga) and immaterial realm (arūparāga) likewise underlie the fine-material and immaterial realms, and are therefore "included in the fine-material and immaterial realms" respectively—just as [they assert]—[it is said: ...

[This refers] to the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas. With reference to them, the question "Is there lust for form? is asked by the proponent of the first position (the Sakavādin), and the admission [of its existence] is by the other.

In that context, "it underlies" (*anuseti*): just as lust for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) underlies the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*)—which is designated as sense-sphere thoughts—by way of co-arising, does he ask:
"Does lust for form likewise underlie the form-sphere (*rūpadhātu*)? And "is included" (*pariyāpanna*): just as that [lust for sense-pleasures] is included in the threefold...
Because it is included within the sense-sphere realm by way of the defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*), it is "included in the sense-sphere realm" (*kāmadhātupariyāpanna*).

[The interlocutor] asks: "Is attachment to form (*rūparāga*) likewise included in the fine-material-sphere realm (*rūpadhātupariyāpanna*)? The other, however, not perceiving his intention, simply assents with "Yes" by way of its acquisition (*laddhi*).
Then, in order to make him perceive that meaning, [the teacher speaks] regarding those things known as wholesome, resultant, and functional...

Having correlated [the text] with the attainment-sphere (*samāpatti*) and so forth, he says "attainment-sphere" and so on in order to inquire. The rest here follows exactly as in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

But does not the statement beginning with "lust for sensual pleasure" (*kāmarāga*) also indicate that only lust for sensual pleasure has the nature of a latent tendency (*anusaya*) and is included within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), and not the others in the other realms?
Commentary on the Discussion of the Included (Pariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā). 8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Undeclared (Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā) 706–708.
Now follows what is called the discussion of the undeclared (abyākata). Therein, [the undeclared] is fourfold, consisting of resultant, functional, material, and Nibbāna.

It is called "indeterminate" (abyākata) because it is without karmic fruition (avipāka). A "view-position" (diṭṭhigata) is so called because it has not been declared as being eternal and so forth—as in the passage: "Vaccha, 'the world is eternal'—this has not been declared by me.

However, there are those, such as the Andhakas and the Uttarāpathakas, who do not accept this distinction and hold the view that a view-position is indeterminate just like the previously mentioned indeterminates.

In order to demonstrate that distinction for them, the question "Is the range of views (diṭṭhigata) indeterminate? was posed by the proponent of the first position (sakavādī), and the affirmation was given by the other.
The rest here follows exactly as in the text. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Indeterminate (Abyākata-kathā).
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Unincluded (Apariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā) §§709–710.

Now follows the discussion called "the unincluded" (apariyāpanna). In this context, since an ordinary person who has attained meditative absorption (jhāna) may be said to be free from passion regarding sense-desires, yet not to be one whose views have vanished, therefore "wrong view" (diṭṭhigata) is what is meant by "the unincluded."
The question belongs to the proponent regarding those who hold such a doctrine, namely the Pubbaseliyas;
the answer belongs to the other. The rest here follows exactly as in the text.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion on the Undeclared.
The Fourteenth Chapter. 15.
The Fifteenth Chapter. 1.
Explanation of the Discourse on Conditionality.

711–717. Now follows the discussion on conditionality (*paccayatākathā*). In this regard, since a state that is a condition by way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) is not a condition by way of the object, contiguity, or immediate condition for those very same states for which it is a root-condition;

or else, since a state that is a condition by way of the object-condition is [likewise] not a condition by way of the immediate or immediate-contiguity condition for those very same states for which it is an object-condition—
The opponent holds the view that "there is no condition; therefore, conditionality is fixed," as is the case with the Mahāsāṅghikas.
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent (sakavādī), and the other party gives his assent. The rest here follows exactly the text of the Pāḷi itself.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Conditionality.
2. Explanation of the Discussion on the Condition of Mutuality (Aññamaññapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā) 718–719.

Now follows the discussion known as the condition of mutuality. In that regard, according to the system for which the formula is simply “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” and for which there is no such statement as “with volitional formations as condition, ignorance arises,” therefore it is only ignorance [that is the condition].

The view that ignorance is a condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), but volitional formations are not a condition for ignorance—as held, for example, by the Mahāsāṅghikas—is addressed here.

With reference to them, the question from the proponent (*sakavādin*) is intended to show that there is indeed mutual conditionality between ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth; the other’s answer is affirmative.

In the phrase "ignorance [is a condition] for volitional formations," only unwholesome volitional formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) are taken; therefore, they are also conditioned by volitional formations.

Regarding "ignorance" (*avijjā*), here the conditionality should be understood by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), presence (*atthi*), non-disappearance (*avigata*), and association (*sampayutta*).

Regarding "craving as a condition for clinging" (*upādānapaccayā taṇhā*), here—with the exception of sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*)—the remaining three types of clinging should be understood as being conditions for craving, just as volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are conditions for ignorance. The rest follows exactly as in the text. Regarding "old age and death as a condition" (*jarāmaraṇapaccayā*):
The question belongs to the opponent’s school, while the response—that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition—belongs to our own school.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of mutual conditionality. 3.
Commentary on the Discussion of Time.

720–721. Now follows the discussion on time (addhā). In this regard, there are those who hold the view that, based on the Sutta passage, “Bhikkhus, there are these three bases for discourse,” there exists a truly established entity called time, which is reckoned as an interval (addhā). To them [it is said]:
“There is no such thing as time established as a real entity, other than being a mere designation (paññatti) of time. Rather, it is simply the aggregates (khandha), such as form and the rest.”

In order to show the distinction [between what is] "fully accomplished" (*pariniṣpanna*) and [what is not], the question "Is time fully accomplished? is asked by the proponent (*sakavādin*), and the other [the opponent] assents.
Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If that is fully accomplished, it must be one or another among form (*rūpa*) and so forth," he says "Form," and so on.
The other denies it. The rest follows exactly as in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Time (Addhākathāvaṇṇanā). 4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Moment, the Instant, and the Hour (Khaṇalayamuhuttakathāvaṇṇanā) 722–723.
This same method applies to the discussions of the moment and so forth as well. For all these—moments and the rest—are merely synonyms for time (addhā).
Commentary on the Discussion of Moments, Seconds, and Hours. 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Taints (Āsava). 724–725.
Now follows what is called the discussion of the taints. In this regard, since there is no other taint beyond the four taints...
There is no [dharma] by which the four taints (āsava) could be subject to taints;

therefore, for those who hold the view that "the four taints are untainted"—such as the Hetuvādins—the question belongs to the proponent of his own position (sakavādin), while the admission belongs to the other.
Then, [the proponent says to him]: "If your taints are untainted, then, this being the case, they must possess the characteristics of the Path and so forth."
He said, "The path for exhorting," and so forth. The rest here is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the taints (āsava). 6. Commentary on the Discussion of Aging and Death (jarāmaraṇa).
726–727. Now follows the discussion on aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

In this context, because aging-and-death is not fully accomplished (*aparinipphanna*), it cannot be said to be either mundane (*lokiya*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*). For in the dyad "mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena," aging-and-death is specified neither under the category of the mundane nor under the category of the supramundane. In that regard, for those who hold this [view]...

The position that aging-and-death of supramundane states is itself supramundane, without taking into account their characteristics—as held, for example, by the Mahāsāṅghikas—is the question posed by the proponent (Sakavādī) with reference to them, and the admission is made by the other (Itarassa). The rest here follows exactly as in the text.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Aging-and-Death.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of Perception and Feeling (Saññāvedayitakathā) 728–729.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Discussion of Perception and Feeling.

In this context, what is called the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*) is not any specific dhamma, but rather the cessation of the four aggregates (*khandha*). Thus, it is neither mundane (*lokiya*) nor supramundane (*lokuttara*).

However, because it is not mundane (*lokiya*), those who hold the view that it is "supramundane" (*lokuttara*)—such as the Hetuvādins themselves—are the ones intended by the questioner of the Sakavādin school, while the other provides the affirmation.
The remainder is exactly like the previous discussion. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Perception and Feeling (*Saññāvedayitakathā*).
8. Commentary on the Second Discussion of Perception and Feeling (Saṃñāvedayitakathā) 730–731.

Now, since that [feeling] is not supramundane, it is therefore mundane. With reference to those who hold this view—such as the Hetuvādins—the question belongs to the proponent of the first position (Sakavādī), and the admission belongs to the other. The remainder is exactly as before.
End of the commentary on the Second Discussion of Perception and Feeling.
9. Commentary on the Third Discussion of Perception and Feeling (Saṃñāvedayitakathāvaṇṇanā) 732.

Now, since there is no fixed rule regarding the mortality of beings such that one could say, "This one is subject to death, this one is not subject to death," there are those who hold the view that even one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling might die; for example:

Regarding the Rājagirikas: in order to demonstrate both the state of being subject to death and the timing of death—even for those who have attained meditative absorption—the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), and the affirmation to the other.
Then, since one who is passing away must indeed possess contact and so forth occurring at the point of death, [the opponent] said "it exists" and so on, in order to challenge him in that manner.
When asked whether one who is intangible (aphassaka) can die, and so forth, he denies it with reference to other beings.

When asked whether such a person could swallow poison, and so forth, he denies it with reference to the power of meditative attainment (samāpatti). In the second instance, he affirms it with reference to the natural state of the body.

However, since this is the case, there is no such thing as the "power of meditative attainment"; for that very reason, he persists in questioning why he has not entered the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti).

733–734. “One would not die” is the question of the opponent. Regarding the opponent’s question, “Is there that fixed course (niyāma)?”, [the Master] rejects it because such a thing as a fixed course does not exist.

The passage beginning with “one possessed of eye-consciousness,” etc., was stated by the proponent of our own school (sakavādin) to show that even in the absence of a fixed course, one dies precisely at the time of death and not at an improper time.
The intended meaning here is as follows: If death were to occur simply through the absence of the path of certainty (*niyāma*), it would also occur for one possessing eye-consciousness.
Consequently, there would be a contradiction with the Sutta which states, "One does not pass away or reappear by means of the five types of sensory consciousness.
Just as there is no death for one possessing eye-consciousness, so too there is none for one who has attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*).
Commentary on the Third Discussion of Perception and Feeling. 10. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning Non-percipient Beings (Asaññasattupikā-kathā). 735.
Now follows what is called the Discussion Concerning Non-percipient Beings. In that context, there is a development of meditation proceeding by way of the fading away of perception (*saññā-virāga*).

Both the attainment of non-perception (*asaññasamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) are called the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*). Thus, there are two attainments of the cessation of perception and feeling:
the mundane (*lokiya*) and the supramundane (*lokuttara*). Among these, the mundane belongs to worldlings (*puthujjana*) and even to non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*);
the supramundane belongs to the noble ones (*ariya*), and it does not belong to non-percipient beings. This, however, is the distinction.

Regarding those who hold the view— such as the Hetuvādins— that the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) is, without distinction, also present in non-percipient beings (*asañña-satta*),
the Sakavādī asks the question directed at them, and the other (the opponent) grants the premise. Then,

because non-greed and the other [wholesome roots] exist for one who has entered the attainment of non-perception (*asañña-samāpatti*), but not for one who has entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), he says "they exist" and so forth in order to challenge them on that basis.
736. Here too, regarding the question "Is one non-percipient?", non-percipient status is admitted because of having attained meditative absorption through the fading away of perception;
and even there, it refers specifically to a non-percipient being (*asaññasatta*). Therefore, by accepting this proposition and establishing a tenet, it is established through a quibble (*chala*).
Alternatively, non-percipient status is admitted here with reference to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); and even there—
For one who has passed away from here as a non-returner, there is only the attainment of cessation; therefore, the doctrine established by this admission is likewise without foundation.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning the non-percipient beings. 11. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Accumulation of Kamma.

737. Now follows the discussion on the accumulation of karma (*kammūpacaya*). In this regard, there is a doctrine held by some—such as the Andhakas and the Sammitīyas—that the so-called "accumulation of karma" is something other than the karma itself, being a mental non-associated factor (*cittavippayutta*), indeterminate (*abyākata*), and without an object (*anārammaṇa*).
With reference to them, the proponent asks, "Is it something other than karma? and the opponent assents. Then [the proponent says to him]: "If [it is] from karma..."
To challenge [the opponent] by suggesting that "the accumulation of karma must be one thing, and the accumulation of contact and so forth must be another," he says, "Contact is different," and so on.
The other rejects this because such a tenet does not exist.

Regarding the questions, "Is it co-nascent with karma? and so forth, he rejects them with reference to what is dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*), but [he would accept them] for what is associated with consciousness (*cittasampayutta*).
He makes his affirmation with a specific intention. Even when asked "Is it wholesome? he affirms with reference to that which is dissociated from consciousness.
The same method applies to the subsequent question, "Is it unwholesome? (740).
But when asked "Does it have an object?", he maintains that it is exclusively without an object; therefore, he rejects it.
"Mind breaking up": when the mind is breaking up, then karma breaks up—this is the meaning.
Alternatively, it is used in the locative sense; the meaning is "when the mind is breaking up. Or rather, this very reading [is preferred].
In that regard, because what is associated (sampayutta) breaks up while what is dissociated (vippayutta) does not break up, he both affirms and denies.
741. "Accumulation of karma occurs within karma": when karma exists, there is an accumulation of karma; or, when karma is established, there is an accumulation of karma.

It is precisely from the accumulation of karma that a result is produced. His position is that even when that karma has ceased, the accumulation of karma persists until the arising of the result, just as a seed persists until the arising of the sprout. Therefore, he asserts this. That very...

Since he holds the view that "action is the accumulation of action, and that is the fruition of action," and that this accumulation of action persists within the action itself until the arising of its fruition, [the author] asks about the identity of these three: "Is fruition with an object?
He asks this in order to challenge him, implying that just like fruition, the state of being subject to fruition (vipākadhammadhamma) is likewise bound to an object.
The other, however, by way of what has been acquired, affirms one [of the two] and denies the other. The same method applies to the reverse order as well.
The rest here is concluded exactly according to the text. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the accumulation of kamma.
The fifteenth chapter.
The third fifty-section concludes. 16.
The sixteenth chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on Subduing (Niggahakathāvaṇṇanā) 743–744.

Now follows what is called the "Discourse on Subduing. In this regard, if those who have attained power and mastery in the world were unable to subdue the mind of another, what would their attainment of power be, and what would their state of mastery be? [It would be nothing at all. Regarding the attainment of power...

However, regarding those who hold the view that "by means of mastery, you certainly restrain another's mind"—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—it is with reference to them that the questioner (the Sakavādin) asks, "Does one restrain another? and the other (the Itaravādin) grants the assent.
In this context, "restrains" means he prevents [the mind] from falling into defilement or transgression. The rest here follows exactly as in the canonical text.
The same method applies to the discussion on "Support" (*paggaha*).
Explanation of the Discussion on "Restraint" (*niggaha*). 3. Explanation of the Discussion on "Bestowing Happiness" (*sukhānuppadāna*).

747–748. Now follows the discussion on the "bestowing of happiness. In this regard, there are those—such as the Hetuvādins—who hold the view that one person bestows happiness upon another, based on the Sutta passage: "Indeed, the Blessed One has brought many things conducive to our happiness.
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent of the first position (Sakavādī), and the admission is given by the other. [The opponent asks: "Does one bestow suffering?"
But when questioned, not seeing such a scriptural passage, he rejects it. Regarding the question "Is it for one's own pleasure? and so forth, he rejects it by saying:
"That which belongs to oneself or another cannot be bestowed; as for that which belongs to that very person, what is there to be bestowed?
Regarding the question "Is it neither for oneself... and so forth, however, he says: "That which is of such a nature is not called 'bestowed'."
He acknowledges this by means of the conviction that it ought to be so. Indeed, it was not stated because of the absence of pleasure such as that of emission and so forth.

The statement "the providers of pleasant things" indicates the Blessed One’s status as a condition for the arising of pleasure in others, not the actual bestowal of pleasure like food and so on; therefore, [that argument] is not a proof.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Bestowing of Happiness. 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Grasping with Attention (Adhigayha-manasikāra-kathā). §§749–753.
Now follows the discourse known as "Grasping with Attention" (adhigayha-manasikāra). In this regard, attention is of two kinds: by way of method (*naya*)...

And by way of the object. Therein, when the impermanence of even a single formation has been seen, there is attention to the remaining formations by way of inference, [thinking], "All formations are impermanent.
However, one who attends to past formations is not able to attend to those in the future.
When attending to any one among the past and so forth, there is attention by way of the object. Therein, regarding the present...
When one is attending [to them], the mind by which one attends cannot itself attend to its own present moment.

In this regard, there are those who hold the view: "One who 'attends'—meaning having grasped, having seized, and having gathered them all together—attends to all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as a single unit," based on such statements as "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
It is just as with the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas; the question was directed at the proponent (*sakavādin*) with reference to them, and the admission was made by the other.

Now, since one who attends to all [of them] together must attend to that very mind with which he attends to them, the opponent said "by that mind" in order to challenge him on the basis of that state of mind.
The other replied: "It is not possible [to attend to them] by making them the object."

He rejects [the claim] with the intention that it must be known. However, because that mind is known through its being recognized as having such a characteristic, he admits it with the intention that that mind is indeed known.
Alternatively, he rejects it on the grounds that that very [object] is not its object. This is by way of the views arisen based on such passages as:
"When one sees with wisdom that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent'."
He admits it. The same method applies to the remaining two questions as well.

However, regarding the phrases "by that contact" and so forth, not seeing any such sūtra, he simply rejects them. In the questions concerning the past and so on, the rejection and admission should be understood according to the method explained below.
The rest follows exactly the text of the Pāḷi itself. The statement beginning with "all formations" is intended to show the underlying method (naya).
It was stated [that they arise] from an object, not at a single moment; therefore, it is not a proof.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of grasping through attention (*adhigayhamanasikārakathā*). 5.
Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Matter is a Root Cause (*rūpaṃ hetūti-kathāvaṇṇanā*).

754–756. Now follows the discussion on whether matter is a cause (*hetu*). In this context, "cause" is a term for the roots of skillfulness (*kusalamūla*) and so forth, as well as for a causal cause (*hetu-hetu*), and even for any kind of condition (*paccaya*).

However, there are those—such as the Northerners (*Uttarāpathaka*)—who, without making this distinction and relying merely on the statement that "the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are causes," hold the view that matter is a cause without qualification.

These questions are posed by the proponent with a specific intention, while the other provides an admission. When he asks, "Is non-greed the cause? Is form reckoned as non-greed the cause?", the other denies it.

The same method applies to the remaining cases. As for the statement, "The great elements are the supporting causes (*upādāyahetu*) of derived matter," here the status of being a cause is stated in the sense of a condition (*paccaya*), not in the sense of a root (*mūla*); therefore, it does not prove [the point].
Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Matter Has Causes (Rūpaṃ hetūtikathāvaṇṇanā).
757–759. In the discussion of whether matter has causes (sahetuka), the meaning should also be understood by this same method.
Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Matter Has Causes (Rūpaṃ sahetukantikathāvaṇṇanā).
7. Explanation of the Discussion on Whether Matter is Wholesome or Unwholesome (Rūpaṃ kusalākusalantikathāvaṇṇanā) §§760–764.

Now follows the discussion entitled "Whether Matter is Wholesome or Unwholesome. In this regard, based on the statement, "Bodily action and verbal action are both wholesome and unwholesome," [it is argued that] matter consisting of bodily intimation and verbal intimation—designated as bodily and verbal action—[is wholesome or unwholesome].
Regarding those who hold the view that "both the wholesome and the unwholesome exist"—namely, the Mahīśāsakas and the Saṃmitīyas—the proponent asks, "Is matter wholesome? and the opponent assents.
Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If matter is wholesome for you, it must be of such a nature," [the proponent] says, "It has an object," and so forth. Hereafter...
The same method applies to the questions on the unwholesome (*akusala*) as well. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of matter as wholesome or unwholesome. 8.
Commentary on the Discussion of Matter as Resultant (*vipāka*).

765–767. Now follows the discussion titled "The Exposition on Matter as Resultant. In this regard, there are those who hold the view that just as the mind and mental factors arise from the performance of karma, so too does matter arising from the performance of karma constitute a resultant (*vipāka*);
such as the Andhakas and the Saṃmitīyas. With reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of our own school (Sakavādī), and the admission is made by the other.
Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If for you form is a result (vipāka), it ought to be of such a kind as this," he said, "It is to be experienced as pleasant," and so forth.
The rest follows exactly as in the text.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding whether form is a result.
9. Discussion on Matter Ending with the Fine-Material and Immaterial Spheres (Rūpaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarantikathāvaṇṇanā) §§768–770.
Now follows the discussion on matter ending with the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

In this regard, that matter which arises because of having performed karma of the sense-sphere is itself of the sense-sphere; therefore, it also [arises] because of having performed karma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

Regarding those who hold the view that there must be matter belonging to the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere—such as the Andhakas—the proponent of the first position asks, "Is there matter belonging to the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere? and the other assents.
The rest here follows the same method as explained below.
The commentary on the discussion concerning matter belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
10. The commentary on the discussion concerning what is included within the fine-material and immaterial realms (rūpārūpadhātupariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā) [§§ 771–775].
Now follows the discussion: "Sensual lust for the fine-material realm is included within the fine-material realm; sensual lust for the immaterial realm is included within the immaterial realm."

It is so called. In this context, since sensual lust is included within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas—that "therefore, attachment to form and attachment to the formless must also be included within the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*)," are the ones referred to.
The question belongs to the proponent (*sakavādī*), and the admission belongs to the other. The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained below.
For in that context, the only distinction is the phrase: "it underlies the form realm; it underlies the formless realm.
This tenet belongs both to the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas; however, this [specific view] belongs to the Andhakas alone. This concludes the commentary on the discussion:
"Sensual lust for the form realm is included within the form realm; sensual lust for the formless realm is included within the formless realm."
Commentary on the Discussion of What is Included in the Form and Formless Realms.
The Sixteenth Chapter.
17. The Seventeenth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Accumulation of Merit by an Arahant (776–779).

Now follows the discussion known as "Is there an accumulation of merit for an Arahant? In this context, regarding those who—such as the Andhakas—hold the view that there is an accumulation of merit for an Arahant upon seeing his acts of giving, sharing, worshipping shrines, and so forth, it is with reference to them [that this discussion is undertaken].
The question is from the proponent; the other [the opponent] assents. Then, in order to challenge him—thinking, "One who is called an Arahant has abandoned both merit and evil;
if he were to perform merit, he would likewise perform evil"—the proponent says, "it is an accumulation of demerit.
The other rejects this, not seeing any such act as the taking of life. Regarding the phrases "meritorious volitional formation" and so forth, there is no karma leading to existence for an Arahant.

"He rejects. Regarding such statements as "one might give a gift," the proponent admits it because there is the actual occurrence of giving and so forth through a functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*).

The other, however, disregarding the consciousness and establishing his tenet by pointing merely to the occurrence of the action, maintains that since it was established through improper reflection (*ayoniso*), it is not truly established.
Commentary on the Discussion: "The Arahant Has an Accumulation of Merit. 2. Commentary on the Discussion: "The Arahant Has No Untimely Death. 780.
Now follows the discussion known as "The Arahant Has No Untimely Death. Regarding this, [the Blessed One said]: "Bhikkhus, I do not..."

Having misunderstood the meaning of the Sutta which says, "I declare that there is no making an end of volitional kamma that has been performed and accumulated without experiencing its result," those such as the Rājagirikas who hold the view that "an Arahant must indeed attain final Nibbāna only after experiencing the ripening of all kamma;
therefore, there is no untimely death for an Arahant."
And [the question concerns] the Siddhatthikas. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of his own view (sakavādin), and the admission is from the other.

Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If there is no untimely death for him, then one should not be called an 'arahant-killer,'" he said, "There is no such thing as an arahant-killer. The other denies this, because of the existence both of deeds of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma) and of persons who commit such deeds.

781. Regarding the question, "Does [kamma] not take effect?"—this is rejected on the basis of the tenet that "as long as previously committed kamma has not reached exhaustion, it does not take effect. The rest here follows exactly according to the text. 782.
This was said with reference to the Sutta beginning, "Bhikkhus, I do not see...":

without having experienced, found, or undergone the result of intentional kamma once performed, there can be no reaching of the end of those kamma-actions—that is, their state of being brought to completion or their being delimited.
I do not say that [the result] occurs only in this very life for those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life, nor beyond that;
for those to be experienced upon rebirth, it occurs immediately after rebirth, having been reborn, and not beyond that;

for those to be experienced in subsequent lives, it occurs when they find an opportunity for ripening, either in such subsequent lives or in other successive turns of existence. Thus, in every way, as long as the turning of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) continues, there is an occasion for the ripening of results.
“There is no place in the world where one who stands can be freed from evil karma.

This being so, the attempt to establish the doctrine that “there is no untimely death for an Arahant” by means of the fabrication that “even karma whose result has not yet been obtained must necessarily be experienced by an Arahant” is indeed a faulty argument.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Absence of Untimely Death for an Arahant.
3. Commentary on the Discussion that All This is Due to Kamma. 783.
Now follows the discussion known as "All This is Due to Kamma. In this regard, there is the sutta: "The world proceeds by means of kamma."
Relying on this, those who hold the view that "this entire cycle of karma, afflictions, and karmic results arises from karma alone"—such as the Rājagirikas and the Siddhatthikas—are being addressed.
With reference to them, the question "Is all this [from karma]? is asked by the proponent of our own position (sakavādī), and the affirmation is given by the other.
Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If that is so, then karma itself would follow from karma," he says: "Karma also..."
He said, "It is karma. The other rejects this, thinking: "If even karma is called 'karma,' then that karma must itself be a result [of something else].

He asks in order to challenge him: "If all this is from karma, then it must have been caused by what was done in the past. The other rejects this out of fear of the doctrine of past-action causality (*pubbekatahetu*).

784. "From the ripening of kamma": he asks this in order to challenge [the opponent] with the thought, "If all this arises from kamma—meaning that whatever kamma served as the cause for what occurred in a past existence was itself kamma in an even earlier existence, then the ripening of kamma (kammavipāka) would result;
thus, you fall into the position that all this is from the ripening of kamma.
The other [responds] that it is like a sprout from a seed, in the case of the present occurrence.

He rejects [the first position] with reference to arising from karma. When asked the second [question], he admits it because that karma, like a seed, proceeds from a previous seed—that is, from prior karma.

The statement beginning with "one might kill a living being" is said to challenge [the opponent]: "If everything were from the ripening of karma, then acts such as the taking of life would be performed solely through the ripening of karma. The other [responds] that even unwholesome volition (*dussīlya-cetanā*)...
He admits to the position that "the result produced by past karma is, in one sense, merely the ripening (vipāka) itself.

Then, in order to challenge him with the argument, "If for you killing (pāṇātipāta) arises from the ripening of karma, then like killing itself, the ripening would also follow as having a fruit," he says it is "with fruit" (saphala).
The other [responds] regarding the fact that killing leads to hell and so forth, thus establishing its state of having a fruit.
One who sees [the result] admits it; however, not seeing the specific place where such-and-such a fruit of karmic ripening occurs, one denies it.

The same method applies to taking what is not given and so forth. When he asks about the fruit of giving by way of the object to be given—asking whether the requisite of medicine for the sick has a fruit—he does so because of the sutta stating, "The world proceeds by means of karma," and thus [he asks] in order to refute the view that "there is no karma."
Having rejected the doctrine of non-action, he demonstrates the doctrine of action—that there is action—and that one is the owner of one's own actions.
It does not mean that everything arises from every kind of action; therefore, it is not the case that [action] is ineffective.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the totality of action.
4. Explanation of the Discourse on What is Bound by the Faculties (Indriyabaddhakathāvaṇṇanā) 786–787.
Now follows the discourse known as "What is Bound by the Faculties. In this context, suffering is twofold:

that which is bound by the faculties (*indriyabaddha*) and that which is not bound by the faculties (*anindriyabaddha*). That which is bound by the faculties is suffering by virtue of being a basis for suffering; that which is not bound by the faculties is suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away.
It is suffering because it is included under the statement, “What is impermanent, that is suffering.

Without accepting this distinction, there are those—such as the Hetuvādins—who hold the view that “only that which is bound to the faculties is suffering for the sake of whose full understanding the holy life is lived under the Blessed One, and not the other.
In order to show that even the other [the unconditioned] is suffering, [the text says]: “And only that which is bound to the faculties... and so forth.

The question was from the proponent; the admission was from the other. Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "Since the Blessed One has stated that 'whatever is impermanent is suffering,' therefore that which is impermanent must necessarily be bound to the sense faculties," he said, "Is only that which is bound to the sense faculties impermanent? and so forth. [The opponent asks:

"Is not that which is not bound to the sense faculties impermanent too? [The proponent replies: "Is not the earth, mountains, rocks, and so forth impermanent even though they are not bound to the sense faculties? This is the meaning.
788. Regarding the question, "Should it not be said that suffering is bound only to the sense-faculties?"—the opponent's admission (*paṭiññā*) is "yes.

For there are objects of suffering and mental distress (*domanassa*) that are not bound to the sense-faculties. Indeed, fire during the heat of summer and wind during the cold of winter are objects of suffering;
likewise, the loss of wealth and so forth are always objects of mental distress. Therefore, even without [being bound to the sense-faculties],...
In the sense of impermanence (*anicca*), that which is not bound by the faculties (*anindriyabaddha*) should be called suffering (*dukkha*).

However, because it is not produced by kamma and the defilements (*kilesa*), it should not be called the Noble Truth of Suffering; likewise, because it is not to be fully understood (*apariññeyya*) by the Path.

Since the cessation of grass, wood, and so forth, or the cessation of the seasonal elements and seeds, is not what is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, therefore [only] that which is bound by the faculties...

He undertakes this [statement] to show the distinction that "this is both suffering and a noble truth," whereas "the other is merely suffering. The statement beginning with "Just as for one bound by the faculties...

illustrates that for one bound by the faculties, there is the full understanding (*pariññā*) [of suffering], and for one who has fully understood it, there is no further arising while living the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
For this very reason, the proponent of our own position (*sakavādin*) offers a rebuttal: "Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering."
However, it is not possible to deny the state of suffering for that which is comprised by verbal expression but is not bound to the faculties; therefore, [the opponent's argument] is not a proof.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding what is bound to the faculties. 5.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Excluding the Noble Path.

789–790. Now follows the discussion called "Excluding the Noble Path. In this regard, there are those—such as the Hetuvādins—who hold the view that "because the Noble Path is called 'the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,' therefore all remaining conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), excluding the Noble Path, are suffering.
With reference to them, the question is asked by the proponent of his own position (Sakavādī), and the other party gives his assent. Then [the proponent says to him]: "If that is so..."

He said, “The origin of suffering, too,” in order to challenge [the opponent] by pointing out that the state of being suffering would also apply to the origin. The other [the opponent] rejects this, referring to the characteristic of being a cause.
Being questioned again, he admits it, referring to its inclusion within the process of occurrence (*pavatta*).
Regarding the questions “only three,” he rejects them for fear of contradicting the Sutta, but he admits them according to his own established position. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the discussion excluding the Noble Path. 6.
The commentary on the discussion that it should not be said that “the Saṅgha accepts an offering. 791–792.
Now follows the discussion titled “It should not be said that the Saṅgha accepts an offering. Regarding this:
“From the ultimate standpoint (*paramatthato*), the Saṅgha is nothing other than the paths and fruits (*maggaphala*); there is no so-called Saṅgha distinct from the paths and fruits.
And since the paths and fruits do not accept anything, it cannot be said that ‘the Saṅgha accepts an offering (*dakkhiṇā*).
This refers to those who hold such a view, namely the Vetullakas known as the Mahāpuññavādins of the present day. It is with reference to them [that this was said].
"It should be said" is the question of the proponent (sakavādin); "it is admitted" is the response of the other.

Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If the Saṅgha were not to accept [the gift], the Teacher would not praise it with such words as 'worthy of offerings' (āhuneyya) and so forth," he said:

"Is the Saṅgha not worthy of offerings? and so on. Regarding the phrase "giving gifts to the Saṅgha," [the opponent asks]: "If those who give to the Saṅgha find no recipients, to whom would they give?"
This was stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent]. The verse, "The fire consumes the oblation," is derived from a non-Buddhist system (parasamaya).
In that context, the phrase "a great cloud" is said with reference to the rain from the cloud; for the earth receives the rain, not the cloud itself.
When it says "the Path receives," he speaks according to the tenet that "the Saṅgha consists of the Paths and Fruits," yet the Saṅgha is not merely the Paths and Fruits themselves.
Furthermore, the Saṅgha is designated based on the aggregates that are purified by the manifestation of the Path and its Fruits;
therefore, this [objection] is not a proof.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion: "It should not be said that the Saṅgha accepts offerings."
7. Commentary on the Discussion: "It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Purifies the Offering" (793–794).
Now follows the discussion titled "It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Purifies the Offering. In this regard, [the opponent argues]: "The Saṅgha consists only of the paths and fruits;
yet these are not capable of purifying an offering. Therefore, it should not be said that the Saṅgha..."
Regarding those who hold the view that "one purifies the offering," just as they do, the question is asked by the proponent (sakavādī) with reference to them, and the answer is given by the other.

The passage beginning with "worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyyo*) is stated to show that "if the Saṅgha were not able to purify the offering, the Teacher would not have praised it in such a way. "Purifies" (*visodheti*) means that one makes it of great fruit.
For in the Saṅgha, what is given in small measure becomes much, and what is given in large measure becomes even greater.
"Worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyya) means deserving of offerings, suitable for offerings; the meaning is that they are capable of purifying the offering.
"They fulfill the offering" means they bring it to completion; the meaning is that they attain a great fruit even from a very small offering. The rest is exactly as explained below.
Commentary on the Discussion: It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Purifies the Offering.
8. Commentary on the Discussion: It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Eats. 795–796.
Now follows the discussion entitled "It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Eats. In that context as well, [it is argued that] only the paths and fruits...

Regarding those who hold the view that "the Saṅgha" is merely a name and does not consume anything at all, and therefore it cannot be said that "the Saṅgha eats, drinks, chews, or tastes"—just as in the case of those very individuals—the question is posed by the proponent of the first position (Sakavādī) with reference to them, and the other (Itarassa) grants the premise. Then [the opponent] says to him:
"If the Saṅgha did not eat, the preparation of meals for the Saṅgha and so forth would be purposeless."
In order to urge [the Buddha], saying, "Would it not be so? he said, "Are there not some who prepare meals for the Saṅgha? and so forth.
The passage beginning with "Eating in a group" was stated for the purpose of urging him, thinking, "If the Saṅgha did not eat, to whom would there be meals for groups and so on?
The passage regarding "the eight drinks" was also for the purpose of urging him, thinking, "If the Saṅgha did not drink, for whom would the Teacher have authorized these drinks?"
It has been stated. The remainder here also should be understood according to the method explained below.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion: "It should not be said that 'the Saṅgha eats.
9. Commentary on the discussion: "It should not be said that 'what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit.'"
797–798. Now follows the discussion on whether it should be said that what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit. In this regard, [the opponent argues]:
"The Saṅgha consists only of the paths and fruits; it is not possible to give anything to them, nor can they accept anything, nor does any benefit accrue to them through giving.
Therefore, it should not be said that what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit."
The question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī) with reference to those who hold such a view—namely, that very same view [as previously stated]—while the other’s response is an admission.
The passage beginning with “worthy of offerings” (āhuneyyo) was spoken in order to show: “If giving to the Saṅgha were not of great fruit, the Teacher would not praise it in this way.
The remainder follows exactly as it appears in the canonical text (pāḷi).
The commentary on the discussion that it should not be said that what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit. 10.
The commentary on the discussion that it should not be said that what is given to the Buddha is of great fruit. 799.
Now follows the discussion called "it should not be said that what is given to the Buddha is of great fruit. In this regard, "the Buddha..."
The Blessed One does not consume anything at all; however, for the sake of conforming to the world, he displays himself as if consuming.
Therefore, because [the gift] provides no benefit, it cannot be said that what is given to him yields great fruit—such is the tenet of certain [opponents], namely those very ones.
With reference to them, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādin), and the admission belongs to the other. Of bipeds...
The passage beginning with "the foremost" (*aggo*) is stated for the purpose of showing that "even when given to a person of immoral conduct among humans, a gift yields a thousandfold merit;
how much more so, then, to such a supreme person (*aggapuggala*)! The rest here follows exactly the text of the Pāḷi.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the great fruitfulness of giving to the Buddha.
11. Explanation of the Discourse on the Purification of the Offering (Dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathāvaṇṇanā) 800–801.
Now follows the discourse known as the Purification of the Offering. In this regard:
"If the offering were purified by the recipient, it would be of great fruit. The gift was given by the donor; the result was produced by the recipient."
“Another might be the doer for another; pleasure and pain would thus be produced by another; one person might act, while another experiences [the result].
Therefore, the purification of a gift comes from the giver alone, not from the recipient;
it is the mental purity of the giver alone that yields the fruit. Such is the doctrine held by those, such as the Uttarāpathakas.
The question is posed by the proponent with a specific underlying intention (*sandhāya*), while the other party provides an admission.

The passage beginning with "worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyya*) is stated for the purpose of showing: "If the gift were not purified by way of the recipient, what would the state of being 'worthy of offerings' and so forth accomplish?
[The phrase] "one person is the agent for another" means that if the donor’s volition of giving were performed by the recipient, it would be logical.
It may be so. However, his volition for giving is purified by depending upon the object known as the recipient, in the sense that it yields a great result;
therefore, this statement, "Giving is purified by the recipient," is not to be criticized.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Purification of the Offering (*Dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathā*).
The Seventeenth Chapter.
18. The Eighteenth Chapter: 1.
Exposition of the Discourse on the Human World.

802–803. Now follows the discussion on the world of humans (*manussaloka*). In this regard, some take a discourse such as, “The Tathāgata was born in the world, grew up in the world, and dwells having overcome the world, unsullied by the world,” and, grasping it incorrectly (*ayoniso*), they maintain: “The Blessed One was reborn in the Tusita heaven and dwells there;
he does not come to the human world. What appears here is merely a created form (*nimmitarūpa*).”

“...shows [the Buddha]. Regarding those who hold such a tenet—just like the Vetullakas of the present day—the question belongs to the proponent of our own school (sakavādī), while the admission belongs to the other.
Then, in order to convince him both by providing an opportunity for questioning and by means of scriptural proof (suttasādhana), he said:
“Is it not the case that [he] exists? and so forth. “Born in the world,” the opponent says, referring to the Tusita heaven. But the Teacher [said this]:...

The term "world" (*loka*) is spoken with reference specifically to the human world (*manussaloka*). Regarding the phrase "having overcome the world," the opponent asserts through his view that [the Buddha] overcame the human world;
however, the Teacher dwelt having overcome the world as an object of perception (*ārammaṇaloka*).

Regarding the phrase "unsullied by the world," the opponent speaks with reference only to being unsullied by the human world; however, the Teacher [is unsullied] regarding the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
He dwelt unsullied by defilements. Therefore, this is not a proof.
Thus ends the commentary on the Discourse on the Human World. 2.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Teaching of the Dhamma.
804–806. Now follows the discussion on the preaching of the Dhamma. Regarding this, there is the view held by certain people—such as the Vetullakas—namely:
"While residing in the Tusita heaven, the Blessed One dispatched a manifested being for the purpose of preaching the Dhamma;
it was that being, and not the Buddha, the Blessed One himself, who preached the Dhamma after receiving the teaching from him, and it was the Venerable Ānanda who delivered it. This is their tenet.
These questions were posed by the proponent with a specific intention, while the other [the opponent] gave his assent.
Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If the Dhamma was taught by him, he alone should be the Teacher," [the proponent] said, "The Victor is manifested," and so forth.
The other, not accepting it as such, rejects it. The rest here is of plain meaning.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Teaching of the Dhamma. 3. Commentary on the Discourse on Compassion (Karuṇākathā). 807–808.
Now follows what is called the discourse on compassion. In this regard, for those who possess lust, [compassion arises] from the misfortune of beloved objects.

Having seen an occurrence that is a counterfeit of compassion arising through the influence of lust, those who hold the view—such as the Uttarāpathakas—that "lust itself is what is called compassion, and since that does not exist in the Blessed One, therefore the Buddha, the Blessed One, has no compassion," are the ones referred to.

The question belongs to the proponent of his own position (the Sakavādin), while the admission belongs to the other. Then, [the opponent asks] him: "This so-called compassion, because of its freedom from defilement..."

Because it has sentient beings as its object, because it is liberation of the mind, and because it possesses eleven benefits, compassion is of the same nature as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables].

Therefore, in order to raise the objection, "If the Blessed One lacks compassion, then loving-kindness and the others would also not exist for him," he said, "There is no loving-kindness in the Buddha, the Blessed One," and so forth. Regarding the question, "Is he devoid of compassion? he did not see such a conventional expression [as being applicable].
He rejects it. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on Compassion. 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Fragrance.

809. Now follows the discussion on the "fragrance-born" (gandhajāta). In this regard, there are those—such as certain Andhakas and Uttarāpathakas—who, out of improper affection for the Blessed Buddha, hold the view:
"The Blessed One’s excrement and urine far surpass other fragrance-born substances;
there is no fragrance-born substance more fragrant than that. These [hold such a view].
The question was asked by the proponent with a hidden intention, while the other [the opponent] gave an explicit admission. The rest here is resolved exactly according to the text.
This concludes the commentary on the *Gandha-jātaka-kathā*. 5. Commentary on the *Ekamagga-kathā*.

810–811. Now follows the discussion on the single path (*ekamaggakathā*). In this regard, there are those who hold the view concerning the Blessed Buddha that, solely through the power of unwise affection, [they believe]:
"The Blessed One, having become a stream-enterer, became a once-returner; having become a once-returner, he became a non-returner; having become a non-returner, he realized arahantship;
and by means of a single noble path (*ariyamagga*), he realized the four fruits. Such as these...
It refers to those very same [phenomena]; with reference to them, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), while the admission belongs to the other.
Then, in order to challenge him by way of combining together the four types of contact and so forth that arise along with the four fruits, he said, "Of the four contacts," and so on.
The passage beginning with "By the path of stream-entry" was stated for the purpose of asking, "By which path does one realize [it]? [The answer is: "By the path of Arahantship."

When this was said, he challenges [the Buddha] on the grounds that there is no abandonment of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth. The Blessed One rejects this, stating that one who has become a Buddha cannot be a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
This same method applies to the two subsequent questions as well. The rest here follows exactly the text of the scripture.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Single Path.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Transition of Jhāna (813–816).
Now follows what is called the discussion on the transition of jhāna. In that regard, for those [who hold] that "here, monks, a monk... [the following applies].
Based on this teaching of sequential progression—“secluded from sensual pleasures, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna; with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, the second jhāna;

the third jhāna; and he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna”—there arises the tenet that “one passes from one jhāna to another jhāna even without the occurrence of the access concentration (upacāra) for each respective jhāna.”
It is just as among the Mahīśāsakas and certain Andhakas; with reference to them, the question was asked by the proponent of his own view, and the admission was made by the other.

Then [the opponent] said to him: "If, without reaching the access to the second jhāna, you pass directly from the first jhāna to the second jhāna itself, then from the first you might pass to the third, and from the second even to the fourth."
He spoke of "the first jhāna," and so forth, in order to raise an objection. The passage beginning with "That which is of the first" was stated for the purpose of raising the objection:
"If the second follows immediately after the first, or if one enters the third and subsequent jhānas from the second and so on, would one enter them by means of a single adverting? [The answer is:
It arises subsequently for one who first attends to the danger in sense pleasures; at the moment of the jhāna...
He attends only to the sign (*nimitta*). He asks this in order to challenge [the opponent] by saying:

"If that very same [sign] were to arise immediately after the first [moment], just as the subsequent impulsion arises after the preceding impulsion, then—setting aside the distinction between first and last—it would, in terms of its characteristic, be that very same thing.
The meaning is to be understood in this way throughout all instances. By means of the phrases beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*), etc.
This explains that the jhānas are taught in a sequential order, not that they arise immediately one after another; therefore, it is not a proof [of immediate succession].
Explanation of the Discussion on the Transition between Jhānas. 7. Explanation of the Discussion on the Intermediate Jhāna (Jhānantarika).
817–818. Now follows the discussion on the intermediate jhāna (*jhānantara*).

In this context, for those who hold the view that "in the fivefold system, five jhānas are analyzed, yet only three types of concentration are mentioned," and who do not understand the scope of the concentration consisting of vicāra alone without vitakka, [they claim] that "between the first and second jhānas there is what is called the intermediate jhāna."
“This is the tenet,” as held by the Saṃmitīyas and certain Andhakas. With reference to them, the question was posed by the proponent of his own view, and the other party gave his assent.
Then, for the purpose of challenging him with the argument: “Meditative absorption (jhāna) is also mental factors (cetasika-dhamma), as are contact (phassa) and the rest;
therefore, if there were such a thing as an ‘interval of absorption,’ there would also have to be intervals of contact and so forth.”
He says, "There is an interval between contacts," and so forth.

And regarding "of the second jhāna": this is stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent] by saying, "If there were such a thing as an 'interval-jhāna,' then the second, third, and subsequent jhānas would also be jhānas, and they too would have to have an interval.
This [objection] is based solely on the absence of such a tenet.
He both denies and admits. Regarding the phrase "of the first," when asked, he admits on the basis of what he has obtained.

(819) "With applied thought and sustained thought," etc., is stated for the purpose of raising an objection: "Since the state of being *samādhi* is common to all three types of concentration, why is it that only the concentration consisting of sustained thought alone is an intermediate *jhāna*, and not the others? What is the specific reason here?
(820–822) "Of two present *jhānas*" refers to the first and second [meditative attainments]; he asks this with reference to them. The other...
He professes the tenet that "among those very present [factors], concentration that is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought alone is called 'jhāna-interval' (jhānantarika).
When asked whether the first jhāna has ceased, he professes that it is not logical for three [mental factors] to occur simultaneously.
According to the fourfold method (catukkanaya), concentration without applied thought and consisting of sustained thought alone is the first jhāna.
He asks. The proponent rejects [the position] because that [state] is absent according to that method. Is it not the case that the intention here in the passage "Are there not three concentrations?
is this: just as among those three concentrations two concentrations are indeed *jhānas* and not intermediate *jhānas*, so too the other must be a *jhāna* and not an intermediate *jhāna*.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Intermediate Jhāna. 8.
Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Has Attained Attaining Jhāna Hearing Sound (823–825).
Now follows the discussion known as "One who has attained attaining jhāna hears sound. In this regard, because of the first [jhāna]...
"Sound is said by the Blessed One to be a thorn to jhāna; if one who has attained [jhāna] does not hear it, how could it be a thorn?
Therefore, one who has attained hears sound"—this is the tenet of those such as the Pubbaseliyas.
With reference to them, the proponent asks the question, and the other gives his assent. "One sees a form with the eye," and so forth, refers to one who has attained [jhāna].
This was said for the purpose of challenging [the opponent] by showing that, at that time, there is no occurrence through the five doors;
and if that were absent, should he hear a sound, he would also see a visible form. It is called "thorn" because it causes distraction.
For when the ear is struck by a coarse sound, there is emergence from the first jhāna; thus this was said, and therefore it is not a proof. As for the second...

The passage beginning with "of the jhāna" and so forth was stated for the purpose of making it understood that "just as no other thorn exists within the attainment, even so there is no hearing of sound"; all of that is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether one who has attained [jhāna] hears sound.
9. Commentary on the Discussion:

Does the Eye See Form? (826–827) Now follows the discussion titled "Does the Eye See Form? In this regard, there are those who hold the view that "the eye-faculty itself sees form," based upon the scriptural statement, "Having seen form with the eye," such as the Mahāsāṅghikas.
These questions were asked with a specific intention by the proponent, while the other [the opponent] gave his assent.
Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If one were to see a form with the eye, would one see form by means of form?", he said, "One sees form by means of form.
The other, having denied this while referring to the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), was questioned again and admitted it while referring to the eye itself. "He understands" (*paṭivijānāti*).
Herein, this is the intended meaning: we ask with reference to the admission that "one sees," not merely to the act of directing the eye.
Therefore, first say: "Does one who possesses the eye cognize form by means of the form?
The other rejects and yet admits it in the same manner as before. Then, [the questioner says] to him: "If that is so, it follows that form is mental consciousness."
He said, "It is called 'name' because it understands that," in order to challenge [the opponent] by stating that form is mental consciousness. The other, finding no foothold, simply rejects it.

He asks, "Is there an adverting of the eye? and so forth, in order to challenge [the opponent] with the thought: "If the eye sees in the sense of understanding, then there must be an adverting of it as well, just as there is for visual consciousness. The other, because...
The eye is not bound by adverting; it does not arise immediately after adverting. Therefore, he rejects [the view] that "it sees" by saying "it does not.
