The same method applies to the phrases "by the ear, sound," and so forth. Here, monks, when it is said, "a monk sees a form with the eye," this is stated according to the method of discourse concerning the constituent factors (*sasambhārakathā*).
For just as one who pierces with an arrow [is said to do so] "with a bow,"...
Just as one who pierces with an arrow is said to "pierce," so too one who sees with eye-consciousness is said to "see with the eye";
therefore, this [argument] is not a proof. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of "one sees a form with the eye."
The Eighteenth Chapter.
19. The Nineteenth Chapter: 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Abandoning of Defilements.
828–831. Now follows the discussion on the abandoning of defilements (*kilesapajahanakathā*). In this regard, there are those—such as certain [sectarians]—who hold the view:

"Since there is such a thing as the abandoning of defilements, and for one who has abandoned defilements, past defilements are indeed abandoned, as are future and present ones; therefore, one abandons past defilements, and likewise future and present ones. Regarding them:

[This concerns] those from the Northern Path. With reference to them, the question beginning with "the past" and so forth belongs to the proponent of our own school (sakavādī), while the admission belongs to the other.

The remainder proceeds exactly according to the text. However, regarding this question of the opponent (paravādī) concerning "one who abandons defilements," since there is no effort to abandon the past and so forth among the categories [of time] for one abandoning defilements—just as there is no effort to discard refuse for one discarding refuse—[the opponent's position fails].

There is indeed effort regarding the defilements; however, when the Noble Path—which has Nibbāna as its object—is set in motion, the defilements do not arise even though they have not yet arisen, and thus they are said to be "abandoned.
Therefore, he rejects [the view] by saying, "It is not so. As for the statement, "By that, one abandons past defilements," and so forth:
since it cannot be said that "there is no abandoning of defilements," [it refers to] those divided into the categories of past and so on.
"It abandons" is stated by way of a figurative expression (*chala*).
This concludes the commentary on the discourse regarding the abandoning of the defilements (*kilesa*). 2. Commentary on the Discourse on Emptiness (*suññata*).

832. Now follows the discourse on emptiness (*suññatā*). In this context, there are two kinds of emptiness: the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) of the aggregates (*khandha*), and Nibbāna.
Among these, the characteristic of non-self may, in one sense, be included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), whereas Nibbāna is not so included at all.
However, without taking this distinction into account, it is said that "emptiness is included within the aggregate of mental formations."
The question belongs to the proponent (*sakavādī*) with reference to those who hold such a tenet (*laddhi*), such as the Andhakas; the answer belongs to the other.
"Signless" (*animitta*) refers to Nibbāna, which is devoid of all signs (*nimitta*). "Desireless" (*appaṇihita*) is also a name for that very same thing. Why, then, is this brought forward?

It is for the purpose of attributing a fault to the doctrine of those who do not admit analysis (*avibhajjavādī*). For according to them, emptiness (*suññatā*) exists only partially, without having been analyzed.
The tenet is that [Nibbāna] is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). For him, it follows that even Nibbāna is included within the aggregate of mental formations.
To impose this fault upon him, the phrase "signless and wishless" (*animittam appaṇihitam*) was brought forward.
The other, not desiring its inclusion, rejects it. [The statement] "the aggregate of mental formations is not impermanent," etc., regarding that which is designated as Nibbāna—
This was stated for the purpose of showing the fault of falling into the state of impermanence regarding emptiness.

(833) Regarding the emptiness of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*): it is said for the purpose of raising an objection, namely, "If the emptiness of one aggregate were included within another aggregate, then the emptiness of the aggregate of mental formations would also have to be included within the remaining aggregates."

It has been stated. The statement that "the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is not to be spoken of [as being included in the remaining aggregates]" and so forth was said for the purpose of demonstrating the reverse: "If the emptiness of the aggregate of formations is not included within the remaining aggregates, then the emptiness of the remaining aggregates is also not included within the aggregate of formations."
834. The sutta, "Bhikkhus, this is empty of formations," has been cited from another school's tradition.
Therein, "formations" refers to the five aggregates, as in the passage, "All formations are impermanent.

And because they are empty of self and what belongs to self, they are emptiness; thus it falls within the scope of the Teaching and is not contradictory, and for that reason it is permitted. However, since this [sutta] does not [teach] emptiness...
This demonstrates that it is included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); therefore, it is not a proof [of the existence of a self].
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on Emptiness (Suññata-kathā). 3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Fruits of Asceticism (Sāmaññaphala-kathā).

835–836. Now follows the discussion on the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). In this regard, it is the established conclusion within our own school that the resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*) of the Noble Path—whether occurring in the cognitive process of the path itself or in the process of the attainment of the fruit—is called a "fruit of recluseship.

However, there are those who do not accept it in that way, but instead hold: "The fruit of recluseship consists both in the abandoning of defilements and in the arising of the fruit; therefore, it is unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)."
"Tenet" (laddhi) refers, for example, to that of the Pubbaseliyas; with reference to them, the question is posed by one of our own school (sakavādī), and the admission is made by the other.

The rest here follows the method already stated below, and thus conforms exactly to the canonical text (pāḷi). This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life (Sāmaññaphala-kathā-vaṇṇanā).
4. Explanation of the Discourse on Attainment (Pattikathāvaṇṇanā) 837–840.

Now follows the discourse known as the *pattikathā*. Regarding this, there are those who hold the view that "whatever is obtained, the obtaining of each of those is called 'attainment' (*patti*), and that [attainment] is unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)," such as, for example, the Pubbaseliyas; it is with reference to them [that the following is said].

The question is from the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is from the other (the opponent). The remainder here also follows exactly the textual recension (pāḷi) because it proceeds according to the method explained below.
The passage beginning with "it should not be said" is stated in order to reveal that tenet by which [the opponent] conceives attainment (patti) to be unconditioned (asaṅkhata).
Therein, the proponent, rejecting [the opponent's view] by saying "it should certainly not be said so," [denies] the status of form and so forth to attainment alone.
He does not accept it. For there is no such thing as a dhamma called "attainment" (patti); nor, however, does he admit the state of being unconditioned (asaṅkhata).

But the other establishes the view that [the unconditioned] exists merely by means of negation; because it is established through improper method (ayoniso), it remains truly unestablished. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Attainment.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on Suchness (Tathatākathāvaṇṇanā) 841–843.
Now follows the discourse known as "Suchness" (tathatā). In this regard, there are those who hold the view:

"There exists for all phenomena such as form (rūpa) and so forth a 'suchness' (tathatā) consisting of their respective intrinsic natures (sabhāva); and because it is not included among the conditioned (apariyāpanna) within the conditioned forms and so forth, it is unconditioned (asaṅkhata)."
Just as in the case of certain people from the Northern Region (Uttarāpathaka), the question was directed at the proponent with reference to them, while the other [the opponent] gave his assent.
The remainder here is also clear because it follows the method explained below. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Suchness (Tathatā).
6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Wholesome (Kusalakathāvaṇṇanā) 844–846.
Now follows the discussion called "the wholesome" (*kusala*). In this context, that which is blameless (*anavajja*) is also wholesome and has a desirable ripening (*iṭṭhapāka*).
"Blameless" means dissociated from the defilements (*kilesa*). This principle applies to all phenomena with the exception of the unwholesome (*akusala*). It has a desirable ripening.
Merit (*puñña*) is that which produces desirable fruit in future births and during the course of existence. This method conforms only to the first term in the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*).

However, for those such as the Andhakas who hold the view that Nibbāna is wholesome merely by virtue of its blameless nature, without taking this distinction into account, [the text points out] the absence of wholesomeness in Nibbāna in the sense of producing a desirable result.
The question is posed by the proponent (sakavādī) in order to illuminate [the matter], while the admission is made by the other (itara) according to his own position.
The remainder here is also of obvious meaning because it follows the method explained below. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Wholesome (kusalakathā).
7. Commentary on the Discussion of Ultimate Certainty (Accantaniyāmakathā) 847.

Now follows the discussion known as the "Discussion of Ultimate Certainty. In this regard, there are certain [teachers] who, relying on the Sutta passage, "Once submerged, he remains submerged," hold the view that "there is ultimate certainty for an ordinary person" (*puthujjana*), such as some [of those belonging to other schools].
The question was directed toward those of the Northern Path by the proponent of the first position (sakavādī), while the other [the opponent] gave his assent.

The phrase "a matricide," and so forth, was stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent] with the thought: "Since one who possesses fixed wrong view and those such as matricides are alike in being fixed in the state of wrongness (micchattaniyāma), those [matricides] must also be absolutely fixed.
The other [the opponent] said: "One who possesses fixed wrong view..."

He rejects [the view] with "No" because of the tenet: "These [beings] are fixed even in another existence as seeds of *saṃsāra*, but these [others] are fixed within this very single individual existence (*attabhāva*). 848.
He asks, "Could doubt arise? meaning, "Could [the thought] 'Is this one fixed or not? arise in such a way?"
The other, seeing no reason for its non-arising, admits [its existence]. But when asked, "Would it not arise?

he admits it with reference to its non-arising in that specific case where one who has cultivated a particular view has entered the certainty of rightness (*niyāma*). When asked, "Is it then abandoned by that?
he denies it because it is not abandoned by the Path; yet he admits it because that view does not manifest with respect to that object. Then...
Since there is no such thing as abandonment apart from the Noble Path, he said, "by the path of stream-entry" and so forth, in order to urge him on that basis.
The other rejects it because [those defilements] have not been abandoned even by that single path. When asked again, "By which?", he said, "by the unwholesome," referring to the wrong path.
(849) "The view of annihilation might arise"—this asks whether the second determination (*niyāma*) has arisen. The other [replies]: "Even those who..."
Because of the statement, "Okkalā, Veyyābhiccas, Natthikavādins, Akiriyavādins, and Ahetukavādins," all three types of fixed wrong views arise in a single individual;
therefore, he admits this.
Then, in order to challenge him by saying, "But surely that [person] is not absolutely fixed," he says "Hañci" (If indeed... and so forth. For one who is absolutely fixed...

For the second rule would then be purposeless. Regarding the question, "Would it not arise?": having grasped that very thing which was taken as "permanent" by the eternalist view, he admits its non-arising with the intention that it will be cut off.

When asked, "Is it abandoned?", he denies it because it has not been abandoned by the Path, yet he admits it because it does not arise according to the method already stated. This also applies to such questions as, "Would the eternalist view arise? and so forth.
The same method applies. The remainder is exactly as stated in the section on doubt (vicikicchā-vāra).
851–852. "It should not be said" is the question of the opponent; "because the Sutta exists" is the admission of one's own school (sakavādin).
However, he is not submerged even in another existence. For it is in this very existence that he is incapable of abandoning that view.
This is the intended meaning here; therefore, that [argument] is not a proof.
This was stated for the purpose of showing that one should seek the meaning without becoming dogmatic regarding mere expressions such as "having emerged at all times, he submerges.
Commentary on the Discussion of Absolute Certainty.
8. Exposition of the Faculties (Indriyakathāvaṇṇanā) 853–856.
Now follows the discourse on the faculties. In this context, mundane faith is simply faith;
it is not the faculty of faith. Likewise, mundane energy... mindfulness... concentration... and wisdom are simply wisdom; they are not the faculty of wisdom.

This is the tenet of those such as the Hetuvādins and the Mahīśāsakas; with reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of our own school (sakavādī), and the admission is given by the other.

Regarding the statement "there are no mundane forms of faith" and so forth: since even mundane states such as faith and the rest are faculties in the sense of being predominant (adhipati-ṭṭhena), and there is no such thing as a "faculty of faith" distinct from faith itself, therefore [the text speaks of] mundane faith and the rest as well.
This was stated for the purpose of showing that they possess the nature of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and so forth.
The passage beginning with "There is a worldly mind" and so on was stated by way of a simile to clarify that meaning:

just as those worldly phenomena such as the mind are the mind-faculty (manindriya) and so forth, so too are worldly faith and the others the faculty of faith and so forth. The rest here follows exactly the text of the Pāḷi.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties.
The Nineteenth Chapter.
20. The Twentieth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Unintentional (Asañcicca-kathāvaṇṇanā) §§857–862.
Now follows the discussion known as the "Unintentional. In this regard, there are those who hold the following view:

"The bases for the immediate [karmas] (ānantariya-vatthu) are indeed grave and heavy; therefore, even if one violates those bases unintentionally, one still incurs an immediate [retribution]. Such is their position, for example:

[This refers] to certain people from the Northern Region (Uttarāpathaka). With reference to them, the question "unintentionally" (*asañcicca*) was asked by the proponent of our own school (*sakavādī*), and the admission [of the contrary] was made by the other on account of his own tenets.
Then, for the purpose of challenging him with the argument:

"Since what is called an 'immediate' (*ānantariya*) deed has reached the status of a full course of action (*kammappatha*), if there could be a breach of a course of action unintentionally, then the remaining [offenses] such as taking life (*pāṇātipāta*) and so forth would also occur unintentionally."
He says, “having unintentionally killed a living being,” and so forth. The other denies this because he lacks such a view.
The rest proceeds exactly according to the text. The question, “Is he not a matricide? belongs to the opponent;
the admission belongs to our own side, referring to killing unintentionally at times such as during medical treatment. This is also the case in the question, “Was the mother not deprived of life?”

The admission regarding the taking of life unintentionally belongs only to the proponent’s own side. However, by not grasping the intended meaning in this way, the other person establishes the position that "it is indeed so.
Because that was established improperly, it remains unestablished. This same method applies even in the case of parricides and the like.
But regarding the schism of the Saṅgha, the schism of the Saṅgha [is admitted] with reference to one who perceives it as a legal act (*dhamma*).

The question regarding the "immediate" (ānantarika) offense belongs to the proponent of the first position (*sakavādin*). Having grasped inappropriately the statement, “Having split a harmonious Saṅgha, one roasts in hell for an eon,” the opponent (*paravādin*) makes his admission.

When questioned again with the word “all,” he denies it with reference to one who perceives it as *dhamma* on his own side, but he admits it with reference to one who perceives it as *dhamma* on the opponent’s side. Thus, [the term] “one who perceives it as *dhamma*” (*dhammasaññī*)...

The same method applies to both questions. As for the statement, "Has it not been said by the Blessed One?", that was spoken solely to demonstrate that one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma (adhammavādī) is destined for immediate rebirth in hell.
In the verse beginning with "He is bound for a state of misery, destined for hell," it is likewise the speaker of non-Dhamma who is intended.
The other [opponent], however, establishes his own position without grasping the underlying intention; because it is established through improper means (ayoniso), it remains truly unestablished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Unintentional Action. 2. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā). 863–865.
Now follows what is called the Discussion of Knowledge. Therein, knowledge is twofold: mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*).
There is also mundane knowledge of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-ñāṇa*) occurring by way of giving and so forth, as well as the knowledge of the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*);

there is also supramundane knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*) and the fruit (*phala-ñāṇa*) which delimits the Truths. However, for those—such as the Hetuvādins—who hold the view that "only the knowledge that delimits the Truths is [true] knowledge and not the other;
therefore, an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) possesses no knowledge," they do so without making this distinction.

These questions are directed toward the proponent, while the other’s response is an admission. The terms “wisdom” (*paññā*) and so forth are stated for the purpose of showing that they are synonyms for knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
By this, he demonstrates: if that person lacks knowledge, then wisdom and the rest are also absent;
but if wisdom and the rest exist, then knowledge also exists. Why? Because wisdom and the rest are not different from knowledge. [The passage beginning with] “the first jhāna” and so forth...

This was stated for the purpose of showing the knowledge of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-ñāṇa*). "One should give a gift," and so forth, refers to the knowledge of the ownership of action (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*).

"One fully understands suffering" indicates specifically the supramundane path-knowledge (*lokuttara-magga-ñāṇa*), yet it does not mean that knowledge is exclusively supramundane. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of knowledge.
3. Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Hell-Wardens (Nirayapālakathāvaṇṇanā) 866.

Now follows the discourse concerning the hell-wardens. In this regard, there are those—such as the Andhakas—who hold the view that "in hell, it is only the kamma of the denizens of hell that slays them by taking on the form of hell-wardens;
there are no such beings as 'hell-wardens'. These [are the ones being refuted].
The question was asked by the proponent with a hidden intention (*sandhāya*), while the other [the opponent] gave his assent.

Then, in order to challenge him with the argument, "If there were no hell-wardens (*nirayapāla*) there, there would also be no infliction of punishments; for when there are punishers, there are punishments," he said, "There are none in the hells," and so forth.
(867–868) He said, "They exist among humans," in order to make it known through direct observation. For just as when there are punishers among humans...
The reason is that "it is likewise there too"—this is the intended meaning here. "Are there [beings] in the hells? is the question of the opponent; "Yes" is the response of the other.
"Neither Vessabhū nor even the King of Petas"—this sutta was cited by the opponent from his own tradition.
However, it was accepted by the proponent as belonging to the domain of the Teaching (Sāsana). In that context, Vessabhū is a certain deity.
"Pettirāja" means a great lord among the spirits (petas) in the spirit realm. Soma and the others are well known. This is what is meant:
these Vessabhū and the rest do not kill a person who, driven away from this world by his own kamma, has reached the other world.
Rather, it is those very kamma-actions by which he was driven there that kill him; thus, one is the owner of one's own kamma (kammassakata).

It illuminates [the existence of hell-wardens], but it does not deny the existence of hell-wardens. Furthermore, the scriptural passages cited by our own proponent, beginning with "Monks," are indeed of explicit meaning (*nītārtha*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Hell-Wardens. 4.
Commentary on the Discussion of Animals.

869–871. Now, there is what is called "animal talk" (*tiracchānakathā*). In that regard, among the gods, divine sons such as Erāvaṇa and others manifest themselves in the form of elephants, horses, and so forth;
yet there are no actual animals there. However, those who—like the Andhakas—hold the view that "there are animals among the gods" because they see divine sons in animal forms, [should be corrected].
The question was posed by the proponent with a hidden intention (*sandhāya*), while the other [the opponent] gave an affirmative answer.

Then, in order to challenge him with the argument, "If there were animals in the celestial realm (*devayoni*), then there would also be gods in the animal realm (*tiracchānayoni*"), he said, "Are there [gods] among the animals? and so forth.
The passage beginning with "insects" (*kīṭa*) was stated to show those beings whose non-existence he maintains. As for "Erāvaṇa," his existence is established in the context of that question.
The admission is that of one's own proponent, not that of an animal.
The phrase "elephant-binders," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of raising the objection: "If elephants and such were there, there would also be elephant-binders and the like.

In this context, "barley-servants" (yāvasika) are those who give barley. "Handlers" (kāraṇika) are elephant-trainers and others by whom they might be subjected to various kinds of training. "Cookers" (bhattakāraka) are...
Just as those who provide food for elephants and other animals do not cry out when they are not fed, so too one who does not desire [the gift] rejects it.
This concludes the commentary on frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*). 5. Commentary on talk concerning the path (*maggakathā*).

872–875. Now follows the discussion on the Path (maggakathā). In this regard, there are those who, based on the Sutta passage—"But previously his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were quite purified"—and relying on the fact that right speech, right action, and right livelihood are dissociated from consciousness, hold the view that "the Path, in its direct sense, consists of only five factors," as for example...
Regarding the Mahīśāsakas, the question "Is it fivefold? refers to the proponent's own school (Sakavādin), while the affirmation belongs to the other.

The statement "Right speech is a path-factor, yet it is not the path," and so forth, is stated according to the tenets of other schools (parasamaya). For in the systems of other schools, right speech and the rest are presented as path-factors.
However, they are described [here] as not being the path because they are material form (rūpa). The passage beginning with "Right view is a path-factor" and so forth...
It is stated for the purpose of showing that there is no such thing as a path-factor that is not a factor of the path.

Furthermore, in the sutta beginning with "But previously indeed for him," it is stated that "bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are perfectly purified" in order to show the state of purity of the practice leading to the goal (*āgamaniyapaṭipadā*)—namely, that the cultivation of the path belongs only to one whose virtue is pure, and not to another; it is not stated for the purpose of showing that these [three] constitute the fivefold nature [of the path] even in their absence.
For this very reason it was said: "In this way, this Noble Eightfold Path reaches the fulfillment of its development.
Thus, the sutta cited by the proponent of the opposing view is of explicit meaning (nītattha). This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Path.
6. Explanation of the Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 876–877.

Now follows the so-called "Discourse on Knowledge. In this regard, concerning the twelvefold knowledge during the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, there are those—such as the Pubbaseliyas—who hold the view that "knowledge based on twelve grounds is supramundane" (lokuttara).
The question was asked by the proponent with a specific intention (*sandhāya*), while the other [the opponent] gave his assent.

Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If that [knowledge] has twelve bases, there ought to be twelve path-knowledges," he said, "Twelve," and so forth. The other rejects this, intending the unity of the path;

for according to each individual truth, there is a diversity of knowledge by way of the knowledge of the truth (*sacca-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of function (*kicca-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of what has been done (*kata-ñāṇa*).
He asserts this by way of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). This same method applies to the passages beginning with "twelve knowledges of the stream-entry path. [Objection:

But has it not been stated by the Blessed One that the Sutta—along with its preliminary and subsequent sections—illustrates the diversity of knowledge, and not that the Noble Path consists of twelve knowledges?
Therefore, [your argument] is not a proof.
Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge.
The twentieth chapter.
The fourth fiftieth section is completed.
21. The Twenty-first Chapter. 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Dispensation (Sāsanakathā). 878.
Now follows what is called the discourse on the Dispensation. In that regard, with reference to the three councils (saṅgīti), [it is said]: "The Dispensation is new..."

Regarding those who hold the view that "it is spoken [by the Tathāgata]," or "there is someone who makes new [teachings] in the Tathāgata’s dispensation," or "it is possible to make new [teachings] in the Tathāgata’s dispensation"— such as certain Northerners—

it is with reference to them that, in all three discourses, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādin) and the admission to the other. The passage beginning with "the foundations of mindfulness" refers to the dispensation.
The name refers both to the noble qualities (ariyadhammā) such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and to the teaching on the wholesome (kusala) and so forth.

In this regard, if the Blessed One had taught foundations of mindfulness and so forth to some [people], yet by performing foundations of mindfulness and so forth for others—excluding those [first group]—or by making the unwholesome and so forth wholesome, he would have made the Dispensation (sāsana) something newly created. Has anyone ever done that?
"Is there anyone who does this? or "Is it possible to do this?"—these three questions are stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent].
In all other respects, the remainder follows exactly as in the text. This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Teaching (*Sāsanakathā*).
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Unsecluded (Avivitta-kathā) 879–880.

Now follows the discourse called "the unsecluded. In this regard, the established conclusion within our own school is that whatever phenomenon is present for a particular person is said to be "unsecluded" from that person.
However, because by an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) the three realms...

"Because phenomena have not been fully understood, he is at that very same moment not devoid of all phenomena belonging to the three realms"—this is the tenet of certain [opponents], such as those very ones [previously mentioned].
With reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent (sakavādī), and the admission is made by the other.

The phrase "by means of contacts," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the fault of the simultaneous occurrence of all contacts and the rest within a single moment. The remainder...
In all cases, the meaning is indeed plain.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on Non-Abandonment (Avivittakathā). 3. Commentary on the Discourse on Fetters (Saññojanakathā).

881–882. Now follows the discussion on the fetters (*saññojana*). In this regard, because an *arahant* does not know everything within the domain of a Buddha, there arises the notion that ignorance (*avijjā*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*) must therefore remain unabandoned in him.
Consequently, those who hold the view that "there is some fetter that has not been abandoned for one who has attained *arahantship*"—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—[are here addressed].

These questions were posed by the proponent of the first position (*sakavādin*), and the other [the opponent] gave his assent. The statement beginning with "Is there any kind of personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi)?
was spoken for the purpose of demonstrating that the Arhat has abandoned all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Regarding the two questions, "Is everything within the Buddha’s domain?", a denial was made because the Arhat lacks the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), not because of a failure to abandon ignorance (*avijjā*) or doubt (*vicikicchā*).

The other, however, establishes the thesis "by that" with reference to the fact that those [fetters] have not been abandoned. Since it is established through improper reflection (*ayoniso*), it remains unestablished.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Fetters (*saññojana-kathā*).
4. Explanation of the Discourse on Psychic Power (Iddhikathāvaṇṇanā) 883–884.
Now follows what is called the discourse on psychic power (*iddhi*). In this context, what is known as psychic power succeeds in some cases and does not succeed in others;
it certainly does not succeed in making things that are impermanent and so forth permanent and so forth. However, regarding a homogeneous continuity (*sabhāgasantati*)—
Whether by transforming [the object] to produce a dissimilar continuity, or by causing it to persist for a much longer duration through a similar continuity,
such an act succeeds in some cases depending on the causes— such as the merit and so forth— of those for whose sake it is performed;
this is like the production of drinking water, ghee, milk, and the like for the sake of monks, or the long-lasting persistence of lamps and other offerings in the enshrinement of a great relic.

"And as if" (*viya ca*)—this is the established conclusion within our own school (*sakasamaya*). However, regarding the venerable Pilindavaccha’s resolve that the king’s palace was indeed gold, the question "Is there psychic power through intention?

(*adhippāya-iddhi*) is asked by the proponent of our own position (*sakavādin*) with reference to those who hold the view that such power exists, such as the Andhakas. In this context, "psychic power through intention" means:
*Adhippāya-iddhi*: the meaning is "success according to one's intention. "Yes" (*āmantā*) is the opponent’s admission, standing merely upon his own tenet.
Then, in order to investigate whether impermanent things and so forth could possess permanence and so forth, he says, "Let trees be ever-green," and so on.
The rest here is of plain meaning. Regarding the establishing of a tenet, [he says], "And you were gold," etc.
It came about through the king’s supportive merit, not solely by the elder’s intention alone. Therefore, that [argument] is not conclusive.
Explanation of the Discussion on Psychic Power. 5. Explanation of the Discussion on the Buddha.

885. Now follows the discussion on the Buddhas (buddhakathā). In this regard, apart from differences in physical form, lifespan, and radiance at various times, there is no such thing as inferiority or superiority among the Buddhas with respect to the remaining Buddha-qualities.
However, for those—such as the Andhakas—who hold the view that there are indeed distinctions [among them], it is with reference to them [that the following is said].
The question "Are there Buddhas? is from the proponent's side; the other's reply is an affirmation.

Then, in order to examine him by means of the Buddha-qualities, [the proponent] says, "By way of the foundations of mindfulness," and so forth. The other, seeing no inferiority or superiority on their part, simply refuses. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Buddhas.
6. Explanation of the Discourse on All Directions (Sabbadisākathāvaṇṇanā) 886.

Now follows the discourse known as "All Directions. Therein, having generated a mental conceptualization regarding the arrangement of world-systems all around—in the four cardinal directions, below, and above—and that Buddhas exist in all world-systems, [the meditator proceeds].
Regarding those who hold the view that "Buddhas abide in all directions," such as the Mahāsāṅghikas:

the question is posed by the proponent of his own school (sakavādī), and the answer is given by the other (itaro). When asked about the "eastern direction," he rejects [the claim] with reference to Sakyamuni.
When asked again, he admits it with reference to one residing in another world-system according to their tenet. What is his name?
The passage beginning with "Bhagavā" was spoken for the purpose of challenging [the interlocutor] by saying, "If you know him, speak of him by way of his name and so forth.
By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on All Directions.
7. Explanation of the Discourse on the Dhamma (Dhammakathāvaṇṇanā) 887–888.

Now, there is that which is called the "Discourse on the Dhamma. In this regard, because form and the other aggregates are determined by their own respective intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) and do not abandon those natures, those who hold the view that "all phenomena (*dhammā*) are determined"—such as the Andhakas and others—[are refuted].
And [the question] regarding certain people from the Northern Region: with reference to them, the proponent asks, "Are they all *dhammas*? and the other assents.
Then, in order to challenge him by saying, "If they are fixed (*niyata*), they must be either fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*) or fixed in truth (*sammattaniyata*);
there is no other kind of 'fixation' apart from these," he says, "Are they fixed in falsehood? and so forth. In that regard, there is also a rejection.
And as for the opponent’s admission: when he says that "form is fixed in the sense of being form," etc., this is stated in order to challenge him on his own terms.
Herein, this is the intended meaning: since "form is fixed in the sense of being form," it must be said with the intention that "form is only form, not of the nature of feeling, and so forth";
it cannot be said otherwise than this. Why? Because of the sense of being form (*rūpaṭṭhato*).

Because there is no other form [to distinguish it from]. For the characteristic of form (*rūpasabhāva*) is the meaning of "form" (*rūpaṭṭha*); and the characteristic of form is form itself, not something other than form.
However, this conventional designation exists for the purpose of establishing its distinction from feeling and the other aggregates.

Therefore, when one says, "Form is determined in the sense of the characteristic of form," it is stated that form is determined. And what is called "determined" refers to that which is fixed in the direction of falsehood (*micchattaniyata*).
Or it may be fixed in rightness; there is no other "fixity" (niyāma) besides this. Now, why does he claim this? It is by way of a different meaning.
In the statement, "matter is fixed in the sense of being matter," the meaning here is that matter is simply matter and not of the nature of feeling and so forth.
Therefore, he claims this. However, since there is no fixity for it other than this, [he repeats] by means of that very same [term].
He said, "To refute by means of the method [of the *nayena*], 'one fixed in wrongness' (*micchattaniyata*)," and so forth.

All of that is of obvious meaning. Therefore, even the thesis that "there is form" (*rūpa*) is indeed unestablished, because it has been established through improper attention (*ayoniso*). This concludes the commentary on the discourse on the Dhamma.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Karma (Kammakathāvaṇṇanā) 889–891.

Now follows the discussion called "Karma. In this regard, there are those who hold the view—such as they themselves do—that "all karma is determinate" because karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth is determinate by virtue of its status as being experienced in the present life and so forth. It is with reference to them that [the following is said]:
The question is from the proponent's side, and the admission is from the other's. "Fixed in the sense of being experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṭṭhena niyata*):
here, "experienced in the present life" means precisely the state of being experienced in the present life.

The proponent’s admission is made with reference to this point: that if it is able to give its result in this very life, it gives it; and if not, it becomes what is called "ineffective action" (*ahosikamma*).

Furthermore, this [kamma] is indeed undetermined (aniyata) by way of its alignment with either wrongness (micchatta) or rightness (sammatta); thus everything should be understood according to the method already explained below.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Kamma. The twenty-first chapter.
22. The Twenty-Second Chapter. 1.
Explanation of the Discourse on the Parinibbāna. 892.
Now follows the discourse known as the *Parinibbānakathā*. In this regard: "Because the Arahant has not yet abandoned the fetters within the domain of the Omniscient One..."

Regarding those who hold the view— such as the Andhakas— that "one attains final nibbāna, therefore there is some fetter not yet abandoned when one attains final nibbāna," the question is posed by the proponent of our own position (Sakavādī), and the admission is made by the other.
The rest here follows the same method as explained below.
Commentary on the Discourse on Final Nibbāna. 2. Commentary on the Discourse on Wholesome Consciousness. 894–895.
Now follows the discourse known as “Wholesome Consciousness. In this regard, since even an Arahant who has attained fullness of mindfulness passes away into final Nibbāna...
Regarding those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas—that one attains final Nibbāna with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and therefore attains final Nibbāna with a wholesome consciousness:
the question was asked by the proponent of the orthodox position (Sakavādī) concerning them, and the other party admitted it.

Then, because what is called "wholesome consciousness" exists by way of the formation of meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth, the opponent said, "meritorious volitional formations," and so on, in order to challenge him on that point.

In this context, everything proceeds exactly according to the canonical text. The phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending" is stated for the purpose of illustrating death without delusion by way of functional mindfulness and clear comprehension at the moment of the impulsion (javana), not for the purpose of illustrating wholesome consciousness. Therefore, it is not a proof [of the presence of wholesome consciousness].
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of wholesome consciousness.
3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Imperturbable (Āneñjakathāvaṇṇanā) 896.

Now follows the discourse known as the "Discourse on the Imperturbable" (Āneñjakathā). In this regard, having observed that the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna while established in the fourth jhāna, there are those—such as certain sectarians—who hold the view:
"An Arahant attains final Nibbāna while established in the imperturbable (āneñja). [The following addresses their position.]
The question was asked by the proponent (sakavādī) with reference to those of the Northern Path (Uttarāpathakas), while the other [the opponent] gave his assent.

"In a natural mind" (*pakaticitte*) means in the life-continuum mind (*bhavaṅgacitte*). For all sentient beings possessing perception, having remained in the life-continuum mind, pass away through the death-moment consciousness (*cuticitta*) at the conclusion of the life-continuum.
Thus he spoke in this way to challenge him on this point. In that regard, although in the four-aggregate existence...
Even the natural consciousness of an Arahant is imperturbable (*āneñja*), yet this question is raised specifically with reference to existence in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*).
Therefore, he said, "Indeed, you should not say so. The rest here is of plain meaning. This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on Imperturbability (*Āneñjakathāvaṇṇanā*).
4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Realization of the Dhamma (Dhammābhisamaya-kathā) 897.

Now follows the discussion known as the "Realization of the Dhamma. In this regard, there are those who hold the view that "there is realization of the Dhamma while lying in the womb," having seen one who was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) in a past existence enter [the womb] and then emerge from it—just as, for example, [the case of] Soṇa Koḷivisa.
This refers to certain people from the Northern Region; the question is posed by the proponent of our own school (sakavādī), while the other party provides the affirmation.

Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If there is the realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*) there, there must also be the causes for that realization of the Dhamma, such as the teaching of the Dhamma," he says:
"Is there a teaching of the Dhamma for one lying in the womb? and so forth. The passage beginning with "Of the sutta... constitutes the section on the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). For, while lying in the womb, for the most part only the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) proceeds.

Therefore, because of the absence of any occurrence consisting of functional states (*kiriyā*), the being is "asleep"; because of the absence of application to mental development (*bhāvanā*), he is "negligent";

and because of the absence of mindfulness and clear comprehension that grasp the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he is called "one of confused mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension. How, then, could there be a breakthrough to the Dhamma for such a person?
Commentary on the Discourse on the Realization of the Dhamma.
5–7. Commentary on the Discourse on Tissa (898–900).
Now follows the discourse known as "Tissa. In that context, regarding the attainment of Arahatship by those who have recently become Stream-enterers:
Having seen Suppavāsā the laywoman’s seven-year-old pregnancy, [some hold] the view that "one can attain Arahantship while lying in the womb";

and having seen in a dream such things as traveling through the air, they hold the views that "there is a realization of the Dhamma" and "there is the attainment of Arahantship therein"—just as those very same people do elsewhere.
It is with reference to them that the question of the proponent of his own position (sakavādin) is asked, and the admission is given.
For the other [case], the remainder here is exactly the same as the previous discussion.
This concludes the commentary on the three-fold discussion. 8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Undeclared (Abyākata-kathā).

901–902. Now follows the discussion on the indeterminate (abyākata). In this regard, concerning those who hold the view that "all the mind of one who has fallen asleep in a dream is indeterminate," based on the statement:

"There is, monks, such a volition (cetanā), and it is indeed beyond conventional designation (abbhohārika),"—referring specifically to certain Northerners (Uttarāpathakas) and others like them—the question belongs to the proponent of our own school (sakavādī), while the admission [of the point] belongs to the opponent.

For the other [case], the rest here follows exactly as in the Pāḷi. The statement that "the mind of one who has gone to sleep is not subject to formal designation" is said with reference to an offense (*āpatti*).

For although unwholesome states of mind may indeed arise in one who has gone to sleep by way of killing living beings and so forth, since there is no violation of the objective basis (*vatthu*), it is impossible to define an offense therein. By this...
For that reason, it is not "not to be discussed" (abbohārika), but rather because it is "indeterminate" (abyākatatta).
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Indeterminate (Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā). 9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Condition of Repetition (Āsevanapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā).

903–905. Now follows the discussion on the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*). In this regard, since all phenomena (*dhammas*) are momentary, nothing whatsoever remains for even a moment to be called "repeating" as a condition of repetition. Therefore, there is no such thing as the state of being a condition of repetition.
As for those who hold the view that nothing arises through the state of being a condition of repetition—just like them [the opponents]:
Having taken these into account, the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādī), while the answer belongs to the other.

Then, in order to establish this by means of the Suttas themselves, the passage beginning with "Is it not said by the Blessed One that killing living beings... was brought forward. All of that is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya).
10. Explanation of the Discourse on Momentariness (Khaṇikakathāvaṇṇanā) 906–907.
Now follows what is called the discourse on momentariness. In this regard, since all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, they must therefore last for only a single moment of consciousness.
For if impermanence is common to all, why is it that one thing breaks up quickly while another takes a long time? What [is the reason]?

Regarding the term "fixed order" (*niyāma*) here, there is the tenet of certain schools—such as the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas—who hold that [all things] exist for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).

With reference to them, the proponent asks whether they are "momentary," and the other assents. Not perceiving such a configuration in the mind regarding the "great earth" and so forth, he rejects it.
As for the "eye-base" (*cakkhāyatana*) and so on, [the opponent objects]: "If all were to be momentary in a single moment of consciousness..."
This was stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent] with the thought: "The eye-base and so forth would arise and cease only together with eye-consciousness and so forth.

However, the other [opponent] denies this with reference to the arising of consciousness in one who has entered the mother's womb, while he admits it by way of its acquisition with reference to the course of existence (*pavatta*).
The rest here is of obvious meaning. Therefore, they are of a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).

Because they are not permanent, he states his own preference for the reason that they last for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*). That is just like what was not stated [previously].
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Momentariness.
The twenty-second section.
23. The Twenty-third Chapter. 1. Explanation of the Discourse on a Single Intention (Ekādhippāyakathā). 908.
Now follows the discourse known as "A Single Intention. In this context, "a single intention" refers to either compassion or a single purposeful aim.
"One who has a single purpose" (*ekādhippāyo*) refers to one who, having performed acts such as worship of the Buddha together with a woman with the thought,
"May we be together in saṃsāra," possesses a single intention by way of a formal aspiration (*paṇidhi*). Regarding those— such as the Andhakas and the Vetullakas—
who hold the view that sexual intercourse should be practiced when two people have such a single purpose, [the text] refers to them.
The question is from the proponent; the admission is from the other. The rest here is established exactly according to the text.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of a Single Intention. 2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Description of an Arahant.

909. Now follows the discussion on the description of an Arahant. In this context, there are certain people—such as some from the Northern Path—who hold the view that "non-human beings engage in sexual intercourse by means of the description of Arahants," having seen wicked bhikkhus who were perfect in deportment and perfect in appearance.
It is with reference to them that the proponent asks the question, and [the opponent] gives the admission.
For the other [type of person]. The rest here is of plain meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse describing the Arahant. 3–7.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Exercise of Sovereign Power at Will.

910–914. Now follows the discussion on the exercise of sovereign power at will. Regarding the *Chaddanta Jātaka* and others, there is the tenet held by certain groups—such as the Andhakas—that "the Bodhisatta goes to a state of ruin for the sake of exercising sovereign power at will;
he enters a womb; he performed austerities; he practiced self-mortification; and he designated another teacher. This is their position.
With reference to these, the question belongs to the proponent, and the admission belongs to the other. The remainder of the first discussion has its meaning already explained.

In the second discussion, the phrase "one possessing psychic power" (*iddhimā*) is stated for the purpose of challenging [the opponent]: if one were to go by way of mastery, acting according to one's desire, then one would go by means of *iddhi*, not by way of karma.
The other, however, in the first part of the inquiry, refers to that which consists of mental cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
He rejects [the first position]. In the second question, he admits it with reference to the power of merit (*puññiddhi*).
In the third discussion, the practice of difficult austerities performed for the sake of exercising power and acting according to one’s own will is categorized as a wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).

Furthermore, the statement beginning with "the world is eternal" is spoken for the purpose of challenging [the opponent] by suggesting that if he were to perform such [austerities], he would also embrace views such as eternalism. The same method applies to the fourth discussion as well.
Commentary on the Discussion of Exercising Authority at Will.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Counterfeits. 915–916.
Now follows what is called the discussion of the counterfeits of lust. Therein, with reference to loving-kindness, compassion, and gladness, [it is said]: "No..."
“Lust is the counterfeit of lust,” and with reference to envy, stinginess, and remorse, “hatred is the counterfeit of hatred,” and with reference to the arousal of laughter,
“delusion is the counterfeit of delusion”; [this was said] regarding the restraint of ill-behaved persons,
the favoring of well-behaved bhikkhus, the censuring of evil, and the praising of what is wholesome, concerning the Venerable Pilindavaccha.

With reference to the doctrine of the outcaste, the doctrine that the Blessed One was a spittle-eater, and the doctrine of the "empty man," as well as the tenet held by some—such as the Andhakas—that "defilement is not like defilement," in all such discussions, the question belongs to one's own side (the proponent) and the admission belongs to the other.
This is because there are no so-called "counterfeits" of contact and the rest that are not actually contact and the rest. Therefore...
In order to challenge the claim that even those things which resemble lust and so forth—namely, non-lust and the rest—do not exist, he says, "Is there no contact? and so on.
The other person rejects this because of the non-existence of those [resemblances]. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on Resemblance.
9. Explanation of the Discussion on the Unestablished (Aparinipphannakathāvaṇṇanā) 917–918.
Now follows the discussion known as "The Unestablished. Therein it is said:
"Only suffering indeed arises; suffering stands and passes away."
"Nothing arises other than suffering; nothing ceases other than suffering.

Relying on this statement, there are those who hold the view that suffering alone is fully established (*pariniṣpanna*), while the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), faculties (*indriya*), and phenomena (*dharma*) are not fully established—such as certain Northerners (*Uttarāpathaka*) and the proponents of Causality (*Hetuvādin*).
Having in mind that "form is unestablished," the proponent of the first position (sakavādī) asks the question, and the other (itarassa) grants the admission.
Then, in order to challenge him with the thought, "If form is unestablished, it could not possess the intrinsic nature of impermanence and so forth," he says, "Form is not impermanent," and so on.
The other, seeing no such form as that [described], rejects it. The proponent of the first position [continues] with the statement, "Is form not impermanent? and so forth.
Having refuted his first tenet, [the Blessed One], asking about the second, said: "Suffering alone is fully established," and so forth.
Then, in order to refute that tenet as well, he said: "Whatever is impermanent... and so forth. Herein, this is the intended meaning:
for it is not only the first Truth (suffering) that is suffering; rather, whatever is impermanent is itself suffering. And form...

It is impermanent; therefore, that too is unconditioned (*pariniṣpanna*). Thus, as for what you say—“Form is unconditioned, while suffering alone is conditioned”—surely you ought not to say, “Suffering alone is conditioned.
This same method applies to the applications beginning with those rooted in feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
However, regarding the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), setting aside...
Nibbāna should be understood as impermanent by way of its relation to all other phenomena. Thus, the faculties are indeed impermanent.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse concerning the unconditioned.
The twenty-third chapter.
The Conclusion:
And to this extent—
by means of four fifties and three sections;
Having compiled all the discourses, numbering one hundred and less than ten,
this commentary on the meaning of the *Kathāvatthu* treatise— which the Conqueror, skilled in the paths of discourse, taught— is now completed.
By whatever merit has been gained by me through compiling this tradition into thirteen recitation sections for the sake of the long endurance of the Dhamma— by that,
may this world, including its humans and devas, [attain happiness].
May [the reader] attain the very flavor of the True Dhamma of the King of Dhamma.
The Commentary on the *Kathāvatthu* is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the *Yamakappakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā* of the *Abhidhammapitaka*: Briefly,
the God of Gods [spoke] to the gods in the abode of the gods;
Having taught the *Kathāvatthu* treatise, he abandoned the defilements.
He who has transcended the realm of Māra, the teacher of the sixth section,
composed the sixth treatise, the *Abhidhamma*, adorned with various methods of reasoning.
This *Yamaka* is a work of the one with dark-blue, stainless body-hair who has arrived;
since it is now the turn for its commentary on that which he taught, therefore this commentary upon it comes forth.
1. The Root Pairs (Mūlayamaka):
Explanation of the Section on Enumeration. 1.
The Root Pairs, the Aggregates Pairs, the Bases Pairs, the Elements Pairs, the Truths Pairs, and the Formations Pairs.

It is said that this treatise is analyzed in ten ways by way of these ten pairs (yamaka): the pair on underlying tendencies (anusaya), the pair on consciousness (citta), the pair on phenomena (dhamma), and the pair on faculties (indriya).
Regarding that, the meaning of the names both for those ten pairs by way of which this treatise is analyzed in ten ways, and for this treatise itself, is as follows:
It should be understood in this way: in what sense is it called a "pair" (*yamaka*)? In the sense of a "pair" (*yugala*).
For a pair is called a "pair" (*yamaka*), as in such expressions as "the Twin Miracle" (*yamakapāṭihāriya*) or "the Twin Sal trees" (*yamakasālā*).
Thus, because they are taught by way of these pairs consisting of dyads, each one among these ten is called a "pair. Furthermore, because of the collective nature of these pairs, all of this—
It should be understood as the *Yamaka* (Pairs) treatise.
Therein, because it was taught by making questions and answers based on the roots, it is first of all called the "Root Yamaka" (*Mūlayamaka*) among the ten [yamakas].

It consists of two sections: the Section of Enumeration (*Uddesavāra*) and the Section of Exposition (*Niddesavāra*). Of these, because they must be explained according to the sequence in which they were enumerated—
The first section on enunciation (*uddesavāra*). Regarding that, the statement: "Whatever states are wholesome, all those have wholesome roots;
or whatever have wholesome roots, all those states are wholesome"—this is the beginning of the *Yamaka* (Pairs).

It is called the "Meaning-Pair" (*atthayamaka*) by way of the two meanings comprised by the wholesome and unwholesome roots; or, it is [the *Yamaka*] by way of those very same meanings, in direct and reverse order.
The nature of the *yamaka* (pairing) should be understood as threefold: either as the *dhammayamaka* (pairing of phenomena) by way of the Dhamma as it occurs in the scriptures;
or as the *pucchāyamaka* (pairing of questions) by way of questions occurring in direct and reverse order. This same method applies to the remaining [sections] as well.

Now, regarding this *Mūlayamaka* taught by way of these *yamas*, first, concerning the section on the enumeration (*uddesavāra*), there is the classification according to the method of the *nayayamaka* (method-pairing), the questions, and the meaning-sections (*atthavāra*).
The establishment of the text should be understood in this way:

based on the initial phrase “wholesome states” in the matrix of the wholesome triad (*kusalattika-mātikā*), there are these four methods—the root method, the root-of-roots method, the rooted method, and the root-of-roots method.
Within each of these methods, there are the root dyads (*mūlayamaka*), the single-root dyads (*ekamūlayamaka*), and the mutual-root dyads (*aññamaññamūlayamaka*).
There are three pairs (yamaka) for each [of the four methods]. Thus, there are twelve pairs in the four methods.
Within each pair, there are two questions by way of positive and negative order, making twenty-four questions in total.
For each question, there are two meanings by way of the conclusion and the doubt, making forty-eight meanings in total.

In this context, regarding the phrase "whatever wholesome states there are," the sense of certainty (*sanniṭṭhāna*) is to be understood in this term, because there is no doubt among wholesome states as to whether they are "wholesome" or "not wholesome.

Regarding the phrase "all those are roots of the wholesome," the sense of doubt (*saṃsaya*) is to be understood in this term, because it is asked by way of inquiry: "Are all those wholesome states roots of the wholesome, or are they not?"
This is to be understood. And this [doubt] was stated for the purpose of illustrating doubt in a matter of doubt for those who are to be trained (*veneyya*);
however, for the Tathāgata, there is no such thing as doubt. This same method applies to the subsequent questions as well.
And just as these four methods are based upon the category of the wholesome (*kusala*), so too within each individual method, there are three pairs of *yamaka*s (twins).
By way of these [three] bases, there are twelve pairs (yamaka). In each pair, by way of two questions each, there are twenty-four questions.
And for each question, by way of two meanings each, there are forty-eight meanings.
It is the same when based on the unwholesome category (akusalapada), and it is the same when based on the indeterminate category (abyākatapada). Thus, all three categories [are treated].
It should be understood that by taking as a basis even the term "name" (*nāmapada*) which was explained by treating [the categories] together, the same applies [to the other terms].

Thus, in the four sections of the Matika of the Wholesome Triplet (*kusalattika*), all sixteen methods (*nayā*), forty-eight pairs (*yamakāni*), ninety-six questions (*pucchā*), and nine hundred and twenty meanings (*atthā*) are stated by way of enumeration.
Up to this point, what is called the "Root Section" (*mūlavāra*) has been first presented.
Following that, nine sections are set forth as synonyms for that same "Root Section" (Mūlavāra), beginning with: "Whatever wholesome states there are, all those have wholesome roots," and so on.

Thus: the Root Section, the Cause Section (Hetuvāra), the Source Section (Nidānavāra), the Origin Section (Sambhavavāra), the Arising Section (Pabhavavāra), the Production Section (Samuṭṭhānavāra), the Nutriment Section (Āhāravāra), the Object Section (Ārammaṇavāra), the Condition Section (Paccayavāra), and the Origination Section (Samudayavāra).
There are ten sections in total. In this regard, since the remaining methods and so forth are to be understood through the same pattern as that presented in the Root Section (Mūlavāra),
it should be understood that across all ten sections there are six hundred methods, four hundred and eighty pairs (yamakas),
nine hundred and sixty questions, and nineteen hundred and twenty topics (atthas) that have been taught.

Thus, first of all, in the section on the summary (uddesa), the establishment of the text (*pāḷivavatthāna*) should be understood by way of the divisions of the method (*naya*), the pairs of questions (*yamaka-pucchā*), and the section on the meaning (*atthavāra*).
The verse beginning "The root, the cause, and the source" is called the summary verse (*uddānagāthā*) for all ten sections.

In that context, "root" (*mūla*) and all the other terms are synonyms for "cause" (*kāraṇa*). For a cause is a "root" in the sense of being a foundation; it is [the basis] for the production of its own fruit.
It is called a *hetu* (cause) because it leads (*hinoti*) and proceeds (*pavattati*). It is called a *nidāna* (source) because it points toward its own fruit as if saying, "Come now, take this!
It is called a *sambhava* (origin) because from it the fruit arises (*sambhoti*). It is called a *pabhava* (source) because it originates (*pabhavati*) [the fruit].

It is called a *samuṭṭhāna* (origination) because the fruit arises therein, or because the fruit arises by means of it. It is called an *āhāra* (nutriment) because it brings forth its own fruit. Because it is not to be rejected...

It is called an *ālambana* because it is that which is taken as an object by its own fruit. It is called a *paccaya* because, depending upon this, the fruit comes into being—that is, it proceeds—without being rejected.
It is called a *samudaya* because from this the fruit arises. In this way, the meaning of these terms should be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the section of the summary.
Commentary on the Section of Exposition (Niddesavāravaṇṇanā) 50.
Now, the section of exposition is commenced by way of the method beginning with "whatever wholesome states," and so forth. Therein, "whatever" is an expression meaning without remainder.
"Wholesome states" refers to those characterized as stated in the word-commentary of the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*), which have blameless and pleasant results.
They have a wholesome nature (*kusalasabhāvā*). "Are they all wholesome roots?"—by this he asks whether they are all exclusively wholesome roots.
"There are only three wholesome roots"—the meaning is that not all of them are wholesome roots; rather, only the three beginning with non-greed (*alobha*) are wholesome roots.
"The remaining wholesome states are not wholesome roots"—this means that the remaining wholesome states, such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth, are not wholesome roots.

They are not [merely] names. Alternatively, the meaning is that the remaining factors, such as contact and so forth, are only wholesome phenomena (*kusala-dhammā*), but they are not themselves wholesome roots (*kusala-mūla*).
Or else, regarding the phrase "those which are wholesome roots": by the second part of the first question, the three beginning with non-greed (*alobha*) are taken as the "wholesome roots.
Are all those phenomena wholesome? That is to say, are all those three phenomena wholesome?
He asks. “Yes,” he says, accepting the wholesome nature of all roots of the wholesome.
This, then, is the meaning of the Root Yamaka according to the method of roots. By this same method, the manner of answering in all the questions is to be understood.
However, wherever there is a specific distinction, that alone we shall explain.

51. First, regarding the "Single Root" (Ekamūla) pair: all those [states] should not be understood as "single-rooted" in the sense of numerical counting—that is, as having one root by way of number—but rather they should be taken in the sense of identity. This is the meaning here: all of them have a common root by way of the wholesome root (*kusalamūla*).
Whatever is the root of contact (*phassa*), that itself is the root of feeling (*vedanā*) and the others. Then, acknowledging their state as such, he addresses them: "Āmantā."
He said: "Arising from the wholesome" (kusalasamuṭṭhāna) indicates material form produced by a wholesome consciousness.

"Having a single root" means having a common root with the wholesome roots such as non-greed and so forth. For just as non-greed and the others are the "roots" of contact and the rest because they serve as their cause-condition (hetupaccaya), so too are they the root of that produced material form;
however, it is not itself wholesome because it lacks the characteristic of wholesomeness.
52. In the *Aññamaññayamaka*, instead of asking "whatever states are wholesome," the question is asked: "Whatever states have a single root by way of a wholesome root. Why?
Because this phrasing also allows for the possibility of that same meaning. The term "wholesome roots" (*kusalamūlāni*) is a qualification of the preceding [term].
For it was stated: "Those roots which arise together"—and these are indeed wholesome roots as well.
This was stated here for the purpose of showing the distinction that even though they are roots of the unwholesome and the indeterminate, they are called "wholesome roots" in this context.
And the phrase "mutually as roots" means that they act as conditions for one another by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*).

Why, in the reverse inquiry concerning that same matter, did it not say, "All those states have a single root in the wholesome root," but instead say, "All those states are wholesome"? [The answer is: because...
Because there is no distinction in meaning. For if the question "Are they of one root by virtue of the wholesome roots?
were asked, the answer would have to be given exactly in the manner stated below—"The roots which arise together"—and in that case, there would be no distinction in meaning.
Therefore, instead of doing it in that way, this question was formulated. By this same method, [the analysis] regarding the mutual roots in the *Mūlamūla-naya* and so forth should also be understood.
The distinction of the questions should be understood.
53–55. In the *Mūlamūla-naya*, he asks: "Are all of them roots of wholesome roots? meaning, "Are all of them roots designated as wholesome roots?
"Having a single root-root" (*ekamūlamūla*) means that they have one and the same root-root in the sense of being identical. "Mutually root-root" (*aññamaññamūlamūla*)...

"Mutually rooted" (*aññamaññamūla*) means the root of one another. "Rooted in mutual roots" (*aññamaññamūlamūla*) means that these have mutual roots as their root in the sense of being a cause-condition (*hetupaccaya*). 56.
In the method of the "rooted" (*mūlaka*), "rooted in wholesome roots" (*kusalamūlaka*) means that these have a wholesome root as their root in the sense of being a cause-condition. 57–61.

In the method of the "rooted in roots" (*mūlamūlaka*), "rooted in wholesome roots" (*kusalamūlamūlaka*) means the root of wholesome states is the "wholesome root. It is precisely in the sense of being a cause-condition.

"Those which have wholesome roots as their root are 'wholesome-rooted' (*kusalamūlamūlaka*). This, first of all, is the specific meaning based on the term "wholesome" (*kusala*) within the questions of the *Nayayamaka*.

62–73. The same method applies to the terms beginning with "unwholesome" (*akusala*). However, this is the distinction: "rootless unwholesome" is stated with reference to delusion (*moha*) associated with doubt (*vicikicchā*) and restlessness (*uddhacca*).
74–85. "Rootless indeterminate" (*ahetukam abyākataṃ*) refers to the eighteen types of consciousness-arising, material form, and Nibbāna. [The compound] "indeterminate-rooted" (*abyākatamūlena*)...
"Not having a single root": here, however, with the exception of matter originated by the rootless indeterminate (*ahetuka-abyākata*), the remainder is obtained.

Matter originated by the rootless indeterminate has a single root in the indeterminate; setting that aside as not being within the scope of this discussion, this answer is given solely by way of what is obtainable from a single [root].
86–97. *Nāmā dhammā* means phenomena designated as "name" (*nāma*). In terms of their actual meaning, these consist of the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*) and Nibbāna.

Regarding "there are exactly nine roots of name": there are nine roots by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate roots. That which is "rootless name" does not share a single root with the [other] roots of name;

thus, all that is rootless consists of the eighteen types of consciousness-arising, together with doubt-accompanied, restlessness-accompanied, and delusion-accompanied consciousness, as well as Nibbāna.

Name and the root of name do not have a single root; for it does not arise together with that [root]. Even in the phrase "name accompanied by a cause [arises] with the root of name," the meaning is "name accompanied by a cause [arises] with the root of name.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout. This concludes the commentary on the section on roots (Mūlavāra).

98–99. The meaning in the sections beginning with the *Hetuvāra* (Cause Section) should also be understood by this same method. The verses beginning with "The root (*mūla*), the cause (*hetu*), and the source (*nidāna*)" have been stated again as a summary (*uddāna*) for all ten sections as they were previously explained.
This concludes the commentary on the Root Pairs (*Mūlayamaka*). 2. The Aggregate Pairs (*Khandhayamaka*).

1. Explanation of the Section on the Enumeration of Designations (Paṇṇatti-uddesa-vāra-vaṇṇanā) Now follows the explanation of the Khandha Yamaka (the Book of Pairs on the Aggregates), which was taught immediately after the Mūla Yamaka (the Root Book of Pairs). In this work, the wholesome and other phenomena already taught in the Mūla Yamaka are here subsumed under the category of aggregates (khandha).
Regarding this, the determination of the textual structure (pāḷi-vavatthāna) should be understood as follows: [The text continues with the formal definitions of the aggregates.]
In this *Khandhayamaka*, there are three major sections: the Section on Designation (*paṇṇattivāra*), the Section on Occurrence (*pavattivāra*), and the Section on Full Understanding (*pariññāvāra*).
Among these, the Section on Designation is so called because it proceeds by way of clarifying the names and designations of the aggregates.
The Section on Occurrence, for its part, clarifies the occurrence of those aggregates—whose names and designations have been clarified by the former—by way of their arising and ceasing.
The Section on Occurrence has been concluded; therefore, it is called the "Section on Occurrence.

The Section on Full Understanding has been concluded by demonstrating, in brief, the three kinds of full understanding regarding the aggregates that occur in this sequence; therefore, it is called the "Section on Full Understanding.
Therein, the Section on Designation is established in two ways: by way of enumeration and by way of exposition. Among the others, there is no separate section for enumeration from the beginning.
From this point on, it is established in a single way by means of questions and answers.

Therein, starting from the phrase "the five aggregates" (*pañcakkhandhā*) and continuing up to the phrase "neither aggregates nor formations" (*na khandhā, na saṅkhārā*), the section on the enumeration of the Section on Designations (*paṇṇattivāra*) should be understood;
its name is also the "Section on Questions" (*pucchāvāra*). Therein, the term "the five aggregates" refers to those things that are to be questioned by way of the *yamaka* (pairing) method.
The enumeration of the aggregates: the aggregate of form … [and so on] … up to the aggregate of consciousness. This is the definition of their names according to their specific divisions.

2–3. Now, by way of these aggregates, there are four sections of method: the section on the purification of terms, the section on the wheel based on the purification of terms, the section on the pure aggregates, and the section on the wheel based on the pure aggregates.
Among these, "form" is the aggregate of form; the aggregate of form is...

Having purified the terms themselves by way of the method beginning with "matter" (rūpa) and so forth, there is the section called the Purification of Terms. That is twofold, according to the direct (anuloma) and reverse (paṭiloma) orders.
Therein, in the direct order, there are five pairs (yamaka), such as: "Matter is the aggregate of matter; the aggregate of matter is matter," and so forth.
In the reverse order as well, there are [pairs] such as: "Not matter, not the aggregate of matter; not the aggregate of matter, not matter," and so forth.

There are exactly five [sections]. Following that is the Section on the Wheel Based on the Purification of Terms (Padasodhanamūlacakkavāra), so called because it proceeds by forming four wheels based on each individual aggregate— such as “matter is the matter-aggregate” and “the aggregates are the feeling-aggregate”—
for those very aggregates that were purified in the section on the purification of terms.
That too is twofold, by way of the direct order (*anuloma*) and the reverse order (*paṭiloma*).
Therein, in the section on the direct order, there are twenty pairs (*yamaka*), four being formed for each of the aggregates as the basis, such as:

“Form is the aggregate of form; the aggregates are the aggregate of feeling,” and so forth. In the section on the reverse order, there are likewise twenty, such as: “Not form, not the aggregate of form; not the aggregates, not the aggregate of feeling,” and so forth.

Following that, the section known as the "Pure Aggregate Section" proceeds by way of the pure aggregates alone, according to the method beginning with “Form is an aggregate; aggregates are form,” and so forth.

In this context, regarding the expressions “aggregates are form” and so on, the meaning to be understood is: “The aggregates are the form aggregate; the aggregates are the feeling aggregate,” and so forth. Why?
Because they are analyzed in this manner in the Explanatory Section (Niddesa-vāra). For there it says: “‘Form is an aggregate,’ yes.”
The aggregates: “The aggregate of form” means that the aggregate of form is both an aggregate and the aggregate of form, while the remaining aggregates are not the aggregate of form.

Thus, by extracting the phrases from “the aggregates are form,” etc., according to the method beginning with “the aggregate of form,” the meaning has been analyzed. For that very reason, this is called the section on the pure aggregates.
For here, as in the *Vacanasodhana*, the mere phrasing is not the authority; rather, the meaning is the authority insofar as pure aggregates are found.

This same method applies to the subsequent sections, such as the *Āyatana-yamaka* and others. Furthermore, this section on pure aggregates is twofold, according to the direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*paṭiloma*) orders.
In that regard, in the direct order, there are such statements as “form is an aggregate” and “aggregates are form,” and so forth.
There are five pairs. In the reverse order as well, there are likewise five, beginning with “Form is not a aggregate; aggregates are not form,” and so forth.
