Following that, by way of the method beginning with “Form is an aggregate; aggregates are feeling,” he proceeds after forming four wheels based on each individual aggregate from among those same pure aggregates. Regarding those based on the pure aggregates:
Because of the presence of the wheels, this is called the “Wheel-Section on the Pure Aggregates.

Therein, regarding the aggregates such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, the meaning should be understood according to the method beginning with “the aggregate of feeling” (*vedanākkhandho*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Section on Exposition (*Niddesavāra*).
That [section] is also twofold, by way of direct order (*anuloma*) and reverse order (*paṭiloma*). Therein, in the direct-order section: “Form... [and so on].
By taking each individual aggregate as the basis, there are four pairs (yamaka) for each—such as "aggregate" and "aggregates," or "feeling" and so forth—making twenty pairs in total.
In the reverse order as well, there are likewise twenty, such as "not form, not aggregate, not aggregates, not feeling," and so on.
Thus, with one hundred pairs and two hundred questions, according to the determination and doubt regarding each question...
Having established two pairs of meanings and being adorned with four hundred meanings, the section on the summary of the Section on Designation (Paṇṇattivāra) should be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the section on the summary of the Section on Designation. 1. Commentary on the Section on the Exposition of Designation (Paṇṇattiniddesavāra).
26. Now, the section on the exposition begins in the manner of "matter is the aggregate of matter" and so forth. Therein, regarding "matter is the aggregate of matter":
whatever is called "matter," all that matter is the aggregate of matter. He asks this for the purpose of clarifying the statement.
As for "lovely matter, pleasant matter, matter, not the aggregate of matter"—here, that which is called "matter" in the phrase "lovely matter, pleasant matter" [is being examined].
That which was stated is matter itself, not the aggregate of matter; this is the meaning.
However, as for that which is the aggregate of matter, it is appropriate to say that it is both matter and the aggregate of matter; this is the meaning.
Regarding the statement "the aggregate of matter is matter," since the aggregate of matter must necessarily be called matter, therefore—
"Commanded," he said. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all the responses. However, where there will be a distinction, we shall explain that specifically.
First, in the *Saññā-yamaka* (Pairs on Perception), "perception of views" refers to the perception of views as it occurs in such passages as "perceptions of proliferation" (*papañca-saññā*).
In the *Saṅkhāra-yamaka* (Pairs on Volitional Formations), "the remaining volitional formations" refers to those in such passages as "Alas, volitional formations are impermanent."
The remaining conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). This same method applies to the reverse order as well.
The Section on the Purification of Terms is finished. 28.

In the Wheel of the Root Section on the Purification of Terms, regarding the statement "the aggregates are the feeling-aggregate" (*vedanākkhandha*): whatever aggregates there may be, are they all the feeling-aggregate?
He asks. This same method applies to the remaining questions as well. Regarding the reverse order, "Are they not aggregates?

Are they not the feeling aggregate?"—here, those phenomena consisting of designations (*paṇṇatti*) and Nibbāna which are not aggregates are, because they are not aggregates, also not the feeling aggregate;
therefore, he says, "Yes. This same method applies to the remaining answers as well.
The Wheel-Section on the Root of Purifying the Categories is finished. 38.
In the Section on Pure Aggregates, it was stated that "whatever is form is an aggregate";
[this section] asks whether all of that is an aggregate. In this regard, whether it be form reckoned as a pleasant form or a gratifying form, or whether it be primary or derived form—
Everything is indeed included within the five aggregates; therefore, he acknowledges it by saying "Yes.

Regarding the second phrase, although one might ask, "Are the aggregates form? since by the word "form" only the aggregate of form is intended, he asks according to the meaning rather than adhering strictly to the phrasing, saying, "Are the aggregates the aggregate of form? Following this same method...
The meaning should be understood in all instances. This same method applies to the subsequent sections on the pairs of bases (*āyatana-yamaka*) and so forth.

Regarding the statement "perception is an aggregate" (*saññā khandho*): whether it be perception consisting of views or perception in its general sense, since all such perceptions possess the nature of an aggregate, it is stated that they are "yes.
The same method applies to the phrase "volitional formations are an aggregate" (*saṅkhārā khandho*); for there is no such thing as a volitional formation apart from the aggregates.
39. In the reverse order, "Is it not matter, is it not an aggregate? asks whether that class of phenomena which is not matter is also not an aggregate.
In the response, however, setting aside matter, the remaining aggregates are not matter;
the meaning is that the aggregates other than matter—namely, feeling and so forth—are indeed aggregates, but they are not matter itself. And matter...
"Excluding the aggregates, the remainder" refers to both Nibbāna and designations (paññatti), which are distinct from the five aggregates.
This same method applies to all subsequent instances where the term "the remainder" occurs.
The section on the pure aggregates is concluded.

40–44. In the section on the Wheel based on the Pure Aggregates (*suddhakhandhamūlacakkavāra*), the meaning of "matter is an aggregate" and so forth should be understood according to the method already explained below.
The section on the Wheel based on the Pure Aggregates is finished. [End of] the commentary on the section on the Exposition of Designations (*paṇṇattiniddesavāravaṇṇanā*).
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra-vaṇṇanā) §§50–205.
Now begins the section on occurrence (*pavattivāra*) according to the method starting with "for whom there is the aggregate of form" (*yassa rūpakkhandho*).

But why is the section on enumeration (*uddesavāra*) not stated here? Because the method has already been shown below. For in the section on enumeration within the section on designations (*paṇṇattivāra*), the method [is as follows]:...

It has been demonstrated. However, since it is possible to understand that [method] here even though it was not explicitly stated, he did not mention it and instead commenced the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*).

In this great section known as the "Section on Occurrence" (*pavattivāra*), there are three intermediate sections: the Section on Arising (*uppādavāra*), the Section on Cessation (*nirodhavāra*), and the Section on Arising and Cessation (*uppādanirodhavāra*).
Among these, the first is called the "Section on Arising" because it demonstrates the characteristic of the arising of phenomena (*dhamma*).
It is so called. The second is called the "Section on Cessation" because it illustrates the characteristic of cessation of those very same phenomena.

The third is called the "Section on Arising and Cessation" because it illustrates the characteristics of both. Furthermore, by the section on arising, only the mode of the arising of phenomena is illustrated;
by the section on cessation, it is shown that "what is called 'arisen' is not permanent. Of those very same [phenomena]...
Impermanence is thus illustrated. By the section on arising and cessation, both of these are shown.
Therein, first, in the section on arising, there are six temporal divisions by way of the three time periods:
the present, the past, the future, the past by means of the present, the future by means of the present, and the future by means of the past. Among these, for that which—
The aggregate of form should be understood as "present" by way of the designation "the aggregate of form arises";
it is stated first because it is extremely easy to understand, since it must be grasped through direct perception regarding present phenomena.
That [aggregate] should be understood as "past" by way of the designation "for whom the aggregate of form arose," since it was previously experienced through direct perception.
The second [type] is stated because the future is more easily understood through inference from past phenomena.
That for which the aggregate of form will arise should be understood as "future" by way of its designation as something yet to come.

The third is stated because it must be grasped through the inference of phenomena already apprehended—both by direct perception and by what was previously experienced—in the thought: "In the future, too, such phenomena will arise."

"For whom the aggregate of form arises, for him the aggregate of feeling has arisen"—this is to be understood as the past by means of the present, through the expression of the past together with the present.
This fourth [formula] is stated because it is more easily understood among the three mixed ones.
"For whom the aggregate of form arises, for him the aggregate of feeling will arise."
The future is to be understood by way of its designation together with the present;
that is stated as the fifth [category] because it is more easily understood in terms of actual fact due to the existence of those phenomena that are to be grasped through direct perception.
"For one in whom the aggregate of form has arisen, the aggregate of feeling will arise"—this is by way of designating the future together with the past.
The future is to be understood by means of the past. That [future] is stated as the sixth because it is difficult to discern by means of the preceding [two].

Thus, among these six divisions of time, regarding this first one—the present—there are three sections: by way of the person (*puggala*), by way of the location (*okāsa*), and by way of both the person and the location (*puggalokāsa*).
Among those, the phrase "of whom" (*yassa*) indicates the arising of the aggregates (*khandhā*) by way of the person.
The Chapter on Persons (*puggalavāra*). “Where” (*yattha*) refers to the Chapter on Location (*okāsavāra*), which demonstrates the arising of the aggregates by way of location.
“In whom and where” (*yassa yattha*) refers to the Chapter on Person and Location (*puggalokāsavāra*), which demonstrates the arising of the aggregates by way of both person and location.

These three chapters, however, having first been demonstrated by way of the direct method (*anulomanaya*), are subsequently demonstrated by way of the inverse method (*paṭilomanaya*). Among them, [the term] “arises” (*uppajjati*)...

The method of direct order (anulomanaya) illustrates arising from the statements: "it has arisen" and "it will arise. The method of reverse order (paṭilomanaya) illustrates non-arising from the statements: "it does not arise," "it has not arisen," and "it will not arise.
In that regard, first, in the present time, according to the method of direct order for the section on persons: "For whom the aggregate of form arises..."
The feeling aggregate arises for him. Or else, for whomsoever the feeling aggregate arises, the form aggregate arises for him.
For whomsoever the form aggregate arises, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, and the consciousness aggregate arise for him.
Or else, for whomsoever the consciousness aggregate arises, the form aggregate arises for him.”

Thus, there are four pairs based on the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*); three pairs based on the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) according to the method beginning with, "For whom the aggregate of feeling arises, for him the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*) arises," and so forth;
two pairs based on the aggregate of perception; and one pair based on the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). Including those not previously mentioned, there are ten pairs.
Among those [questions] based on the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), only the first of the four was answered in full.

The remaining ones were abbreviated for the sake of brevity in the text, as their answers are identical to it. Regarding those based on the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth, the answer is likewise uniform:
“Yes” (*āmantā*). Therefore, those too were abbreviated for the sake of brevity in the text. Thus, these [questions] concern the present time.

It should be understood that in the section on persons (*puggalavāra*), by means of the single-pair exposition (*ekayamaka-vissajjana*) within the method of direct order (*anulomanaya*), ten pairs are effectively expounded.
And just as there are ten in the section on persons, so too there are ten in the section on bases (*okāsavāra*), and ten in the section on persons and bases (*puggalokāsavāra*);

thus, in the three sections concerning the present time, there are thirty pairs in the method of direct order. And just as it is in the method of direct order, [so it is in the method of reverse order].
In the same way for the reverse order as well, there are sixty pairs (yamaka) in the present time.
Among these, it should be understood that there are one hundred and twenty questions and two hundred and forty meanings.

Thus, in each of the remaining five divisions of time, there are six sections based on the distinctions of persons and so forth, according to the direct and reverse orders. In each section, there are ten [questions].

"Having made sixty sets of six pairs" means three hundred pairs. Together with the previous ones, these amount to three hundred and sixty pairs, seven hundred and twenty questions, fourteen hundred and forty meanings.
This, first of all, is the determination of the text in the section on arising (*uppādavāra*). And just as it is in the section on arising, so it is also in the section on cessation (*nirodhavāra*).

Regarding the sections on arising and cessation: in every major section on the course of existence (*pavattimahāvāra*), it should be understood that there are eighty thousand pairs of questions, two thousand six hundred questions, and four thousand two hundred and thirty questions.
However, in the Pāḷi, within the sections on arising and cessation, for each respective section among the three unmixed divisions of time:

Having answered each pair (yamaka) individually, [the others] are abbreviated. Among the three mixed temporal divisions, even in those cases rooted in the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-khandha) and so forth—such as “for whom the aggregate of feeling arises, for him the aggregate of perception (saññā-khandha) has arisen”—one pair is answered according to this method.
However, in the section on arising and cessation (uppādanirodha-vāra), that [pair] is indeed answered across all six temporal divisions.

The remaining [questions] are abbreviated because their answers are identical to those already given. This concludes the determination of the textual structure (*pāḷi-vavatthāna*) for the entire Great Chapter on Occurrence (*pavatti-mahāvāra*).
However, for the purpose of analyzing the meaning (*attha-vinicchaya*), the following characteristic should be understood:
in this Great Chapter on Occurrence, five answers to four questions are inserted into twenty-seven places, and therein the analysis of the meaning is carried out.
It should be understood. In this context, there are four types of questions:

the preliminary question (*purepañha*), the subsequent question (*pacchāpañha*), the complete question (*paripuṇṇapañha*), and the futile question (*moghapañha*). For in each pair (*yamaka*), there are two questions; and for each question, there are two phrases.
Among these, in the answer to whichever question the arising or the cessation of the aggregate (*khandha*) mentioned by a single phrase is obtained—

This is called a "prior question" (purepañha). However, that question by which, in its answer, the arising or the cessation of the aggregates grasped by both terms is obtained, this is called a "subsequent question" (pacchāpañha).
Furthermore, that question by which, in its answer, the arising or the cessation of the aggregate grasped by even a single term [is obtained], or of the aggregates grasped by both terms...
That for which an affirmation or an obtaining is found is called a "complete question" (*paripuṇṇapañha*).

However, that question for which, in its answer, a negation or a prohibition is found is called a "vain question" (*moghapañha*). Since this [vain question] cannot be understood unless it is shown, we shall therefore demonstrate it.

Regarding the question, “Where the aggregate of form does not arise, there the aggregate of feeling does not arise,” in this answer, “it arises,” the arising of the aggregate of feeling—which was already included by that single phrase—is obtained;
thus, this and other such questions are to be understood as *purepañha* (simple questions). “For whom the aggregate of form...”
However, regarding the question, “If for one [a consciousness] had arisen, did his aggregate of feeling arise?”— in this response,
“Yes,” the arising in the past of whichever being it may be of the material and feeling aggregates included by those two terms is obtained.
Thus, this and other questions of a similar nature should be understood as *pacchāpañha* (subsequent questions).
Regarding this first question, "Does the aggregate of feeling arise for one in whom the aggregate of form arises?",
in this response beginning with "For those being reborn among the non-percipient beings," in this section it is stated: "For those being reborn among the non-percipient beings,
the aggregate of form arises, but the aggregate of feeling does not arise for them."
The arising of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), which is included by a single term alone, is obtained.

In this section—“For those being reborn in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra*), their aggregate of form arises and their aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) arises”—the arising of both the aggregates of form and feeling, which are included by two terms, is also obtained. Thus, this and another...
A question of this kind should be understood as a "complete question" (*paripuṇṇapañho*). "A question of before and after" (*purepacchāpañho*) is also a name for this very same type.
For in its answer, in the first section, only the arising of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), which is comprised by a single term, is shown;

whereas in the second section, the arising of the aggregates of form and feeling (*rūpavedanākkhandhā*), which are comprised by two terms, is shown. And it is by this very characteristic [that it is so called].
Where the arising or the cessation of an aggregate included by a single term is obtainable,
that is called a "prior question. Where the arising or the cessation of aggregates included by even two terms is obtainable,
that is called a "subsequent question."
Regarding the question, “For whom the aggregate of form did not arise, for that person did the aggregate of feeling not arise?”—
in this answer, “No,” a negation is obtained. Regarding the question, “For whom the aggregate of form arises,
for that person does the aggregate of feeling cease?”— in this answer, “No,” a prohibition is obtained.
Therefore, this twofold question and others of a similar kind should be understood as "vain questions" (*moghapañha*). They are also called "empty questions" (*tucchapañha*).
Thus, first of all, the four types of questions should be understood. [The four ways of answering are:

answering by following the sequence of the text (*pāḷigatiyā*), answering with a counter-question (*paṭivacanavissajjanaṃ*), answering by showing the actual form (*sarūpadassanena*), and answering by way of negation (*paṭikkhepena*).

These five types of answers—namely, the categorical answer, the analytical answer, the answer by way of a counter-question, the answer by way of a refutation, and the answer by way of setting aside—are what are called "answers.
Among these, that answer which, being the very words of the text (*pāḷi*), explains the meaning is called an "answer according to the course of the text" (*pāḷigatiyā vissajjana*).
That is found in the "Prior Questions" (*purepañha*). For example: "Where the aggregate of form does not arise, there the aggregate of feeling [does not arise]."
For in the question, "Does it not arise?", the answer "It arises" proceeds by answering the meaning while remaining as the very words of the text (*pāḷipada*).
Therefore, in such instances, the answer should be understood as following the course of the text.
However, that answer which answers the meaning by way of a direct response is called an "answering-response" (*paṭivacanavissajjana*). That [occurs] in the subsequent question.

It is so. For regarding the question, "Has the aggregate of feeling arisen for one for whom the aggregate of form arose?", this answer, "Yes," has proceeded by answering the meaning through the very act of providing a reply;
therefore, in such instances, it should be understood as an answer given by way of a direct response (*paṭivacanavissajjana*). As for that answer which is [given] in its own form...
Having shown [the question], it provides the answer; this is called an answer by way of showing the specific form (*sarūpadassana*).
This is found in the case of a complete question. For instance, regarding the question: "In whom does the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) arise?

In him does the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) arise?"—this answer, "In those being reborn as non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*)," indicates that "in these [beings] the aggregate of form arises..."

And when it is asked, "Does the aggregate of form arise for one for whom the aggregate of feeling does not arise?", the answer proceeds by providing an illustration through a similar case (*sarūpadassana*), resolving the meaning as follows: "For such a person, both the aggregate of form and the aggregate of feeling arise.
Therefore, in such instances, the answer should be understood as being given by means of an illustration through a similar case.
However, as for that answer which—due to the non-existence of such a thing—resolves the question by way of a negation of the object (*atthapaṭikkhepa*):

To answer by way of negation is what is called an answer by rejection (*paṭikkhepena vissajjana*). When one answers a question by denying the existence of a matter because such a thing cannot be obtained at a single moment, this is called an answer by denial (*paṭisedhena vissajjana*).
This is found in the "Futile Questions" (*moghapañha*): "For whom the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) had not arisen, for him the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) had not arisen?"

For this question, the answer is “it does not exist”; since it answers the question by negating the meaning—that is, by stating that no such being exists—one should understand that in such instances the answer is given by way of negation.
However, for the question, “Does the feeling aggregate cease for one in whom the form aggregate arises? the answer is “no.”
This answer proceeds by answering the question through the negation of the underlying meaning— that in a single moment of rebirth-linking, cessation cannot be found together with arising;
therefore, in such instances, the answer should be understood as one given by way of negation.
Now, these four questions and these five answers must be inserted into twenty-seven places;
they should be understood as follows: "beings reborn in the non-percipient realm" is one place;
"among those non-percipient beings there" is one; "of the non-percipient beings" is one; "beings passing away from the non-percipient realm" is one.
One [case] for those being reborn in the formless realm (*arūpa*); one for "there, in the formless realm" (*tattha*); one for "the formless ones" (*arūpānaṃ*);

one for those passing away from the formless realm; one for those having their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) in the formless realm; one for those attaining final nibbāna (*parinibbāyanta*) in the formless realm;
and one for those who, having been reborn in the formless realm, will attain final nibbāna; and one for those being reborn in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra*). In the five-aggregate realm...

"Among them": one [refers to] "those in the five-aggregate realm"; one [refers to] "those passing away from the five-aggregate realm"; one [refers to] "those in their final existence in the five-aggregate realm";
one [refers to] "those attaining final nibbāna in the five-aggregate realm"; one [refers to] "those being reborn in the Suddhāvāsa [heaven]";
one [refers to] "among them in the Suddhāvāsa"; one [refers to] "those in the Suddhāvāsa"; one [refers to] "those attaining final nibbāna in the Suddhāvāsa"; [this applies] to all of them.
"Of those being reborn" is one [category]; "of all those passing away" is one; "of those in their final existence by way of commonality to all" is one;
"of those attaining Parinibbāna" is one; "of those being reborn in the fourfold or fivefold [planes of existence]" is one;
and "of those passing away" is one. Thus, these five answers to these four questions [are contained] within these twenty-seven [categories].

Having inserted [the relevant terms] into their respective places, the determination of the meaning (*atthavinicchaya*) should be understood within this Great Chapter on Occurrence (*pavattimahāvāra*).
For when one who answers a question understands it thus, the answer is well-given; and when one determines the meaning, it is well-determined.
Herein, this is the method: "For whom the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) arises" refers to that person who possesses the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*).
The aggregate of form arises. He asks: "Does the aggregate of feeling arise for him? meaning that the aggregate of feeling also arises for him at that very same moment.
"For those being reborn among the non-percipient beings" means for those being reborn into the state of non-percipient beings by way of a mindless rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"For them, the aggregate of form arises" means that for them, the aggregate of form arises with absolute certainty.
It indeed arises. During the course of existence (pavatta), for those who have arisen, the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) both arises and ceases;
therefore, instead of saying "of non-percipient beings," it is said "of those being reborn as non-percipient beings. Yet, for them, the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) does not arise;
because they are without consciousness, the aggregate of feeling does not arise at all. This is the first of the twenty-seven positions.

In this context, for one whose question is complete, the answer is given by showing the actual form of the preceding section. "For those being reborn in the five-aggregate realm" means for those being reborn in existence consisting of the five aggregates by way of rebirth-linking that is a mixture of the material and immaterial.
For them, both the aggregate of material form and the aggregate of feeling arise; thus, for them, the aggregates known as material form and feeling arise invariably.
Two aggregates indeed arise [there]. However, during the course of existence (*pavatta*), those aggregates that have arisen therein both arise and cease;
therefore, instead of saying "of those belonging to the five-aggregate realm," it is said "for those being reborn into the five-aggregate realm.

The answer. By this method, all answers are to be understood.

But what is the authority for the fact that arising and cessation were not mentioned here in the context of the process of existence (pavatti)? It is the Canon itself. For in the Canon:

There is an extremely authoritative proof for the fact that cessation is nameless.

For, at the moment of the dissolution of the death-consciousness of those attaining final Nibbāna in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa), there is no possibility of counting the aggregates of perception that had arisen and ceased during the course of existence starting from rebirth-linking.
Even so, it is impossible to reach a definitive conclusion that "the aggregate of perception did not cease for them there."
It should be understood that because it exists as something already arisen, cessation is not included in the process [of arising].

Thus, having understood the characteristic of necessity regarding arising and cessation here, one should understand the determination of the meaning of the answers given in various places by taking only rebirth-arising and only death-cessation. That...

Having fully demonstrated the meaning of the decisions,

Since the sequence of answering the questions has already been explained in detail here,
