"The remaining is cessation" refers to cessation by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-nirodha*), suppression (*vikkhambhana-nirodha*), eradication (*samuccheda-nirodha*), and tranquilization (*paṭippassaddhi-nirodha*).
And there is the cessation through momentary dissolution. The remainder is the path;
thus [the texts] speak of "at that time there is a fivefold path, an eightfold path, a wrong path, a pedestrian path, a cart path," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the section on designations (paṇṇattivāra).
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra-vaṇṇanā) 27–164.
Now, regarding the positive method (anulomanaya) of the Person Chapter (puggalavāra) within this Section on Occurrence, concerning the present time:
"For whom the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) arises, for him the truth of the origin (samudayasacca) arises; or else, for whom the truth of the origin arises..."

"the truth of suffering arises for him. Having taken both what is obtainable and what is not obtainable from among the three [yamakas] based on the truth of suffering, the two based on the truth of the origin, and the one based on the truth of cessation, there should be six yamakas according to the text.
Among these, since neither arising nor cessation is applicable to cessation, therefore...
Three pairs (yamakas) are presented: two based on the truth of suffering together with the truths of origin and the path; and one based on the truth of origin together with the truth of the path.
This same method applies to its reverse order as well, and to the sections on the bases (okāsavāra) and so forth.
Thus, in all these sections, the enumeration of the pairs should be understood by way of three pairs each.

In this *Atthavinicchaya*, however, the following is the characteristic: in the section on the process of occurrence (*pavattivāra*) for this *Saccayamaka*, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) is simply not found at all.
Among the remaining three truths, the truths of origin (*samudayasacca*) and the path (*maggasacca*) are found exclusively within the process of occurrence.
The truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), however, is found both in the process of occurrence and in the moments of death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-paṭisandhi*). As for the present and so forth...
Three times are obtainable with respect to both death and rebirth-linking, as well as the course of existence.
Thus, the analysis of the meaning here should be understood according to whatever is applicable in each case.
Herein, this is the key to the method: "of all those who are being reborn" includes even those in the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), for they too...

They arise by means of the truth of suffering alone. The phrase "of a consciousness dissociated from craving" is stated for the purpose of showing the arising of one portion within both the truth of suffering and the truth of origin.
Therefore, it should be understood specifically in terms of the fivefold plane (pañcavokāra).
However, in the fourfold plane (catuvokāra), at the moment of the arising of a fruit-attainment consciousness dissociated from craving, not even a single truth [arises].

It does not arise. This [case] is not to be included here. Regarding the phrase "and their truth of suffering" (*dukkhasaccaṃ*): this was said with reference to the fact that at that moment, with the exception of craving (*taṇhā*), the remainder is called the truth of suffering. The same principle applies to the moment of the arising of the Path (*magga*).
However, in that case, matter (*rūpa*) alone is called the truth of suffering; the remaining factors associated with the Path are not.

They are dissociated from truth. For that very reason it is said: "In the immaterial realm, at the moment of the arising of the path, the truth of the path arises for them, but the truth of suffering does not arise for them.

For all those being reborn, and during the course of existence at the moment of the arising of a consciousness dissociated from craving—therein, meaning at that moment of rebirth, or at the moment of the arising of a consciousness dissociated from craving for them.
Thus, in this context, the occasion should be understood by way of moments. This same method applies to other such cases as well.

"Of those who have not fully realized" means of beings who have not attained the full realization (abhisamaya) consisting in the penetration of the Four Truths. "Of those who have fully realized" means of those who have realized the Truths.
By means of this introductory method, the determination of the meaning should be understood in all instances.
Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra-vaṇṇanā). 3.

Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra-vaṇṇanā) 165–170. In the Section on Full Understanding, there are three types: full understanding as the known (ñātapariññā), full understanding by scrutinization (tīraṇapariññā), and full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā). Herein...
Full understandings are obtained. However, since there is no such thing as full understanding regarding supramundane states, only two truths are included here.
Among them, the statement "he fully understands the truth of suffering" is said by way of the full understandings of knowing and scrutinizing.

The statement "he abandons the truth of the origin" is by way of the full understanding of abandoning what has been known. Thus, the meaning in all instances should be understood by way of these full understandings.
The commentary on the section on full understanding is finished. The commentary on the Twin Verses on the Truths is completed.
6. The Twin Verses on Formations (Saṅkhārayamaka).
1. Commentary on the Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra-vaṇṇanā) 1.
Now follows the commentary on the "Yamaka on Formations" (Saṅkhārayamaka), which was taught immediately after the "Yamaka on Truths.
This section consists of a summary of a portion of those wholesome and other phenomena taught in the "Root Yamaka," arranged according to how they are applicable. Within this [section], too:

The three great sections beginning with the Section on Designation (Paṇṇattivāra), as well as the remaining subdivisions beginning with the Intermediate Section (Antaravāra), are to be understood in the same manner as explained below.
However, there is this distinction here: first, in the Section on Designation, just as the aggregates and other phenomena were enumerated below—“Form is the aggregate of form;
the eye is the eye-base; the eye is the eye-element; suffering... [and so forth].

The section on the purification of the terms beginning with “the truth of suffering” has commenced. Instead of commencing in that manner, first the three formations were analyzed and shown by way of the statement:

“In-breathing and out-breathing are bodily formations. In this context, the formation of the body is the “bodily formation. [As it is said: “In-breathing and out-breathing are bodily; these states are bound up with the body.”
According to this explanation, because it is the result of the kamma-born body which serves as its cause, it is called "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).
Another method: it is called a "formation" (*saṅkhāra*) because it is formed (*saṅkhariyati*). By what is it formed? By the body.
For this [breath] is formed by the kamma-born body, just as air is formed by a bellows; thus, it is a formation of the body, hence "bodily formation. By the body...

The meaning is: what is the wind of inhalation and exhalation? Furthermore, according to the statement, “Friend Visākha, it is after first thinking and pondering that one subsequently breaks forth into speech;

therefore, initial application and sustained application are the verbal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*). It is called a *saṅkhāra* because it forms (*saṅkharoti*). What does it form? Speech. It is a verbal formation because it is a formation by means of speech. [It is so called] because it originates the breaking forth of speech.

This is the name for the pair consisting of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). Furthermore, because of the statement, “Perception and feeling—these mental states are bound to the mind,” it is also conditioned by the third factor; thus, it is a *saṅkhāra*. By what is it conditioned? By the mind.

Having used the genitive case in the sense of the instrument, it is called "mental formation" (*cittasaṅkhāra*), meaning the formation of the mind. [This applies] to all those things originated by the mind.

This is a designation for mental states (*cetasika-dhamma*). However, because initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) have been taken separately due to their nature as verbal formations (*vacī-saṅkhāra*), it is said: "excluding initial application and sustained application. 2–7.

Now begins the section on the purification of the terms "body" (*kāya*) and "bodily formation" (*kāya-saṅkhāra*). In its forward order (*anuloma-naya*), there are three [sub-sections], and in its reverse order (*paṭiloma-naya*)...
"Three" refers to the six pairs (*yamaka*). In the section on the Wheel of the Root-Analysis of Words (*padasodhanamūlacakkavāra*), there are twelve pairs:

six in the forward order and six in the reverse order, each consisting of two [formulations] based on each individual formation (*saṅkhāra*). However, in the section on Pure Formations (*suddhasaṅkhāravāra*), as in the sections on the Pure Aggregates (*suddhakhandhavāra*) and so forth, it is stated:
"Form is an aggregate, aggregates are form; the eye is a base (*āyatana*), bases are the eye," and so on.
The pairs (yamakāni) are stated according to this method. Thus, instead of saying "the body is a formation; formations are the body," it is said in the manner of "bodily formation, verbal formation;

verbal formation, bodily formation," and so forth. In this way, there are three in the direct order—two based on the bodily formation and one based on the verbal formation—and three in the reverse order;
thus, there are six in total in the section on the pure (suddhika-vāra).
The pairs (yamakāni) have been stated. For what reason? Because there is no meaning [to be derived] by way of individual, pure terms.

For instance, in the *Khandha-yamaka* and other such works, since it is intended to refer to aggregates distinguished by form and so forth, as well as bases and so forth distinguished by the eye and so forth, one finds expressions such as "form is an aggregate" (*rūpaṃ khandho*), "an aggregate is form" (*khandhā rūpaṃ*), "the eye is a base" (*cakkhu āyatanaṃ*), and "a base is the eye" (*āyatanā cakkhū*) by way of individual, pure terms.
There is a distinct meaning [in such cases]. Likewise, here there is no such thing as "the body is a formation" or "formations are the body.
Rather, by both terms, "body-formation" (*kāya-saṅkhāra*), only one single meaning is obtained.

Because there is no such meaning when using the simple individual terms "inhalation" or "exhalation," it was not stated as "the body is a formation" or "formations are the body. [The phrase] "the body is a body-formation," etc., [is used instead].
However, it might be said [that this is incorrect]. That too is not tenable, because the formations intended here have not been included by means of the terms "body," "speech," and "mind.
For this is the section on pure formations (*suddhasaṅkhāra-vāra*). In the purification of terms (*padasodhana*), however, a word is considered tenable even without its specific meaning;
thus, that method was adopted there. But here, [the distinction is made] between bodily formation and speech-formation, etc., and between speech-formation...

Because the mental formations and so forth are other than the bodily formations and so forth, and the bodily formations are other than the verbal formations and so forth, there are six pairs (yamakas) formed by taking each formation as a basis and making two for each—namely, "bodily formation is verbal formation" and "verbal formation is bodily formation.
Among these, by including what was not previously mentioned, only three are obtained. Therefore, in order to show those very ones:

Six pairs have been stated: three for the direct order (*anulomana*) and three for the reverse order (*paṭilomana*). However, the section on the wheel based on the root of pure formations (*suddhasaṅkhāramūlacakkavāra*) is not included here.
Thus should the section on the summary (*uddesavāra*) of the section on the formal definitions (*paṇṇattivāra*) be understood.

In the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*), first regarding the direct order (*anuloma*): since it is not only the body and so forth that are the names for bodily formations and so forth, [the following applies].
Therefore, the negation "no" is employed. In the reverse order, "neither body nor bodily formation":

he asks whether that which is not the body is also not the bodily formation. "Bodily formation, not body, bodily formation": the meaning is that the bodily formation is not the body, yet it is precisely this [same thing] that is the bodily formation.
"The remainder": it is not merely the other two formations that remain; rather, [it refers to] that which is distinct from the bodily formation.
But all the rest—the entire range of phenomena (dhamma) classified as conditioned, unconditioned, and conceptual—is neither body nor bodily formation;
by this method, the meaning should be understood in all the subsequent answers.
This concludes the commentary on the section on designations (paṇṇattivāra).
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) 19.
Now, in this Section on Occurrence, regarding the Positive Method (anulomanaya) of the Chapter on Persons (puggalavāra) during the present time:
"In one for whom bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) arises, does verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra) arise?"—there are two [questions] based on bodily formation, and [one] based on verbal formation.

In the "one" [section], only three pairs (yamakas) are obtained; these alone are taken up. This same method applies to the reverse order as well, and also to the section on the bases (okāsavāra), etc.
Thus, here in all the sections, the enumeration of the pairs should be understood by way of three pairs in each.
However, regarding the determination of the meaning (atthavinicchaya) here, this is the characteristic: for in this *Saṅkhārayamaka*, [regarding] "in-breaths and out-breaths..."

From such statements as, "at the moment of arising of applied thought and sustained thought," it should be understood that the distinction of time—present and so forth—is to be taken by way of occurrence (*pavatti*), and not solely by way of death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-patisandhi*).

Furthermore, from statements such as, "in the second jhāna, in the third jhāna, there the bodily formation arises," it should be known that even the jhāna is included by way of its sphere (*okāsa*). Thus, herein, whatever...
The determination of the meaning should be understood according to each respective case that is obtained.
Herein, this is the methodological introduction: "without applied thought and sustained thought" is said with reference to the second and third jhānas.
"Of those" means of those possessing the second and third jhānas. "Of sense-sphere beings" means of beings arisen in the sense sphere. "Of fine-material-sphere deities."
However, there are no in-breaths and out-breaths [in the formless realm]. For those in the formless sphere, material form itself does not exist.

The phrase "without in-breaths and out-breaths" is stated with reference to the arising of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) in beings reborn in the realms of form and formlessness.

21. Regarding "in the first jhāna of the sense-sphere": this refers to the first jhāna that has arisen on the plane of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-bhūmi*). It is [said] by way of the mere factors (*aṅga*).

And here, the first jhāna is to be understood, not only by way of absorption (appanā). For even in a state of mind that has not reached absorption—namely, a mind accompanied by initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra)—these two formations certainly arise.

Regarding the phrase "at the moment of the mind's dissolution": this is stated because the bodily formation is exclusively originated by the mind. For it is the mind *while arising* that originates either material or immaterial phenomena, not the mind while dissolving.

37. "When the second consciousness of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) is occurring" means when the second life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness [following] rebirth-linking is occurring. Granted, this would not arise for them even while the rebirth-linking consciousness itself is occurring;
however, this was stated in order to show that it certainly does not arise as long as the resultant consciousness continues in uninterrupted succession.
Or else, [it refers to] by means of the resultant consciousness of whichever jhāna...
They have been reborn; that which arises even for a hundred or a thousand [beings] is the very first consciousness.

However, the second consciousness—the adverting consciousness (āvajjana-citta) prompted by the desire for existence (bhava-nikanti)—is dissimilar to the resultant consciousness (vipāka-citta). It should be understood that this was said with reference to that [second consciousness].
44. "Of those endowed with the final consciousness" means of those who are possessed of the absolute final consciousness, which does not lead to rebirth-linking (appaṭisandhika-citta).

"Of those whose taints are destroyed. "The final consciousness is without initial application and sustained application" is stated with reference to the death-consciousness of the fine-material sphere belonging to the second jhāna, and the death-consciousness of the immaterial sphere belonging to the fourth jhāna. "Of them" refers to those such as the possessors of the final consciousness. 79.
Regarding the statement, "For whom bodily formation ceases, for him mental formation ceases," here it is a matter of necessity.
"Yes," is the reply given because the bodily formation ceases at the same moment as the mental formation. But it is not so for the mental formation with respect to the bodily formation. Why?
Because the mental formation arises and ceases even without the bodily formation; however, the bodily formation is originated by the mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*).

The air of inhalation and exhalation is derived matter produced by consciousness. Having arisen at the moment of the arising of consciousness, it persists until sixteen other moments of consciousness have arisen; it ceases together with the very last of those sixteen.
Thus, from the moment it arises together with a particular consciousness, it ceases together with the seventeenth [consciousness].
It ceases. It does not cease at the moment of arising or the moment of presence of any consciousness, nor does it arise at the moment of presence or the moment of dissolution.
This is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of mind-originated matter; thus, it is stated that "yes," because it necessarily ceases in the same moment as the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*).
As for what is [stated] in the Sinhalese commentary on the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*:
It was stated that “matter originated by consciousness ceases at the moment of arising of the seventeenth consciousness,” but this contradicts the following canonical text.
Furthermore, since the canonical text is more authoritative than the commentary, what is stated in the canon alone is the valid authority. 128.
Regarding the statement, “For whom bodily formation arises, for him vocal formation ceases”: herein, because bodily formation...
At the moment of the arising of consciousness, it arises, yet at that very moment, applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) do not cease; therefore, the negation "no" is employed.

By this methodological approach, the determination of the meaning should be understood in all instances. The section on full understanding (*pariññāvāra*) remains as it was previously. This concludes the commentary on the section on occurrence (*pavattivāra*).
The commentary on the *Saṅkhāra-yamaka* is finished.
7. The *Anusaya-yamaka*:
Commentary on the Section of Enumeration Distinguished by the Divisions.
1. Now follows the commentary on the meaning of the *Anusaya Yamaka* (the Book of Latent Tendencies), which is taught immediately after the *Saṅkhāra Yamaka*.

In this regard, having first summarized a portion of those wholesome and other phenomena already taught in the *Mūla Yamaka* according to how they occur, the textual arrangement (*pāḷivavatthāna*) of this *Anusaya Yamaka* must be understood. For in this *Anusaya Yamaka*, as in the *Khandha Yamaka* and others—
Without teaching it in that manner, the exposition of the text was presented by another method. How so?

First, in order to cause the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) to be grasped through three modes—namely, by way of delimitation (*pariccheda*), enumeration (*uddesa*), and the place of origin (*uppattiṭṭhāna*)—three sections were taught:

the section on delimitation, the section on the enumerated delimitation, and the section on the place of origin. Then, by way of the seven great sections (*mahāvāra*), regarding the underlying tendencies...
Having thus joined [the factors], the teaching on the pairs (*yamakadesanā*) was given.

In this context, the section titled "The Section on Delimitation" (*paricchedavāra*) is so called because the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are taught by delimiting them through a numerical boundary, stating: "There are exactly seven beings, neither more nor less.

The passage beginning with "the underlying tendency to sensual lust" (*kāmarāgānusayo*) and ending with "the underlying tendency to ignorance" (*avijjānusayo*) provides the mere names for those [tendencies] already delimited by the section on delimitation.
Because they are taught by specifying, “These indeed are those,” it is called the section on the specification of the delimited.

Because it is taught that “the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies here... pe ... the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies here,” thus showing, “In these specific places these underlying tendencies underlie,” it is called the section on the locus of arising.
Now, regarding those seven great sections by means of which the Twin Exposition was formulated in connection with the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), their names are as follows:

the Section on Underlying Tendencies, the Section on Possessing Underlying Tendencies, the Section on Abandoning, the Section on Full Understanding, the Section on Having Abandoned, the Section on Arising, and the Section on Elements.
Among these, the first is the Section on Underlying Tendencies. It is twofold, according to the methods of direct and reverse order.

In that regard, within the method of conformity (*anulomanaya*), there are three intermediate sections based on the person (*puggala*), the object (*okāsa*), and both together, according to the formula: "In whom it underlies, in what it underlies, and in whom and in what it underlies.

Among these, in the first section concerning the person: "In whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) underlies, in him the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) underlies;
or else, in whom the underlying tendency of aversion underlies, in him the underlying tendency of sensual lust..."

"It underlies [the mind]; in one in whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance underlie.
Or else, in one in whom the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies, the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies.
These are the six pairs based on the underlying tendency to sensual lust. Again, by way of including what was not previously included:

There are five rooted in the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), four rooted in the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), three rooted in the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), two rooted in the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*), and one rooted in the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*).

Thus, all twenty-one [types] have a single root. Furthermore, there are those mentioned as: "In whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion both underlie."
There are five based on dyads, four based on triads, three based on tetrads, two based on pentads, and one based on a hexad;
thus there are another fifteen. Together with the previous twenty-one, there are thirty-six pairs in the section on persons (*puggalavāra*).
Likewise in the section on bases (*okāsavāra*), and likewise in the section on persons and bases (*puggalokāsavāra*).

In the method of direct order (*anulomanaya*), there are one hundred and eight pairs (*yamaka*). Likewise in the method of reverse order (*paṭilomanaya*), there are two hundred and sixteen pairs in the section on underlying tendencies (*anusaya*);
from that, the questions are double, and the meanings are to be understood as double again. And just as it is here, so it is for these [sections]:
the section on underlying tendencies, the section on abandoning, the section on full understanding, the section on what has been abandoned, and the section on arising.

In each of the five sections, there is a calculation based on pairs (*yamaka*). It should be understood that the questions are double the number of the pairs, and the meanings are double the number of the questions.
However, here is the distinction regarding the first three sections:
in the section on the bases (*okāsa*), instead of saying "wherever" (*yattha tattha*), the teaching is given using the ablative case, "whence" (*yato tato*). The rest is exactly the same.
Furthermore, this final section on the elements (*dhātu-vāra*) is established in two parts: the section of questions (*pucchā-vāra*) and the section of answers (*vissajjana-vāra*).

In its section of questions, after stating, "one who has passed away from the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and is being reborn in the sense-sphere element," it does not say, "or one who is being reborn in the sense-sphere element and has passed away from the sense-sphere element. What is the reason? Because there is no difference in meaning.

For these two questions have indeed the same meaning; therefore, after asking each single question from each pair of dyads, at the conclusion of all the questions, the answer was given according to the sequence of the questions itself, in the manner beginning with:
"In one who passes away from the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) and is reborn in the sense-sphere realm, do seven underlying tendencies (anusaya) underlie? and so forth.

In that regard, there are six pure questions: “For one who has passed away from the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) and is being reborn in the sense-sphere realm, the fine-material-sphere realm (rūpadhātu), the immaterial-sphere realm (arūpadhātu), the non-sense-sphere realm, the non-form-sphere realm, or the neither-form-nor-non-form-sphere realm”;

and “for one being reborn in the non-sense-sphere realm, the non-form-sphere realm, the non-fine-material-sphere realm; the non-form-sphere realm, the non-sense-sphere realm, or the non-fine-material-sphere realm.”
Including the three mixed questions, there are nine positive (anuloma) questions rooted in the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*).

Likewise, there are nine rooted in the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*) and nine rooted in the immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*), making twenty-seven positive questions in total. Similarly, there are twenty-seven negative (paṭiloma) questions rooted in "not the sense-sphere element," "not the immaterial element," and "not the non-immaterial element.
Furthermore: "Not in the sense-sphere element, not in the immaterial element, not in the fine-material element, not in the non-immaterial element..."
“Not in the sense-sphere realm, nor in the form-sphere realm”—these are twenty-seven questions based on the dyads.

When all are combined, there are eighty-one questions. The answers are given here according to these [questions]. This is the establishment of the text (*pāḷivavatthāna*) for the Section on Elements (*dhātuvāra*).
In this way, the establishment of the text for the entire *Anusaya-yamaka* (Duality of Latent Dispositions) should be understood.
From the beginning, however, wherever anything remains unclear, this is the analytical discussion on those points:
In what sense are they called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*)? In the sense of lying latent (*anusayana*). What is this so-called sense of lying latent? It is the sense of being unabandoned.
For it is in the sense of being unabandoned that these lie latent within this or that personal continuum; therefore, they are called "latent tendencies. They are said to "lie latent" (*anusenti*)...
The meaning is that they arise having obtained a corresponding cause. Now, it might be argued:

"The state of being a latent tendency (*anusaya*) is the mode of being unabandoned; and it is not logical to say that a mode which is unabandoned arises; therefore, latent tendencies do not arise. To this, the reply is as follows:
the latent tendency is the mode of being unabandoned; however, a latent tendency is a defilement that has become firmly established in the sense of being unabandoned.

It is said: "That [craving] is associated with consciousness, possesses an object, and, in the sense of having a condition, is accompanied by a cause; it is exclusively unwholesome, whether past, future, or present.
Therefore, it is appropriate to say that it 'arises. Herein, this is the proof:
first, in the Abhidhamma, in the *Kathāvatthu*, it is stated: 'The underlying tendencies (anusaya) are indeterminate; the underlying tendencies are rootless.'"
All doctrines [asserting] that "the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are dissociated from consciousness" have been refuted.

In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, having posed the question, "Does one abandon defilements (kilesa) in the present?", it is stated that "one abandons the entrenched underlying tendency," because of the existence of the present state of the underlying tendencies.
However, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇi*, in the word-commentary on delusion (moha), it says: "the underlying tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya), the obsession of ignorance (avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna)..."

“Delusion, which is ignorance-clad, is an unwholesome root; at that time, this is what constitutes delusion. Thus, the state of the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) having arisen together with an unwholesome mind is stated.
Furthermore, in this very *Anusayayamaka*, within one of the seven great sections concerning the section on arising, it says:
“In whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust arises, in him the underlying tendency to aversion arises,” and so forth.

It has been stated. Therefore, it should be understood that what was said—that "they 'follow' (anuseti) means they arise having obtained a corresponding cause"—is well-stated according to this scriptural authority (*tantippamāṇa*). Furthermore, what was said—that "it is associated with consciousness and possesses an object," and so forth—is also well-stated.
For this so-called latent tendency (*anusaya*) is indeed a fully established unwholesome dhamma associated with consciousness.

The conclusion must be reached here. Regarding the terms "underlying tendency of sensual lust" (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and so forth: it is sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) that, in the sense of being unabandoned, is the underlying tendency (*anusaya*);
thus, it is called the "underlying tendency of sensual lust. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
This concludes the commentary on the section of the summary dealing with the delimitation and definition.
Commentary on the Section on the Basis of Arising (Uppattiṭṭhānavāra-vaṇṇanā) 2.
Now, in order to reveal the basis for their arising, he said: "Where does the underlying tendency to sensual lust lie latent?
and so forth. Therein, "in two feelings of the sense-sphere" means in the two feelings of pleasure and equanimity within the plane of the sense sphere.
Regarding the statement "the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies [feeling] here," it arises in these two types of feeling.
Furthermore, this tendency underlies them in two ways: by way of co-nascence and by way of object.
It arises both as something co-nascent with unwholesome pleasant feeling and with unwholesome neutral feeling; and it also arises taking those feelings as its object.
The meaning is "it arises. However, the remaining feeling—whether it be wholesome, resultant, or functional feeling of the sense sphere—arises by making only the object its condition.

While this underlying tendency (anusaya) lies latent within two types of feeling in the sense sphere, it likewise lies latent within the perception, formations, and consciousness associated with those feelings.
For it is not possible for one who has an underlying tendency toward feelings to be free from those [other factors] associated with them.
It could either be non-co-nascent with perception and the other [mental factors], or perception and the others could arise without making that [object] their object.
Even though this is so, nevertheless, because these two feelings alone— being pleasant and peaceful—
are pre-eminent among the remaining associated states for the arising of the underlying tendency to sensual lust in the sense of being an "enjoyment," therefore, regarding the two feelings...
"Herein, the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies [the mind]," it is said; for it is by way of its grossness that it is easy to awaken those who are to be awakened.
But surely, when this [tendency] underlies by way of its object, it does not only underlie these two feelings and the states associated with feeling;
rather, it also underlies desirable forms and so forth. And this has been stated in the Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa:

“Whatever in the world is of a pleasant nature and of a gratifying nature, herein the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) underlies beings”—this is stated in this treatise within the section on the underlying tendencies (anusaya-vāra), in the method of reverse order. “Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust does not underlie, there the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) does not underlie”:
in regard to painful feeling, the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), herein the underlying tendency to sensual lust [does not underlie].

"It does not underlie [it], nor does the underlying tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya) underlie it there. In the non-included (apariyāpanna), neither the underlying tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) nor the underlying tendency of views underlies it.

For here, because it is stated that it does not underlie painful feeling itself and in the form-element and so forth, it refers to painful feeling together with its associated states, and to the states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres together with their respective bases.
It is said that [the underlying tendency] underlies the remaining [objects], namely, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—excluding the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*).

Why is this not stated here? Because they are not gross (*anoḷārika*). For, according to the method explained below, while feelings themselves are gross, these [visible forms and so forth] are not gross;
therefore, it was not stated that [the underlying tendency] underlies these visible forms and so on. However, in terms of actual meaning (*attha*), it is as follows:
It is found. Therefore, it should be understood that even in these [beings], the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) still underlies them.

For the Teacher does not teach everything everywhere. Rather, according to the capacity of beings who are to be enlightened, he teaches whatever is applicable in some cases and does not teach it in others.
Thus, having asked in some instances whether the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) underlies [them], [he answered accordingly].

“Regarding all phenomena included within the entire personal aggregate (*sakkāya*), the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) underlies them”—whatever is obtainable therein has been fully stated.

In another place, by way of answering: “In the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*), the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*), the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), and the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) underlie; in the sensual element (*kāmadhātu*), in two types of feeling, the underlying tendency to doubt...”
Without stating everything that is obtainable— namely, that in the pleasant feeling the underlying tendency to sensual lust,

the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views persist; and in painful feeling, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to ignorance persist—
he has instead spoken only of the three feelings together with the form and formless realms.
However, immaterial phenomena associated with feeling and all material phenomena have not been mentioned here.
Even though they have not been mentioned, the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) still underlies them.

In the same way, even though a desirable object such as visible form has not been mentioned here, the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) still underlies it. Thus, first of all, the basis for the underlying tendency to sensual lust should be understood.
Regarding the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), however, because of the statement "in painful feeling," three types of feeling are the basis for its latent presence:
the two kinds of mental pain-feeling (*domanassavedanā*) and the bodily pain-feeling associated with body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*).

This tendency underlies these mental pain-feelings in two ways: by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of object (*ārammaṇa*); whereas in the remaining bodily pain-feelings, it underlies them only by way of object.
It underlies [them]. Underlying those feelings, it likewise underlies the aggregates of perception and so forth that are associated with them.
For whatever feeling this [latent tendency] is co-nascent with, it is also co-nascent with the perception and other factors associated with that feeling.
And whatever object the feeling takes as its objective support, the perception and other factors associated with it take that same object. Nevertheless, even though this is so, because...

Painful feeling alone, because it is experienced as unpleasant and painful, is predominant over the other associated states in the sense that it provides no gratification and serves as the basis for the arising of the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya).
Therefore, it is said: "Herein, the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent in painful feeling.
For [the Buddha] teaches those to be trained according to what is coarse, so as to awaken them easily.
But surely, while this underlying tendency (anusaya) lies latent by way of its object, it does not lie latent only in painful feeling and in the states associated with it;
rather, it also lies latent in undesirable forms and so forth? For this has also been stated in the Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa:
"In whatever in the world is an unlovely form, an unpleasant form, therein the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) lies latent in beings. And in this [text] as well...

In the *Paṭṭhāna*, in the section on the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) under the method of reverse order, it is stated: “In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) does not underlie there, but the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) does not fail to underlie there.

In the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*), the immaterial realm (*arūpadhātu*), and the unconditioned (*apariyāpanna*), neither the underlying tendency to aversion nor the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies there. For here, in the two feelings of the sense-sphere...

Because it is stated that [the latent tendencies] do not underlie the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth, it follows that—excluding the two feelings together with their associated states, the nine states belonging to the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, and the supramundane states—the remaining [latent tendencies] underlie form and the other aggregates.

Why is this not stated here? Because they are not coarse (*anoḷārika*). For, according to the method explained below, in the case of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*), [the latent tendencies] do not underlie it.

However, because these [other feelings] are not gross (*oḷārika*) while those [unpleasant feelings] are gross, it was not stated that the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) underlies these [latter] forms and so forth.
Yet, in terms of actual meaning, this is obtainable; therefore, it should be understood that the underlying tendency to aversion does indeed underlie these as well.
But are the other two types of feeling not objects for aversion, or do they not have desirable objects? No, they are not.
They exist. In one who has fallen away from jhāna, sorrow arises with respect to those feelings, together with the associated mental states, due to remorse.
Furthermore, sorrow arises even for one who recollects the transformation of a desirable object already obtained, or the non-obtainment of one not yet obtained.
Yet that is merely a state of sorrow; it is not the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*).
For the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) is a firmly established defilement that has arisen by way of striking against an undesirable object;

therefore, although aversion arises here together with mental grief (*domanassa*), it does not constitute the underlying tendency to aversion because it fails to perform its own function as aversion, and thus it falls outside the conventional usage [of the term].
Just as, for example, [the underlying tendency to killing] does not exist alongside the volition of taking life...

Even when ill will has arisen, it is not called mental action (*manokamma*); it becomes something that does not count [as such]. Likewise, the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) does not exist;

it becomes something that does not count [as such]. And this was also said with reference to a certain kind of displeasure (*domanassa*) directed toward a desirable object or even based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*):
"Whatever displeasure or aversion of such a kind there is, he abandons it; he does not [cling] therein..."
“The underlying tendency to aversion underlies it. In this way, the locus for the underlying tendency to aversion is to be understood.
As for the underlying tendency to conceit, however, based on such statements as “in two feelings within the sense-sphere realm,” its threefold locus is:
the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm, and the fine-material and immaterial realms. Regarding that [tendency], in unwholesome feelings, there is the underlying tendency to sensual lust...

It should be understood as being co-nascent with the latent tendencies (*anusaya*). However, among all the associated states within the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), as well as in the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpadhātu*), it lies latent solely by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*). Furthermore, in the reverse order of the section on latent tendencies:
"In unpleasant feeling and in the unconditioned (*apariyāpanna*), the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) does not lie latent."

Because it is stated that “the underlying tendency to conceit does not underlie,” this [tendency] underlies all remaining material and immaterial phenomena—excluding only painful feeling and the ninefold supramundane dhammas.
Thus should the locus of the underlying tendency to conceit be understood.
As for the underlying tendencies to views and doubt, however, they do not underlie at all within supramundane dhammas; rather, they underlie only those dhammas belonging to the three planes.

However, it underlies all [of them] as well. Therefore it was said: "Among all phenomena included within the personal existence (sakkāya), here the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) underlies; here the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) underlies.

In that context, "among all phenomena included within the personal existence" means among all phenomena included within the personal existence in the sense of being dependent upon the cycle of saṃsāra. Furthermore, therein...
They underlie by way of underlying tendencies co-arising with the five types of consciousness.

Alternatively, they underlie by way of underlying tendencies toward the object at the time they occur directed toward those five types of consciousness or other phenomena belonging to the three planes.
In this way, the locus of the underlying tendency to views and the underlying tendency to doubt should be understood.

As for the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), although it might be said that "it underlies two feelings in the sense-sphere realm" by way of being a co-nascent underlying tendency— since it arises in the four types of consciousness dissociated from views—
it nevertheless acquires only phenomena of the fine-material and immaterial spheres when it arises together with the two feelings within the sense-sphere realm. In the sense-sphere realm...
It does not take even a single dhamma included in the mundane as its object; therefore, having established a restriction by way of the underlying tendency toward the object, it is said:
"In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, the underlying tendency to lust for existence underlies.
Furthermore, this lust is twofold, by way of sensual lust and lust for existence. Therein, sensual lust [underlies] the two feelings in the sense-sphere element.

It is said that "it underlies. However, if the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) were also spoken of in this same way as attachment to sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*), the teaching would seem to be confused with attachment to sense-pleasures.
Therefore, having divided the defilement of attachment into two types, this teaching was given in order to show the distinction between attachment to existence and attachment to sense-pleasures.
In this way, the locus for the underlying tendency of attachment to existence should be understood.
The underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya), however, underlies all phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence. Therefore it is said:

"In this regard, the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies all phenomena included within the personality-heap (sakkāya). Its state as a co-nascent underlying tendency should be understood with respect to the twelve types of consciousness-arising.
As for its mode of taking an object, there is no phenomenon of the three planes that it does not arise in reference to.

Thus should the basis for the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of ignorance (*avijjā*) be understood. This concludes, for now, the exposition of the analysis within the sections on delimitation, the section on the enumeration delimited by the [preceding] section, and the section on the origin.
This is the commentary on the section on the origin.
The Great Section.
1. Commentary on the Chapter on Latent Dispositions (Anusayavāra) 3.
Regarding the first of the seven great chapters, the Chapter on Latent Dispositions (Anusayavāra), concerning the statement:

"In one for whom the latent disposition of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) underlies, does the latent disposition of aversion (paṭighānusaya) also underlie?", the answer given there—"Yes"—is not well-given.
It appears as if they do. Why? Because sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*paṭigha*) do not arise at the same moment. For instance, in such passages as:
"When the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) arises for someone, does the sense-base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) arise for them?

Yes," or "At the moment of the arising of inhalation and exhalation, both bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) arise," the sense-bases of mind and mental objects [are mentioned].
The bodily formations and verbal formations arise simultaneously, but sensual lust and aversion do not.
Sensual lust arises in eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed, while aversion arises in two types accompanied by displeasure;
thus, there is no simultaneous arising of these two, and therefore a negation such as "no" should have been made here. Yet, that was not done.

However, because the reply "Yes" (*āmantā*) has been given, one must understand this passage differently from the preceding sections, not by taking it as the conventional usage of "presently occurring" in the sense of the present moment (*khaṇapaccuppanna*).
How so? By way of its being unabandoned (*appahīna*).
For it is with reference to this state of being unabandoned that this conventional usage of "it underlies" (*anuseti*) is stated as a present tense.

It does not refer to the state of being present at the moment. And because it was stated with reference to the state of not having been abandoned, therefore, regarding the question, "In whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies, in him the underlying tendency to aversion underlies," the meaning should be understood as follows:

in whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust has not been abandoned and has not been brought to the state of being subject to non-arising, in him the underlying tendency to aversion has also not been abandoned.
And because, among those [latent tendencies], whichever one is not abandoned, the others are likewise not abandoned, therefore it was said:

“Yes. If that is so, regarding what was asked in the section on arising above—“For whom the latent tendency of sensual lust arises, for him does the latent tendency of aversion arise?”—and the answer given was “Yes,” how should the meaning be understood there? There too...
This is either by way of non-abandonment itself when there is a condition for arising, or by way of the non-obstruction of arising.

For example, when painters and others have begun works such as painting but have not yet finished their tasks, even at a moment when they are not performing those tasks, if they are seen in various places by friends, companions, and so forth, and asked, "What are you doing these days? they reply, "We are doing painting; we are doing woodwork..."

They say, "We do [it]. Although they do not actually perform them at that specific moment because their work is continuous, nevertheless, by taking into account both the moments when it has been done and the moments when it ought to be done, they are indeed said to be doing it.

In the same way, in whichever continuum the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have not been abandoned, or in whichever continuum there exists a condition for their arising such that their arising is unobstructed—

In this context, even at the moment when [the latent tendency] has not yet arisen, one should understand the meaning as follows: "For one in whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) arises—taking into account both what has previously arisen and what will arise at another time—the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) necessarily arises as well.

This same method applies to all subsequent answers of this kind. Regarding the phrase "but not for him" (*no ca tassa*), this refers to the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) in respect of sensual lust and ill-will (*byāpāda*).

It is stated because [the defilements] have been abandoned without remainder. "Of three persons" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*).

"Of two persons" refers to the stream-enterer and the once-returner. This same method applies to similar instances further on as well. 14. Regarding the first and second questions of the section on bases (*okāsavāra*):
because the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) exists in the two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The underlying tendency to aversion underlies painful feeling; therefore, a negation was made with the word “no.
In the third question, because both [tendencies] underlie both feelings within the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu), the reply “yes” was given.

However, in the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu), there is a place of arising for the underlying tendency to conceit that is not shared with the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Therefore, it is said: "And there is no underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) therein.
Following this method, one should understand the common and uncommon bases of arising by examining the section on the bases of arising for all [underlying tendencies]. 20.
In the inquiry based on pairs, since the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion do not arise in the same place, [they are treated as distinct].
They do not take a single dhamma as their object; therefore, the negation "it does not exist" is made. This is the intended meaning here:
there is simply no such place where these two underlying tendencies (anusaya) could lie latent. Therefore, the question "Where does the underlying tendency of conceit lie latent?
is indeed a non-question. This same method applies to other similar cases as well.

27. In the section on the world of persons (*puggalokāsa*), "of four" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*), and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*). 36.
In the method of reverse order, the question "for whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) does not underlie" asks about the non-returner.
56. "In all cases, for two persons the underlying tendency of sensual lust does not underlie" refers to the non-returner and the arahant. [This applies] in the realm of sense-desire (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the phrase "in the three feelings" (*tīsu vedanāsu*), by the mention of "feelings," it should be understood that there is an inclusion of all sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*), including those associated with feeling as well as their bases and objects.
This concludes the analytical exposition for the section on latent tendencies (*anusaya-vāra*).
This is the commentary on the section on latent tendencies.
2. Commentary on the Section on "With Underlying Tendencies" (Sānusayavāra), §§ 66–131.

Regarding the section on "with underlying tendencies," the phrase "one who has an underlying tendency toward sensual lust" (*kāmarāgānusaya*) is like a person afflicted by a chronic disease such as jaundice:
as long as one is not freed from that disease, one remains diseased even at moments when that specific illness is not manifest.

It is so called. Thus, for a being subject to defilement who proceeds through the round of existence, as long as the underlying tendencies (anusaya) have not been eradicated by the Noble Path, that being is indeed said to "possess underlying tendencies" even at those moments when those tendencies are not actually arising.
It is with reference to such a state of possessing underlying tendencies that it was stated: “Yes. The rest here is exactly the same as in the section on underlying tendencies.
However, in the section on the bases (*okāsavāra*), when it is stated, "In the fine-material element and the immaterial element,

one is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) therein," the person's state of being possessed of that underlying tendency would be made known in those elements, but the place of origin of the underlying tendency would not be made known.
Since this section was commenced for the purpose of showing the place of origin of the underlying tendency, therefore, by means of the underlying tendency to conceit from that [section]...

It is said, "one who possesses underlying tendencies. For this being the case, by the phrase "possessing the underlying tendency of conceit arising from those two elements," the locus of the arising of the underlying tendency is shown. However, since the meaning of this question has not yet been stated, the meaning of the first question would not be clear;
therefore, it was not stated first. Consequently, that [first question] should be understood as follows: "From which [state] does one possess the underlying tendency of sensual lust?"

Since one who has the underlying tendency (anusaya) due to the arisen latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya), does he also have the underlying tendency due to the arisen latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya)?
Because these two do not arise from the same point, a negation is made with the word "no.
An Arahant is "in all places" means that an Arahant is free from any underlying tendency arising in regard to any phenomena whatsoever.
For this reason, the locative case alone has been employed in all instances where it is required without exception. By this method, the determination of the meaning in all cases should be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning latent tendencies (*sānusayavāra*).
3. Explanation of the Chapter on Abandoning (Pajahana-vāra) 132–197.

Regarding the phrase "he abandons" (*pajahati*) in the chapter on abandoning: he abandons by means of the full understanding of abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*) through each respective path, bringing about the state of non-arising in the future.
"Yes, venerable sir" (*āmantā*) is the reply referring to one who stands at the stage of the non-returner path (*anāgāmī-magga*).

"It abandons that which is to be abandoned by one function" is said with reference to abandonment as a single function (*pahāna-ekaṭṭhatā*). "No" is a negation with reference to the stage of the path of arahantship.
"From which he abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust" means from which the underlying tendency to sensual lust that arises [therein] is abandoned.
"The eighth person" refers to the stage of the path of stream-entry when counted in reverse order starting from the stage of the fruit of arahantship.
The "eighth" (aṭṭhamaka) is as follows. In the reckoning of those worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya), the Arahant is first because he is the foremost of those worthy of offerings;
the one standing on the path to Arahantship is second; the Non-returner (anāgāmī) is third... [and so on] ...the one standing on the path to stream-entry (sotāpatti) is eighth.

He is what is meant here by "the eighth. Or rather, this is merely a conventional designation for him. Excluding both the one possessing the path of non-returning and the eighth, the remainder are [the others].

Together with the worldling (puthujjana), there are those in training (sekkha) and those beyond training (asekkha). For among them, the worldling does not abandon [the defilements] due to the absence of full understanding through abandonment (pahānapariññā).
The others [do so] because those underlying tendencies (anusaya) have been abandoned. "Of the two possessing the path" means excluding the two who possess the path.
By this method, the analysis is to be understood in all instances.
Commentary on the Chapter on Abandoning (Pajahanavāra). 4. Commentary on the Chapter on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra), §§198–263.

Regarding the phrase "he fully understands" in the Chapter on Full Understanding: he fully understands by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*). The rest here is exactly according to the method explained below. For this chapter, like the Chapter on Abandoning, is answered solely by way of the position of the Path (*magga*).
Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding. 5. Commentary on the Section on Abandonment (264–274).

In the section on abandonment, the teaching is undertaken specifically from the standpoint of one who has attained the fruit [of the path]. For in the case of a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), both these underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have been abandoned; therefore, it is said: "Yes, they have."

275–296. Regarding the section on the bases (*okāsa-vāra*), it is stated that after asking, "Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) is abandoned, is the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) there also abandoned?
one cannot say either that it is abandoned or that it is not abandoned. Why is that? Because their respective bases for arising are not common.

For the basis for the arising of the underlying tendency to sensual lust is one thing, and the basis for the underlying tendency to aversion is another. This is because the path has not been developed... [of the person whose path is undeveloped].
And wherever a latent tendency arises, once the Path has been cultivated, it is said to be abandoned right there.

In this regard, since the latent tendency of aversion does not arise where the latent tendency of sensual lust resides, nor does the latent tendency of sensual lust arise where the latent tendency of aversion resides, it cannot be said of that [person] there whether the tendency is abandoned or unabandoned. For it is only in its own place of arising...
The underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) has been abandoned; because it has not been abandoned in that [state], one cannot say that it is abandoned there.
Because it does not exist in that which is the basis for the arising of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, one cannot say that it is not abandoned there.

Regarding the statement, "Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust is abandoned, there the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) is abandoned," this refers to a common locus (*sādhāraṇaṭṭhāna*).
It is said, “Yes,” with reference to this. For the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies the two feelings in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The underlying tendency to conceit underlies those same two feelings as well as those in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and arūpadhātu*). Having set aside its own unique domain, in the common domain it is said to be abandoned along with that [sensual lust].
Therefore, it is said, “Yes. By this method, it applies to every section concerning the spheres (*okāsa*).
The state of being abandoned and the state of not being so should be understood. However, regarding the instances where it is stated "it does not exist," the analysis is exactly as explained above.
The section on persons and bases follows the same pattern as the section on bases. 297–307.

In the reverse order, the phrase "for whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust is unabandoned" refers, by way of the ordinary person (*puthujjana*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*).
He asks this because, although these two underlying tendencies (anusaya) remain unabandoned by the six types of persons from the worldling up to those standing on the path of non-returning,
here the persons standing on the paths are not intended— since it is stated further on, "of three persons" and "of two persons," etc.— therefore,
he says "Yes" with reference only to the worldling, the stream-enterer, and the once-returner.

It has been stated. "Of two persons" refers to the stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and the once-returner (sakadāgāmī). In this manner, the analysis in the section on persons (puggalavāra) is to be understood.

308–329. The sections on the bases (okāsavāra) and the persons and bases (puggalokāsavāra), however, are to be understood by the same method as explained below. This concludes the commentary on the section on what has been abandoned (pahīnavāra).
6. Explanation of the Section on Arising (Uppajjanavāra):
330. The section on arising is exactly like the section on underlying tendencies (anusaya). 7.
Explanation of the Section on the Inquiry into Elements (Dhātupucchāvāra)

332–340. Regarding the section on questions in the Chapter on Elements (*dhātuvāra*): first, as for "how many latent tendencies (*anusaya*) lie latent," it means how many latent tendencies lie dormant by being continuous within the continuum (*santāna*).
"How many latent tendencies do not lie latent" means how many latent tendencies do not lie dormant by not being continuous within the continuum.
"How many latent tendencies are subject to analysis" means how many latent tendencies are to be analyzed in this way: "they lie latent" or "they do not lie latent."
The meaning [is as follows]. Whatever else might need to be said here has already been stated below in the section on the analysis of the text (*pāḷivavatthāna*).

Furthermore, in the section of the detailed exposition (*niddesavāra*), the statement that "in some, seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) lie latent" is made with reference to worldlings (*puthujjana*).

"For some, five" is stated with reference to stream-enterers and once-returners. For in their case, since the underlying tendency to views and the underlying tendency to doubt have been abandoned, only five underlying tendencies remain.
In this context, the meaning of the word "underlie" (*anusenti*) should not be taken as "arise," as it was understood in the section on underlying tendencies;
why? Because they do not arise at that moment. [This refers to] the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).
For when one is being reborn, both resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*) and matter produced by kamma arise; there is no unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*).
Furthermore, the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) arise during moments of unwholesome consciousness, not during moments of resultant consciousness.

Therefore, because they do not arise at that [resultant] moment, the meaning should not be understood in that way. How, then, should it be understood? It should be understood according to how it is possible.
It should be understood. And how is it obtained? By way of being unabandoned.

For just as a person endowed with a wholesome or indeterminate state of consciousness is called "one with lust," "one with hatred," or "one with delusion" because lust, hatred, and delusion have not been abandoned, so too, because they have not been abandoned through the cultivation of the Path, those respective underlying tendencies (anusaya) are said to underlie that particular person even at the moment of rebirth-linking.

Furthermore, it should be understood that they are not merely called "latent tendencies" (anusaya) because they are spoken of as such; rather, they are so called precisely because they have not been abandoned.

There is no such thing as a "breakdown" of latent tendencies. For whatever [tendency] in whom lies latent, it remains latent; whatever does not lie latent, it simply does not lie latent. One cannot say, "This one has it latent and this one does not," or "In this case it is latent and in that case it is not"; thus they must be analyzed.

There is no such thing as a latent tendency (*anusaya*) that does not exist. The statement that "for someone being reborn in the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*), three [latent tendencies] remain" is said with reference to a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
For him, all four latent tendencies—sensual lust, aversion, views, and doubt—have been abandoned without remainder;
only the other three remain unabandoned. Therefore it is said: "For some, three latent tendencies still underlie."
"Not in the sense-sphere realm" means that because rebirth in the sense-sphere realm is excluded for one who is passing away from it, the meaning is that [rebirth occurs] in the remaining two realms.

"Or among beings" is stated with the restriction "or among beings" because for a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) who has passed away from the form realm, there is no such thing as rebirth in the sense-sphere realm;
this occurs only for an ordinary person (puthujjana). [This applies to] one who has passed away from the formless realm into the sense-sphere realm...
The same principle applies here as well in the phrase, "for one being reborn, there are seven. Why is there no rebirth in the fine-material element (rūpadhātu)?

Because of the absence of the fine-material-sphere jhāna that produces rebirth. For he has been reborn in that element by completely transcending perceptions of form; thus, the fine-material-sphere jhāna does not exist for him there. Due to its absence...

It should be understood that there is no rebirth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the statement "for one who has passed away from the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*), it is not the desire realm," here only the formless realm itself is intended.
By this method, the meaning should be understood in all the responses. This concludes the commentary on the section on the realms (*dhātuvāra*).
