Even though these were not explicitly mentioned, they are shown by this very [passage]. However, because the unwholesome is to be abandoned absolutely, the wholesome absolutely to be developed, and the supramundane indeterminate to be realized, it is said:
"He abandons the faculty of mental grief," "He develops the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'," and "He realizes the faculty of one who has known."
It has been stated. Furthermore, the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) is both to be developed and to be realized;

it is included here specifically by way of its development. In that regard, there are two types of persons: one who possesses the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmimagga*) and one who possesses the path of arhatship (*arahattamagga*).
Among them, one is said not to abandon the faculty of mental distress (*domanassindriya*) because he is unable to completely eradicate it. The other, however, has abandoned the defilements.
"He does not fully understand the eye-faculty" means he does not fully understand it because of his inability to bring about its non-arising.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all the answers.
This concludes the commentary on the Chapter on Full Understanding (*pariññāvāra*).
The commentary on the *Indriya-yamaka* is finished.
And at this point— the concluding discourse:
Standing by whose instruction, one who has completed his task is perfected in duty;
even the youth, having transcended [worldly bonds], is well-established in the discipline of that refuge.
In the midst of the assembly of gods, in the city of the gods, by the God of all gods—
That which is called the *Yamaka* has been elucidated by me, the stainless Loma.
In order to demonstrate the method for establishing the textual basis (*pāḷi*), the questions and their answers,
and the principles of meaning (*atthanaya*), I have commenced this commentary on the *Yamaka*.
This [work], which has many obstacles in the world,
has today reached its conclusion through five recitation sections of the *tantī* without hindrance.
May everyone likewise reach their own completion.
May the heart's desires of all beings bring about welfare and happiness.
The Commentary on the Yamaka (The Book of Pairs) is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the *Paṭṭhānappakaraṇa-ṭīkā* of the *Abhidhammapitaka*:
The God beyond gods, worshipped by gods and dānavas,
Having taught this compendium, the Twin [Nikāya], he who is pure in self-restraint— then,
for the sake of its meaning and its doctrine which are profound,
the Great Hero, the seventh among seers, [taught] the next [work].
Known by the name *Paṭṭhāna*, the destroyer of name-and-form taught a discourse adorned with an exceedingly profound method.
Now, since the turn has come for its detailed commentary, [I shall provide it].
"Therefore, I shall explain it; listen to it with concentrated minds. This is the commentary on the enumeration of conditions (*paccayuddesavaṇṇanā*).
For indeed, in the *Anuloma Paṭṭhāna*, the Blessed One, relying upon twenty-two triads, expounded what is known as the *Tika Paṭṭhāna*.
Based on the hundred dyads (*duka*), what is called the "Establishment of Dyads" (*duka-paṭṭhāna*) has been demonstrated.
Following that, having taken the twenty-two triads (*tika*) and added them to the hundred dyads, what is called the "Establishment of Dyads and Triads" (*dukatika-paṭṭhāna*) is shown.

After that, having taken the hundred dyads and added them to the twenty-two triads, what is called the "Establishment of Triads and Dyads" (*tikaduka-paṭṭhāna*) is shown. As for the triads, they are [treated] only among the triads themselves.

Having included [the triplets] within the triplets, what is called the "Exposition of Triplets" (Tikapaṭṭhāna) is shown. And having included [the couples] within the couples, what is called the "Exposition of Couples" (Dukapaṭṭhāna) is shown. Thus:
"The excellent Exposition of Triplets and the supreme Exposition of Couples..."
The dyad and the triad, and the triad and the dyad;
the triad and the triad, and the dyad and the dyad—
these six methods in the direct order are profoundly deep.
In the *Paccanīyapaṭṭhāna* (Negative Conditional Relations) as well, there is the *Tikapaṭṭhāna* based on twenty-two triplets; the *Dukapaṭṭhāna* based on one hundred couplets;

the *Dukatikapaṭṭhāna* consisting of those twenty-two triplets combined with those one hundred couplets; the *Tikadukapaṭṭhāna* consisting of those one hundred couplets combined with those twenty-two triplets;
and [finally] the *Tikapaṭṭhāna* consisting of those triplets combined with triplets themselves.
It is called the *tika-paṭṭhāna*. By including [the factors] only in pairs, it is called the *duka-duka-paṭṭhāna*.
Thus, even in the reverse order (*paccanīya*), the *Paṭṭhāna* is demonstrated by means of six methods. Therefore it was said:
“The excellent *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, the supreme *Duka-paṭṭhāna*...”
The dyad and the triad, and the triad and the dyad;
the triad and the triad, and the dyad and the dyad—
these six methods in the section on opposites are profoundly deep.
Following that, by this same method, six methods (nayas) are shown for the positive-negative (anuloma-paccanīya) combinations as well. Therefore he said:
“The excellent and most supreme Paṭṭhāna consists of the Triplets and the Couplets;
namely, the Triplet-Couplet, the Couplet-Triplet, and the Triplet-Triplet.”
“Threefold and threefold, and twofold and twofold—these six methods in the Positive-Negative [analysis] are very profound.
Immediately following that, the Negative-Positive [analysis] is demonstrated by these same six methods. Therefore he said:
“The excellent and most supreme *tika-paṭṭhāna*,
the *duka-tika*, the *tika-duka*,
the *tika-tika*, and the *duka-duka*;”
“The methods in the reverse-conformity are very profound.

Thus, there are six *paṭṭhānas* in the conformity, six in the reverse, six in the conformity-and-reverse, and six in the reverse-and-conformity; this is what is called “the Great Treatise on the Foundations of Phenomena (Paṭṭhāna), which is the Compendium of the Twenty-four Universal Foundations (*samantapaṭṭhāna*)”.
In that context, it is by way of the compendium of those twenty-four universal foundations that this is called “the Compendium of the Twenty-four Universal Foundations.”
It is called the *Paṭṭhāna-mahāpakaraṇa* (The Great Treatise on Conditional Relations). The meaning of the names of both those [previous treatises] and this treatise should be understood as follows.

In what sense is it called *paṭṭhāna*? It is in the sense of various kinds of conditions (*paccaya*). For the syllable *pa-* indicates the sense of "various kinds," while the word *ṭhāna* signifies "condition.
Indeed, in such expressions as "skill in *ṭhāna* and *aṭṭhāna*" (skill in what is possible and what is impossible), the condition is referred to as *ṭhāna*.
Thus, because it is taught by way of various types of conditions, each individual section among these twenty-four sections is called a *paṭṭhāna*.
Furthermore, this entire treatise should be understood as a *paṭṭhāna* by virtue of being a collection of these sections.
Another method: in what sense is it a *paṭṭhāna*? In the sense of analysis (*vibhajana*). “It is establishing, it is setting forth, it is disclosing... [etc.]
For in the passage where it is stated, “it is analysis and making plain,” *paṭṭhāna* is understood in the sense of analysis (*vibhajana*).
Thus, because wholesome and other states are analyzed by way of causes, conditions, and so forth, each one among these twenty-four *paṭṭhānas* is called a *paṭṭhāna*.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this entire treatise is called *paṭṭhāna* as a collection of these *paṭṭhānas*.
Another method: In what sense is it called *paṭṭhāna*? In the sense of being set forth (*paṭṭhita*). The meaning is "in the sense of going.
For in the passage where it is said, "The cattle have been set forth at the cow-pen" (*goṭṭhā paṭṭhitagāvo*), that by which they are called "cattle set forth" is, in actual fact, "going.
Thus, regarding the all-knowing knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*)—which moves without attachment—in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and other treatises where the method is not overly prolix...

Because it proceeds without attachment by attaining the method explained in detail regarding the wholesome and other states— which are divided according to the distinctions of the root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*) and so forth—
each one among these twenty-four "foundations" (*paṭṭhāna*) is called a "foundation.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this entire treatise, as a collection of these foundations, is called "The Foundation" (*Paṭṭhāna*).
In this context, first, regarding the *anuloma* (direct order), it is called the *Tika-paṭṭhāna* because it is taught by way of triplets. Its word-analysis (*padaccheda*) is as follows:
"The *paṭṭhāna* (foundation) of triplets exists herein" is thus the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*. The meaning is that various kinds of conditions for the triplets exist in this teaching.
In the second interpretation as well, it is simply the *paṭṭhāna* of triplets, hence the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, by way of the root-cause condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth.

The meaning is "the analysis of the triads. In the third interpretation, the *tikapaṭṭhāna* (Triad-System) refers to the triads themselves which have attained expansion through their differentiation by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth;
the meaning is that it is the ground for the unimpeded movement of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

The same method applies to the *dukapaṭṭhāna* (Dyad-System) and the others as well. Having thus understood the six systems in the direct order (*anuloma*), [one should likewise understand them] in the reverse order (*paccanīya*) and so forth.
These are to be understood by this method.

However, because these—consisting of six each in the forward order (*anuloma*), the reverse order (*paccanīya*), the forward-and-reverse order (*anuloma-paccanīya*), and the reverse-and-forward order (*paccanīya-anuloma*)—amount to twenty-four, they are called "the twenty-four universal foundations" (*samantapaṭṭhāna*). Thus...

This Great Treatise on the *Paṭṭhāna*, known as the Compendium of the Twenty-four *Samantapaṭṭhānas*—that is, the twenty-four *Samantapaṭṭhānas* consisting of the Minor *Paṭṭhāna*—is so called by way of their collective synthesis.

Furthermore, because it is expounded in dependence upon the triads (*tika*) and so forth, it is designated as "the Triad *Paṭṭhāna*, the Dyad *Paṭṭhāna*, ... [and so on] ... the Dyad-Dyad *Paṭṭhāna*."

Without referring to those [categories] already mentioned, in order to show the conditions by way of which those triads and so forth are analyzed, the section first called the "Enumeration of the Schedule" (mātikānikkhepavāra) was stated; this is also known as the "Analysis of Conditions" (paccayavibhaṅgavāra).
It is twofold: by way of enumeration (uddesa) and exposition (niddesa). Of these, the enumeration is: "Root condition... pe ... non-disappearance condition."
In this context, that which is both a cause (*hetu*) and a condition (*paccaya*) is called the "cause-condition" (*hetupaccaya*).

Having been a cause, it is a condition; what is meant is that it is a condition by way of its state as a cause. This same method applies to the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and the others as well. In this regard, "cause" (*hetu*) is a designation for a member of a statement, a reason, and a root.
For in common usage, in such expressions as "the proposition is the cause," "cause" refers to a member of a statement. However, in the Teaching (*sāsana*), [it refers to the roots].

In such passages as “Those phenomena that arise from a cause,” it refers to a *kāraṇa* (efficient cause). In such passages as “There are three roots of the wholesome, three roots of the unwholesome,” it is called a *hetu* (root-cause).
That is what is intended here. As for the term *paccaya* (condition), its etymological meaning is this:
it is a *paccaya* because something goes (*eti*) by depending (*paṭicca*) upon it; the sense is that it functions without being rejected by that [dependent]. For whatever phenomenon...
Whether a phenomenon persists or arises, it does so without rejecting the dhamma; thus, it is said that this is its condition (*paccaya*).

By way of characteristic, however, a condition is characterized by being helpful. For whatever phenomenon is helpful for the persistence or the arising of another phenomenon, that is called its condition.
Condition (*paccaya*), cause (*hetu*), reason (*kāraṇa*), and source (*nidāna*) are synonyms.

“Sambhava” (origination) and “pabhava” (source) are identical in meaning but differ in phrasing. Thus, in the sense of being a root it is a cause (*hetu*), and in the sense of being an assistant it is a condition (*paccaya*).
In brief, a phenomenon that is an assistant in the sense of being a root is a causal condition (*hetupaccaya*).

For it establishes the state of wholesomeness and so forth in wholesome states and the like—just as the seeds of rice and so forth do for rice and the like, or as the color and other qualities of a gem do for the radiance of a gem; such is the view of the teachers.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). However, this being the case, the status of being a root-cause condition (*hetupaccayatā*) does not apply to the material phenomena (*rūpa*) originated by those [mental states].
For that [root-cause] does not establish their state as wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth; yet it is not the case that it is not a condition. For this has been said:

"Roots are a condition, by way of the root-condition, for those states associated with roots and for the material phenomena originated by them. And regarding rootless consciousnesses (*ahetukacitta*),...
Without this [distinction], the state of being indeterminate (abyākata-bhāva) would be established.

Furthermore, even for those states that possess causes, their status as wholesome (kusala) and so forth is dependent upon appropriate attention (yonisomanasikāra) and the like, not dependent upon associated causes (sampayutta-hetu).
And if the status of being wholesome and so forth were to exist in associated causes by their very nature (sabhāvatova), then it would be dependent upon causes in those things associated with them.

Non-greed may be either wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*). Since it exists in both ways, therefore, just as with the associated states, so too should the wholesomeness and other qualities of the roots be sought.

However, if one does not take the meaning of "root" for the roots to be their status as establishing factors of wholesomeness and so forth, but rather takes it to mean their status as establishing factors of being well-established, nothing is contradicted. Having obtained the root-condition...
For indeed, those states that possess a root are firm and well-established, like trees with deep roots; however, those without a root are not well-established, like moss or seeds such as sesame.
Thus, a state that is beneficial by way of providing a foundation through the accomplishment of a state of being well-established should be understood as the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*).
Next, the state that is beneficial to other states by way of being an object is the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).

Although it begins with the statement, “The visible-object base is [the condition] for the eye-consciousness element,” it concludes with: “Whatever states, having whatever states as their object, arise—whether they be consciousness or mental factors—those states are conditions for those states by way of the object-condition. Therefore, there is no [state]...

There is no such thing as "dhamma" [in the sense of a non-existent object]. For just as a weak man stands up and remains standing only by leaning on a staff or a rope, so too do states of consciousness and mental factors (cittacetasika-dhammā) arise and persist only by taking objects such as visible forms (rūpa) and so forth.
Therefore, all those things that serve as the objects (ārammaṇa) for states of consciousness and mental factors—
It should be understood as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
A factor that assists by way of being predominant is the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*). It is twofold: by way of co-nascent [predominance] and by way of object [predominance].
Among these, "predominance of desire (*chanda-adhipati*) [is a condition] for those states associated with desire and for the material phenomena originated thereby..."

From such statements as “it is a condition by way of predominance-condition,” it should be understood that the four factors known as desire (chanda), energy (viriya), consciousness (citta), and investigation (vīmaṃsā) are co-nascent predominance-conditions;

however, they do not function as such simultaneously. For when consciousness proceeds having made desire its primary and chief factor, then desire alone is the predominance, not the others. This same principle applies to the remaining factors as well.
However, that state by way of which non-material states arise when it is treated with esteem is their object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*).

Therefore it was said: "Whatever states, whether consciousness or mental factors, arise by way of treating whatever state as estimable, those [former] states are a condition for those [latter] states by way of the predominance condition."
A state that assists by way of immediate succession is the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*). A state that assists by way of contiguity is the contiguity condition (*samanantara-paccaya*).
These two conditions are elaborated upon in many ways; however, the essential point here is this:

namely, that the mind-element (*manodhātu*) which follows immediately after eye-consciousness, and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) which follows immediately after the mind-element, and so forth.
The restriction of consciousness succeeds only by means of the preceding consciousness and not otherwise;
therefore, a state that is capable of producing a corresponding arising of consciousness immediately after itself is the proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*). For this very reason it was said:
"The proximity condition consists of the eye-consciousness element and the states associated with it, [in relation] to the mind-element and the states associated with it..."

“...is a condition for states by way of proximity-condition,” and so forth. That which is the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*) is itself the immediate-condition (*samanantara-paccaya*). Here, the difference is merely in the phrasing, as in the cases of accumulation and continuity, or as in the *adhidhamma-nirutti-duka* and others; in terms of meaning, however, there is no difference. As for the statement, “Because of being immediately subsequent... [The text continues: ...it is said that the state of being immediately subsequent (*addhānantaratā*) is the characteristic of the proximity-condition. But what is this state of being immediately subsequent? It is the state of having no interval between the cessation of the preceding state and the arising of the succeeding state. For example, when one consciousness has ceased and another consciousness arises, or when one mental state has ceased and another mental state arises, there is no other state intervening between them. This is called the state of being immediately subsequent. Because of this state of being immediately subsequent, it is the proximity-condition. Furthermore, the state of being immediately subsequent is also the immediate-condition. Why? Because the proximate state is precisely the immediate state. Therefore, the characteristic of the proximity-condition is the state of being immediately subsequent. However, the characteristic of the immediate-condition is not merely the state of being immediately subsequent. What then? It is the state of being immediately subsequent together with the quality of being the most proximate. For example, when one consciousness has ceased and another consciousness arises, although there is no other state intervening, the preceding consciousness is the most proximate to the succeeding consciousness; therefore, it is the immediate-condition. The teachers' opinion is that "it is an immediate condition (anantarapaccaya), and it is a proximate condition (samanantarapaccaya) by virtue of its temporal immediacy. This contradicts such statements as:

"For one emerging from cessation, the wholesome attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of being a proximate condition," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding what they say there—"the capacity to arouse phenomena..."—this too is problematic.

As for the claim that "it does not fall away, but because they have been obstructed by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*), the states do not arise immediately thereafter," this too establishes precisely the absence of immediate succession.
For we also say exactly this: that there is no immediate succession in that case due to the power of cultivation.
And since there is no immediate succession, therefore there is no status as a condition of immediate proximity (*samanantarapaccayatā*).
This is not tenable. For their position is that the "immediately preceding condition" (samanantara-paccaya) exists because of their temporal contiguity.
Therefore, without forming a dogmatic attachment, one should understand that the distinction here lies merely in the phrasing and not in the meaning. How so?

Because there is no interval between them, they are "without interval" (anantarā). Because they are perfectly without interval due to the absence of any spatial configuration, they are "immediately preceding" (samanantarā).
A phenomenon that, while arising, assists by its very state of arising is a conascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), like a lamp for illumination.
It is sixfold by way of the immaterial aggregates and so forth. As it is said: "The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of the conascence condition;
the four great elements are a condition for one another... [and so on]... at the moment of descent [into the womb]."
"Name-and-form is a condition for one another... mental states and mental factors are conditions for matter originated by mind... the great primary elements are conditions for derived matter...

material phenomena are at times a condition for immaterial phenomena by way of the co-nascence condition, and at times they are not a condition by way of the co-nascence condition. This was said with reference specifically to the heart-base.
A phenomenon that assists another by way of its mutual production and support is the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*).

It is like a tripod of three staffs supporting one another. It is threefold, consisting of the immaterial aggregates and so forth. As it is said: "The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of the mutuality condition;
the four great elements... [and] at the moment of descent [into the womb], name-and-form is a condition for one another by way of the mutuality condition."
A phenomenon that assists by way of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and by way of support (*nissaya*) is a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), such as earth for trees and canvas for paintings.

This should be understood in the same manner as explained under "conascence" (*sahajāta*): "The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of support-condition. Furthermore, the sixth category here is: "The eye-base is [a condition] for the eye-consciousness-element..."
The sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body are a condition by way of support for body-consciousness and for those states associated with it.

Whatever material form depending upon which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element proceed, that material form is a condition by way of support for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and for those states associated with them. Thus it is analyzed.

Regarding the term *upanissaya-paccaya* (decisive support condition), its etymological meaning here is as follows: it is called *nissaya* because it is not rejected by its own fruit, which exists in dependence upon it.
Just as *upāyāsa* (agitation) means intense agitation (*bhuso āyāso*), so too *upanissaya* means intense support (*bhuso nissayo*).
This is a designation for a powerful cause. Therefore, it is a phenomenon that assists by way of being a powerful cause.

It should be understood as the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). It is threefold: object-decisive support (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*), proximity-decisive support (*anantara-upanissaya*), and natural decisive support (*pakata-upanissaya*).
Among these: "Having given a gift, having undertaken virtue, and having performed the Uposatha rite, one esteems and reviews it;
one esteems and reviews past deeds well-performed; having emerged from a meditative absorption..."
"One reviews jhāna making it an object of esteem; trainees review change-of-lineage making it an object of esteem; they review purification making it an object of esteem;

and trainees, having emerged from the path, review the path making it an object of esteem"—in such a manner, the decisive support by way of object (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) is treated without making any distinction from the dominance by way of object (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
It is analyzed. In this context, whatever object the mind and mental factors arise by treating as important is, by necessity, the powerful object (*balavārammaṇa*) among their objects.
Thus, in the sense of being treated as important, it is the object-dominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*);
in the sense of being a powerful cause, it is the object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*). In this way, their distinction should be understood.

The proximity-decisive-support condition (*anantarūpanissaya*) is also analyzed without making any distinction from the proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*), according to the method beginning with: "Preceding wholesome aggregates are a condition for subsequent wholesome aggregates by way of the decisive-support condition.
However, in the presentation of the matrix (*mātikānikkhepa*), these are [distinguished] as: "the eye-consciousness element and its associated [states]..."
The distinction in their presentation arises because the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) is mentioned in such a manner as,

"And mental phenomena are a condition for the mind-element and for the phenomena associated with it by way of the immediate condition," and the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is mentioned in such a manner as, "Preceding wholesome phenomena are a condition for succeeding wholesome phenomena by way of the decisive support condition."
It exists; even so, it attains a state of oneness in meaning.

Nevertheless, because each [preceding consciousness] has the capacity to give rise to its own corresponding succeeding state of consciousness, the quality of "immediacy" (*anantaratā*) should be understood; and because the preceding consciousness possesses a powerful efficacy in producing the succeeding consciousness, it should be understood as an "immediate decisive support condition" (*anantarūpanissaya*).
For example, among the root-conditions (*hetu-paccaya*) and others, [it supports] some phenomenon...
It arises even without a [preceding] consciousness, whereas the immediately preceding consciousness does not arise without it; there is indeed no arising of consciousness without [a cause].

Therefore, it is a powerful condition (*balavapaccaya*). Thus, the relation of proximity (*anantarapaccaya*) should be understood as being by way of the arising of a suitable consciousness immediately following its own [predecessor], while the relation of proximity-support (*anantarūpanissaya*) is by way of a powerful cause; such is the distinction between them.
Natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) means a decisive support that is natural. "Natural" refers to things produced within one's own continuum, such as faith, virtue, and so forth;
or things utilized, such as climate and food. Alternatively, a decisive support by its very nature is a "natural decisive support";
the meaning is that it is unmixed with objects (*ārammaṇa*) or immediate antecedents (*anantara*). Regarding this: "Natural decisive support—faith..."

Relying upon [a certain person], one gives a gift, undertakes moral discipline, performs the Uposatha rite, arouses jhāna, arouses insight, arouses the Path, arouses direct knowledge, or arouses meditative attainment.
Relying upon moral discipline… learning… generosity… wisdom, one gives a gift… [and so on] … arouses meditative attainment. Faith… moral discipline… [and so on].

The manifold classification should be understood according to this method: “Learning... generosity... wisdom is a condition for faith... virtue... learning... generosity... wisdom by way of decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*),” and so forth.
Thus, these qualities beginning with faith are called “natural decisive supports” (*pakatūpanissaya*) because they are both natural and possess the sense of being powerful causes.
A state that, having arisen earlier, assists by its presence as a supporting condition is the *purejāta-paccaya* (pre-arising condition).

This is elevenfold, consisting of the bases and objects at the five doors and the heart-base. As it is said: "The eye-base is a pre-arising condition, by way of the pre-arising condition, for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated with it. [So too are] the ear... nose... tongue... body-base..."

The base of visible form, the base of sound, the base of odor, the base of flavor, and the base of tangible objects are related to body-consciousness and its associated mental states by way of the condition of pre-existence (*purejāta-paccaya*).

The bases of visible form, sound, odor, flavor, and tangible objects are related to mind-element (*manodhātu*) and its associated mental states by way of the condition of pre-existence. Whatever material form depending upon which the mind-element [arises]...
When the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element proceed, that form is a pre-arising condition for the mind-element and for the states associated with it;
it is a pre-arising condition for the mind-consciousness-element and for the states associated with it at some times,
but at other times it is not a pre-arising condition.

A non-material phenomenon that assists pre-arisen material phenomena by way of providing support is a postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*), like the volition of desire for food in the bodies of young vultures. Therefore it is said:
"Postnascent states of consciousness and mental factors are a condition, by way of postnascence condition, for this pre-arisen body."

The *āsevanapaccaya* (repetition condition) is a state that assists subsequent states in attaining a state of proficiency and strength by way of repetition, like prior application to books and so forth.
It is threefold, according to wholesome, unwholesome, and functional javanas. As it is said:
"Preceding wholesome states are related to succeeding wholesome states by way of the repetition condition."

Condition: Preceding unwholesome states... [and so on] ...or functional-ineffective states are related to subsequent functional-ineffective states by way of the condition of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*).
A state that assists by means of the state of activity known as mental application (*cittapayoga*) is the kamma-condition (*kamma-paccaya*). It is [of two kinds]: asynchronous (*nānākkhaṇika*)...
Furthermore, it is twofold by way of both wholesome and unwholesome volition that is co-nascent with [the resultant], as well as by way of all volition generally. As it is said:
"Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition for resultant aggregates and for kamma-produced matter by way of kamma-condition;
volition is a condition for associated states and for matter originated by them by way of kamma-condition."
A resultant state that, by its quality of being effortless and peaceful, assists toward the state of being effortless and peaceful, is a resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*).

It serves as a resultant condition for mind-produced matter during the course of existence (*pavatta*), for the matter of past deeds (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and for all associated states everywhere.
As it has been said: "One resultant indeterminate aggregate is a condition for three aggregates and for mind-produced matter."
Material phenomena are related to material phenomena by way of resultant condition... [as before] ...At the moment of rebirth-linking, one resultant indeterminate aggregate...
[as before] ...two aggregates are related to two aggregates and to the kamma-produced material phenomena by way of resultant condition.
Aggregates are related to the physical basis by way of resultant condition.
The four nutriments (*āhāra*) that assist by way of supporting both the material and the immaterial are the nutriment condition (*āhārapaccaya*). As it is said:

"Physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) is a condition for this body by way of the nutriment condition; the immaterial nutriments are a condition for associated states and for the material phenomena originated by them by way of the nutriment condition.
Furthermore, in the *Pañhāvāra* (the Chapter on Questions), regarding the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*):

It is also said: "Nutriments that are indeterminate by way of result (vipākābyākatā) are a condition, by way of nutriment-condition (āhārapaccaya), for the associated aggregates (sampayuttakānaṃ khandhānaṃ) and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā rūpānaṃ).

The twenty faculties, excluding the female faculty (itthindriya) and the male faculty (purisindriya), are the faculty-condition (indriyapaccaya) in the sense of being supportive through their predominance (adhipati).

Among these, the five beginning with the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*) are conditions for immaterial phenomena alone; the remaining ones are conditions for both material and immaterial phenomena. As it is said:

"The eye-faculty is a condition by way of faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated with it; the ear... nose... tongue... and body-faculty are conditions by way of faculty-condition for the body-consciousness element and for the states associated with it. The material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is a condition for kamma-produced materiality (*kaṭattārūpa*)."

It is a condition by way of faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*). The immaterial faculties are a condition by way of faculty-condition for the associated states and for the material phenomena produced by them.

Furthermore, in the *Pañhāvāra* (Chapter on Questions), it is also stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate faculties are a condition by way of faculty-condition for the associated aggregates and for the [material] phenomena born of kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*)."

In the sense of being closely reflected upon, with the exception of those factors that are supportive, the two types of bodily feeling—pleasure and pain—and all seven jhāna factors (whether wholesome or otherwise) are the jhāna condition for the two sets of fivefold consciousness. As it is said:

"The jhāna factors are a condition by way of jhāna condition for the states associated with jhāna and for the material phenomena originated by them. However, in the *Pañhāvāra* (Chapter on Questions), at the moment of rebirth-linking...

It is also stated: "The jhāna factors that are indeterminate by way of result (vipākābyākatāni) are a condition for their associated aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of the jhāna-condition.
Furthermore, the twelve path factors—classified as wholesome and so forth—which are helpful in the sense of leading out from this or that [state], are the path-condition (maggapaccaya).
As it is said: “The path factors are a condition, by way of path-condition, for those states associated with the path and for the material phenomena originated by them.

However, in the *Pañhāvāra*, it is stated: “At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate path factors are a condition, by way of path-condition, for the associated aggregates and for the material phenomena produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*). Yet, these two [statements] are not...
It should be understood that, by way of the conditions of jhāna and path, these are found respectively in the two types of fivefold sense-consciousness and in rootless consciousness.

The immaterial states that assist through the state of association—defined as having the same physical basis, the same object, simultaneous arising, and simultaneous cessation—are the associated condition (*sampayuttapaccaya*).
As it is said: "The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of the associated condition."

Material phenomena that assist immaterial phenomena, and immaterial phenomena that assist material phenomena, by not reaching the state of having a single basis (*ekavatthuka*) and so forth, are related to one another by way of dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*). This is threefold, according to the categories of conascence, post-nascence, and pre-nascence. For it has been said:
"Conascent wholesome aggregates are related to mind-produced matter by way of dissociation condition."
Post-nascent wholesome aggregates are related to this pre-nascent body by way of dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*).

Furthermore, in the analysis of co-nascence regarding the indeterminate category: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate aggregates are related to the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) by way of dissociation condition.
Aggregates are related to the physical heart-base, and the physical heart-base is related to the aggregates, by way of dissociation condition."
"...is a condition," it is said. However, the pre-arisen [condition] should be understood solely by way of the bases (vatthu) such as the eye-faculty and so forth.

As it has been said: "The pre-arisen eye-base is a condition for eye-consciousness... [and so on] ...the body-base is a condition for body-consciousness by way of dissociation-condition (vippayuttapaccaya).
The base is a condition for resultant-indeterminate and functional-indeterminate aggregates; the base is a condition for wholesome aggregates."
The basis (vatthu) is a condition for unwholesome aggregates by way of the dissociation-condition (vippayutta-paccaya).
An existing phenomenon that assists another such phenomenon by way of providing support through its presence characterized by the present moment is the presence-condition (atthi-paccaya).
This [condition] exists by way of the immaterial aggregates, the great elements, mind-and-matter, consciousness, mental factors, the great elements, the sense bases, and the physical basis (vatthu).
The matrix is set forth in seven ways. As it has been said: "The four formless aggregates are a condition for one another by way of the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*);
the four great elements are [a condition] for one another; at the moment of descent [into the womb], name-and-form are [a condition] for one another;

mental states and mental factors are [a condition] for mind-originated matter, for the great elements, and for derived matter; the eye-base is [a condition] for the eye-consciousness-element... and so on."
The body-base … pe … the visible-form base … pe … the tangible-object base is a condition by way of presence-condition for the body-consciousness element and for the states associated with it.
The visible-form base … pe … the tangible-object base is a condition by way of presence-condition for the mind-element and for the states associated with it.
Whatever material form depending upon which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness element [arise] … [is a condition by way of presence-condition].
And that material form is a condition by way of presence-condition for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental states associated with them.

In the Section on Questions (Pañhāvāra), however, having set forth conascence, prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty, first regarding conascence: "One aggregate is a condition for three aggregates and for mind-originated material phenomena..."
The exposition is made according to the method beginning with: "Visible forms are a condition for [mental states] by way of the presence-condition.
Regarding the pre-arisen: the exposition is made by way of the pre-arisen eye and so forth. Regarding the post-arisen:
the exposition is made by way of the condition of the post-arisen mind and mental factors for this pre-arisen body. As for nutriment and faculties, however: "Edible food... [and so on].
"The material life-faculty is a condition, by way of presence-condition, for the kamma-produced material phenomena.
Thus is the exposition made.
[The mind-element] is helpful by providing an occasion for the occurrence of the immaterial states arising immediately after itself; it is that which has ceased in immediate succession.

Non-material phenomena (arūpadhammā) are the non-existence condition (natthipaccaya). As it is said: "Mind and mental factors that have ceased immediately prior are a condition for present mind and mental factors by way of the non-existence condition.

Because they are helpful by virtue of having disappeared, they are also the disappearance condition (vigatapaccaya). As it is said: "Mind and mental factors that have just disappeared are a condition for present mind and mental factors by way of the disappearance condition."

The states that are presence-conditions (atthipaccaya-dhamma) should be understood as the non-disappearance-condition (avigatapaccaya) because they provide assistance by way of their non-disappearance.

However, this dyad was stated either for the sake of the Teacher’s pedagogical skill or according to the needs of those to be trained; it is like the dyad of "associated with a root" (hetusampayutta) being stated even after the dyad of "with root" (sahetuka) has already been mentioned.
Now, for the purpose of avoiding confusion regarding these twenty-four conditions:
The exposition should be understood according to the nature of the phenomena, according to time, according to their various classifications,

and according to the arising from conditions. Therein, "according to the nature of the phenomena" means that among these conditions, the root-condition (hetupaccaya) is, first of all, a portion of the mental phenomena within the categories of both mind and matter.

The object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) consists of all mental and physical phenomena (*nāma-rūpa-dhammā*), together with their conceptual designations (*paññatti*). In the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) is a portion of mental phenomena;
likewise for the conditions of kamma, jhāna, and the path. Object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) consists of all objects worthy of being treated as important.

The conditions of proximity (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), post-nascence (*pacchājāta*), repetition (*āsevana*), fruition (*vipāka*), association (*sampayutta*), absence (*natthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*) [are explained accordingly].

They are merely mental phenomena (*nāmadhamma*). Since *nibbāna* is not included therein, it is also appropriate to say that it is a portion of mental phenomena. The pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) is a portion of material phenomena (*rūpa*).

The remaining conditions are, according to their occurrence, both mental and material phenomena. Thus, first, the analysis should be understood here from the perspective of the phenomena themselves. As for "from the perspective of time":
In this [dependent origination], fifteen conditions are present; five are past;
and one is both past and present. Thus it relies on two times.
Three are of all three times, and some are also free from time.

Among these, the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*), and the fifteen conditions consisting of co-nascence, mutuality, support, prenascence, postnascence, fruition, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance, are all present phenomena. The five conditions—proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance—are past only.
However, the single kamma-condition depends upon both the present and the past times.

The remaining three conditions—the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), and the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*)—belong to all three times;
however, because they include Nibbāna along with its designation (*paññatti*), they are also timeless. Thus, the analysis herein should be understood according to time as well.
The meaning of these two phrases—“from the division into various kinds” and “as arisen by way of condition”—will become clear in the section on the exposition (Niddesavāra).
This concludes the commentary on the enumeration of conditions (Paccayuddesavaṇṇanā). Now follows the exposition of conditions (Paccayaniddesa).
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Root Condition (Hetupaccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) Now, in order to demonstrate all those conditions by explaining them in the order they were enumerated, it is said:
"The root condition: roots are a condition, by way of the root condition, for the states associated with the roots and for the material phenomena originated by them," and so forth.
In this context, "root condition" (*hetupaccaya*) is the extraction of the term to be analyzed first of all in the sequence established among the twenty-four conditions.
It should be understood that for the remaining conditions as well, the answer is formulated by first extracting the term to be analyzed in the same manner.
This, however, is the connection here: that which was listed in the enumeration of conditions as "root condition."

Thus, from the detailed exposition, it should be understood as follows: "Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for states associated with roots and for the material phenomena originated thereby.
By this method, the connection should be understood through the answering of the passage to be analyzed for all conditions.

Now, regarding the phrase "the roots [are conditions] for those associated with roots": why is it stated as "the roots [are conditions] for those associated with roots," rather than simply saying "for those associated with roots"?
It is because of the establishment of both the condition and the conditioned.

For if it were said "for those associated with roots," the meaning would be that [the roots] are a condition by way of the root-condition for those things associated with the root. This being the case...
The determination of conditions— such as "this specific phenomenon is a condition by way of the root-condition"— would not be discernible. Furthermore,
if one were to disregard the meaning of "root-associates" (hetusampayuttaka) as those associated with the root,

and instead take the meaning to be that "the root is a condition by way of the root-condition for any associates whatsoever," then even eye-consciousness and the rest, which are dissociated from the root, would [likewise be so].
Even wholesome states and so forth are associated with the cause only through association.

In that case, the determination of conditions—namely, "this cause is the condition for such-and-such an associated state"—would not be discerned. Therefore, while determining both the condition and the conditioned, he said:
"Causes [are conditions] for those associated with the cause. The meaning of this is: for those associated with the cause.
That which is the associated cause of wholesome and other states is a condition by way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*).
Even there, instead of simply saying "condition," the expression "by way of the root-condition" is used for the purpose of precluding any other mode of being a condition for the root.

For this root is a condition both as a root-condition and also as a co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and other types of conditions. Among these, that which [occurs] by way of the co-nascent and other conditions...
The state of being a condition exists in other ways as well; therefore, it is stated "by way of the root-condition" (*hetupaccaya*) in order to exclude those.
Even so, why is it said "associated with the roots" (*hetusampayuttakānaṃ*) instead of saying "associated with that" (*taṃsampayuttakānaṃ*)?
It is because that which is to be demonstrated is not yet manifest. For if it were said "associated with that," [the question would arise: by what means do they become "associated with that"? This...
The word "name" (nāma) is to be demonstrated as something unmanifest. Because it is unmanifest, those factors associated with it are called "associated with that";
in order to show this by its very nature, the phrase "associated with causes" (hetusampayuttakānaṃ) is stated.

However, in the case of the term "originated from that" (taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ), the inclusion of the word "that" (taṃ) is made because what is to be demonstrated is manifest. This, then, is the point here.
The meaning is as follows: those things which have both the roots and the states associated with the roots as their origin are "originated from them" (*taṃsamuṭṭhānāni*).
The meaning of "of those originated from them" is: of those produced by both the roots and the states associated with the roots.
By this, he includes mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*). But does that [matter] also originate from something other than the mind? Yes.
It originates. For indeed, all mind and mental factors, having come together as one, originate matter.
However, in the teaching on mundane phenomena (*lokiyadhamma*), because of the predominance of the mind, such matter is called "mind-originated" (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*). Therefore it was said:
"Mind and mental factors are a condition for mind-originated matter by way of the co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*)."
If this is so, why is it not stated here as well—instead of saying "of those originated by that"—simply "citta-samutthānānaṃ" (of those originated by consciousness)?

It is because [the term] includes even those not originated by consciousness. For in the *Pañhāvāra* (Chapter on Questions), it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate roots are a condition, by way of the root-condition, for the associated aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma."
For the sake of including that [matter], instead of saying here "arisen from consciousness" (*cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ*), it is said "arisen from those" (*taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ*).

Its meaning is as follows: although they do not produce matter born of consciousness, those roots and the states associated with the roots have these [material qualities] as their source by way of such conditions as co-nascence;
thus, they are "arisen from those. Of those arisen from those, which are born of consciousness during the course of existence (*pavatta*) and at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)—
"Even for the material phenomena produced by kamma (kaṭattārūpa), the cause is a condition by way of the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya).
By this method, the meaning should be understood in other instances where the phrase "produced by that" (taṃsamuṭṭhāna) occurs.
But why is this root-cause a root-cause condition for the material phenomena produced by kamma only at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), and not during the course of existence (pavatti)?
Because at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the material phenomena born of kamma have an existence dependent upon consciousness.
For at the moment of rebirth-linking, the occurrence of kamma-born material phenomena is dependent on consciousness; they arise and persist by the power of consciousness.
At that moment, consciousness is unable to produce consciousness-born material phenomena, nor can those [kamma-born phenomena] arise or persist without consciousness.
Therefore it was said: "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form; when consciousness is established, there is the descent of name-and-form.
However, in the course of existence, even though these [faculties] exist in the mind, their occurrence is dependent on kamma, not dependent on the mind.
Furthermore, they arise even for those who have attained the cessation of perception and feeling, even though the mind is absent.
But why is it that at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), consciousness is unable to produce mind-born matter (cittajarūpa)?

It is because it is weak due to being impelled by the force of karma (*kammavega*) and having no established basis (*appatiṭṭhitavatthu*). For at that time, it is impelled by the force of karma and—because its pre-arising bases (*purejātavatthu*) are absent—it lacks an established basis;
thus it is weak. Therefore, it is like a man who has just fallen down a precipice and cannot perform any craft.

It is not able to produce or generate form; rather, only kamma-born matter remains in the place where mind-originated matter stands. And that [kamma-born matter] stands in the place of the seed for kamma-born matter itself. Kamma, however, is like a field, and the defilements are like water.
Therefore, even though the field and the water exist, at the time of the first arising, the growth of a tree occurs through the power of the seed.

Just as at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the material body arises through the power of consciousness, so too, even when the seed has vanished, the tree continues to grow higher and higher through the power of earth and water.
It should be understood that in the same way, the occurrence of the materiality of past action (*kaṭattārūpa*) takes place through kamma alone, even without consciousness.
And this has been said: "Kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture."

Furthermore, this meaning should be understood by way of the "bases" (okāsa) alone. For there are three bases: the base of name (nāmokāsa), the base of form (rūpokāsa), and the base of both name and form (nāmarūpokāsa).
Among these, the immaterial existence (arūpabhava) is called the base of name; for there, immaterial phenomena arise even without a material condition such as the heart-base (hadayavatthu).
The non-percipient existence (asaññabhava) is called the base of form; for there, even the mere rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) [does not arise].
Material phenomena arise even without the condition of the immaterial. The five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) is called the sphere of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

For therein, at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), neither do immaterial phenomena arise without even a minimal amount of physical basis (vatthurūpa), nor do material phenomena born of kamma arise without the rebirth-linking consciousness.
The arising of the material and immaterial occurs as an inseparable union (yuganaddha). Just as [it would be impossible] in the case of a kingdom with its owner and its king...
In a house with good gatekeepers, there is no first entry without the king’s command; however, at a later time, even without a command, entry occurs solely by the power of the previous command.

In the same way, in the five-aggregate plane, there is no first arising of matter by way of rebirth-linking without the co-nascent and other conditions provided by the king that is the rebirth-linking consciousness. At a later time...

However, even without the influence of the co-nascent and other conditions for rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), the process of existence (*pavatti*) proceeds from karma that has already gained entry by virtue of its prior influence.

Since the non-percipient state (*asaññabhava*) is not a formless realm (*arūpokāsa*), matter (*rūpa*) proceeds there even without formless conditions, due to the presence of the non-percipient sphere; it is like a man in an ownerless empty house or in his own house.

It is like entering [a house]. Since the immaterial existence (arūpabhava) is not a place for form, immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) proceed there even without a condition consisting of form, because there is another space.
However, the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava) is a place for both form and the immaterial;

thus, at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhikkhaṇa), there is no arising of forms here without a condition consisting of the immaterial. Therefore, this cause [of the arising of form] exists only in rebirth-linking.
It is a condition for the material phenomena produced by past karma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*), but it does not cause them to arise.
Now, when it is stated that "the roots are a condition for co-nascent [phenomena] by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*)," is not all this meaning already included?
Why, then, is this further specified: "for the states associated with the roots and for the material phenomena originated by them"?
Because it excludes the status of being a condition for the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*) and so forth during the course of existence (*pavatti*).

For if that were the case, then those matter-produced-by-kamma and those produced by temperature and nutriment which arise at the same moment as the cause during the course of existence would also have to be considered "cause-condition" (*hetupaccaya*) for that cause;
yet it is not a condition for them. Therefore, regarding their status as conditions...
It should be understood that this was taken for the purpose of exclusion.
Now, the exposition to be understood here should be given by way of these two phrases: "according to the division into various types" and "according to the arising from conditions.

Among these, regarding "according to the division into various types": this so-called cause, by way of its genus, is divided into the wholesome (*kusala*), unwholesome (*akusala*), resultant (*vipāka*), and functional (*kiriya*).
It is fourfold. Therein, the wholesome root is fourfold according to the difference in planes, namely, the sense-sphere and so forth;

the unwholesome root is only of the sense-sphere; the resultant root is fourfold according to the difference in planes, namely, the sense-sphere and so forth; and the functional root is threefold: of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
Therein, the wholesome root of the sense-sphere is threefold by name, according to non-greed and the others.
The same method applies to the wholesome roots of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth. The unwholesome roots are threefold by way of greed (*lobha*) and the rest.

However, the resultant and functional roots are each threefold by way of non-greed (*alobha*) and the rest. Yet, according to their association with this or that consciousness, there is indeed a manifold variety of these various roots.
Thus, first, the analysis should be understood here by way of its manifold variety.
"By way of being conditionally arisen": the meaning is that the exposition should also be understood thus: "By this condition these states arise; this is the condition for these named states.

In this regard, first, within the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), the wholesome root of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala-hetu*) is a root-condition for both the states associated with itself and the mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*) in the realms of sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) and fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*).

In the immaterial realm (*arūpabhava*), it is a condition for associated states alone. A wholesome root of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacarakusalahetu*) is a root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) for both associated states and mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*) in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*) and the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*) alone. A wholesome root of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacarakusalahetu*) is similar to a wholesome root of the sense-sphere.

Likewise is a wholesome root not included [within the realms] (*apariyāpannakusalahetu*); likewise is an unwholesome root (*akusalahetu*). A resultant root of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacaravipākahetu*)...

Furthermore, in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) alone, the resultant root-cause (vipākahetu) is a root-condition for the mental states associated with itself, for the kamma-produced material phenomena (kaṭattārūpa) at rebirth-linking, and for the mind-originated material phenomena during the course of existence.
In the fine-material existence (rūpabhava), the resultant root-cause of the fine-material sphere is a root-condition for those very same types of phenomena mentioned above.

In the immaterial existence (arūpabhava), the resultant root-cause of the immaterial sphere is a root-condition only for the associated mental states. As for the resultant root-cause not included within the realms of existence (apariyāpanna-vipākahetu):

In the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), the root condition (*hetupaccaya*) is a condition for both the associated mental states and the mind-originated matter; in immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), it is a condition for immaterial phenomena alone.

However, among functional roots (*kiriyahetu*), even though they belong to the three planes of existence, the condition is similar to that of wholesome roots (*kusalahetu*). Thus, the analysis [of the root condition] should be understood here also by way of what arises through that condition.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Root Condition.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Object Condition.
In the exposition of the object condition, "visible base" (*rūpāyatana*) refers to the base known as visible form. The same method applies to the remaining [bases] as well.
"Of the eye-consciousness element" means of the element designated as eye-consciousness. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"Of those associated with it" means of the three aggregates associated with that eye-consciousness element;
[it is] the visible-object base that serves as the object-condition for all four aggregates having the sensitive eye-faculty as their physical basis.
The meaning is "condition. This same method applies to the following cases as well.

For the mind-element (*manodhātu*)—that is, for all three types of mind-element together with their associated mental states—the five sense bases beginning with the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) are conditions by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), but not within a single moment.
"All phenomena" refers to these five beginning with the visible-form base, as well as all remaining knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*); these six...

The meaning is that, setting aside the [six] elements, the remaining mental-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu), together with its associated states, is a condition by way of object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya).

By the phrase "taking whatever state as an object," it is meant that those states which have been described as the objects of these seven consciousness-elements become an object-condition precisely at the moment they arise having made those elements their object.

He demonstrates that they "exist. Furthermore, he demonstrates that even while existing, they do not exist as one; rather, whatever [consciousness] arises with reference to whatever [object], those respective [objects] serve as the object-condition for each of those [consciousnesses] individually.
It should be understood that the statement "they arise" is spoken by way of including all time, just as it is said, "rivers flow" or "mountains stand."

Therefore, it is established that whatever [mental states] have arisen, and whatever will arise, with respect to these [objects], all of them have arisen and will arise solely by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). "States of consciousness and mental factors" is a specific illustration of those states referred to as "whatever states.
"Those respective states" refers to those respective objective states. Of these...
"Of these" means of those various states of consciousness and mental factors. This, then, is the commentary on the text here.
Now, as for this so-called "object," it is sixfold by way of categories: the object of visible form, the object of sound, odor, flavor, tangible object, and mental phenomena.
Therein, setting aside the concept (paññatti), the remainder is, according to plane: belonging to the sense sphere... [etc. ...or unincluded (apariyāpanna).
It is fourfold. Therein, the sense-sphere consciousness is fivefold, by way of the division into wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material;

the fine-material-sphere consciousness is threefold, by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional; likewise the immaterial-sphere consciousness; and the non-encompassed (supramundane) is threefold, by way of wholesome, resultant, and Nibbāna.
Or alternatively, all of this is [fivefold] by way of the division into wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, material, Nibbāna, and conceptualization (paññatti).
It is sevenfold. Therein, the wholesome is fourfold according to the distinction of planes; the unwholesome belongs only to the sense-sphere plane;

the resultant belongs to the four planes; the functional belongs to three planes; the material is of one plane, namely the sense-sphere alone; Nibbāna is also of one plane, being entirely non-included (apariyāpanna);
and the conceptual (paññatti) is independent of any plane. Thus, herein, it is according to the distinction of various modes.
The detailed exposition should be understood.
When this object is thus divided, an object consisting of sense-sphere wholesome states is the object of these:

sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, fine-material-sphere wholesome consciousness, unwholesome consciousness, sense-sphere resultant consciousness, sense-sphere functional consciousness, and fine-material-sphere functional consciousness.

The object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) pertains to six groups. An object belonging to the fine-material-sphere wholesome (rūpāvacara-kusala) serves as the object-condition for five of those six groups, excluding the sense-sphere resultant (kāmāvacara-vipāka).

An object belonging to the immaterial-sphere wholesome (arūpāvacara-kusala) serves as the object-condition for the sense-sphere wholesome, the fine-material-sphere wholesome, the immaterial-sphere wholesome, the unwholesome (akusala), and the immaterial-sphere resultant.

It is the object-condition for these eight groups: [the wholesome and unwholesome of the sense sphere], the functional of the sense sphere, the functional of the fine-material sphere, and the functional of the immaterial sphere.
An object that is unincluded (apariyāpanna) and wholesome is the object-condition only for the wholesome and functional consciousnesses of the sense and fine-material spheres.
An unwholesome object is [the object-condition] for the wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses of the sense and fine-material spheres.
The object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) pertains to these six groups: [it is the object-condition] for sense-sphere resultant, and for sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere functional states.

An object that is a sense-sphere resultant state is the object-condition for these six groups: sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, sense-sphere resultant, and sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere functional states. An object that is a fine-material-sphere resultant state...

The object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) pertains to these five groups: wholesome states of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, unwholesome states, and functional states of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere.
Furthermore, the object-condition for the resultant states of the immaterial sphere also pertains to these same five groups.
The object-condition for the resultant states not included in the mundane spheres pertains only to the wholesome and functional states of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere.
It is an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

An object that is sense-sphere functional (*kāmāvacara-kiriya*) is an object-condition for these six groups: sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, sense-sphere resultant, and sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere functional. An object that is fine-material-sphere functional...
Among these six groups, the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) exists for five of the groups, excluding the sense-sphere resultant group.

The object of immaterial-sphere functional consciousness is the object-condition for those five [immaterial-sphere resultant] groups and for the immaterial-sphere functional group—thus it is the object-condition for these six groups. The material object, consisting of the aggregate of matter produced by the four origins, is likewise an object-condition.

It is the object-condition for these six groups: wholesome states of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, unwholesome states, sense-sphere resultant states, and sense-sphere and fine-material sphere functional states.
That which has Nibbāna as its object is the object-condition for these six:
wholesome states of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, wholesome-resultant states (because they are not included in the mundane), and sense-sphere and fine-material sphere functional states.

It is an object-condition for those [states] that are present. Some maintain that it is also an object-condition for wholesome and functional states of the fine-material sphere; this should be examined according to logic.
However, the various kinds of conceptual objects (*paññatti-ārammaṇa*) are the object-condition for these nine types:
wholesome states of the three planes, unwholesome states, resultant states of the fine-material sphere, resultant states of the immaterial sphere, and functional states of the three planes.

It is an object-condition for those that are present. In this context, whichever object is the condition for whichever [mental states], those [states] are called "arisen from that respective condition.
Thus, the analysis here should be understood also by way of what has arisen from conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the object-condition.

3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Dominant Condition (Adhipatipaccaya-niddesa) Regarding the phrase "dominant by desire" (*chandādhipati*) in the exposition of the dominant condition: it is a dominant factor (*adhipati*) designated as "desire.
Having made desire the primary burden and having made desire the foremost at the moment of the arising of consciousness, this refers to the desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) that has arisen.

This is the name. The same method applies to the rest as well. But why, when in the exposition of the root condition it was stated, "Roots [are conditions] for those associated with roots," is the teaching here not given in that same way—by saying "Predominance is a condition for those associated with predominance"—but rather by the method beginning, "Desire-predominance is a condition for those associated with desire," and so forth?
It is because they do not exist simultaneously in a single moment. For in the former method, two or three roots [can coexist] even in a single moment.

The root-cause condition (*hetu-paccaya*) exists in the sense of being a root, because it does not abandon its state of being an auxiliary. The dominant condition (*adhipati*), however, is an auxiliary in the sense of being preeminent;

yet, there cannot be many things that are preeminent at one and the same moment. Therefore, even for those [factors] that have arisen together, there is no status as a dominant condition at one and the same moment.
Because of the absence of that status as a dominant condition at one and the same moment—
"Here, the teaching has been given thus.

Having thus shown the co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*), [the text] now begins with "whichever state one esteems highly" (*yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ garuṃ katvā*) and so forth, in order to show the object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
Therein, "whichever state" (*yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ*) means whichever state that serves as an object. "Esteeming highly" (*garuṃ katvā*)...
By way of respect and esteem, or by way of gratification, it is to be held dear, valued, not abandoned, and not disregarded.
"Those various states" refers to those various states worthy of respect. "Of those various" refers to those various states that exercise respect.
"By way of the predominance condition" means it serves as a condition by way of the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipatipaccaya*).
This, then, is the commentary on the text here.

This "predominance" (adhipati), moreover, is twofold: by way of co-nascence (sahajāta) and by way of object (ārammaṇa). Among these, that which is co-nascent is fourfold by way of desire (chanda) and so forth.

Each of those is fourfold according to plane (bhūmi) by way of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth. Among those, the sense-sphere [predominance] is threefold by way of the wholesome (kusala), the unwholesome (akusala), and the functional (kiriya).
It is threefold. However, here, when referring to the unwholesome, the predominance of investigation (*vīmaṃsādhipati*) is not obtained.
The fine-material and immaterial-sphere [predominances] are twofold by way of wholesome and functional; the non-included [predominance] is twofold by way of wholesome and resultant.

As for objective-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), it is sixfold according to the classification of its types, namely: the wholesome, the unwholesome, the resultant, the functional, the material, and Nibbāna. Thus, herein, it is distinguished by various modes.
The analysis should be understood as follows.
When this [classification] is thus divided, first regarding the co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*):

at the time of arising, when any one of desire (*chanda*) and so forth acts as the predominant factor among the two-rooted or three-rooted consciousness-moments designated as wholesome or functional of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), [it is the co-nascent predominance].

It is a predominance condition for the states associated with itself as well as for mind-produced matter. This same principle applies to what is termed wholesome and functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
However, this [predominance] is obtained exclusively [in those cases], for those states do not arise without a co-nascent predominance.
That which is termed wholesome and functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) is similar to the fine-material-sphere predominance within the fivefold existence (*pañcavokāra*).

In the fourfold plane (catuvokāra), however, only associated states (sampayuttadhamma) serve as the predominance condition (adhipatipaccaya). Likewise, all sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) predominances arising therein do so as well.

Furthermore, in the fivefold plane (pañcavokāra), an unperturbed (apariyāpanna) state—whether wholesome (kusala) or resultant (vipāka)—is invariably a predominance condition for both associated states and for mind-originated matter (cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa). In the fourfold plane, [it functions similarly].

Only for immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*). In the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*), unwholesome states (*akusala*) are exclusively a predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) for associated mental states within consciousnesses fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*), as well as for the matter originated by that consciousness.
Indeterminate states are a predominance condition for those same [mental states] at the time they themselves exercise predominance within both the sensual and fine-material realms (*rūpabhava*).
In the immaterial realm, they are a predominance condition only for immaterial phenomena. This...
Such is the method regarding the co-nascent predominance (sahajātādhipati).
Regarding objective predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), however, wholesome states of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) serve as the objective-predominance condition for these two groups:

wholesome states of the sense sphere and unwholesome states accompanied by greed (lobha). This also applies to the fine-material and immaterial spheres when wholesome states serve as the objective-predominance.

The same method applies here. Furthermore, a wholesome state not included within the mundane (apariyāpanna-kusala) serves as an object-predominance condition for both wholesome states associated with knowledge and functional states associated with knowledge belonging to the sense sphere.
An unwholesome state called "object-predominance" refers to a mental arising accompanied by greed; it serves as an object-predominance condition only for unwholesome states accompanied by greed.

[The predominance condition] exists. However, the predominance of an object that is a resultant [state] belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) is a predominance-condition only for unwholesome states accompanied by greed.

Likewise, the predominance of an object that is a resultant [state] belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) [functions similarly]. Furthermore, the predominance of an object that is a resultant [state] belonging to the supramundane (lokuttara) is a predominance-condition only for wholesome or functional states associated with knowledge belonging to the sense-sphere. [This classification is made] according to the distinctions of the sense-sphere and so forth.
Furthermore, all three types [of objects] serve as the object-predominance condition only for unwholesome states accompanied by greed.
The aggregate of form, comprised of matter produced by the fourfold origination, serves as the object-predominance condition only for unwholesome states accompanied by greed.
Nibbāna serves as the object-predominance condition for wholesome states associated with knowledge and for functional states associated with knowledge belonging to the sense-sphere.
The predominance condition (adhipatipaccaya) applies to these four groups: wholesome supramundane states and their supramundane resultants.
Thus, the analysis here should be understood also by way of the state of being produced by conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the predominance condition.

4. Explanation of the Description of the Proximity Condition (Anantara-paccaya-niddesa) In the description of the proximity condition: "By the mind-element" (manodhātu) means by the resultant mind-element (*vipāka-manodhātu*). "By the mind-consciousness-element" (manoviññāṇadhātu) means by the rootless resultant mind-consciousness-element whose function is investigating (*santīraṇa*).
