Following that, however, [there occur] the functions of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), impulsion (*javana*), registration (*tadārammaṇa*), and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

The mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) should have been mentioned; however, even though they were not explicitly stated, they are to be understood by this same method. Thus, having shown the method, the teaching was condensed.

Furthermore, it should be understood that those [elements] are included in the sixth method beginning with "preceding wholesome states" (*purimā purimā kusalā dhammā*), and for that reason they are not mentioned here.
In that context, "preceding, preceding" refers to the wholesome impulsion-moments (*javana-dhamma*) that have just passed away at all six doors.
[They] should be seen. "Of each subsequent [consciousness]" means precisely those that arise immediately after. "Wholesome" refers to wholesome states of a similar kind.

As for "indeterminate," this is stated with reference to the object-attaining consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) following a wholesome state.

In the section based on the unwholesome, "indeterminate" refers specifically to those termed object-attaining and life-continuum. In the section based on the indeterminate, "indeterminate" [refers to those same types].

This same principle applies to the process-consciousnesses occurring in the course of functional, resultant, and indeterminate states— whether proceeding by way of adverting and impulsion, or by way of the life-continuum—

from the moment of the functional mind-element up to the mind-consciousness-element performing the function of determining, as well as to those occurring in the five sense doors immediately following determining,

and in the mind door immediately following adverting. Regarding "wholesome" states, this refers to those occurring in the five sense doors immediately after determining, and in the mind door immediately after adverting.
[This refers to] the first impulsion wholesome states. The same method applies to the word "unwholesome" as well.
"Of whichever [states]" refers to all those phenomena that serve as immediate conditions (*anantarapaccaya*). This is the summary characteristic; this, then, is the commentary on the text here.
Furthermore, this so-called immediate condition consists solely of the immaterial dhammas of the four planes, excluding Nibbāna.
It should be understood. By way of birth, it is divided into four types: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional.
Among these, the wholesome is fourfold according to the distinctions of the sense-sphere and so forth; the unwholesome belongs only to the sense-sphere; the resultant belongs to all four planes;
and the functional condition (anantarapaccaya) belongs to those same planes. Thus, the analysis here should be understood through its various modes of classification.

When analyzed in this way, here a wholesome state of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-kusala) serves as the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) only for a wholesome state of the sense-sphere that is similar to itself.
However, a wholesome state of the sense-sphere associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta-kāmāvacara-kusala) serves as the proximity condition for these three groups:
the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), and the supramundane (lokuttara). Thus, the wholesome state of the sense-sphere...

And it is the immediate condition for these four groups: for sense-sphere resultant [consciousness], for fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere resultant [consciousness], and for supramundane resultant [consciousness] associated with knowledge.
Wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere is the immediate condition for these three groups:
for wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere, for sense-sphere resultant consciousness associated with knowledge, and for fine-material-sphere resultant consciousness.

The wholesome consciousness of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara-kusala*) is the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for those two types of fruition (*vipāka*), for its own wholesome fruition, and thus generally for four groups.

Specifically, however, the wholesome consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-kusala*) is also the proximity condition for the supramundane fruition known as the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). The same applies to the wholesome consciousness of the supramundane (*lokuttara-kusala*).

It is a condition by way of proximity (anantara-paccaya) only for supramundane resultant consciousness. An unwholesome state is [a condition] generally for both the unwholesome and for wholesome-unwholesome resultant consciousness.
Specifically, however, here an unwholesome state associated with pleasant or neutral feeling is also a condition for the resultant consciousness of the fine-material and immaterial spheres;
thus, it serves as a condition by way of proximity for these four groups.
The resultant consciousness of the sense sphere—whether associated with knowledge or dissociated from knowledge—is the proximity condition for the functional advertence of the sense sphere;
furthermore, the resultant consciousness associated with knowledge here is also the proximity condition for the fine-material and immaterial sphere resultants arising by way of rebirth-linking.
Thus, it is the proximity condition for these four groups. The fine-material sphere resultant is [the proximity condition] for the sense-sphere resultant accompanied by roots.
The resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere is the proximity condition for these four groups:

the resultant consciousness of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, and the functional adverting consciousness of the sense-sphere. The immaterial-sphere resultant consciousness is the proximity condition for three groups:

the three-rooted resultant consciousness of the sense-sphere, the immaterial-sphere resultant consciousness, and the functional adverting consciousness of the sense-sphere. The supramundane resultant consciousness...

It is the proximity condition for four groups: for the resultants of the sense sphere with three roots, and for the resultants of the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the supramundane.

Sense-sphere functional consciousness is the proximity condition for sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome consciousness, for the resultants of the four planes, and for functional consciousness of the three planes.
The functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere is the proximity condition for nine groups:

it is the proximity condition for the threefold-rooted resultant consciousness of the sense-sphere, the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere, and the functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere. The functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere is the proximity condition for five groups:

it is the proximity condition for the threefold-rooted resultant consciousness of the sense-sphere, the resultant consciousness of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, the supramundane resultant consciousness, and the functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere.
"It is the proximity condition for the five groups. Thus, the analysis here should be understood also by way of what has arisen through conditions.
Explanation of the Description of the Proximity Condition. 5.
Explanation of the Description of the Immediate Condition.

5. The exposition of the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-paccaya*) follows the same method as this. These two conditions, however, are of great extent; therefore, their detailed exposition should be understood by examining them in relation to the arising of all types of consciousness.
Explanation of the Exposition of the Condition of Immediate Succession. 6. Explanation of the Exposition of the Condition of Co-nascence (*sahajāta-paccaya*).

6. In the exposition of the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), "mutuality" (*aññamañña*) means one [factor] for another. By this, he illustrates both the state of being a condition and the state of being conditionally arisen for these phenomena at a single moment.
"At the moment of descent" (*okkantikkhaṇe*) refers to the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*).
For at that moment, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is as if descending, as if leaping forth from the world beyond.
It arises as if entering and descending into this world; therefore, that moment is called the "moment of descent" (*okkantikkhaṇo*).

And here, by "matter" (*rūpa*), only the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) is intended. For that [base] exercises the function of a co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) for the mind, and the mind exercises it for that [base], each upon the other.
By "mind and mental factors" (*cittacetasika*), the four aggregates during the course of existence (*pavatti*) are meant. By "co-nascent condition" (*sahajātapaccayena*)...

In this context, material phenomena produced by consciousness (cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa) do not exercise the function of a condition for consciousness and mental factors; therefore, they are not described as "mutually" related.

Likewise, derived matter (upādārūpa) does not so relate to the primary elements (bhūta). As for "material phenomena [are conditions] for immaterial phenomena," this refers to the heart-base being a condition for the four aggregates.
"At some time" means at a certain time. "By way of the co-nascence condition" refers to the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

This was stated with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). The statement “not by way of the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*)” was made with reference to the process of active occurrence (*pavatti*).
This [condition], however, is established in six categories as follows: “The four formless aggregates (*arūpa-khandha*) are a condition for one another by way of the co-nascent condition.
Among these, three categories are stated by way of mutual reciprocity (*aññamañña*), while three are not stated by way of mutual reciprocity.
In this regard, in the first section, the immaterial alone is both the condition and the conditionally arisen;

in the second, the material alone; in the third, name-and-form; in the fourth, the condition is immaterial and the conditionally arisen is material; in the fifth, both the condition and the conditionally arisen are material alone;
and in the sixth, the condition is material and the conditionally arisen is immaterial. This, then, is the commentary on the text here.
This conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), however, is divided into five types according to its nature: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material.
Therein, the wholesome is fourfold according to plane; the unwholesome is of one kind; the resultant is fourfold; that termed functional is threefold;
and the material is of one kind, being exclusively of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Thus, first, it is classified here according to its various modes of differentiation.
The detailed exposition should be understood.

Thus, when these are analyzed, wholesome states belonging to the four planes act as a conascence condition for both the mental factors associated with themselves and for the mind-originated matter within the five-aggregate existence;
likewise does the unwholesome. As for that which occurs here in the formless realm...
That which arises is the conascence condition for immaterial phenomena alone.
The resultant consciousness of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere is the conascence condition for both mind-produced matter and its associated mental states.
However, that matter which it does not produce here is the conascence condition for its associated mental states alone. That which [arises] at rebirth-linking...

When it arises, it is also a conascence condition for kamma-produced material phenomena (*kaṭattārūpa*). A fine-material-sphere resultant consciousness is a conascence condition only for its associated states.

A supramundane resultant consciousness is a conascence condition for both its associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-aggregate plane, and for immaterial states alone in the four-aggregate plane.
Sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere functional consciousnesses are conascence conditions for their associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-aggregate plane.
It is a co-nascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) in the fourfold existence (*catuvokāra*), specifically for the immaterial states.

Functional states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kiriya*) are invariably a co-nascence condition for both their associated mental states and for the mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*).
Regarding matter produced by the four [causes], one great primary element (*mahābhūta*) is a co-nascence condition for three others, and three are a co-nascence condition for one.
Two [great elements] are related to two [other great elements] by way of co-nascence condition; the great elements are related to derived matter by way of co-nascence condition.
At the moment of rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, the physical basis (vatthurūpa) is related to the resultant aggregates by way of co-nascence condition.

Furthermore, among those [derived matters] produced by temperature, mind, and nutriment, the great elements are related both to one another and to derived matter by way of co-nascence condition. Thus it is here.
The exposition of the analysis [of phenomena] should also be understood by way of their being conditionally arisen.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya). 7.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Mutuality Condition (aññamañña-paccaya).
7. In the exposition of the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), the text is presented according to the first three sections of the exposition of the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).
Since the commentary thereon is identical to what has already been stated, it is not repeated here.
Furthermore, this mutuality condition is divided into five types by way of genus: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and materiality.

Therein, the wholesome is fourfold by way of plane; all [the details] are exactly like those previously mentioned. Thus should the exposition be understood here according to its various classifications.
When thus divided, all wholesome states belonging to the four planes act as a mutual condition for the states associated with themselves.

...is a condition. Likewise for the unwholesome (akusala). However, in the case of resultant (vipāka) states, sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere resultants are a condition for the physical basis (vatthurūpa) at rebirth-linking, and during the course of existence (pavatta), they are a condition only for their associated mental states. Immaterial-sphere and supramundane (lokuttara) resultants are a condition only for the states associated with themselves by way of mutuality-condition (aññamañña-paccaya).
All functional (kiriya) states as well are a condition for their associated states only by way of mutuality-condition.

Condition: Regarding matter produced by the four [other] origins, one great primary element is a condition for three [great primary elements], three are a condition for one, and two are a condition for two, by way of mutual conditionality.

In the rebirth-linking of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, the physical basis (vatthurūpa) is a condition for the resultant aggregates by way of mutual conditionality. Among those produced by temperature, mind, and nutriment...

The great primary elements themselves are a condition for the great primary elements by way of mutual conditionality; thus, herein the exposition should be understood also from the perspective of what has arisen through conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the mutual condition.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Support Condition (Nissaya-paccaya-niddesa):

In the exposition of the support condition, after demonstrating the method of co-nascence support (sahajāta-nissaya) by way of the first five sections of the exposition of the co-nascence condition, it further demonstrates the method of pre-nascence support (purejāta-nissaya) by means of the sixth section.

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "the eye-base for the eye-consciousness-element" is commenced. Therein, the phrase "depending on which form" is stated with reference to the physical base (vatthurūpa).

Depending on that [base], these seventy-five types of consciousness proceed: namely, the threefold mind-element and, excluding the immaterial resultant, the seventy-two kinds of mind-consciousness-element. This, first of all, is the explanation here.

The commentary on the text. This condition of dependence (*nissayapaccaya*) is likewise divided into five types according to the classification of the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth by way of birth.
Therein, the wholesome is fourfold according to plane; the unwholesome is of one kind; the resultant (*vipāka*) is fourfold;
that termed functional (*kiriya*) is threefold; and matter (*rūpa*) is of only one kind. Thus should the exposition be understood here according to its various modes of division.

When analyzed in this way, here even wholesome states of the four planes act as a support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) for the associated aggregates and for mind-produced matter in the five-aggregate realm. The same applies to unwholesome states.
However, that which arises here in the immaterial realm acts as a support condition only for immaterial phenomena. As for the resultant states of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere...

In the course of existence (*pavatta*), it is a support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) for both the associated mental states and for mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*); at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it is also a support condition for kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).
The immaterial-sphere resultant (*arūpāvacara-vipāka*) is a support condition for the associated aggregates (*khandha*) alone.

The supramundane resultant (*lokuttara-vipāka*) is a support condition for the associated states and mind-originated matter in the five-aggregate plane (*pañcavokāra*); in the four-aggregate plane (*catuvokāra*), it is a support condition for the immaterial [states] alone.

The support condition (nissaya-paccaya) exists. Functional states (kiriyā) of the sense-sphere and the formless sphere are a support condition for both their associated mental states and for mind-originated matter in the fivefold plane; in the fourfold plane, they are a support condition for immaterial states alone.
Functional states of the fine-material sphere are invariably a support condition for both their associated mental states and for mind-originated matter.

In the case of matter originated by the fourfold origination, one great primary element is related to three [other] great primaries, three to one, and two to two; the great primaries are related to derived matter;

and the heart-base (vatthurūpa) is related to the wholesome and unwholesome states of the four planes in the five-aggregate existence, as well as to the remaining resultant states of the other planes, excluding the immaterial-sphere resultants and the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness.
Regarding "the functional [states] of the three planes": this serves as the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) for these four groups of phenomena.

The five bases, beginning with the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), serve as the support condition for the five consciousnesses, beginning with eye-consciousness, together with their associated mental states.

Furthermore, among those things originated by temperature, mind, and nutriment, the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as the support condition both for other great primary elements and for derived matter (*upādārūpa*). Thus it is here.
The exposition of the analysis [of phenomena] should also be understood from the perspective of what has arisen through conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the description of the dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya). 9. Commentary on the description of the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

9. In the exposition of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), "the preceding, the preceding" refers to those immediately past in the case of the proximity-decisive support (*anantara-upanissaya*);
however, in the cases of the object-decisive support (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*) and the natural-decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*), they are more remote by way of various mental paths (*vīthi*).

These three groups are found under the heading of the wholesome (*kusala*) by way of the wholesome; yet, a wholesome state does not obtain as the immediate past for an unwholesome state. For that very reason...
It is said: “A certain unwholesome state is a condition for unwholesome states by way of the decisive-support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). For this [is explained as follows]:

“A wholesome state is a condition for an unwholesome state by way of the decisive-support condition; [namely,] objective decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya) and natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya).
Objective decisive support: having given a gift, undertaken virtue, and performed the Uposatha duty, one esteems that...”
Having done so, one relishes and delights in it; esteeming that, lust arises and wrong view arises.
Esteeming past deeds well-performed, one relishes and delights in them; esteeming those, lust arises and wrong view arises.
Having emerged from jhāna, one esteems the jhāna, relishes and delights in it; esteeming that, [lust arises and wrong view arises].
Lust arises; wrong view arises. Natural strong-dependence (*pakatūpanissaya*): depending on faith, one arouses conceit and adopts wrong view.
Depending on virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, one arouses conceit and adopts wrong view.
Faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom [are related] to lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, and aspiration...

This was said with reference to this method: "It is a condition by way of decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). This was stated with reference specifically to the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) as it appears in the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), by way of the method beginning with "he gives a gift.

However, unwholesome states do not serve as an object-decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) for wholesome states. Why? Because they do not arise by taking those [wholesome states] as an object of respect.
Thus, it should be understood that just as with the proximity-decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*), the object-decisive support is likewise not found here. By means of the unwholesome...

In the section on the indeterminate (*abyākata*), only the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) is not found. This is because indeterminate states do not regard unwholesome states as venerable.
However, since the proximity condition (*anantarattā*) is found there, the phrase "for some" (*kesañci*) is not stated in this context.
But in the three systems—indeterminate, wholesome, and unwholesome—the three types of predominance conditions are indeed found for the indeterminate. As for the person (*puggala*)...
"Also lodgings"—this pair is stated by way of natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*). For these two are powerful conditions for the occurrence of both wholesome and unwholesome states.
Furthermore, their status as a condition here should be understood in a figurative sense (*pariyāyavasena*). This, then, is the commentary on the text.
Now, this so-called decisive support condition consists of all phenomena belonging to the four planes of existence, together with certain designations (*paññatti*).

As for its classification, it is threefold by way of object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), decisive-support-strong-dependence (*upanissaya*), and so forth. Among these, object-strong-dependence is not distinct from object-predominance;

thus, it should be understood according to its various sub-classifications in the same manner as explained above. Decisive-support-strong-dependence is not distinct from the proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*);
that too should be known according to its various sub-classifications in the same manner as explained above.
Their determination regarding their arising through conditions should also be understood by the same method explained there.

However, natural strong-dependence (pakatūpanissaya) is fivefold according to the classification of birth—namely, wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material—and it is manifold according to the classification of the planes of the wholesome and so forth.
Thus, first, the determination should be understood here according to its various modes of classification.

When this is thus divided, here the wholesome states of the three planes (*tebhūmaka-kusala*) serve as the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) for four groups: for wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states of all four planes. Supramundane states do not serve as such a support for the unwholesome.
However, according to the method of our teacher—who says, "The supramundane dhamma has been produced"—it also serves as a support for the unwholesome of others. For whom...
Or, for one who arouses a longing for the unsurpassed liberations that will arise in the future, it is exactly the same according to this method.
Unwholesome [kamma] is the natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) for all aggregates belonging to the four planes; likewise is the resultant [kamma] of the three planes.
Regarding supramundane resultants, the three lower fruits belong to the unwholesome alone, while the highest fruit belongs to the wholesome as well.

Furthermore, according to the previous method, for anyone else—or whoever it may be—in whose continuum supramundane (lokuttara) fruition arises, that entire supramundane fruition becomes a natural strong support (pakatūpanissaya) for all wholesome and other immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha).
Even that which is termed functional (kiriya) serves as a natural strong support for the unwholesome and other aggregates belonging to the four planes;
likewise does that which is termed material (rūpa). However, materiality itself...
According to the method presented in this great treatise, the *Paṭṭhāna*, the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is not found;
however, it is appropriate to say that it is found according to the method of the Suttantas. Thus, the analysis should be understood here also by way of the conditioned state (*paccayuppanna*).
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the decisive support condition.

10. Explanation of the Exposition of the Pre-arisen Condition (Purejātapaccaya-niddesa) Regarding the phrase "conditioned by the pre-arisen condition" (*purejātapaccayena paccayo*): here, "pre-arisen" (*purejāta*) refers to that which is the condition for something else;
it is that which has arisen prior to it, having passed beyond the moment of birth (*jātikkhaṇa*) and reached the moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*).

The phrase "eye-base," and so forth, is stated by way of the pre-arising of the physical basis (*vatthu-purejāta*). The phrase "visible-object-base," and so forth, is by way of the pre-arising of the object (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*).
"At some times by way of the pre-arising condition" is stated with reference to the course of existence (*pavatti*);

"at some times not by way of the pre-arising condition" is stated with reference to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Thus, in every respect, in the five doors by way of the physical basis and the object, and in the mind-door...

This text is presented here by way of the basis (*vatthu*); however, since it is stated in the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*) that "for those in training (*sekkhā*) or worldlings (*puthujjana*), the eye is a pre-arisen object (*ārammaṇapurejāta*) when they contemplate it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self," the pre-arisen object is certainly found in the mind-door (*manodvāra*) as well.
But here, the teaching is given in an abbreviated manner; this, then, is the commentary on the text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*) in this context.

This prior-nascence condition (*purejātapaccaya*), however, consists solely of material phenomena (*rūpa*). Moreover, it is exclusively the eighteenfold materiality that has passed beyond the moment of arising and reached the moment of presence.
All of this is established in two ways: as base-prior-nascence (*vatthupurejāta*) and object-prior-nascence (*ārammaṇapurejāta*).
Among these, the eye-base … pe … the body-base, which is the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*), constitutes base-prior-nascence.

[This is] the name. As for the rest—whether included in this textual passage or not—the twelvefold materiality consisting of visible form, sound, odor, flavor, the four elements, the three faculties, and physical nutriment is called the object-prenascence condition (*ārammaṇa-purejāta-paccaya*).
Thus, the analysis here should be understood according to its various classifications.
When analyzed in this way, here the eye-base is a condition by way of pre-nascence condition for two types of eye-consciousness;

likewise, the other four bases are conditions for the ear-consciousness and so forth. However, excluding the two sets of fivefold consciousness and the four immaterial-sphere resultants, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states belonging to the four planes are [conditioned] by the heart-base.

It is a pre-arising condition for the mind and mental factors. However, the five objects such as visible form and so forth are exclusively pre-arising conditions for the two sets of fivefold consciousness and the mind-element.

Furthermore, this eighteen-fold material form is a condition for sense-sphere wholesome [consciousness], for fine-material-sphere wholesome [consciousness], for super-knowledge wholesome [consciousness], for unwholesome [consciousness], and for sense-sphere resultant [consciousness] that takes it as its object.

The pre-arising condition (purejāta-paccaya) applies to these six groups: [the resultants] of the sense-sphere, the functional of the sense-sphere, and the functional of direct-knowledge (abhiññā) of the fine-material sphere.
Thus, the exposition should be understood here also by way of the conditioned states (paccayuppanna).
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the pre-arising condition.

11. Explanation of the Description of the Postnascence Condition (Pacchājātapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā) In the description of the postnascence condition: "Postnascent" means arisen while that body, which serves as their condition, has already arisen and is persisting.
"Of the prenascence" means of that which was born prior to their arising; having passed the moment of its own birth...
"Of one who has attained stability. "Of this body" means of this body, which is reckoned as consisting of material phenomena (rūpa) derived from the four origins or the three origins.

And here, the "body originated by the three [origins]" should be understood as the body of the Brahmā-parisajja and others, due to the absence of that originated by nutriment. This is the commentary on the text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*) herein.
Furthermore, this so-called "postnascent condition" (*pacchājātapaccaya*) is, in brief, as follows:

Excluding the immaterial-sphere resultants, the remaining immaterial aggregates of the four planes are divided into four types according to their mode of birth: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional.
Thus, the analysis here should be understood through these various classifications.
Now, when these have been so divided, the wholesome and unwholesome [states] of the four planes that arise in the five-aggregate existence at the moment of their arising—
Having passed away, it becomes a postnascent condition for the material body—which arises from four or three origins—once that body has reached its state of existence.

Regarding resultant states as well, with the exception of rebirth-linking resultants, all remaining sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere resultants are exclusively postnascent conditions for that same body.
Furthermore, supramundane resultants arising in the five-aggregate plane are also postnascent conditions for that very same body.
The functional states of the three planes, when arisen in the five-aggregate realm, also serve as a postnascent condition for the body of the aforementioned kind.
Thus, the analysis here should be understood also by way of what arises from this condition.
Explanation of the Description of the Postnascent Condition.

12. Commentary on the Exposition of the Condition of Repetition (Āsevanapaccaya-niddesa) In the exposition of the condition of repetition, the phrase "each preceding [state]" (purimā purimā) should be understood as referring only to those states that have immediately passed away, according to all the methods [of the Abhidhamma].
Why, however, is it not stated here as in the case of the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya), "each preceding wholesome state [is a condition] for each subsequent wholesome state"?
Why has no exposition been made [of indeterminate phenomena] together with those of different classes, according to the method beginning with "of indeterminate phenomena"?

Because they are incapable of causing one to grasp their own course. For phenomena of different classes, while establishing through the quality of repetition (*āsevana-guṇa*) the state of being skilled, powerful, and habitual for other formless phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*) of different classes, are unable to cause them to grasp their own course, which is defined by their own states such as the wholesome (*kusala*).

Therefore, instead of providing a detailed exposition (niddesa) for all of them together, it should be understood that a detailed exposition has been made for those [mental states] which, through the practice known as "habitual tendency" (vāsanā), are capable of causing their own state—characterized as wholesome and so forth—to become more proficient, stronger, and more distinguished, by means of association with those of a similar nature.
Now, why is the resultant indeterminate (vipākābyākata) not included? Because of the absence of habitual practice (āsevanā).
For a result (vipāka), having reached the state of being a result by way of karma and being transformed by karma, proceeds without effort and is weak;

thus, having been made to grasp its own intrinsic nature and cultivated through the quality of repetition (āsevana-guṇa), it is neither able to produce another result, nor does it arise by taking up the influence of a previous result. It is projected by the force of karma.
However, because it arises as if it had fallen [from its previous state], there is no repetition (āsevana) whatsoever in the case of resultant consciousness;

thus, due to the absence of repetition, the resultant is not included [among the conditions]. Furthermore, even though this [resultant] arises immediately after wholesome, unwholesome, or functional consciousness, it does not take on the quality of repetition because its mode of existence is bound to the specific karma; therefore, wholesome states and the others do not serve as its repetition-condition (āsevana-paccaya). Moreover, these [resultants] are excluded because they belong to different classes (nānājātika).
They do not exist [as distinct entities]. However, there is no difference in their nature (nānājātikatta) in terms of plane or object.

Therefore, even wholesome sense-sphere functional states and sublime wholesome functional states are indeed the repetition condition (āsevanapaccaya) for the wholesome adaptation consciousness that has formations as its object, and for the wholesome change-of-lineage consciousness that has Nibbāna as its object. This, then, is the commentary on the textual passage (pāḷivaṇṇanā).
Furthermore, this repetition condition is, first of all, wholesome by way of its intrinsic nature (jāti).

It is established in three ways: as unwholesome, functional-indeterminate, and resultant-indeterminate. Among these, the wholesome is threefold according to plane: sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, and immaterial-sphere.
The unwholesome belongs only to the sense-sphere. The functional-indeterminate is likewise threefold: sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, and immaterial-sphere.
There is no such thing as a supramundane condition of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*). Thus, it is here distinguished by its various classifications.
The detailed exposition should be understood.
When these are thus divided, here, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness conditions only its own immediate successor, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness.

Furthermore, that which is associated with knowledge among these conditions wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere and wholesome consciousness of the immaterial sphere, which have a feeling similar to its own.

Supramundane wholesome states are the condition of repetition for these [three] groups. However, fine-material-sphere wholesome states are [the condition of repetition] only for fine-material-sphere wholesome states;

immaterial-sphere wholesome states are [the condition of repetition] only for immaterial-sphere wholesome states. Unwholesome states, moreover, are the condition of repetition only for unwholesome states.
As for functional states, first, those classified as sense-sphere functional are [the condition of repetition] only for sense-sphere functional states. Furthermore, regarding those here—

Associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*), it is a condition by way of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*) for these groups: for functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kiriya*) that has feeling similar to its own, and for functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara-kiriya*).
However, that which is reckoned as functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere is a condition by way of repetition only for functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere;

and that which is reckoned as functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere is a condition by way of repetition only for functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere. As for resultant consciousness (*vipāka*), however—

There is no single dhamma that serves as a repetition-condition (āsevanapaccaya) for even a single dhamma that is a result (vipāka). Thus, the analysis here should be understood also by way of what arises through conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the repetition-condition.

13. Commentary on the Exposition of the Kamma Condition In the exposition of the kamma condition, "kamma" refers exclusively to volitional action (*cetanā-kamma*). "And from the having-been-done of kamma" means the material phenomena that have arisen from the having-been-done of kamma.
"By way of the kamma condition" means [the capacity] to produce its own fruit even at the end of many millions of eons.
The meaning is: by way of the asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika) kamma-condition acting as a support. For wholesome or unwholesome kamma does not yield its fruit at the very moment of its own occurrence.

If it were to do so, then a human being who performs wholesome kamma leading to the world of the gods would become a god at that very moment through its power. However, at a time other than the moment when it was performed...

Even though it does not exist [at that time], solely by virtue of having been performed (*kaṭattā*), when the remaining conditions are assembled, it produces its fruit either in this very life, in the next birth, or in some subsequent period—just as a former act of craftsmanship, though ceased, serves as a basis for a later act of craftsmanship at a different time.
Therefore, it is called the "kamma-condition of asynchronous moments. As for the phrase "volition [is the condition] for associated states," whatever...

Volition [is the condition] for the states associated with itself. By the phrase "for those originated by it," the materiality produced by past action (*kaṭattārūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking is also included.
The expression "by way of kamma-condition" is stated with reference to co-nascent volition;
for whatever co-nascent volition exists among the wholesome and other types, it is beneficial to the remaining states by way of its functional nature, which is termed the activity of consciousness.
It exists. Therefore, it is called the "simultaneously-arisen kamma-condition" (*sahajāta-kamma-paccaya*). This, then, is the commentary on the textual passage (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*) here.
As for this kamma-condition, in terms of its meaning (*atthato*), it is simply volition (*cetanā*) belonging to the four planes.

For that [volition] is divided into four types according to the distinction of birth: wholesome (*kusala*), unwholesome (*akusala*), resultant (*vipāka*), and functional (*kiriya*). Among these, the wholesome [volition], according to the planes, consists of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.
It is divided fourfold: unwholesome is of one kind, resultant is fourfold, and functional is threefold; thus should the analysis here be understood according to its various classifications.
When it is thus divided, herein, co-nascent wholesome sense-sphere volition [is the cause] for the states associated with itself in the fivefold plane...
Furthermore, for mind-originated matter, it is only in the fourfold plane (*catuvokāra*) that there is a co-nascent kamma-condition (*sahajāta-kammapaccaya*) for the associated aggregates.

Having arisen and ceased, however, it becomes a condition by way of asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*) for its own resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by past action (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).
And this occurs only in the fivefold plane (*pañcavokāra*), not elsewhere. Co-nascent wholesome volition of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala-cetanā*)...

It is a condition, by way of co-nascence-kamma-condition (*sahajāta-kamma-paccaya*), exclusively for the states associated with itself as well as for the mind-originated material phenomena (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*).

However, having arisen and ceased, it is a condition, by way of asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*), for its own results as well as for the material phenomena produced by past action (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).

Furthermore, wholesome volition (*kusala-cetanā*) that is co-nascent with the immaterial-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) and the supramundane (*lokuttara*) is, in the five-aggregate realm, a condition for the states associated with itself...

Furthermore, it is a condition, by way of the co-nascence kamma-condition (*sahajāta-kamma-paccaya*), for mind-originated material phenomena and, in the fourfold plane (*catuvokāra*), for the associated aggregates alone.
Having arisen and ceased, both of these [types of volition] are a condition, by way of the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*), for their own respective resultant aggregates.
Co-nascent unwholesome volition is [a condition], in the fivefold plane (*pañcavokāra*), for the aggregates associated with itself...

Furthermore, in the fourfold plane (catuvokāra), resultant volition (vipākacetanā) is a condition by way of co-nascence-kamma-condition (sahajāta-kamma-paccaya) for mind-originated matter and for the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) themselves.
Having arisen and ceased, it is a condition by way of asynchronous kamma-condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) for the resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by past karma (kaṭattā-rūpa).
From the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, resultant volition is a condition for the states associated with itself and for mind-originated matter during the course of existence (pavatta).
At rebirth-linking, it is a condition for the kamma-produced material phenomena by way of the conascence-kamma-condition.
Immaterial-sphere resultant volition is a condition only for the states associated with itself by way of the conascence-kamma-condition.

Supramundane resultant volition is a condition, in the five-aggregate plane, for both the states associated with itself and for mind-originated matter; in the four-aggregate plane, [it is a condition] for the states associated with itself.

The immaterial [kamma] is a condition by way of the co-nascent kamma-condition (sahajāta-kamma-paccaya). Functional volition (kiriyacetanā) belonging to the three planes is a condition by way of the co-nascent kamma-condition for both the associated states and the mind-produced matter in the fivefold plane (pañcavokāra).
However, that which arises here in the immaterial realm is a condition by way of the co-nascent kamma-condition for immaterial states alone;
thus it is also [to be understood] here by way of the produced-from-conditions (paccayuppanna).
"The exposition should be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the kamma-condition. 14.
Commentary on the exposition of the result-condition (*vipāka-paccaya*).

14. In the exposition of the resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*), the phrase "the four aggregates are resultants" is stated because material phenomena (*rūpa*) originating from kamma are not considered resultants;
therefore, having said "resultants," it specifies "the four aggregates. Thus, this passage in the text is presented solely by way of the resultant condition for immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).
However, in the Chapter on Questions (*Pañhāvāra*), it says: "One indeterminate resultant aggregate [is related] to three aggregates..."

"Also, it is a condition for mind-originated material phenomena by way of the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*). At the moment of rebirth-linking, one resultant indeterminate aggregate is a condition for three aggregates and for the material phenomena born of kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) by way of the resultant condition.

Because this has been stated, the resultant condition is obtained even for material phenomena originated by mind and originated by kamma. However, in this context, it is treated with a remainder [of other conditions].

"The instruction has been given"—this, first of all, is the commentary on the text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*) here. As for this resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*), it is of one kind by way of its nature as a result;

however, it is divided into four types according to the distinction of planes, such as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth. Thus, the exposition (*vinicchaya*) should be understood here through these various modes of classification.

When analyzed in this way, here the resultant consciousness of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere acts as a resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*) for the states associated with itself during the course of existence—for mind-produced matter—and at rebirth-linking, for kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattā-rūpa*). The immaterial-sphere resultant acts as such a condition for the states associated with it alone.
The supramundane resultant acts as such a condition for the states associated with it and for mind-produced matter within the fivefold plane of existence.
Furthermore, in the four-aggregate plane, it is a condition for the resultant aggregates alone; thus, the analysis should be understood here also by way of what has arisen through conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the resultant condition.

15. Explanation of the Description of the Nutriment Condition (Āhāra-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) In the description of the nutriment condition, "edible food" (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) refers to the nutritive essence (ojā) within the material phenomena produced by the four continuities; that is what is called "nutriment.
However, because it performs the function of nutriment only after being made into morsels and swallowed—not while remaining outside—it is therefore [called edible food].
Instead of simply saying "nutriment," it is stated as "edible nutriment" (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*). It is called "edible" because its substance must be made into morsels and swallowed.
The "formless nutriments" are the nutriments of contact, volition, and consciousness. Regarding the phrase "arising from that," here too, those arising from kamma are indeed what are intended.
For this has been stated in the *Pañhāvāra*: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, the resultant indeterminate..."
Nutriment is a condition by way of nutriment-condition for the aggregates associated with it and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa).
This, then, is the commentary on the textual passage here.
Furthermore, this nutriment-condition consists, in brief, of only four things: edible food, contact, volition, and consciousness.

These are the mental phenomena (dhammas). Therein, excluding edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), the remaining three immaterial foods are divided fourfold according to their nature as wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya).
Furthermore, they are divided manifoldly by way of the distinction of planes: the wholesome is fourfold, the unwholesome is singlefold, the resultant is fourfold, and the functional is threefold.
However, edible food is indeterminate (abyākata) by nature, and by plane—
"Belonging to the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacaro vā*): thus should the analysis herein be understood according to its various classifications.

When analyzed in this way, even though they belong to the four planes, the three wholesome nutriments (*kusala-āhāra*) act as nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*) for both the states associated with themselves and for mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*) within the fivefold existence (*pañcavokāra*). However, excluding the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the remainder...
In the formless realm, nutriment is a condition by way of nutriment-condition (āhāra-paccaya) only for the associated mental states. This same principle applies to unwholesome nutriments as well.

However, the resultant nutriments of the four planes are nutriment-conditions for their associated states everywhere. Furthermore, the resultant [nutriments] of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, when arising during the course of existence (pavatta) in the five-aggregate realm, are nutriment-conditions for mind-produced matter; and at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), they are also nutriment-conditions for kamma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa).
They exist as nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*). However, supramundane states are conditions only for mind-produced matter; those arisen in the formless realm are not conditions for matter.
Furthermore, the three functional nutriments belonging to the three planes are conditions for both associated mental states and mind-produced matter in the five-aggregate realm;
but those of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere are conditions only for associated mental states in the formless realm.

It is a condition by way of nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*). Although edible food produced by the four continuities is stated without distinction as "of this body," specifically here it acts as a nutriment-condition by being both the producer and the sustainer of matter originated by nutriment;
whereas for the remaining eight continuities, it acts only as a sustainer.

"It is a condition by way of the nutriment-condition (āhāra-paccaya)"—thus, in this context, the analysis should be understood also from the perspective of that which has arisen through conditions. This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the nutriment-condition.
16. Commentary on the Exposition of the Faculty-Condition (indriya-paccaya)
16. In the exposition of the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya-niddesa*), "eye-faculty" (*cakkhundriya*) refers to the faculty known as the eye.

"By way of the faculty-condition" means that, having itself arisen prior [to its effects], it serves as a condition by way of the faculty-condition from the moment the immaterial phenomena begin to arise until their dissolution.
The same method applies to the ear-faculty and the others. Regarding the phrase "immaterial faculties," here the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*) is also included.
It is included. Regarding the phrase "arising from that," here too, as in the method explained below, kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*) is also included.

For this has been stated in the *Pañhāvāra*: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate faculties are a condition by way of faculty-condition for the associated aggregates and for kamma-produced matter. Thus, first, the commentary on the text should be understood in this way.
This faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya), however, is established by way of twenty faculties, excluding the female faculty (itthindriya) and the male faculty (purisindriya).
For although the female and male faculties are the seeds for the female sex characteristics, male sex characteristics, and so forth,
they do not [constitute this condition] because those sex characteristics are absent even while the [faculties] exist during the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*.
They exercise the conditionality of faculties (indriya-paccayatā) toward those [states], not toward others.

For there is no instance where the faculty-condition, at its own existing moment, does not exercise the conditionality of faculties toward the states inseparable from it; therefore, those [other states] do not have these as their faculty-conditions.
However, for those to whom these [faculties] serve as seeds, they constitute the state of natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) according to the Suttanta method.
They partake [of it]. Thus, the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya) should be understood as established by way of twenty-two faculties.
As for its classification, it is divided fivefold according to the types of consciousness:

wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material form. Among these, the wholesome is fourfold according to the planes; the unwholesome belongs only to the sense-sphere; the resultant is fourfold; that termed functional is threefold; and material form belongs only to the sense-sphere.
Thus it is divided in many ways; this, firstly, is how the exposition should be understood here by way of its various classifications.

When thus divided, even that which belongs to the four planes—wholesome [consciousness]—is a condition for both the associated states and the mind-produced matter in the five-aggregate plane by way of the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*); likewise, the unwholesome [consciousness]. However, excluding...

Wholesome states of the fine-material sphere and the remaining wholesome and unwholesome states are conditions by way of faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) only for associated states in the immaterial sphere.
Resultant states belonging to the four planes are invariably conditions by way of faculty-condition for their associated states.
Furthermore, those of the sense-sphere and fine-material spheres, arising here in the five-aggregate plane during the course of existence, [act as conditions] for mind-produced matter.

At rebirth-linking, even the kamma-produced material phenomena (kaṭattārūpa) act as a condition for material phenomena by way of the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya). Supramundane [faculties] act as conditions only for mind-originated material phenomena.
The supramundane resultant faculties that arise in the immaterial plane are not conditions for material phenomena.

The functional faculties (kiriyindriya) belonging to the three planes act as conditions, in the five-aggregate realm, for both associated states and mind-originated material phenomena; likewise for those belonging to the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere.
However, in the immaterial realm (ārūpa), they exercise their function as faculty-conditions (indriya-paccaya) only for the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma).

Among the sixfold material faculties (rūpindriya) consisting of the eye-faculty and so forth, the eye-faculty exercises its function toward the two types of eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) that are associated with wholesome, unwholesome, or resultant [states].

Likewise, the ear-faculty and the others exercise their functions toward the corresponding ear-consciousness and so forth; and the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) [exercises its function toward the associated states].

At the moment of the persistence of the material phenomena co-nascent with itself, it is a condition for them by way of the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*). However, it does not possess the state of being a co-nascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccayatā*) itself;
thus, the analysis here should be understood also from the perspective of that which has arisen through conditions.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Faculty-Condition (*Indriya-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*).

17. Commentary on the Exposition of the Condition of Jhāna (Jhānapaccayaniddesa) In the exposition of the condition of jhāna, "jhāna factors" refers to the seven factors—namely, initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (somanassa), grief (domanassa), equanimity (upekkhā), and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā)—that arise in all remaining types of consciousness, excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness. Of these five...

However, because they are merely the point of contact for the groups of consciousness, even though equanimity, pleasure, and pain exist within them, they are not designated as jhāna factors due to the absence of the mode of sustained contemplation (*upanijjhānākāra*).
Furthermore, because that [contemplation] has been cut off, they are likewise not designated as jhāna factors in the remaining types of rootless consciousness (*ahetuka*).
Here too, it should be understood that "arisen from that" includes both mind-produced matter and kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*). For this has been said:

In the section on questions: “At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate jhāna factors are a condition, by way of the jhāna-condition, for the associated aggregates and for the materiality of the kamma-born.

This, then, is the commentary on the textual passage here. However, although this jhāna-condition is established by way of the seven jhāna factors, it is divided according to its types into the wholesome, the unwholesome, the resultant, and the functional.
It is divided fourfold, and again fourfold by way of the planes; it is divided twelvefold—once, fourfold, and threefold.
Thus, the exposition should be understood here according to its various modes of classification.
When it is thus divided, even the wholesome jhāna-factor of the four planes [is present] in the five-aggregate realm as well as among the associated states.

With the exception of the fine-material-sphere [consciousness], the remaining consciousness-originated matter is a condition by way of the jhāna-condition for associated states in the immaterial sphere.

The same method applies to the unwholesome as well. During the course of existence, sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere resultant [consciousness] is a condition by way of the jhāna-condition for both associated states and consciousness-originated matter; at rebirth-linking, it is a condition for associated states and—

It is a condition for the kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*), for the immaterial-sphere resultant (*āruppavipāka*) and its associated states alone, and also for that supramundane resultant which arises in the immaterial sphere.
However, in the five-aggregate plane, it is also a condition by way of the jhāna-condition for the mind-originated matter.
Furthermore, in the five-aggregate plane, even the functional jhāna-factor belonging to the three planes is a condition for the associated states as well as for the mind-originated matter.
Furthermore, whatever arises here in the formless realm is a condition for its associated states by way of the jhāna-condition.
Thus, the exposition should be understood here also by way of what has arisen through conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the jhāna-condition.
18. Explanation of the Exposition of the Path Condition (Maggapaccayaniddesa) Regarding the phrase "path factors" (maggaṅgāni) in the exposition of the path condition:

these refer to wisdom (paññā), applied thought (vitakka), right speech (sammāvācā), right action (sammākammanta), right livelihood (sammājīva), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), wrong speech (micchāvācā), wrong action (micchākammanta), and wrong livelihood (micchājīva)—as they arise in all remaining types of consciousness, with the exception of rootless (ahetuka) states of consciousness.
These are the twelve factors. However, because the Path has no preceding cause [in its own arising], the path-factors are not mentioned among the rootless consciousnesses (*ahetuka-citta*).
Regarding the phrase "arising from that" (*taṃsamuṭṭhāna*), here too, the matter-form produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) is indeed included. For this has been stated in the *Pañhāvāra*:
"At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the resultant indeterminate path-factors [are the cause] for the associated aggregates produced by kamma."
“And [it is] a condition for material phenomena by way of the path-condition.

This, then, is the commentary on the text here. Now, although this path-condition is established by way of the twelve path-factors, it is fourfold according to the classification of its types—namely, as wholesome and so forth—and the wholesome and so forth are further divided into twelve ways according to the classification of planes such as the sense-sphere and so forth; thus, it is here [treated] by way of these various classifications.

The detailed exposition should be understood [in this way]. Thus, when analyzed here, the wholesome path-factor belonging to the four planes is a condition for both the associated mental states and the consciousness-originated matter in the five-constituent realm;

however, excluding the fine-material sphere, the remainder is a condition for the associated mental states alone by way of the path-condition in the immaterial realm—just as in the case of the jhāna-condition.
"It should be expanded" means that in this context, the exposition (vinicchaya) is to be understood also by way of what has arisen through conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the description of the path condition. 19.
Commentary on the Description of the Association Condition.
19. In the exposition of the associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*), the text is self-evident.
This so-called associated condition, in brief, consists of all immaterial aggregates (*arūpa-khandha*).

However, in its detailed classification, it is divided in many ways according to its nature—such as the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth—and according to its plane—such as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth. Thus, it should be understood here through these various modes of classification.

The analysis: Thus, when these wholesome aggregates belonging to the four planes are distinguished, one aggregate is a condition for three aggregates, three for one, and two for two; in this way, all of them are mutually conditions by way of the associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*).
This same method applies to the unwholesome, resultant, and functional aggregates. Thus, here [the analysis] is also presented from the perspective of what arises through conditions.
“The determination is to be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the associated condition (sampayutta-paccaya). 20.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Dissociated Condition (vippayutta-paccaya).

20. In the exposition of the dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*), the phrase "material phenomena (*rūpino dhammā*) are non-material" should first be understood by way of the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) and the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*) and so forth.
For among material phenomena, these six components alone serve as a dissociation condition for the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).
Although the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) and the others are objects (*ārammaṇadhamma*) and thus dissociated phenomena, [they are not included here].
But they do not exist as dissociation conditions. Why? Because there is no possibility of association.
For the immaterial aggregates arise as if emerging from within the bases such as the eye;
thus, a doubt arises there: "Are these associated with these [bases], or are they dissociated? However, as for the objects...
Since they serve merely as objects for those states that arise dependent upon a physical basis, there is no suspicion of association with them.
Thus, because there is no suspicion of association, they are not dissociation conditions (*vippayutta-paccaya*).

However, this status of being a dissociation condition should be understood only in the case of the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*) and so forth. And this has also been stated in the *Pañhāvāra*: "The physical basis is a condition for wholesome aggregates..."

It is a condition by way of dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*). The physical basis (*vatthu*) is a condition by way of dissociation-condition for unwholesome aggregates (*akusala-khandha*).
The eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) is a condition by way of dissociation-condition for eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*). The ear... nose... tongue...

body-base is a condition by way of dissociation-condition for body-consciousness (*kāya-viññāṇa*). The physical basis is [a condition] for resultant-indeterminate (*vipāka-abyākata*) and functional-indeterminate (*kiriya-abyākata*) [states].
"It is a condition for the aggregates by way of the dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*).
Furthermore, this statement "immaterial states [are conditions] for material states" should be understood with reference to the four aggregates.
For among immaterial states, only the four aggregates serve as dissociation conditions for co-nascent and prenascent material states; Nibbāna does not.
However, even though it is formless, it does not serve as a dissociation condition for form. For it is said: "There is association with four [factors] and dissociation with four.
Thus, the status of being a dissociation condition should be understood as belonging only to the four formless aggregates (arūpakkhandha).
And this has also been stated in the Pañhāvāra: "Co-nascent wholesome aggregates are a dissociation condition for mind-produced matter..."
Condition: Postnascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for this prenascent body by way of dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*).
At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate aggregates are a condition for the kamma-produced material phenomena (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) by way of dissociation-condition;
likewise, aggregates are a condition for the physical heart-base. Thus, in this context, the commentary on the canonical text (*pāḷi*) should be understood.
Now, this so-called dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*) consists, in brief, of material and immaterial phenomena occurring within the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).

Among these, the material is divided sixfold by way of the physical bases (*vatthu*) and the sense organs such as the eye; the immaterial is divided fourfold by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states that arise in the five-aggregate existence.
According to its plane, it is [further divided] by way of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.

There is a division into eleven ways: fourfold, singlefold, threefold, and threefold. For the fruition of the formless realm (*ārūppavipāka*) does not function as a dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*);
thus, the analysis here should be understood according to these various modes of classification.
Now, when [the mind] has thus been divided, both the wholesome and unwholesome [states] arising in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) belong to the four planes.
It is a condition for the materiality produced by the mind itself, through the condition of co-nascence and dissociation.

Furthermore, having passed the moment of arising and reached the moment of presence, it is a condition for the pre-nascent body of materiality—whether produced by the four [mental] origins or the three [mental] origins—through the condition of post-nascence and dissociation. And herein, "body produced by the three" refers to that which is produced by nutriment.
The body of the Brahmapārisajja and other deities is to be understood by way of non-existence (abhāva).

However, sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere resultant [kamma] acts as a condition for mind-originated matter during the course of existence (pavatta), and for kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa) at rebirth-linking, by way of the conascence-disjoined condition (sahajāta-vippayutta-paccaya).
Supramundane resultant [kamma] acts as a condition for mind-originated matter alone. All three types of this [resultant kamma], moreover, [act as a condition] for pre-nascent [matter].
The body, whether arising from four causes or three causes, is a condition for [consciousness] by way of the postnascent dissociation condition.

Furthermore, functional states belonging to the three planes are a condition for mind-originated matter by way of the conascent dissociation condition; and [those same states] are a condition for the prenascent body, whether arising from four causes or three causes, by way of the postnascent dissociation condition.
Among the material phenomena existing in six ways, however, the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) at the moment of rebirth-linking—
It is a condition, by way of co-nascence and dissociation condition, for the resultant states of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere;

and it is a condition, by way of prenascence and dissociation condition, for the wholesome and unwholesome states of the four planes arising during the course of existence, for the resultant states of the three planes (excluding the two fivefold sense-consciousnesses), and for the functional states of the three planes.
The eye-base and so forth are conditions, by way of prenascence and dissociation condition, for eye-consciousness and so forth.
"Condition": thus, herein the exposition should be understood also by way of that which has arisen through conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the dissociation condition. 21.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Presence Condition.

21. In the exposition of the presence condition (*atthipaccaya*), the presence condition is demonstrated by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) through such phrases as "the four aggregates," and by way of pre-nascence (*purejāta*) through such phrases as "the eye-base. In the passage "depending on whatever form," the presence condition is demonstrated by way of both co-nascence and pre-nascence.
Thus, this text [deals] specifically with the presence conditions of co-nascence and pre-nascence.

[The condition] has been introduced. In the section on questions (*paṇhāvāra*), however, because it is introduced by way of these—conascence (*sahajāta*), prenascence (*purejāta*), postnascence (*pacchājāta*), nutriment (*āhāra*), and faculty (*indriya*)—the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*) is also obtained by way of postnascence, nutriment, and faculty.
But here, the teaching is given with a remainder; this, then, is the commentary on the text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*) in this context.
This condition called "presence" (atthipaccaya), however, is twofold: by way of mutual relation and not by way of mutual relation. Therein, mutual relation is threefold:

immaterial with immaterial, material with material, and material-immaterial with material-immaterial. For in the passage, "The four aggregates are immaterial," the immaterial is stated as being with the immaterial by way of all mental states that arise.
In the passage, "The four great elements... [the material is stated as being with the material].

Matter is [related] to matter by way of all its continuities. In the phrase “name-and-form at the moment of descent,” both the rebirth-linking aggregates and the physical basis are stated as form-and-non-form by way of the form and non-form themselves. There is also a threefold mutual relationship:
“non-form to form, form to form, and form to non-form,” where, in this context, it refers to the five-aggregate plane (the mind and mental factors being the non-form).

It has been stated that "the formless is a condition for form. In the passage, "The great primary elements [are conditions] for derived forms," form is said to be a condition for form by way of all three periods of time (past, present, and future).

In passages such as, "The eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness-element," form is stated to be a presence-condition for the formless by way of its status as a physical basis (vatthu) or an object (ārammaṇa).
Briefly stated, the presence condition (*atthipaccaya*) consists of both mind and matter that have reached the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution];
it is also appropriate to say it comprises the five present aggregates. By way of classification according to type, it is divided into five kinds:
wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material. Among these, the wholesome is twofold by way of conascence and post-nascence; likewise, the unwholesome is twofold.
And [it is] designated as resultant and functional. Among these, the wholesome is divided fourfold according to the distinctions of the sense-sphere and so forth;

the unwholesome belongs only to the sense-sphere; the resultant belongs to all four planes; and that which is designated as functional belongs to three planes. That which is designated as material is a presence-condition belonging only to the sense-sphere.
It, moreover, is twofold by way of conascence and prenascence. Therein, the five bases are the objects.
Furthermore, the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is either conascent or pre-arisen relative to those [mental states] that have arisen previously.

However, as it appears in the *Pañhāvāra* (Chapter on Questions), nutriment (*āhāra*) and the faculties (*indriya*) do not admit of such divisions as "conascent" and so forth. Thus should the analysis here be understood according to its various classifications.

When these have been thus distinguished, even a wholesome state of the four planes is a conascent presence-condition (*sahajāta-atthipaccaya*) in the five-aggregate realm; for example, "one aggregate..."
In the manner beginning with "of the three aggregates," etc., with the exception of the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala*),

the remainder— whether in the formless realm (*ārūpa*) or elsewhere— is a conascent wholesome state-by-presence condition for the mutually related aggregates and for mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*). Furthermore,
this [wholesome state] belonging to the four planes serves as the body in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra*) for a body that is produced by four or three types of origination.
A posteriorly arisen wholesome state is a condition by way of presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*). The same method applies to the unwholesome as well.

For that too, in the five-aggregate realm, it is a condition by way of presence for the associated aggregates and for mind-originated matter; in the four-aggregate realm, it is a condition by way of presence for the associated aggregates alone. In the five-aggregate realm, it is a condition for the body that is originated by the four [great elements] or originated by the three [great elements].
The postnascent unwholesome state is a condition by way of presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*).

However, as for the resultant [states] of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, the presence-condition is invariably a condition by way of conascence-presence-condition (*sahajāta-atthipaccaya*) for both the aggregates and the kamma-produced matter at the moment of rebirth-linking.
During the course of existence (*pavatta*), however, it is a condition for the associated aggregates and...

It is a condition for mind-originated matter by way of the co-nascence-presence condition; and it is a condition for the body originated from the four [great elements] or the three [great elements], when that body has reached the stage of duration, by way of the post-nascence-presence condition.

However, immaterial-sphere resultant and supramundane resultant arising in the formless realm are conditions only for the aggregates associated with themselves by way of the co-nascence-presence condition. As for supramundane resultant in the five-aggregate plane...
The associated aggregates and mind-produced matter are related to [the mind] by way of the condition of presence as co-nascent;
the body produced by four or three [mental] origins is related [to the mind] by way of the condition of presence as postnascent.
The functional fine-material-sphere presence-condition is related to the associated aggregates and mind-produced matter by way of the condition of presence as co-nascent.
[Material] nutriment is a presence-condition for the body produced by four or three [bases].
However, in the formless realm, sense-sphere, and fine-material-sphere [nutriment] is a presence-condition by way of co-nascence only for the associated aggregates;

in the five-aggregate realm, it is also a presence-condition by way of co-nascence for mind-produced matter, and a presence-condition by way of post-nascence for the body produced by four or three [bases].

The presence condition (*atthipaccaya*), however, when classified as material form (*rūpa*), is fourfold: conascent (*sahajāta*), prenascence (*purejāta*), nutriment (*āhāra*), and faculty (*indriya*).

Among these, the conascent presence condition for material form exists in four ways according to the four modes of origination (*samuṭṭhāna*). Therein, that which is originated by kamma is as follows:

one great primary element (*mahābhūta*) [is the condition] for three great primary elements; three for one; two for two; and the great primary elements are [the condition] for derived material form (*upādārūpa*).

Thus it is a condition by way of the conascence-presence condition (*sahajāta-atthi-paccaya*). At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the physical basis (*vatthu-rūpa*) is a condition for the resultant aggregates (*vipāka-khandha*) of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere by way of the conascence-presence condition.
Furthermore, among those [aggregates], the matter produced from the three [mental] origins is a condition for one great primary (*mahābhūta*) by way of the conascence-presence condition;
