three [great primaries] are a condition for one; two are a condition for two; and the great primaries are a condition for the derived matter (*upādārūpa*). Thus it is by way of the conascence-presence condition.
It is a condition. The presence-prenascence condition (*purejātathitipaccaya*), however, is twofold: by way of base-prenascence (*vatthupurejāta*) and object-prenascence (*ārammaṇapurejāta*).
Both of these types should be applied and understood according to the method already explained below under the prenascence condition (*purejātapaccaya*).

The nutriment-presence condition (*āhāratthitipaccaya*) should also be applied according to the method already applied below under the edible-nutriment condition (*kabaḷīkārāhārapaccaya*). Here, moreover, in its own unceased moment...

It is called the "presence condition" (atthi-paccaya) by virtue of its state as a condition. The material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) should also be applied here in the same manner as it was explained previously in the application of the material life-faculty within the section on the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya).
However, in this context, it is also called the presence condition by virtue of its state as a condition precisely at its own unceased moment;
thus should the analysis be understood here even from the perspective of what has arisen through conditions.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Presence Condition (Atthipaccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā). 22. Commentary on the Exposition of the Absence Condition (Natthipaccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā). 22.
In the exposition of the absence condition, the term "immediately ceased" (*samanantaraniruddha*) means having been immediate [to the present] by way of another arising of consciousness.

"Samanantaraniruddhā" means "immediately ceased. "Paṭuppannānaṃ" means "of the present. By this, he establishes the state of non-existence as a condition (natthipaccaya) in the sense of providing space.
For if the preceding states, by way of their cessation, did not provide the opportunity for the occurrence of the succeeding states, those succeeding states would lack the status of being present;
such is the commentary on the text here. All the rest is the same as in the case of the proximity-condition (anantarapaccaya).

It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Here, the only difference is in the characteristic of the conditions; however, there is no distinction between the conditions themselves and the phenomena produced by those conditions.

Yet, in that [previous] context, both the conditions and the conditionally arisen phenomena were shown in their specific forms according to the method beginning with, “The eye-consciousness element and the states associated with it [are conditions] for the mind-element,” and so forth. But here, on the other hand—
“Mind and mental factors that have just ceased [are conditions] for presently arisen mind and mental factors”—
all these have been shown collectively by way of their cessation and arising.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the absence condition (*natthipaccaya*).

23. Commentary on the Exposition of the Disappearance Condition (Vigatapaccaya-niddesa) In the exposition of the disappearance condition (*vigatapaccaya*), "disappeared immediately after" (*samanantaravigata*) means disappeared at that very moment.

By this, he shows that the status of being a condition for the disappearance condition exists precisely through its state of disappearing. Thus, there is a difference between the non-existence condition (*natthipaccaya*) and this [disappearance condition] merely in their verbal expression.
There is no diversity; there is no "there is not.
Explanation of the Description of the Dissociated Condition (vigatapaccaya). 24.
Explanation of the Description of the Non-Dissociated Condition (avigatapaccaya).

24. In the exposition of the non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*), the meaning of the phrases "the four aggregates," and so forth, should be understood in exactly the same manner as that stated in the exposition of the presence condition (*atthi-paccaya*). For even in this condition, there is a difference only in the phrasing, but not in the actual meaning; it is identical to the presence condition.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Non-disappearance Condition.
Discourse on Miscellaneous Determinations in the Exposition of Conditions:
Now, for the purpose of clarifying the range of knowledge regarding these twenty-four conditions shown through the summary and the exposition, [the following is presented].

Because many phenomena have the state of being a single condition; because a single phenomenon has the state of having many conditions; because a single condition has the state of being many conditions;
by way of similarity of conditions; by way of dissimilarity of conditions; by way of pairs; by way of productive and non-productive; by way of universal and non-universal;
by way of the various classifications such as "matter is the condition for matter"; and by way of the different types of existence—of these...
The detailed analysis should be understood by way of ten points. Regarding the first point, "the state of being a single condition for multiple phenomena":
among these twenty-three conditions—with the exception of the kamma-condition—multiple phenomena act together as conditions in the remaining twenty-three.
However, the kamma-condition is only a single phenomenon, namely volition (*cetanā*). Thus, in this context, regarding multiple phenomena...
The analysis [of conditions] should be understood by way of their being single conditions.
Regarding the fact that a single state can have multiple conditions: first, in the case of the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*), non-delusion (*amoha*) is a single state;

it does not function as a condition solely through the relations of prior-arising, nutriment, or jhāna, but rather functions as a condition by way of the remaining twenty relations. Likewise, non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adosa*) also function as conditions through the relations of faculty (*indriya*) and path (*magga*).
They are not [conditions] by way of the remaining eighteen conditions; rather, they are conditions by way of the remaining [eighteen] conditions.
Greed and delusion are also not resultant conditions (*vipāka-paccaya*); rather, they are conditions by way of the remaining seventeen conditions.

Hatred is also not a predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*); rather, it is a condition by way of the remaining sixteen conditions. Regarding the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*)...
The eye-consciousness element is a condition in four ways: by way of object-prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance; likewise for the mind-element and the rootless mind-consciousness element.
However, for the root-possessing [mind-consciousness element], it is also a condition by way of object-predominance and object-strong-dependence.
By this method, the manifold conditional status of all phenomena that serve as object-conditions should be understood.

Regarding the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), the various modes of being a condition for objective-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) should be understood in the same manner as explained under the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
Among the co-nascent predominances (*sahajātādhipati*), volition (*vīmaṃsā*) is a condition in twenty ways, just like the non-delusion root (*amohahetu*).
Desire (*chanda*) is not a condition by way of root, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, or path; it is a condition for the remaining seventeen conditions.
It is a condition by way of [the remaining] conditions. Consciousness is not a condition as root, pre-existence, kamma, jhāna, or path;
it is a condition by way of the remaining nineteen conditions. Energy is not a condition as root, pre-existence, kamma, nutriment, or jhāna;
it is a condition by way of the remaining nineteen.

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*anantara-paccaya*), among the four aggregates mentioned in the sequence beginning with "the eye-consciousness element," the feeling aggregate is not a condition by way of the roots, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, or path conditions; it is a condition by way of the remaining nineteen.
The perception aggregate is also not a condition by way of the faculties or jhāna conditions; it is a condition by way of the remaining seventeen.
It exists. Within the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), roots (*hetu*) are conditions by way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) according to the method already stated;

desire (*chanda*) and energy (*vīriya*) are conditions by way of the predominance-condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) according to the very same method already stated. Contact (*phassa*) is not a condition by way of the root-, prenascence-, kamma-, faculty-, jhāna-, or path-conditions;
it is a condition by way of the remaining eighteen [modes]. Volition (*cetanā*) is a condition by way of the root-, prenascence-, faculty-, jhāna-, and path-conditions.
It is not a condition. By way of the remaining nineteen, it is a condition. Applied thought (*vitakka*) is not a condition by way of root, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, or faculty;
it is a condition by way of the remaining nineteen. Sustained thought (*vicāra*) is also not a condition by way of path;
it is a condition by way of the remaining eighteen. Rapture (*pīti*) is a condition by way of those same [eighteen]. One-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*)...
The root, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, and jhāna conditions do not exist [for it], but it exists as a condition for the remaining twenty.
Faith does not exist as a root, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, jhāna, or path condition, but it exists as a condition for the remaining eighteen.
Mindfulness exists as a condition for those same [eighteen] plus the path condition, thus for nineteen. The life faculty...

It acts as a condition by way of the eighteen [mental factors] that proceed from faith. Moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*), excluding the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) from among those, act as conditions by way of the remaining seventeen.

Likewise, the pairs beginning with bodily tranquility (*kāya-passaddhi*), among the "inclusionary" (*yevāpanaka*) factors, as well as resolve (*adhimokkha*), attention (*manasikāra*), equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*), and compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*). As for the abstinences (*viratiyo*), however—
Together with those very same conditions as path-conditions, there are eighteen ways of being a condition. If one removes the result-condition from that [list], wrong view becomes seventeen ways;
if one adds to those the same [factors] as kamma- and nutriment-conditions—namely, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood—it becomes nineteen ways.
Shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, conceit, sloth, torpor, and restlessness are conditions by way of root, prenascence, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path.
They do not [act as conditions] for themselves, but they do act as conditions for the remaining sixteen types of conditions.

Doubt, envy, stinginess, and worry act as conditions for the aggregate of consciousness in fifteen ways, having excluded the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) from that list. The fact that these possess multiple modes of conditioning should be understood in the same manner as explained for the predominance condition.
This same principle applies to the contiguity condition (*samanantara-paccaya*) as well.

Regarding the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), the fact that each single phenomenon among the four aggregates possesses multiple modes of conditionality should be understood according to the method already explained.

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) act as conditions in nine ways: by way of object (*ārammaṇa*), object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), co-nascence (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), decisive support (*upanissaya*), prenascence (*purejāta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*). The heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) acts as a condition in ten ways: by way of those same [nine] and by way of dissociation (*vippayutta*).

[The condition] exists. In the case of the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), there is nothing new. In the case of the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), the eye-base and so forth act as conditions in nine ways:

by way of object (*ārammaṇa*), predominance (*adhipati*), support (*nissaya*), decisive support (*upanissaya*), prenascence (*purejāta*), faculty (*indriya*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*). In the case of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*), there is nothing new.

In the case of the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), the bases of visible form, sound, odor, and taste act as conditions in six ways: by way of object, predominance, decisive support, prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance.
Only this much here is new; there is nothing new regarding the postnascent and other [types of conditions].
In the nutriment condition, edible food acts as a condition in six ways: by way of object, object-predominance, decisive support, nutriment, presence, and non-disappearance.
Among the faculty and other [conditions], there is nothing new. Thus, the analysis should be understood here also by way of one state having many types of conditional relations.
"Because a single condition possesses the state of being many conditions": this means that among the conditions such as the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and others,
whatever mode and whatever sense in which any one particular condition acts as a condition for the arisen states, without abandoning that mode and that sense,
it simultaneously possesses the state of being many conditions for those same states by way of other modes and other senses.
It goes; the meaning is that its classification should be understood from its state as many conditions. For example:

non-delusion (*amoha*) is a root condition (*hetu-paccaya*). Without relinquishing its status as a root condition, it also attains the state of being many conditions in eleven other ways by way of predominance (*adhipati*), conascence (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), result (*vipāka*), faculty (*indriya*), path (*magga*), association (*sampayutta*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*).
From non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adosa*), there are likewise predominance, faculty, and path conditions.
Excluding those three, they become various conditions by way of the remaining factors. This applies only to the resultant roots (*vipākahetu*);
however, in the case of wholesome functional states (*kusalakiriya*), the status of being a resultant condition (*vipākapaccayatā*) is excluded.
Excluding those three—greed, hatred, and delusion—as well as the four [roots] including the resultant, they become various conditions by way of the remaining factors.

The object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), while not relinquishing its status as an object condition, also functions as various other conditions in seven other ways—namely, by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), support (nissaya), decisive support (upanissaya), prenascence (purejāta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). This is the maximum limit in this context;
however, when immaterial phenomena or past and future material phenomena serve as an object condition, they function only as object-predominance and object-decisive-support.
More is obtained [in this way]. Under the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is similar to non-delusion (*amoha*).

The desire-to-act (*chanda*) as a predominance condition, without relinquishing its status as a predominance condition, becomes a multiple condition in eight other ways by way of the conascent, mutuality, support, resultant, associated, dissociated, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
Energy (*vīriya*) functions as those same [conditions] as well as the faculty and path conditions.
By way of these [three], it also becomes a manifold condition in ten other ways.
Having removed the path-condition from that [list] and inserted the nutriment-condition, by way of these, it becomes a manifold condition in ten ways beyond the predominance-condition.
As for objective-predominance, however, it is according to the method already stated below under the object-condition.
The state of being multiple conditions should be understood.

The proximity and contiguity conditions, while not relinquishing their status as proximity and contiguity conditions, also become multiple conditions in five other ways by way of decisive support, kamma, repetition, absence, and disappearance. It is the volition of the Noble Path itself...
And herein, it receives the status of a kamma-condition, while the remaining phenomena do not.

The conascence-condition, without relinquishing its nature as a conascence-condition, attains the state of being a manifold condition in fourteen other ways by way of root, predominance, mutuality, support, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. This too is the highest limit.
Furthermore, it should be understood that here, by way of the co-nascent object (*vatthusahajāta*) and so forth, there is an absence of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) and others.

The same principle applies to the mutuality-condition (*aññamaññapaccaya*). As for the support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*), while not relinquishing its status as a support-condition, it functions—by excluding itself, the six conditions consisting of the proximity, contiguity, post-nascence, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions, and the twenty-four remaining conditions—as the support-condition among those twenty-four conditions.
It also becomes a condition in seventeen other ways. This too is merely the highest limit;

however, it should be understood that here, by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*), the support (*nissaya*), and so forth, there is also the presence of conditions such as the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and others.

Within the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), the object-decisive-support (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*) is similar to the object-dominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*). The proximity-decisive-support (*anantara-upanissaya*) is the state of being the proximity-decisive-support condition.
Without abandoning its own nature, it also becomes a condition in six other ways by way of immediate, contiguous, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions.
Herein, only the volition of the Noble Path receives the status of a kamma-condition, and not the remaining states.
A natural strong-dependence condition is itself a natural strong-dependence condition. A prenascence condition [retains] its own status as a prenascence condition.

Without abandoning its object, it also becomes a condition in eight other ways by way of object, object-predominance, support, decisive support, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. This too is merely a description of the maximum;
however, in this case, the status of support, faculty, and dissociation conditions is not obtained for the object-prenascence [condition]. Beyond this...

It should be understood as being both obtainable and unobtainable. The postnascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), without relinquishing its own nature as a postnascent condition, becomes a multiple condition in three other ways by way of dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata).

The repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya), without relinquishing its status as a repetition condition, [becomes so] by way of proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), decisive support (upanissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata).
By way of these [factors], it also becomes a manifold condition through another five modes.

As for the kamma-condition, while not relinquishing its status as a kamma-condition, it first becomes a manifold condition through another nine modes by way of conascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance, all occurring at the same moment (*ekakkhaṇika*).
At different moments (*nānākkhaṇika*), it becomes a manifold condition by way of decisive support, proximity, contiguity, absence, and disappearance.
By way of these [factors], it also becomes a manifold condition through another five modes.

The resultant condition, without relinquishing its status as a resultant condition, also becomes a manifold condition through another fourteen modes by way of the root, predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, kamma, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. Regarding the nutriment condition, edible food...
Nutriment, without relinquishing its status as a nutriment condition, also functions as various other conditions in two further ways by way of presence and non-disappearance.
The remaining three [nutriments], likewise without relinquishing their status as nutriment conditions,
function accordingly as predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, kamma, result, faculty, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
By way of these, they also become multiple conditions in another eleven ways.

Regarding the faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*), the five material faculties, without relinquishing their status as faculty conditions, also become multiple conditions in another five ways by way of support, prenascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. The material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) also...
Without relinquishing its status as an indriya-condition, it also becomes a multiple condition in two other ways by way of presence (atthi) and non-disappearance (avigata).

The immaterial faculties (*arūpino indriyāni*), likewise, without relinquishing their status as indriya-conditions according to their respective natures, become multiple conditions in thirteen other ways by way of root (hetu), predominance (adhipati), conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), result (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), jhāna, path (magga), association (sampayutta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). The jhāna-condition [remains] a jhāna-condition...

Without relinquishing its own nature as a path-condition, it also functions as various other conditions in ten ways, according to its specific suitability, by way of being co-nascent, mutual, support, resultant, faculty, associated, dissociated, presence, and non-disappearance. Without relinquishing its own nature as a path-condition,
it likewise functions as those ten factors mentioned for the jhāna-condition— namely, the roots and predominants— as well as these others, according to its specific suitability.
By way of these [factors], it also becomes a manifold condition in another twelve ways.

The associated condition (sampayutta-paccaya), without relinquishing its status as an associated condition, becomes a manifold condition in another thirteen ways according to its specific suitability by way of root, predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
The dissociated condition (vippayutta-paccaya) [becomes a manifold condition] by way of its status as a dissociated condition...

Without abandoning [its own nature], it becomes a condition for others in seventeen ways according to its suitability, by excluding six conditions—namely, those designated as *anantara*, *samanantara*, *āsevana*, *sampayutta*, *natthi*, and *vigata*—and by way of the remaining ones.
Therein, the analysis of the conditions for both the material and the immaterial should be understood. The presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*) is the state of being a presence-condition.

Without abandoning the five conditions known as proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance, it functions as various other conditions in eighteen ways according to its specific suitability by way of the remaining factors.

The absence condition (*natthi-paccaya*) and the disappearance condition (*vigata-paccaya*) are similar to the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*). The non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*) is indeed similar to the presence condition (*atthi-paccaya*).
In this way, the analysis should also be understood here by means of a single condition having the nature of multiple conditions.

Regarding "similarity of conditions": among these twenty-four conditions, the proximate (anantara), immediate (samanantara), proximity-strong-dependence (anantarūpanissaya), repetition (āsevana), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata) conditions are similar;

likewise, the object (ārammaṇa), object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), and object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya) conditions are similar. It is by this method that similarity of conditions is to be understood here.
The analysis should be understood.
Regarding "dissimilarity of conditions": here, the prenascence condition is dissimilar to the postnascence condition;
likewise, the association condition is dissimilar to the dissociation condition, the presence condition to the absence condition, and the disappearance condition [to the non-disappearance condition].
By means of this method, the analysis here should also be understood even through the dissimilarity of conditions (*paccaya-visabhāga*).
As for "as pairs" (*yugala-ka*): among these, the analysis should be understood as being in pairs by virtue of these reasons:
similarity of meaning, similarity of sound, opposition in time, cause-and-effect relationship, and mutual opposition. [The terms] *anantara* and *samanantara*.
Indeed, a pair is so called because of similarity in meaning. A pair is so called because of similarity in sound in the case of the support (nissaya) and decisive-support (upanissaya) conditions;

because of opposition in time in the case of the prenascence (purejāta) and postnascence (pacchājāta) conditions; because of cause-and-effect relationship in the case of the kamma-condition and resultant-condition (vipāka-paccaya); and because of mutual opposition in the case of the associated (sampayutta) and dissociated (vippayutta) conditions.
Likewise, there are pairs in the case of the presence (atthi) and absence (natthi) conditions, and in the case of the disappearance (vigata) and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions.
Thus, the analysis should be understood here even by way of pairs. Regarding the classification as "productive" (*janaka*) and "non-productive" (*ajanaka*):

among these, the conditions of immediate (*anantara*), contiguous (*samanantara*), proximity (*anantarūpanissaya*), natural-proximity (*pakatūpanissaya*), repetition (*āsevana*), asynchronous (*nānākkhaṇika*), kamma, absence (*natthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*) are exclusively productive, not non-productive.
The postnascent condition (*pacchājāta*) is merely supportive, not productive. The remaining conditions are both productive and non-productive.
The meaning is "supporting. Thus, in this context, the analysis should be understood both in terms of what produces and what does not produce [results].

Regarding the categories of "all-bases" (*sabbaṭṭhānika*) and "not-all-bases": among these, the co-nascent (*sahajāta*), support (*nissaya*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*) conditions are called "all-bases";
the meaning is that they serve as the basis and the cause for all conditioned phenomena, whether material or mental. By means of these...

There is not even a single dhamma that arises without [these conditions]. The object (ārammaṇa), object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), absence (natthi), disappearance (vigata), natural-decisive-support (pakatūpanissaya), repetition (āsevana), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions are called "not having all things as their locus" (asabbatṭhānika). This means they do not serve as the locus or cause for all material and immaterial dhammas;
rather, they serve as the locus and cause only for the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha). For it is only immaterial dhammas that arise by means of these conditions, not material dhammas.
The pre-arisen and post-arisen conditions are also not all-pervasive, because they function as conditions for only the immaterial and material phenomena respectively.
Furthermore, the remaining conditions mentioned are not all-pervasive because they are causes for the arising of only certain material and immaterial phenomena.
Thus, in this context, the distinction between what is all-pervasive and what is not all-pervasive should be understood.

Regarding the phrase "from the conceptualization of 'form as form,' etc.," among these twenty-four conditions, there is not even a single condition that, being exclusively material, serves as a condition for materiality alone;
however, there is indeed one that, being exclusively material, serves as a condition for the immaterial alone.
Which one is it? It is the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*). For the prenascence condition is exclusively...

Materiality itself, having become [a condition], is a condition for immateriality alone. There is no such thing as materiality itself, having become [a condition], being exclusively a condition for both the material and the immaterial;
however, there is that which, having become exclusively immaterial, is a condition for immateriality alone. But what is this?
It is sixfold by way of the immediately preceding, the equal-and-immediate, the habitual, the associated, the presence, and the absence conditions. For it...
Everything, having been exclusively non-material, becomes a condition for what is non-material.
There is also that which, although being exclusively non-material, is a condition for what is exclusively material. But which one is this? It is the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).
For that, having been exclusively non-material, is a condition for matter alone; yet it is exclusively a non-material phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*) itself.
There is also a condition for both the material and the immaterial. But what is it? It is fivefold by way of root-cause, kamma, result, jhāna, and path.
For all of these, being exclusively immaterial, serve as conditions for both material and immaterial phenomena.
However, there is no such thing as a condition that, being exclusively both material and immaterial, serves as a condition for the material alone; rather, [it serves] for the immaterial alone.

What, then, is this? It is both the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). For these two, being exclusively material or immaterial, serve as conditions for the immaterial alone.
However, there is also that which, being exclusively material or immaterial, serves as a condition for both the material and the immaterial.
What, then, is this? It is by way of the dominant, conascent, mutuality, support, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
It is ninefold. For all of it, being exclusively either material or immaterial, serves as a condition only for the material or the immaterial;
thus, the analysis here should be understood even through such alternatives as "material for material" and so forth.
Regarding "by way of the distinction of existence": among these twenty-four conditions, first, in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*), no condition whatsoever [is absent].
It is not obtained [in that case]. However, in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*), twenty-one conditions are obtained, excluding the three:

the prenascence, postnascence, and dissociation conditions. In the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*), only seven are obtained: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, kamma, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance.
Furthermore, in external matter not bound to faculties, [seven are obtained] by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, presence, and non-disappearance.
"Only five are obtained"—thus should the exposition here be understood even by way of the classification of existence (*bhava*).
The commentary on the section on the exposition of conditions (*paccayaniddesavāra*) is finished. The section on questions (*pucchāvāra*).
1. Commentary on the Positive Order of Conditions (*Paccayānulomavaṇṇanā*).

Thus, in the Great Treatise on the *Paṭṭhāna*—which comprises twenty-four sections of the *Paṭṭhāna* such as the Positive *Paṭṭhāna* and so forth, arranged by way of the Triplets (*tika*) and so on—this is called the "Triplet *Paṭṭhāna*" because it is expounded based upon those triplets, and the "Couplet *Paṭṭhāna"*... [and so forth].

It is called "the establishment by twos. Without taking those [twos] into account, first, having shown by way of both summary and exposition those very conditions by means of which those triads and so forth were analyzed—
by means of this section known as the "Enumeration of the Schedule" and the "Analysis of Conditions"—
now, because it was explained in reliance upon those triads and so forth, this is the "Establishment by Threes" (*tikapaṭṭhāna*).

"Dependent on the unpleasant... [and so on] ...dependent on the unpleasant and the unpleasant," it is said. Having expanded and demonstrated those triplets and so forth by way of these conditions, the teaching is presented through seven great sections based on each individual triplet and dyad.

Their names are as follows: the Section on Dependent (Paṭicca-vāra), the Section on Co-nascent (Sahajāta-vāra), the Section on Conditions (Paccaya-vāra), the Section on Support (Nissaya-vāra), and the Section on Conjoined (Saṃsaṭṭha-vāra).
The section on association and the section on inquiry.
Therein, the "Dependent Section" is so called because it is stated by way of the expression of dependence, as in: "Dependent upon a wholesome state, a wholesome state [arises].
The "Conascent Section" is so called because it is stated by way of the expression of conascence, as in: "Conascent with a wholesome state, a wholesome state [arises]."
The section called "Co-nascence" has been stated. It is not different in meaning from the preceding "Dependence" section.

However, the first was stated for the sake of those who understand by way of the designation "dependent," while the second is for the sake of those who understand by way of the designation "co-nascent.
In both of these, the conditions and the conditioned phenomena should be understood by way of both material and immaterial phenomena.

And these [factors] are indeed co-nascent; neither pre-nascent nor post-nascent ones are obtained. However, the section on conditions called "conditioned by a wholesome state, a wholesome state [arises]" is stated by way of expressing the conditions.

That too should be understood as being solely in terms of material and immaterial states, just like the two preceding sections. But here, a pre-nascent condition is also obtained. This is its [distinction].

There is a distinction from the first two sections. Immediately following that is the section called the "Dependence Section" (*nissayavāra*), which is stated by way of expressing dependence as: "Depending on a wholesome state, a wholesome state [arises].
This is not different in meaning from the preceding "Condition Section" (*paccayavāra*).
However, it was stated first for those who understand by way of the expression "condition," whereas this is stated by way of the expression "dependence."

The second [section] is by way of those who are awakening. Following that, the section called the "Conjoined Section" (saṃsaṭṭhavāra) is stated by way of the designation of conjoining, as follows: "A wholesome state conjoined with a wholesome state.

The section called the "Associated Section" (sampayuttavāra) is stated by way of the designation of association, as follows: "A wholesome state associated with a wholesome state. This [latter] is [similar] to the former.
In terms of meaning, this section on "associated" (saṃsaṭṭha) is not different from the preceding one.

However, it is stated first for the sake of those who understand by way of the designation "associated," while the second is stated for those who understand by way of the designation "conjoined" (sampayutta).

In both of these cases, the conditions and the conditionally arisen states should be understood as referring exclusively to immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma). As for the seventh section, since "a wholesome state [is a condition] for a wholesome [state]... [the text continues].

Having extracted each respective question by way of the method beginning with "the state is a condition for the state as a root-condition" (*dhammassa hetupaccayena paccayo*), and having again analyzed all those questions—

rendering them free from tangles and free from thickets— by way of the method beginning with "wholesome roots [are a condition] for the associated aggregates" (*kusalā hetū sampayuttakānaṃ khandhānaṃ*),
that section is designated as the "Section on Questions" (*pañhāvāra*) precisely because the questions have been thoroughly analyzed.
[The section] is concluded. Herein, both the conditions and the conditionally arisen states are to be understood by way of both material and immaterial phenomena.
Among these, that which is called the "first chapter on dependence" is twofold: by way of enumeration (*uddesa*) and by way of exposition (*niddesa*).
Therein, the first is the chapter of enumeration, which is also called the "chapter of inquiry" (*pucchāvāra*). It is also called the "chapter of formal definitions" (*paṇṇattivāra*).

It is called "nāma" (name). For it is called the "Section on Enumeration" (*uddesavāra*) because wholesome states and so forth are enumerated by way of the root-conditions and other conditions of wholesome states and so forth;

the "Section on Inquiry" (*pucchāvāra*) because the arising of wholesome states and so forth is inquired into by way of the root-conditions and other conditions dependent upon wholesome states and so forth;

and the "Section on Designation" (*paññattivāra*) because the arising of wholesome states and so forth is designated by way of the root-conditions and other conditions dependent upon wholesome states and so forth.

25–34. In this regard, there may be the following hypothetical question: "Dependent on a wholesome state (*kusala dhamma*), could a wholesome state arise by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*)? Herein, the meaning is as follows: "If a wholesome state were to arise by way of the root-condition, could it be that it [arises] dependent on a wholesome state?
Or alternatively: "That wholesome state which arises dependent on a wholesome state..."
"Could it arise through the condition of a cause"—this is the meaning here. In that context, *paṭi* functions in the sense of similarity;
for a similar person is called a *paṭipuggala*, and a similar part is called a *paṭibhāga*. *Icca* is a word expressing the desire to go.
Having combined both [words], *paṭicca* means "having gone toward," that is, having reached [it] by way of a state of similarity known as simultaneous arising.

This means: "having attained the state of arising together with that. The question is asked: "Could a wholesome dhamma arise by way of the root condition (hetupaccaya) depending upon a wholesome dhamma through such a state of simultaneous arising?

Alternatively, *paṭicca* means "having made a condition. And that act of making a condition is found both in the case of the prenascence condition (*purejāta*) and the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta*).
Here, "conascent" (sahajāta) is intended. The same method applies to such passages as, "Dependent on a wholesome state, an unwholesome [state arises]," and so forth.

In that regard, although there is no unwholesome state dependent on a wholesome state by way of conascence, nevertheless, in this section of questions, both that which is obtainable in meaning when being answered and that which is not obtainable—all of it—[is to be considered].
This has been extracted by way of the questions. However, in the subsequent answers, that which is not applicable has been discarded, and only that which is applicable has been answered.
Thus, having understood both the meaning and the course of the questions herein, the classification of the questions should now be understood by way of enumeration.

For here, beginning with the term "wholesome" (*kusala*) in the phrase "dependent on a wholesome state" (*kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca*), [the sequence extends] up to the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
There are three questions; again, starting from that same beginning, there are three [questions] ending with the classification of dyads by way of the wholesome, the indeterminate, and so forth;

and again, starting from that same beginning, there is one [set] ending with the triads. Thus, there are seven questions beginning with the wholesome—namely, "dependent on a wholesome state," and so on—likewise those beginning with the unwholesome, likewise those beginning with the indeterminate, likewise those beginning with both the wholesome and the indeterminate, and likewise those beginning with both the unwholesome and the indeterminate.

There are forty-nine questions regarding the root-condition (hetupaccaya) based on the wholesome triad (kusalattika), by way of all seven sets of seven— beginning with the wholesome-unwholesome, and beginning with the wholesome-unwholesome-indeterminate.
Among these, there are nine ending with the single-rooted, nine ending with the single-rooted dyad, three ending with the single-rooted triad, and [nine] ending with the dyad-rooted single.
Nine [combinations] end with two roots; three end with three roots; three end with one root; three end with two roots;
and one ends with three roots—thus they should be understood according to the roots as well.
And just as there are forty-nine [combinations] in the case of the root condition, so it is for the object condition and the others; thus, in all twenty-four conditions—
One thousand and one hundred, and another seventy-six;
these questions are combined together in the Single Root Guide (Ekamūlaka-naya). 35–36.

Following that, the Double Root Guide (Dumūlaka-naya) is commenced, beginning with the root conditions of cause (hetu), object (ārammaṇa), and so forth. Therein, the dyad of cause and object... [and so on].
The "duo of absence of root" (hetu-avigata-duka) consists of twenty-three duos together with the root-condition (hetu-paccaya).
Among them, just as in the case of the root-condition, there are forty-nine questions for the duo of root-object (hetu-ārammaṇa-duka), of which only two are shown in the Pāḷi.

And just as there are forty-nine in the duo of root-object, so it is in the duos of root-predominance (hetu-adhipati-duka) and the rest. Therein, by way of the first question, there is the duo of root-predominance.

Having shown three dyads in sequence—the dyad of immediate cause (*hetānantara-duka*) and the dyad of cause and immediate antecedent (*hetu-samanantara-duka*)—the dyad of cause and non-disappearance (*hetu-avigata-duka*) is shown at the conclusion;
the rest is abbreviated. Furthermore, the section on the questions here should be understood as follows:
one thousand and one hundred and twenty-seven.
In the twenty-three chapters [of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*], there are questions based on two roots (*dumūlaka*). 37.

Following that, the method of three roots (*timūlaka*) begins, starting with the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), and the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*).
Therein, together with the dyad of root and object, for each one of the twenty-two conditions beginning with the predominance-condition...
By way of arrangement, there are twenty-two triads (*tīkā*). Among these, having shown the first and second triads by way of the first inquiry, the final triad is shown; the rest is abbreviated.
Just as with the dyads (*dukas*), so too with the triads—one should apply fifty-one [modes] to each individual triad, and thus to all twenty-two triads.
One thousand and seventy-eight questions in total arise from the reckoning of questions in the method based on the triple root (tikamūlaka). 38.
Following that is the method based on the quadruple root (catumūlaka): the root-cause condition, the object condition, the predominance condition, and the proximity condition.

It has begun. Therein, by way of combining each [condition] with the twenty-one conditions—beginning with the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*)—along with the first tetrad, there are twenty-one tetrads. Having shown two of those tetrads, the rest have been abbreviated.
Here too, having taken forty-nine [factors] in each tetrad, [the same applies] to all twenty-one tetrads.
There are one thousand questions and twenty-nine others;
thus, by way of number, there are these questions in the Fourfold Root (Catummūlaka) method.
Following that, beginning with the Fivefold Root (Pañcamūlaka) and continuing up to the All-Root (Sabbamūlaka), the teaching was given; all of that, having been condensed—
Having combined what was stated below with what is to be stated above, the method is shown in the Pāḷi:
“One should expand [the exposition] by not becoming confused regarding the single-rooted, double-rooted, triple-rooted, four-rooted, five-rooted, and all-rooted [categories].
Among these, that which is to be said concerning the single-rooted and so forth has already been stated. However, regarding the five-rooted [category], by means of the first tetrad—
Together with the twenty conditions beginning with the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-paccaya*),
there are twenty-five groups of five by way of combining each one of them. Calculating forty-nine for each of those—
there are nine hundred and eighty questions, and another [set] beyond that.
In the *Pañcamūlaka* method, the questions arise from enumeration.

In the *Chamūlaka*, by way of combining each [condition] with the nineteen conditions—beginning with the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*)—along with the first pentad, there are nineteen hexads.
Calculating fifty-nine for each of those, there are nine hundred and thirty-one questions. Furthermore: "Nine hundred questions, and thirty-one beyond that."
The questions arise from enumeration within the system based on the sixfold root.

In the system based on the sevenfold root, by way of combining each [condition] with the eighteen conditions—beginning with the mutuality condition and so forth—together with the first sixfold set, there are eighteen heptads.
Calculating forty-nine for each of those, there are eight hundred and eighty-two questions beyond that.
The questions arise from enumeration within the sevenfold method.

In the eightfold method, by combining each of the seventeen conditions—beginning with the dependence condition (*nissaya-paccaya*)—with the first heptad, there are seventeen groups of eight. Calculating forty-nine for each of those, there are:
Eight hundred and thirty-three questions in total.
The questions arise from enumeration within the "Rooted in Eight" method (*aṭṭhamūlaka*).

In the "Rooted in Nine" method (*navamūlaka*), by way of combining each [condition] with the first group of eight among the sixteen conditions—such as the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) and the rest—there are sixteen groups of nine.
Calculating forty-nine for each of those, there are seven hundred and eighty-four questions. Furthermore: Seven hundred questions, and eighty-four beyond that.
The questions are formed by way of enumeration in the Ninefold Root Guide (Navamūlaka-naya).

In the Tenfold Root Guide (Dasamūlaka), by combining each of the fifteen conditions—beginning with the prior-condition (purejāta-paccaya) and so forth—with the first ninefold set, there are fifteen decads. Calculating forty-nine for each of those, it is said:
"Seven hundred questions, and thirty-five more than that."
In the *Dasamūlaka* (Ten-Root) method, the questions arise from enumeration.

In the *Ekādasamūlaka* (Eleven-Root), by combining each [condition] with the first tenfold set and with the fourteen conditions beginning with the postnascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*), there are fourteen elevenfold sets. Calculating forty-nine [questions] for each of these, it is said:
"Six hundred and eighty-six questions, and more than that."
In this [work], the questions are calculated based on the elevenfold root.

In the twelvefold root, by way of combining each factor with the first elevenfold root across the thirteen conditions—beginning with the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya)—there are thirteen twelvefold sets. Calculating forty-nine [questions] for each of these, there are:
Six hundred and thirty-seven questions in total.
The questions are formed by way of enumeration according to the twelvefold method.

In the thirteenfold method, by combining each of the twelve conditions—beginning with the kamma-condition—with the first twelvefold set, there are twelve thirteenfold sets. Calculating forty-nine for each of these, it says:
"Five hundred and eighty-eight further questions."
The questions arise from enumeration according to the method based on the thirteenfold root.

In the fourteenfold root, by combining each [condition] with the eleven conditions—beginning with the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*)—along with the first thirteenfold root, there are eleven fourteenfold sets. Calculating forty-nine for each of those, it says:

"Five hundred and thirty-nine questions. (Note: This refers to 11 × 14 = 154; 154 × 49 = 7,546; however, the traditional calculation here accounts for specific exclusions, resulting in the stated total of 539.)
The questions arise from enumeration in the fourteen-rooted method.

In the fifteen-rooted method, by combining each of the ten conditions—beginning with the nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*)—with the first fourteenfold set, there are ten fifteenfold sets. Calculating forty-nine for each of those, there are:
Four hundred and ninety questions in total. Thus it is said.
The questions are formed by way of enumeration according to the fifteenfold method.

In the sixteenfold method, there are nine sets of sixteen by way of combining each [of the factors] with the first fifteenfold set, across the nine conditions beginning with the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*).
Making forty-nine [questions] for each of those— Four hundred and forty-one, and yet another.
The questions arise from enumeration according to the method based on the sixteenfold sets.

In the seventeenfold set, by way of combining each [condition] with the first sixteenfold set among the eight conditions—beginning with the condition of jhāna—there are eight seventeenfold sets. Making forty-nine [questions] for each of those, there are:
Three hundred and ninety-two questions, and another two hundred and ninety.
The questions arise from enumeration according to the method based on the seventeenfold sets.

In the eighteenfold set, by way of combining each [condition] with the first seventeenfold set among the seven conditions beginning with the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*), there are seven eighteenfold sets.
Calculating forty-nine for each of those—there are three hundred and forty-four questions.
The questions are formed by way of enumeration according to the eighteen-rooted method.

In the nineteen-rooted method, by combining each [of the factors] with the first eighteen-rooted set, there are six sets of nineteen through the application of each to the six conditions, beginning with the associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*).
Calculating fifty-nine for each of those, it says: "Two hundred and ninety-four, and four more."
The questions arise from enumeration in the nineteenfold method.

In the twentyfold root, by way of combining each [condition] with the first nineteenfold [method] among the five conditions beginning with the dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*), there are twenty-five [questions].
Making forty-nine for each of those—there are two hundred and forty-five questions.
The questions arise from enumeration in the twentyfold root-method.

In the twenty-onefold root-method, by way of combining each [condition] with the four conditions—beginning with the presence condition (*atthipaccaya*)—along with the first twentyfold method, there are four sets of twenty-one.
Making forty-nine for each of those, the total number of questions combined is one hundred and ninety-six.
Calculated by those who know the characteristics according to the method of the twenty-onefold scheme:

in the twenty-two-fold root scheme, there are three sets of twenty-two, each formed by combining the first twenty-onefold scheme with each of the three conditions beginning with the "absence" condition (*natthi-paccaya*).
Having calculated forty-nine for each of these, [the total is] one hundred and forty-four, and another seven.
The questions are formed by way of enumeration in the section based on twenty-two root-conditions.

In the section based on twenty-three root-conditions, there are two sets of twenty-three questions each, according to the method of combining each [condition] with the first set of twenty-two, regarding the two conditions of absence (vigata) and non-absence (avigata).
Calculating forty-nine for each of those two—thus, eighty-nine questions in this context are recognized by way of enumeration.

In this twenty-third [chapter], which is based on twenty-three [conditions], the twenty-fourth base, however, should be understood by way of the combination of all conditions; for that very reason, it is called the "base of all.
In that regard, there are exactly forty-nine questions, all of which are formulated by taking only the term "root condition" (hetupaccaya).

The questions, which were explained in detail by the Teacher to the assembly of devas according to the sequence beginning with those having a single root and ending with those having all roots, are here presented in brief.
Furthermore, this is the numerical summary of them all:
in the method of the single-rooted [questions], there are one thousand one hundred and seventy-six.

And the questions have arrived. In the method of the root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*), having counted forty-nine by means of that very same root, these are to be taken here under the root-cause condition;
the remainder should be inserted into the roots of the remaining conditions. Under the two-root [method], there are one hundred twenty-seven;
under the three-root, one thousand seventy-eight; under the four-root, one thousand twenty-nine; and under the five-root...
There are nine hundred and eighty in the root of six; nine hundred and thirty-one in the root of five; eight hundred and seventy-two in the root of seven;
eight hundred and thirty-three in the root of eight; seven hundred and eighty-four in the root of nine;
seven hundred and thirty-five in the root of ten; and six hundred and eighty-six in the root of eleven.
In the twelvefold root, there are six hundred and thirty-seven; in the thirteenfold root, five hundred and eighty-eight;
in the fourteenfold root, five hundred and thirty-nine; in the fifteenfold root, four hundred and ninety;
in the sixteenfold root, four thousand seven hundred and forty-one; in the seventeenfold root, three hundred and ninety-two; and in the eighteenfold root—
There are three hundred forty-three based on nineteen roots, two hundred ninety-four based on twenty roots,
two hundred forty-five based on twenty-one roots, one hundred ninety-six based on twenty-two roots,
ninety-eight based on twenty-three roots, and forty-nine based on all roots; thus, beginning with the "root" category (hetupada),...
Regarding the classifications beginning with those having a single root:
"There are fourteen thousand and seven hundred questions concerning the causal terms alone, according to the divisions beginning with the single root."

39–40. Having thus demonstrated the classification of questions starting from the single-root method up to the all-root method, beginning with the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*), he now says, "Could a wholesome state arise dependent on a wholesome state by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*)," etc., in order to demonstrate [the analysis] beginning with the object-condition. Therein, "by way of the object-condition":

"Conditioned by cause" (*hetupaccayā*): up to this point, the method based on a single root has been shown, beginning with the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and ending with the cause condition.
Following that, the method based on two roots is commenced, beginning with "conditioned by object, conditioned by predominance" (*ārammaṇapaccayā adhipatipaccayā*).
Therein, having shown this first dyad as well as the dyad of object and non-disappearance (*ārammaṇa-avigata-duka*), the remainder is abbreviated. [The section begins: "Conditioned by object..."

The "condition by way of cause" (*hetupaccaya*)—this concluding dyad has not been shown. However, if it appears in some version of the textual tradition (*vācanāmagga*), that very version should be accepted.

Following that, without showing the triads and so forth based on the "condition by way of object" (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), in order to show the single factors and so forth beginning with the "condition by way of dominance" (*adhipatipaccaya*), [the text says]: "Condition by way of dominance," "condition by way of proximity" (*anantarapaccaya*).
Only these—namely, the condition as immediate antecedent (samanantara-paccaya), the condition as co-nascent (sahajāta-paccaya), and the condition as mutuality (aññamañña-paccaya)—are mentioned;
this should be understood either by way of a single root or by way of all roots. 41.
Following that, beginning with the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya), only those based on two roots are shown: "by way of the non-disappearance condition..."

The section beginning with "condition by way of cause" (*hetupaccaya*) is commenced. Therein, after stating three dyads in sequence—namely, the dyad of non-disappearance by way of cause (*avigata-hetuduka*), the dyad of non-disappearance by way of object (*avigatārammaṇaduka*), and the dyad of non-disappearance by way of predominance (*avigatādhipatiduka*)—a single dyad, the dyad of non-disappearance and disappearance (*avigatavigataduka*), is shown at the conclusion.

Then, in order to show the triple-rooted [formula] by way of the condition of non-disappearance alone, it says: "By way of the condition of non-disappearance, by way of the condition of cause, by way of the condition of object..."

Having stated three triads in sequence—“conditioned by non-disappearance, conditioned by root, conditioned by predominance; conditioned by non-disappearance, conditioned by root, conditioned by proximity”—and having stated the final triad as “conditioned by non-disappearance, conditioned by root, conditioned by disappearance,” he then shows the fourfold root [analysis] by way of the non-disappearance condition alone: “Conditioned by non-disappearance, conditioned by root...”

Having stated two sets of four—namely, "conditioned by object, conditioned by predominance, conditioned by non-disappearance, conditioned by root, conditioned by object, and conditioned by proximity"—the term "conditioned by disappearance" was extracted and set aside, while everything else was abbreviated. To demonstrate that state of abbreviation, [it says]:
"For each single term, there is one based on a single root, one based on two roots, and one based on three roots..."
It is said: "The entire root [analysis] should be expanded out by one who is not confused.

Therefore, just as there are one hundred and seventy-six questions based on the single-root [analysis]—starting with the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and proceeding according to the terms beginning with "root," and so forth up to forty-nine [questions] for the all-root [analysis]—in the same way, starting with each individual [condition] such as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), and proceeding according to the terms beginning with "object" (*ārammaṇa*), etc., [the analysis should be expanded].
For each single word, there are one hundred and seventy-six questions based on a single root... [and so on] ...up to forty-nine questions based on all roots.
Thus, for each individual word, there are fourteen thousand seven hundred questions, categorized by the single-root basis and so forth.
This is the numerical extent of these [questions] across all twenty-four conditions:
Three hundred thousand eight hundred and fifty-two questions regarding the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*) have been well analyzed according to the method of positive formulation (*anulomanaya*).
And just as it is with the wholesome triad, so it is with the feeling triad (*vedanāttika*) and the others; thus, in all twenty-two triads—
Sixty-one thousand, six hundred and seventy-seven;
one hundred thousand questions, according to their classification within the threefold division,
have been condensed into this path of recitation.
In the *Duka*, however, regarding the statement, "Could it be that, dependent on a root-dhamma, a root-dhamma arises by way of root-condition?"—thus, dependent on a root, a root;
dependent on a root, a non-root; dependent on a root, both root and non-root;
dependent on a non-root, a non-root; dependent on a non-root, a root; dependent on a non-root, both root and non-root; and [dependent on] a root...
Dependent on a non-root and a root; dependent on both a root and a non-root, there is a non-root;

and dependent on both a root and a non-root, there are both a root and a non-root—thus, for each of the dyads among the root-condition and the others, there are nine questions for each individual condition.
Starting with the root-condition as the first, there are two hundred and sixteen questions in the single-rooted section. Among those:
Only nine questions, unmixed with others, are to be taken for the root-condition (hetupaccaya); the remaining eight have been taken by way of the [other] sections.
From among those twenty-three sections beginning with the "root-dyad" (dukamūlaka), this is the numerical limit: having removed one nonad from each section up to the "all-root" (sabbamūlaka).
First, regarding the root-dyad, there are two sets of more than one hundred and sixteen questions shown under the single-rooted (ekamūlaka) [sections].
Subtracting nine, there are two hundred and seven questions; then, subtracting nine from that, there are one hundred and ninety-eight in the three-rooted [set].

Thus, by successively subtracting nine from each preceding total, there are one hundred and eighty-nine in the four-rooted, one hundred and eighty in the five-rooted, one hundred and seventy-one in the six-rooted, one hundred and sixty-two in the seven-rooted, and one hundred and fifty-three in the eight-rooted.
In the nine-rooted [formula], there are one hundred and forty-four; in the ten-rooted, one hundred and thirty-five; in the eleven-rooted, one hundred and twenty-six;
in the twelve-rooted, one hundred and seventeen; in the thirteen-rooted, one hundred and eight; in the fourteen-rooted, ninety-nine;
in the fifteen-rooted, ninety; in the sixteen-rooted, eighty-one; in the seventeen-rooted, seventy-two; and in the eighteen-rooted—

There are sixty-three [questions] based on nineteen roots, fifty-four based on twenty roots, forty-five based on twenty-one roots, thirty-six based on twenty-two roots, eighteen based on twenty-three roots, and nine based on all roots.
Just as these two hundred and sixteen questions are presented by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) starting from the single-root basis... [and so on] ...up to the basis of all roots.

Nine. Likewise, beginning with each one among the object-condition and the others, according to the sequence of terms such as "object" (*ārammaṇa*), there are two hundred and sixteen questions for each term based on the single-rooted [analysis]... and so on, up to nine for the all-rooted [analysis].
Thus, for each term, there are two thousand seven hundred questions, categorized by the single-rooted and other types. Of these—
This is the numerical limit for all twenty-four conditions:
Sixty-four thousand and eight hundred questions are recognized in the method of direct order (anuloma) for the simple condition-by-cause (hetu-duka) alone.
And just as it is with the dyad on roots, so it is with the dyads on "with-cause" and the rest;
thus, in the entire hundred of dyads, the wise state: Six million and four hundred thousand, And eighty thousand more—these are the questions in the hundred of dyads.
This, then, is the enumeration of the questions in the Pure Triplets and the Couplets of the Paṭṭhāna.
Furthermore, after taking twenty-two triplets and adding them to the hundred couplets, that which is taught as the "Couplet-Triplet Paṭṭhāna" is presented there, beginning with:
"Could it be that, dependent on a causal wholesome state, a causal wholesome state arises?"
"By way of root-condition": in this manner, by combining each of the twenty-two triads with one hundred duads,
the delimitation should be understood by taking all of them— beginning with those having a single root— as explained in the method stated below for the questions that are to be demonstrated.
Furthermore, after that, having taken one hundred dyads (*duka*) and inserted them into twenty-two triads (*tika*),

the so-called *Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna* was taught. Therein as well, in the manner of "Could a wholesome causal state arise conditioned by a wholesome causal state through the condition of cause (*hetupaccaya*)?",
each one of the hundred dyads is to be demonstrated by being combined with the twenty-two triads.
The delimitation should be understood by taking all [the questions]—beginning with those having a single root and so forth—in the manner explained below the questions.
Furthermore, that which is taught thereafter, having been included within the triplets themselves, is called the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*; therein also it is said:
"There may be a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling dependent upon a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling..."
"Could a state associated [with consciousness] arise by way of the root condition?"—
in this manner, each one of the twenty-two triads should be combined with the remaining twenty-one triads;
the delimitation of all these questions, beginning with those having a single root, is to be understood according to the method explained below.
Furthermore, when the so-called *Duka-Duka-Paṭṭhāna* was taught by grouping [the factors] into pairs after that point, even there— in the case of the statement,
"Dependent on a state that is a root and accompanied by a root, a state that is a root and accompanied by a root may arise by way of the root-condition"—
each single pair among those one hundred pairs must be shown by being joined with the remaining ninety-nine pairs.
The delimitation should be understood by taking all [the questions] according to the method explained below, starting from those with a single root and so forth.
For it was precisely after the Tathāgata had shown all these various classifications that he taught the Dhamma to the assembly of devas;
however, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) explained the teaching to him by way of a mere demonstration of the method, summarizing it as: "Today this and that has been taught."
The Elder also set forth the method of recitation by way of summary alone; that very method established by the Elder was then included in the compilation at the time of the Council.
To demonstrate this method of summary, the following verse was placed: "The excellent *Tikapaṭṭhāna* and the supreme *Dukapaṭṭhāna*. Its meaning is as follows:
"The excellent *Tikapaṭṭhāna*" refers to the preeminent *Tikapaṭṭhāna*; and "the supreme *Dukapaṭṭhāna*" refers to the most excellent *Dukapaṭṭhāna*.
“Dukatikañceva” means the *dukatika-paṭṭhāna*. “Tikadukan” means the *tikaduka-paṭṭhāna*. “Tikatikañceva” means the *tikatika-paṭṭhāna*. “Dukadukan” means the *dukaduka-paṭṭhāna*.
“Cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā” means that these six methods—the *tikapaṭṭhāna* and so forth—are to be understood as very profound in their direct order (*anuloma*). Therein, two...

The *anulomas* consist of the *dhammānuloma* and the *paccayānuloma*. Therein, *dhammānuloma* refers to the teaching that proceeds by way of the positive exposition (*anulomadesanā*) of those phenomena included in the matrices (*mātikā*) of the Abhidhamma, such as: "Dependent on a wholesome phenomenon, a wholesome phenomenon [arises].
*Paccayānuloma* refers to the twenty-four conditions, such as: "By way of the root condition, by way of the object condition," and so forth.
That which proceeds by way of teaching in direct order is called "conditionality in direct order" (paccayānuloma).

In that regard, the verse cited earlier in the commentary—“The triads and the excellent Paṭṭhāna... these six methods in direct order are very profound”—was spoken with reference to the "direct order of phenomena" (dhammānuloma).
However, here this verse [is spoken] with reference to that same direct order of phenomena.

This was stated with reference to the *paccayānuloma* (the forward order of conditions). Therefore, regarding the commentary verse which says, "The six methods in the forward order are very profound," the meaning should be understood as follows:
in the *dhammānuloma* (the forward order of phenomena), the six methods beginning with the *tikapaṭṭhāna* (the triads) are very profound.
However, in this particular context, within the *paccayānuloma* as it occurs in the sequence "conditioned by root, conditioned by object," these [methods] belong to the *dhammānuloma*.
The meaning should be understood as follows: "The six methods, beginning with the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*, are very profound.

Among these, in the *Anuloma* (Positive) section of the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*, this classification of questions for the "Dependent" chapter (*paṭiccasamuppādavāra*) within the "Enumeration" (*paṇṇatti*) section is shown by way of the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*) alone, having been condensed.
However, not even a single question is shown for the remaining triads or for the other *Paṭṭhānas*.

Furthermore, in the subsequent sections such as the "Co-arising Chapter" (Sahajātavāra), instead of posing questions according to the "Wholesome Triad" (Kusalattika), only the answers are shown according to what is applicable.

However, because of the statement, "The six methods in the forward order are very profound," these six methods of the *Paṭṭhāna* should be presented by posing questions within this "Conditionality in Forward Order" (Paccayānuloma). *Paṭṭhāna* (The Great Treatise on Relations)
For this is the burden of the teachers who provide such expositions.
2. Commentary on the Negative (Paccanīya) Section 42–44.
Now follows the negative section. To demonstrate it: "Dependent upon a wholesome state, a wholesome state [may arise]."

The passage beginning with "Could it arise without the condition of root" (*uppajjeyya na hetupaccayā*) and so forth is commenced. Therein, the scope of the questions is exactly equal to that of the positive formulation (*anuloma*). For this very reason, it is stated here:

"Just as the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) was explained in detail in the positive formulation, so too should the non-root-condition (*nahetupaccaya*) be explained in the negative formulation (*paccanīya*).
Furthermore, at the conclusion, it says: "Just as in the positive formulation there was a single root for each individual term..."
"It should be expanded in the reverse order as well, from the two-rooted, the three-rooted, and the four-rooted up to the twenty-three-rooted"—so it is said.
This "twenty-three-rooted" is stated here with reference specifically to the two-rooted [section].
However, at the conclusion, there is indeed the "all-rooted" and even the twenty-four-rooted; all of that is merely abbreviated.
"And the excellent Paṭṭhāna in three ways... and so on, up to "...the six methods in the negative (paccanīya) are very profound. Here too, there are two negatives:

the negative of phenomena (dhamma-paccanīya) and the negative of conditions (paccaya-paccanīya). Among these, by way of the teaching of the negative—namely, "dependent on a non-virtuous phenomenon, a non-virtuous phenomenon [arises]"—with respect to those phenomena comprised by the headings of the Abhidhamma matrix such as "virtuous phenomena" (kusalā dhammā):

That which proceeds by way of the opposition of phenomena (*dhammapaccanīya*) is as follows: "Not by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), not by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*)," and so forth.
That which proceeds by way of the teaching of the opposition of the twenty-four conditions is called the opposition of conditions (*paccayapaccanīya*).

Therein, the following verse from the sub-commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) below—“The *tika* and the excellent *Paṭṭhāna*... [etc. ...the six methods in the opposition are very profound”—refers to the opposition of phenomena (*dhammapaccanīya*).

[The previous statement] was spoken with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). However, here this verse is spoken specifically with reference to the "opposites of conditions" (*paccayapaccanīya*) within the conformity to the Dhamma (*dhammānuloma*).
Therefore, regarding the commentary verse, “Six methods are very deep in the opposites,” the meaning should be understood as follows:

in the opposites of the Dhamma, the six methods beginning with the *Tikapātthāna* (the Threefold Exposition) are very deep. But in this particular context, the root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*) is not [included].

"Not by way of object-condition" (*nārammaṇapaccayā*): thus, regarding the negative formulation of conditions as they occur, it should be understood that these six methods, beginning with the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, are extremely profound within the positive formulation (*dhammānuloma*) alone.
Among those, this [section] belongs to the "Dependent Chapter" (*paṭiccavāra*) within the *Anulomika-paṭṭhāna* itself, by way of the mere "Wholesome Triad" (*kusalattika*).

In the section on the formulated categories (*paṇṇattivāra*), the classification of questions has been shown in abbreviated form. However, in the remaining triads (*tikesu*) and the remaining *Paṭṭhāna* sections, not even a single question has been shown.
Furthermore, in the subsequent sections such as the "Co-nascent" (*sahajāta*) chapter, questions have not been raised even for the "Wholesome Triad" (*kusalattika*);
instead, only the answers have been shown according to what is applicable. [As it is said: "Six in the negative. (*Cha paccanīyamhi*)

Furthermore, because of the statement, “The method is very profound,” these six methods of the *Paṭṭhāna* regarding the inverse of conditions (*paccayapaccanīya*) should be extracted and demonstrated by way of questions.
For this is the burden of the teachers who expound the *Paṭṭhāna*.
3. Commentary on the Positive-Negative Method (*Anulomapaccanīyavaṇṇanā*)

45–48. Now follows the positive-negative (anuloma-paccanīya) method. To demonstrate this, the following is commenced: "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state may arise by way of the root condition (hetu-paccaya), but not by way of the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya)," and so forth.
Therein, regarding the phrase "by way of the root condition, not by way of the object condition...
[and so on] ...by way of the root condition, not by way of the non-disappearance condition," for the term "root" (hetu), with respect to the remaining twenty-three [conditions]...

By way of combining each of the conditions with [the others], there are twenty-three positive-negative combinations based on the single-rooted [method] beginning with the root-condition (*hetu-pada*).
In each of those, making forty-nine [combinations], there are eleven hundred and twenty-seven questions.
However, in the double-rooted [method] (*dumūlaka*), by way of combining the root and object-conditions (*hetu-ārammaṇa-pada*) with each of the remaining twenty-two conditions...

Regarding the "twenty-two positive-negative" combinations: thus, for all those stated in the positive order—beginning with the single-rooted and so forth—the number of questions should be understood by way of omitting one term at a time from each [set] and considering the remainder.

Furthermore, among these single-rooted and other combinations, both those questions that have been included in the canonical text (pāḷi) and those that have not should all be understood according to the method explained below.
“The excellent *Paṭṭhāna* in three sections... the six methods (*naya*) in the positive-negative [analysis] are very profound.

Herein, according to the method explained below, there are two types of positive-negative analysis: the positive-negative analysis of phenomena (*dhamma*) and the positive-negative analysis of conditions (*paccaya*).

Among these, regarding the phenomena included by the headings of the Abhidhamma matrix (*mātikā*), such as “wholesome phenomena” (*kusalā dhammā*), [the analysis begins with] “the wholesome... [and so forth].

"Dependent on a wholesome state, an unwholesome state [does not arise]"—this is called the "positive-negative sequence of states" (*dhammānulomapaccanīya*), as it proceeds by way of a positive-negative teaching.

"By way of the root condition, not by way of the object condition"—this is called the "positive-negative sequence of conditions" (*paccayānulomapaccanīya*), as it proceeds by way of a positive-negative teaching regarding the terms found among the twenty-four conditions. Therein, below...

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, this verse—“The *Tika* and the excellent *Paṭṭhāna*... the six methods (*naya*) in the positive-negative [analysis] are very profound”—was spoken with reference to the positive and negative analysis of phenomena (*dhamma*).

Here, however, this verse is spoken specifically regarding the positive analysis of phenomena (*dhammānuloma*), with reference to the positive-negative analysis of conditions (*paccayānulomapaccanīya*).
Therefore, [the phrase] “the six methods in the positive-negative [analysis] are very profound” [is used].
In the commentary on the verse, the meaning should be understood as follows: "The six methods, beginning with the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, are very profound in the positive and negative order of the Dhamma.

However, in this particular context, regarding the positive and negative order of conditions as they occur—namely, that "root-conditions are not object-conditions"—the meaning should be understood thus:
"These six methods, beginning with the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, are very profound specifically within the positive order of the Dhamma."
