Among those, regarding the positive (anuloma) section, this classification of questions has been shown here in the "Exposition of Terms" (paṇṇattivāra) of the "Dependent Chapter" (paṭiccavāra) by way of the wholesome triad (kusalattika) alone from the *Tikapapaṭṭhāna*.
However, not even a single question has been shown for the remaining triads or in the remaining sections of the *Paṭṭhāna*.
Furthermore, in the subsequent sections such as the "Co-nascent Chapter" (sahajātavāra), it is [shown] by way of the wholesome triad as well.

Without extracting the "tails," only the answers as they are obtained have been shown. However, because of the statement, "The six methods in the Positive-Negative [section] are very profound," these six *paṭṭhāna* methods in this Positive-Negative Conditionality (*paccayānulomapaccanīya*) should be extracted and shown by way of questions.
For this is the burden of the teachers who expound the *Paṭṭhāna*.
4. Explanation of the Negative-Positive (Paccanīyānuloma) [49–52].

Now follows the negative-positive method. To demonstrate this, the following is commenced: “Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state may arise by way of the object condition, but not by way of the root condition,” and so forth. In that context, there are questions of the positive-negative type.

The scope of the questions is indeed equal [to that of the previous sections]. Furthermore, regarding the "Single Root" and so forth, all questions—both those that have appeared in the text and those that have not—are to be understood according to the method explained below.
Also, in the passage beginning with "And the excellent Paṭṭhāna, the Triads... the six methods of the negative-positive are very profound," it is here too [as stated] below.
In the same manner as previously stated, there are two types of positive concomitance (*paccayānuloma*):
the positive concomitance of the negation of states (*dhammapaccanīyānuloma*) and the positive concomitance of the negation of conditions (*paccayapaccanīyānuloma*).

Among these, the "positive concomitance of the negation of states" refers to the teaching that proceeds by way of the negation-positive concomitance—such as "dependent on a non-virtuous state, a virtuous state [arises]"—concerning those states comprised by the matrix headings (*mātikāpada*) of the Abhidhamma, such as "virtuous states."

The name is as follows: “Not by way of root-condition, but by way of object-condition. This is called the *paccayapaccanīyānuloma* (the positive-negative-positive method regarding conditions), which proceeds by way of teaching the positive and negative relations among the twenty-four conditions for those terms found therein.
Regarding this, it was stated in the sub-commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) above: “The triads and the excellent *Paṭṭhāna*... the six methods in the negative-positive [analysis] are very profound.”

This verse was spoken with reference to the "conformity to the opposition of the Dhamma" (*dhammapaccanīyānuloma*). However, here this verse is spoken with reference to the "conformity to the opposition of conditions" (*paccayapaccanīyānuloma*) within the "conformity to the Dhamma" itself.

Therefore, regarding the statement in the Commentary, "The six methods in the conformity to the opposition are very profound," the meaning is that the six methods, such as the *Tikapaṭṭhāna* and so forth, are very profound within the "conformity to the opposition of the Dhamma."

It should be understood. In this section, however, regarding the positive sequence of conditions (*paccaya-paccanīyānuloma*)—such as "not-root condition" (*nahetupaccayā*) and "object condition" (*ārammaṇapaccayā*)—it should be understood that these six methods, beginning with the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, are extremely profound within the positive sequence of phenomena (*dhammānuloma*) alone.
Among those, even by way of the mere wholesome triad (*kusalattika*) within the positive sequence of the *Paṭṭhāna* itself, this [is the treatment] for the "Dependent Chapter" (*paṭicca-vāra*).

In the section on definitions (*paṇṇattivāra*), the classification of questions was shown by way of abbreviation. However, among the remaining triads (*tikes*) and the remaining *Paṭṭhāna* sections, not even a single question was shown.
Furthermore, in the subsequent sections such as the "Co-nascent Section" (*sahajātavāra*), questions were not raised even for the "Wholesome Triad" (*kusalattika*);
instead, only the answers were shown according to what is applicable. [As it is said: "Six in the negative-positive (*paccanīyānuloma*)."

Furthermore, because of the statement, "The methods are very profound," these six methods of the *Paṭṭhāna*—the positive and negative applications of conditions (*paccaya-paccanīya-anuloma*)—should be extracted and demonstrated by way of questions.
For this is the burden of the teachers who expound the *Paṭṭhāna*. The commentary on the section of questions is concluded.
1. Commentary on the Wholesome Triplet (Kusalattikavaṇṇanā) 1.1.
Commentary on the Chapter on Dependence (Paṭiccavāravaṇṇanā) 1.1.1.
Positive Conditionality (Paccayānuloma)
(1. The Section on Analysis (Vibhaṅgavāra) 53.

Now, regarding those immeasurable questions shown in the Section on Formulations (Paṇṇattivāra)—beginning with the forty-nine [questions] based on the wholesome triad (kusalattika) by way of the root-condition (hetupaccaya) and so forth, and presented merely as an illustration of the method—therein, of the wholesome, unwholesome, and so on...

Because there is no simultaneous arising [of wholesome and unwholesome states], those questions such as, “Dependent on a wholesome state, an unwholesome state arises by way of root-condition,” do not receive an answer.
Setting those aside, in order to answer those [questions] that do receive an answer, this [text] begins with:
“Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of root-condition,” and so forth.
The section on the exposition of the "Dependent Chapter" (paṭiccasamuppādavāra) has commenced according to the method.
Herein, it might be asked: "If these forty-nine questions—beginning with the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya)—do not receive a complete answer, then for what reason were they shown?
Should not only those that do receive answers be shown? Yes, they ought to be shown.

It might be so. However, if they were to be shown in that manner, they would have to be demonstrated in all the *tikas*, *dukas*, *patthānas*, and so forth—without making any abbreviations—in each individual *tika*, *duka*, *dukatika*, *tikaduka*, *tikatika*, and *dukaduka*. Why?
Because those [factors] which one obtains in the *Kusala-tika* are not the same as those obtained in the *Vedanā-tika* and others. [This applies to] the *Dhammānuloma-paccanīya*.

And in the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, in the exposition of the "Tenfold Application of Initial Application" (*vitakkattika*) and the "Threefold Application of Joy" (*pītittika*), all of these receive an exposition;
therefore, according to the highest limit, however many questions there ought to be for each triad, they have all been shown in the "Wholesome Triad" (*kusalattika*).
For among those thus shown, having set aside those that do not receive an exposition therein, those that do receive it—
Since it is said, "These, when explained, can easily be understood," they are all shown in the *Kusala-ttika* (the triad of the wholesome) for the purpose of easy comprehension.
However, among these, those that do not receive a formal answer (*vissajjana*) should be excluded, and it should be understood that only those which do receive an answer are actually answered.

In that context, "dependent on a wholesome state" refers to the division consisting of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-kkhandha*) and so forth, among the wholesome states belonging to the four planes of existence.
"Depending on one dhamma" means having returned [to it], having reached a state of similarity defined by simultaneous arising;

the meaning is that one has entered into a state of arising together with that [dhamma]. "A wholesome dhamma" refers to a single dhamma—classified as the aggregate of perception and so forth—among the wholesome dhammas of the four planes.
"Arises" means it proceeds from its moment of arising until its passing away into cessation.
"Is produced" (*nibbattati*) is also the meaning. It acquires itself; what is meant is that it reaches the three moments, beginning with arising (*uppāda*).
By "root-condition" (*hetu-paccaya*), it is by means of the wholesome root which establishes the state of being a root-condition.
Having thus given the answer "it arises" (*uppajjati*) to the question "would it arise? (*uppajjeyya*), [the author] now states, depending on which phenomenon...
In order to show that phenomenon which arises by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), he said, "the wholesome is one aggregate," and so forth.
Therein, "one" refers to any one among the four beginning with feeling (*vedanā*).

"Three aggregates" refers to the remaining three aggregates, setting aside whichever specific factor was taken as the condition. "Three aggregates" [refers to] whichever one of the aggregates beginning with feeling is excluded.
"Arises" refers to that which has been included; setting that aside, there are three remaining [cases].
"Dependent on two aggregates" means dependent on any two aggregates among the six dyads, such as the feeling-perception dyad and so forth.

"Two aggregates" means that, setting aside whichever ones have been taken as the condition, the remaining two aggregates arise by way of the root-condition (hetupaccaya) being established through the wholesome root (kusalahetu). This is the meaning.
However, because there is no such thing as one aggregate being a condition for only one or two aggregates, nor two aggregates being a condition for only one aggregate, it was not stated:
"dependent on one aggregate, one aggregate [arises]; dependent on one aggregate, two aggregates [arise];
dependent on two aggregates, one aggregate [arises]. [It was stated: "dependent on a wholesome state, an indeterminate state [arises]..."
The meaning in [terms such as] "arises" (*uppajjati*) and so forth should also be understood according to the method already stated.

Regarding the phrase "matter produced by mind" (*cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ*), this was said to show that which, being co-nascent with the wholesome (*kusala*) and receiving it as a root-condition (*hetupaccaya*), possesses the sense of "co-nascence" (*sahajāta*) within the sense of "dependent origination" (*paṭicca*).
This same principle applies in other instances of this kind further on as well.

Regarding the phrase "resultant-indeterminate and functional-indeterminate": here, it is "rootless" (*ahetuka*) because of the absence of root-conditions (*hetu-paccaya*). Furthermore, the immaterial-sphere resultant (*āruppa-vipāka*) should not be included, as it does not arise together with material form (*rūpa*).

The mention of "at the moment of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi-kkhaṇe*) is stated for the purpose of showing the arising of the indeterminate—namely, that which is reckoned as "kamma-produced matter" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*)—dependent upon the indeterminate. As for "resultant-indeterminate," in that context...
This is stated by way of the indeterminate that exists at the present moment. The statement, "dependent on the aggregates there is the basis;

dependent on the basis there are the aggregates," is stated for the purpose of showing the arising of the aggregates dependent on the basis, even though the basis has already been included by the inclusion of "matter produced by kamma" (kaṭattārūpa).
The passage beginning with "one great primary element" is stated for the purpose of showing the arising of the indeterminate materiality dependent on the indeterminate materiality.
Furthermore, the interpretation of the meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated in the passage beginning with "one aggregate.

Having thus explained the arising of primary elements (bhūta) dependent on primary elements within the indeterminate materiality, he now states "dependent on the great elements, mind-originated [materiality]" and so forth, in order to show the arising of derived materiality (upādārūpa) dependent on the primary elements. This being the case, [the question arises: why is it said only "derived materiality"?
It should be stated [that it arises dependent on the aggregates]; why then are the other two mentioned?

It is for the purpose of showing that it also arises dependent on the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*). For that which was shown below as "matter originated by mind and matter produced by kamma" does not arise dependent on the aggregates alone;
rather, this is stated to show that it also arises dependent on the great primary elements.

This is how it should be understood. In this context, mind-originated [materiality] occurs only during the course of existence (*pavatta*), whereas produced materiality (*kaṭattārūpa*) occurs at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as well.
"Derived materiality" (*upādārūpa*) is a qualification of both of these.
In the phrase "dependent on wholesome aggregates and great primaries," only the great primaries originated by mind are included.
Regarding "matter derived from mind" (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*), both primary matter (*bhūtarūpa*) and derived matter (*upādārūpa*) are included here.
For, according to the method beginning with "dependent on one great element, three great elements [arise]," primary matter arises dependent on the aggregates and the great elements;

and according to the stated method, "derived matter arises dependent on the great elements," derived matter is also included. This refers to both the unwholesome (*akusala*) and the indeterminate (*abyākata*).
The same method applies to the answers to the questions as well. Thus, nine questions regarding the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) have been answered.
For it is only these that are found here; the remaining forty are "vain questions" (*mogha-pucchā*) and have therefore not been answered.

By this same method, the meaning of the questions and answers regarding the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and the others should also be understood. However, in each respective case, we shall examine only those matters that are worthy of investigation.

54. Regarding the object condition (ārammaṇapaccaya), since matter does not arise by way of being an object condition for [consciousness], among those nine [questions] involving a mixture of matter, only three questions were answered, excluding the others.

For that very reason, after stating "the aggregates depend on the physical basis" (vatthuṃ paṭicca khandhā), it was not stated that "the physical basis depends on the aggregates" (khandhe paṭicca vatthū); for the latter does not arise by way of the object condition.

55. Regarding the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), the term "resultant-inefficient" (*vipākābyākata*) is stated specifically with reference to the supramundane (*lokuttara*). For that very reason, the phrase "at the moment of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhikkhaṇe*) is not included here. The remainder is exactly the same as under the root condition (*hetupaccaya*). 56.

Since matter is not obtained even in the conditions of proximity (*anantara*) and contiguity (*samanantara*), there are likewise only three questions, just as in the case of the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

57. Regarding the co-nascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*), the phrase "at the moment of rebirth-linking" is stated by way of rebirth-linking in the five-aggregate plane (*pañcavokāra*). [As for] below...
Furthermore, the term "at the moment of descent" (*okkantikkhaṇe*) found in the *Paccayavibhaṅga* is identical in meaning to this [term];

here, there is only a difference in phrasing. Moreover, because of the statement, "The descent into the womb occurs through the conjunction of three factors," "descent" (*okkanti*) is a name specifically for rebirth-linking in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra*).
"Rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*), however, is common to all states of existence. But here—
By the statement beginning with “matter produced by kamma” (*kaṭattā-rūpa*), only rebirth-linking in the five-aggregate plane is intended.

For that [rebirth-linking] encompasses both the state of being a condition for matter and the state of being conditionally arisen, as well as the state of being a condition for the immaterial; therefore, it is included so that the answer may be complete.
“One external great primary” refers to a great primary among earth, stones, and so forth, which are not bound up with sense faculties.

This was said with intentional meaning (*saṇdhāya*). For in the section on the Analysis of Conditions (*Paccayavibhaṅgavāra*), the four great elements were taken by combining the internal and external together;
that was indeed a concise teaching. This, however, is a detailed teaching;
therefore, showing everything by way of analysis, he said, "One external great element," and so forth. [This refers to] one great element of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*).
"Dependent on" (*paṭicca*) is stated by way of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) originating from the two continuities (*santati*).

"Derived form" (*upādārūpa*) is stated by way of temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*) form. However, "kamma-born form" (*kaṭattārūpa*) dependent on the great primaries is stated specifically by way of kamma-originated form.

In the section on the mutuality condition (*aññamaññapaccaya*), it is stated: "dependent on the aggregates (*khandha*) there is the basis (*vatthu*); dependent on the basis there are the aggregates. This is said to show the mutual conditionality of all four aggregates together with the basis.

59. Regarding the dependence condition (*nissaya-paccaya*): since the meaning of "dependence" (*paṭicca*) is the meaning of "co-arising" (*sahajāta*), therefore that status as a dependence condition shown previously in the section on the analysis of conditions (*paccaya-vibhaṅga*) for the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth is not included here.

For the eye-base and so forth function as conditions by being pre-arisen (*purejāta*), whereas here only that which is co-arisen is applicable. Precisely for this reason it was said: "The dependence condition..."
“It is similar to the co-nascence condition. 60.
Regarding the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), because there is no decisive support condition for material form (*rūpa*), only three answers are obtained;
therefore it is said, “it is similar to the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). In that context, although not all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [states]...
They obtain the object-strong-dependence condition (ārammaṇūpanissaya). It should be understood that this is stated with reference to those who do indeed obtain it.

61. Regarding the pre-nascence condition (purejātapaccaya): "dependent on the basis as a pre-nascence condition" means that they arise by depending on the basis, thereby establishing the state of being a pre-nascence condition through that basis.
"One resultant indeterminate aggregate"—here, regarding that which is resultant indeterminate...

The physical basis (*vatthu*) is a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) at the moment of descent [into the womb]; however, because that belongs to the section on the pre-nascent condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), it should not be included here.

Furthermore, those wholesome states (*kusala*) and so forth which do not obtain the pre-nascent condition in the immaterial realm (*ārūpa*) should also not be included here, as they likewise belong to the section on the pre-nascent condition.
The object (*ārammaṇa*), however, does not invariably obtain the status of a pre-nascent condition. This refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) and the others.

For [the Abhidhamma] establishes that only eye-consciousness and the others have the status of a pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), whereas for the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), even past and future things serve as objects.
Therefore, it is not included here. For this teaching is according to the aggregates (*khandha*), not according to the consciousness elements.
And by the teaching, "one resultant indeterminate aggregate," all consciousness elements are included, not merely the eye-consciousness element and the rest.
A posteriorly arisen state is not a condition for the wholesome or unwholesome; nor, even with respect to the indeterminate, is it a supporting condition rather than a productive one.
Therefore, since there is not even a single dhamma that can be said to "arise by way of posteriority-condition," no answer has been given according to the posteriority-condition.

62. Regarding the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*): while it is true that not all functional states (*kiriya*) receive the condition of repetition, they are nevertheless described as "functional-indeterminate" (*kiriyābyākata*) from the perspective of those that do so.

Therefore, it should be understood that here only functional impulsion (*javanakiriya*) is intended. 63. Regarding the condition of kamma (*kammapaccaya*): in the case of wholesome and unwholesome states, the condition of kamma should be understood as being simultaneous (*ekakkhaṇika*). The same applies to functional-indeterminate states.

However, in the case of resultant-indeterminate states, it may also be asynchronous (*nānākkhaṇika*), as is the case for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), as well as for mind-originated matter.
However, [the arising] of kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*) is of different moments; likewise for the matter of non-percipient beings.
Herein, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is kamma-produced matter. The remainder is not stated to be derived matter (*upādārūpa*) exclusively because it is kamma-originated.
Even so, here only that which is kamma-originated is intended.

64. Regarding the condition of ripening (*vipāka-paccaya*), since neither wholesome, unwholesome, nor functional states are obtained, the answer is given solely by way of the indeterminate (*abyākata*).
"Mind-originated" means mind-originated specifically as resultant mind (*vipāka-citta*).

"Matter due to past action" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) refers, according to what is applicable, to both the sense-faculty matter and the base matter. "Derived matter" (*upādā-rūpa*) refers to the remaining derived matter existing at that time.

65. Regarding the nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*), it should be understood that for all wholesome and other aggregates (*khandha*) as well as for mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*), their arising occurs by way of immaterial nutriment (*arūpāhāra*).
Likewise, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), this applies to the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

"Mind-produced" refers to that produced by the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and other such states of consciousness. "Nutriment-produced" refers to that produced by physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*). "Mind-produced" refers specifically to that produced by wholesome and unwholesome consciousness.
In the section on the Analysis of Conditions (*Paccayavibhaṅga*), edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) was shown first according to the sequence of the nutriments;
however, here it should be understood that the immaterial nutriments are shown first by way of the question, "What is wholesome dhamma? (66).
In the analysis of conditions regarding the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*), the eye-faculty and the others were shown first according to the sequence of the faculties.
Here, however, by way of an inquiry into the wholesome and so forth, the conditionality of the immaterial faculties (*arūpindriya*) is first shown.

In that context, among the wholesome and so forth, the immaterial faculties are to be understood according to their occurrence. For non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is also present even within the materiality of the primary elements (*bhūtarūpa*). 67.
Regarding the conditions of the jhānas and the path, the answer is exactly like that of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*); for this very reason, it is stated here: "similar to the root-condition."

68. The answer regarding the association condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*) follows the same pattern as the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*); for that very reason, it is stated here that it is "similar to the object condition.
69. Regarding the dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*): "The basis is the dissociation condition" means that they arise depending on the basis as the dissociation condition;
the meaning is that they arise by establishing the state of being a dissociation condition through the basis. "The aggregates are the dissociation condition" [means the same].

"Dependent on the aggregates, by way of dissociation-condition": the meaning is that [the mind-produced matter] arises while establishing a state of dissociation-condition with respect to the aggregates.
"The aggregates are a dissociation-condition for the basis": dependent on the basis, the aggregates are a dissociation-condition;
the meaning is that they arise while establishing a state of dissociation-condition with respect to the basis. Mind-originated matter...

"Dependent on the aggregates, by way of dissociation condition" means that mind-originated matter arises dependent on the aggregates, establishing the state of dissociation condition with respect to those aggregates.
The meaning in the remaining answers—such as "the physical basis [is] by way of dissociation condition," and so forth—should also be understood according to the same method already stated.
And here, regarding the indeterminate resultant [states], by the inclusion of the "physical basis,"...
The eye and so forth are to be included. The passage beginning with "one great primary" (*mahābhūta*) is stated to show the conditionality of the indeterminate materiality (*rūpa-abyākata*).
"Mind-produced" (*citta-samutthāna*) refers both to that produced by an indeterminate mind and to that produced by wholesome or unwholesome minds. 70.

In the presence condition (*atthi-paccaya*), everything follows the same course as the conascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*). For this very reason, it is stated here that it is "similar to the conascence condition."
71–72. *Natthi* and *vigata* belong to the category of object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), while *avigata* belongs to the category of conascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).

For this very reason, it is said here: "similar to the object-condition" and "similar to the conascence-condition. This is stated by way of summarizing these twenty-three conditions as they have been shown.
They should be expanded upon according to those questions that receive an answer; that is, they should be detailed by way of those [questions] for which a response is obtained.

This is the commentary on the meaning of the "Dependent Chapter" (*paṭiccasamuppādavāra*) in the positive order of conditions (*paccayānuloma*), starting from the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) and based on the single-rooted combinations, as presented in the explanation of the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*).
(2. The Numerical Chapter (*saṅkhyāvāra*): 73.
Now, regarding those response-sections (*vissajjanavāra*) obtained here for each individual condition, such as the root-condition and so forth, by way of enumeration:

To demonstrate this, the section beginning with "nine by way of cause" (*hetuyā nava*) is commenced. Therein, "nine by way of cause" means there are nine rounds of questions and answers regarding the causal condition (*hetupaccaya*).
Namely: from the wholesome, the wholesome; from the wholesome, the indeterminate; from the wholesome, both the wholesome and the indeterminate;
from the unwholesome, the unwholesome; from the unwholesome, the indeterminate; from the unwholesome, both the unwholesome and the indeterminate; and from the indeterminate, the indeterminate.
With the wholesome and indeterminate, the indeterminate; with the unwholesome and indeterminate, the indeterminate.
Regarding the object condition (*ārammaṇa*), there are three: with the wholesome, the wholesome; with the unwholesome, the unwholesome; with the indeterminate, the indeterminate.

Regarding the predominance condition (*adhipati*), there are nine, which are exactly as stated for the root condition (*hetu*). For it is said that among the twelve conditions, there are nine [types] for each. This applies to all of them as well.
The questions and answers regarding these are exactly like those for the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*). However, there is a distinction in the *Vibhaṅga*.

It is stated that among the ten conditions, there are three [questions] for each. In all of them, the questions and answers are similar to those for the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). Yet, there is a distinction in the *Vibhaṅga*:
for in the answer to the "indeterminate" section of the mutuality-condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), material form (*rūpa*) is also included.
Likewise for the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*). In the repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*), neither resultant states nor process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*) are obtained.
In the resultant condition (*vipāka*), there is only one [type], namely the indeterminate (*abyākata*) alone. Thus, here in brief, the delimitation of the sections is threefold: nine, three, and one.
In detail, across all twenty-three conditions, there are twelve groups of nine, ten groups of three, and one group of one.
There are one hundred thirty-nine [factors], and there are one hundred thirty-nine questions. "One hundred thirty-nine answers to questions" is also a name for that same work. 74.

Having thus shown the enumeration in the single-rooted [analysis] beginning with the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), the detailed exposition for the subsequent double-rooted (*dumūlaka*) and other [analyses] follows.
Having condensed the teaching shown under the "Single Root" (ekamūlaka), and taking only the number actually found therein, [the author] states "Under the 'Two Roots' (dumūlaka), first:
from the root-condition (hetupaccaya) there are three [in relation] to the object-condition (ārammaṇa)," etc., in order to show the division of sections. Herein, this is the characteristic:

even if a condition has a large number of instances, when conjoined with one that has a small number of instances, it becomes equal in number to that [smaller one]. Therefore it was said: "From the root-condition..."
"Regarding the object, there are three. This means that in the dyad of root and object, only the three answers mentioned under "object" are obtained.
However, when the same number is joined with the same number, it remains as an unimpaired number. Therefore it is said:
"With the root condition, there are nine [answers] for the dominant condition. Thus, in the dyad of root and dominance, exactly nine answers are obtained.
Meaning: In the case of "result" (*vipāka*), there is one; that is, in the "Root-Result" dyad (*hetu-vipāka-duka*), only one single answer is obtained for the result.
In this way, first, the delimitation of the sections in the "Two-rooted" (*dumūlaka*) [analysis] should be understood.

75. This same characteristic applies to the "Three-rooted" (*timūlaka*) and subsequent analyses as well. Therefore he said: "By way of root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), and predominance..."
"Three": this means that in the triads of cause, object, and predominance, only the three answers mentioned under the object condition are obtained.
This same method is to be applied everywhere.
Regarding the twelvefold root, however, the resultant condition is not obtained; therefore, under the repetition condition, there are three [answers] for kamma.
Having stated [the nutriment] and not touching upon its ripening (*vipāka*), it is said: "three in regard to nutriment. This same method applies to the "thirteen roots" and so forth.
However, having condensed them, twenty-three roots are shown here. That [nutriment] is twofold: either accompanied by habituation (*sāsevana*) or accompanied by ripening (*savipāka*).
Therein, the first—accompanied by habituation—is shown; it receives only three answers. Therefore it was said:

“With the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya) in the non-disappearance (avigate), there are three. However, that which is accompanied by fruition (savipāka) does not receive the condition of repetition;

therefore, setting that aside, and for the purpose of showing the enumeration by way of fruition, one method was first shown immediately following [the previous section] as: “With the condition of root (hetupaccaya)…pe… with the condition of fruition (vipākapaccaya), there is one in nutriment (āhāra).
Only after that was the twenty-three-rooted method shown. Now, regarding these two twenty-three-rooted [methods]:
Although there is no fruition condition (*vipāka-paccaya*) in one case and no repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*) in the other, the post-nascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) exists in both.
By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī-sadda*), these should be understood as having twenty-three roots.

Among them, in the case of "with repetition" (*sāsevana*), there are three answers in every instance by way of the repetition condition; in the case of "with fruition" (*savipāka*), there is only one by way of the fruition condition.
This is the enumeration beginning with the root-cause (hetu-paccaya) among those starting from the single-rooted (ekamūlaka).
As for what was stated immediately after the root-cause section— namely, "When [the mind] is fixed on the object (ārammaṇa), there are exactly three questions in all cases"—

that refers to the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) as the starting point, and applies everywhere, both in the single-rooted and in the double-rooted (dumūlaka) and subsequent sections, within the category of the object-term.
This was stated for the purpose of showing that in the remaining combinations of conditions, where there ought to be nine [questions], there are only three;
however, in the case of the "resultant" (vipāka) term, in its combination with the "resultant" term and in the remaining combinations of conditions, there is only one question.
Thus, as we said below: "Even a condition of many counts [is combined] with one of few counts..."
"Joined with that, it becomes of the same category"—this has indeed been well said.

Now, regarding those [conditioned states] such as the "single-rooted" which are to be shown by way of conditions like the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), among them, the single-rooted is not shown even under a single condition because it is identical to the single-rooted by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*). By way of the object-condition:
However, in order to demonstrate the calculation based on the "root of the deficient" (dumūlaka), it is stated: "From the object condition, there are three with the root condition;

three with the predominance condition... pe ... three with the non-disappearance condition. And here, although one should have said, "From the object condition, there are three with the predominance condition...

pe ... three with the non-disappearance condition," those conditions such as the root condition and so forth which have a higher number of counts [are mentioned] together with those that have lower counts and those that have equal counts.

In order to show the enumeration obtained when [the conditions] are combined, the root condition (hetupaccaya), although it stands before the object condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) in the sequence, is placed after it; thus it is said: "From the object condition, there are three with the root condition.
By this, he makes it clear that the object condition—whether by way of a greater number or an equal number—is [to be understood].
Or, when combined with the condition of nutriment, it undergoes the divisions of the "two-by-three" and so forth;
in all such cases, it should be understood that there are exactly three answers to the questions. However, in the combination with the condition of resultant (vipāka), only one [answer] is obtained;

since this will be made clear by the enumeration beginning with the resultant condition, it is not shown here. And as for this enumeration shown under the "two-rooted" (dumūlaka) section, it applies to the "three-rooted" (timūlaka) and subsequent sections as well.
This is the enumeration; those based on three roots and so forth have not been detailed here by way of the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).

Now, in order to show the enumeration among those based on two roots and so forth by way of the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) and others, it is said: "Under the root condition (*hetu*), there are nine [types] of predominance conditions," and so on.
In that case as well, the arrangement of the conditions should be understood according to the method already stated. And just as with the predominance condition...
In the case of the root-condition (*hetu*), there are nine; likewise for the remaining conditions that have the same enumeration as the root-condition, there are also nine.
Thus, when combining those with the same enumeration as whichever condition stands at the beginning, the enumeration is made according to that which stands at the beginning.
But when combining those with a lower enumeration than that [initial condition], the enumeration is made according to those very ones with the lower enumeration.

It should be understood that [the conditions] exist. And just as they are explained by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), so too they are not elaborated in detail for those following it—such as the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) and the rest—by way of the dominant condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), nor for the triads and so forth.

Therefore, the enumeration should be established everywhere according to the method of counting shown in the dyads (*dumūlaka*). For this very reason it was said: "One should count them by way of the path of recitation, making each individual condition the root."
Commentary on the Positive Order of Conditions.
Chapter on "Dependent" (Paṭicca-vāra).
Commentary on the Negative Order of Conditions (Paccaya-paccanīya-vaṇṇanā).

86–87. As for the "Negative Condition" (paccayapaccanīya), however, because it is not found in the section on the wholesome—since a wholesome state does not arise without the root-condition (hetupaccaya)—therefore the passage beginning with "dependent on an unwholesome state" is commenced. In that context, "not-root-condition" (nahetupaccaya) is the negation of the root-condition;
the meaning is that it arises by means of another condition, apart from the root-condition. [This refers to] that which is accompanied by doubt (vicikicchāsahagata).
Regarding "delusion accompanied by restlessness": this indeed acts as a root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) for both the associated mental states and for mind-originated matter;
however, because there is no other associated root-cause present, it does not arise by way of a root-condition.
Thus, with the exception of the root-condition, it arises through the remaining conditions appropriate to itself. This same method applies to all negations of conditions.
The meaning should be understood. "Rootless, resultant-indeterminate" is to be understood specifically in terms of the origination of matter.
This same method applies to other such cases as well.

88. Regarding the non-predominance condition (*na-adhipati-paccaya*): although there is indeed a predominance factor (*adhipati*), it is [classified here] because of the absence of a second predominance factor alongside itself.

It does not receive the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*). However, while delusion (*moha*) accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*) or restlessness (*uddhacca*) is rootless (*ahetuka*), the predominances themselves are not likewise without a predominance.

Rather, at the time when wholesome states and so forth arise without making any one among desire (*chanda*) and the others their predominance, all those wholesome states and so forth are "without a predominance" (*nirādhipati*).
Therefore, unlike delusion, it is merely a case of lacking a specific predominance.
It should be understood that this teaching, beginning with "dependent on one aggregate, three aggregates [arise]," was given by way of a comprehensive summary, without excluding anything. 89.

In the cases of the immediate (nānantara) and the contiguous (samanantara), unlike the object-condition (ārammaṇa), only material form is the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna). Therefore it is said:
“It is not like the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya),” it is said. Thus, the co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) is excluded.
As this is so, the dependence (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions are also excluded. Why? Because without these, nothing whatsoever arises.
For even setting aside the co-nascence, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions, not even a single material or immaterial phenomenon arises; therefore, they are excluded.

90. In the analysis of the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), at the moment of rebirth-linking, it should be understood that, dependent upon the resultant indeterminate aggregates, there arises the "matter produced by kamma" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*), excluding the heart-base.
91. In the analysis of the strong-dependence condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), matter alone is the conditionally arisen state, for it does not receive strong-dependence.
As for the immaterial, although it may not receive the object-strong-dependence or the natural-strong-dependence, it does receive the immediate-strong-dependence.
But it does not exist [in that way]. Therefore it was said: "It is not similar to the object condition. 92.
Regarding "mind-originated matter is not [conditioned] by the prenascence condition," this is stated with reference to the fivefold plane of existence (*pañcavokāra*).
93. Regarding "not by the postnascence condition": here, the co-nascence and prenascence conditions are included. Therefore...

The textual passage here is similar to that for the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*); since it was already explained in detail under the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), it is abbreviated here.

Regarding the repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*), wholesome and unwholesome states are to be understood by way of the first impulsion (*javana*), and likewise for functional-inefficient (*kiriya-abyākata*) states.

However, the textual passage here should also be understood according to the detailed explanation given under the predominance condition. For this very reason, it is said: "Nor is there a post-nascence condition..."
“Even the condition of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*) is not the same as the condition of predominance (*adhipati-paccaya*). (94–97) Regarding the condition of kamma (*kamma-paccaya*):

resultant volition (*vipāka-cetanā*) does not receive the condition of asynchronous kamma (*nānā-khaṇika-kamma-paccaya*), and thus it is not included. Regarding the condition of nutriment (*āhāra-paccaya*): only certain types of matter (*rūpa*) are the conditioned states (*paccayuppanna*).

The same applies to the condition of faculty (*indriya-paccaya*). (98) Regarding the condition of jhāna (*jhāna-paccaya*): both the fivefold sense-consciousness phenomena and certain types of matter are the conditioned states. For, within the fivefold sense-consciousness...

Feeling (*vedanā*) and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) are not included as conditions for *jhāna* because, due to their weakness, they do not reach the characteristic of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*).

99–102. In the case of the non-path condition (*namaggapaccaya*), the conditionally arisen factors consist of rootless resultant and functional states, as well as certain types of materiality (*rūpa*). In the cases of the non-associated (*nasampayutta*), non-absent (*nonatthi*), and non-disappeared (*novigata*) conditions, only materiality is the conditionally arisen factor. Therefore it is said: "It is similar to the object condition (*nārammaṇapaccaya*). 103.
Regarding the non-root condition (*nahetu*), the statement "two" follows the enumeration based on a single root, exactly as in the text.
104. Regarding the statement "In the case of *dumūlaka* [two-rooted], with the exclusion of root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), there is one":

although, when combining a lower number with a higher number, it ought to be two according to the lower number—just as in the case of the non-root condition—it is stated as "one" here because, by way of the exclusion of object-condition, immaterial phenomena have been omitted;
this refers to the arising of indeterminate material form in dependence upon indeterminate [consciousness].

It has been stated. This same method applies to all [combinations], even those consisting of single factors. However, regarding the phrase "two," it should be understood that there are two instances obtained by way of the "not-root" (na-hetu) condition at the stated positions. 105–106.

But in all cases beginning with the "three-rooted" (ti-mūlaka), because the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) is not excluded, there is only one answer; this is the calculation for the single-rooted (eka-mūlaka) combinations and so forth, starting from the "not-root" condition in the negative (paccanīya) analysis.
107–130. As for the non-object condition (*nārammaṇa-paccaya*) and the others, since they are similar to what was previously stated in the single-rooted [analysis], they are not shown here either.
By way of the non-object condition in the two-rooted [analysis], "one" under the non-object condition and the non-root condition is exactly as stated in the non-root two-rooted [analysis].
"Five" under the non-predominance condition should be understood by way of what was obtained under the non-object condition; thus it is in all the combinations.

The enumeration should be understood by way of the condition itself when it has fewer members. And wherever the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) enters, there matter alone is the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna).

The same method applies to the places where the proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), mutuality (aññamañña), strong-dependence (upanissaya), nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), association (sampayutta), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata) conditions enter. Regarding the nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path conditions, the answers are identical in all instances.
The tetrad beginning with "nasahajāta" is likewise excluded here; this is the defining characteristic in this context.
By means of this characteristic, one should understand the enumeration among all the "two-rooted" (dumūlaka) and subsequent groups by first observing: "This condition is the root;
this is the two-rooted here, this is the three-rooted, and this is the all-rooted," and then applying the count according to the condition that has the lowest number.
Commentary on the Negative Enumeration of Conditions.
Commentary on the Positive-Negative Enumeration of Conditions (131–189).
Now, in order to show the enumeration for the positive-negative enumeration, [it says]: "From the root condition, five do not exist in the object condition," and so forth.

It has been undertaken. Therein, when the root, predominance, path, and presence conditions are established in the forward order (anuloma), these eight conditions—the four universal conditions beginning with conascence, and the four conditions of nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path—are not obtained in the reverse order (paccanīya).
For a phenomenon arising by way of the root condition and so forth, if it does not obtain these eight conditions...

There is no such thing [as a non-arising of the condition]. However, when the object, proximity, contiguity, decisive support, association, presence, and disappearance conditions are established in the forward order (*anuloma*), those based on the immaterial sphere (*arūpaṭṭhānika*) are not obtained in the reverse order (*paccanīka*).

This is because those arising by way of the object condition and so forth do not fail to obtain the proximity, contiguity, and other such conditions. Regarding the conascence, mutuality, support, kamma, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance conditions:
However, among those established in the direct order (*anuloma*), only the four universal conditions (*sabbaṭṭhānika*) are found; they are not obtained in the inverse order (*paccanīka*).

For there is no dhamma that arises by way of these conditions which does not obtain the universal conditions. There is no place for the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) in the direct order.
Thus, regarding the remaining [conditions] established in the direct order, those which are obtained and those which are not—

They are not found; having observed this, it should be understood that in all the methods beginning with the "root-of-two" (dumūlaka), the enumeration is to be understood by way of the lower counts alone when combining those respective conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the Positive-Negative (Anuloma-Paccanīya) Conditions.
Commentary on the Positive Order of the Negative Conditions (Paccayapaccanīyānulomavaṇṇanā) 190.
Now, in order to show the enumeration in the positive order of the negative conditions, the passage beginning "With the non-root condition, two in the object-condition" is commenced.
Therein, when the root condition stands in its negative form, all remaining conditions—excluding the predominance condition—are obtained in their positive order.
However, the "post-nascence" condition is not found at all in the direct (anuloma) order.

Among those nine conditions stated as "only for immaterial states," with the exception of "prenascence" and "repetition," when the remaining seven are established in the inverse (paccanīka) order, the remaining immaterial bases are not found in the direct order.
For that which does not arise by way of object and so forth does not [function as] the "proximity" condition and the rest.

[It] obtains [them]. However, as for the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) result, it obtains the "pre-arisen" (purejāta) condition; and all results, together with the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu), obtain the "repetition" (āsevana) condition and the subsequent conditions such as "immediately preceding" (anantara), even though they do not arise [at that moment]. Therefore, it is said: "excluding the pre-arisen and repetition conditions.
When the pre-arisen, post-arisen, repetition, resultant, and dissociated conditions stand as opposites, one is excluded and the remainder [are taken].

They are obtained in the direct order (*anuloma*). In the case of the kamma-condition (*kammapaccaya*), when considered in the reverse order (*paccanīka*), all except for the result-condition (*vipākapaccaya*) are obtained in the direct order.

When the nutriment- and faculty-conditions (*āhāra-indriya*) are considered in the reverse order, with the exception of the universal conditions (*sabbaṭṭhānika*) and the mutual, kamma, nutriment, and faculty-conditions, the remaining ones are not obtained in the direct order; the others [are obtained] according to their applicability.

They are obtained. Under the condition of jhāna, when standing in opposition, they are not obtained. Under the conditions of root, predominance, repetition, and path, when standing in conformity, they are not obtained.
Under the condition of path, when standing in opposition, the conditions of root and predominance, when standing in conformity, are not obtained.
Under the condition of dissociation, when standing in opposition, with the exception of the prenascence condition, the remaining ones are obtained in conformity.

Thus, when those various conditions are presented in reverse order, one should understand the enumeration by way of the combined total of the fewer counts for whichever [factors] are not obtained in direct order;
this is to be known through the combination of those respective conditions.

Furthermore, regarding the methods beginning with the "Two-rooted" (Dumūlaka), whatever dyads and so forth are shown starting from whichever particular condition, [they should be understood accordingly].
Those [conditions] should be carefully observed exactly as they have been shown according to the various conditions that are obtained or not obtained.
In this context, when showing the method of the "two-rooted" and so forth by way of non-cause (nahetu), it is stated: "Non-cause condition, non-object condition...
pe ...non-repetition condition," and then it is said, "Everything is the same up to repetition."
Its similarity [to the previous section] should be understood through such statements as, “In the case of conascence, there is one when excluding mutual condition,” and so forth.
As for that which is written in the Sinhalese language, “When ‘not-kamma’ is counted, it takes five,” its meaning is as follows:

starting from the “not-root” condition and continuing thus up to the “not-kamma” condition, when combined with the “not-kamma” condition, there is one in the case of conascence; thus, exactly five are shown.
Conditions are obtained in the direct order (anuloma), not otherwise. Thus, in other such instances as well, one should grasp only the intended meaning without adhering to the literal phrasing.
For such phrasing was written by the ancients in their respective languages merely for the purpose of establishing a mnemonic convention.

Furthermore, in this reverse-analogical sequence (*paccanīyānuloma*), among the phenomena that have arisen through conditions, there is a phenomenon that receives the condition of kamma but not the condition of faculty (*indriya-paccaya*).
This should be understood by way of the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) in the case of non-percipient beings and in the course of existence within the five-aggregate realm.

There is a phenomenon that receives the condition of the path (*magga-paccaya*) but not the condition of root (*hetu-paccaya*). This is by way of the delusion (*moha*) co-arising with doubt (*vicikicchā*) and restlessness (*uddhacca*).

It should be understood: there is a state (dhamma) that receives the condition of jhāna but not the condition of path (magga). This should be understood by way of the mind-element (manodhātu) and the rootless mind-consciousness-element (ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu).

In those places where kamma-produced material phenomena (kaṭattārūpa) receive the condition of kamma solely by way of asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika) kamma, there the material states do not receive the conditions of root, predominance, fruition, faculty, jhāna, or path; this applies to all locations.

They are not contrary conditions. Since there is no predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) in rootless states, the section on enumeration here should be understood without confusion by way of these miscellaneous factors as well.

In this regard, the method is as follows: regarding the statement "with the exception of the root condition, there are two in the object condition," first, in that context, it refers to rootless delusion (*ahetuka-moha*) and rootless resultant and functional [consciousness] (*ahetuka-vipāka-kiriya*).
And [it is] conditionally arisen; therefore, with reference to the unwholesome arising from the unwholesome and the indeterminate arising from the indeterminate, it is said here that "there are two.

This same method applies to the remaining [types of consciousness] as well. However, in the case of repetition (*āsevana*), the resultant (*vipāka*) is not obtained, and likewise for the functional mind-element (*kiriya-manodhātu*).

Therefore, in this context, the indeterminate arising from the indeterminate should be understood by way of the functional root-cause mind-consciousness-element (*kiriya-hetumanoviññāṇadhātu*). Regarding the resultant:

In the "ekanta" (exclusive) section, that which is indeterminate arises only from the indeterminate. In the "magge" (path) section, that which is unwholesome arises only from the unwholesome. 196–197.
In the "nārammaṇamūlaka" (not-rooted-in-object) section, the statement "five by way of root" is said with reference to material form (*rūpa*) alone.
For that [material form] arises dependent upon five categories: wholesome, unwholesome, indeterminate, wholesome-indeterminate, and unwholesome-indeterminate. This applies to all pentads.
The same method applies here. "Mutually one" is said with reference to both the primary material phenomena (*bhūtarūpa*) and the physical basis (*vatthu*).

For these arise through mutual conditionality (*aññamañña-paccaya*), not through object conditionality (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). The same method applies to the triad as well. 198–202. Regarding the section on non-predominance (*nādhipati-mūlaka*):

"Nine by way of root" refers to those very factors stated under the root-condition in the positive order (*anuloma*). "Three," and so forth, are also exactly like those stated previously in the positive order. "Two" in the triad on non-root is exactly like those stated previously under the object-condition in the absence of the root-condition.

203–233. In the *Napurejātamūlaka*, the seven [answers] under the heading of "cause" (*hetu*) are exactly as those shown previously under "prenascence" (*purejāta*) by way of the method beginning with, "In the formless realm, dependent on one wholesome aggregate...
This same method applies to all the sevens. In the *Nakammamūlaka*, regarding the three [answers] under the heading of "cause" and so forth, volition (*cetanā*) alone is the conditionally arisen.
Therefore, this refers to the arising dependent upon the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
"Three" has been stated. By this method, the enumeration should be understood in those places where "one, two, three, five, seven, nine" occurs.
However, these three enumerations—"four," "six," and "eight"—do not exist at all.
This concludes the commentary on the positive and negative conditions.
The commentary on the section on "Dependent" (paṭiccasamuppādavāra) is completed.
2. Commentary on the Section on "Conascent" (sahajātavāra) §§234–242.
In the section on "Conascent," the phrase "conascent with a wholesome state" means conascent with that [wholesome] state in dependence upon a wholesome state.
The meaning is "having sacrificed. The rest here is to be understood according to the method already stated in the section on "dependent" (*paṭicca*).
However, at the conclusion of this [section], the statement "dependence is co-nascence;
co-nascence is dependence" is said for the purpose of showing that there is no difference in meaning between these two sections. For in meaning, these two are indeed not different.

Even though this is so, these terms are stated for the purpose of defining their respective meanings. For in such passages as “dependent on the eye and forms,” it is said that something arises dependent [on others] even when it is not co-nascent (*asahajātā*). Furthermore, even though it is co-nascent, derived form (*upādārūpa*) is not a condition for primary form (*bhūtarūpa*).

Thus, by means of the section on "dependent" (*paṭiccasāsanavāra*), the state of being a co-nascent condition is shown; and by means of the section on "co-nascent" (*sahajātavāra*), the sense of "dependent" is shown.

Both of these have been stated in order to determine the state of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*) for that which has already been mentioned. Furthermore, both have been stated according to the inclinations of those who understand in that way, as an elegance of teaching, and by way of knowing the distinctions of the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*).
The commentary on the section on the co-nascent is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Conditions (Paccayavāra) 243.

In the section on conditions, "conditioning a wholesome state" means that, having established oneself in a wholesome state, one makes that wholesome state a condition by way of support (*nissaya*). "Conditioning one wholesome aggregate" means [conditioning] a wholesome...
It is said that, with one aggregate acting as a support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*), three aggregates arise by way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*).

In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for all the remaining cases. The statement, "conditioned by the [heart-]base, there arise resultant-indeterminate or functional-indeterminate aggregates," is stated with reference to the process of existence within the fivefold plane (*pañcavokāra*);
for it is in the course of existence within the fivefold plane that these aggregates [arise].

A pre-arisen (purejāta) physical basis (vatthu) is a support-condition (nissaya-paccaya). However, because the meaning of "dependent" (paṭicca) is the meaning of "co-arisen" (sahajāta), this principle does not apply in the section on "dependent" (paṭicca-vāra);

thus, with reference only to the co-arisen physical basis at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it is stated: "Dependent on the physical basis, the aggregates [arise]. This is also the case in such passages as:
"With one wholesome aggregate and the physical basis as conditions, three aggregates [arise]," and so forth.
The meaning should be understood by this same method.

The statement, "conditioned by an indeterminate state, there arise both wholesome and indeterminate states," is said with reference to the simultaneous arising of wholesome and indeterminate states by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*).
For, at the moment of the arising of the wholesome, the wholesome aggregates arise depending upon the physical basis (*vatthu*).
And depending on the great primary elements (mahābhūta) produced by mind, the derived matter (upādārūpa) produced by mind arises together with them by way of the root condition (hetupaccaya).

Thus, it should be understood that this was said with reference to the simultaneous arising of the conditioned states by way of the root condition, even though there is diversity among the indeterminate (abyākata) states that serve as conditions. This same principle applies in other such instances as well.

This is the method. Thus, in this condition of cause (*hetu-paccaya*), seventeen questions have been answered by making both the co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and the pre-nascent (*purejāta*) conditions function as a support-condition (*nissaya-ṭṭhena*).
Therein, both the aggregates (*khandha*) and the primary elements (*bhūta*) are taken by way of co-nascence, while the physical basis (*vatthu*) is taken by way of both co-nascence and pre-nascence.
However, in the section on "dependent" (*paṭicca-vāra*), only a co-nascent condition is obtained; therefore, there are only nine questions therein.

The answers have been given. Regarding these seventeen questions answered here, in the case of answers beginning with one and ending with one—such as among the wholesome states and so forth—from a single condition, there is a single conditionally arisen state.
In the case of answers beginning with one and ending with two—from a single condition, there are various conditionally arisen states.

In the case of answers beginning with two and ending with one—from various conditions, there is a single conditionally arisen state. In the case of answers beginning with two and ending with two—from various conditions, there are various conditionally arisen states.
248–252. By this same method, the classification of questions and answers regarding the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and the others should also be understood.

As for what was stated regarding the object-condition—that "with the physical basis as condition, the aggregates arise"—that was said with reference specifically to the resultant aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
This applies to eye-consciousness and the rest, which arise by way of the object-condition depending upon the indeterminate (abyākata).

These are stated for the purpose of showing the distinctions. Furthermore, it is stated that "the basis is a condition" for the purpose of showing the arising of resultant and functional indeterminate states during the course of existence (*pavatta*).
The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before.

Thus, in this object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), seven questions are answered by making both the conascent (*sahajāta*) and the prenascence (*purejāta*) conditions. Among those, the aggregates [are treated] by way of conascence;...
The bases are included by way of both the conascent (*sahajāta*) and the prenascence (*purejāta*) relations; however, the eye-base and so forth are taken only by way of prenascence.
In the section on "Dependent" (*paṭicca*), however, only the conascent relation is obtained as a condition. Therefore, only three questions are answered therein.

(253–254) Regarding the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), it should be understood that the resultant-indeterminate (*vipākābyākata*) is exclusively supramundane (*lokuttara*). Because of the absence of material form (*rūpa*), the immediate (*anantara*) and contiguous (*samanantara*) conditions are similar to the object condition (*ārammaṇa*). The same method applies subsequently to the repetition (*āsevana*), absence (*natthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*) conditions.

255. Regarding the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), "kamma-produced matter" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) refers to that which is designated as derived matter (*upādārūpa*). This is stated with reference specifically to the matter of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*). The five bases, such as the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), are stated by way of the five-aggregate plane (*pañcavokāra*). 256–257.

Regarding the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), it is stated that it is "just like the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*)," which is said with reference to the similarity of their respective explanations. However, there is a difference among the phenomena produced by these conditions. 258.

Regarding the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), it is stated to be similar to the object condition both because of the absence of matter (*rūpa*) therein and because of the similarity of their explanations.
259–260. The meaning of *vatthu-purejāta-paccaya* and so forth should be understood according to the method explained in the section on the "Dependent" (*paṭicca*) analysis.

261–266. Regarding the "kamma-condition" (*kammapaccaya*), there are three: conditioned by the wholesome (*kusala*), there arise the wholesome, the indeterminate (*abyākata*), and the wholesome-indeterminate; thus, three should be understood. The same method applies to the unwholesome (*akusala*) as well. 267–268. Regarding the "dissociation-condition" (*vippayutta-paccaya*):
"the aggregates as dissociation-condition" means [arising] in dependence upon the aggregates as a dissociation-condition.
The meaning is "they arise. "The aggregates are related to the basis by way of dissociation-condition" means that the aggregates, depending upon the basis, arise by way of dissociation-condition.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated below.
269–276. Now, in order to show the answers obtained by way of enumeration, he says: "In the case of root-cause, seventeen," and so forth.
In that context, regarding the "seventeen by way of cause": through the wholesome, there is the wholesome, the indeterminate, and both the wholesome and the indeterminate;
thus, by way of the wholesome, three are stated—namely, two beginning with one and ending with one, and one ending with a dyad.

Likewise, there are three by way of the unwholesome. Through the indeterminate, there is the indeterminate, and by that same [indeterminate], the wholesome, the unwholesome, and both the wholesome and the indeterminate.
[The combinations are as follows: unwholesome and indeterminate; from the wholesome and indeterminate, [arise] the wholesome, the indeterminate, and the wholesome-indeterminate;
from the unwholesome and indeterminate, [arise] the unwholesome, the indeterminate, and the unwholesome-indeterminate—thus seventeen [combinations] are to be understood.

Regarding the objects (*ārammaṇe*), there are seven: through the wholesome, [arises] the wholesome; through the unwholesome, the unwholesome; through the indeterminate, the indeterminate, the wholesome, and the unwholesome; through the wholesome-indeterminate, the wholesome; and through the unwholesome-indeterminate, the unwholesome—thus seven.
"In resultant [consciousness] there is one" means that by way of the indeterminate, it is only indeterminate. Thus, in this context, there are three groupings: seventeen, seven, and one.

Among these, having carefully observed all of them—the twelve groups of seventeen, the ten groups of seven, and the single group of one—the enumeration for the subsequent combination of conditions, such as those beginning with "two triads," should be understood according to the principle of a diminishing count.
Since it is indeed possible to know the limits of the sections by means of this calculation regarding the "root-of-two" (dukamūla) and so forth,

the passage beginning with "With a wholesome state as condition, seven [states] in the object-condition" is commenced; this is done not by referring to "a wholesome state conditioned by a wholesome state," but rather to show the limits of the sections by way of calculation alone.
In this context, a wholesome state arises conditioned by a wholesome state through the condition of root and the condition of object.
Taking one wholesome aggregate as a condition, three aggregates [arise]—in this manner, the answers obtained regarding the object-condition should be expanded upon.
This, first of all, is the method for the direct order (*anuloma*).
277–285. However, since the wholesome (*kusala*) is not obtained in the negative (inverse) order, the exposition is commenced by taking the unwholesome (*akusala*) state as the condition;
this proceeds exactly according to the text. Whatever needs to be said here has already been stated in the inverse section of the "Dependent" (*paṭicca*) chapter.

286–287. As for this section on the negative (paccanīya) which has been presented as a summary of the responses, it was stated beginning with "four in the case of non-root" (*na-hetuyā cattāri*) in order to show them by way of enumeration.
In that context, there are six summaries: four, seventeen, seven, five, three, and one.
By means of these, the enumeration should be understood regarding the combination of conditions in the *duka*, *tika*, and so forth. For whichever condition [is taken] as the seventeen...

One obtains the [first] answers; together with that, in the case of a combination with an equal number, seventeen are obtained, and in the case of a combination with a lesser number, the remaining six sections are also obtained.
Thus, in the other cases as well, setting aside the higher section, equal and lesser numbers are obtained.
And here, the rule is that more [conditions] than this are not obtained. However, when there is no contradiction, equal or fewer meanings are obtained.
Therefore, it is stated here: "With the exclusion of the root condition (na-hetu-paccaya), one [condition] is not the object condition (nārammaṇa)," and so forth.

For in this context, since four are mentioned under the exclusion of the root condition and five under the exclusion of the object condition, it should have been said: "By way of the root condition, four."
It may be that because it is conjoined with the object, the objective phenomenon (ārammaṇadhamma) is contradicted;

thus, the three answers—"conditioned by an unwholesome phenomenon, an unwholesome phenomenon [arises]"; "conditioned by an indeterminate phenomenon, an unwholesome [phenomenon arises]"; and "conditioned by both unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena, an unwholesome [phenomenon arises]"—are omitted. Conditioned by an indeterminate phenomenon...

"Indeterminate" is stated as only one [category] by way of matter (*rūpa*). Thus, having understood what is contradictory and what is non-contradictory in all instances, the available delimitation should be known.
Furthermore, this is merely a demonstration of the method (*naya*): "four by way of predominance" (*adhipati*) are precisely those obtained by way of root-cause (*hetu*).
This same method applies to the remaining tetrads as well.

"In the immediate condition, one" means that it is indeterminate by way of the indeterminate, both in terms of mind-produced matter arising from a rootless consciousness and the remaining types of matter.
In this manner, the appropriate matter should be understood for all the "ones. "In the prenascence condition, two":
here too, one might say there are four by way of the non-root condition; however, because it is combined with the prenascence condition, it is indeterminate.

With unwholesome states as condition, there is the unwholesome; and with both unwholesome and indeterminate states as condition, there is the unwholesome—these two answers, by way of the priority of the physical basis (*vatthupurejāta*), are omitted.
However, in the formless realm (*ārūpa*), two are stated by way of rootless delusion (*ahetuka-moha*) and rootless functional (*ahetuka-kiriya*).

Regarding "not-dissociation" (*navippayutta*), there are two: these two are by way of rootless unwholesome and rootless functional [states] in the formless realm. Regarding "not-absence" (*nonatthi*) and "not-disappearance" (*novigata*), [there are none].
In the "one" [category], it should be understood as indeterminate by way of all indeterminate matter. Among the triads and so forth, there is nothing new.
288. However, in the section based on the "not-object" root, the phrase "five by way of not-predominance" refers only to those already obtained under the "not-object" condition.

Regarding "one by way of not-kamma," here one should understand that which is indeterminate by way of indeterminate matter, excluding both mind-produced matter and kamma-born matter, and taking the remaining matter into account.
289–296. In the section based on predominance (*adhipati*), there are seven [answers] for "not-prenascence" (*napurejāta*); these are the same as those obtained under "not-prenascence.

For "not-postnascence" (*napacchājāta*), there are seventeen; these seventeen are likewise obtained therein. The sections based on "not-immediate" (*nānantara*), "not-simultaneous" (*nasamanantara*), "not-mutuality" (*naaññamañña*), "not-strong-dependence" (*naupanissaya*), "not-association" (*nasampayutta*), "not-absence" (*nonatthi*), and "not-disappearance" (*novigata*) are exactly the same as those based on "not-object" (*nārammaṇa*).
By this mere demonstration of the method, one should understand what has been stated and what remains to be understood, and what is obtainable and what is not obtainable, in all cases.
The commentary on the Negative (Paccanīya) is finished.

297–328. By means of this very same method of definition, one should understand the enumeration, the limits, what has been included and what is yet to come, and what is obtainable and unobtainable, by placing the Positive (Anuloma) first for the Positive-Negative (Anulomapaccanīya), and by placing the Negative first for the Negative-Positive (Paccanīyānuloma).
The commentary on the section on conditions (*paccayavāra*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the section on support (*nissayavāra*). 329–337.
In the section on support, "supported by a wholesome state" means supported by a wholesome state in the sense of being its foundation (*patiṭṭhaṭṭhena*).
The meaning is "having made. The rest here is to be understood according to the method already stated in the section on conditions (*paccayavāra*).
However, at the conclusion of this [section], the statement: “Conditionality (*paccayatta*) is indeed support-ness (*nissayatta*);

support-ness is indeed conditionality,” is said for the purpose of showing that there is no difference in meaning between these two sections. For in meaning, these too are like [the terms] *paṭicca* and *sahajāta*.
They are not different in nature. Even so, they are stated for the purpose of defining their respective meanings.
For in such cases as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," even that which exists at a different moment without depending [on another] is said to "arise with a condition.
Likewise, among things such as pieces of wood standing together by leaning against one another, one is not the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) for the other. Thus...
Derivative form (*upādārūpa*) is certainly not a support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*) for the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Thus, both of these have been stated in order to determine that what was called "condition" in the section on conditions is a support-condition, and what was called "support" in the section on supports possesses the nature of being either co-nascent (*sahajāta*) or pre-existent (*purejāta*).

Furthermore, this is done by way of the inclination of those who understand in such a manner, through the elegance of the teaching, and for the sake of knowing the distinctions of the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
And these two have also been explained.
This concludes the commentary on the section on dependence (nissayavāra). 5. Commentary on the section on association (saṃsaṭṭhavāra).

338–346. In the section on association (*saṃsaṭṭha-vāra*), "associated with a wholesome state" means having made a wholesome state a condition in the sense of association, by way of the characteristics of simultaneous arising and so forth.

"Associated with one wholesome aggregate" means that, having made one wholesome aggregate a condition through association, three aggregates arise by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*). Thus it is said.
It exists. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

However, regarding this root condition (*hetupaccaya*), three questions are answered by way of making it a condition for immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) alone in the sense of association (*sampayoga*). And just as it is with the root condition, so it is with the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and the others;
there is only a single answer in the case of the resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*).
347–350. Now, in order to show the answers according to their number, it is said: "Three by way of cause," and so forth. Therein, among the "all-pairs" (sabbatika), the rule is simply this:
with the wholesome, the wholesome; with the unwholesome, the unwholesome; with the indeterminate, the indeterminate.
However, among the "singletons" (ekaka), only the indeterminate is obtained by way of the indeterminate. Thus, here, regarding the twenty-two [questions]...
