Regarding the conditions, there are three in the nutriment condition and one in the resultant condition—thus there are two limits. In the postnascent condition, there is no conformity.

Therefore, by means of these alone—namely, "three" and "one"—in the combinations of conditions within the dyads, triads, and so forth, wherever the resultant condition enters, there the count should be understood as "one," and in the remaining cases, "three.
The rest here in the direct order (anuloma) is of obvious meaning.
351–354. However, because wholesome states are not obtained in the negative (paccanīya) analysis, the answer is given starting with the unwholesome; that [explanation] is of obvious meaning.

359. As for what was stated here—"In the negative analysis, two in the case of non-root," etc.—to show the number of sections in the answers, it says "two, three, one," which constitutes three sections. By means of these, in the combinations of conditions within the *duka*, *tika*, and so forth, [the following occurs]:
The enumeration should be understood. Here too, when enumerations of a higher number are combined with an enumeration of a lower number, only the lower enumeration is obtained;

when combined with an equal enumeration, the equal enumeration is obtained. And because here only immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā) are conditionally arisen, therefore, by way of not-root, not-predominance, not-prenascence, not-postnascence, not-repetition, not-kamma, not-resultant, not-jhāna, not-path, and not-dissociation:
Only ten conditions are shown from the perspective of opposition; the remaining fourteen are not obtained.
Even among those that are obtained, when the resultant condition is produced, neither kamma nor resultant [conditions] are obtained. 360–368.

"With the non-root condition, there are two through the non-predominance [condition]" means that only the two obtained under the non-root condition are present. This is also the case for the other two [conditions].

The same method applies. "In the case of 'not-kamma,' one": having taken rootless functional volition (*ahetuka-kiriya-cetanā*) as the conditionally arisen, the indeterminate is answered by the indeterminate.
"In the case of 'not-resultant,' two": there are two due to rootless delusion-functional states (*ahetuka-moha-kiriya*). "In the case of 'not-jhāna,' one":

the answer regarding the indeterminate should be understood by way of rootless fivefold sense-consciousness (*ahetuka-pañcaviññāṇa*). "In the case of 'not-path,' one": the answer regarding the indeterminate is by way of rootless resultant and functional states (*ahetuka-vipāka-kiriya*).
By this method, the meaning should be understood in all combinations. 369–383.
In the positive-negative (anuloma-paccanīya) analysis, only the ten factors mentioned below—beginning with "not-root" (nahetu)—are obtained from the negative perspective, and no others.
Even among those that are obtained, when "root" (hetu) stands in the positive position, "jhāna" and "path" (magga) are not obtained in the negative position.
All should be understood according to the method explained below.

384–391. In the negative-positive (paccanīyānuloma) sequence regarding those arisen by way of the non-root condition (*na-hetu-paccaya*), only rootless delusion (*ahetuka-moha*) receives the jhāna and path conditions;

the rest do not. In the case of the non-jhāna condition (*na-jhāna-paccaya*), there are also eight rootless consciousnesses. [In the case of] the non-kamma condition (*na-kamma-paccaya*) and the non-root condition (*na-hetu-paccaya*)...
By way of neither predominance condition nor prenascence condition, there is one [way] with respect to the object:

in the formless realm, by way of rootless functional volition, the indeterminate is related to the indeterminate. By this method, the enumeration for all cases should be understood according to what is obtained and what is not obtained.
Commentary on the Chapter on Association. 6. Commentary on the Chapter on Conjunction (Sampayutta-vāra), §§ 392–400.
In the Chapter on Conjunction, "conjoined with a wholesome state" means that a wholesome state is a condition by way of conjunction (sampayutta-paccaya) [for another].
The meaning is "having made. The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on *saṃsaṭṭha* (conjoined).
At the conclusion, however, the statement, "What is called being conjoined (*saṃsaṭṭhatta*) is associatedness (*sampayuttatta*);

what is called associatedness is being conjoined," is said for the purpose of showing that there is no difference in meaning between these two sections. For in meaning, these too are dependently arisen and co-nascent.
They are non-distinct in their nature, like conditions and supports. Nevertheless, they are stated for the purpose of defining their respective functions.
For in such expressions as “the horses are yoked together” (*saṃsaṭṭhā yojitā*), even that which is not associated (*asampayutta*) is called “conjoined” (*saṃsaṭṭha*).
And in such passages as “that investigation which is accompanied by indolence, associated with indolence,” even that which is not conjoined and is intermingled is called “associated” (*sampayutta*).

Thus, both of these have been stated in order to establish the state of association for that which has the characteristic of arising together (ekuppāda-lakkhaṇa) through the section on association (saṃsaṭṭha-vāra), and to establish the state of association for that which is associated (sampayutta) through the section on association (sampayutta-vāra).

Furthermore, they are taught according to the inclinations of those who understand in such a way, as a display of the teaching, and for the purpose of knowing the various divisions of the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).
And these two have also been explained.
This concludes the commentary on the section on associated states (*sampayutta-vāra*).
Now, among those six sections, there is a certain condition that does not exist exclusively in the forward order (*anuloma*), but rather only in the reverse order (*paccanīka*).

It persists; there is that which does not persist in an absolute contrary manner, but persists only in a conformable manner; and there is that which persists neither exclusively in a conformable manner nor exclusively in a contrary manner.
This should be understood as a miscellaneous exposition (*pakiṇṇaka*). In this regard, the first question is to be understood by way of what is subsequently arisen (*pacchājāta*);
the second, by way of the Great Tetrad (*mahācatukka*); and the third, by way of those remaining factors that are applicable.
7. Commentary on the Analysis of the Section of Questions (Pañhāvāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 401–403.

In the Section of Questions, in order to show the answers according to the possible occurrences for the questions to be extracted from the Triplet of the Wholesome (*kusalattika*)—beginning with “A wholesome state may be a condition, by way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*), for a wholesome state”—the wholesome state [is discussed].
It is said: "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of the root-condition," and so forth.
This wholesome state, when arising itself, arises by means of twenty-two conditions, excluding the postnascent and the resultant.
When acting as a condition for a wholesome state, it arises by means of twenty conditions, excluding the prenascence, postnascence, resultant, and dissociation conditions.

...is a condition. Therefore, in order to show those conditions by which the wholesome is a condition for the wholesome in their proper sequence, the passage beginning with "by the root-condition" (*hetupaccayena*) is commenced.

Therein, instead of saying—as was done in the section on the Analysis of Conditions (*paccayavibhaṅga*)—"of states associated with roots" (*hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ*), it says "roots... [and so forth].
The teaching was given as "of the associated aggregates. The purpose for making that very statement is this:
in that context, it was said "of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*) in order to illuminate the sense of emptiness (*suññaṭṭha*).

Here, however, it is said "of aggregates" (*khandhānaṃ*) in order to illuminate the sense of a heap (*rāsaṭṭha*), showing that the phenomena arising from conditions arise as a heap, not individually. Or else, [it is used] in the *Paṭiccasamuppāda-vāra* and so forth...
The teaching on the conditions arising by way of the aggregates has been presented; for that same reason, it is presented here as well in that very sequence.

But why have these been presented in this manner? It is for the purpose of showing their distinctions without confusion. For if it were stated in the manner beginning with "dependent on one state, the remaining states," it would not be possible to specify, "depending on such-and-such a state, such-and-such a state [arises]."

In order to know the conditions and the conditionally arisen states without confusion, it might be argued that if this were the case, the summary (uddesa) and the exposition (niddesa) would be indistinguishable.
Therefore, it should be understood that they are presented in this way for the purpose of showing their distinct classification without confusion.
The phrase "of those originated by consciousness" is stated to show specifically which kind of indeterminate state serves as a root-condition (hetupaccaya) for another.
In the *Paccayavibhaṅga*, however, without making a division by way of the wholesome and so forth, but for the purpose of showing materiality arisen through all causes in their general sense,
it is stated as "produced by that" (*taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ*) rather than saying "mind-produced" (*cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ*). Therefore, in that context,
both the materiality produced by indeterminate causes and the "kamma-wrought" materiality at the moment of descent [into the womb] are included.
By this method, the meaning should be understood in the remaining similar answers as well.
404. "Having given a gift" means having relinquished the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*). Alternatively, the volition (*cetanā*) by which that [object] is given is itself the "gift.
"Having given" means having purified and made clean that volition. "Having undertaken virtue" means [by way of] the five factors, etc.
Having undertaken the perpetual precept (*niccasīla*). By this, only the abstinence through formal undertaking (*samādānavirati*) is shown.

However, the abstinence through attainment (*sampattavirati*) and the abstinence through eradication (*samucchedavirati*) are not mentioned because they are not well-known in the world as "virtue" (*sīla*). Even though they are not mentioned, they nevertheless serve as object-conditions (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
Among these, the abstinence through eradication is an object only for the wholesome [consciousness] of those in training (*sekkha*), and not for others. The Uposatha ritual—
"Having performed" means having performed the eightfold Uposatha observance on Uposatha days as it is stated: "One should not kill a living being, nor take what is not given.
He reflects upon that: both a trainee (sekkha) and an ordinary person (puthujjana) reflect upon that wholesome state, and even an Arahant reflects upon it.
For even for an Arahant, wholesome karma previously performed remains wholesome; however, the mind by which he reflects [is itself wholesome].
That is what is called functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*). Therefore, it is not included in this context of "this wholesome state [is the cause] for a wholesome state.

Regarding the phrase "previously well-performed," it should be understood that those acts performed "having given, having undertaken, having done" were mentioned as being proximate, whereas these are not proximate.
Alternatively, by "giving and so forth," the remaining wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) are meant.
This was said in order to show [this]. "Having emerged from jhāna" means having emerged from jhāna; or rather, this is the very reading of the text (*pāḷi*).
"The trainees' change-of-lineage" is said with reference to the stream-enterer, for he reviews the change-of-lineage.
"Purification," however, is said with reference to the once-returner and the non-returner, for their consciousness is called purification.

"Trainees" (sekkhā) refers to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. "Having emerged from the paths" means having emerged from the paths they themselves have attained by way of transcending the path, the fruit, and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
However, there is no such thing as reviewing after having emerged from the pure path itself.
Regarding the phrase "the wholesome as impermanent," here it should be understood as the wholesome of the three planes that has entered into insight (vipassanā), namely, the wholesome of insight.

But [the object] is only that of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). By "knowledge of the minds of others" (cetopariyañāṇa), he shows the wholesome [consciousness] of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).

By "the base of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatana) and so forth, he shows only the wholesome [consciousness] of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) arising by way of having the wholesome of the immaterial sphere as its object.

By "wholesome aggregates are the object of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power" (iddhividhañāṇa) and so forth, he shows it by way of the phenomena (dhamma), without referring to a person (puggala). For that very reason, here below—
Although the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) has already been mentioned, it is stated again here.
"He relishes" means that he experiences and is attached by means of consciousnesses associated with greed accompanied by joy (*somanassa*).
"He delights" means that through the influence of craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*), he rejoices and becomes elated; this refers to delighting in views (*diṭṭhābhinandanā*).
Or one relishes it. "Lust arises" means that for one who is gratifying [the object], lust indeed arises. This is stated by including all eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed (*lobha*).

"Wrong view arises" means that for one who relishes it, wrong view—associated with all four types of consciousness in the manner of "self" and "belonging to self," and so forth—arises. Furthermore, for one who has reached a state of indecision here, doubt arises.
For one who has fallen into distraction, there is restlessness; for one who feels remorse, thinking "Alas, what a good deed I have not done," there is grief.
"Taking that as an object" means taking those well-performed deeds as the object—this is the meaning.
For this is a singular substitution for a plural, or it is singular by way of genus.

406. "An Arahant, having emerged from the path" means having emerged by way of transcending the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) that immediately follows the fruition within the cognitive process of the path.
His reviewing consciousnesses, moreover, are functional-indeterminate (kiriya-abyākata).

Having thus shown the object-condition for the functional-indeterminate, he said "or those in training," etc., in order to show it again for the resultant-indeterminate (vipāka-abyākata). [In the case of] the wholesome...
"Ceased" means when the cognitive process of insight (vipassanā-javana) has been cut off. "Resultant" refers to a resultant consciousness of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-vipāka).

"Taking that as its object" (tadārammaṇatā) means by way of taking that as its object; the meaning is that it arises having made the wholesome state previously contemplated—which served as the object for that wholesome impulsion—its own object.
And it does not arise solely by way of taking that as its object, but also by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti).
For indeed, when resultant [consciousness] takes kamma as its object, it has a wholesome object for one who has grasped rebirth-linking;
however, because that is difficult to discern, it is not shown here.

The passage beginning "He relishes the wholesome" is stated to show the resultant with a wholesome object at the conclusion of an unwholesome javana. "Of the resultant of the base of infinite consciousness... [etc.]

Although this is difficult to discern, it is stated here in terms of its potential occurrence, because it does not actually arise as the object-condition (*tadārammaṇa*) for the sublime resultant consciousness.

"Of functional [consciousness]" refers to the functional consciousness that has attained Arahatship and enters the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) either in reverse order or by skipping stages (*ekantarika*).
"Of the knowledge of others' minds" and so forth refer to the adverting [consciousness] mentioned later.

[The following] are to be applied. The meaning here is this: the wholesome aggregates that constitute the adverting consciousness (*āvajjanā*) of these [states] are a condition for them by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
407–409. "Lust" (*rāga*) refers to one's own lust or another's lust; however, in this context, the explanation is more evident from the standpoint of one's own lust.
"Relishes" (*assādeti*) and so forth have meanings already explained. Regarding the three beginning with doubt (*vicikicchā*), however, because there is an absence of anything to be relished...
“Experiences with relish” is not stated [here]. However, a view arises in this context;

because the phrase “experiences with relish” has been omitted, it was not stated first according to the established sequence. Among doubt and the others, each corresponding category was stated first, and then each subsequent one was stated immediately after it.
And regarding these [defilements] such as lust and so forth, [one thinks]: “Why do evil states arise in me?”

Alternatively, the arising of mental distress (*domanassa*) should be understood as occurring through intolerance, or through remorse and so forth, thinking: "An evil deed has been done; a cruel deed has been done. 410.

Regarding the phrase "the eye is impermanent": by way of the sequence of insight (*vipassanā*), eleven types of form are included because they are prominent—namely, the coarse sense bases (*oḷārikāyatana*) and the physical basis of the heart (*vatthurūpa*).
Furthermore, the sense base of visible form and the others are included because they serve as the objects (*ārammaṇa*) for eye-consciousness and the other types of consciousness.
However, because this teaching is given by way of the groups of consciousness (*viññāṇakāya*) and not by way of the elements (*dhātu*), the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is not included.
In this manner, what is included and what is excluded should be understood in all instances.
(411) "They review the fruit" and "they review Nibbāna" is stated for the purpose of showing the object of the skillful reviewing consciousness.
413–416. In the exposition of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), wholesome states of the four planes are shown by way of those who are still in training (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana);
likewise in the exposition of conascent-predominance (sahajātādhipati). Because the Arahant has attained the supreme state (uttamadhamma), there is no esteem for mundane wholesome states;
therefore, only the highest path (aggamagga) is shown.

417. Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*anantara-paccaya*), the phrase "the preceding ones" refers to wholesome states (*kusala*) spoken of collectively, whether they belong to the same plane (*ekabhūmaka*) or different planes (*nānābhūmaka*).

"Adaptation (*anuloma*) to change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*)," and "adaptation to purification (*vodāna*)" are stated by way of different objects (*nānārammaṇa*). "Change-of-lineage to the Path (*magga*)," and "purification to the Path" are stated by way of different planes.
In the expression "wholesome to emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*)," however, "wholesome" refers to the wholesome states of the three planes (*tebhūmaka-kusala*).
"Emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) refers to the resultant consciousness of the three planes. They emerge from those wholesome impulsion-cognitive series; therefore it is called "emergence. That is twofold:
the object-identical registration (*tadārammaṇa*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). Among these, for sense-sphere wholesome [consciousness], both types of emergence occur;
for sublime [wholesome], only the life-continuum occurs. As for the statement "the path [is the cause] of the fruit": because...

Supramundane resultant [consciousness] is not called "emergence" because it is included within the cognitive process of impulsion (*javana-vīthi*); therefore, it is mentioned separately. Regarding "conformity for one in training":
wholesome [consciousness] does not immediately follow that of one beyond training; therefore, he makes this distinction.

"By the attainment of fruition" refers to the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and the fruit of non-returning. "By the attainment of fruition" [specifically here] refers to the attainment of the fruit of non-returning.
In the unwholesome (akusala), both types of emergence (vuṭṭhāna) are obtained. Regarding the resultant-indeterminate (vipākābyākata) and the functional-indeterminate (kriyābyākata):

here, it should be understood that the resultant-indeterminate [emerges] only from resultant-indeterminate states, and the functional-indeterminate [emerges] only from functional-indeterminate states. The sequence beginning with "the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) emerges into adverting (āvajjanā)" is stated by way of a mixed classification.
In that context, "functional" refers to the sense-sphere functional (kāmāvacara-kiriya). That [functional state] is the emergence for both types [of indeterminate states].

...is the proximity condition; [the same applies to] sublime [states], which are [proximity conditions] for the life-continuum alone. Thus, regarding those [cases] begun below in the Exposition of the Analysis of Conditions with the statement:

"Preceding wholesome states are a condition for subsequent wholesome states by way of the proximity condition"—namely, wholesome for wholesome, wholesome for indeterminate, unwholesome for unwholesome...

The unwholesome [condition] to the indeterminate, the indeterminate to the indeterminate, the indeterminate to the wholesome, and the indeterminate to the unwholesome—these seven permutations are shown.
By way of these, the proximity condition (anantarapaccaya) is analyzed here in brief.
However, in detail, herein—
One should carefully observe its exposition as tenfold, seventeenfold, sixty-fourfold, and also manifold.
For this proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) does not receive an exposition merely as sevenfold; rather, wholesome [consciousness] [arises] from wholesome...
[The wholesome] to [the wholesome]; the unwholesome to the unwholesome result; the result to the result and the functional;
the functional to the wholesome, the unwholesome, the unwholesome result, and the functional—thus it receives its exposition in ten ways.
Not only in ten ways, however: the wholesome [is related] to the wholesome, to the wholesome result, and to the unwholesome result; the unwholesome to the unwholesome and to the unwholesome result.

A wholesome resultant [consciousness] [is related] to a wholesome resultant [consciousness]; a wholesome resultant [consciousness] to a wholesome resultant, an unwholesome resultant, and functional [consciousnesses]; an unwholesome resultant [consciousness] to an unwholesome resultant, a wholesome resultant, and functional [consciousnesses]; a functional [consciousness] to a functional, wholesome, unwholesome, wholesome resultant, and unwholesome resultant [consciousness].
Thus, it receives its exposition in seventeen ways.
And it is not only in seventeen ways that it receives its exposition; it is also obtained in sixty-six ways. How so?

For sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is the proximity condition for the fourfold wholesome [consciousness] according to the distinction of planes; whereas fine-material and immaterial wholesome consciousness are the proximity conditions only for those belonging to their own respective planes.
Thus, wholesome consciousness is a sixfold proximity condition for wholesome consciousness. Sense-sphere wholesome consciousness...
However, [the result] of sense-sphere wholesome [kamma] is the result of sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, fine-material-sphere resultant, immaterial-sphere resultant, and supramundane resultant;
fine-material-sphere wholesome [is the result] of fine-material-sphere resultant and sense-sphere wholesome resultant;
immaterial-sphere wholesome [is the result] of sense-sphere wholesome resultant, fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere, and supramundane resultant.
Supramundane wholesome [consciousness] is the proximity condition in twelve ways for supramundane resultant [consciousness].
Unwholesome [consciousness] is the proximity condition in five ways for unwholesome [consciousness], unwholesome resultant [consciousness], and wholesome resultant consciousness of the three planes.

Sense-sphere wholesome resultant [consciousness] is the proximity condition for sense-sphere wholesome resultant [consciousness], unwholesome resultant [consciousness], and fine-material-sphere resultant [consciousness].
Regarding "of the immaterial-sphere resultant": the sense-sphere wholesome resultant is a fourfold proximity condition for the resultant;
the fine-material-sphere resultant is a threefold proximity condition for the wholesome resultant of the three planes;
the immaterial-sphere resultant is a twofold proximity condition for the immaterial-sphere resultant and the sense-sphere wholesome resultant; [and] the supramundane resultant...
Regarding "of the wholesome resultant of the four planes": there is the proximity condition in four ways. Thus, the wholesome resultant is a proximity condition for the resultant in thirteen ways.
The unwholesome resultant is a proximity condition for the unwholesome resultant and for the sense-sphere wholesome resultant—thus in two ways.
Thus, in every respect, the resultant is a proximity condition for the resultant in fifteen ways.

Furthermore, wholesome-resultant consciousness of the sense sphere is a condition by way of proximity for functional consciousness of the sense sphere; likewise for unwholesome-resultant consciousness; likewise for fine-material-sphere resultant consciousness;
and likewise for immaterial-sphere resultant consciousness. Thus, resultant consciousness is a condition by way of proximity for functional consciousness in four ways.

Functional consciousness of the sense sphere is a condition for functional consciousness of the three planes; and functional consciousness of the fine-material and immaterial spheres is a condition for those of the fine-material and immaterial spheres respectively.
Kiriya (functional) is a condition for kiriya by way of fivefold immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*).

Sensuous-sphere kiriya is [a condition] for both unwholesome-resultant and four-plane wholesome-resultant; fine-material-sphere kiriya is [a condition] for sensuous-sphere wholesome-resultant, fine-material-sphere resultant, and immaterial-sphere kiriya is [a condition] for four-plane wholesome-resultant as well—thus, kiriya is a condition for resultants by way of elevenfold [classification].
The proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*). However, sense-sphere functional consciousness is a proximity condition for both sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome consciousness;
thus, it serves as a proximity condition for both the wholesome and the unwholesome in two ways. In this manner, it receives its designation even in sixty-four ways.
And not only in sixty-four ways, but it certainly receives it in many ways as well. How so? The first great wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere...
Thus, by way of the preparatory application (*pādakayoga*) for one’s own [wholesome states] and for the four wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*),
for the twenty-one wholesome states consisting of the sixteen accompanied by joy and the supramundane (*lokuttara*),

and for the eleven sense-sphere resultant states (*kāmāvacara-vipāka*) that arise at the conclusion of the impulsion (*javana*) as registration (*tadārammaṇa*) and life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), as well as for the fine-material and immaterial sphere resultant states that proceed solely as life-continuum—

Thus, for twenty-one wholesome states and thirty-two resultant states—namely, the twelve supramundane resultants that occur by way of the attainment of fruition—it serves as the proximity condition for these fifty-three consciousnesses. The same applies to the second wholesome consciousness.
However, excluding the third and fourth [wholesome consciousnesses], it is also the proximity condition for the wholesome states of the higher planes and the supramundane resultants.
And [the first two] are conditions for the remaining twenty-one types of consciousness. The fifth and sixth [types of consciousness] are conditions for thirty-three:
for themselves, for the nine wholesome states of equanimity belonging to the higher planes, and for twenty-three resultant states. The seventh and eighth are conditions for twenty-one only.
The five wholesome states of the fine-material sphere are conditions for their own subsequent wholesome states of the fine-material sphere, and for all four...
[This applies] to ten [types of consciousness]: the four great resultants associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta-mahāvipāka*) and the five fine-material-sphere resultants (*rūpāvacara-vipāka*).
By this same method, among the immaterial-sphere wholesome states (*arūpāvacara-kusala*), the first [wholesome state] is the condition for eleven [states], including its own resultant;
the second, for twelve; the third, for thirteen; the fourth, for fourteen; and [the fifth], for fifteen, including the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Supramundane wholesome [states] produce only their own respective results. Among the eight unwholesome states accompanied by greed, each one produces its result for twenty-one types of consciousness:
the eleven sense-sphere resultant mind-consciousness elements, the nine sublime resultants, and its own respective final [resultant].
The two [unwholesome states] accompanied by grief produce their results for six types of consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
For seven [consciousnesses]: for the seven sense-sphere resultant mind-consciousness elements (kāmāvacara-vipāka-manoviññāṇadhātu), including itself as the last.

For twenty-one: for the eleven sense-sphere resultant mind-consciousness elements—consisting of the two accompanied by doubt and restlessness together with the rootless resultant accompanied by joy—and for the nine fine-material and immaterial-sphere resultants, including itself as the last.
The five wholesome-resultant sense-consciousnesses [are conditions] for the wholesome-resultant mind-element; the mind-element is [a condition] for the two resultant mind-consciousness-elements.
Among those two, the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*) is [a condition] for twelve:

for ten resultant mind-consciousness-elements when they function as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) at the time of the object-representation (*tadārammaṇa*), and for its own subsequent functional mind-element of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*). The rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-aheutuka-manoviññāṇadhātu*)...
However, [it is the cause] for exactly twelve: the two-fold adverting mind-element, the adverting mind-consciousness-element, and the ten resultant mind-consciousness-elements.

It is the cause for twenty-one: the ten sense-sphere resultant mind-consciousness-elements (excluding those accompanied by joy and those that are rootless), the resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, and the two types of adverting consciousness; excluding the two-rooted resultants.

In the case of the sublime (mahaggata) resultant [consciousness], it is the condition for the remaining twelve. In the case of the five fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) resultants, it is the condition for nineteen:

namely, the seventeen types of three-rooted wholesome-resultant rebirth-linking consciousnesses of the three planes, and the two types of adverting consciousness. Among the immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara) resultants, the first is the condition for nine:

namely, the three-rooted wholesome-resultant rebirth-linking consciousnesses of the sense sphere, the four immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses, and the four mind-door adverting consciousnesses. The second...
Excluding the lower resultant [consciousness], it is the cause for eight; excluding the first two lower ones, it is the cause for seven;

excluding the first three lower ones, it is the cause for six; and excluding the four supramundane resultants, it is the cause for fourteen—namely, the thirteen three-rooted resultants and its own last one.
The five unwholesome-resultant sense-consciousnesses [condition] the unwholesome-resultant mind-element; the mind-element [conditions] the unwholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element.

At the time of its own object-ascertaining, at the moment of death, and as rebirth-linking and life-continuum, it conditions the other nine sense-sphere resultants accompanied by equanimity and the two limited functional states accompanied by equanimity.
Of twelve. The functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) [is a condition] for ten types of consciousness:

for nine types of three-rooted resultant consciousness occurring as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in the five-aggregate plane during the arising of laughter; for five types of joy-accompanied resultant consciousness occurring as registration (tadārammaṇa);

and for its own subsequent [consciousness]. Thus, by including what was not previously included, it is a condition for thirteen. Excluding the functional investigating consciousness (voṭṭhabbanakiriyā)...
The functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) [is the cause] for forty-five types of consciousness:

for ten sense-sphere functional states, and for fifteen resultant states that occur as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in the five-aggregate realm—namely, the wholesome and unwholesome states of the sense sphere.
The pair of sense-sphere functional states accompanied by joy and associated with three roots is [the cause] for thirteen states that occur as the life-continuum...
By way of taking what has not been previously taken, there are twenty-two [types of consciousness]: the two types of twice-rooted joy-accompanied functional consciousness;

the five twice-rooted resultant consciousnesses that arise by way of registration (*tadārammaṇa*) from those with three roots; the four fine-material-sphere functional consciousnesses occurring by way of preparation (*parikamma*); the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship; and one's own last [consciousness]. As for the aforementioned [types of consciousness]...
By including the thirteen life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousnesses, the five [consciousnesses] that have those as their object (tadārammaṇa), and one’s own last [consciousness],

there are seventeen through the inclusion of what was previously excluded. The two types of sense-sphere functional (kiriya) consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with three roots arise for those same thirteen life-continuum consciousnesses,
for the six resultant consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity that occur as tadārammaṇa, and for the preliminary (parikamma) stage.

By including what was not previously included, there are twenty-four [consciousnesses]: one active consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), four active consciousnesses of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, and its own last [moment].
By including what was not previously included, there are thirteen [consciousnesses] for the two types of functional consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with two roots:
those same thirteen life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) states, six registration (*tadārammaṇa*) states, and its own last [moment].
Of eighteen [types of consciousness]. In the case of fine-material-sphere functional [consciousness], each one [is the condition] for nine:

for the five-aggregate three-rooted life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and for its own immediately preceding [functional consciousness], making ten. In the case of immaterial-sphere functional [consciousness], the first is [the condition] for eleven:
for the five-aggregate nine life-continuums and for the four-aggregate one’s own immediately preceding [consciousness]. The second is [the condition] for the four-aggregate...
One obtains two life-continuum (bhavaṅga) states. For the third, three; for the fourth, four, as well as the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
Among these, each one in its respective order serves as an immediate condition (anantarapaccaya) for eleven, twelve, thirteen, and fifteen [subsequent states].
Thus it receives its designation in many ways. Therefore it was said:
“One should carefully observe the exposition in ten ways, in seventeen ways, in sixty-four ways,
and also in many ways. The conditions beginning with the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-paccaya) have already been explained.
423. “Depending on faith as a decisive support” (*upanissaya*) means having made faith in such things as karma, the fruit of karma, this world, and the next world one’s decisive support.

Just as a man, believing that there is water beneath the surface of the earth, digs into the earth, so too the faithful son of good family, believing in the fruit and the benefit of giving and other virtues, performs acts of giving and so forth.
He causes it to proceed. Therefore, it is said: "by relying upon faith.
In the phrases "relying upon virtue" and so forth, the meaning is: "having made these qualities such as virtue, etc., the decisive support (upanissaya).
For one who is virtuous, being skilled in the power and the benefits of virtue, relies upon virtue and gives gifts to those possessed of virtue, [proceeding] higher and higher.
He undertakes moral discipline that is perfectly pure and unbroken; he performs the uposatha rites on the fortnightly days beginning with the fourteenth;
and relying upon the perfection of virtue, he gives rise to the meditative absorptions (jhānas) and other qualities.

Furthermore, having penetrated—by means of wisdom consisting of learning—the fact that all attainments depend upon meritorious deeds such as giving, and the distinction between the defilement and purification of those very acts such as giving, [he practices].

One who is established [in virtue], relying upon what has been heard, engages in giving and the other perfections. One who is generous and devoted to generosity gives a gift by relying upon his own perfection of generosity;
being virtuous, he understands that "what is given bears great fruit" and thus undertakes moral discipline and performs the Uposatha rites.
With a mind purified by such practice, he generates the meditative absorptions (jhānas) and so forth. Likewise, one who possesses wisdom [cultivates] both the welfare of this world and the next...

Investigating the means for transcending the world, he thinks: "By this practice, it is possible to accomplish both welfare in this world and welfare in the next world, as well as the means for transcending the world.
Relying on wisdom (*paññā*), he engages in giving and the other perfections.
For it is not only faith and the rest that serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for giving and so forth; they also [serve as such] for one's own future state.

Since even faith and the other [faculties] that are arising have only the decisive support (upanissaya) as their condition, it is therefore said: "Faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom [are the conditions] for faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

Regarding "preliminary work" (parikamma), one should understand it as the preliminary stage prior to the immediate [moment], rather than taking the immediately preceding moment. This applies to the knowledge of the passing away according to deeds (yathākammūpagañāṇa).
Regarding "of the knowledge of future states" (*anāgataṃsañāṇassa*): these two are merely the preliminary work (*parikamma*) for the divine eye; there is no separate preliminary work for them.
These are simply peripheral knowledges (*paribhaṇḍañāṇāni*) of the divine eye itself; they succeed only when that [divine eye] succeeds.

Nevertheless, because of the specific inclination toward them, it should be understood that the preliminary work for the divine eye is also their preliminary work. For these [knowledges] are not [attained] by everyone.
For those possessing the divine eye, these two lead to the same destination. Therefore, a specific preliminary practice (*parikamma*) must be undertaken here.

Regarding "the divine eye and the divine ear-element": for one who, having seen forms at a distance, desires to hear their sounds, the purity of the divine eye serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the purity of the divine ear-element.
Furthermore, by way of the desire to go there after hearing those sounds, etc., [the divine ear-element serves as the support for the divine eye].

The divine ear-element is a decisive support for the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*). Thus, in all cases, the nature of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccayatā*) should be understood by way of its being an auxiliary to this or that [state].
Regarding "the attainment not yet arisen in dependence upon the path": because the obstacles have been loosened by means of this or that path.
And because they abandon the obstacles to each respective attainment (*samāpatti*), the path is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for that attainment.

"They practice insight" means they practice insight for the sake of attaining progressively higher paths. The phrase "of the analytical knowledge of meaning" (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) and so forth is stated because the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) are accomplished precisely through the acquisition of the path.
And once these have been thus accomplished, subsequently, with respect to various objects...
The path itself is called the decisive support (upanissaya) for its own occurrence.
Relying on faith, one arouses conceit (*māna*); that is, one brings about the conceit, "I am faithful, I am confident. One adopts a wrong view (*diṭṭhi*);
that is, having proceeded by means of faith toward various statements, one does not examine the meaning with wisdom.

One adopts a view by way of such [assertions] as "there is a person. One arouses conceit, thinking, "I am virtuous, learned, generous, and endowed with wisdom," regarding virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
Furthermore, one adopts a view by giving rise to the conceit of views—just like the conceit of pride—regarding virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "of lust" and so forth, [one adopts a view] by depending upon the excellence of faith and the other qualities.
At the time of self-praise, each of those qualities serves as a decisive support (upanissaya) for lust; at the time of disparaging others, for hatred; for delusion associated with both;
for the aforementioned types of conceit and views; and for the aspiration toward the attainment of existence and enjoyments by relying on the perfection of faith and so forth.
Thus, only mundane wholesome states are shown here. However, the supramundane is peaceful and sublime.

It is the supreme destroyer of unwholesome states. Therefore, unlike the moon which is the basis for darkness and ignorance, it is not taken as a supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for the unwholesome.
The passage beginning with "he torments himself" (*ātāpeti*) is stated for the purpose of showing that these are indeterminate (*abyākata*) phenomena by way of bodily suffering.
For one who is faithful, relying on faith, does not hesitate—thinking "it is too cold" or "it is too hot"—but performs various kinds of construction work, service, and so forth.
One torments and afflicts oneself; having acquired wealth, one experiences suffering rooted in the pursuit of the thought, "I shall perform meritorious deeds.

Even a virtuous person, for the sake of guarding their virtue, torments and afflicts themselves by living in the open air and so forth, and experiences suffering rooted in the pursuit of the thought, "I shall live as an alms-collector" and so forth.
One who is learned, practicing in accordance with his learning according to the method already described,
torments himself and torments others, and experiences suffering rooted in seeking. One who is generous, through his inclination toward generosity,
renounces without remainder even those requisites sufficient for his own maintenance, or else renounces his limbs and so forth.
While doing so, he torments and afflicts himself; for the sake of acquiring the requisites that must be renounced, he experiences suffering rooted in the search for them.

Even one possessed of wisdom, thinking "I shall increase my wisdom further," relies on his state of wisdom and—disregarding cold, heat, and so forth—exerts himself in recitation and mental attention, thereby tormenting and afflicting himself.
Having seen the danger in wrong livelihood and the benefit in right livelihood, one abandons wrong livelihood and seeks a means of subsistence through a pure livelihood;
yet, while doing so, one experiences suffering rooted in that very search. Regarding "bodily happiness":
this refers to the time when one makes use of the requisites for comfort that have arisen by depending upon the excellence of faith and other such qualities.

And at the time of the arising of bodily pleasure— namely, for the body touched by sublime matter originated by faith and so forth, and for the body touched by matter originated by joy and rapture rooted in non-regret through the influence of those [qualities]—
as well as at the time of the arising of suffering in the manner already described, and at the time of being subjected to execution, imprisonment,
and so forth by those unable to endure the excellence of qualities such as faith; and also at the time of the arising of the pleasure of resultant (vipāka) that has arisen from past kamma (kaṭattā).

Regarding bodily suffering, however, at the time when the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) occurs by depending on faith and the other [faculties], each one among these should be understood as a condition for that attainment of fruition by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). "Wholesome kamma" refers to wholesome volition (*cetanā*);
it is a decisive support condition for its own result, but this must be strong volition, not weak.
The story is as follows: It is said that a certain woman, wishing to hang herself, fastened a rope to a tree and made her preparations.

Then, during the night, a thief approached her house and, thinking, "I will bind something with this rope and carry it off," drew near with a knife to cut it. Thereupon, that rope became a venomous snake and hissed.
He did so. The thief, terrified, retreated. The woman, having gone out from her own dwelling, placed her neck in a noose made of rope and hanged herself, thus passing away.
In this way, a powerful volition (cetanā) wards off obstacles and becomes the decisive support (upanissaya) for its own fruition.
However, this should not be taken as an absolute rule; for it is karma that has already found its opportunity which creates an obstacle to fruition.
Having been obstructed, it ripens; however, it should not be said that karma which produces a result is not a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for that result.

Here, "karma" should be understood as belonging to all four planes. As for what is stated later, "the path [is the condition] for the attainment of fruition," that is said with reference to non-consciousness (*acetanā*).
By this, he illustrates: whatever phenomenon produces a result, that [is the condition] for itself...
"It is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the result of maturation (*vipāka*).

Regarding the statement "one kills a living being depending on lust": one kills a living being either toward that object toward which one is lustful, or toward that which is hostile to it, or for its sake.
The same principle should be understood for the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth. [The word] *sandhiṃ*...
"He cuts off" is said by way of taking what is not given. In that context, "a joint" refers to a house-joint (a point of entry).
"He carries off by ambush" means he carries it off after hiding. "He makes a single-house raid" means he plunders by surrounding many people together at a single house.
"He stands in ambush" means he performs the work of highway robbery. Regarding the phrases beginning with "relying on hatred," [the result is] harm...
"Having made the hatred arisen by way of [the thought] 'He has wronged me,' etc., the proximate cause (upanissaya).

Having made delusion the proximate cause means having made the delusion that conceals the danger in killing living beings, etc., the proximate cause. Having made pride the proximate cause means having made the pride [thinking], 'Why should I not be able to kill?
Why should I not be able to take? the proximate cause; or, having been despised by someone..."
"He is despised and reviled" means having made that self-contempt (*omāna*) his decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"Relying on a view" means relying on a view as a decisive support, like the brahmins and others in sacrifices, or like the *pādasika* and *milakkha* tribes.
"Relying on a wish" means: "If this specific thing of mine succeeds, I shall perform such an offering for you."
Likewise, having made a prayer consisting of supplicating a deity, such as:

"Kill such-and-such a person and give [him] to me," or "Bring what belongs to such-and-such a person," or "Come and be my companion while I am performing these deeds"—having thus made such a wish the decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, and wish—these are [the conditions] for lust. Herein, lust is also the decisive support for lust.
The same applies to hatred and the rest; this method is identical for hatred and so forth as well.
Regarding "killing is the condition for killing": because one stands in non-restraint, a killer kills yet another living being.
Or, one who was killed by him may be harassed by his kinsmen and friends, and [the killer] then kills yet another among them. Thus, killing is a condition for killing.
It is a condition by way of decisive support (upanissaya-paccaya). Furthermore, in the case of stealing another's property after having killed the owner of the goods or their guardian;
in the case of violating another's wife after having killed her husband; in the case of speaking falsehood, saying "I did not kill him";

in the case of instigating malicious talebearing for the purpose of concealing what has been done or for the purpose of doing what has not been done; and likewise, in the case of uttering harsh speech—[these are conditions by way of decisive support].

In the speaking of idle chatter; in coveting the wealth and requisites of others belonging to another whom one has killed, thinking, "May the friends and relatives of him who was killed by me be cut off";

and at the time of grasping a wrong view through such practices as self-mortification, thinking, "In this way my killing of living beings will be exhausted"—therein lies killing. This also applies to taking what is not given and the other [precepts].
It serves as a decisive support (*upanissaya*). By this same method, the meaning should be understood for the wheels rooted in taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), and so forth.

Regarding "the act of matricide is [the condition] for the act of matricide": this refers either to one who, seeing another killing his mother, thinks "it is permissible to do so" and then kills his own mother;
or to one who, having killed her in one existence, kills her again in a subsequent existence; or to one who kills her in that very same existence.

In this case, the kamma of matricide becomes the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for another kamma of matricide either by repeatedly commanding, "Go, kill my mother," or by administering a second blow when death is certain from two blows.
The remaining [types of kamma] should also be understood according to their respective application by this same method. For strong wholesome kamma [overcomes] weak unwholesome kamma...

They say that because there is no decisive supporting condition (*upanissaya*), the teaching was given solely by way of the immediate retribution of the courses of action (*kammapathānantariya-kamma*).
That should not be accepted as absolute. For after committing acts such as the destruction of life, when one is reproached with "Why did you do this?", one may even give way to mere anger;
one also becomes remorseful. And when even a slight defilement arises, one increases it.
One commits a transgression. Therefore, a strong [state] is indeed a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for a weak one, and a weak state is also a decisive support for a strong one.

As for what was stated in the commentary on the summary of the *Paccayavibhaṅga*—namely, "it is a decisive support in the sense of being a powerful cause"—that was said because of the power of the causal state itself, not because of the phenomena that constitute the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). [This applies to] kamma and the defilements (*kilesa*).
For indeed, both the strong and the weak possess causes for strength.

In such passages as "one gives a gift depending on lust," one gives a gift depending on lust for either rebirth or wealth, thinking, "O, may I be reborn in the company of the Cātumahārājika devas. This applies also to the undertaking of virtue and the performance of the Uposatha duties.

The same method applies here. However, when one arouses jhāna for the purpose of suppressing lust, insight (vipassanā) for the purpose of abandoning lust, and the Path (magga) for the purpose of eradicating it, one is said to arouse them "by depending on lust" (upanissāya).

But when one arouses direct knowledge (abhiññā) and meditative attainment (samāpatti) for the purpose of attaining a state free from lust, one is said to arouse them "by depending on lust," for it is only at that point that one becomes truly "free from lust."
"By means of faith": this refers to the faith that arises through giving and so forth; the same method applies to virtue and the other factors as well.

For just as one who, while producing faith and the rest by way of giving and so forth, is said to produce them "by depending on lust," it should be understood that lust and the like likewise serve as the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for faith and the rest.
"For the purpose of warding off that": for the purpose of resisting or repelling that.
The meaning is: "for the purpose of not providing an opportunity for the ripening [of the result]. Let it be so in the case of those actions that involve resistance (*sappaṭighāta*);

but as for those immediate (*ānantariya*) karmas that do not involve resistance (*appaṭighāta*), why is it said of them, "for the purpose of counteracting that"? It is because of the inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) of that person.
For his inclination was, "I shall set this in motion for the purpose of counteracting that"; taking that into account, it was stated thus.
"Tormenting oneself depending on lust": wherever one is lustful, seeing that attainment comes through hardship, one acts in this way;
all of this is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

"Of bodily pleasure" refers either to the pleasure obtained by performing wholesome deeds through the transcendence of lust and so forth, or to the pleasure obtained by indulging in sense pleasures while failing to see their danger due to lust and so forth.
"Of arisen pleasure" means either of the pleasure arisen through such means as self-mortification (*ātāpana*), or of the suffering arisen through execution, imprisonment, and so forth,
caused by lust and other defilements. "By the attainment of the fruit" means either by that which has been produced after completely cutting off lust and the rest,
or by that which has been entered into by one who is distressed by them.

In such passages as "bodily pleasure" (*kāyikaṃ sukhaṃ*), when pleasure has arisen, for one who relishes it and repeatedly produces it through similar conditions, the preceding [moment] becomes the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the subsequent one.

However, in the case of those who excessively indulge in fire-warming and so forth during cold weather, there is pleasure in the prior stage and pain in the later stage—as in the verse: "O happy indeed is the life of the wandering nun Missā... [and so on].

"Contact with a hairy youth on the arm"—for one who thus falls into the state of being drunk with sensual pleasures, the bodily pleasure found here is [no match for] the bodily suffering of a denizen of hell;

however, for one who is happy by virtue of being free from disease and enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), that bodily pleasure serves as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the attainment of fruition. Furthermore, pleasure exists for the sake of counteracting suffering.

For one who serves for the sake of warding off suffering, bodily pain—having suppressed an affliction just as the Blessed One did while entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti)—serves as a decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for both bodily pleasure and the attainment of fruition.
A favorable season is a condition for pleasure and the attainment of fruition, while an unfavorable season is a condition for pain. [This applies to] an unfavorable season.

Or, for one who wishes to experience the pleasure arisen by means of the materiality produced through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) after having mastered [the jhānas], even an unsuitable temperature serves as a condition for the fruition attainment (*phalasamāpatti*). The same principle applies to food and lodgings.

Furthermore, the phrases "bodily pleasure" and so forth are merely presented together here; however, their status as conditions should be understood according to the method explained below. Fruition Attainment.
“Of bodily pleasure” means of the pleasure arisen by way of the material form produced from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
For he, having emerged from that attainment, experiences it.
In such expressions as “giving based on bodily pleasure,” [the thought is]: “O, may this pleasure of mine not decline!”
Either by way of the non-decline of what has already been attained; or by way of the attainment of what has not yet been attained, thinking, "O, may I reach such happiness in the future";

or even regarding suffering, either by way of the decline of what has been attained, thinking, "O, may my suffering diminish," or by way of the aspiration for its non-arising, thinking, "May such [suffering] not arise in the future. This refers to happiness and suffering.

The state of decisive support (*upanissayatā*) should be understood. The weather, food, and lodging are exactly as described by the aforementioned method. Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "bodily happiness," because it is said:
"It is good indeed, dear Moggallāna, to go for refuge to the Buddha," even for those who have attained happiness, [it is said]:
"Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, who teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding of such suffering."
Faith arises even in those who have encountered suffering. One should fulfill the precepts and other virtues for the sake of union with happiness and separation from suffering;
therefore, happiness and suffering are shown as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for faith and the other [faculties]. Temperature and the other [conditions] should also be applied accordingly.
Regarding such statements as "one kills a living being depending on bodily happiness," one should follow the same method already explained.
The state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for pleasure and the other [mental factors] should be understood.

In this analysis of decisive support, however, the wholesome is a decisive support for the wholesome in three ways, for the unwholesome in two ways, and for the indeterminate in three ways. The unwholesome is a decisive support for the unwholesome in three ways, and for the wholesome in one way.

The indeterminate [state] is [related] to the indeterminate in two ways. The indeterminate is also related to the indeterminate in three ways; likewise to the wholesome, and likewise to the unwholesome.

Thus, it should be understood that the decisive support (upanissaya) has been classified in twenty-three ways: as eightfold for the wholesome, sixfold for the unwholesome, and ninefold for the indeterminate.
424. The eye and so forth are mentioned as "pre-arisen" (*purejāta*) by way of their grossness. However, the water element and so on are also indeed pre-arisen objects.
The statement, "The base (*vatthu*) is a pre-arisen eye-base," and so on, was said to show that which, being a base, is pre-arisen.
The phrase "the base for resultant indeterminate states" was said with reference to the pre-arisen condition during the course of existence (*pavatti*).
425. "Of this body born afterwards" (*pacchājāte imassa kāyassa*) refers to the body composed of the four great elements (*cātumahābhūtika*).

"Conditioned by way of posteriority-condition" (*pacchājātapaccayena paccayo*) means being a condition by way of providing support (*upatthambhana*) after having been born later. Because it is a condition precisely in the sense of being a supporter, it is called the "posteriority-condition" (*pacchājātapaccaya*);
thus it is presented in the forward order (*anuloma*) within this section of questions.

426. Regarding the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), the reason for the separate mention of "adaptation" (*anuloma*) and "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhu*), and so forth, should be understood according to the method already explained below.

427. Regarding the condition of kamma (*kammapaccaya*), in the phrase "wholesome volition [is a condition] for its associated states," the term "conascent" (*sahajāta*) is not used because there is no distinction here between conascence and asynchronous (non-conascent) relations.
However, in the section dealing with the indeterminate (*abyākata*), that distinction does exist; therefore, in that case—
[This] has been stated. The grasping of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is performed by way of the material phenomena produced by kamma (kaṭattārūpa).

Regarding the phrase "volition is the condition for the physical basis" (vatthu): although at the moment of rebirth-linking immaterial phenomena, established upon the physical basis, proceed by way of the physical basis as their condition, it is nevertheless stated [in this way] to show that volition is also a condition for the physical basis itself.
428. Regarding the condition of kamma-result (vipāka-paccaya), the meaning should be understood in the section on rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) by this same method.

429–438. Regarding the condition of nutriment (āhāra-paccaya): "For this body" means for this body composed of the four great elements (cātumahābhūtika) that proceeds by way of the four continuities (catusantati).
It is a condition by way of the condition of nutriment through the mode of producing that which is originated by nutriment, and through the mode of supporting the remainder.

In the sections on the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya) and so forth, the section on rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-vāra) should be understood in the same manner as already stated. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the analysis of the Question Section (pañhāvāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
[Now follows] the forward calculation (anuloma-gaṇanā) for the arrangement of the Question Section.
439. Now, in order to show here the answers obtained according to their numerical count, it is said:
"Seven by way of cause," and so forth. Therein, "seven" means: by way of the wholesome, there are three—wholesome, indeterminate, and wholesome-indeterminate;

likewise by way of the unwholesome; and by way of the indeterminate, there is only the indeterminate. Thus there are seven. "Nine by way of object" refers to those beginning with a single root and ending with a single [result].
Nine. Ten by way of predominance: wholesome [states] are related to wholesome [states] both as co-nascent and as object;

to unwholesome [states] as object only; and to indeterminate [states] both as co-nascent and as object; and to wholesome-indeterminate [states] as co-nascent only—thus there are four rooted in the wholesome.
Unwholesome [states] are related to unwholesome [states] both as co-nascent and as object; and to indeterminate [states]...
Likewise, for the unwholesome and the indeterminate, there are three rooted in the unwholesome due to co-nascence.
The indeterminate [state] is related to the indeterminate through both co-nascence and object; likewise for the wholesome and the unwholesome, it is related through object alone.
Thus, there are three rooted in the indeterminate, making ten in total. Herein, objective predominance is obtained in seven ways, and likewise, co-nascent predominance is obtained in seven ways.
In the "immediate" (anantara) condition, there are seven: two rooted in the wholesome, likewise two rooted in the unwholesome, and three rooted in the indeterminate—thus making seven.
In the "contiguous" (samanantara) condition, these same seven apply. In the "co-nascent" (sahajāta) condition, there are nine:

three rooted in the wholesome, three rooted in the unwholesome, one rooted in the indeterminate, and likewise one rooted in both the wholesome and the indeterminate, and one rooted in both the unwholesome and the indeterminate.
Thus there are nine. Regarding "three by way of mutuality": wholesome [states] with wholesome, unwholesome with unwholesome, and indeterminate with indeterminate—thus there are three.

Regarding "thirteen by way of dependence": there are three rooted in wholesome [states] through co-nascence alone; likewise three rooted in unwholesome [states]; likewise three rooted in indeterminate [states].
Herein, however, pre-nascence is also included. For the indeterminate [state] is [dependent] upon the indeterminate.
It is both co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and pre-nascent (*purejāta*); for the wholesome, it is only pre-nascent, and likewise for the unwholesome.

Again, the wholesome and indeterminate [states] are [conditions] for the wholesome by way of being co-nascent and pre-nascent, and for the indeterminate by way of being co-nascent alone; likewise for the unwholesome and indeterminate—thus there are thirteen.
"Nine in the case of decisive support (*upanissaya*)" means nine from the single root to the end of the single section. Twenty-three divisions are shown in their analysis (*vibhaṅga*).

Among these, there are seven in the case of object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya), seven in the case of proximity-strong-dependence (anantarūpanissaya), and nine in the case of natural-strong-dependence (pakatūpanissaya).
Regarding the "three in the case of prenascence" (purejāta): the indeterminate [state] is [conditioned by] the indeterminate, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—thus there are three.

Regarding the "three in the case of postnascence" (pacchājāta): the wholesome [is conditioned by] the indeterminate, the unwholesome [is conditioned by] the indeterminate, and the indeterminate [is conditioned by] the indeterminate.

Thus there are three [ways] for [the condition of] repetition (*āsevana*); these three are similar to one another. For [the condition of] kamma, there are seven, which are similar to the [condition of] root (*hetu*). Among those, in two of the responses, even asynchronous kamma (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma*) is included;
in five, only conascent kamma is included. For [the condition of] result (*vipāka*), there is one: the indeterminate conditioned by the indeterminate.

For nutriment (*āhāra*), faculty (*indriya*), jhāna, and path (*magga*), there are seven, which are exactly like the [condition of] root. However, here the faculty [condition] is [treated] by way of both the conascent and the pre-arising [modes].

[The condition] that has arrived: in the case of association (*sampayutta*), there are three [conditions] similar to those of mutuality (*aññamañña*); in the case of dissociation (*vippayutta*), there are five.

Thus, from the perspectives of co-nascence (*sahajāta*), post-nascence (*pacchājāta*), and so forth, the indeterminate (*abyākata*) arises with the wholesome (*kusala*) and the unwholesome (*akusala*); the indeterminate arises with the indeterminate through co-nascence, pre-nascence (*purejāta*), and post-nascence;
and the wholesome arises with the indeterminate through the pre-nascence of the physical basis (*vatthu-purejāta*), as does the unwholesome—this constitutes one wholesome root (*kusalamūla*).
One unwholesome root and three indeterminate roots—thus there are five.

Regarding "thirteen by way of presence": through co-nascence, the wholesome is associated with the wholesome; through co-nascence and post-nascence, the wholesome is associated with the indeterminate;

and through co-nascence alone, the wholesome is associated with both the wholesome and the indeterminate—thus there are three wholesome roots. Likewise for the unwholesome roots. [The remaining are] through co-nascence, pre-nascence, post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty.
Furthermore, the indeterminate [state] conditions the indeterminate by way of object-prenascence (vatthārammaṇa-purejāta);

the wholesome [state] is conditioned by the indeterminate by way of base-prenascence (vatthu-purejāta) and object-prenascence; likewise for the unwholesome. The wholesome and the indeterminate are conditioned by the unwholesome by way of conascence-prenascence (sahajāta-purejāta).

That same [wholesome state] is conditioned by the indeterminate by way of conascence-postnascence-nutriment-faculty (sahajāta-pacchājāta-āhāra-indriya), and by way of conascence-prenascence. That same [wholesome state] is conditioned by the indeterminate by way of conascence-postnascence-nutriment-faculty.

Thus there are thirteen. Regarding the "non-existent" (natthi) and "disappeared" (vigata) conditions, seven are similar to the "immediately preceding" (anantara). Regarding the "not-disappeared" (avigata) condition, thirteen are similar to the "existent" (atthi).
Thus, in this context, there are seven numerical groupings: one, three, five, seven, nine, ten, and thirteen. Among these, by way of result (vipāka), there is only one single;

by way of mutuality (aññamañña), prenascence (purejāta), postnascence (pacchājāta), repetition (āsevana), and association (sampayutta), there are five triads; and by way of dissociation (vippayutta)...
There is one pentad; ten heptads by way of root, proximity, contiguity, kamma, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, presence, and non-disappearance;
three nonads by way of object, conascence, and decisive support; one decad by way of predominance;
and three tredecads by way of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance—thus, in each respective section where the conditions are specified.

Having carefully observed by way of enumeration, the counting should be understood according to those [factors] in the combination of conditions (*paccaya-saṃsandana*) within the groups of two, three, and so forth.
However, those conditions which are dissimilar (*visabhāga*) or incompatible (*viruddha*) with other conditions should not be combined with them.

For example: for the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*), there are the object, proximity, contiguity, decisive support, prenascence, postnascence, kamma, repetition, nutriment, jhāna, absence, and disappearance conditions.
Excluding the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), the remaining predominances are dissimilar (*visabhāga*); those beginning with the conascent (*sahajāta*) are similar (*sabhāga*).

Why? Because of their presence and absence in that manner. For when something is the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) for certain factors, it is also their conascent and other such conditions, but it is not their object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and so forth;
thus, the object and other such conditions are called its "dissimilar. Therefore, that...
These [factors] should not be combined with those [others], nor with that [factor].

The relations of prenascence, postnascence, association, dissociation, presence, absence, disappearance, and non-disappearance are mutually contradictory; these too should not be combined with one another.

Having excluded those combinations that are inadmissible, in order to show briefly the possible combinations that can be made with those that are admissible, it is said: "With the root condition and the predominance condition, there are four," and so forth.

In this context, although there ought to be seven instances by way of the lower count when the root condition is combined with the dominant condition, nevertheless, because among the dominants only wisdom (*vīmaṃsā*) is a root condition and not the others, the phrase "four" is stated by excluding the dissimilar ones and taking only the similar ones. These are to be understood as follows: a wholesome state...

A wholesome state is related to a wholesome state by way of root-condition and predominance-condition; wholesome investigation is related to its associated aggregates by way of root-condition and predominance-condition; a wholesome state is related to an indeterminate state by way of root-condition and predominance-condition;
wholesome investigation is related to mind-originated matter by way of root-condition and predominance-condition; a wholesome state...
A wholesome and indeterminate state is related to a wholesome and indeterminate state by way of root-condition and predominance-condition.
Wholesome investigation is related to its associated aggregates and mind-produced matter by way of root-condition and predominance-condition.
An indeterminate state is related to an indeterminate state by way of root-condition and predominance-condition; [this includes] resultant-indeterminate states.
Functional-ineffective investigation [is related] to the associated aggregates and to mind-produced matter.

Herein, only supramundane resultant-ineffective states are to be taken. However, object-condition, proximity-condition, and so forth, are not applied because they belong to a different category (*visabhāga*).
By this method, that which is obtainable and that which is not obtainable in all instances [should be understood].
Having understood this, the alternatives should be extracted according to what is obtainable.
"Seven in co-nascence" means they are obtained precisely within the root-cause (hetu). "Three in mutuality" means they are obtained precisely within pure mutuality (aññamañña).

"Seven in dependence" means they are obtained precisely within the root-cause. "One in resultant" means it is obtained precisely within pure resultant (vipāka). Regarding the faculties and the path...
"Forty" refers to the same method as stated below. "Three in association" refers to those obtained in pure association (*suddhika-sampayutta*).
"Three in dissociation" should be understood by taking matter originated from wholesome and other types of consciousness as the conditionally arisen (*paccayuppanna*).
"Seven in presence and non-disappearance" are those obtained in the root-cause (*hetu*) condition.

441–443. Having thus demonstrated the enumeration according to the "two-rooted" method by way of those eleven conditions—beginning with the predominance condition—with which the root-condition (hetupaccaya) finds its application, [the author] now states, "root, conascent, dependence, presence, non-disappearance:
seven," and so forth, establishing the characteristic for the purpose of demonstrating it in the "three-rooted" methods and beyond. [In the manuscripts...]
However, they write the names of the conditions with missing syllables, such as *nissaupanissaadhipāti*; this was written merely for the sake of providing a technical designation (*saññā*).
Therefore, in such instances, the text (*pāḷi*) should be made complete. As for this grammatical rule (*lakkhaṇa*) that has been established, it illustrates this:
when this root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) combines with the four [others] beginning with co-nascence (*sahajāta*), its own...
In the *Vibhaṅga*, one obtains seven answers. However, if the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*) enters here, one obtains the three obtained in the mutuality [section].
If the association condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*) enters, one obtains those same three.
If the dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*) enters, one obtains the three obtained in the root-dissociation dyad (*hetu-vippayutta-duka*). If the fruition condition (*vipāka-paccaya*)...
When it enters [into combination] with all those factors of similar result (*vipākasabhāga*), it receives its answer in exactly this same way.

However, if here the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) and the path-condition (*magga-paccaya*) enter [into combination], one receives only the four [answers] obtained in the "two-rooted" (*dumūlaka*) combinations along with them.
If, together with those, the mutuality-condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*) enters, then among the four [answers] shown in the "root" (*hetu*) and "predominance" (*adhipati*) dyads—

Regarding the answers: having excluded the two [answers]—“a wholesome state [is related] to an indeterminate state” and “a wholesome state [is related] to both a wholesome and an indeterminate state”—one obtains the remaining two.
Even if the associated condition (sampayutta-paccaya) enters therein, one still obtains those same two.
However, if the dissociated condition (vippayutta-paccaya) enters, one obtains the other two. Furthermore, if...
Among these, the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya) enters [the calculation] in every instance, obtaining exactly one [count].
However, when conditions such as predominance (adhipati) are excluded from the enumeration—being fewer than those in the dyads beginning with root (hetu) and predominance—one obtains only four.

When conditions that enter into the enumeration of fewer types are included, one obtains two or one according to their influence. Thus is the enumeration obtained through the combination of various conditions.
Having understood this, the enumeration in the *Timūlaka* and other sections should be extracted.
