Among these combinations, the first four combinations are stated generally with respect to all nine causes as being without result (*avipāka*). However, in the case of an indeterminate [cause] responding to an indeterminate [result], a resultant cause (*vipākahetu*) is also found here.
The five combinations following those are stated with respect to the resultant cause. Among them, all [of these] are co-nascent results (*sahajāta-vipāka*).

And there are also material phenomena co-nascent with the result (vipāka). Among these, in the first case, during the process of integration (ghaṭana), both results and the material phenomena originated by them are found;
in the second, both results and the physical basis (vatthurūpa) at rebirth-linking; in the third, only immaterial phenomena;
in the fourth, only material phenomena originated by resultant consciousness; and in the fifth, only the physical basis.
The fifteen combinations following that are associated with the faculties and the path, and are stated by way of the root of non-delusion (*amoha*).
Among them, the first nine are without a dominant influence (*nirādhipati*), while the last six possess a dominant influence (*sādhipati*).

Even among those without a dominant influence, the first four are stated generally as applying everywhere by way of non-delusion, while the last five are by way of resultant non-delusion (*vipākāmoha*).
In that context, regarding the first [set] among those without a dominant influence (*anādhipatika*), the "four" are exactly as shown below in the "Dominant Cause" dyad (*hetādhipatiduka*).

In the second, mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*) is excluded. In the third, the physical basis-matter (*vatthurūpa*) is excluded. In the fourth, only matter is obtained: wholesome states [are related] to mind-originated matter, and indeterminate [states] to that which is originated by them. Those following this are associated with kamma-result (*vipāka*).

The five [factors] are exactly as described in the method stated below. Among those with a predominating cause (*sādhipatika*), the first three combinations are stated generally by way of both resultant and non-resultant causes.

Among these, in the first, the four [factors] are exactly as described in the method. In the second, the material (*rūpa*) factor is excluded; in the third, the immaterial (*arūpa*) factor is excluded.
The three following [combinations] are stated by way of resultant causes. Among these, in the first, both the material and immaterial factors are obtained.

In the second [formula], there is only the immaterial; in the third, only the material. Thus, having understood the enumeration as it occurs through the combination of various conditions, the enumerations for those beginning with the "three-rooted" should be extracted.
The section on the Root Condition is finished.

444. Even in the section based on the object-condition (*ārammaṇamūlaka*), seven conditions—namely, the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) and the others—are similar to the object-condition; the remaining sixteen are dissimilar. Therefore, having not combined those [dissimilar ones], only these seven are combined.
Among them, there are seven for the predominance condition: a wholesome state [is related] to a wholesome state, to an unwholesome state, and to an indeterminate state.
Thus, there are three wholesome roots, one unwholesome root, and [three] indeterminate roots.

"Three" refers to the seven [roots]. "Three in the case of support" (nissaya) refer only to the indeterminate roots by way of the physical basis (vatthu). "Seven in the case of decisive support" (upanissaya) are the same as the preceding ones.

"Three in the case of prenascence" (purejāta) are the indeterminate roots by way of both the physical basis and the object (ārammaṇa). "Three in the case of dissociation" (vippayutta) are by way of the physical basis alone.

"Three in the cases of presence and non-disappearance" (atthi-avigata) are by way of both the physical basis and the object. However, just as in the section on the root of cause (hetumūlaka), for the purpose of showing the characteristics—
Thus, combinations have been set forth for the root-objects and so on as well. 445.

Regarding that, first, there are five combinations set forth here under the "root-object" section. Among them, the first is accompanied by predominance (*sādhipatika*) by way of object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
Therein, the term "beings" (*satta*) refers precisely to those answers already obtained in the "Object-Predominance" dyad (*ārammaṇādhipatiduka*).

The second [set] is without a dominant influence (*nirādhipatika*). Therein, "three" refers to the indeterminate roots (*abyākatamūla*) by way of both the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*), or by way of the object alone.
The third is stated by way of the support (*nissaya*). Therein, "three" refers to the indeterminate roots by way of the physical basis.

The fourth and fifth possess a dominant influence (*sādhipatika*). Among them, in the fourth, "one" refers to an indeterminate root by way of both the physical basis and the object, or by way of the object alone.
"Unwholesome. In the fifth [section], "one" refers to the unwholesome root based on the dependent (nissaya) condition.
Thus, here too, the enumeration within the triads and so forth should be understood according to what is applicable. The same applies to the sections beginning with the predominance (adhipati) root.
However, rather than providing a detailed application by way of object (ārammaṇa), faculty (indriya), and result (vipāka), I shall state only what is appropriate to be said in each respective place.

446. In the section on predominance (adhipati), under the heading of conascence (sahajāta), there are seven factors: by way of conascent predominance, there are three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, and one indeterminate root.
However, objective predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) is not obtained together with conascence, nor is conascence obtained together with objective predominance.
Under the heading of mutuality (aññamañña), there are three; this is likewise by way of conascent predominance alone. Under the heading of dependence (nissaya)...
"Eight" refers to the three roots of the wholesome, the three roots of the unwholesome, and the two roots of the indeterminate.

For an indeterminate dominant condition is a support for an indeterminate state both by way of co-nascence and by way of object, whereas it is a support for an unwholesome state only by way of object;
however, it is not so for a wholesome state in either way. Thus, there are only two indeterminate roots, making eight in total. [In the case of] decisive support...
The seven are exactly like those for the object-condition (*ārammaṇa*). For the pre-nascent condition (*purejāta*), there is one: an indeterminate predominance by way of object for the unwholesome.

For the resultant condition (*vipāka*), there is one: the indeterminate for the indeterminate supramundane. Regarding nutriment and the others, the seven are already obtained from the single-rooted section below.
For the dissociation condition (*vippayutta*), there are four: the indeterminate for the wholesome, likewise for the unwholesome, and the indeterminate for the indeterminate.
And it is wholesome. Among the "existent" and "not yet disappeared" [factors], there are eight [combinations] that are exactly like those based on support (nissaya).

447–452. However, regarding the combinations here, instead of joining them with objects (ārammaṇa) and so forth in successive order, they are first joined with the "existent" and "not yet disappeared" factors.
Why is this? Because they are mixed with both types of predominance (adhipati). Therein, in the first combination, by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati):
The basis is obtained as the object; in the second, for one who esteems and relishes [it] by way of dependence, it is the basis alone;

in the third, by way of co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*), wholesome states and so forth [are predominant] over material phenomena, and by way of objective predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), the basis [is predominant] over the unwholesome.
The three subsequent combinations are stated by way of objective predominance. Therein, in the first, "seven" refers to...
These are exactly as stated below. In the second [section], "one" refers to pre-arisen bases and objects for the unwholesome. In the third, only the base is for the unwholesome.
The three combinations following that are stated by way of co-nascent predominance (sahajātādhipati), being common to both resultant and non-resultant states.
Therein, in the first, both the material and immaterial are obtained; in the second, only the immaterial; in the third, only the material. After that—
The next three are stated by way of predominance over resultant [states]. Among those, in the first both the material and immaterial [factors] are obtained;
in the second, the immaterial; and in the third, the material alone. Following that, six combinations associated with nutriment and faculties are stated by way of predominance over consciousness.
Therein, three are non-resultant and three are with-resultant. Among those, the enumeration is quite evident. Following that—

Six combinations have been stated in the same way by way of energy as the dominant factor (*adhipati*). But surely, according to the sequence of the dominant factors, they should have been stated first by way of energy as the dominant factor;
why were they not stated in that manner? Because they are similar to the combinations stated later by way of the cause (*hetu*).
For the combinations stated later by way of the cause [begin] with non-delusion (*amoha*), because of its having investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) as the dominant factor.
And because investigation brings about right view, these [factors] are associated with the Path. Energy, too, is the Path by virtue of being right effort as opposed to wrong effort;
thus, its conjunction with that [Path] is similar to the conjunctions stated later by way of cause. Having reversed [the order], they are stated [here].
In those cases as well, the enumeration is quite evident.
453–456. Regarding the seven [types of conditions] based on the immediate (*anantara*) and the contiguous (*samanantara*): the wholesome is [the condition] for the wholesome and the indeterminate;
likewise the unwholesome; and the indeterminate is [the condition] for all three. Thus there are seven. Regarding the action [condition], there is one:

the wholesome volition of the Path is [the condition] for its own indeterminate resultant. However, among these, the combinations are exactly three each. These have been stated according to the most frequent sequence.

457–460. Among those based on the co-nascent, mutual, and support conditions, those very same conditions that were stated in the "Pairs" (Duka-mūlaka) section are identical to those established at the beginning.

Therefore, having understood the enumeration in the "Pairs" section, the enumeration for all combinations should be known by way of the lower number among those conditions combined in the subsequent sections. Therein, in the "Co-nascent" (Sahajāta) section, there are ten.
Incidents. Among them, five have no result (avipāka), and five have results (savipāka). Regarding those that have no result:
first, for a wholesome [consciousness], there are four—wholesome for wholesome and indeterminate, wholesome-indeterminate for wholesome-indeterminate, and wholesome-indeterminate for indeterminate;

likewise for the unwholesome; and for the indeterminate, there is only one—indeterminate for indeterminate. Thus, there are nine. Among these, regarding the eight beginning with the wholesome and unwholesome...
In the [first] answers, both the immaterial and mind-produced matter are obtained. In the indeterminate [answers], the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) is also included.

In the second combination, among the indeterminate answers, only the physical basis is obtained among the material phenomena; in the third, in all three [types of consciousness], only the immaterial [phenomena] are obtained;
in the fourth, only mind-produced matter is obtained; and in the fifth, at rebirth-linking, the immaterial factors are obtained together with the physical basis.

Among those with resultant [factors], in the first [combination] both the resultant and the matter originated by resultant consciousness are obtained; in the second, both the resultant and the physical basis (vatthurūpa) are obtained;
in the third, only the resultant is obtained; in the fourth, only that originated by resultant consciousness is obtained;

and in the fifth, only the physical basis is obtained. There are six combinations based on mutuality (aññamañña). Among these, the first three are non-resultant, and the latter three are with resultants. Their enumeration is quite evident.

461. In the section based on the dependence condition (*nissayamūlaka*), regarding the dependence condition (*nissayapaccaya*), there are three [results] in the object-condition (*ārammaṇa*); these are to be understood by way of wholesome states, etc., that arise having made the physical basis their object.
Regarding the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*), there is one; this refers to unwholesome [states] that have arisen having made the physical basis a decisive support as an object.
The remainder is to be understood according to the method already explained below in the section based on two conditions (*dumūlaka*).

462–464. In this dependence condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), however, there are twenty combinations. Among them, the first six combinations are stated by way of both pre-arising (*purejāta*) and co-arising (*sahajāta*);
after that, four are by way of pre-arising alone; and after that, ten are by way of co-arising alone.
Therein, in the first combination, "thirteen" refers to those mentioned specifically in the analysis of the dependence condition. In the second, "eight" refers to...
There are seven by way of the conascence-predominance condition, and eight including the unwholesome [state] when taking the physical basis as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya).

In the third [section], the seven are obtained as the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya). In the fourth, the five are obtained as the dissociation-condition (vippayutta-paccaya). In the fifth, there are four:
the wholesome and so forth for mind-originated [matter], and the physical basis for the unwholesome. In the sixth, there are three: the wholesome and so forth for mind-originated [matter].

By way of pre-arising (*purejāta*), there are four [bases]; in the first, three are for the wholesome and so forth, while the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the eye and other faculties are for the indeterminate (*abyākata*).

In the second, the physical basis alone is for the wholesome and so forth. In the third, one is for the unwholesome. In the fourth, the eye and other faculties are for the fivefold consciousness (*viññāṇapañcaka*).
By way of co-arising (*sahajāta*), ten are divided into two types—resultant and non-resultant—in the section on co-arising roots.
These should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. 465.

Regarding the seven conditions based on decisive support (*upanissaya*) with respect to the object (*ārammaṇa*): these are obtained only within the decisive support of the object (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*). Regarding the seven conditions based on predominance (*adhipati*): these are the same [as those mentioned above].

Regarding the two conditions of proximity (*anantara*) and contiguity (*samanantara*): these are obtained only within the proximate decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*). Regarding the condition of dependence (*nissaya*): there is one, namely, the physical basis (*vatthu*).

For unwholesome [states]: in the case of the "pre-arisen" (purejāta) condition, there is one [way], namely as its own basis (vatthu) or object (ārammaṇa). In the case of the "repetition" (āsevana) condition, there are three ways by way of proximity (anantara) and decisive support (upanissaya).
In the case of the "kamma" condition, there are two ways by way of natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya). However, supramundane wholesome volition (cetanā) is also a proximity-decisive-support.

In the case of the "dissociation" (vippayutta) condition, there is one way by way of object-decisive-support; likewise for the "presence" (atthi) and "non-disappearance" (avigata) conditions. In the case of the "absence" (natthi) and "disappearance" (vigata) conditions, there are seven ways, which are exactly the same as those for the proximity condition.
466. Furthermore, there are seven combinations based on decisive support (*upanissaya*). Among these, the first three are stated by way of objective decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*).

Therein, in the first, there are seven [cases]: wholesome [states] for wholesome and so forth; likewise, the indeterminate for the indeterminate; and the unwholesome for the unwholesome alone—thus there are seven.
In the second, there is one: the indeterminate eye-faculty and so forth for the unwholesome. In the third, the [heart-]base is for the unwholesome.
The next two are stated by way of immediate and natural decisive support (*anantara-ūpanissaya*). Among them, the enumeration is indeed evident.

The following two are stated by way of immediate and natural decisive support. Therein, in the first case, they should be understood as being conditions through the state of mundane wholesome and unwholesome volition;
in the second, only supramundane wholesome [volition].

467–468. Regarding the "pre-arisen" (purejāta) root, there are three [conditions] for the indeterminate (abyākata) in relation to the wholesome (kusala) and so forth as the object (ārammaṇa). There is one [condition] by way of predominance (adhipati): the indeterminate [is a condition] for the unwholesome (akusala).
The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. Herein, however, there are seven combinations (ghaṭanā). Among them, the first is stated by way of both the basis (vatthu) and the object;
the second, by way of the basis alone; the third, by way of the object; and the fourth, by way of the time when the basis becomes the object.

The fifth [condition] is by way of the predominance of the object; the sixth is by way of the time of the predominance of the object for the basis; the seventh is by way of the eye and so forth. 469–472.

In the section based on the postnascent, twenty conditions are not applicable; only three obtain application. Here there is only one combination, which should be understood by way of the body’s wholesome states and so forth. In the section based on repetition (*āsevana*) as well, there is only one combination. 473–477.
In the section based on kamma, "one" in the immediate sequence is stated by way of path-volition (*maggacetanā*). Regarding "three" in the mutuality (*aññamañña*) condition: here...

In the case of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the physical basis (*vatthu*) must also be included. Regarding "two in the case of decisive support" (*upanissaya*), these are precisely those mentioned below by way of the proximate decisive support (*anantara-upanissaya*) and the natural decisive support (*pakata-upanissaya*).
In this manner, the remaining [categories] should also be understood according to the method explained below. Herein, however, there are eleven combinations.
Among them, the first two are distinct due to the division between natural decisive support and proximate decisive support, and by way of asynchronous (*nānā-khaṇika*) kamma.
These have been stated. The four that follow are stated by way of kamma that is simultaneous with its result, whether it be resultant (*vipāka*) or non-resultant (*avipāka*).
Therein, in the first [case], mind-produced matter is obtained together with the immaterial; in the second, the physical basis (*vatthu*) is obtained together with the immaterial;
in the third, the immaterial alone; and in the fourth, mind-produced matter alone. However, in the case of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) is also obtained.

It is obtainable. The five [factors] following that have resultant fruit (*savipāka*); they are exactly as explained in the method below. In the section on the root of result (*vipākamūlaka*), the five combinations (*ghaṭanā*) have their meanings already made clear. 478–483.
In the section on the root of nutriment (*āhāramūlaka*), the seven and so forth are exactly as explained in the method above. However, there are thirty-four combinations here; among them—
