484–495. In the section based on faculties (*indriyamūlaka*) regarding the "pre-arisen" (*purejāta*), the single [condition] refers to the indeterminate being conditioned by the indeterminate through the faculty of eye (*cakkhundriya*) and so forth.
The remainder of the "two-rooted" (*dumūlaka*) section should be understood according to the method explained below. However, the combinations (*ghaṭanā*) here amount to seventy-six.
In that regard, in the first [section], all the faculties are found in the sense of being conditions.
In the second, the material life-faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*) is excluded, for it does not serve as a support. In the third, the immaterial faculties are [conditions] for material phenomena.
In the fourth, the eye and so forth are [conditions] for eye-consciousness and so forth. The nine subsequent combinations are stated by way of co-nascent immaterial faculties.
Then, by way of the nine faculties that constitute the path; then, the nine that constitute the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga);
then, the nine that constitute both absorption and the path; then, the nine by way of the mind-faculty alone; then, the six with predominance (adhipati);
then, the six associated with the path by way of energy (vīriya); and then, the nine without predominance and the six with predominance by way of the root of non-delusion (amoha).
Among all these, those that are incompatible and those that are compatible with the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*) should be understood according to the method explained below.
496–500. In the section based on jhāna as well, the "two-rooted" (*dumūlaka*) combinations should be understood according to the method explained below.

However, there are thirty-six combinations here; among them, the first nine do not touch upon the state of faculties (*indriya*) or the path (*magga*), but deal solely with the common jhāna factors (*jhāna-aṅga*).
These have been stated. Following those, nine [jhānas] are by way of being factors of jhāna that are faculties; then nine by way of being factors of jhāna that are the Path;
then nine by way of being factors of jhāna that are both faculties and the Path. In each of these four sets of nine, the first four in each set are common to both resultant and non-resultant states.
At the end of each set, the five are exclusively resultants, according to the method already explained below.

501–508. The "Roots of the Path" (maggamūlaka) should also be understood according to the same method as explained for the "Roots of the Tree" (dumūlaka). However, there are fifty-seven combinations here.
Among them, the first nine are stated solely by way of the pure path (*suddhika-magga*), without touching upon the state of faculties (*indriya*) or jhāna.

Following those, nine are by way of the path as consisting of faculties; then nine by way of the path as consisting of jhāna; and then nine by way of the path as consisting of both faculties and jhāna.
Then, by way of the path as a dominant factor (adhipati), there are six; then, by way of the path without a dominant factor (nirādhipati) as a cause (hetu), nine;
then, by way of the path with a dominant factor as a cause, six. Among these, in the groups of nine there are five results each, and in the groups of six there are three results each.
The remaining ones are common, and they follow the same method explained below.

509–510. In the section based on association (*sampayutta-mūlaka*), the "two-rooted" (*dumūlaka*) treatment has its meaning already explained. Here, however, there are only two combinations: one is stated by way of commonality, and the other by way of result (*vipāka*). 511–514.

In the section based on dissociation (*vippayutta-mūlaka*), the "two-rooted" treatment likewise has its meaning already explained. There are, however, thirteen combinations here. Among these, in the first [set], "five" refers to:
(1) wholesome [states] with respect to the indeterminate; (2) likewise, unwholesome [states]; and (3) indeterminate [states] with respect to all three [types]. Here...

And these [factors], such as dissociation and so forth, are both co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and post-nascent (*pacchājāta*) or pre-nascent (*purejāta*). In the second [category], there are only the pre-nascent and co-nascent;
in the third, those same [factors] by way of predominance (*adhipati*). Therein, the wholesome [state] is related to the indeterminate in that manner, as is the unwholesome;
but the indeterminate is related to the indeterminate by way of object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), and to the unwholesome as well—thus there are four. In the fourth, there are three.
Wholesome states and so forth [are conditions] for the indeterminate. Herein, the faculties are both material and immaterial. In the fifth [section], the conditions are exclusively immaterial;

in the sixth, they are exclusively material by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*); in the seventh, they are wholesome and indeterminate by way of insight (*vipassanā*), while for the unwholesome, it is the physical basis alone by way of gratification (*assāda*).
In the eighth, it is that same [basis] for the unwholesome; in the ninth, the eye and so forth are [conditions] for the indeterminate.

In the tenth [condition], the wholesome and so forth are related to mind-originated [material phenomena]; in the eleventh, the physical basis (vatthu) is related to the aggregates during rebirth-linking;

in the twelfth, the aggregates during rebirth-linking are related to the kamma-produced material phenomena (kaṭattārūpa); in the thirteenth, the aggregates during rebirth-linking are related to the physical basis. 515–518.

In the section based on the presence-condition (atthipaccaya), regarding the decisive support (upanissaya), there is one instance: the indeterminate is related to the unwholesome by way of object-decisive-support (ārammaṇūpanissaya).
The rest at *Dumūlaka* is self-evident. Here, however, there are twenty-nine combinations.

Among them, in the first, conditions by way of conascence, prenascence, and postnascence are obtained for the immaterial bases, objects, great primaries, faculties, and nutriment. In the second, postnascent physical nutriment is not obtained.
The third and fourth [combinations] above follow the first and second combinations together with the predominance condition.

[The groups] have been made. Furthermore, in the first [group], the fifth was made together with the four nutriments (*āhāra*), the sixth together with the material faculties (*rūpindriya*), and the seventh together with both material and immaterial faculties.
Alternatively, in the second [group], the seventh was made together with the faculties.
In the first and second [groups], the eighth and ninth were made together with the dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*). Among those, the ninth—
With the inclusion of the dominant condition (*adhipati*), it becomes the tenth. Then, in the eleventh, the basis (*vatthu*) is lost due to the condition.
In the twelfth, only immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) are the conditions; in the thirteenth, both the basis and the object (*ārammaṇa*);

in the fourteenth, the basis alone; in the fifteenth, the object alone; in the sixteenth, both the basis and the object; but in the seventeenth, that very same [pair] functions by way of the object-dominant condition (*ārammaṇādhipatibhāvena*).
In the eighteenth [condition], that same [relationship] occurs by way of object-predominance (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*); in the nineteenth, the eye and so forth are themselves the conditions.
These nineteen miscellaneous combinations are stated excluding co-nascence (*sahajāta*). Those following thereafter, ten in number, are stated by way of co-nascence.

519. In the cases of *natthi* and *vigata*, just as with those rooted in *anantara* and *samanantara*, there are only three combinations by way of *upanissaya*, *āsevana*, and *kamma*; *avigata*-rooted [conditioning] is exactly like *atthi*-rooted [conditioning].
Furthermore, all these combinations mentioned in this section of questions are of two kinds only:
miscellaneous and conascent. Among these, for all [conditions], beginning with those rooted in the object (*ārammaṇa*), the conascent [conditioning] comes first.

Those not included [in the above categories] are called miscellaneous (*pakiṇṇaka*). Among them, there are five based on the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-mūlaka*), six based on the predominance-condition (*adhipati-mūlaka*),

three each based on the proximity-condition (*anantara-mūlaka*) and the contiguity-condition (*samanantara-mūlaka*), ten based on the support-condition (*nissaya-mūlaka*), seven based on the decisive-support-condition (*upanissaya-mūlaka*),

seven based on the prenascence-condition (*purejāta-mūlaka*), one based on the postnascence-condition (*pacchājāta-mūlaka*), likewise one based on the repetition-condition (*āsevana-mūlaka*), and [one] based on the kamma-condition (*kamma-mūlaka*).

Two are rooted in nutriment, one is rooted in faculty, four are rooted in dissociation, nineteen are rooted in presence, three are also rooted in absence, and likewise in disappearance. Nineteen are rooted in non-disappearance;
thus, all together they amount to one hundred and three. However, these are called "miscellaneous" because they function as co-nascent and supporting conditions.
However, those [conditions] that are obtained as co-nascent are called "co-nascent combinations" (*sahajātaghaṭanā*).
These are not found among the root-conditions for objects, nor among the root-conditions for the immediate, contiguous, prenascence, postnascence, repetition, absence, or disappearance conditions;

for these conditions are not conditions for things that are co-nascent. And just as they are not conditions for co-nascent things, so it is with the root, co-nascence, mutuality, resultant, jhāna, path, and association conditions.
Regarding "those not co-nascent" (*asahajātānaṃ*): in the root of cause (*hetumūlaka*), all twenty-four combinations are indeed co-nascent combinations (*sahajātaghaṭanā*).

Likewise, there are twenty-four in the root of predominance (*adhipatimūlaka*), ten in the root of co-nascence (*sahajātamūlaka*), six in the root of mutuality (*aññamaññamūlaka*), ten in the root of dependence (*nissayamūlaka*), nine in the root of kamma (*kammamūlaka*), five in the root of result (*vipākamūlaka*), thirty-three in the root of nutriment (*āhāramūlaka*), and [thirty-three] in the root of faculty (*indriyamūlaka*).
In the case of the seventy-two rooted in jhāna there are thirty-six; in those rooted in the path, fifty-seven; in those rooted in association, two;
in those rooted in dissociation, four; in those rooted in presence, ten; and in those rooted in non-disappearance, ten.
Thus, all together they amount to three hundred and twelve. So, these are the previous three hundred and twelve.
"Three hundred" refers to all four hundred and fifteen combinations that have appeared in the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*).

Among these, those conditioning states (*paccayadhamma*) which do not become manifest by way of their names should also be shown within the combinations stated at the outset of the methods beginning with the "root of cause" (*hetumūlaka*), according to the general categories of resultant and non-resultant. For there are only twelve causes.
The six objects, the four predominants, the four nutriments, the twenty faculties, the seven factors of absorption, and the twelve path-factors—
these are called the conditioned phenomena (*paccaya-dhammā*). Among these, those states which are exclusively wholesome,
exclusively unwholesome, exclusively wholesome-resultants, exclusively unwholesome-resultants, and exclusively resultants...

Having carefully observed those [factors] which are non-resultant, those which are resultant therein should be joined to the resultant-combinations, and those which are non-resultant to the non-resultant-combinations,
as appropriate. This is the forward calculation for the combination of the Chapter on Questions (*pañhāvāra*).
Commentary on the Negative (Paccanīya) Extraction 527.

Now follows the negative [section]. Therein, just as in the "Dependent" (Paṭicca) section and others, questions that are obtainable according to the method beginning with, "Dependent upon an unwholesome state, an unwholesome state arises by way of not-root condition," are [to be applied] to those [states] that are obtainable.

[The conditions] have been explained in detail according to their specific forms. Without expanding further in this way, in order to show the negative (paccanīya) relationship concisely by means of a single characteristic, the compilers of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī extracted the conditions for the wholesome and so forth in the positive (anuloma) order, beginning with the formula:
"A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya)," and so on.
Furthermore, those conditions [are presented] by way of their collective groups.
It is not by way of each single condition alone; therefore, those which are shown there as groups should be understood by analyzing them.
For all these twenty-four conditions are included within eight conditions. Within which eight? Namely:
object (ārammaṇa), conascence (sahajāta), decisive support (upanissaya), prenascence (purejāta), postnascence (pacchājāta), kamma, nutriment (āhāra), and faculty (indriya).

How so? Excluding these eight conditions, among the remaining sixteen, six conditions—the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*), the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*), the jhāna condition (*jhāna-paccaya*), the path condition (*magga-paccaya*), and the association condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*)—invariably exist as co-nascent; because they function as conditions only for those things that are co-nascent, they are included within the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).

Furthermore, the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*), the contiguity condition (*samanantara-paccaya*), the repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*), the absence condition (*natthi-paccaya*), and the disappearance condition (*vigata-paccaya*)...

The five [mental aggregates], having arisen and ceased, enter into the category of decisive support (*upanissaya*) by way of the characteristic of immediate decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*), because they serve as conditions for those very states that arise immediately after them.
The support condition (*nissayapaccaya*) is twofold, divided into conascent (*sahajāta*) and pre-arisen (*purejāta*).
Among these, the conascent support enters into the category of the conascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*), because it serves as a support condition only for those states that are conascent with it.
The pre-arisen support (purejāta-nissaya) is included within the pre-arisen condition (purejāta-paccaya).
The dominant condition (adhipati-paccaya) is also twofold, by way of co-nascent dominance (sahajātādhipati) and object dominance (ārammaṇādhipati).

Therein, co-nascent dominance is included within the co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya), because it functions as a dominant condition only for those things that are co-nascent with it. Object dominance...

Since it is indeed an object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), it is included within the condition of strong-dependence (*upanissayapaccaya*) by virtue of the characteristic of object-strong-dependence.

The dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*) is threefold, being divided into conascence, prenascence, and postnascence. Among these, the conascent dissociation [condition] is included within the conascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) because it functions as a dissociation condition only for those things that are conascent. The prenascence dissociation...
Because it arises first and serves as a condition for those things that arise later, it is included within the *purejāta* (pre-arising) condition.

Because it arises later and serves as a condition by way of providing support for those things that have already arisen, the *pacchājātavippayutta* (dissociation from what is later-arisen) falls under the *pacchājāta* (later-arising) condition.
The *atthi* (presence) and *avigata* (non-disappearance) conditions are included within the *sahajāta* (conascent), *purejāta*, *pacchājāta*, *āhāra* (nutriment), and *indriya* (faculty) conditions.
And among the "present" (atthi) and "non-disappearance" (avigata) conditions, they are established through six divisions according to each one.

Therein, co-nascent presence and non-disappearance [conditions] exist because they function as the presence and non-disappearance conditions for those very things that are co-nascent; thus, they are included within the co-nascent condition.
Pre-nascent [presence and non-disappearance] are included within the pre-nascent condition because, having arisen earlier, they function as a condition for those things arising later.

Those that arise later, having arisen subsequently, are included in the condition of post-nascence (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) because they act as a supporting condition for those that have already arisen.
Those that function as nutriment are included in the condition of edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra-paccaya*).
Those that function as faculties are included in the condition of the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya-paccaya*). Thus, these sixteen conditions are [subsumed] within these eight.
It should be understood that they are included within the conditions (*paccaya*).
Furthermore, there is indeed a mutual inclusion among these eight conditions as well.

For the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), which was explained first, is twofold—divided into the dominant (*adhipati*) and the non-dominant (*anadhipati*). Among those, that which has become dominant [is included] by way of the characteristic of the decisive support-object (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*).
It is included within the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*). When it is not a dominant factor (*anadhipati*), it is simply a pure object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).

The kamma condition is also twofold: by way of conascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of asynchronous (*nānākkhaṇika*). Among these, conascent kamma is included only within the conascence condition, because it functions as a kamma condition only for those states that are conascent with itself. Asynchronous kamma, however, [is divided] by way of being powerful or weak...

It is twofold. Therein, powerful kamma becomes a condition for phenomena subject to ripening solely as an *upanissaya* (decisive support) condition; thus, it is included within the *upanissaya* category.
However, even powerful kamma is a condition for material phenomena, and weak kamma for immaterial phenomena, only by way of the *nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya* (kamma condition of different times).

The nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*) is also twofold, according to whether it pertains to the material or the immaterial. Therein, immaterial nutriment [is a condition] only for those things co-nascent with itself.

"It is a condition" means it is included within the category of co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*). Material nutriment (*rūpāhāra*) is not a condition for [nutriments] that are co-nascent, prenascent, or postnascent.
However, having passed its own moment of arising and reached the moment of presence (*ṭhiti*), it accomplishes the state of being a nutriment condition;
thus, it is indeed a nutriment condition. The faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*) is also twofold, consisting of the material and the immaterial. Among these, the immaterial faculty condition...
Because it establishes the faculty-conditionality only for those phenomena co-nascent with itself, it is included within the category of "co-nascent" (sahajāta) alone.
Furthermore, the material faculty-condition (rūpindriya-paccaya) is twofold, distinguished as internal and external.

Among these, the internal faculty-condition, having arisen previously, serves as the faculty-condition for eye-consciousness and the other consciousnesses that arise subsequently, together with their associated mental states.

The phrase "it exists" includes it only within the *purejāta* (pre-arisen) condition. As for the external condition called the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*), this refers to the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*).
Although it acts as a condition for co-nascent states, it does so solely by way of maintenance and not by way of generation; thus, it is indeed an "indriya-paccaya.
In this way, it should be understood that these eight conditions also include one another. This, first of all, is...
The method of inclusion for the remaining sixteen conditions among the eight conditions is by way of their mutual relationship.
Now, regarding each one of these eight conditions, those among the twenty-four conditions that fall under its inclusion should be understood.
In this regard, first of all, within the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), which is the very first of the eight, it is simply the object condition itself.
It is included [in this category], but not the remaining twenty-three. In the second [section], regarding the co-nascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*), there are:

the root condition (*hetupaccaya*), the co-nascent predominance condition (*sahajātādhipatipaccaya*), the co-nascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*), the mutuality condition (*aññamaññapaccaya*), the co-nascent dependence condition (*sahajātanissayapaccaya*), the co-nascent kamma condition (*sahajātakammapaccaya*), the resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*), the co-nascent nutriment condition (*sahajātaāhārapaccaya*), the co-nascent faculty condition (*sahajātaindriyapaccaya*), the jhāna condition (*jhānapaccaya*), the path condition (*maggapaccaya*), and the association condition (*sampayuttapaccaya*).
The co-nascence-dissociation condition, the co-nascence-presence condition, and the co-nascence-absence condition—these fifteen conditions are included [in this category].
In the third, the decisive-support condition, there is the object condition that has become the dominant condition, and the dominant condition that has become the object;
as well as the proximity, contiguity, decisive-support, and repetition conditions, which are asynchronous.
The nine conditions—namely, the strong kamma condition (balavakamma-paccaya), the absence condition (natthi-paccaya), and the disappearance condition (vigata-paccaya)—are included [in this category].

In the fourth, the pre-arising condition (purejāta-paccaya), there are six conditions: the pre-arising support condition (purejāta-nissaya-paccaya), the pre-arising condition (purejāta-paccaya), the pre-arising faculty condition (purejāta-indriya-paccaya), the pre-arising dissociation condition (purejāta-vippayutta-paccaya), the pre-arising presence condition (purejāta-atthi-paccaya), and the pre-arising non-disappearance condition (purejāta-avigata-paccaya).

They are included. In the fifth [section], on the postnascent condition, these four conditions are included: the postnascent condition, the postnascent dissociation condition, the postnascent presence condition, and the postnascent disappearance condition.
In the sixth, on the kamma condition, only the asynchronous kamma condition is included. In the seventh, on the nutriment condition, only by way of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*)...

These three conditions—nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*), presence-of-nutriment condition (*āhāra-atthi-paccaya*), and non-disappearance-of-nutriment condition (*āhāra-avigata-paccaya*)—are included.

In the eighth, the faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*), these three conditions—physical life-faculty condition (*rūpa-jīvitindriya-paccaya*), presence-of-faculty condition (*indriya-atthi-paccaya*), and non-disappearance-of-faculty condition (*indriya-avigata-paccaya*)—are likewise included.
Thus, within each one of these eight conditions, these...

Having understood that these conditions are included [within the categories], it should be known that those which are included in a particular category are already accounted for by the enumeration of that category.
Thus, by way of these eight conditions which include all conditions, regarding the forty-nine questions—

In this "Counter-Sequence" (*paccanīya*), these fifteen questions—beginning with “A wholesome state is a condition, by way of object-condition, for a wholesome state”—have been extracted and answered.

Among them, there are four questions beginning with the wholesome: (1) wholesome for wholesome, (2) wholesome for unwholesome, (3) wholesome for indeterminate, and (4) wholesome for both wholesome and indeterminate; likewise, there are [four] beginning with the unwholesome.
There are three [questions] beginning with the indeterminate: "The indeterminate [arises] from the indeterminate," "the indeterminate from the wholesome," and "the indeterminate from the unwholesome.

Then there are four [questions] ending with the "two-rooted" (dumūlaka): "The wholesome and the indeterminate [arise] from the wholesome," likewise "from the indeterminate," "the unwholesome and the indeterminate from the unwholesome," and likewise "from the indeterminate. Among these, in the first question:
All those things that ought to be cultivated have been included and stated as three conditions in the second [chapter], two in the third, one in the fourth,
three in the fifth, two in the sixth, five in the seventh, one in the eighth, seven in the ninth, three in the tenth, three in the eleventh,
two in the twelfth, four in the thirteenth, two in the fourteenth, and likewise in the fifteenth.
There are only four. These are not stated as "conascence condition" (*sahajāta-paccaya*), but rather as "conascent and postnascent" (*sahajātaṃ pacchājātaṃ*).
The reason for this we shall explain later.
In brief, however, there are only six limits of conditions here: one, two, three, four, five, and seven.
This is the section on the questions in the Negative Mode (*paccanīya*) according to the highest limit:
both the determination of the questions and the determination of the conditions shown by grouping those respective conditions together.

For among the twenty-four negative conditions, such as "not-root-condition" (*na-hetu-paccaya*) and so forth, in each single negative condition, no further questions or conditions are found beyond this point; they are found only below. Therefore:

In those questions where only a single condition is stated— such as, “A wholesome state is a relatedness-condition, by way of co-nascence, for a wholesome and indeterminate state”— when that specific condition is excluded,

those questions fall away. However, in the question where it is stated, “A wholesome state is a relatedness-condition, by way of object-condition or decisive-support-condition, for an unwholesome state...”
"...condition"—thus two conditions have been mentioned.

Therein, even though one condition has been excluded by the phrase "not by way of object-condition," that inquiry still applies by virtue of the other condition. However, when both of those two conditions are excluded, that section is cut off.
In the same way, regarding those inquiries where three, four, five, or seven [conditions are involved]...
Or they may not be obtained; setting aside those requisites that are prohibited, those questions are indeed obtainable by way of the remaining ones.
However, when all requisites are prohibited, all those sections are cut off—this alone is the defining characteristic here.
By this characteristic, starting from the beginning, the requisites stated in brief for those various questions—
The specific divisions and the omissions of these respective questions regarding each respective opposite condition should be understood.
Herein, this is the detailed explanation: first, in the initial question, nineteen conditions are shown by way of three [general] conditions.
How so? For a wholesome state is not a condition for a wholesome state except by way of the prenascence, postnascence, resultant, and dissociation conditions.
Of the remaining twenty, there is one object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*);

however, it is stated that fifteen conditions, by way of a comprehensive inclusion, are included within the conascent (*sahajāta*) conditions. Among those, when the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) is excluded, there are fourteen.
Furthermore, since the wholesome [state] is neither a result-condition (*vipāka-paccaya*) nor a dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*) for the wholesome, those two being removed—
With reference to the remaining twelve [types of consciousness], it is stated that they are related by way of the conascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).
Regarding the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) as well, it is stated that nine conditions are included by way of a comprehensive inclusion.

Among those, the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) acting as a predominance, and the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) acting as an object, are both subsumed under the decisive-support itself by way of the object-decisive-support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*). However, the wholesome...

Since a wholesome state does not serve as a asynchronous kamma-condition for another wholesome state, that [condition] is excluded; referring to the remaining six, it is stated that they are conditions by way of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
Thus, in the first question, nineteen conditions should be understood as being shown through three types of conditions.
Among those, in this negation of the root-condition (*hetu-paccanīya*), it is said: "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of the non-root-condition."
Having given a gift, undertaken virtue, or performed the Uposatha rite, one reviews that;

or one reviews what was well-performed in the past—having extracted [the examples] in this manner according to the method stated under the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and so forth, the text should be shown.
However, when the object-condition is excluded, having removed its detailed exposition and inserted the detailed exposition of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), [the text should be shown].
That very same text should be shown; this same method applies to the negations of the remaining conditions as well.
However, regarding those sections that are omitted when that condition is negated, we shall explain them later.
In the second question, however, three conditions are shown by means of two conditions. How so? For the wholesome [condition] [is related] to the unwholesome...
It does not function as a condition by way of the immediate (anantara) and other such relations.

Therefore, setting those aside, with reference to the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and the natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya)—which are included under the decisive support condition (upanissayapaccaya) by way of the object-decisive-support (ārammaṇūpanissaya)—it is said: "it is a condition by way of the decisive support condition.
Consequently, the pure object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) is a predominance condition by way of object-predominance, and it is a decisive support condition.
In the second question, it should be understood that these three conditions are shown by way of two conditions.
In the third question, however, eighteen conditions are shown by way of five conditions. How so?

For a wholesome [state] is not a condition for an indeterminate [state] except by way of the conditions of mutuality, prenascence, repetition, result, and association; it is [a condition] by way of the remaining nineteen.

Among those, the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) is one. However, because a wholesome state does not serve as a condition for an indeterminate state by way of mutuality, resultant, or association, and because the root condition (*hetupaccaya*) has been excluded while the kamma condition (*kammapaccaya*) has been taken separately, these five [conditions] are removed;
thus, ten conditions are shown by way of co-nascence (*sahajata*). Having set aside the six mentioned previously by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*),...
The remaining five [paccayas] are by way of repetition (āsevana). Post-nascence (pacchājāta) alone is likewise;

thus, although the kamma-paccaya is twofold—by way of co-nascence (sahajāta) and asynchronous (nānākhaṇika)—it should be understood that in this third question, these eighteen paccayas are shown through five paccayas.
However, in the fourth question, ten are shown by means of a single paccaya. How so? For a wholesome [state] is related to the wholesome and the indeterminate by way of co-nascence (sahajāte).
Among the fifteen stated [conditions], there is no condition by way of mutual, resultant, associated, or dissociated conditions; the root-condition (hetupaccaya) is excluded.
Thus, having set aside these five, it should be understood that the remaining ten conditions are shown here by means of a single condition.

And just as it is in these four questions beginning with the wholesome (kusala), so too in the four questions beginning with the unwholesome (akusala), it should be understood that those very same conditions are shown by those respective conditions.
529. Next, regarding the three questions beginning with the indeterminate (*abyākata*), twenty-three conditions are shown by means of seven conditions in the first question.
How so? For the indeterminate is a condition for the indeterminate by way of all twenty-four conditions.
However, when the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) is excluded, there are twenty-three. Among those, the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) is only one. Why is this? [Because...]
In this context, however, the nutriment and faculty conditions are taken separately for the purpose of including those that are not conascent.
Therefore, having set aside these three, twelve conditions are shown by way of conascence.

These [twelve] consist of the six mentioned above by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), the single one by way of prenascence, and likewise the postnascence, nutriment, and faculty conditions; thus, by means of these seven conditions, these...
It should be understood that twenty-three conditions have been shown. In the second [section], twelve are shown by way of three conditions. How so? The object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) is one;

however, by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*), there are six shown: the object-decisive-support, the object-dominance, the immediate, the contiguity, the absence, the disappearance, and the decisive-support conditions.
By way of the prenascence condition (*purejāta*), there are five: prenascence, support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus, in this case, by way of these three...
It should be understood that these twelve conditions have been demonstrated by means of [other] conditions. The same method applies to the third [section] as well.

530. Regarding the four questions based on pairs that follow thereafter, in the first question, instead of saying "by way of co-nascence condition and prenascence condition," it is stated as "co-nascent and prenascence.
By means of these two, through the modes of dependence (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata)—

Three conditions have been shown. For although wholesome aggregates, together with the physical basis (*vatthu*), establish the state of being a condition for the wholesome when occurring simultaneously, they do not constitute a "conascence condition" (*sahajāta-paccaya*) because of their admixture with the physical basis.

Therefore, it is said that among those conascent factors, by way of the dependence (*nissaya*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*) conditions, they are "conascent. The same applies to the physical basis as well.
This is the method. For although that [nutriment] is indeed pre-arisen, it does not function as a pre-arisen condition because it is mixed with the aggregates;
it is merely called "pre-arisen" by way of its being a support and so forth for those things that are pre-arisen.
In the second question, regarding what are stated as the four—conascent, post-arisen, nutriment, and faculty—by way of the conascent, support, presence, and non-disappearance conditions...
Four conditions are shown. For in this section, the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) is obtained; the post-nascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) and others are not obtained.
However, this is stated by way of the nutriment and faculty conditions—which are classified as post-nascent—and by way of presence and non-disappearance.
For wholesome aggregates and indeterminate great elements are [conditions] for derived matter by way of the co-nascence condition and the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*).

By way of the presence and non-disappearance conditions, there are four types of conditions. However, postnascent wholesome [states] are conditions by way of presence and non-disappearance for those very same primary elements and their derived matter.
Edible food is also a condition by way of presence and non-disappearance for the prenascent body together with the postnascent wholesome states. The material life-faculty is also...
With regard to postnascent wholesome states, they are related to kamma-produced matter solely by way of the presence and non-disappearance conditions.
Thus, with reference to these four modes of conditionality, it was said: "Conascent, postnascent, nutriment, and faculty.
However, in this context, the postnascent nutriment and faculty conditions are simply not applicable. This also applies to the two subsequent questions concerning mixed unwholesome states.
"By this same method": in this way, the classification of the conditions stated here concisely in response to those various questions should be understood.
However, we shall explain later, in each respective condition, whether those various questions are answered or not answered.
This concludes the commentary on the meaning of the "Exposition of the Reverse Order."
Commentary on the Negative Enumeration (Paccanīyagaṇanavaṇṇanā) 532.
Now, these fifteen sections beginning with “A wholesome state [is related] to a wholesome state” have been shown by way of the positive order (anuloma).
Since these same [sections] also exist in the negative order (paccanīya), and there are none beyond them—though they do occur below [the positive order]—therefore...
In order to show, by way of enumeration starting from the beginning, which specific sections are obtainable for each respective condition in its opposite form,
the passage beginning with "Fifteen in the case of not-root" (*nahetuyā*) is commenced.
Therein, fifteen [sections] are obtained for "not-root" (*nahetuyā*) by way of all the conditions as they have been shown.

The root condition (hetupaccaya) enters into the "not-object" (nārammaṇa) category. In each respective instance, the pure object condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) is excluded, while those instances receive their classification through the remaining conditions. And just as it is for the "not-object," so it is for the others as well.

The root condition enters into the "conascent" (sahajāta) category. And in each respective instance, it is excluded from the "strong-dependence" (naupanissaya) and "contiguity" (naanantara) categories.
Thus, the conditions established in the reverse order are excluded; the various sections receive their respective answers by way of the remaining conditions.
However, regarding "not-by-conascence" (*nasahajāte*): "A wholesome state [is related] to a wholesome and an indeterminate state;
an unwholesome state to an unwholesome and an indeterminate state; both wholesome and indeterminate states to a wholesome state; and an unwholesome..."
The two categories "the indeterminate and the states are unwholesome" and so forth—these four sections are omitted.
For among these four, in the first two, there is only one single summary of conditions stated by way of eleven types of conditions, namely, "conditioned by way of co-nascence condition.
When that [co-nascence] is excluded, they do not receive an answer in any other manner. In the latter two...
With reference to the conditions of dependence (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata), it is stated: "conascent and pre-arisen.

When those [conditions] are excluded from the conascent, the remaining ones—namely, the root-cause (hetu) and so forth, as well as the pre-arisen conditions of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance—do not receive a response;
therefore, these four sections are omitted. With reference to the remaining ones, it is stated: "eleven."

In this regard, it might be asked: "Just as those sections were obtained when *hetu* was excluded by way of the remaining factors such as *adhipati*, why are they not likewise obtained when *sahajāta* is excluded by way of the remaining factors such as *hetu*? [The answer is: Because they are non-exclusive (*nippadesa*).
For *hetu* and the others are exclusive (*sappadesa*) with respect to co-nascent states only in part; therefore, when they are excluded, [the sections] for the others...
By way of that, those two alternatives are obtained. However, the co-nascent [condition] includes all causes and so forth without exception;
therefore, when that is excluded, they are all excluded. For there are no such things as causes and conditions that are not co-nascent.
Thus, because the co-nascent is without exception, when it is excluded, both of those two alternatives are also excluded.

They are not obtained. However, in the sections where the answers are given as "conascent" (*sahajāta*) and "prenascent" (*purejāta*), although there is indeed no conascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) at all, it is because here the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) themselves serve as conditions by way of support (*nissaya*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*);
and since when conascence is excluded, the support, presence, and non-disappearance conditions that are invariably conascent are thereby excluded as well. Therefore...
Because those [states] have been excluded, those [same] four modes are not obtained; thus, in every respect, these four modes are omitted here.
It is stated that there are eleven [modes] by way of the remaining states alone.
The same four modes are also omitted for the mutually-arisen, supported, and associated [states]. Why? Because they share the same concomitant course (sahajātagatika).

For just as the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), being itself an immaterial dhamma, takes up the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpa-kkhandha*) in their entirety, so too do the mutuality (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), and association (*sampayutta*) conditions. Therefore, because they share the same status as co-nascent conditions, it should be understood that when these [conditions] are excluded, those [same] permutations (*vāra*) are not obtained.
Hence it was said: "Not in mutuality, eleven; not in support, eleven; not in association, eleven."

In this regard, it might be argued: although these [mental factors] are co-nascent with respect to the four aggregates—classified as wholesome and so forth—because they include them without distinction, a wholesome state, however, does not act as a condition for a wholesome or indeterminate state in any way other than as a co-nascent condition;
therefore, when that [condition] is excluded, let that category be dropped. But [what of] a wholesome state in relation to wholesome and indeterminate states?

Why, when mutual conditionality (*aññamañña-paccaya*) is excluded, is that category [of conditions] also lost? Because the occurrence [of phenomena] exists by way of the nature of mutually conditioned states.

For just as wholesome and indeterminate states are not merely co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*) for a wholesome state, yet their occurrence does exist by way of co-nascent states through such conditions as the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), so too when mutual conditionality is excluded...

Thus that category is excluded; likewise here too, because of the existence of occurrence by way of co-nascence and so forth through the medium of states that are mutual conditions, when that [category] is rejected, that category is excluded. For this is the meaning of the phrase "conditioned by way of not-mutual-condition":

those states which have been included under the heading of mutual condition—there is no conditionality by means of them. And a wholesome state [is a condition] for wholesome and indeterminate states...

When acting as a condition by way of being co-nascent and so forth, it acts as a condition only through those phenomena that are mutual-conditions; therefore, when that [mutual-condition] is excluded, that category is eliminated.
Just as that category is eliminated, so too are the remaining three—thus all four of those categories are eliminated.
Regarding the phrase "eleven in the case of non-dependence," here too, because in those categories the phenomena are exclusively co-nascent conditions...
They are dependent; therefore, when dependence is excluded, they fall away. Regarding "thirteen in the case of not-prenascence":
having removed the two from the two-rooted section mentioned in the response concerning "conascence and prenascence," there are thirteen.

For just as those [factors] do not receive a response in terms of the presence, existence, and non-disappearance conditions of only the prenascence factors when conascence is excluded, so too it is with prenascence.
When [the condition] is excluded, they do not receive an answer by way of only those conascent [states] that are related as presence and non-disappearance;
therefore, having removed them, it should be understood that there are thirteen.
Regarding the statement "fifteen in the postnascent," here [it refers to] either "being a condition by way of the postnascent condition" or "the conascent is the postnascent..."
In those places where it is stated as "nutriment" or "faculty," those questions are also found by way of the remainder, excluding only the "postnascent" (pacchājāta) condition;

therefore, they are stated as fifteen only. Regarding the phrases "not-kamma" and so forth, since even kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path are merely portions of the four aggregates classified as wholesome and so on, [the questions] are formulated by way of the remaining phenomena, excluding those specific factors.
The single question-and-answer regarding "conascent states being conditions" is not omitted. Regarding "eleven in the case of the non-associated":

since, in those four sections, associated states are conditions by way of the conascent and other conditions, it should be understood that those very sections are excluded by the negation of the associated condition. Regarding the non-dissociated...
There are nine [ways]: four ending with the single-rooted *dumūlaka*, and two ending with the single-rooted *dukā*.

These six modes are invariably associated with states that function as dissociation-conditions (*vippayuttapaccaya*). Since they serve as conditions by way of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and so forth, when dissociation is excluded, all of them are likewise eliminated;
thus, only nine are obtained. Therefore it was said: "Not in dissociation... (*na-vippayutte*).

"Are they new? No; even when those [conditions] have not ceased, they should be understood as being the same. For those sections are exclusively associated with states that possess the conditions of presence (atthi) and non-disappearance (avigata);

therefore, they are excluded when those [conditions] are negated. As for those [sections] that do apply, the answers should be formulated by way of the object (ārammaṇa) or by way of the immediate (anantara) and so forth.
[This applies] to the fivefold division consisting of conascence (sahajāta), prenascence (purejāta), postnascence (pacchājāta), nutriment (āhāra), and faculty (indriya).
They should not be formulated by way of dissociated states that are either present or non-disappeared.

Having thus demonstrated the enumeration in the negative (paccanīya) section where it was obtained, the following—"Fifteen [conditions] are not-root conditions for not-object conditions," and so forth—is commenced in order to demonstrate the enumeration of conditions by way of the double-rooted (dumūlaka) and subsequent groups. Among those, regarding the pairs based on the not-root root-condition:
When an over-counting is combined with an under-counting, it becomes an under-counting.

In the section on the three bases (*timūlaka*) regarding the "not-strong-dependence" (*naupanissaya*) condition, two instances—namely, "the wholesome for the unwholesome" and "the unwholesome for the wholesome"—are omitted. Why?
Because the "not-strong-dependence" condition is not conjoined with the "object" (*ārammaṇa*) condition. For, by way of the object condition, [the strong-dependence] functions...

And this is their occurrence. Both of those [conditions] have been rejected. Furthermore, object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) is indeed included by the inclusion of object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya).
In the "six-root" table as well, there are thirteen under non-strong-dependence; thus they remain thirteen. In the "seven-root" table, however, there are seven under non-strong-dependence;
because it is combined with non-conascence (nasahajāta), when the four [conditions] are excluded from there, [the relationship is] "the wholesome [is related] to the wholesome."

“Wholesome [dhamma] for unwholesome, unwholesome for unwholesome, and unwholesome for wholesome”—these four function by way of immediate-proximity-decisive-support (anantarūpanissaya) and natural-decisive-support (pakatūpanissaya), and thus eight are excluded; therefore, it is said that there are seven by way of the remainder.
“In the case of ‘not-prenascence,’ eleven”: because they are combined with ‘not-co-nascence’ (nasahajāta), there are eleven. “In the case of ‘not-postnascence,’ nine.”

Among those eleven, having removed twice those two [factors] ending in "indeterminate" from the dumūlaka (two-rooted) sections—where they have received the designations of co-nascence, post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty—there remain nine by way of the remaining factors.
For although they are excluded from co-nascence, they are not abandoned because of their status as post-nascent;
however, when both co-nascence and post-nascence are excluded, they are abandoned. Thus, there are nine by way of the rest.
It has been stated. In the section on the eight roots, regarding the "not-root" condition (*na-nissaya*), there are eleven; all of this is exactly as stated below.

In the section on the nine roots, regarding the "not-strong-dependence" condition (*na-upanissaya*), there are five: the three beginning with the wholesome (*kusala*) and ending with the indeterminate (*abyākata*) in the two-rooted [section], and the two beginning with the indeterminate in the two-rooted [section].
Among these, the answer should be understood by way of asynchronous karma, edible food, material phenomena, the life-faculty, and postnascent states.
In the cases of "not-prenascence" such as "five," etc., they are the same. In "not-postnascence," there are three;

these are the remaining ones from the "two-rooted" [formulas] obtainable by way of postnascence, excluding the two with the indeterminate as their fruit. In "not-dissociation" as well, those same three. In "not-presence," there are two:
wholesome and unwholesome [states] by way of asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika) kamma, [acting as conditions] for kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa). [The same applies to] resultant [matter].
In this context, [the combination] is not obtained because it is not conjoined with the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*). In the elevenfold group, the enumeration is exactly as stated below.
In the twelvefold group, regarding "one" in the case of kamma, it is "abyākata by abyākata. And therein, the answer should be understood by way of nutriment and faculties (*āhāra* and *indriya*).
In all cases from the thirteenfold group onwards, wherever "one" occurs, this very same [method] is to be adopted.
Regarding nutriment (*āhāra*), however, the answer should be understood by way of the faculties (*indriya*); regarding the faculties, it should be understood by way of nutriment.

In the cases of the fourteen root-conditions (*mūla*) and so forth, because they are combined with kamma-condition (*kamma-paccaya*), the "not-present" (*no-atthi*) and "not-disappeared" (*no-vigata*) conditions are not obtained;

therefore, they are not mentioned. The phrases "not-nutriment-condition" (*nāhāra-paccaya*) and "not-jhāna-condition" (*najhāna-paccaya*) are stated excluding the faculty-condition. Therefore, in those instances, one [condition] should be understood by way of the faculties.

The condition "not-resultant" (navipāka-paccaya) excluding the condition "not-faculty" (naindriya-paccaya) is stated with the nutriment-condition (āhāra) removed; therefore, in that case, one [condition] should be understood by way of nutriment.
However, as for these two [conditions] standing in opposition (paccanīya), there is no counting [of them], and thus they are not shown together.
This concludes the root-section on "not-root" (nahetu-mūlaka).

534. Even in the cases beginning with "not rooted in an object" (*nārammaṇamūlaka*), there are only four limits for the enumeration of roots—namely, fifteen, thirteen, eleven, and nine—in all the dyads.
However, in the triads and so forth, when many conditions are combined, other enumerated answers—limited to seven, five, three, two, or one—are indeed obtained.
Among these, whatever is obtained through the combination of whichever conditions, that [is the answer].
Having carefully observed that according to the method explained below, it should be extracted.

In all these [charts], beginning with those rooted in non-object (nārammaṇa-mūlaka), the wheels are constructed by first connecting them with the "root-cause" (hetu) term—having transcended terms such as "non-object" (nārammaṇa)—and then forming the circles.
However, because they are exactly like those described under the "not-root" (na-hetu-mūlaka) section, they will not be shown in detail.

These have been shown in brief. In this regard, just as in the section on "not-root" (nahetu), although the "not-object" (nārammaṇa) and "not-strong-dependence" (naupanissaya) conditions each receive fifteen instances individually, they receive thirteen when combined; likewise, in all cases, they receive exactly thirteen.
And just as there are seven instances for the "not-strong-dependence" condition when combined with "not-object" and "not-conascence" (nasahajāta), so too...
There are seven [conditions] together with the non-predominance (naupanissaya) and object (nārammaṇa) conditions, as well as the non-conascence (nasahajāta) condition. 538.

Under the non-dependence (nanissaya) condition and the non-predominance condition, there are three [results] excluding the post-nascence (napacchājāta): the wholesome (kusala) and so forth, ending with the indeterminate (abyākata). Among these, the kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa) and nutriment-produced matter (āhārasamutthāna) are the conditioned states (paccayuppanna). 543–544.
In the fourfold groups rooted in nutriment and faculties, because they are not combined with the non-kamma (nakamma) condition, they are excluded from those rooted in the non-root (nahetu).

They are obtained exclusively [in this way]. Excluding those under the heading of "not-root-condition" (*na-indriya-mūlaka*) and "not-strong-dependence" (*na-upanissaya*), as well as "not-prenascence" (*na-purejāta*), one should state:
"In 'not-nutriment' (*nāhāre*), there are three. Thus, having combined these two conditions starting from the "not-faculty-condition" (*na-indriya-paccaya*), it is stated:

"...from the not-faculty-condition...pe... from the not-strong-dependence-condition, in 'not-nutriment,' there are three. From the not-faculty-condition...pe... from the not-prenascence-condition, in 'not-nutriment,' there are three."

The meaning is that, together with these conditions, the calculation for the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya) must also be performed. In that context, "three" refers specifically to the wholesome (kusala) and so forth, excluding the indeterminate (abyākata).
Therein, the wholesome and unwholesome [states] are related to the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa) and to the pre-arisen body by way of the post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya);

however, the indeterminate mind and mental factors are related [to those same things] by way of the post-nascence condition alone—it is by virtue of these [distinctions] that [the calculation is made].
Three answers should be given. However, because it is not combined with the "subsequently-arisen" (napacchājāta) condition hereafter, it is stated that there are "not two [conditions] for nutriment.
In that context, only this much is applicable: wholesome [consciousness] as a condition for the indeterminate by way of "produced materiality" (kaṭattārūpa), and likewise unwholesome [consciousness].
But since nutriment has been excluded, edible nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) does not obtain the state of being a condition even by way of "existence" (atthi) and "non-disappearance" (avigata).

545. In the fourfold root of that which has non-dissociation as its root, there are five [conditions] in the case of non-predominance: namely, (1) a wholesome [state] to a co-nascent wholesome [state];

(2) a wholesome [state] to the indeterminate [state] reckoned as *kaṭattā-rūpa*; (3) an unwholesome [state] to a co-nascent unwholesome [state]; likewise, (4) [an unwholesome state] to the indeterminate [state] reckoned as *kaṭattā-rūpa*;
and (5) an indeterminate [state] to a co-nascent indeterminate [state]. Thus there are five. [This applies to] the non-dissociation condition... pe ...in the case of non-predominance.
"Three" refers to the three—wholesome and so forth—as previously explained, [which serve as conditions] for the indeterminate. 546.
"Nine by way of the non-presence condition, not by way of the root condition": nine are stated for the non-presence condition by way of the non-root condition.

For all of these are obtained through the relations of proximity, contiguity, and decisive support, beginning with a single root and ending with a single [condition]. "Nine also by way of the non-object condition."
Those same [factors], standing on the "not-object" condition (*nārammaṇa*), should be made two by means of the "not-strong-dependence" (*naupanissaya*).

Up to the "support" (*nissaya*) as well— in the method based on the root "not-existence" (*noatthi*)— by proceeding according to the wheel-binding method starting from "not-existence-condition, not-root-condition,

not-object-condition," one should proceed by standing on the not-object-condition with either these three, or with any one of those following it, such as the "not-predominance" (*nādhipati*) conditions, and so forth.
The meaning is that one should proceed until reaching the *nissaya-paccaya*, and then two answers regarding the *naupanissaya* (non-strong-dependence condition) must be given.
Having thus established the characteristic, he again speaks of the two [answers] for the *naupanissaya* by taking seven conditions starting from the *anārammaṇa* (non-object) up to the *nissaya*.

In that context: "not being a presence-condition (*no-atthi*), not being a root-condition (*na-hetu*), and not being an object-condition (*anārammaṇa*) [are the conditions for] the non-strong-dependence."
"Two, not by way of presence-condition, not by way of root, object, or predominance-conditions, and not by way of strong-dependence-condition:
two"—thus, starting from "not by way of object," the application should be made with all the terms ending with "support," both preceding and following.
Here, "two" refers to wholesome [kamma] for the indeterminate and unwholesome [kamma] for the indeterminate; this is by way of asynchronous kamma producing "kamma-born matter" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).

These [factors] are to be understood by way of their conditions. Together with the "not-strong-dependence" (na-upanissaya) category, there are two [factors] in all instances of "not-prenascence" (na-purejāta) and so forth.
However, the "kamma-condition" (kammapaccaya) is not included here; for if that were included, even those two cases would be cut off, and no answer at all could be obtained.
Thus, in whatever combination of whichever [factors] with whichever [others], one should determine what is obtained and what is excluded.
Having carefully observed all of that, the enumeration for all the opposites should be extracted.
This concludes the commentary on the enumeration of opposites. [Now begins] the commentary on the positive-negative sequence.

550. In the positive-negative method (*anuloma-paccanīya*), there are seven [conditions] under "root" (*hetu*) and nine under "object" (*ārammaṇa*); thus, in the positive method. And in the negative method (*paccanīya*), there are fifteen under "not-root" (*na-hetu*) and fifteen under "not-object" (*nārammaṇa*).

Among the conditions obtained through these counts, for whichever condition stands in the positive method, together with the instances obtained in the positive method, [one should consider] those among the instances obtained in the negative method of whichever condition stands in the negative method.

The number should be understood by way of these similar sections. For in the positive (anuloma) order, under the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*), seven sections are obtained, namely "seven in the case of the root";
in the negative (paccanīya) order, under the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), fifteen are obtained, namely "fifteen in the case of the non-object.
Among those, together with the seven stated for the root condition, within the fifteen stated for the non-object condition, [there occurs] "the wholesome for the wholesome..."
“Of the indeterminate, of the wholesome-indeterminate; of the unwholesome, of the unwholesome and of the indeterminate; of the unwholesome-indeterminate;
