Likewise, regarding decisive support (*upanissaya*), by way of object-decisive support...
Four [types of relations] have been stated. However, the combinations (*ghaṭanā*) here are only one.

Regarding the root-conditions such as the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), etc., one should understand the enumeration of the connections and combinations by carefully observing everything—both what is obtained and what is not obtained—in accordance with the method explained below. 83–87.
In the Negative (Paccanīya) section, having extracted the conditions from the Positive (Anuloma) side according to the method stated for the Wholesome Triplet (*kusalattika*), therein...
By way of the nine occurrences obtained through the method of reverse counting, nine [conditions] are shown for all conditions under the heading of "not-root" (*nahetu*).
These are presented by way of the nine answers beginning with the single root and ending with the single condition:
"A state associated with pleasant feeling is related to a state associated with pleasant feeling by way of the not-root condition."

The text should be cited and demonstrated according to the method beginning with: “Having given a gift with a consciousness associated with pleasant feeling, [the result arises] as a condition,” and so forth.

However, regarding the combination of conditions here, the statement “there are eight [conditions] excluding the root-cause condition... pe ... excluding the decisive-support condition” should be understood by way of asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*). For weak kamma does not serve as a decisive support for its own result; it functions solely as an asynchronous kamma-condition.

It is a condition. The rest here—namely, in the positive-negative, negative-positive, and negative-positive-positive combinations—can be calculated according to the method stated below by way of the number of occurrences obtained through the conjunction of those respective conditions; therefore, it has not been detailed.
This concludes the commentary on the Triplet of Feeling (Vedanāttika).

3. Commentary on the Triplet of Resultant States (Vipākattika) 1–23. Regarding the "Resultant Triplet," concerning the statement "a resultant state arises dependent upon a resultant state by way of the root condition" (*hetupaccaya*), there are thirteen sections (*vāra*) that have been explained for the root condition.
To show these by means of a numerical summary, it is stated: "Thirteen under the root [condition]."

The same method applies to the sections beginning with "five objects" and so forth. Thus, there are six numerical limits here—namely, thirteen, five, nine, seven, three, and two—and by means of these, the enumeration in the combination of conditions should be understood according to the method explained below. 24–52.
In the negative (paccanīya) section as well, [it is stated]: "Dependent on a resultant state, a resultant state arises not by way of the root condition."
The ten instances stated for the not-root condition (*na-hetu-paccaya*) are condensed and shown by way of enumeration as "ten in not-root.
The same method applies to "five in not-object" (*na-ārammaṇe*) and so forth.
Thus, there are eight numerical limits here—namely, ten, five, thirteen, twelve, two, one, nine, and three—and it is by means of these that the conditions are combined below.
The enumeration should be understood in detail according to the method already stated. However, the text has been abbreviated;
it should be understood by combining the positive-negative and negative-positive sequences according to these very sections (vāra) defined by their respective numerical limits.
The "Co-nascent Section" (Sahajātavāra) follows this same single method. The "Condition," "Support," "Conjoined," and "Associated" sections proceed exactly as they appear in the text.

92. Regarding the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), "when wholesome and unwholesome [states] have ceased" means: when the wholesome has occurred by way of insight (*vipassanā*) and the unwholesome has occurred by way of attachment (*sārajjanā*) and so forth, having ceased;
"then the resultant arises as registration" (*tadārammaṇatā*) means that the sense-sphere resultant (*kāmāvacara-vipāka*) arises as registration.
However, those who hold that registration occurs at the conclusion of insight-impulsions (*vipassanājavana*) and of doubt (*vicikicchā*) and restlessness (*uddhacca*)...

Those who say "it does not exist" should be refuted by this textual tradition. That "wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space is a condition for the functional consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness by way of object-condition" is stated with reference to one who, having attained Arahantship, enters the meditative attainments in reverse order that he had never previously entered.
By this method, one should apply [this principle] carefully to all the answers.
The meaning should be understood by examining the Pāli text.
In the cases of "seven with respect to cause," "nine with respect to object," "ten with respect to predominance," and so forth,
[the analysis] proceeds by way of conascence-predominance, object-predominance, conascence-dependence, pre-nascence-dependence, and immediate-strong-dependence.

By way of object-strong-dependence, natural strong-dependence, conascence-dissociation, and pre-existence-post-existence-dissociation—wherever, however, and however many answers are obtainable, there they should all be noted accordingly.
Likewise, in the negative and other modes, the extraction is by way of the positive; from the positive...

The counting of the possible permutations for those [factors] that have been obtained by way of the negative method, the synthesis of conditions, the counting of available permutations in the positive-negative and negative-positive methods—
whether based on causes and so forth— as they occur through both the pure synthesis and the combined synthesis, and the non-availability of those not obtainable:
all this should be understood according to the method explained below.
And as it is here, so it is with the subsequent triplets and dyads. For the *Paṭṭhāna* treatise is indeed infinite and immeasurable within the Canon itself.
Even for one who has attained an exceedingly long life, that lifespan would not suffice to explain its meaning word by word.
Nor, if one were to explain only a portion of it and then indicate the remainder by way of method, would the purpose be achieved.
Since this has been understood, we shall not say even this much further from hereon;

rather, regarding the remaining triads and dyads, because their modes have not been stated below, we shall state only that which must necessarily be said. As for what we shall pass over without stating, that is to be understood by the method of the Pāḷi itself.
Explanation of the Triplet on Resultant (Vipāka).
4. Commentary on the Triplet of the Clung-to (Upādinnattika) 51.

In the section on questions for the Triplet of the Clung-to and Subject to Clinging (Upādinnupādāniyattika), the statement that "the physical basis is a condition for the aggregates subject to clinging by way of the pre-arising condition" (purejātapaccaya) is said with reference to the process of existence (pavatti). However, in the case of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), that [basis] does not function as a pre-arising condition. 72.
Edible food that is clung-to and subject to clinging is a condition for the body that is clung-to and subject to clinging by way of the nutriment condition (āhārapaccaya).

Regarding the term "nutriment" (*paccaya*): here, "edible nutriment that is clung-to and subject to clinging" refers to the nutritive essence (*ojā*) situated within the material phenomena produced by kamma. "Of the body that is clung-to and subject to clinging" means it is a condition for that very same body of matter produced by kamma by way of nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*).
It is a condition by way of maintaining and supporting the *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by kamma), just like the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*).

Not by way of being a producer. As for the claim that the nutritive essence (*ojā*) in the body of a living frog or similar creature serves as a nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*) for the bodies of snakes and others who have swallowed it while they remain alive—that should not be accepted.
For the nutritive essence in one living body does not establish the status of a nutriment-condition for another body.
Regarding the phrase "of a body that is non-clung-to but subject to clinging" (*anupādinnupādāniyassa kāyassa*): [the following applies here...]

It is also obtained by way of producing. Regarding the phrase "of that which is acquired and subject to clinging, and of that which is not acquired but subject to clinging," one is mentioned by way of supporting and the other by way of producing, or both are mentioned solely by way of supporting.
Furthermore, when two nutriments act as conditions together, they are only supporters, not producers. The rest here is [as follows].
This should be understood by carefully examining the Pāli text itself.
[End of] the Commentary on the Clung-to Triplet (Upādinnattika). 5–22. Commentary on the Defiled Triplet (Saṅkiliṭṭhattika), etc.

In the "Triplet on the Corrupt and Corruptible," everything should be understood according to the method already stated for the "Triplet on the Wholesome. 79. Regarding the "Triplet on Applied Thought":

the "preliminary work" (*parikamma*) for the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds is simply the preliminary work for the divine eye; it is the preliminary work for the purpose of producing that [knowledge].
However, this is said with reference to the preliminary work at the time of employing [the knowledge] once it has arisen.
The rest here follows exactly according to the text (Pāḷi). 82.

This was stated by way of the registration-moment, the life-continuum with that as its object (tadārammaṇa-bhavaṅga), and the root-life-continuum (mūla-bhavaṅga). All else here should be understood solely according to the text.
In the "Triplet on Seeing" (Dassana-ttika), regarding such passages as "lust to be abandoned by seeing arises," for the worldling (*puthujjana*), that which is to be abandoned by seeing...

It arises. Even for a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāya pahātabba*) [does not arise]; thus it should be understood that for each successive higher stage, the corresponding lower stages do not arise.

A state to be abandoned by seeing (*dassanena pahātabbo dhammo*) does not serve as a condition for a state to be abandoned by cultivation by even a single condition. The rest here should be followed according to the text in the *Kusalattika*.
It should be understood according to the characteristics already stated.

Regarding the triad of "having roots to be abandoned by vision," the classification of those factors having roots to be abandoned by vision and so forth is to be understood by the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*.
Delusion accompanied by doubt and restlessness is included in the third category because it is rootless (*ahetuka*).

Thus, having understood this classification of those "with roots to be abandoned" (*pahātabbahetuka*)— wherein those for whom there is a root to be abandoned by seeing or by cultivation are "with roots to be abandoned," while those for whom such a root does not exist are "neither by seeing nor by cultivation with roots to be abandoned"—
the remainder should be understood according to the characteristics already shown in the "Triplet on What is to be Abandoned by Seeing" and the "Triplet on the Wholesome."

In the "Leading to Accumulation" (ācayagāmi) triad, as well as in the "Dependent" (paṭicca) and "Associated" (saṃsaṭṭha) sections, the positive (anuloma) relations are exactly like those in the "Wholesome Triad" (kusalattika). The remainder proceeds exactly according to the text, both in terms of the answers and the enumeration.
In the "Trainee Triad" (sekkhattika), a state belonging to one beyond training (asekkha) is not a condition for a state of one in training (sekkha) by any kind of condition.

However, a state of one in training is an immediate (anantara), natural (pakata), and decisive support (upanissaya) condition for a state of one beyond training. The rest here proceeds exactly according to the text; likewise for the "Limited Triad" (parittattika).
In the triad of limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*), "volition with immeasurable object" refers to the change-of-lineage volition (*gotrabhucetanā*) of those in training (*sekkhā*);
it is also appropriate to call it "reviewing volition. Regarding "resultants with limited objects": at rebirth-linking, the object is the kamma;

during the course of existence, it consists of visible forms and so forth as objects by way of eye-consciousness and the rest, as well as limited objects grasped by the impulsion (*javana*) through the process of registration (*tadārammaṇa*).

[This refers to] those [states] arisen having made an object. However, those who say, "There is no rebirth-linking by means of the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū-citta*)," should be refuted by this Sutta.
The rest here should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi itself. The triad of the inferior (*hīna*) is similar to the triad of the defiled (*saṅkiliṭṭha*).

In the triad of the fixed-in-falsity (*micchattaniyata*), that which is fixed-in-falsity [is the cause] for that which is fixed-in-truth (*sammattaniyata*), or that which is fixed-in-truth [is the cause] for that which is fixed-in-falsity.
In some cases, there is no condition by way of a condition. There is no such thing as a state fixed in falsehood or fixed in truth that is devoid of co-nascent predominance.
In the case of that which is fixed in truth, object-prenascence is absolutely absent; in the case of that which is fixed in falsehood, object-prenascence may exist.
Taking an indefinite consciousness as its object, a fixed wrong view might arise. As for the remaining [types of consciousness], they [take] the fixed...
With reference to [the path], that which is fixed-in-wrongness does not arise; no state whatsoever arises by making that which is fixed-in-wrongness its object.
A wholesome state is not a decisive-support condition for that which is fixed-in-wrongness. The rest here should be understood according to the method stated in the Pāḷi.
In the "Dependent" section of the Positive Order within the triad of objects beginning with the Path, there is no resultant condition. Regarding the kamma-condition as well, in this...
The "various-momentary" (nānākkhaṇika) triad is not obtained; likewise for the "arisen" triad and the "past" triad.

Regarding the negative formulation, the statement "rootless with the Path as object" refers to a rootless consciousness that has the Path as its object, specifically intending the adverting consciousness (āvajjana).
The rest here should be understood according to the text itself.

In both the *Uppanna-ttika* (Triplet on the Arisen) and the *Atīta-ttika* (Triplet on the Past), the sections beginning with the "Dependent" (*paṭicca*) chapter do not exist; only the "Investigation" (*pañhā*) chapter is found there. Why?
Because the "Dependent" chapter and the others apply only to co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and pre-arisen (*purejāta*) states. However, these two triplets consist of a mixture of past and future states.
Furthermore, in the *Uppanna-ttika*, even conditions belonging to the "immediately preceding" (*anantara*) category are not found. Why? Because in the *Uppanna-ttika*, [the past...]

By way of non-existence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, these two states—namely, the arisen and the unarisen—are not conditions for these two [other states], the arisen and the unarisen, by any kind of condition whatsoever.
However, these two—the unarisen and that which is subject to arising—are conditions for the arisen by way of two conditions:
the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and the decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). The rest here is in the Pāḷi.
This should be understood according to the same method already explained.
In the triad of the past, the present is not a condition for the past and future, nor are the past and future conditions for the past and future by any kind of condition.
Furthermore, Nibbāna is found neither as a condition nor as a conditioned state in either of these two triads.
In this case as well, it should be understood according to the method presented in the Pāḷi itself. In the triad of "internal," the category of "internal-external" is not included.

This is because both groups designated as "internal-external" are neither conditions nor conditionally arisen when taken together; therefore, [the example is] like a mustard seed placed on the palm of the hand.
It should be understood that even visible form (*vaṇṇa*) does not become a single object together with the color of the palm of the hand.
And just as the category of "internal-external" (*ajjhatta-bahiddhā*) is absent here, so too in this triad of "internal objects," the category of "internal-external objects" is not found.
The remainder proceeds exactly according to the text.

In the *Sanidassana-ttika* (the triad on the visible), the meaning should also be understood according to the text itself. Here, the enumeration should be understood by condensing the sections as they appear in the text and correlating them according to the method explained below.
This concludes the commentary on the *Dhammānuloma-tika-paṭṭhāna*. 2.
Commentary on the *Duka-paṭṭhāna* (The Couplets)
In the *Duka-paṭṭhāna* as well, the answers to the questions and the enumerations for all the dyads should be understood according to the method presented in the Pāḷi.
Furthermore, herein, the answer to the "With-cause and Cause-associated" dyad is similar to the answer to the "Cause" dyad;
likewise for the "Causes and With-cause" dyad and the "Causes and Cause-associated" dyad, as well as for the "Conditioned and Determined" dyads.

"This dyad should be treated just like the 'with-conditions' dyad"—this was stated because, although the "unconditioned" (asaṅkhata) is indeed conditioned (saṅkhata) by way of being without conditions, it does not admit of a conjunction with that which is unconditioned.
The dyads concerning "consciousness with an object," "associated with consciousness," and "conjoined with consciousness" also have identical answers;
likewise for the groups (gocchaka) of "taints" (āsava), "floods" (ogha), and "yokes" (yoga), for these three also have identical answers to one another.

Furthermore, these dyads are similar: the worldly (lokiya), with-outflows (sāsava), fetterable (saṃyojaniya), bondable (ganthaniya), hindranceable (nīvaraṇiya), adhered-to (parāmaṭṭha), and defiled (saṅkilesika) dyads;

and the dyads that are dissociated from outflows (āsavavippayutta), with-outflows (sāsava), dissociated from fetters (saṃyojanavippayutta), fetterable (saṃyojaniya), dissociated from bonds (ganthavippayutta), bondable (ganthaniya), dissociated from hindrances (nīvaraṇavippayutta), hindranceable (nīvaraṇiya), dissociated from adherence (parāmāsavippayutta), adhered-to (parāmaṭṭha), dissociated from defilements (kilesavippayutta), defiled (saṅkilesika), included (pariyāpanna), surpassable (sauttara), and so forth.

The dyad of defilements (kilesaduka) is similar to the dyad of fetters (saṃyojanaduka). Also similar are the dyads of the defiled (saṅkiliṭṭha), associated with defilements (kilesasampayutta), associated with hindrances (nīvaraṇasampayutta), to be abandoned by vision (dassanenapahātabba), and subject to fear (saraṇa).

They are the same. Likewise, the dyads consisting of both defilements and defiled hindrances, as well as both hindrances and the defilements associated with them, and both defilements and the states associated with defilements—by this method, it should be understood that the explanations for all dyads that are identical in meaning are likewise identical.
Furthermore, in the entire *Paṭṭhāna*, no dyad is found that can be understood by anyone [as distinct from these].
[The same applies to] those that are both taints (*āsava*) and associated with taints.

Furthermore, in such pairs as "fetters and those associated with fetters," "bonds and those associated with bonds," "hindrances and those associated with hindrances," and "defilements and defiled states," neither the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*) nor the asynchronous kamma condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*) is found.
In the case of "not-root and with-root" and "rootless and not-root," the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*) [is not found].

There are none. Among these pairs—(1) those that are both roots and associated with roots, (2) those that are both taints and associated with taints, and (3) those that are both knots and associated with knots—the categories of "not-root," "not-jhāna-factor," and "not-path-factor" are not found.

[However, they are found among] those that are both fetters and associated with fetters, those that are both hindrances and associated with hindrances, and those that are both defilements and associated with defilements. Defilements...
Furthermore, among these [twenty-two pairs], the "not-root condition" (nahetupaccaya) is not obtained by way of delusion (moha) accompanied by doubt (vicikicchā) or restlessness (uddhacca);

likewise, the "not-jhāna" and "not-path" conditions are not obtained. Thus, having examined what is obtainable and what is unobtainable in all the pairs, the enumeration of the doors should be understood according to the text itself.
Commentary on the Pairs (Dukapaṭṭhāna).
3. Commentary on the Pairs and Triads (Dukatika-paṭṭhāna):
In the Pairs and Triads, it is said: "Dependent on a root wholesome state, a root wholesome state arises by way of the root condition."

Thus, the teaching has been given in brief by way of merely raising the questions. However, a detailed exposition could be stated according to the method beginning with, "Dependent on wholesome non-greed, there arise non-hatred and non-delusion," and so forth;

since that can be understood even without being explicitly stated by means of the method shown below, not even a single term or a single condition was mentioned. As for this teaching that was given in brief:
Thus it should be understood how [the remaining sections] are to be treated.

For, having joined the "wholesome" category with the "cause" dyad, all available conditions were shown by way of both the positive (anuloma) and negative (paccanīya) methods in the section on "Dependent" (paṭicca). However, the positive-negative, negative-positive, and positive-positive methods, as well as the "conascent" (sahajāta) section and so forth, were not shown;
rather, it was simply stated that "[they] should be expanded out in the very same manner as the 'Dependent' section."

It has been stated. In the section on questions (pañhāvāra), without answering the questions themselves, but merely setting forth the headings of the questions, the conditions obtained by way of the positive and negative methods alone have been shown.

And it is stated that just as with the "wholesome" category, so too the "unwholesome" and "indeterminate" categories should be demonstrated by joining them with the "root" dyad, thus explaining the triad of the "root-wholesome-dyad."
Following that, twenty-one dyads and triads beginning with "the state associated with pleasant feeling as its cause" (*hetu-sukhāya-vedanā-sampayutta-dhamma*) and so forth are shown.

However, since there is no such thing as a cause that is both visible and impinging (*sanidassana-sappaṭigha*) or invisible and impinging (*anidassana-sappaṭigha*), the terms "visible and impinging" and "invisible and impinging" are not combined with the term "cause."

They were not combined. Thus, having combined twenty-two triplets (tike) with the dyads (duka) of "with-root" (sahetuka) and so forth according to their availability, they were then further combined with all the dyads beginning with the "with-root" dyad and ending with the "having-a-refuge" (saraṇa) dyad.
In that regard, whichever term does not enter into combination with whichever other term is simply not found in the text (pāḷi).
Thus, having combined twenty-two triplets (tikes) with one dyad (duka), and again twenty-two with another, and another twenty-two—
thus twenty-two triplets are combined with the dyad-terms found in succession within a hundred dyads;
having taken these twenty-two triplets and inserted them into the hundred dyads, the so-called *Dukatika-paṭṭhāna* has been taught.

In this regard, wherever an abbreviation has been made in the text by showing the method, the full expansion of that [abbreviation] should be understood according to the method shown in those respective places.
This concludes the commentary on the *Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna*.
4. Commentary on the Tikaduka Paṭṭhāna:

In the Tikaduka Paṭṭhāna as well, the teaching is given merely by way of setting forth the questions, such as: "Dependent upon a wholesome state that is a root-cause (hetu), a wholesome state that is a root-cause arises by way of the root-condition (hetupaccaya).
In this regard, just as below the wholesome category was [treated] together with the Hetuduka, so too here...
Having thus combined [the factors] according to all conditions in all sections, a concise exposition has been given;
in this same way, having combined the "root-condition" (hetupada) with the wholesome triad (kusalattika), a concise exposition has been given for all sections according to all conditions.
And just as with the root-condition, so too the "non-root-condition" (nahetupada) is combined with the wholesome triad, forming the wholesome-triad-root-dyad (kusalattikahetuduka).

It is concluded. Following that, twenty-one triads and dyads, such as the triad of feeling and the dyad of root, are shown by way of the method beginning with "the state associated with pleasant feeling is a root" and so forth.
Thus, having combined the dyad of roots with the twenty-two triads, [the author] again combines the dyad of "with-root" and the others with those same [triads].
All the *dukas* (pairs) have been combined according to their availability, concluding with the *saraṇa-duka*.
Here too, whichever term does not fit into the arrangement has been rejected right within the text itself.
Having thus taken one hundred *dukas* and inserted them into twenty-two *tikas* (triplets), that which is called the *Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna* was taught. Therein also, by whichever method the text—
This method has been stated in brief; it should be understood in detail according to each respective system.
This concludes the commentary on the *Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna*. 5.
Commentary on the *Tikatika-paṭṭhāna*.

In the *Tikatikapaṭṭhāna* as well, the teaching is given in brief by way of the formulation of the questions alone: "Dependent on a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling, a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling arises by way of the root condition.
And herein, the wholesome triad is [combined] with the feeling triad and so forth, while the feeling triad and so forth are [combined] with the wholesome triad.
In this way, triplets have been inserted precisely within the triplets themselves. Whenever one term does not connect with another term, that [term] is omitted;
thus, in all the conditions, the sections and the method of enumeration are shown according to what is actually obtainable.
Therefore, these should be understood by carefully examining the text (*pāḷi*). And just as it is with the wholesome triplet (*kusalattika*), so it is with the others.
The triads beginning with feeling should be understood by being combined with that [tetrad] and its subsequent members; likewise, each individual triad should be combined with the remaining ones.
And the rest should be understood by being combined with those.
This concludes the commentary on the *Paṭṭhāna* of the Triads and Triads.
6. Commentary on the Exposition by Twos In the Exposition by Twos as well, the teaching is given in brief by way of the formulation of the questions alone:
“Dependent on a state that is both a root and accompanied by roots, a state that is both a root and accompanied by roots arises by way of the root condition.
Therein, the dyad of roots [is explained] by means of the dyad of states accompanied by roots and so forth; the dyad of states accompanied by roots and so forth...

And they are joined with that [first dyad]. Each individual dyad, however, should be joined with the remaining ones, and the remaining ones should be joined with those [preceding ones] in successive order.
For this is called the "Foundation of Relations of Dyads upon Dyads" (*dukadukapaṭṭhāna*), taught by "inserting dyads into dyads.
Therefore, here the joining of all dyads with all other dyads should be understood; however, the text has been abbreviated. By whichever [dyad]...
And whatever term does not go into conjunction with any other term, that term is omitted from the teaching.
This concludes the commentary on the *Duka-paṭṭhāna*.
Up to this point—
The excellent and most supreme *Paṭṭhāna* consists of:
the triad with the dyad, the dyad with the triad, the triad with the dyad, and the dyad with the dyad;
the triad with the triad, and the dyad with the dyad.
"The six methods in the direct order (anuloma) are very profound"—this is explained by the verse cited in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. In the *Dhammānuloma Paṭṭhāna*, six methods are demonstrated.
However, here, according to the conditions (paccaya), there are four methods—direct order and so forth—in each individual *paṭṭhāna*; thus, by one...
By way of method, it should be understood that the *Anuloma-paṭṭhāna* (Positive Exposition) itself is adorned with twenty-four systems.
7–12. Commentary on the *Paccanīya-paṭṭhāna* (Negative Exposition).
Now, [the exposition] which has received its name from the negative relationship of phenomena by way of the negation of terms such as "wholesome" (*kusala*) and so forth—

In order to demonstrate the negative conditional relations (*paccanīyapaṭṭhāna*), the following is commenced: "Dependent on a non-wholesome state, a non-wholesome state arises by way of the root condition," and so forth.
Therein, "dependent on a non-wholesome state" excludes the status of being a condition for a wholesome state.
"A non-wholesome state arises" excludes the arising of a wholesome state. Therefore, [the text continues]: "One unwholesome or indeterminate aggregate..."
"Dependent on [this], there arise the three unwholesome or indeterminate aggregates and mind-produced matter"—in such a manner should the question here be answered.

1. Now, among wholesome and other states, without rejecting the state of being a condition (*paccaya-dhamma*), but by way of rejecting the wholesomeness and so forth of that which has arisen through conditions (*paccayuppanna*), the *Anuloma-paccanīya Paṭṭhāna*—so named for its positive-negative treatment of phenomena—is shown. To this end, the following is commenced:
"Dependent on a wholesome state, a non-wholesome state arises by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*)," and so forth. Therein, "wholesome" (*kusala*)...
“Dependent on a wholesome state” allows for the status of being a condition for the wholesome; “a wholesome state does not arise” prohibits the arising of that very same wholesome state.
Therefore, the answer is shown by way of such formulations as “dependent on wholesome aggregates, mind-originated matter,” and so forth;
all of this should be carefully observed by consulting the Pāḷi text itself.

1. Now, regarding wholesome and other states, the Negative-Positive Conditional Relations—so named because it is established by way of the negative and positive order of phenomena—is that which, while excluding the conditioning state among wholesome and other states, does not exclude the wholesomeness and other qualities of the conditioned state.
In order to demonstrate this, it is begun: "Dependent on a non-wholesome state, a non-wholesome state arises by way of the root-condition," and so forth.
Therein, "dependent on a non-wholesome state" excludes the status of being a condition for what is wholesome.
"A non-wholesome state arises" allows for the arising of the unwholesome. For that which is "non-wholesome" may be either unwholesome or indeterminate (abyākata). And that...
There is no wholesome state that arises by making co-nascence a condition;

therefore, the teaching is given by way of the unwholesome and the indeterminate. In this context, the answer should be understood as follows: "In dependence on one unwholesome aggregate, three aggregates [arise]"—thus, the answer regarding the unwholesome dhamma in dependence [on another] is to be known. "An indeterminate dhamma arises with root-condition": this...

However, the question [concerning] the indeterminate resultant and the indeterminate functional has already been answered thus: "Dependent on one aggregate that is indeterminate resultant or indeterminate functional, there arise three aggregates and mind-originated matter.
Thus, for all questions, the answer given is exactly as it appears in the Pāḷi, corresponding to the meaning of what was not answered and what was answered.

Concluding Statement:
[This work was composed] by one adorned with faith, wisdom, and energy that are supremely pure; endowed with a multitude of virtues such as virtue, conduct, sincerity, and gentleness;
capable of plunging into the depths of both his own and other systems; possessed of analytical discernment; and [versed] in the various divisions of the scriptural tradition of the Three Piṭakas.

In the Teacher’s dispensation, together with its commentaries, there were Elders who were lamps of the Theravamsa; whose intellects were firmly established in superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) adorned with various qualities such as the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) and surrounded by the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā);

who were great poets and preeminent debaters, speakers of reasoned and excellent words, endowed with the grace of sweet and noble speech arising from the perfection of their composition through the power of unimpeded knowledge; and who were great expounders of the Dhamma.
This commentary on the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka was composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa—
so called by his teachers— who was an ornament to the lineage and possessed vast, purified intelligence:
"May it endure in the world as long as those seeking to cross over the world [remain]."
Thus it shines forth for noble sons, as the method for the purification of wisdom:
that even the mere name "Buddha" occurs in this world for the pure-minded Tathāgata, the Great Seer and Foremost of the World.
The commentary on the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is completed.
